empathy.patient_summary:
Thank you for coming in today and for sharing what has been happening with your eye. You are doing the right thing by getting this checked out, and we want to make sure you have all the information you need in plain language.

Here is what we know so far: You have been having a sharp, sudden pain in your left eye that lasts only a split second. This has happened about 4 times in the past 8 hours. Both of your eyes have also been watering more than usual. You mentioned you were worried about allergies and a detached retina — and we want to address both of those concerns honestly.

The good news is that your symptoms do not strongly point to a detached retina. A detached retina usually does NOT cause sharp pain. It typically causes flashing lights, floating spots, or a shadow across your vision — none of which you have reported. That is reassuring.

Regarding allergies: while allergies can cause watery eyes, they do NOT usually cause the kind of sharp, stabbing pain you are describing. So allergies alone are unlikely to explain everything that is happening.

What our medical team IS focused on right now are two main possibilities that need to be checked urgently:

1. A condition called INTERMITTENT ANGLE-CLOSURE GLAUCOMA. Think of your eye like a drain in a sink. In some people, the drain can become temporarily blocked, causing pressure to build up inside the eye. This pressure spike can cause a sudden, sharp pain — exactly like what you are describing. This is something that MUST be checked today because, if left untreated, it can cause permanent vision loss. The important thing to know is that it IS treatable when caught early.

2. A condition called RECURRENT CORNEAL EROSION SYNDROME. The cornea is the clear front surface of your eye, like a windshield. Sometimes a tiny patch of the surface layer can briefly lift or slip, causing a sudden electric-shock-like pain that lasts only a split second. This matches your description very closely. This condition is NOT immediately dangerous to your vision, but it does need treatment to prevent it from happening again and again.

Both of these conditions are manageable. The most important thing right now is getting the right eye tests done today so we know exactly what we are dealing with.
empathy.what_this_means:
Let us break down the two most likely explanations for your symptoms in simple terms.

POSSIBILITY 1 — PRESSURE BUILDUP IN YOUR EYE (Intermittent Angle-Closure Glaucoma): Inside your eye, there is a fluid that constantly flows in and out, like water in a fish tank. In some people, the tiny drainage channel for this fluid can get temporarily blocked — like a clogged drain. When this happens, pressure builds up quickly inside the eye, causing a sudden sharp pain. Then the blockage releases on its own, the pressure drops, and the pain goes away — until it happens again. This is why your pain comes and goes in split-second bursts. Your age (54) and the pattern of your pain make this an important possibility to check. The test to detect this is quick and painless — a doctor simply measures the pressure in your eye.

POSSIBILITY 2 — SURFACE OF THE EYE SLIPPING (Recurrent Corneal Erosion Syndrome): Imagine the surface of your eye is like a tile floor. Normally the tiles stick firmly to the floor. In some people, a tile can briefly lift up and then snap back down — causing a sudden sharp pain for just a moment. This is what may be happening to the surface layer of your eye. It can cause watery eyes as a reflex reaction, and the pain is often described as electric or stabbing — lasting only a fraction of a second. This condition is very treatable with special eye drops and ointments.

Both conditions are detectable with simple eye tests that an eye specialist (ophthalmologist) will perform today.

right_now: STAY at the medical facility — do not leave before being seen by the eye doctor. This visit is classified as urgent and you should be seen very soon.

Tell the doctor or nurse if you notice ANY of the following during your wait: sudden blurring of vision, seeing rainbow-colored rings or halos around lights, nausea or feeling like you might vomit, a shadow or curtain appearing across your vision, or if the pain becomes much more severe or constant.

Do NOT use any eye drops you may have at home (including allergy eye drops, redness-relief drops, or any drops that say they dilate or enlarge your pupils) until the doctor has examined you and given you the all-clear. Some common eye drops can make certain eye conditions much worse.

Do NOT take antihistamine medications (allergy pills like Benadryl, Claritin, Zyrtec, or similar) until the doctor has ruled out the pressure-buildup condition. These medications can sometimes trigger a dangerous pressure spike in people whose eye drainage channels are narrow.

Tell the doctor your COMPLETE list of all medications, vitamins, and supplements you take — even ones you take occasionally. Some common medications (including certain antidepressants, bladder medications, cold and flu tablets containing pseudoephedrine, and seizure medications) can affect eye pressure.
Tell the doctor about any allergies you have — especially to antibiotics or sulfa drugs (sulfonamides).
Tell the doctor if you have asthma, COPD, a slow heart rate, or any heart conditions — this is important for deciding which medications are safe for you.

Answer the doctor's questions about your symptoms as clearly as you can — especially: Do you see halos or rainbow rings around lights? Do you feel nauseous during the pain episodes? Does anything seem to trigger the pain (blinking, cold air, bright light)? Have you noticed any blurred vision or shadows?
this_week: Attend ALL follow-up appointments that are scheduled for you before you leave today — especially any appointment for your RIGHT eye. Even though your pain is in your left eye, the doctor may recommend a preventive procedure for your right eye as well.
Fill any prescriptions given to you today and start them exactly as directed. Do not skip doses.

If you are prescribed hypertonic saline eye drops (Muro 128 — a special thick saltwater eye drop), make sure you buy the correct product. Ask the pharmacist to help you find it. It is NOT the same as regular artificial tears or contact lens solution.

If you are prescribed a bedtime eye ointment, use it EVERY night at bedtime without skipping — this is the most important dose for preventing the sharp pain from happening while you sleep or when you first wake up.

If you are prescribed artificial tears, make sure they say PRESERVATIVE-FREE on the label (look for 'PF' in the name). Regular artificial tears used many times a day can actually irritate your eye surface.

If you are prescribed an oral antibiotic called doxycycline, take it with a full glass of water and protect your skin from the sun during the treatment period — this medication can make your skin burn more easily in sunlight. Use sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher) every day.
Avoid rubbing your eyes — rubbing can trigger the surface-slipping type of pain and make it worse.
Sleep with a humidifier in your bedroom if possible — keeping the air moist helps your eye surface heal overnight.
ongoing: Use your eye drops and ointments consistently every day, even on days when you feel fine. These treatments work best when used regularly, not just when you have pain.
Wear protective eyewear (wraparound glasses or goggles) in windy, dusty, or outdoor environments to protect your eye surface.
Avoid environments with very dry air (airplanes, air-conditioned offices) for long periods without using your lubricating eye drops.

Keep a simple diary of your eye pain episodes — note the date, time, how long the pain lasted, what you were doing when it happened, and whether you saw any halos or felt nauseous. This information is very helpful for your eye doctor at follow-up visits.
Attend all scheduled ophthalmology (eye specialist) follow-up appointments — do not skip these even if you are feeling better.

Tell any new doctor, dentist, or pharmacist that you have been evaluated for a possible narrow eye drainage channel (angle-closure glaucoma) — this affects which medications are safe for you going forward.

Do not start any new medications — including over-the-counter allergy medications, cold medicines, or sleep aids — without first checking with your eye doctor or pharmacist that they are safe for your eyes.

medications_explained.name: Hypertonic Saline Eye Drops 5% (Brand name: Muro 128 Drops)
medications_explained.what_it_is: A special thick saltwater eye drop — much saltier than regular eye drops or artificial tears.
medications_explained.why_you_need_it: The surface layer of your eye may be holding too much water, making it weak and prone to slipping. These drops gently draw out that extra water, making the surface stronger and less likely to slip and cause pain.
medications_explained.how_to_use: Put 1 to 2 drops in your affected eye 4 times a day while you are awake (roughly every 4 to 6 hours). You may feel a brief sting when you put them in — this is normal and will pass quickly.
medications_explained.important_warning: Make sure you buy the RIGHT product. Ask the pharmacist for Muro 128 DROPS (5% sodium chloride). Do NOT confuse this with regular artificial tears, regular saline, or contact lens solution — they are completely different products.
medications_explained.prescription_needed: No — available over the counter at the pharmacy.

medications_explained.name: Hypertonic Saline Eye Ointment 5% (Brand name: Muro 128 Ointment)
medications_explained.what_it_is: A thick gel version of the saltwater drops, designed to stay in your eye overnight.
medications_explained.why_you_need_it: Many people with your type of eye condition have their worst pain episodes when they first wake up in the morning. This is because the eye surface can dry out and stick to the eyelid during sleep. This ointment prevents that from happening by keeping your eye surface moist and protected all night.
medications_explained.how_to_use: Apply a small amount (about the size of a grain of rice) inside your lower eyelid at bedtime ONLY. It will blur your vision significantly — this is expected and normal. Use it ONLY at bedtime, never before driving.
medications_explained.important_warning: This ointment will make your vision very blurry. Do not drive or do anything that requires clear vision after applying it. Use it only at night.
medications_explained.prescription_needed: No — available over the counter at the pharmacy.

medications_explained.name: Preservative-Free Artificial Tears (Examples: Systane Ultra PF, Refresh Optive PF, TheraTears)
medications_explained.what_it_is: Gentle lubricating eye drops that supplement your natural tears.
medications_explained.why_you_need_it: Your eye surface needs to stay moist to heal properly and to prevent the sharp pain episodes. These drops act like a protective coating for the surface of your eye.
medications_explained.how_to_use: Use 1 to 2 drops in both eyes every 1 to 2 hours while you are awake, or whenever your eyes feel dry or uncomfortable.
medications_explained.important_warning: You MUST use the PRESERVATIVE-FREE version. Look for the words 'Preservative-Free' or the letters 'PF' on the label. If you use regular artificial tears (with preservatives) this many times a day, the preservative chemical can actually damage your eye surface and make things worse. Ask the pharmacist to help you find the right product.
medications_explained.prescription_needed: No — available over the counter at the pharmacy.

medications_explained.name: Doxycycline 50mg Tablets (if prescribed)
medications_explained.what_it_is: A low-dose antibiotic tablet taken by mouth — but in your case, it is NOT being used to fight an infection.
medications_explained.why_you_need_it: At this low dose, doxycycline works differently — it blocks certain chemicals in your body that break down the 'glue' holding your eye surface together. By blocking these chemicals, it helps your eye surface stick properly and stops the slipping that causes your sharp pain. You would take this for about 3 months.
medications_explained.how_to_use: Take one 50mg tablet twice a day (morning and evening) with a full glass of water. Take it with food to reduce stomach upset.
medications_explained.important_warning: This medication makes your skin much more sensitive to sunlight. Wear sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher) every day during your 3-month course, even on cloudy days, and avoid prolonged sun exposure. Do not take this if you are allergic to tetracycline antibiotics — tell your doctor about any antibiotic allergies.
medications_explained.prescription_needed: Yes — requires a prescription from your doctor.

medications_explained.name: Eye Pressure-Lowering Drops (Timolol, Brimonidine, Dorzolamide — if prescribed by the eye doctor)
medications_explained.what_it_is: Prescription eye drops that reduce the pressure inside your eye.
medications_explained.why_you_need_it: If the eye doctor finds that the pressure inside your eye is too high, these drops will bring it down quickly and safely. High eye pressure is what causes the sharp pain in the pressure-buildup type of glaucoma.
medications_explained.how_to_use: Exactly as directed by the eye doctor. After putting in the drops, press gently on the inner corner of your eye (near your nose) with your finger for 2 minutes. This stops the medication from draining into your throat and reduces side effects.
medications_explained.important_warning: Tell the doctor BEFORE receiving these drops if you have asthma, COPD, a slow heart rate, or any heart conditions. One of these drops (timolol) can cause breathing problems in people with asthma. The doctor needs to know this before giving it to you.
medications_explained.prescription_needed: Yes — administered and prescribed by the eye doctor.

empathy.lifestyle_tips:
Here are some practical things you can do at home to help manage your symptoms and support your recovery. Many people find these small changes make a real difference.

PROTECT YOUR EYES AT NIGHT: The sharp pain you are experiencing often happens first thing in the morning, or even wakes people up from sleep. This is because the eye surface can dry out and stick to the eyelid during sleep. Using the bedtime eye ointment consistently every night is one of the most effective things you can do to prevent this.

KEEP THE AIR MOIST: Dry air — especially from air conditioning, heating systems, or fans blowing near your face — can dry out your eye surface and trigger pain episodes. A simple bedroom humidifier can make a meaningful difference. Many people in your situation find this helps significantly.

DO NOT RUB YOUR EYES: We know it can be tempting, especially when your eyes are watering and uncomfortable. But rubbing can trigger the surface-slipping type of pain and can make healing take longer.

WEAR PROTECTIVE GLASSES OUTDOORS: Wind, dust, and debris can irritate your eye surface. Wraparound sunglasses or safety glasses when you are outside — especially on windy days — can help protect your eyes.

TAKE SCREEN BREAKS: If you spend a lot of time looking at a computer, phone, or TV screen, you blink less than normal. This dries out your eye surface. Try the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Use your lubricating drops before long screen sessions.

AVOID TRIGGERS UNTIL CLEARED BY YOUR DOCTOR: Until your eye doctor has completed all the tests and given you the all-clear, try to avoid dim or dark environments (like movie theaters or dark rooms) and avoid lying face-down. In some people with the pressure-buildup type of eye condition, these situations can make the pressure spike worse.

STAY HYDRATED: Drinking enough water throughout the day supports your overall eye health and tear production.

You are taking an important step by seeking care today. Even small, consistent changes like using your drops every day and protecting your eyes at night can make a meaningful difference in how quickly you recover and how often the pain episodes happen.
when_to_get_help: CALL 911 OR GO TO THE EMERGENCY ROOM IMMEDIATELY if you experience sudden, severe eye pain that does not go away on its own within a few minutes — especially if it is much worse than what you have experienced so far.
GO TO THE EMERGENCY ROOM IMMEDIATELY if your vision suddenly becomes blurry, dim, or you lose any part of your vision in either eye.

GO TO THE EMERGENCY ROOM IMMEDIATELY if you start seeing rainbow-colored rings or halos around lights — especially streetlights or lamps. This can be a sign that pressure is building up dangerously inside your eye.
GO TO THE EMERGENCY ROOM IMMEDIATELY if you feel nauseous or vomit along with eye pain. Nausea with eye pain is a warning sign that eye pressure may be dangerously high.

GO TO THE EMERGENCY ROOM IMMEDIATELY if you see flashing lights (like camera flashes or lightning bolts) in your vision, or if you notice a dark shadow, curtain, or veil appearing across part of your vision. These are warning signs of a retinal problem.

GO TO THE EMERGENCY ROOM IMMEDIATELY if your eye becomes red, the colored part of your eye looks cloudy or hazy, or your pupil (the dark circle in the center of your eye) looks larger than usual or does not react normally to light.
CALL YOUR EYE DOCTOR URGENTLY (same day) if the sharp pain episodes become more frequent, last longer than a few seconds, or feel more severe than before.
CALL YOUR EYE DOCTOR URGENTLY if you notice any new changes in your vision between now and your follow-up appointment.

CALL YOUR DOCTOR OR PHARMACIST if you experience any unexpected reactions to your medications — such as difficulty breathing, a very slow heartbeat, severe dizziness, or significant worsening of eye discomfort after starting new drops.

Here is what we want you to hold onto: the conditions that are most likely causing your symptoms are both well-understood and very treatable. Many thousands of people experience exactly what you are going through, and with the right care — which you are already receiving — the vast majority of them do very well.

The fact that your vision has not changed, that you are not seeing flashing lights or floating spots, and that the pain resolves on its own are all genuinely reassuring signs. The medical team is being thorough precisely because they want to make sure nothing is missed — not because they expect the worst.

You are not facing this alone. Your medical team is working carefully to find the right answer for you, and you will leave today with a clear plan. Take it one step at a time, follow the instructions you have been given, and do not hesitate to reach out if anything changes or if you have questions. You are in good hands.

PRIORITY 1 — Tonometry (Goldmann applanation preferred; non-contact acceptable for screening): Measure IOP BOTH eyes immediately. Target: identify IOP >21 mmHg (abnormal) or >30 mmHg (emergency). CRITICAL CAVEAT: Normal IOP between episodes does NOT exclude intermittent angle-closure glaucoma — document time of measurement relative to last pain episode.

PRIORITY 1 — Pupil assessment (both eyes, in dim and bright light): Assess for mid-dilated (4-6mm), poorly reactive or non-reactive pupil in left eye — pathognomonic for acute angle-closure. Assess relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) — presence suggests optic nerve or retinal pathology.

PRIORITY 1 — Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with fluorescein staining: Evaluate corneal epithelial integrity (RCES, foreign body, abrasion), fluorescein uptake pattern (linear = abrasion; dendritic = HSV keratitis; punctate = dry eye/exposure), anterior chamber depth (Van Herick grading), anterior chamber inflammation (cells and flare = uveitis), corneal edema (angle-closure), conjunctival injection pattern (ciliary flush = anterior segment pathology; diffuse = conjunctivitis).

PRIORITY 1 — Visual acuity testing (Snellen chart, both eyes, with and without correction): Establish baseline; detect asymmetry suggesting unilateral pathology; reduced VA in affected eye during or after episode suggests IOP spike or corneal pathology.

PRIORITY 2 — Gonioscopy (Goldmann 3-mirror or Zeiss 4-mirror lens): Gold standard for anterior chamber angle assessment. Mandatory if IOP elevated or Van Herick grade I-II. Differentiates open angle (Shaffer grade III-IV) from narrow angle (Shaffer grade I-II) from closed angle (Shaffer grade 0). Identifies peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) indicating prior angle-closure episodes. Cannot be substituted by any other test for definitive angle-closure diagnosis.

PRIORITY 2 — Dilated fundus examination (AFTER angle-closure definitively excluded by gonioscopy): 90D or 78D lens evaluation of: optic nerve head (cup-to-disc ratio, rim tissue, ISNT rule), retina for detachment/tears/lattice degeneration, macula, vitreous for posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) with Weiss ring.

PRIORITY 2 — Confrontational visual field testing: Rapid screening for retinal detachment field defects, glaucomatous field loss, or neurologic field defects. Formal Humphrey visual field testing (24-2 or 30-2) if optic nerve pathology suspected.

PRIORITY 3 — Anterior segment OCT (AS-OCT): Non-contact imaging of anterior chamber angle — useful when gonioscopy is not immediately available or for documentation. Measures anterior chamber depth, angle opening distance, trabecular-iris space area. Increasingly used as adjunct to gonioscopy.

PRIORITY 3 — B-scan ocular ultrasound: Indicated if media opacity (corneal edema, hyphema, dense cataract) prevents adequate fundus visualization. Evaluates for retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage, choroidal detachment, intraocular mass.

PRIORITY 3 — Corneal topography/tomography (Pentacam or Orbscan): Identifies anterior basement membrane dystrophy (ABMD/map-dot-fingerprint dystrophy) as predisposing condition for RCES; maps corneal irregularity; measures anterior chamber depth and angle parameters.

PRIORITY 3 — Schirmer's test and tear break-up time (TBUT): Quantifies tear production and stability to evaluate dry eye disease contribution to bilateral lacrimation and potential RCES predisposition. Schirmer I (without anesthesia) <10mm/5min = abnormal; TBUT <10 seconds = abnormal.
ANCILLARY — Blood pressure measurement: Hypertension contributes to ocular vascular events; hypertensive retinopathy evaluation during fundus exam.
ANCILLARY — Point-of-care blood glucose: Diabetic ocular complications (neovascular glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy) if diabetes history unknown.

NEUROLOGIC REFERRAL TRIGGER — MRI brain with posterior fossa protocol (gadolinium): Indicated if complete ophthalmologic workup is negative and trigeminal neuralgia V1 remains on differential. Evaluates for neurovascular compression of trigeminal nerve root, demyelinating lesions (MS), or posterior fossa mass.
final_result.patient_summary:
Thank you for coming in today and for sharing what has been happening with your eye. You are doing the right thing by getting this checked out, and we want to make sure you have all the information you need in plain language.

Here is what we know so far: You have been having a sharp, sudden pain in your left eye that lasts only a split second. This has happened about 4 times in the past 8 hours. Both of your eyes have also been watering more than usual. You mentioned you were worried about allergies and a detached retina — and we want to address both of those concerns honestly.

The good news is that your symptoms do not strongly point to a detached retina. A detached retina usually does NOT cause sharp pain. It typically causes flashing lights, floating spots, or a shadow across your vision — none of which you have reported. That is reassuring.

Regarding allergies: while allergies can cause watery eyes, they do NOT usually cause the kind of sharp, stabbing pain you are describing. So allergies alone are unlikely to explain everything that is happening.

What our medical team IS focused on right now are two main possibilities that need to be checked urgently:

1. A condition called INTERMITTENT ANGLE-CLOSURE GLAUCOMA. Think of your eye like a drain in a sink. In some people, the drain can become temporarily blocked, causing pressure to build up inside the eye. This pressure spike can cause a sudden, sharp pain — exactly like what you are describing. This is something that MUST be checked today because, if left untreated, it can cause permanent vision loss. The important thing to know is that it IS treatable when caught early.

2. A condition called RECURRENT CORNEAL EROSION SYNDROME. The cornea is the clear front surface of your eye, like a windshield. Sometimes a tiny patch of the surface layer can briefly lift or slip, causing a sudden electric-shock-like pain that lasts only a split second. This matches your description very closely. This condition is NOT immediately dangerous to your vision, but it does need treatment to prevent it from happening again and again.

Both of these conditions are manageable. The most important thing right now is getting the right eye tests done today so we know exactly what we are dealing with.
safety_warnings: CRITICAL PRESCRIBING SAFETY — Do NOT administer any mydriatic/pupil-dilating agents (tropicamide, phenylephrine, cyclopentolate) until acute/intermittent angle-closure glaucoma is definitively excluded by gonioscopy. CRITICAL PRESCRIBING SAFETY — Do NOT prescribe topical or systemic antihistamines (diphenhydramine, loratadine, cetirizine, olopatadine, ketotifen) until angle-closure glaucoma is definitively excluded. Anticholinergic/mydriatic properties of antihistamines can precipitate acute angle-closure crisis in anatomically predisposed individuals.

CRITICAL PRESCRIBING SAFETY — Do NOT apply topical corticosteroids until HSV keratitis is definitively excluded by fluorescein slit-lamp staining. Application of steroids to an HSV dendritic ulcer causes corneal melting and perforation — a blinding complication.

Multiple drug classes can precipitate angle-closure episodes in susceptible individuals: anticholinergics, first-generation antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, SSRIs/SNRIs (especially paroxetine), topiramate, sulfonamide antibiotics, sympathomimetics (pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine), and adrenergic bronchodilators. If any of these are identified, they may be the precipitating cause of the episodic pain and must be flagged immediately.

Nasolacrimal occlusion technique (finger pressure at inner canthus for 2 minutes post-instillation) is MANDATORY to minimize systemic beta-blockade. Risk of bronchospasm, bradycardia, hypotension, and masking of hypoglycemia. Asthma and COPD status must be confirmed before administration — these are absolute contraindications.

Patient allergy history is documented as 'none' but this must be explicitly verified by the treating clinician before administration. Do not administer concurrently with systemic acetazolamide — additive carbonic anhydrase inhibition increases toxicity risk (metabolic acidosis, electrolyte disturbance). Intermittent angle-closure produces brief, recurrent episodes of IOP spike causing sharp pain, tearing, and may resolve spontaneously between attacks — perfectly matching the microsecond-to-seconds episodic pattern with 4 episodes in 8 hours. Absence of reported halos, nausea, vomiting, or headache slightly lowers confidence but these symptoms must be actively queried as patients often underreport. LR+ for episodic unilateral sharp eye pain in age >50 male: ~4.5. Lacrimation as associated finding adds modest support (LR+ ~2.1). Post-test probability estimated 50-55%. diagnosis.clinical_reasoning_summary: This 54-year-old male presents with a diagnostically challenging pattern of episodic microsecond-duration sharp left eye pain (4 episodes in 8 hours) with bilateral excessive lacrimation. The triage team appropriately flagged intermittent angle-closure glaucoma as the primary concern, and this remains the most dangerous diagnosis to exclude. However, my analysis reveals that the microsecond duration of pain is actually MORE consistent with corneal foreign body (blink-triggered pain) or trigeminal neuralgia (V1 branch) than with classic angle-closure episodes, which typically last minutes to hours. This represents an important anchoring bias check — the triage framing should not cause premature closure on angle-closure to the exclusion of corneal pathology. My differential is led by intermittent angle-closure glaucoma (52%) and corneal foreign body/abrasion (48%) as near co-equal leading diagnoses, with dry eye neuropathic pain (35%) as a secondary consideration. Allergic conjunctivitis (20%) is unlikely given the sharp pain quality — itching, not sharp pain, is the hallmark of allergic disease. Retinal detachment (15%) is included as a must-not-miss despite poor clinical fit, as the patient specifically raised this concern and dilated fundus exam is required. Trigeminal neuralgia V1 (12%) is an important alternative that would completely change management from ophthalmologic to neurologic. The critical immediate steps are: tonometry to measure IOP, slit-lamp with fluorescein to evaluate corneal integrity, pupil assessment for mid-dilation, and gonioscopy if angle-closure is suspected. Crucially, pupils must NOT be dilated until angle-closure is excluded, as dilation can precipitate acute angle-closure crisis. The five follow-up questions targeting halos/nausea, pain triggers, visual symptoms, environmental exposures, and refractive history would substantially narrow this differential before or concurrent with the ophthalmologic examination.

specialist.reason_for_consultation: 54-year-old male with episodic microsecond-duration sharp left eye pain (4 episodes in 8 hours) with bilateral excessive lacrimation. Triage ESI-2. Must exclude acute/intermittent angle-closure glaucoma, recurrent corneal erosion syndrome, corneal foreign body, HSV keratitis, and retinal detachment. Patient self-concerned about allergies and retinal detachment.
specialist.specialist_assessment:
This is a diagnostically nuanced ophthalmologic presentation requiring urgent specialist evaluation. The constellation of episodic microsecond-duration sharp unilateral left eye pain with bilateral excessive lacrimation in a 54-year-old male generates a focused differential with two near-co-equal leading diagnoses and several must-not-miss conditions.

LEADING DIAGNOSIS 1 — RECURRENT CORNEAL EROSION SYNDROME (RCES) [Estimated probability: 50-55%]: The microsecond duration of pain is the single most discriminating feature in this case. Classic intermittent angle-closure glaucoma episodes typically last minutes to hours, not microseconds. In contrast, RCES produces sudden, electric, microsecond-to-second sharp pain caused by abrupt epithelial detachment from Bowman's layer — a pathophysiologically instantaneous event perfectly matching this pain character. Bilateral reflex lacrimation is a hallmark corneal irritation response. The episodic recurrence (4x/8 hours) is consistent with repeated epithelial micro-detachment events. Predisposing conditions include anterior basement membrane dystrophy (ABMD/map-dot-fingerprint dystrophy), prior corneal trauma (often forgotten by patient), and dry eye disease — all plausible at age 54. This diagnosis is frequently missed in emergency settings and misattributed to conjunctivitis or dry eye.

LEADING DIAGNOSIS 2 — INTERMITTENT ANGLE-CLOSURE GLAUCOMA (IACG) [Estimated probability: 45-50%]: This remains the must-not-miss vision-threatening diagnosis. Age 54, male sex, episodic unilateral sharp eye pain, and excessive lacrimation are all consistent. Intermittent angle-closure produces transient IOP spikes causing sharp pain and tearing that can resolve spontaneously between attacks, leaving the patient asymptomatic and with normal IOP at time of examination. The absence of reported halos, nausea, vomiting, and headache slightly argues against but these symptoms must be actively queried — patients frequently underreport or fail to connect them to eye pain episodes. The atypically brief pain duration may represent early or mild IOP spikes, or may reflect the patient's subjective perception of a longer event. Each untreated intermittent episode causes progressive trabecular meshwork damage and cumulative optic nerve injury. This diagnosis cannot be excluded without gonioscopy.

SECONDARY DIAGNOSIS — CORNEAL FOREIGN BODY [Estimated probability: 35-40%]: Blink-triggered microsecond sharp pain with reflex lacrimation is the classic presentation of a retained corneal or subtarsal foreign body. Patients frequently do not recall the inciting exposure event. Slit-lamp with fluorescein staining is diagnostic. This is the most common cause of acute sharp eye pain in the emergency setting and must be excluded before other diagnoses are pursued.

TERTIARY DIAGNOSIS — TRIGEMINAL NEURALGIA V1 BRANCH [Estimated probability: 12-15%]: The microsecond electric-shock pain quality is actually more characteristic of trigeminal neuralgia than of glaucoma. V1 (ophthalmic) branch TN produces periorbital/intraocular electric pain of microsecond-to-seconds duration in episodic paroxysms — precisely matching this presentation. Age 54 is within the peak onset range. Lacrimation is not a primary TN feature, which argues against, but autonomic features can accompany V1 TN. If complete ophthalmologic workup is negative, neurologic evaluation with MRI brain/posterior fossa is mandatory.

HSV KERATITIS [Estimated probability: 10%]: Herpes simplex keratitis produces sharp eye pain and lacrimation; dendritic ulcer on fluorescein staining is pathognomonic. Critical to identify as inadvertent steroid application causes corneal perforation.

RETINAL DETACHMENT [Estimated probability: 5-8%]: Patient's primary concern but poor clinical fit. Retinal detachment is characteristically painless, presenting with photopsia, floaters, and curtain visual field defect — none of which are reported. Sharp pain is not a feature of RD unless complicated by secondary angle-closure or inflammation. However, dilated fundus examination is mandatory after angle-closure is excluded to rule out peripheral retinal breaks, lattice degeneration, and posterior vitreous detachment.

ALLERGIC CONJUNCTIVITIS [Estimated probability: 8-10%]: Patient's self-diagnosis. Bilateral lacrimation is consistent but sharp stabbing unilateral pain is NOT a feature of allergic conjunctivitis — itching is the hallmark. Allergic conjunctivitis may coexist as a contributor to bilateral tearing but cannot explain the pain. CRITICAL SAFETY NOTE: Antihistamines (topical or systemic) must NOT be prescribed until angle-closure glaucoma is definitively excluded, as their anticholinergic/mydriatic properties can precipitate acute angle-closure crisis in anatomically predisposed individuals.

CRITICAL PRESCRIBING SAFETY ALERT: Before any medications are administered, a complete medication history is mandatory. The following drug classes can precipitate acute angle-closure in susceptible individuals and must be identified: anticholinergics, first-generation antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, SSRIs/SNRIs (particularly paroxetine), topiramate, sulfonamides, and sympathomimetics (pseudoephedrine). If the patient is currently taking any of these agents, they may be the precipitating cause of intermittent angle-closure episodes.
diagnostic_criteria_applied: AAO Preferred Practice Pattern — Primary Angle Closure Disease 2021: Intermittent angle-closure glaucoma diagnostic criteria applied — episodic eye pain, lacrimation, age >40, unilateral distribution. Patient meets 3/4 major criteria (pain, lacrimation, age); halos/nausea not yet confirmed. Gonioscopy required for definitive classification as PACS/PAC/PACG.

IOP Threshold Criteria (AAO/EGS): IOP >21 mmHg = abnormal; IOP >30 mmHg in symptomatic patient = diagnostic emergency requiring immediate intervention. Normal IOP between episodes does NOT exclude intermittent angle-closure — this is a critical diagnostic pitfall.

RCES Diagnostic Criteria (AAO Corneal/External Disease PPP 2019): Episodic sudden sharp eye pain + slit-lamp evidence of epithelial irregularity/defect + fluorescein pooling in erosion site. Predisposing conditions: ABMD, prior trauma, dry eye. Patient meets clinical pain criteria; slit-lamp confirmation required.

International Headache Society (IHS) Trigeminal Neuralgia Criteria (ICHD-3): Recurrent paroxysmal unilateral facial/periorbital pain lasting microseconds to 2 minutes, electric/stabbing quality, triggered by innocuous stimuli, confined to trigeminal distribution. Patient meets pain character and duration criteria; trigger zone and distribution confirmation required.

Retinal Detachment Risk Stratification (AAO PPP 2019): Age >50 (present), male sex (present), myopia status unknown, prior surgery unknown, trauma unknown, floaters/photopsia absent (argues strongly against active RD). Low-intermediate risk for RD; dilated fundus exam still required.

TFOS DEWS II Dry Eye Diagnostic Criteria 2017: Paradoxical reflex tearing + ocular surface symptoms. Bilateral lacrimation consistent with dry eye contribution; OSDI questionnaire and TBUT testing would formally assess.

Fluorescein Staining Grading (Oxford Scale): To be applied during slit-lamp examination — Grade 0 (no staining) to Grade V (severe confluent staining). Any uptake in corneal epithelium confirms corneal pathology.

Van Herick Grading System for Anterior Chamber Depth: Grade I (<1/4 corneal thickness) = high risk for angle-closure; Grade II (1/4) = moderate risk; Grade III-IV = low risk. To be assessed at slit-lamp prior to gonioscopy decision.
specialist.risk_stratification: HIGH RISK — ESI-2 assignment confirmed and appropriate. This patient carries high risk for two distinct vision-threatening conditions simultaneously: (1) Intermittent angle-closure glaucoma — each untreated episode causes irreversible trabecular meshwork damage and cumulative optic nerve injury; 50% of untreated fellow eyes develop acute attack within 5 years; permanent vision loss occurs in 25-50% of untreated acute angle-closure crises. (2) Recurrent corneal erosion syndrome — while not immediately vision-threatening, repeated erosion events cause progressive corneal scarring and can lead to permanent visual impairment if untreated. Risk-modifying factors elevating this patient's risk profile: Age 54 (peak incidence decade for both IACG and RCES), male sex (higher RD risk, more severe angle-closure presentations), unknown refractive status (hyperopia = 3-5x increased angle-closure risk), unknown medication history (potential angle-closure precipitants), no prior ophthalmologic history (no baseline IOP or anterior chamber angle documentation), recurrent pattern (4 episodes/8 hours suggests active ongoing pathology rather than isolated event). The combination of unknown angle anatomy, recurrent episodic pain, and age >50 mandates emergent ophthalmologic evaluation regardless of current IOP measurement.
specialty_specific_tests: PRIORITY 1 — Tonometry (Goldmann applanation preferred; non-contact acceptable for screening): Measure IOP BOTH eyes immediately. Target: identify IOP >21 mmHg (abnormal) or >30 mmHg (emergency). CRITICAL CAVEAT: Normal IOP between episodes does NOT exclude intermittent angle-closure glaucoma — document time of measurement relative to last pain episode.

PRIORITY 1 — Pupil assessment (both eyes, in dim and bright light): Assess for mid-dilated (4-6mm), poorly reactive or non-reactive pupil in left eye — pathognomonic for acute angle-closure. Assess relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) — presence suggests optic nerve or retinal pathology.

PRIORITY 1 — Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with fluorescein staining: Evaluate corneal epithelial integrity (RCES, foreign body, abrasion), fluorescein uptake pattern (linear = abrasion; dendritic = HSV keratitis; punctate = dry eye/exposure), anterior chamber depth (Van Herick grading), anterior chamber inflammation (cells and flare = uveitis), corneal edema (angle-closure), conjunctival injection pattern (ciliary flush = anterior segment pathology; diffuse = conjunctivitis).

PRIORITY 1 — Visual acuity testing (Snellen chart, both eyes, with and without correction): Establish baseline; detect asymmetry suggesting unilateral pathology; reduced VA in affected eye during or after episode suggests IOP spike or corneal pathology.

PRIORITY 2 — Gonioscopy (Goldmann 3-mirror or Zeiss 4-mirror lens): Gold standard for anterior chamber angle assessment. Mandatory if IOP elevated or Van Herick grade I-II. Differentiates open angle (Shaffer grade III-IV) from narrow angle (Shaffer grade I-II) from closed angle (Shaffer grade 0). Identifies peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) indicating prior angle-closure episodes. Cannot be substituted by any other test for definitive angle-closure diagnosis.

PRIORITY 2 — Dilated fundus examination (AFTER angle-closure definitively excluded by gonioscopy): 90D or 78D lens evaluation of: optic nerve head (cup-to-disc ratio, rim tissue, ISNT rule), retina for detachment/tears/lattice degeneration, macula, vitreous for posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) with Weiss ring.

PRIORITY 2 — Confrontational visual field testing: Rapid screening for retinal detachment field defects, glaucomatous field loss, or neurologic field defects. Formal Humphrey visual field testing (24-2 or 30-2) if optic nerve pathology suspected.

PRIORITY 3 — Anterior segment OCT (AS-OCT): Non-contact imaging of anterior chamber angle — useful when gonioscopy is not immediately available or for documentation. Measures anterior chamber depth, angle opening distance, trabecular-iris space area. Increasingly used as adjunct to gonioscopy.

PRIORITY 3 — B-scan ocular ultrasound: Indicated if media opacity (corneal edema, hyphema, dense cataract) prevents adequate fundus visualization. Evaluates for retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage, choroidal detachment, intraocular mass.

PRIORITY 3 — Corneal topography/tomography (Pentacam or Orbscan): Identifies anterior basement membrane dystrophy (ABMD/map-dot-fingerprint dystrophy) as predisposing condition for RCES; maps corneal irregularity; measures anterior chamber depth and angle parameters.

PRIORITY 3 — Schirmer's test and tear break-up time (TBUT): Quantifies tear production and stability to evaluate dry eye disease contribution to bilateral lacrimation and potential RCES predisposition. Schirmer I (without anesthesia) <10mm/5min = abnormal; TBUT <10 seconds = abnormal.
ANCILLARY — Blood pressure measurement: Hypertension contributes to ocular vascular events; hypertensive retinopathy evaluation during fundus exam.
ANCILLARY — Point-of-care blood glucose: Diabetic ocular complications (neovascular glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy) if diabetes history unknown.

NEUROLOGIC REFERRAL TRIGGER — MRI brain with posterior fossa protocol (gadolinium): Indicated if complete ophthalmologic workup is negative and trigeminal neuralgia V1 remains on differential. Evaluates for neurovascular compression of trigeminal nerve root, demyelinating lesions (MS), or posterior fossa mass.
specialist_red_flags: EMERGENT — Mid-dilated (4-6mm), poorly reactive or fixed pupil in left eye: Pathognomonic for acute angle-closure glaucoma crisis. Requires immediate IOP-lowering therapy and urgent ophthalmology intervention within minutes to hours.

EMERGENT — IOP >30 mmHg on tonometry: Acute angle-closure crisis. Initiate immediate medical therapy (topical timolol 0.5%, brimonidine 0.2%, dorzolamide 2%, pilocarpine 1-2%; systemic acetazolamide 500mg if no contraindications) and arrange emergency laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI).
EMERGENT — Corneal edema (cloudy/hazy cornea on slit-lamp): Indicates severely elevated IOP causing corneal endothelial decompensation — acute angle-closure crisis until proven otherwise.

URGENT — Dendritic ulcer on fluorescein staining: HSV keratitis. Do NOT apply corticosteroids. Initiate topical antiviral therapy (acyclovir 3% ointment 5x/day or ganciclovir 0.15% gel 5x/day) and arrange urgent ophthalmology follow-up.

URGENT — Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) in left eye: Indicates optic nerve or extensive retinal pathology on the affected side. Requires urgent dilated fundus examination and possible neuroimaging.

URGENT — Anterior chamber cells and flare on slit-lamp: Anterior uveitis/iritis. Requires urgent ophthalmology evaluation, identification of underlying systemic cause (HLA-B27 associated conditions, sarcoidosis, syphilis), and topical corticosteroid therapy.

URGENT — Shaffer grade 0-I on gonioscopy (closed or critically narrow angle): Confirms angle-closure mechanism. Requires laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) — prophylactic LPI also recommended for fellow eye given bilateral anatomic predisposition.
URGENT — Peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) on gonioscopy: Evidence of prior angle-closure episodes with permanent trabecular damage. Indicates more advanced disease requiring aggressive management.

URGENT — Retinal break, tear, or detachment on dilated fundus exam: Surgical emergency. Immediate retinal surgery consultation required. Macula-on detachment: surgery within hours. Macula-off detachment: surgery within 24 hours.

URGENT — Optic nerve cupping >0.7 cup-to-disc ratio or asymmetric cupping (>0.2 difference between eyes): Suggests glaucomatous optic neuropathy — may indicate prior undetected angle-closure episodes causing cumulative damage.
IMPORTANT — Halos around lights confirmed on history: Significantly increases probability of angle-closure glaucoma (LR+ 4.2). Escalates urgency of gonioscopy.
IMPORTANT — Nausea/vomiting associated with pain episodes: Classic vagal response to acute IOP elevation. Strongly supports angle-closure mechanism.
IMPORTANT — Pain triggered by dim lighting or entering dark room: Pupillary dilation in dim light can precipitate angle-closure in narrow-angle eyes — highly specific for angle-closure mechanism.
IMPORTANT — Trigger zone identified (touch, cold air, chewing precipitating pain): Strongly supports trigeminal neuralgia diagnosis (LR+ ~6.0) — redirects workup to neurology.
PRESCRIBING SAFETY — Do NOT administer mydriatics (tropicamide, phenylephrine, cyclopentolate) until angle-closure definitively excluded by gonioscopy.
PRESCRIBING SAFETY — Do NOT prescribe antihistamines (topical or systemic) until angle-closure excluded — anticholinergic/mydriatic properties can precipitate acute angle-closure crisis.
PRESCRIBING SAFETY — Do NOT apply topical corticosteroids until HSV keratitis excluded by fluorescein staining — steroid application to HSV dendritic ulcer causes corneal melting and perforation.

treatment_algorithm.step_1_conservative: Immediate cessation of any medications that can precipitate angle-closure (anticholinergics, first-generation antihistamines, sympathomimetics, topiramate, TCAs, SSRIs/SNRIs). Avoid dim lighting and dark environments until angle-closure excluded. Avoid prone positioning. Do NOT self-administer any eye drops until evaluated.
treatment_algorithm.step_2_first_line_pharmacological: If IOP >21 mmHg confirmed on tonometry: Topical timolol 0.5% one drop affected eye (reduces aqueous production). Topical brimonidine 0.2% one drop affected eye (reduces aqueous production and increases uveoscleral outflow). Topical dorzolamide 2% one drop affected eye (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor). Topical pilocarpine 1-2% one drop affected eye (miotic — constricts pupil to open angle). If IOP >30 mmHg or severe: Acetazolamide 500mg IV or PO (systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) — requires prescription and physician administration.
treatment_algorithm.step_3_second_line: If medical therapy fails to lower IOP adequately within 1-2 hours: Hyperosmotic agents — IV mannitol 1-2 g/kg over 45 minutes (hospital administration only). Oral glycerol 1 g/kg if IV access unavailable and patient not diabetic.
treatment_algorithm.step_4_definitive_interventional: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI): Definitive treatment. Creates a small hole in peripheral iris to allow aqueous flow and prevent pupillary block. Performed by ophthalmologist. Prophylactic LPI also recommended for the fellow (right) eye given bilateral anatomic predisposition. Success rate >90% for preventing future acute attacks.
treatment_algorithm.step_5_surgical: If LPI fails or is not technically feasible (corneal edema, small iris): Surgical peripheral iridectomy. Clear lens extraction (CLE) — EAGLE Trial evidence supports CLE superiority over LPI for IOP control and quality of life in established angle-closure disease. Trabeculectomy or tube-shunt surgery if glaucomatous optic nerve damage present.
treatment_algorithm.step_6_fellow_eye: Prophylactic LPI to right eye within 1-2 weeks of left eye treatment — 50% of untreated fellow eyes develop acute attack within 5 years.

treatment_plans.first_line: IMMEDIATE: Urgent ophthalmology evaluation within 1-2 hours. Tonometry (IOP measurement both eyes). Gonioscopy. Slit-lamp exam. Pupil assessment. Do NOT dilate pupils until angle-closure excluded. If IOP elevated: topical timolol 0.5% + brimonidine 0.2% + dorzolamide 2% + pilocarpine 1-2% administered by ophthalmologist. Definitive: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI).

medications.name: Timolol 0.5% ophthalmic solution
medications.frequency: Twice daily (or as directed by ophthalmologist in acute setting)
medications.duration: As directed by ophthalmologist — may be ongoing if IOP remains elevated
medications.mechanism: Reduces aqueous humor production by ciliary body
contraindications: Asthma or COPD (bronchospasm risk — ABSOLUTE contraindication)
warnings: Significant systemic absorption via nasolacrimal duct (~80%) — apply nasolacrimal occlusion (finger pressure at inner corner of eye for 2 minutes) after instillation to minimize systemic absorption
Can mask hypoglycemia symptoms in diabetics
Can cause depression, fatigue, sexual dysfunction systemically
Punctal occlusion technique mandatory to reduce systemic side effects
medications.monitoring: Heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory status after administration
drug_interactions: Systemic beta-blockers: additive bradycardia/hypotension
Calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem): risk of AV block
Digoxin: additive bradycardia
medications.administration_note: PHYSICIAN/OPHTHALMOLOGIST ADMINISTERED in acute setting — requires prescription

medications.name: Brimonidine 0.2% ophthalmic solution
medications.frequency: Three times daily (or as directed by ophthalmologist in acute setting)
medications.duration: As directed by ophthalmologist
medications.mechanism: Reduces aqueous humor production AND increases uveoscleral outflow
contraindications: MAO inhibitor use (ABSOLUTE — severe hypertensive crisis risk)
warnings: Drowsiness and fatigue common
Ocular allergy develops in up to 15% of patients with prolonged use
Dry mouth
Rebound hyperemia
medications.monitoring: Blood pressure, alertness level
drug_interactions: MAO inhibitors: CONTRAINDICATED — severe hypertension
Tricyclic antidepressants: additive hypotension
CNS depressants: additive sedation
Antihypertensives: additive hypotensive effect
medications.administration_note: Requires prescription — ophthalmologist administered in acute setting

medications.name: Dorzolamide 2% ophthalmic solution
medications.frequency: Three times daily
medications.duration: As directed by ophthalmologist
medications.mechanism: Inhibits carbonic anhydrase in ciliary body, reducing aqueous humor production
warnings: Bitter taste after instillation (nasolacrimal drainage)
Ocular burning and stinging
Corneal edema with long-term use in susceptible patients
Sulfonamide cross-reactivity — obtain allergy history
medications.monitoring: Renal function if prolonged use, corneal clarity
drug_interactions: Systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide): additive effect and toxicity — do not combine
High-dose aspirin: increased acetazolamide toxicity if used together
medications.administration_note: Requires prescription

medications.name: Pilocarpine 1-2% ophthalmic solution
medications.frequency: Every 15 minutes x 2 doses in acute setting, then as directed
medications.duration: Acute phase only — typically discontinued after LPI
medications.mechanism: Contracts iris sphincter muscle causing miosis (pupil constriction), pulling iris away from trabecular meshwork to open angle
medications.expected_IOP_reduction: Adjunctive — primarily opens angle mechanically rather than reducing IOP directly
contraindications: IOP >50 mmHg (ischemic iris — pilocarpine ineffective and may worsen)
warnings: Brow ache and headache from ciliary muscle spasm — common and expected
Miosis causes dim vision — warn patient, especially for driving
Systemic cholinergic effects if absorbed: sweating, salivation, bradycardia (rare with topical)
Retinal detachment risk with high myopia — assess before use
medications.monitoring: Pupil size response, IOP response, patient comfort
drug_interactions: Anticholinergic medications: pharmacodynamic antagonism — reduces pilocarpine efficacy
Systemic cholinergic agents: additive cholinergic toxicity
medications.administration_note: Requires prescription — ophthalmologist administered in acute setting. NOT to be self-administered.

medications.name: Acetazolamide 500mg
medications.frequency: Single dose IV (preferred in acute setting) or PO if IV unavailable
medications.duration: Acute phase only — bridge to definitive LPI
medications.indication: Reserved for IOP >30 mmHg or inadequate response to topical agents
warnings: Metabolic acidosis with repeated dosing
Electrolyte disturbances (hypokalemia) — monitor potassium
Paresthesias (tingling in extremities) — common and expected
Kidney stone risk with prolonged use
Nausea, vomiting, malaise
Aplastic anemia (rare but serious — idiosyncratic)
medications.monitoring: Electrolytes (potassium), renal function, acid-base status, CBC with prolonged use
drug_interactions: Aspirin/salicylates: increased acetazolamide toxicity
Lithium: increased lithium excretion
Metformin: increased lactic acidosis risk
Topiramate: additive metabolic acidosis and kidney stone risk
medications.administration_note: Hospital administration only — requires prescription and physician oversight

treatment_plans.condition: Recurrent Corneal Erosion Syndrome (RCES) — Leading Diagnosis by Pain Character

treatment_algorithm.step_1_conservative: Preservative-free lubricating eye drops (artificial tears) every 1-2 hours while awake. Lubricating eye ointment (e.g., Refresh PM, Lacrilube) at bedtime — critical to prevent epithelial desiccation during sleep when erosions most commonly occur. Avoid rubbing eyes. Protective eyewear in windy/dusty environments. Humidifier in bedroom.
treatment_algorithm.step_2_first_line_pharmacological: Hypertonic saline eye drops 5% NaCl (e.g., Muro 128 drops) 1-2 drops affected eye 4x daily — reduces epithelial edema and strengthens epithelial adhesion. Hypertonic saline ointment 5% NaCl at bedtime — most important dose for preventing nocturnal erosions. Preservative-free artificial tears (e.g., Systane Ultra PF, Refresh Optive PF) every 1-2 hours.
treatment_algorithm.step_3_second_line: Topical antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g., erythromycin ointment or moxifloxacin drops) if active erosion present to prevent secondary infection. Bandage contact lens (BCL) — soft therapeutic contact lens worn continuously for 1-3 months to protect healing epithelium and prevent recurrent detachment. Requires ophthalmologist fitting and monitoring.
treatment_algorithm.step_4_adjunctive: Oral doxycycline 50-100mg daily for 3 months — reduces matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) activity that degrades epithelial basement membrane adhesion complexes. Evidence: multiple prospective studies showing reduced recurrence rate. Topical vitamin A (retinol) drops — promotes epithelial differentiation and basement membrane synthesis.
treatment_algorithm.step_5_interventional: Anterior stromal puncture (ASP): Fine needle creates micro-scars in Bowman's layer to anchor epithelium — effective for peripheral erosions. Epithelial debridement with diamond burr polishing: Removes abnormal epithelium and polishes Bowman's layer to promote proper re-adhesion. Phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK): Excimer laser ablation of superficial corneal stroma — most effective for RCES associated with anterior basement membrane dystrophy (ABMD). Success rate 70-90% for refractory cases.
treatment_algorithm.step_6_surgical: Superficial keratectomy: Surgical removal of abnormal epithelium and anterior stroma — reserved for refractory cases failing all other interventions.

treatment_plans.first_line: Urgent ophthalmology evaluation for slit-lamp with fluorescein staining to confirm diagnosis. Immediate: preservative-free artificial tears + hypertonic saline 5% drops (daytime) + hypertonic saline 5% ointment (bedtime). Oral doxycycline 50mg twice daily for 3 months if diagnosis confirmed.

medications.name: Sodium Chloride 5% Hypertonic Saline Eye Drops (Muro 128 or equivalent)
medications.frequency: 4 times daily (every 4-6 hours while awake)
medications.duration: 3-6 months minimum; may be indefinite for prevention
medications.mechanism: Osmotically draws fluid from edematous corneal epithelium, reducing swelling and strengthening epithelial-stromal adhesion
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to sodium chloride preparations
warnings: Temporary stinging and burning upon instillation — expected and normal
Blurred vision immediately after instillation — clears within minutes
Do not use with contact lenses in place (unless bandage contact lens prescribed by ophthalmologist)
medications.monitoring: Symptom frequency and severity — track number of erosion episodes per week
medications.administration_note: Available OTC — pharmacist consultation recommended for proper technique

medications.name: Sodium Chloride 5% Hypertonic Saline Ophthalmic Ointment (Muro 128 Ointment)
medications.frequency: Once daily at bedtime — MOST IMPORTANT DOSE
medications.duration: 3-6 months minimum
medications.mechanism: Maintains corneal hydration balance overnight, prevents epithelial desiccation during sleep when lid movement is absent and erosions most commonly occur
warnings: Causes significant blurring of vision — use ONLY at bedtime
Temporary eye irritation upon waking — normal
Do not drive after application
medications.monitoring: Morning symptoms — if pain upon waking, this is classic RCES and confirms diagnosis
medications.administration_note: Available OTC — critical that patient uses this at bedtime consistently

medications.name: Preservative-Free Artificial Tears (e.g., Systane Ultra PF, Refresh Optive PF, TheraTears)
medications.frequency: Every 1-2 hours while awake, or as needed for comfort
medications.duration: Ongoing — indefinite for dry eye management and RCES prevention
medications.mechanism: Supplements natural tear film, reduces ocular surface friction, promotes epithelial healing
warnings: MUST use preservative-free formulation if using more than 4 times daily — preservatives (benzalkonium chloride) are toxic to corneal epithelium with frequent use and can worsen RCES
Avoid formulations containing benzalkonium chloride (BAK) — check label
Refrigeration not required but may improve comfort
medications.monitoring: Symptom relief, frequency of use
medications.administration_note: OTC — pharmacist can assist with selection of preservative-free formulation

medications.name: Doxycycline 50mg
medications.class: Tetracycline antibiotic (used here for anti-MMP/anti-inflammatory properties, NOT antimicrobial)
medications.frequency: Twice daily (or 100mg once daily)
medications.duration: 3 months
medications.mechanism: Inhibits matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-2, MMP-9) that degrade epithelial basement membrane adhesion complexes (hemidesmosomes, anchoring fibrils) — addresses the underlying pathophysiology of RCES
medications.evidence: Multiple prospective studies and case series demonstrate 60-80% reduction in RCES recurrence with 3-month doxycycline course
contraindications: Pregnancy (Category D — teratogenic, causes fetal bone/tooth abnormalities)

pico_question.P: 54-year-old male with episodic sharp left eye pain (microsecond duration, 4 episodes in 8 hours) and bilateral excessive lacrimation, no reported vision loss, halos, or nausea
pico_question.I: Clinical evaluation for acute/intermittent angle-closure glaucoma, corneal pathology, retinal detachment, and allergic conjunctivitis including tonometry, slit-lamp exam, gonioscopy, and dilated fundus examination
pico_question.C: Alternative diagnoses: recurrent corneal erosion syndrome, dry eye disease, trigeminal neuralgia, allergic conjunctivitis, retinal detachment
pico_question.O: Primary: preservation of vision and prevention of permanent optic nerve damage; Secondary: accurate diagnosis, appropriate triage to ophthalmology, reduction in intraocular pressure if elevated, prevention of acute angle-closure crisis

acute_angle_closure_glaucoma.source: American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) Preferred Practice Pattern — Primary Angle Closure Disease, 2021

key_recommendations.recommendation: Intermittent angle-closure glaucoma (IACG) should be suspected in patients with episodic eye pain, headache, blurred vision, or halos, even when asymptomatic between episodes. Gonioscopy is mandatory to assess anterior chamber angle.
key_recommendations.evidence_grade: A (Strong — based on consistent observational evidence and expert consensus)
key_recommendations.clinical_note: Microsecond-duration sharp pain episodes are atypical for classic AACG but may represent early or intermittent angle-closure events or corneal pathology. Both must be urgently evaluated.

key_recommendations.recommendation: Intraocular pressure (IOP) measurement via tonometry is the first-line urgent assessment. IOP >21 mmHg is abnormal; IOP >30 mmHg in symptomatic patient is diagnostic emergency.
key_recommendations.clinical_note: IOP may be normal between intermittent episodes — a normal IOP does not exclude intermittent angle-closure glaucoma.

key_recommendations.recommendation: Laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) is the definitive treatment for primary angle-closure suspect (PACS), primary angle closure (PAC), and primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG). Prophylactic LPI recommended for fellow eye.
key_recommendations.evidence_grade: A — supported by EAGLE Trial (RCT, Lancet 2016) and multiple systematic reviews
key_recommendations.clinical_note: EAGLE Trial (n=419): Clear-lens extraction superior to LPI for IOP control and quality of life in established angle-closure disease. LPI remains first-line for acute/intermittent presentations.

key_recommendations.recommendation: Do NOT administer mydriatic (pupil-dilating) agents until angle-closure glaucoma is definitively excluded. Dilation can precipitate acute angle-closure crisis.
key_recommendations.evidence_grade: A — strong consensus, supported by pathophysiological mechanism
key_recommendations.clinical_note: Critical safety recommendation — consistent with triage agent flag.

key_recommendations.recommendation: Acute angle-closure crisis management: Topical beta-blockers (timolol 0.5%), alpha-2 agonists (brimonidine), carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (dorzolamide), and pilocarpine 1-2% to constrict pupil. Systemic acetazolamide 500mg IV/PO if IOP severely elevated.
key_recommendations.evidence_grade: B — based on observational studies and expert consensus; limited RCT data for acute phase

recurrent_corneal_erosion_syndrome.source: AAO Preferred Practice Pattern — Corneal/External Disease, 2019; UK Royal College of Ophthalmologists Guidelines 2020

key_recommendations.recommendation: Recurrent corneal erosion syndrome (RCES) should be considered in patients with sudden, sharp, episodic eye pain — classically upon waking but can occur at any time. Microsecond-duration sharp pain is highly characteristic of RCES.
key_recommendations.evidence_grade: B — based on cohort studies and case series
key_recommendations.clinical_note: RCES is a CRITICAL differential diagnosis in this patient. The microsecond duration of pain is MORE consistent with RCES than with angle-closure glaucoma. RCES occurs when the corneal epithelium fails to adhere properly to Bowman's layer, causing sudden epithelial detachment.

key_recommendations.recommendation: Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining is essential to identify epithelial defects, map basement membrane dystrophy, or identify anterior basement membrane dystrophy (ABMD/map-dot-fingerprint dystrophy) — the most common predisposing condition for RCES.
key_recommendations.evidence_grade: A — standard of care, expert consensus

key_recommendations.recommendation: First-line treatment: Preservative-free lubricating eye drops (artificial tears) during day, lubricating ointment at night. Hypertonic saline drops (5% NaCl) to reduce epithelial edema.
Refractory RCES: Anterior stromal puncture, phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK), or epithelial debridement with diamond burr polishing.
key_recommendations.evidence_grade: B — supported by multiple case series and retrospective cohort studies

retinal_detachment.source: AAO Preferred Practice Pattern — Posterior Vitreous Detachment, Retinal Breaks, and Lattice Degeneration, 2019; NICE Guideline NG228 2023

key_recommendations.recommendation: Retinal detachment (RD) presents classically with sudden onset of floaters, photopsia (flashes of light), and a curtain/shadow over visual field — NOT typically with sharp pain. Pain is NOT a primary feature of retinal detachment.
key_recommendations.evidence_grade: A — well-established clinical presentation from large cohort studies
key_recommendations.clinical_note: Patient's concern for retinal detachment is understandable but the pain character (sharp, microsecond) is atypical for RD. However, dilated fundus exam should still be performed after angle-closure is excluded to rule out peripheral retinal breaks or lattice degeneration.

key_recommendations.recommendation: Any patient with new-onset floaters, flashes, or visual field defect requires urgent dilated fundus examination within 24 hours. Rhegmatogenous RD is a surgical emergency.
Risk factors for RD include: myopia (RR 3.0-5.0), prior eye surgery, trauma, family history, age >50. This patient's age (54) places him in elevated risk category.

allergic_conjunctivitis.source: AAO Preferred Practice Pattern — Conjunctivitis 2018; ARIA Guidelines 2020; ACAAI Guidelines

key_recommendations.recommendation: Allergic conjunctivitis typically presents with bilateral itching, watering, redness, and chemosis — NOT with sharp unilateral pain. Sharp pain is NOT a feature of allergic conjunctivitis and should prompt evaluation for other diagnoses.
key_recommendations.clinical_note: Bilateral lacrimation may have an allergic component, but the sharp unilateral pain requires separate urgent evaluation. Allergic conjunctivitis does NOT cause the pain pattern described.

key_recommendations.recommendation: First-line treatment for allergic conjunctivitis: Topical antihistamine/mast cell stabilizer combination (olopatadine, ketotifen). Oral antihistamines for systemic symptoms. Avoid topical vasoconstrictors (tetrahydrozoline) — rebound hyperemia risk.

dry_eye_disease.source: TFOS DEWS II Report 2017; AAO Preferred Practice Pattern 2018

key_recommendations.recommendation: Paradoxical reflex tearing (excessive lacrimation) is a hallmark of dry eye disease — ocular surface desiccation triggers reflex hypersecretion from lacrimal glands. Sharp episodic pain can occur with severe dry eye or exposure keratopathy.
key_recommendations.evidence_grade: A — TFOS DEWS II systematic review
key_recommendations.clinical_note: Dry eye disease should be considered as a contributing factor to bilateral lacrimation, though it does not fully explain the sharp episodic unilateral pain.

relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.drug_pair: Timolol (topical beta-blocker) + Systemic beta-blockers (if patient is on any)
relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.mechanism: Additive systemic beta-blockade — topical timolol has significant systemic absorption (~80% via nasolacrimal duct)
relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.clinical_effect: Bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, masking of hypoglycemia symptoms
relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.management: Obtain complete medication history before prescribing. Contraindicated in asthma, COPD, bradycardia, heart block. Use betaxolol (cardioselective) if beta-blocker required in at-risk patients.

relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.mechanism: Acetazolamide displaces salicylates from protein binding; salicylates inhibit renal tubular secretion of acetazolamide
relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.clinical_effect: Increased acetazolamide toxicity (metabolic acidosis, CNS depression); salicylate toxicity
relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.management: Monitor for toxicity if both used; avoid combination in high-dose salicylate therapy

relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.mechanism: Pharmacodynamic antagonism — anticholinergics cause mydriasis, opposing pilocarpine's miotic effect
relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.clinical_effect: Reduced efficacy of pilocarpine in angle-closure treatment; risk of precipitating acute angle-closure crisis
relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.management: Identify all anticholinergic medications (antihistamines, antidepressants, antipsychotics, bladder medications). These medications can precipitate angle-closure in susceptible individuals.

relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.drug_pair: Topical antihistamines (for allergic conjunctivitis) — Anticholinergic effect
relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.mechanism: Antihistamines have anticholinergic properties causing pupillary dilation (mydriasis)
relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.clinical_effect: Can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma crisis in anatomically predisposed individuals
relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.management: DO NOT prescribe topical or systemic antihistamines until angle-closure glaucoma is definitively excluded. This is a critical prescribing safety concern for this patient.
relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.evidence_grade: A — well-established, multiple case reports and pharmacological mechanism

relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.drug_pair: Brimonidine (alpha-2 agonist) + MAO inhibitors or tricyclic antidepressants
relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.mechanism: Additive hypotensive effect; MAOIs inhibit brimonidine metabolism
relevant_medications_for_angle_closure_t.management: Contraindicated with MAOIs. Use with caution with TCAs. Obtain full medication history.
