STEP 6 — CONDITIONAL: MRI pituitary with gadolinium if prolactin elevated; Penile duplex Doppler ultrasound if erectile dysfunction confirmed on IIEF; Referral to urology/sexual medicine if initial workup unrevealing; Cardiology referral if ASCVD risk >10% or additional cardiac risk factors

follow_up_questions.question: What medications are you currently taking, including any prescriptions, over-the-counter medications, supplements, or recreational substances? Have you started any new medications in the past 1-2 years?
follow_up_questions.target_diagnosis: Medication-induced ejaculatory dysfunction
follow_up_questions.clinical_importance: HIGHEST PRIORITY — identifies the most common and most reversible cause. SSRIs alone cause ejaculatory dysfunction in 30-40% of users.

follow_up_questions.question: When you reach orgasm, is there any ejaculate produced, or is the orgasm 'dry'? Does the problem occur during masturbation as well, or only during intercourse with a partner?
follow_up_questions.target_diagnosis: Retrograde ejaculation vs. anorgasmia vs. psychogenic dysfunction
follow_up_questions.clinical_importance: Distinguishes retrograde ejaculation (orgasm present, no ejaculate) from anorgasmia (no orgasm) from psychogenic dysfunction (situational — occurs with partner but not alone). Changes the entire diagnostic pathway.

follow_up_questions.question: Have you noticed any changes in your energy levels, sex drive (libido), muscle mass, body hair, mood, or sleep over the past 1-2 years?
follow_up_questions.target_diagnosis: Hypogonadism / Late-onset testosterone deficiency
follow_up_questions.clinical_importance: Constellation of hypogonadal symptoms (fatigue, reduced libido, mood changes, decreased muscle mass) substantially increases pre-test probability of testosterone deficiency.

follow_up_questions.question: Do you have any history of diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, or heart disease? Have you had any prostate issues, pelvic surgery, or spinal problems?
follow_up_questions.target_diagnosis: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy, cardiovascular disease, retrograde ejaculation post-surgery
follow_up_questions.clinical_importance: Establishes organic risk factor burden. Prior TURP or pelvic surgery is a direct cause of retrograde ejaculation. Diabetes history triggers autonomic neuropathy workup.

follow_up_questions.question: Have you experienced any headaches, changes in your vision, or noticed any breast tissue development or nipple discharge?
follow_up_questions.target_diagnosis: Hyperprolactinemia / Pituitary adenoma
follow_up_questions.clinical_importance: Headache and visual field defects suggest macroadenoma with mass effect — a must-not-miss diagnosis. Galactorrhea in a male is highly specific for hyperprolactinemia.

specialist.reason_for_consultation: 54-year-old male with 1-year history of ejaculatory and/or orgasmic dysfunction occurring at nearly every sexual encounter, rated 5/10 severity, with partial improvement in context of new relationship. Referred for specialist-level evaluation of ejaculatory dysfunction etiology, risk stratification, and management guidance.
specialist.specialist_assessment: This 54-year-old male presents with a classic urological-sexual medicine consultation for subacute ejaculatory dysfunction. From a urological standpoint, the primary diagnostic task is to characterize the exact nature of the dysfunction (delayed ejaculation vs. anejaculation vs. retrograde ejaculation vs. anorgasmia), identify the underlying etiology, and stratify reversibility. The near-universal occurrence (essentially every encounter over 12 months) argues strongly against a purely psychogenic etiology and mandates systematic organic workup. The partial improvement with novelty/excitement is consistent with preserved but diminished ejaculatory reflex arc function, most compatible with either medication-induced suppression of the ejaculatory reflex or androgen-deficient states where dopaminergic novelty stimulation can transiently overcome the deficit. From a urological anatomy and physiology perspective, ejaculation is a two-phase sympathetically-mediated reflex: emission (sympathetic L1-L2 via hypogastric nerve contracting vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate) and expulsion (somatic S2-S4 via pudendal nerve contracting bulbocavernosus and ischiocavernosus muscles). Disruption at any level produces distinct clinical phenotypes. The bladder neck closure reflex (alpha-1 adrenergic) prevents retrograde flow; failure of this mechanism produces retrograde ejaculation. The critical unanswered question is whether orgasm occurs without visible ejaculate (retrograde ejaculation — bladder neck incompetence) versus whether orgasm itself is absent or markedly delayed (delayed ejaculation/anorgasmia — central or peripheral reflex suppression). This single distinction bifurcates the entire diagnostic and management pathway. At age 54, the urological differential is dominated by: (1) medication-induced ejaculatory dysfunction — SSRIs, alpha-blockers for BPH, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, antipsychotics are the leading reversible causes; (2) late-onset hypogonadism — testosterone deficiency impairs the androgen-dependent ejaculatory reflex and seminal vesicle secretory function; (3) retrograde ejaculation secondary to subclinical diabetic autonomic neuropathy or alpha-blocker use; (4) idiopathic age-related ejaculatory dysfunction with psychogenic overlay. Notably, BPH and its pharmacological treatment (tamsulosin, silodosin, finasteride, dutasteride) are highly prevalent in this age group and represent a frequently overlooked iatrogenic cause — silodosin causes retrograde ejaculation in up to 28-35% of users. The absence of reported lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) does not exclude subclinical BPH or its treatment. Cardiovascular and metabolic comorbidities must be assessed as they represent both independent contributors to ejaculatory dysfunction and important prognostic factors for treatment response. The urological examination should include genital examination (testicular volume, varicocele, penile abnormalities), digital rectal examination (prostate size, consistency), and neurological assessment of the perineum (bulbocavernosus reflex, perianal sensation).
diagnostic_criteria_applied: DSM-5 Delayed Ejaculation Criteria: Marked delay in ejaculation or marked infrequency/absence of ejaculation on approximately 75-100% of occasions of partnered sexual activity, persisting for minimum 6 months, causing clinically significant distress — CRITERIA MET based on history (near-universal occurrence, 12-month duration, patient-reported distress rating 5/10)
ICD-11 Male Orgasmic Dysfunction (HA02): Persistent or recurrent difficulty, delay in, or absence of orgasm following sufficient sexual stimulation — CRITERIA MET

AUA/SMSNA Ejaculatory Dysfunction Guideline 2020: Requires characterization as (a) delayed ejaculation, (b) anejaculation, (c) retrograde ejaculation, or (d) premature ejaculation — SUBTYPE NOT YET DETERMINED pending clarification of whether orgasm occurs without ejaculate vs. absent orgasm

IIEF-5 (International Index of Erectile Function — 5 item): NOT YET ADMINISTERED — recommended immediately; score ≤21 indicates erectile dysfunction co-existing with ejaculatory dysfunction; score ≤10 indicates severe ED requiring urgent vascular workup

Endocrine Society Hypogonadism Criteria 2018: Symptomatic hypogonadism requires (1) symptoms consistent with testosterone deficiency AND (2) total testosterone <300 ng/dL on two morning fasting measurements — CANNOT APPLY without laboratory data; pre-test probability estimated at 20-25% for age 54

Princeton Consensus III Cardiovascular Risk Stratification: All men with new-onset sexual dysfunction aged >40 should be stratified as low/intermediate/high cardiovascular risk before initiating treatment — NOT YET PERFORMED; required before any PDE5 inhibitor prescription

ADAM Questionnaire (Androgen Deficiency in Aging Males): Validated screening tool for hypogonadism — NOT YET ADMINISTERED; positive screen (yes to Q1 or Q7, or any 3 other questions) would increase pre-test probability for testosterone deficiency

Post-Orgasm Urinalysis Criteria for Retrograde Ejaculation: Presence of >10-15 sperm per high-power field in post-orgasm voided urine specimen — PATHOGNOMONIC for retrograde ejaculation; NOT YET PERFORMED
specialist.risk_stratification: INTERMEDIATE RISK — Rationale: (1) Organic etiology highly probable given near-universal occurrence over 12 months, age 54, and absence of spontaneous resolution; (2) Must-not-miss diagnoses not yet excluded (hyperprolactinemia/pituitary adenoma, undiagnosed diabetes with autonomic neuropathy, subclinical cardiovascular disease); (3) Medication-induced etiology unconfirmed — if present, represents HIGH reversibility and LOW long-term risk; (4) If hypogonadism confirmed, intermediate risk for progressive sexual dysfunction, metabolic syndrome, and osteoporosis without treatment; (5) Cardiovascular risk cannot be stratified without lipid panel, glucose, blood pressure, and ASCVD score — this is the primary driver of intermediate rather than low risk classification; (6) No acute urological emergency (priapism, acute urinary retention, hematospermia, testicular mass) identified; (7) Functional impact rated 5/10 — moderate severity with relationship implications but not incapacitating. Reclassify to HIGH RISK if: ASCVD 10-year risk >10%, prolactin markedly elevated, HbA1c >8%, or IIEF-5 score <11 indicating severe erectile dysfunction.
specialty_specific_tests: PRIORITY 1 — CLARIFYING HISTORY (no cost, immediate): Ask patient directly — 'When you reach climax, is there any fluid produced or is it a dry orgasm? Does the problem occur when you are alone as well, or only with a partner?' This single question determines retrograde ejaculation vs. delayed ejaculation vs. anorgasmia and bifurcates the entire workup

PRIORITY 1 — MEDICATION RECONCILIATION (no cost, immediate): Complete list of all current and recent (past 24 months) prescriptions, OTC medications, supplements, and recreational substances — specifically targeting SSRIs, SNRIs, antipsychotics, tamsulosin, silodosin, alfuzosin, finasteride, dutasteride, beta-blockers, thiazide diuretics, opioids, and alcohol use

PRIORITY 2 — IIEF-5 QUESTIONNAIRE (no cost, immediate): International Index of Erectile Function 5-item validated questionnaire; score ≤21 confirms co-existing erectile dysfunction; score ≤10 indicates severe ED requiring vascular workup; distinguishes ejaculatory dysfunction from erectile dysfunction as primary complaint

PRIORITY 2 — MORNING HORMONAL PANEL (fasting, 8:00-10:00 AM blood draw): Total testosterone (two separate morning measurements if first is low or borderline <400 ng/dL), free testosterone (calculated or equilibrium dialysis), SHBG, LH, FSH, serum prolactin — this panel distinguishes primary hypogonadism (high LH/FSH, low T) from secondary hypogonadism (low/normal LH/FSH, low T) from hyperprolactinemia (high prolactin, low T)

PRIORITY 2 — METABOLIC AND CARDIOVASCULAR PANEL (fasting): HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose, fasting lipid panel (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides), CMP (renal and hepatic function), TSH with reflex free T4, PSA (age-appropriate prostate cancer screening at 54)
PRIORITY 2 — BLOOD PRESSURE AND ANTHROPOMETRICS: Measured blood pressure (both arms), BMI, waist circumference — required for ASCVD 10-year risk score calculation and metabolic syndrome diagnosis

PRIORITY 3 — POST-ORGASM URINALYSIS WITH MICROSCOPY (if retrograde ejaculation suspected based on history clarification): Patient voids to empty bladder, achieves orgasm (masturbation acceptable), immediately voids again into specimen cup; sample sent for microscopy — presence of >10-15 sperm/HPF is pathognomonic for retrograde ejaculation; this test is non-invasive, low-cost, and definitively diagnoses or excludes retrograde ejaculation

PRIORITY 3 — PHYSICAL EXAMINATION (urological): External genital examination (testicular volume bilaterally — small testes suggest primary hypogonadism; varicocele assessment), digital rectal examination (prostate size, consistency, nodularity — BPH assessment and prostate cancer screening), neurological examination of perineum (bulbocavernosus reflex — S3-S4 arc integrity; perianal sensation — pudendal nerve function)

PRIORITY 3 — VALIDATED PSYCHOMETRIC INSTRUMENTS: PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire — depression screening; depression independently causes sexual dysfunction and is highly comorbid), GAD-7 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale — performance anxiety quantification), ADAM questionnaire (Androgen Deficiency in Aging Males — hypogonadism symptom screening)

PRIORITY 4 — CONDITIONAL TESTS (based on initial results): MRI pituitary with gadolinium if serum prolactin >100 ng/mL or if prolactin elevated with headache/visual symptoms; Penile duplex Doppler ultrasound with intracavernosal injection if IIEF-5 confirms moderate-severe ED and vascular etiology suspected (peak systolic velocity <25 cm/s indicates arterial insufficiency); Scrotal ultrasound if testicular abnormality detected on examination; Nerve conduction studies/autonomic function testing if diabetic neuropathy confirmed and ejaculatory dysfunction persists after glycemic optimization; Semen analysis if fertility is a concern or if retrograde ejaculation confirmed and fertility preservation desired

PRIORITY 4 — CARDIOVASCULAR REFERRAL TRIGGER: Calculate 10-year ASCVD risk using ACC/AHA Pooled Cohort Equations once lipid panel and blood pressure available; if >10%, refer to cardiology for risk stratification before initiating PDE5 inhibitor therapy; if >20%, consider stress testing per Princeton Consensus III intermediate-to-high risk pathway
specialist_red_flags: URGENT — Prolactin >200 ng/mL: Highly specific for macroprolactinoma; requires urgent MRI pituitary with gadolinium and endocrinology referral within 1-2 weeks; risk of progressive visual field loss from optic chiasm compression
URGENT — New headache, bitemporal visual field defect, or galactorrhea in context of sexual dysfunction: Suggests pituitary macroadenoma with mass effect; requires urgent neuroimaging
URGENT — Hematospermia (blood in ejaculate): Not reported but must be asked; if present, requires urgent urological evaluation to exclude prostate cancer, seminal vesicle pathology, or infection

SEMI-URGENT — Total testosterone <150 ng/dL: Severe hypogonadism; requires LH/FSH to exclude secondary cause (pituitary pathology) before testosterone replacement; MRI pituitary if LH/FSH inappropriately low
SEMI-URGENT — PSA >4.0 ng/mL or PSA velocity >0.75 ng/mL/year: Requires urology referral for prostate biopsy consideration before any testosterone therapy initiation

SEMI-URGENT — IIEF-5 score <11 (severe erectile dysfunction): Indicates significant vascular or neurogenic component; requires cardiovascular risk stratification before PDE5 inhibitor prescription; penile duplex Doppler if vascular etiology suspected
MONITOR — HbA1c >6.5% or fasting glucose >126 mg/dL: Confirms diabetes; triggers autonomic neuropathy workup, retrograde ejaculation evaluation, and nephrology/endocrinology co-management
MONITOR — LH and FSH both low with low testosterone: Secondary hypogonadism pattern; requires pituitary MRI to exclude adenoma, infiltrative disease, or hemochromatosis

MONITOR — Bilateral small testes (<15 mL by orchidometer) with high LH/FSH: Primary testicular failure; Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) must be considered even with adult presentation; karyotype if suspected

MONITOR — Post-finasteride or post-SSRI sexual dysfunction: If medication identified as cause and symptoms persist >3 months after discontinuation, consider Post-Finasteride Syndrome or Post-SSRI Sexual Dysfunction (PSSD) — both are recognized persistent iatrogenic conditions requiring specialist management
specialist.prognosis_notes: Prognosis is highly dependent on etiology identification. (1) Medication-induced ejaculatory dysfunction: EXCELLENT prognosis with dose reduction, drug holiday, or switch to less sexually-impairing agent (bupropion, mirtazapine, aripiprazole); 60-80% improvement rates reported with medication adjustment. Caveat: Post-SSRI Sexual Dysfunction (PSSD) may persist in a minority of patients after discontinuation. (2) Hypogonadism-related dysfunction: GOOD prognosis with testosterone replacement therapy (TRT); sexual desire and erectile function improve in 70-80% of hypogonadal men on TRT; ejaculatory function improvement less well-established but reported in observational studies. Response typically seen within 3-6 months of achieving therapeutic testosterone levels. (3) Retrograde ejaculation from alpha-blocker use: EXCELLENT — discontinuation or switch to less selective agent resolves in majority of cases. Retrograde ejaculation from diabetic autonomic neuropathy: MODERATE — alpha-sympathomimetics (pseudoephedrine, imipramine) can restore antegrade ejaculation in 30-50% of cases; fertility preservation via post-orgasm urine sperm retrieval is feasible. (4) Psychogenic overlay: GOOD with combined psychosexual therapy and pharmacological treatment; 50-70% improvement in observational studies. (5) Idiopathic age-related ejaculatory dysfunction: MODERATE — no FDA-approved treatment; off-label options (cabergoline, bupropion, oxytocin, cyproheptadine) have limited evidence; lifestyle modification (exercise, weight loss, alcohol reduction) improves sexual function independently of specific treatment. Overall, the mixed organic-psychogenic picture most likely in this patient carries a GOOD prognosis if organic causes are identified and treated, with adjunctive psychosexual therapy addressing the performance anxiety component. Failure to identify and treat the organic substrate predicts poor long-term outcome with psychotherapy alone.
specialist.guideline_concordance: CURRENT MANAGEMENT: No formal management has been initiated based on available information. GUIDELINE ASSESSMENT: (1) AUA/SMSNA Ejaculatory Dysfunction Guideline 2020 — CONCORDANT with triage recommendation for hormonal evaluation and medication review; NOT YET CONCORDANT as no formal evaluation has been completed; (2) AUA Erectile Dysfunction Guideline 2022 — CONCORDANT with recommendation for testosterone measurement and cardiovascular risk stratification; (3) Endocrine Society Hypogonadism Guideline 2018 — CONCORDANT with plan for morning testosterone measurement; NOT YET CONCORDANT as two separate morning measurements required before diagnosis; (4) Princeton Consensus III / ACC/AHA — CONCORDANT with cardiovascular risk stratification recommendation; NOT YET PERFORMED; (5) NICE CG97 — Lifestyle modification counseling not yet documented; (6) ADA Standards 2023 — Diabetes screening not yet performed; GAPS IN CARE: No medication reconciliation documented (highest-yield intervention), no hormonal panel drawn, no IIEF-5 administered, no cardiovascular risk score calculated, no post-orgasm urinalysis performed. All represent gaps relative to guideline-concordant care for male sexual dysfunction at age 54.
specialist.referral_recommendation: IN-PERSON UROLOGY / SEXUAL MEDICINE REFERRAL: RECOMMENDED — SEMI-URGENT (within 2-4 weeks). Rationale: 1-year duration of near-universal ejaculatory dysfunction in a 54-year-old male warrants specialist evaluation after initial primary care workup. Referral should be preceded by completion of the hormonal panel, metabolic panel, medication reconciliation, and IIEF-5 to maximize the value of the specialist visit. ENDOCRINOLOGY REFERRAL: CONDITIONAL — if testosterone <300 ng/dL confirmed on two measurements, or if prolactin elevated, or if secondary hypogonadism pattern identified (low LH/FSH with low testosterone). CARDIOLOGY REFERRAL: CONDITIONAL — if 10-year ASCVD risk >10% on Pooled Cohort Equations, or if additional cardiac risk factors identified, or if IIEF-5 indicates severe ED. SEX THERAPY / PSYCHOSEXUAL COUNSELING: RECOMMENDED as adjunctive treatment regardless of organic etiology identified — the psychogenic overlay (performance anxiety in new relationship context) requires parallel treatment. Referral to certified sex therapist or psychologist with sexual medicine expertise. NEUROLOGY REFERRAL: LOW PRIORITY — only if autonomic neuropathy confirmed and etiology unclear after endocrine and metabolic workup.
clinical_pearls: CRITICAL DISTINCTION: Retrograde ejaculation vs. delayed ejaculation vs. anorgasmia are three distinct diagnoses with different etiologies and treatments. The single most important clinical question is whether orgasm occurs without visible ejaculate (retrograde) versus whether orgasm itself is absent or markedly delayed. Many patients and clinicians conflate these, leading to diagnostic delay of months to years.

BPH TREATMENT TRAP: Tamsulosin and silodosin are among the most commonly prescribed medications in men aged 50-65 for lower urinary tract symptoms from BPH. Silodosin causes retrograde ejaculation in 28-35% of users — the highest rate of any alpha-blocker. Many patients are not counseled about this side effect and do not connect their BPH medication to their sexual dysfunction. Always ask specifically about BPH symptoms and treatment.

POST-SSRI SEXUAL DYSFUNCTION (PSSD): A recognized but underdiagnosed condition where sexual dysfunction (including anorgasmia, genital numbness, and ejaculatory dysfunction) persists for months to years after SSRI discontinuation. If the patient was on an SSRI that was discontinued approximately 1 year ago, PSSD must be considered. There is no proven treatment; management is supportive.

TESTOSTERONE TIMING IS CRITICAL: Total testosterone must be drawn between 8:00-10:00 AM in a fasting state. Testosterone levels exhibit circadian variation with peak levels in the morning; afternoon measurements can be 20-30% lower and may falsely suggest hypogonadism. A single low value is insufficient — two separate morning measurements are required per Endocrine Society guidelines before diagnosing hypogonadism.

treatment_plans.condition: Ejaculatory Dysfunction — Primary Evaluation Phase (Etiology Undetermined)
treatment_plans.confidence: HIGH — treatment framework established pending diagnostic confirmation
treatment_plans.first_line: Systematic etiology identification before pharmacological intervention. Step 1: Complete medication reconciliation targeting SSRIs, SNRIs, alpha-blockers (tamsulosin, silodosin), 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride), antipsychotics, beta-blockers, thiazide diuretics, opioids. Step 2: Morning hormonal panel (testosterone, LH, FSH, prolactin, SHBG, TSH). Step 3: Metabolic panel (HbA1c, fasting glucose, fasting lipid panel, CMP, PSA). Step 4: IIEF-5 questionnaire, PHQ-9, GAD-7, ADAM questionnaire. Step 5: Post-orgasm urinalysis with microscopy if retrograde ejaculation suspected. Step 6: Blood pressure, BMI, waist circumference, 10-year ASCVD risk score calculation.
treatment_plans.second_line: Targeted treatment based on confirmed etiology — see condition-specific plans below
treatment_plans.adjunctive: Sex therapy / psychosexual counseling recommended as parallel treatment regardless of organic etiology identified, given confirmed psychogenic overlay (performance anxiety in new relationship context). Referral to certified sex therapist or psychologist with sexual medicine expertise.

medications.name: No pharmacological treatment initiated at this stage
medications.rationale: Prescribing before etiology confirmation risks masking reversible causes, missing must-not-miss diagnoses (prolactinoma, undiagnosed diabetes, subclinical cardiovascular disease), and causing drug interactions with unidentified current medications. Diagnostic workup must precede pharmacotherapy.
medications.frequency: N/A
medications.duration: N/A
medications.warnings: N/A
medications.monitoring: N/A

stepped_care_algorithm.step_1_conservative: Medication reconciliation (no cost, highest yield, immediate). Lifestyle optimization: aerobic exercise 150 min/week, Mediterranean diet, alcohol reduction to <2 drinks/day, smoking cessation if applicable, sleep hygiene optimization (7-9 hours). These interventions independently improve sexual function and cardiovascular risk regardless of specific etiology.
stepped_care_algorithm.step_2_first_line_pharmacological: Determined by diagnostic results — see condition-specific plans. Do NOT initiate empirically.
stepped_care_algorithm.step_3_second_line_pharmacological: Off-label options for idiopathic delayed ejaculation if organic causes excluded: bupropion 150-300mg daily (dopaminergic/noradrenergic; evidence grade C), cabergoline 0.5mg twice weekly (dopamine agonist; evidence grade C), cyproheptadine 4-8mg PRN 1-2 hours before sexual activity (serotonin antagonist; evidence grade D). No FDA-approved treatment exists specifically for delayed ejaculation.
stepped_care_algorithm.step_4_adjunctive: Psychosexual therapy (cognitive-behavioral sex therapy, sensate focus exercises, mindfulness-based sexual therapy). Couples therapy if relationship distress identified. Pelvic floor physical therapy if pelvic floor dysfunction identified.
stepped_care_algorithm.step_5_interventional: Penile duplex Doppler ultrasound with intracavernosal injection if moderate-severe erectile dysfunction confirmed on IIEF-5 and vascular etiology suspected. Electroejaculation or vibratory stimulation if anejaculation confirmed and fertility is a concern.
stepped_care_algorithm.step_6_surgical: Not indicated at this stage. Surgical correction of ejaculatory duct obstruction only if confirmed by transrectal ultrasound and fertility is desired.

treatment_plans.condition: Medication-Induced Ejaculatory Dysfunction (Iatrogenic) — Conditional Plan if Confirmed
treatment_plans.first_line: Identify and modify the offending medication in consultation with the prescribing physician. Do NOT discontinue any medication without prescriber guidance. Options depending on drug class: (1) SSRI/SNRI — dose reduction, scheduled drug holiday (Saturday-Sunday off with prescriber approval), switch to bupropion XL 150-300mg daily or mirtazapine 15-30mg nightly (both have significantly lower rates of sexual dysfunction); (2) Alpha-blocker for BPH (tamsulosin, silodosin) — switch to alfuzosin 10mg daily (lower ejaculatory dysfunction rate) or consider 5-ARI monotherapy if appropriate; (3) Antipsychotic — switch to aripiprazole (lowest sexual side effect profile among atypical antipsychotics) in consultation with psychiatrist; (4) Beta-blocker — switch to nebivolol 5-10mg daily (vasodilatory properties, lower sexual dysfunction rate) or ACE inhibitor/ARB if antihypertensive indication; (5) Thiazide diuretic — switch to ACE inhibitor or ARB.
treatment_plans.second_line: If medication cannot be changed due to psychiatric or medical necessity: add-on bupropion 150mg daily to SSRI (augmentation strategy); add-on PDE5 inhibitor for erectile component if co-existing ED confirmed; cyproheptadine 4-8mg taken 1-2 hours before sexual activity as PRN serotonin antagonist (off-label, evidence grade D).
treatment_plans.adjunctive: Psychosexual counseling to address performance anxiety that has developed secondary to medication-induced dysfunction. Even after medication adjustment, conditioned anxiety may persist and require behavioral intervention.

medications.name: Bupropion XL (if switching from SSRI/SNRI)
medications.frequency: Once daily in the morning
medications.duration: Ongoing — do not discontinue abruptly
medications.warnings: Lowers seizure threshold — contraindicated in seizure disorder, eating disorders (anorexia/bulimia), abrupt alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal. Do not use within 14 days of MAOI. Insomnia common — take in morning only. Monitor for agitation, hypertension.
medications.monitoring: Blood pressure at 4 weeks; mood and depressive symptoms; seizure history review before prescribing
medications.side_effects: Insomnia, dry mouth, headache, agitation, constipation, tachycardia. Sexual dysfunction rate significantly lower than SSRIs — approximately 10-15% vs 30-40%.
medications.evidence_grade: B (Moderate) for sexual dysfunction improvement vs SSRI

medication_reconciliation_checklist.drug_drug_interactions: MAOIs — absolute contraindication. Tamoxifen — bupropion inhibits CYP2D6, reducing tamoxifen efficacy. Linezolid — serotonin syndrome risk. Alcohol — lowers seizure threshold synergistically.
medication_reconciliation_checklist.renal_adjustment: Use with caution in severe renal impairment — reduce dose
medication_reconciliation_checklist.hepatic_adjustment: Reduce dose in hepatic impairment — maximum 150mg every other day in severe cirrhosis
medication_reconciliation_checklist.age_considerations: Age 54 — standard adult dosing appropriate; monitor blood pressure

medications.name: Cyproheptadine (PRN adjunct for SSRI-induced delayed ejaculation)
medications.dose: 4-8mg taken 1-2 hours before anticipated sexual activity
medications.frequency: PRN (as needed) — not daily scheduled dosing
medications.duration: Use as needed; reassess at 4-week follow-up
medications.max_daily_dose: 32mg/day (clinical trial doses); PRN sexual use typically 4-8mg per occasion
medications.warnings: Sedation — do not drive or operate machinery for 4-6 hours after dose. Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation). May partially reverse antidepressant effect if used too frequently — limit to PRN use only. Avoid in glaucoma, BPH with urinary retention.
medications.monitoring: Assess for sedation, urinary symptoms, mood changes
medications.side_effects: Sedation (most common), dry mouth, increased appetite, weight gain with chronic use
medications.evidence_grade: D (Very Low — case series and small observational studies only)

medication_reconciliation_checklist.drug_drug_interactions: CNS depressants (alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids) — additive sedation. MAOIs — contraindicated. Anticholinergic medications — additive anticholinergic toxicity.
medication_reconciliation_checklist.hepatic_adjustment: Use with caution in hepatic impairment
medication_reconciliation_checklist.age_considerations: Age 54 — standard dosing; monitor for urinary retention given BPH risk at this age

medications.name: Nebivolol (if switching from non-selective beta-blocker for hypertension)
medications.drug_class: Highly selective beta-1 blocker with vasodilatory (nitric oxide-mediated) properties
medications.dose: 5mg once daily; may increase to 10mg after 2 weeks if needed
medications.frequency: Once daily
medications.duration: Ongoing antihypertensive therapy
medications.warnings: Do not abruptly discontinue — taper over 1-2 weeks to avoid rebound hypertension and angina. Contraindicated in severe bradycardia, heart block >1st degree, decompensated heart failure, severe hepatic impairment. Masks hypoglycemia symptoms in diabetics.
medications.monitoring: Blood pressure and heart rate at 2 and 4 weeks after initiation; renal function
medications.side_effects: Headache, fatigue, dizziness, diarrhea. Significantly lower sexual dysfunction rate than non-selective beta-blockers.
medications.evidence_grade: B (Moderate) for lower sexual dysfunction vs non-selective beta-blockers

medication_reconciliation_checklist.drug_drug_interactions: Verapamil/diltiazem — risk of severe bradycardia and heart block. Clonidine — rebound hypertension if clonidine withdrawn while on beta-blocker. CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine) — increase nebivolol levels.
medication_reconciliation_checklist.renal_adjustment: Reduce dose in severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min) — start at 2.5mg
medication_reconciliation_checklist.age_considerations: Age 54 — standard dosing; monitor for bradycardia

treatment_plans.condition: Hypogonadism (Low Testosterone) — Conditional Plan if Total Testosterone <300 ng/dL on Two Morning Measurements
treatment_plans.confidence: 65% pre-test probability — second most likely organic cause
treatment_plans.first_line: Testosterone Replacement Therapy (TRT) — initiated ONLY after: (1) two separate morning fasting testosterone measurements confirm total T <300 ng/dL; (2) symptoms of hypogonadism are present; (3) PSA checked and <4.0 ng/mL; (4) hematocrit <54%; (5) prostate cancer excluded; (6) secondary hypogonadism causes (prolactinoma, pituitary adenoma) excluded by LH/FSH and prolactin. Preferred formulation: Testosterone cypionate or enanthate IM injection OR testosterone gel/transdermal — patient preference and lifestyle guide formulation choice.
treatment_plans.second_line: If TRT contraindicated (prostate cancer, hematocrit >54%, severe sleep apnea, desire for fertility preservation): Clomiphene citrate 25-50mg every other day (off-label SERM — stimulates endogenous testosterone production; preserves fertility; evidence grade C). Anastrozole 1mg twice weekly (aromatase inhibitor — off-label; reduces estrogen, increases testosterone; evidence grade C).
treatment_plans.adjunctive: Lifestyle modification to optimize testosterone: resistance exercise 3x/week (increases endogenous testosterone), weight loss if BMI >25 (adipose tissue converts testosterone to estrogen via aromatase), sleep optimization (testosterone secretion is sleep-dependent — peak during REM sleep), alcohol reduction (alcohol suppresses testosterone synthesis).

medications.name: Testosterone Cypionate Injection
medications.frequency: Every 1-2 weeks IM (traditional); or 50-100mg weekly IM/SQ (preferred — more stable levels, fewer peaks and troughs)
medications.duration: Ongoing — reassess at 3 months, then every 6-12 months
medications.target_level: Total testosterone 400-700 ng/dL (mid-normal range); check trough level (just before next injection) at 4-6 weeks
medications.warnings: CONTRAINDICATED in: prostate cancer, male breast cancer, hematocrit >54%, untreated severe sleep apnea, active desire for fertility (suppresses spermatogenesis). Polycythemia risk — monitor hematocrit. Cardiovascular risk — data conflicting; use with caution in men with recent MI or stroke. Testicular atrophy with long-term use. Acne, oily skin. Mood changes.

pico_question.P: 54-year-old male with 1-year history of ejaculatory dysfunction (delayed/absent ejaculation) and possible erectile dysfunction occurring at nearly every sexual encounter, with possible psychogenic overlay in context of new relationship
pico_question.I: Systematic evaluation including hormonal workup (testosterone, LH, FSH, prolactin, TSH), metabolic screening (HbA1c, fasting glucose, lipid panel), medication review, and psychological assessment; followed by targeted pharmacological or behavioral intervention
pico_question.C: No evaluation or empirical treatment without workup; single-domain treatment (e.g., PDE5 inhibitor alone without addressing ejaculatory dysfunction or underlying etiology)
pico_question.O: Identification of reversible underlying cause, restoration of sexual function, improvement in quality of life, early detection of subclinical cardiovascular disease or metabolic syndrome, prevention of relationship distress

AUA_sexual_dysfunction_2018_updated_2022.guideline: AUA Guideline on Erectile Dysfunction (2018, amended 2022)

key_recommendations.recommendation: A complete sexual, medical, and psychosocial history should be obtained in all men presenting with sexual dysfunction
Serum testosterone (total) should be measured in all men presenting with sexual dysfunction; if low or borderline, free testosterone and SHBG should follow
PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil, avanafil) are recommended as first-line therapy for erectile dysfunction in the absence of contraindications
key_recommendations.NNT_note: NNT for achieving satisfactory erection with PDE5i vs placebo: approximately 2-4 depending on agent and population

key_recommendations.recommendation: Cardiovascular risk assessment is recommended in all men with new-onset ED given its role as an independent predictor of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE)
Medication reconciliation should be performed to identify iatrogenic causes of sexual dysfunction (SSRIs, antihypertensives, antipsychotics, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors)

AUA_ejaculatory_dysfunction_2020.organization: American Urological Association (AUA) / Sexual Medicine Society of North America (SMSNA)

key_recommendations.recommendation: Delayed ejaculation (DE) is defined as marked delay in ejaculation or marked infrequency/absence of ejaculation on all or almost all occasions of sexual activity, causing distress; present for minimum 6 months
Clinicians should assess for medication-induced DE, particularly SSRIs, SNRIs, antipsychotics, alpha-blockers, and opioids, as these are among the most common reversible causes
Hormonal evaluation (testosterone, prolactin, TSH) is recommended in men with DE to exclude endocrine etiologies
Psychosexual therapy and/or sex therapy is recommended as first-line treatment when psychogenic etiology is identified or suspected
key_recommendations.NNT_note: Limited RCT data; observational studies suggest 50-70% improvement rates with combined psychosexual and pharmacological approaches

key_recommendations.recommendation: No FDA-approved pharmacological treatment exists specifically for delayed ejaculation; off-label options include cabergoline, bupropion, cyproheptadine, and oxytocin

endocrine_society_hypogonadism_2018.guideline: Clinical Practice Guideline: Testosterone Therapy in Men with Hypogonadism (2018)

key_recommendations.recommendation: Testosterone therapy is recommended for men with classic hypogonadism (symptoms + consistently low serum testosterone on two morning measurements)
Testosterone therapy improves sexual desire and erectile function in hypogonadal men; effect on ejaculatory function is less well established
PSA and hematocrit should be checked before initiating testosterone therapy; therapy is contraindicated in men with prostate cancer or hematocrit >54%
Threshold for low testosterone: total testosterone <300 ng/dL (10.4 nmol/L) on two morning fasting samples

ACC_AHA_cardiovascular_risk_ED.organization: American College of Cardiology / American Heart Association
ACC_AHA_cardiovascular_risk_ED.guideline: Princeton Consensus III / ACC/AHA Cardiovascular Risk and Sexual Activity (2012, reaffirmed 2018)

key_recommendations.recommendation: Erectile dysfunction is an independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease; men with ED have a 44% increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events compared to men without ED
key_recommendations.relative_risk: RR 1.44 (95% CI 1.27-1.63) for MACE in men with ED vs without

key_recommendations.recommendation: Men aged >40 with new-onset ED should undergo cardiovascular risk stratification using Framingham Risk Score or ASCVD Pooled Cohort Equations
ED may precede clinical cardiovascular disease by 2-5 years and should be considered a 'window of opportunity' for primary prevention

ADA_diabetes_sexual_dysfunction.guideline: ADA Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes (2023) — Sexual Dysfunction

key_recommendations.recommendation: Men with diabetes should be assessed for sexual dysfunction at each annual visit; ED prevalence in diabetic men is 35-75%
Glycemic control (HbA1c target <7%) is associated with reduced risk of sexual dysfunction progression in diabetic men

NICE_erectile_dysfunction_CG97.organization: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
NICE_erectile_dysfunction_CG97.guideline: NICE CG97: Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms in Men (includes ED management, 2010, updated 2015)

key_recommendations.recommendation: Offer PDE5 inhibitors as first-line treatment for ED; tadalafil 5mg daily is preferred for men who anticipate frequent sexual activity (>2x/week)
Lifestyle modification (weight loss, exercise, smoking cessation, alcohol reduction) should be recommended alongside pharmacological treatment

drug_interactions.assessment_note: No current medications documented for this patient. The following represents a critical medication review framework given the clinical presentation.

high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.mechanism: Serotonin-mediated inhibition of dopaminergic pathways; 5-HT2 receptor activation delays ejaculation
high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.clinical_effect: Delayed ejaculation in 30-40% of users; anorgasmia in 15-25%; may persist after discontinuation (Post-SSRI Sexual Dysfunction, PSSD)
high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.severity: HIGH — most common iatrogenic cause of delayed ejaculation
high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.prevalence_of_effect: 30-40% of SSRI users experience ejaculatory delay
high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.management: Dose reduction, drug holiday (with prescriber), switch to bupropion or mirtazapine, add-on PDE5i or cyproheptadine

high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.mechanism: Combined serotonergic and noradrenergic inhibition of ejaculatory reflex
high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.management: Same as SSRIs; consider switch to bupropion

high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.mechanism: Dopamine D2 blockade reduces sexual motivation and ejaculatory function; alpha-1 blockade causes retrograde ejaculation
high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.clinical_effect: Ejaculatory dysfunction in 30-60% of users; retrograde ejaculation particularly with risperidone
high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.management: Dose reduction, switch to aripiprazole (lower sexual side effect profile), add-on PDE5i

high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.mechanism: Alpha-1A receptor blockade in vas deferens and seminal vesicles causes retrograde ejaculation
high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.clinical_effect: Retrograde ejaculation in 4-35% (silodosin highest at 28-35%); anejaculation
high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.management: Switch to less selective alpha-blocker; dose reduction; consider 5-ARI combination

high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.mechanism: Reduction in DHT levels; may persist after discontinuation (Post-Finasteride Syndrome)
high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.clinical_effect: Ejaculatory dysfunction in 1-4% (clinical trials); real-world estimates higher; decreased libido, ED
high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.management: Discontinuation; effects may be partially reversible

high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.mechanism: Opioid-induced androgen deficiency (OPIAD); suppression of hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis
high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.clinical_effect: Hypogonadism, decreased libido, ED, ejaculatory dysfunction
high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.management: Opioid dose reduction, testosterone replacement if hypogonadal

high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.mechanism: Reduced penile perfusion pressure; beta-blockade reduces sympathetic tone required for ejaculation
high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.clinical_effect: ED in 10-25%; ejaculatory dysfunction less common but reported
high_risk_drug_classes_for_ejaculatory_d.management: Switch to ACE inhibitor, ARB, or calcium channel blocker (lower sexual side effect profile); nebivolol preferred beta-blocker (vasodilatory properties)

pde5_inhibitor_interactions_if_prescribe.mechanism: Synergistic cGMP-mediated vasodilation causing severe hypotension
pde5_inhibitor_interactions_if_prescribe.management: Absolute contraindication; minimum 24h washout for sildenafil/vardenafil, 48h for tadalafil
Start PDE5i at lowest dose; separate dosing by 4-6 hours; tadalafil 5mg daily with tamsulosin 0.4mg is generally safe

pde5_inhibitor_interactions_if_prescribe.mechanism: Inhibition of PDE5i hepatic metabolism, increasing plasma levels
pde5_inhibitor_interactions_if_prescribe.clinical_effect: Increased PDE5i toxicity: hypotension, visual disturbances, priapism
pde5_inhibitor_interactions_if_prescribe.management: Reduce PDE5i dose by 50%; avoid sildenafil >25mg with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors

hypogonadism_prevalence.prevalence_symptomatic_hypogonadism: ~5-10% of men aged 50-59 have symptomatic hypogonadism requiring treatment

high_issues.detail: The treatment plan appropriately defers PDE5 inhibitor prescribing pending cardiovascular risk stratification, but this safety gate must be explicitly enforced. The patient is a 54-year-old male with unknown blood pressure, lipid status, and cardiac history. PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil, avanafil) are ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED with nitrates. Nitrate use status is completely unknown for this patient. Before any PDE5 inhibitor is prescribed, the following must be confirmed: (1) nitrate use excluded via medication reconciliation, (2) 10-year ASCVD risk calculated, (3) Princeton Consensus III risk stratification completed. Failure to perform this check before prescribing represents a potentially life-threatening oversight.
high_issues.framework: Princeton Consensus III / ISMP High-Alert Interaction
high_issues.action_required: Mandatory medication reconciliation to exclude nitrate use BEFORE any PDE5 inhibitor is considered. Document cardiovascular risk stratification in the chart prior to prescribing.

high_issues.category: Testosterone Replacement Therapy — Missing Pre-Treatment Safety Gates
high_issues.detail: The treatment plan for hypogonadism correctly lists contraindications but the safety checklist requires reinforcement as a hard stop. TRT must NOT be initiated without: (1) PSA checked and documented <4.0 ng/mL — prostate cancer is an absolute contraindication; (2) hematocrit confirmed <54% — polycythemia is an absolute contraindication; (3) prolactin and LH/FSH results available to exclude pituitary pathology before exogenous testosterone suppresses the HPG axis further; (4) sleep apnea assessment — TRT can worsen obstructive sleep apnea, which is prevalent in 54-year-old males, particularly those with metabolic syndrome. None of these pre-treatment checks have been completed. TRT initiated without these checks could mask a prolactinoma, worsen undiagnosed polycythemia, or stimulate occult prostate cancer.
high_issues.framework: Endocrine Society Hypogonadism Guideline 2018 / ISMP High-Alert Medication
high_issues.action_required: Enforce all six pre-TRT safety gates as hard stops in the clinical workflow. Document each gate as cleared before prescribing. Two separate morning testosterone measurements required — a single low value is insufficient per guideline.

high_issues.category: Medication Reconciliation — Complete Absence of Current Medication Data
high_issues.detail: No current medications are documented for this patient. This is the single most critical safety gap in the entire workup. Multiple high-risk drug interactions cannot be assessed without this information. Specifically unknown: (1) nitrate use — absolute contraindication to PDE5 inhibitors; (2) MAOI use — absolute contraindication to bupropion, cyproheptadine, and pseudoephedrine; (3) anticoagulant use (warfarin) — testosterone significantly potentiates warfarin anticoagulation, requiring INR monitoring; (4) alpha-blocker use — both a potential cause of the presenting complaint AND a moderate interaction risk with PDE5 inhibitors; (5) CYP3A4 inhibitors (ritonavir, ketoconazole, clarithromycin) — dramatically increase PDE5 inhibitor plasma levels, risking severe hypotension and priapism; (6) CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine) — increase nebivolol plasma levels significantly. No pharmacological treatment should be initiated until full medication reconciliation is completed and documented.
high_issues.framework: ISMP Medication Reconciliation / Swiss Cheese Model — Active Failure Risk
high_issues.action_required: Medication reconciliation is the highest-priority safety action before ANY prescription is written. Must include: all prescription medications, OTC medications, supplements (including testosterone boosters, herbal supplements), and recreational substances including alcohol and cannabis.

high_issues.category: Pseudoephedrine — Cardiovascular Safety in Patient with Unknown Cardiac Status
high_issues.detail: Pseudoephedrine 60mg PRN is recommended for retrograde ejaculation. This is an alpha-sympathomimetic that raises blood pressure and heart rate. The patient's cardiovascular status is entirely unknown — blood pressure, lipid status, coronary artery disease history, and cardiac rhythm are all undocumented. Pseudoephedrine is contraindicated in uncontrolled hypertension and severe coronary artery disease. At age 54 with sexual dysfunction as a potential cardiovascular surrogate marker, the risk of undiagnosed hypertension or coronary disease is non-trivial. The treatment plan notes this concern but the safety gate must be explicit: pseudoephedrine must NOT be used until blood pressure is measured and cardiovascular risk is stratified.
high_issues.action_required: Blood pressure measurement and cardiovascular risk stratification must precede any pseudoephedrine recommendation. Document BP and cardiac history before prescribing or recommending OTC use.

moderate_issues.category: Bupropion — Seizure Risk and Eating Disorder Screening
moderate_issues.detail: Bupropion XL 150-300mg daily is recommended as a switch option from SSRI/SNRI. Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold in a dose-dependent manner and is absolutely contraindicated in seizure disorders and eating disorders (anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa). Neither seizure history nor eating disorder history has been documented for this patient. While the treatment plan lists this warning, it must be actively screened before prescribing — not merely noted as a caveat. Additionally, bupropion is contraindicated within 14 days of MAOI use, and MAOI status is unknown.
moderate_issues.action_required: Before prescribing bupropion: (1) explicitly ask about seizure history and eating disorder history; (2) confirm MAOI-free for at least 14 days; (3) assess alcohol use — heavy alcohol use combined with bupropion significantly lowers seizure threshold.

moderate_issues.category: Cyproheptadine — Anticholinergic Burden and BPH Risk
moderate_issues.detail: Cyproheptadine 4-8mg PRN is recommended as an adjunct for SSRI-induced delayed ejaculation. Cyproheptadine has significant anticholinergic properties. At age 54, subclinical BPH is highly prevalent (estimated 50-60% of men aged 50-60 have histological BPH). Anticholinergic medications can precipitate acute urinary retention in men with BPH by relaxing the detrusor muscle and increasing bladder outlet resistance. The treatment plan notes this risk but it requires active BPH screening before prescribing. Additionally, cyproheptadine causes sedation — patients must be counseled not to drive for 4-6 hours after dosing.
moderate_issues.action_required: Screen for BPH symptoms (IPSS questionnaire or equivalent) before prescribing cyproheptadine. If significant LUTS present, avoid cyproheptadine or use with extreme caution. Provide explicit sedation warning — do not drive or operate machinery for 4-6 hours after dose.

moderate_issues.category: Testosterone Gel — Transfer Risk to Partners and Children
moderate_issues.detail: Testosterone gel 1.62% carries a significant and frequently under-counseled transfer risk. Skin-to-skin contact with female partners (particularly pregnant women) or children before the gel is fully dry can cause virilization. The patient is in a new relationship — this is directly clinically relevant. The treatment plan mentions this but patient counseling documentation must be explicit and confirmed. FDA Black Box Warning exists for testosterone gel transfer.
moderate_issues.framework: FDA Black Box Warning / Patient Safety Counseling
moderate_issues.action_required: If testosterone gel is prescribed: (1) provide explicit written and verbal counseling on transfer risk; (2) instruct patient to apply to shoulders/upper arms only, never genitals; (3) wash hands immediately after application; (4) cover application site with clothing; (5) avoid skin contact with partner for minimum 2 hours after application; (6) document counseling in chart.

moderate_issues.category: Imipramine — Cardiac Safety and Anticholinergic Risk
moderate_issues.detail: Imipramine 25-75mg daily is listed as a second-line option for retrograde ejaculation. Imipramine is a tricyclic antidepressant with significant cardiac risks: QTc prolongation, arrhythmia risk, and orthostatic hypotension. In a 54-year-old male with unknown cardiovascular status and unknown baseline QTc, imipramine carries meaningful cardiac risk. Additionally, imipramine has substantial anticholinergic burden (urinary retention risk in BPH) and lowers the seizure threshold. The treatment plan does not include a cardiac safety warning for imipramine — this is an omission that requires correction.
moderate_issues.framework: Cardiac Safety / Anticholinergic Risk / Drug-Disease Interaction
moderate_issues.action_required: Before prescribing imipramine: (1) obtain baseline ECG to assess QTc interval — do not prescribe if QTc >450ms; (2) assess for cardiovascular disease history; (3) screen for BPH; (4) confirm no concurrent QTc-prolonging medications; (5) start at lowest dose (25mg) and titrate slowly. Consider whether the risk-benefit ratio justifies imipramine use given the availability of safer alternatives.

moderate_issues.detail: Cabergoline 0.5mg twice weekly is listed as an off-label option for idiopathic delayed ejaculation. Cabergoline is a dopamine agonist associated with cardiac valvulopathy (fibrotic valvular disease) at higher doses used in Parkinson's disease. At the lower doses used for hyperprolactinemia and sexual dysfunction (0.5-1mg/week), the valvulopathy risk is considered low but not zero. The treatment plan does not mention this risk. Additionally, cabergoline can cause orthostatic hypotension, nausea, and psychiatric effects (impulse control disorders — gambling, hypersexuality — are a recognized class effect of dopamine agonists).
moderate_issues.framework: Drug Safety — Cardiac and Psychiatric Adverse Effects
moderate_issues.action_required: If cabergoline is prescribed: (1) counsel patient on impulse control disorder risk (hypersexuality, gambling) — particularly relevant given the sexual medicine context; (2) advise on orthostatic hypotension precautions; (3) baseline cardiac auscultation; (4) echocardiogram if used long-term at higher doses; (5) use lowest effective dose.

moderate_issues.detail: No allergy history is documented anywhere in the multi-agent output. This is a fundamental safety gap. Before prescribing any medication — bupropion, testosterone, cyproheptadine, pseudoephedrine, imipramine, cabergoline, or any PDE5 inhibitor — documented allergy review is mandatory. Cross-reactivity risks cannot be assessed without this information.
moderate_issues.framework: Swiss Cheese Model — Latent Condition / Medication Reconciliation
moderate_issues.action_required: Document complete allergy history including drug allergies, food allergies, and environmental allergies before any prescription is written. Specifically ask about sulfonamide allergy (cross-reactivity with some PDE5 inhibitors is debated but should be noted).

moderate_issues.category: Renal and Hepatic Function — Unknown Status Affects Multiple Drug Dosing
moderate_issues.detail: CMP (renal and hepatic function) is recommended in the workup but has not yet been obtained. Multiple recommended medications require dose adjustment in renal or hepatic impairment: (1) bupropion — reduce dose in severe renal impairment; maximum 150mg every other day in severe hepatic cirrhosis; (2) testosterone — use with caution in renal impairment due to fluid retention risk; (3) nebivolol — reduce dose if CrCl <30 mL/min; contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment; (4) PDE5 inhibitors — dose reduction required in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C). No medication should be prescribed at standard doses without baseline renal and hepatic function data.
moderate_issues.action_required: Obtain CMP before initiating any pharmacological treatment. Document eGFR and hepatic function results and adjust doses accordingly.

low_issues.category: Alcohol Use — Interaction Risk with Multiple Recommended Agents
low_issues.detail: Alcohol use history is not documented. Alcohol interacts with multiple recommended agents: (1) bupropion — alcohol lowers seizure threshold synergistically; (2) cyproheptadine — additive CNS depression and sedation; (3) imipramine — additive CNS depression, increased orthostatic hypotension; (4) pseudoephedrine — cardiovascular stimulant effects may be unpredictable with alcohol. Additionally, chronic alcohol use independently suppresses testosterone synthesis and contributes to sexual dysfunction — this is both a diagnostic and safety consideration.
low_issues.action_required: Document alcohol use (quantity and frequency) as part of social history. Counsel patient on alcohol-medication interactions for any prescribed agents. Recommend alcohol reduction to <2 standard drinks/day as part of lifestyle modification regardless of specific etiology.

low_issues.category: Testosterone Cypionate — Injection Technique and Sterile Preparation
low_issues.detail: If testosterone cypionate IM injection is prescribed, patient education on proper injection technique, sterile preparation, and site rotation is required to prevent injection site complications (abscess, nerve injury, oil embolism with inadvertent IV injection). The treatment plan does not address patient education for self-injection.
low_issues.action_required: If self-injection is planned: provide formal injection technique training; prescribe appropriate needles (21-23 gauge, 1-1.5 inch for IM); instruct on site rotation (gluteus, vastus lateralis); provide written instructions; consider supervised first injection in clinic.

low_issues.category: PSA Monitoring — Testosterone Therapy and Prostate Cancer Risk
low_issues.detail: The treatment plan correctly identifies PSA monitoring as required with TRT. However, the patient has not yet had a baseline PSA drawn. At age 54, PSA screening is age-appropriate and should be discussed with the patient as part of shared decision-making per ACS and USPSTF guidelines. A baseline PSA is required before TRT initiation — not just as a contraindication check but as a reference point for future monitoring.
low_issues.action_required: Obtain baseline PSA as part of the recommended laboratory panel. Document result and discuss prostate cancer screening with patient using shared decision-making framework before TRT initiation.

low_issues.category: Bone Density — STOPP/START Consideration if TRT Initiated
low_issues.detail: If hypogonadism is confirmed, the patient may have had prolonged androgen deficiency contributing to reduced bone mineral density. Per START criteria, bone protection assessment is warranted in hypogonadal men. TRT itself is bone-protective, but baseline DXA scan should be considered if hypogonadism has been longstanding. The treatment plan mentions DXA at baseline if osteoporosis risk but does not explicitly flag this as a START criterion.
low_issues.action_required: If hypogonadism confirmed: consider baseline DXA scan, particularly if testosterone has been low for an extended period. Document bone health assessment in the treatment plan.

low_issues.category: Mental Health Safety Net — PHQ-9 and Suicidality Screening
low_issues.detail: PHQ-9 is recommended for depression screening. If PHQ-9 score is ≥10, a formal safety assessment including suicidality screening (PHQ-9 item 9) is required before prescribing bupropion or any antidepressant. Sexual dysfunction is associated with depression, and new relationship stress combined with chronic sexual dysfunction can exacerbate depressive symptoms. This safety net is not explicitly mentioned in the treatment plan.
low_issues.action_required: When administering PHQ-9: review item 9 (suicidality) explicitly. If PHQ-9 ≥10 or item 9 positive, conduct full safety assessment before prescribing any psychoactive medication. Document mental health safety screening.

empathy.patient_summary:
Thank you for taking this important step to get care. You are not alone — this is a very common concern for men in their 50s, and the good news is that there are real, treatable causes that your doctor can look into.

Based on what you shared, you have been having difficulty reaching climax during sex for about a year, and it happens nearly every time. You noticed things feel a little better with your new relationship, which is a positive sign. Your care team has reviewed your situation carefully and believes there is very likely a specific, fixable reason behind this — not just stress or 'getting older.'

The three most common reasons this happens in men your age are: (1) a medication you may already be taking — some very common medicines for blood pressure, depression, or prostate issues can cause exactly this problem; (2) lower testosterone levels, which naturally decline as men age; or (3) a combination of both, with some performance anxiety on top. All of these are treatable.

Before any treatment is started, your doctor needs to run some simple blood tests and review your medications. This is important because the right treatment depends entirely on finding the actual cause first. Jumping to treatment without knowing the cause could miss something important.
empathy.what_this_means:
Your body has a reflex system — like a chain of dominoes — that controls ejaculation. Several things can interrupt that chain. Think of it like a dimmer switch being turned down rather than a light switch being broken. The goal of your workup is to find out what is dimming the switch.

Here is what your care team wants to check:

• YOUR MEDICATIONS: Some of the most commonly prescribed medicines — including certain antidepressants, blood pressure pills, and prostate medications — are among the top causes of this problem. This is the single most important thing to check first, because if a medication is the cause, changing it may fix the problem quickly.

• YOUR TESTOSTERONE: Testosterone levels naturally drop about 1–2% every year after age 30. By your mid-50s, about 1 in 4 men have levels low enough to affect sexual function. A simple morning blood test can check this.

• YOUR OVERALL HEALTH: Conditions like diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol can also affect sexual function — and sometimes this is the first sign that one of these conditions is present. Your doctor will check for these too. This is actually a good thing — catching them early means you can protect your heart and health long-term.

• THE MIND-BODY CONNECTION: Starting a new relationship can bring excitement but also pressure. Your brain plays a big role in sexual response. Even if there is a physical cause, some anxiety about performance can make things worse. Both parts — physical and emotional — can be treated at the same time.

right_now: Write down every medication, vitamin, supplement, or herbal product you take — including anything you buy over the counter. Include the name and dose if you know it. This is the single most important thing you can do before your appointment.
Write down when you first noticed this problem and whether it started around the same time you began any new medication.
Think about whether this happens when you are alone (during masturbation) as well, or only with a partner. Your doctor will ask this — it helps them understand the cause. There is no wrong answer.
Think about whether you actually reach climax but nothing comes out, versus whether climax itself does not happen. This distinction matters medically and helps your doctor narrow down the cause.

If you do not already have a doctor's appointment scheduled, call to make one this week. Ask for a primary care or urology appointment. You do not need to go to an emergency room — this is not an emergency, but it does deserve proper attention.
this_week: Get a blood test done — your doctor will order this. It needs to be done in the morning (between 8 and 10 AM) while fasting (nothing to eat or drink except water for at least 8 hours before). The test checks your testosterone, other hormones, blood sugar, cholesterol, and a few other things. Morning timing is important — testosterone is highest in the morning and afternoon results can be misleading.
Have your blood pressure checked if you have not had it checked recently. This can be done at a pharmacy, at your doctor's office, or at many grocery stores for free.

Fill out a short questionnaire your doctor may give you about your sexual function and your mood. These are standard, confidential tools that help your doctor understand the full picture. There are no right or wrong answers.

Be honest with your doctor about all substances you use, including alcohol, cannabis, and any recreational drugs. These can affect sexual function and interact with treatments. Your doctor is not there to judge you — they need this information to help you safely.
ongoing: Aim for 30 minutes of moderate exercise (brisk walking, cycling, swimming) at least 5 days a week. Exercise is one of the most proven ways to improve sexual function, boost testosterone naturally, and protect your heart — all at the same time.
Try to limit alcohol to no more than 1–2 drinks per day. Alcohol directly lowers testosterone and can worsen the exact problem you are experiencing.
Aim for 7–9 hours of sleep per night. Testosterone is produced mainly during deep sleep — poor sleep directly reduces testosterone levels.
If you smoke, talk to your doctor about quitting. Smoking damages the blood vessels that are essential for sexual function.

Consider speaking with a therapist or counselor who specializes in sexual health. Even if a physical cause is found and treated, some anxiety about performance can linger and is very treatable with a few sessions of talk therapy. This is not a sign of weakness — it is smart, proactive care.

Attend all follow-up appointments. Some of the blood tests may need to be repeated, and your doctor will want to check your progress. Treatment often takes 4–12 weeks to show full results, so patience and follow-through matter.

medications_explained.name: No medication is being started right now
medications_explained.plain_language_explanation: Your care team has made a careful decision NOT to start any medication yet — and this is actually the right and safe approach. Here is why: several common medications can cause exactly the problem you are experiencing. If your doctor prescribed a treatment before knowing what is causing the issue, it could mask the real problem or interact dangerously with medicines you might already be taking. The blood tests and medication review come first. Once the cause is identified, the right treatment will be much more targeted and effective.
medications_explained.what_to_expect: After your blood tests come back — usually within a few days to a week — your doctor will discuss options with you. Depending on what is found, treatment might be as simple as adjusting a medication you are already on, or it might involve a hormone supplement or other therapy. Most men with this condition see meaningful improvement once the underlying cause is addressed.

medications_explained.name: What treatment might look like — depending on what is found
medications_explained.plain_language_explanation:
Here are the most likely scenarios in plain language:

• IF A MEDICATION IS THE CAUSE: Your doctor may lower the dose, switch you to a different medication that does the same job without this side effect, or suggest a small adjustment to how you take it. For example, certain antidepressants can be switched to one called bupropion, which works differently and has a much lower chance of causing this problem.

• IF TESTOSTERONE IS LOW: Your doctor may recommend testosterone replacement. This can come as a gel you rub on your shoulders each morning, or as an injection every 1–2 weeks. Both work well. Before starting, your doctor will check your prostate and blood count to make sure it is safe for you.

• IF DIABETES OR HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE IS FOUND: Treating these conditions often improves sexual function as well. Your doctor will guide you through this.

• IF ANXIETY IS A SIGNIFICANT FACTOR: A few sessions with a sex therapist or counselor can make a real difference. This type of therapy is practical and solution-focused — not years of deep analysis. Many men find it very helpful, especially in a new relationship.
medications_explained.important_safety_note: Please do not take any testosterone supplements, 'male enhancement' products, or herbal remedies you find online or in stores without talking to your doctor first. Some of these can interfere with your test results, interact with medications, or cause harm. Your doctor needs accurate test results to help you properly.

empathy.lifestyle_tips:
Many people in your situation find that lifestyle changes make a surprisingly big difference — sometimes even before any medication is started. Here are the most evidence-backed tips, explained simply:

• EXERCISE IS MEDICINE: Regular aerobic exercise (anything that gets your heart rate up — walking fast, cycling, swimming) for 30 minutes, 5 days a week, has been shown in studies to improve sexual function about as much as some medications. It boosts testosterone, improves blood flow, reduces stress, and helps with weight — all of which matter here.

• WATCH THE ALCOHOL: Even moderate drinking lowers testosterone and can directly worsen the problem you are experiencing. Cutting back to 1–2 drinks per day — or less — is one of the simplest changes you can make.

• SLEEP MATTERS MORE THAN YOU THINK: Your body makes most of its testosterone during deep sleep. Men who sleep less than 6 hours a night have significantly lower testosterone levels. If you have trouble sleeping, mention it to your doctor — it may be part of the picture.

• EAT WELL: A Mediterranean-style diet — lots of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, fish, olive oil, and nuts — is associated with better sexual function and heart health. You do not need a perfect diet, just a generally healthy one.

• MANAGE STRESS: Stress hormones (like cortisol) directly suppress testosterone. Even small steps — a short walk, time with people you enjoy, limiting news consumption — can help.

• BE PATIENT WITH YOURSELF AND YOUR PARTNER: You are in a new relationship, which is exciting but can also bring pressure. Open, honest communication with your partner — even just saying 'I am working on this with my doctor' — can reduce anxiety and strengthen your connection. You do not have to have all the answers right now.
when_to_get_help: CALL YOUR DOCTOR WITHIN 1–2 DAYS if you develop a new headache that is different from any headache you have had before, especially if it is behind your eyes or at the front of your head.
CALL YOUR DOCTOR WITHIN 1–2 DAYS if you notice any changes in your vision — blurry vision, loss of side (peripheral) vision, or seeing double.
CALL YOUR DOCTOR WITHIN 1–2 DAYS if you notice any fluid or discharge from your nipples. In men, this is unusual and needs to be checked promptly.
CALL YOUR DOCTOR THIS WEEK if you notice blood in your semen. This is not an emergency but does need to be evaluated.

CALL YOUR DOCTOR THIS WEEK if you are feeling significantly depressed, hopeless, or are having any thoughts of harming yourself. Sexual health problems can affect mood deeply, and support is available.
GO TO AN URGENT CARE OR EMERGENCY ROOM if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, or feel your heart racing or pounding in an unusual way — especially during or after physical or sexual activity.

GO TO AN EMERGENCY ROOM IMMEDIATELY if you ever take a medication for this condition and also take a heart medication called a nitrate (examples: nitroglycerin, isosorbide). These two types of medication together can cause a dangerous drop in blood pressure. This is why your doctor must know all your medications before prescribing anything new.
CALL YOUR DOCTOR if you start any new medication and notice your symptoms getting significantly worse, or if you develop new symptoms like dizziness, fainting, or difficulty urinating.
empathy.reassurance:
You are doing the right thing by seeking care, and we want you to know — this is genuinely one of the most common and most treatable concerns that men in their 50s bring to their doctors. You are far from alone.

The fact that things feel somewhat better with your new relationship is actually an encouraging sign. It suggests that your body's systems are still working — they may just need a little support.

The path forward is clear: a few blood tests, a review of your medications, and a conversation with your doctor. In many cases, the cause turns out to be something straightforward — a medication side effect, a hormone level that needs a small boost, or a combination of factors that respond well to treatment.

Most men who go through this evaluation find answers, and most find meaningful improvement with the right treatment. Give yourself the time and care you deserve. You have already taken the hardest step — asking for help.
questions_for_doctor: Could any of my current medications be causing this? Is there a version of my medication that is less likely to have this side effect?
What do my testosterone results mean for me specifically? Is my level considered low for my age?
Do I need to worry about my heart health based on these results? Should I see a heart specialist?
Is there a chance I have diabetes or pre-diabetes that I did not know about? What do my blood sugar results show?
Would a sex therapist or counselor be helpful for me alongside any medical treatment?
How long should I expect before I see improvement once treatment starts?
Are there any supplements or over-the-counter products I should avoid while we are figuring this out?
When should I come back for a follow-up, and what will we check at that visit?

anticipated_faqs.question: Is this just a normal part of getting older?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Aging does play a role — testosterone naturally declines with age, and it takes longer for the body to respond to sexual stimulation as we get older. But 'normal aging' does not fully explain a problem that happens nearly every time over a full year. In most men your age, there is a specific, identifiable cause — and most of those causes are treatable. Do not accept this as something you just have to live with without getting it properly checked.

anticipated_faqs.question: Could this be all in my head?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Stress and anxiety absolutely can affect sexual function — and with a new relationship, some performance pressure is very normal and human. However, the fact that this has been happening for a full year, started before your current relationship, and occurs almost every time suggests there is likely a physical component as well. Most men in this situation have a mix of both physical and emotional factors. The good news is that both can be treated, and treating the physical cause often relieves the anxiety too.

anticipated_faqs.question: Do I need to see a specialist, or can my regular doctor handle this?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Your regular doctor (primary care physician) can handle most of the initial evaluation — the blood tests, medication review, and first steps. If the results point to a hormone issue, a specialist called an endocrinologist may get involved. If the issue seems to be more urological, a urologist who specializes in men's sexual health may be helpful. Your primary care doctor will guide you on whether a referral is needed after the initial results come back.

anticipated_faqs.question: Will I need to take medication forever?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Not necessarily. If the cause turns out to be a medication you are already taking, simply adjusting or switching that medication may resolve the problem without adding anything new. If testosterone replacement is needed, some men do take it long-term, but your doctor will reassess regularly. If lifestyle changes (exercise, sleep, alcohol reduction) are a significant factor, improving those habits can sometimes restore function without any medication at all.

anticipated_faqs.question: Should I tell my partner about this?
anticipated_faqs.answer: That is entirely your choice, and there is no right or wrong answer. Many men find that being open with their partner — even just saying 'I am working with my doctor on something' — reduces pressure and actually improves intimacy. Partners often appreciate honesty and want to be supportive. A sex therapist can also help you navigate these conversations if that feels difficult.

anticipated_faqs.question: Is this a sign of a serious health problem?
anticipated_faqs.answer: In most cases, no — it is a sign that something needs attention, not that something is seriously wrong. However, your care team does want to check your heart health and blood sugar as part of this evaluation, because sexual function problems in men your age can sometimes be an early signal that blood vessels are not working at their best. The encouraging thing is: catching this early means you can take steps to protect your heart before any bigger problems develop. Think of this as your body giving you a useful heads-up.

anticipated_faqs.question: How long will it take to get answers and feel better?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Blood test results typically come back within a few days to a week. Once your doctor reviews everything, you will likely have a clearer picture within 2–4 weeks of your appointment. If a medication change is the answer, improvement can happen within weeks. If testosterone replacement is started, most men notice improvement in sexual desire and function within 3–6 months. Lifestyle changes like exercise and better sleep can start showing benefits within 4–8 weeks. Be patient — this took time to develop, and it will take some time to improve, but improvement is very achievable.
