anchoring_bias_check.initial_anchor: Cannabis smoke exposure as primary irritant — this is the most obvious explanation and may cause premature closure.
anchoring_bias_check.unexplained_by_anchor: The microsecond duration of pain is unusually brief even for irritant conjunctivitis. Pure chemical irritation typically produces more sustained burning/stinging rather than lancinating microsecond pain. This feature is better explained by neuralgic or corneal nerve mechanisms.
anchoring_bias_check.alternative_explanations_for_unexplained: Microsecond pain quality points toward: (1) corneal foreign body with intermittent contact during blinking, (2) trigeminal/supraorbital neuralgia, (3) tear film breakup with corneal nerve exposure in dry eye. The smoke exposure may be coincidental or a contributing rather than primary factor.
anchoring_bias_check.availability_bias_check: Cannabis use is increasingly common; clinicians may over-attribute symptoms to this exposure. The unilateral nature and neuralgic pain quality deserve independent evaluation regardless of exposure history.
anchoring_bias_check.unifying_diagnosis_consideration: Smoke-induced tear film disruption causing corneal epithelial exposure → episodic corneal nerve stimulation (microsecond pain) + reflex tearing + conjunctival hyperemia. This unified model explains all features including the atypical pain duration.
anchoring_bias_check.atypical_presentation_considered: Pre-eruptive HZO without rash is a classic diagnostic pitfall in patients >50 with unilateral periorbital pain.

discriminating_features.finding: Corneal dendrites or pseudodendrites on fluorescein staining
discriminating_features.diagnosis_targeted: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus vs. HSV keratitis

discriminating_features.finding: Visible foreign body or focal fluorescein uptake on slit-lamp
Elevated intraocular pressure (>21 mmHg) with narrow angle on gonioscopy
Vesicular rash in V1 dermatome or Hutchinson's sign (tip of nose)
Bilateral symptoms or response to topical antihistamine
Abnormal tear break-up time (<10 seconds) and Schirmer's test

recommended_tests: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with fluorescein staining and cobalt blue light — PRIMARY TEST: rules out corneal foreign body, abrasion, dendrites (HSV/HZO), and assesses corneal epithelial integrity
Upper eyelid eversion and inspection of superior tarsal conjunctiva — rules out subtarsal foreign body
Intraocular pressure measurement (non-contact tonometry or Goldmann applanation) — rules out angle-closure glaucoma
Careful V1 dermatome skin inspection (forehead, scalp, tip of nose) — screens for pre-eruptive or early HZO rash
Tear break-up time (TBUT) assessment — evaluates for dry eye/tear film instability
Schirmer's test — quantifies aqueous tear production if dry eye suspected
Anterior chamber depth and angle assessment (gonioscopy if IOP elevated) — rules out narrow-angle anatomy
MRI brain with gadolinium (deferred, only if ocular causes excluded and neuralgic etiology suspected) — evaluates for trigeminal nerve compression or demyelination

follow_up_questions.question: Do you notice the sharp sensation more when you blink, or does it occur independently of blinking?
follow_up_questions.diagnosis_targeted: Corneal foreign body (pain with blinking) vs. trigeminal neuralgia (spontaneous, trigger-independent) vs. tear film breakup (occurs during prolonged eye opening)

follow_up_questions.question: Have you noticed any skin sensitivity, tingling, or rash on your forehead, scalp, or the tip of your nose on the left side?
follow_up_questions.diagnosis_targeted: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus — Hutchinson's sign and prodromal dermatomal symptoms are critical screening questions

follow_up_questions.question: Do you experience any halos around lights, blurred vision during or after the episodes, or headache associated with the eye pain?
follow_up_questions.diagnosis_targeted: Acute angle-closure glaucoma (halos, blurred vision) vs. migraine-associated ocular symptoms

follow_up_questions.question: Do you have a history of cold sores (oral herpes), prior eye infections, or have you ever been told you have herpes of the eye?
follow_up_questions.diagnosis_targeted: HSV keratitis — prior HSV-1 infection significantly increases risk of ocular reactivation

follow_up_questions.question: Does the eye feel gritty or like something is in it between the sharp episodes, and is it worse in the morning or later in the day?
follow_up_questions.diagnosis_targeted: Dry eye syndrome (worse later in day, gritty sensation) vs. blepharitis (worse in morning with crusting) vs. foreign body (constant gritty sensation)

specialist.reason_for_consultation: 54-year-old male with 3-day history of episodic unilateral left lateral ocular pricking sensation (microsecond duration, 2-3x/day), ipsilateral redness and tearing, following cannabis smoke exposure in an enclosed garage. Referred for specialist evaluation to exclude corneal foreign body, abrasion, herpes zoster ophthalmicus, angle-closure glaucoma, and to guide management of possible irritant/allergic conjunctivitis.
specialist.specialist_assessment: This 54-year-old male presents with a classic triad of unilateral ocular irritation: episodic sharp/pricking sensation, conjunctival hyperemia, and reflex tearing in the context of a confirmed chemical irritant exposure (cannabis smoke, enclosed space). From an ophthalmologic standpoint, the differential is led by irritant conjunctivitis secondary to cannabis smoke (acrolein, formaldehyde, THC-mediated vasodilation), followed closely by dry eye disease with episodic corneal nerve stimulation (age-appropriate, smoke exacerbates evaporative tear film instability), and corneal foreign body or superficial abrasion from smoke particulates. The microsecond duration of pain is the most diagnostically challenging feature: pure irritant conjunctivitis typically produces sustained burning rather than lancinating microsecond pain. This quality is better explained by intermittent corneal nociceptor firing during tear film breakup, a loose particulate foreign body making intermittent contact with the corneal epithelium during blinking, or — at lower probability — a neuralgic mechanism (supraorbital/V1 branch). Must-not-miss diagnoses requiring active exclusion include: (1) Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus in pre-eruptive prodromal phase — age 54 is within the elevated incidence bracket (6-8 per 1000 person-years), unilateral V1-distribution pain is the prodromal hallmark, and absence of rash at 3 days does not fully exclude this diagnosis; (2) Corneal foreign body — cannot be excluded without slit-lamp examination and fluorescein staining; (3) Intermittent angle-closure glaucoma — episodic unilateral eye pain and redness in a 54-year-old male mandates IOP measurement and anterior chamber assessment; (4) HSV keratitis — prior HSV-1 infection history must be elicited. The unilateral nature of this presentation is the single most important feature driving the ophthalmologic workup: bilateral irritant or allergic conjunctivitis would be expected from bilateral smoke exposure, and the unilateral predominance elevates suspicion for a structural, infectious, or neuralgic etiology independent of the exposure history. Current management has not been initiated, which is appropriate pending examination. Empirical topical antihistamine therapy without slit-lamp exclusion of corneal pathology would be premature and potentially harmful if a foreign body or herpetic lesion is present.
diagnostic_criteria_applied: TFOS DEWS II Diagnostic Criteria for Dry Eye Disease (2017): Symptom score + at least one positive sign (TBUT <10s, Schirmer <5mm/5min, corneal fluorescein staining score ≥2). Patient meets symptomatic threshold; objective testing required to confirm.

International Headache Society (IHS) Trigeminal Neuralgia Criteria (ICHD-3): Recurrent unilateral facial pain, lasting from a fraction of a second to 2 minutes, severe intensity, electric shock/shooting/stabbing quality, precipitated by innocuous stimuli. Patient's microsecond duration meets the lower bound; however, absence of trigger points and presence of ocular signs reduce fit.

AAO Preferred Practice Pattern — Conjunctivitis (2018): Unilateral presentation mandates exclusion of corneal pathology, foreign body, and infectious etiology before diagnosis of allergic or irritant conjunctivitis is assigned.

AAO Preferred Practice Pattern — Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (2019): Any patient ≥50 with unilateral periocular pain should be screened for HZO prodrome; Hutchinson's sign (nasal tip involvement) increases specificity for ocular involvement. Currently low suspicion but active exclusion required.

Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma Diagnostic Criteria: Elevated IOP >21 mmHg, narrow anterior chamber angle on gonioscopy, corneal edema, mid-dilated non-reactive pupil. Patient lacks classic features but episodic unilateral pain/redness in age-appropriate demographic mandates IOP measurement.

Corneal Foreign Body/Abrasion: Fluorescein staining with cobalt blue light showing focal epithelial defect or visible foreign body on slit-lamp biomicroscopy is diagnostic. Cannot be excluded clinically without examination.
specialist.risk_stratification: INTERMEDIATE — Age 54 in elevated HZO and glaucoma risk bracket; unilateral presentation atypical for bilateral irritant exposure; microsecond pain quality suggests corneal nociceptor or neuralgic mechanism beyond simple irritation; 3-day duration without resolution. Downgrade to LOW after normal slit-lamp, normal IOP, and clear V1 dermatome confirmed. Upgrade to HIGH if vesicular rash, vision change, corneal dendrites, or IOP >21 mmHg identified.
specialty_specific_tests: PRIORITY 1 — Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with fluorescein staining and cobalt blue light illumination: Gold standard for corneal epithelial integrity assessment; identifies foreign bodies, abrasions, dendrites (HSV/HZO pseudodendrites), and corneal edema. Cannot be substituted by any other test.

PRIORITY 1 — Upper and lower eyelid eversion with inspection of tarsal conjunctiva: Rules out subtarsal foreign body lodged in superior or inferior fornix — a common cause of episodic unilateral sharp ocular pain that is missed without lid eversion.

PRIORITY 1 — Non-contact tonometry (or Goldmann applanation tonometry): Intraocular pressure measurement to exclude angle-closure glaucoma. Normal IOP <21 mmHg; elevated IOP with narrow angle on slit-lamp warrants urgent gonioscopy.

PRIORITY 1 — V1 dermatome skin inspection (forehead, scalp, periorbital skin, nasal tip): Clinical screen for pre-eruptive or early HZO vesicular rash; Hutchinson's sign (vesicles at nasal tip) indicates nasociliary nerve involvement and high risk of ocular complications.

PRIORITY 2 — Tear Break-Up Time (TBUT): Fluorescein instillation followed by measurement of time to first tear film break under cobalt blue light. TBUT <10 seconds supports dry eye disease diagnosis. Non-invasive TBUT (NIBUT) preferred if available.

PRIORITY 2 — Schirmer's Test Type I (without anesthesia): Measures reflex and basal tear secretion. <10mm/5min suggests aqueous deficient dry eye. Schirmer's Type II (with anesthesia) measures basal secretion only.

PRIORITY 2 — Anterior chamber depth and angle assessment on slit-lamp: Van Herick technique (peripheral anterior chamber depth <1/4 corneal thickness suggests narrow angle). If narrow angle identified, formal gonioscopy required.

PRIORITY 2 — Lid margin and meibomian gland assessment: Inspect for blepharitis (lid margin erythema, telangiectasia, collarettes, meibomian gland plugging). Meibomian gland expression to assess lipid quality. Meibography if available.

PRIORITY 3 — Conjunctival swab for VZV PCR: Only if clinical suspicion for HZO is elevated after examination (e.g., corneal dendrites, skin changes, or persistent unexplained unilateral pain). Not required as first-line.

PRIORITY 3 — MRI brain with gadolinium (trigeminal protocol): Deferred; indicated only if complete ophthalmologic workup is negative and neuralgic etiology remains suspected. Evaluates for vascular compression of trigeminal nerve root, demyelinating plaques (MS), or posterior fossa lesion.

PRIORITY 3 — Corneal confocal microscopy: Specialist-level imaging of corneal nerve fiber density and morphology; useful if neuropathic corneal pain or small fiber neuropathy suspected after standard workup is unrevealing.

ADJUNCT — Allergy skin prick testing or specific IgE panel (cannabis/hemp allergens): If allergic conjunctivitis is confirmed as primary diagnosis after structural pathology excluded; referral to allergy-immunology for formal evaluation.
specialist.severity_assessment: Current Severity: MODERATE-LOW (5/10 patient-reported, episodic, non-vision-threatening at present). Ophthalmologic Severity Classification: Grade 2/5 on the Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI) spectrum — symptomatic with functional impact but no objective vision loss or corneal compromise confirmed. The episodic microsecond nature limits functional impairment between episodes. However, the potential underlying diagnoses span a wide severity spectrum: irritant conjunctivitis (Grade 1 — self-limiting), dry eye disease (Grade 1-3 — chronic but manageable), corneal foreign body (Grade 2-3 — requires intervention, risk of secondary infection), HZO prodrome (Grade 4-5 — vision-threatening if untreated, requires urgent antiviral therapy), and angle-closure glaucoma (Grade 5 — ophthalmic emergency if confirmed). Functional visual acuity is reported as unaffected, which is reassuring. Pain severity of 5/10 is consistent with corneal surface pathology rather than deep ocular or neuralgic pain (which typically scores 7-10/10). Prognosis is excellent if the diagnosis is irritant conjunctivitis or dry eye (expected resolution within 1-2 weeks with appropriate management and irritant avoidance). Prognosis is guarded if HZO or corneal foreign body with secondary infection is the underlying etiology — both require prompt intervention to prevent permanent corneal scarring and vision loss.
diagnostic_criteria: TFOS DEWS II Dry Eye Disease Diagnostic Criteria (2017) — requires positive symptom score AND at least one objective sign
IHS ICHD-3 Trigeminal Neuralgia Criteria — microsecond to 2-minute unilateral lancinating pain; patient meets duration lower bound only
AAO Conjunctivitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2018) — unilateral presentation mandates structural/infectious exclusion before allergic/irritant diagnosis
AAO Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus Preferred Practice Pattern (2019) — age ≥50 with unilateral periocular pain requires HZO screening
Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma Diagnostic Criteria — IOP >21 mmHg + narrow angle + unilateral pain/redness; patient lacks classic features but IOP measurement mandatory
Corneal Foreign Body/Abrasion Diagnostic Standard — fluorescein staining with cobalt blue light showing focal epithelial defect; gold standard, cannot be excluded clinically
specialist_red_flags: Vesicular rash on forehead, scalp, or nasal tip (Hutchinson's sign) — immediate upgrade to urgent; initiate antiviral therapy within 72 hours
Corneal dendrites or pseudodendrites on fluorescein staining — HSV keratitis or HZO; urgent ophthalmology management required
IOP >21 mmHg with narrow anterior chamber angle — intermittent angle-closure glaucoma; urgent IOP-lowering therapy and laser peripheral iridotomy referral
Development of photophobia — suggests anterior uveitis, corneal ulcer, or HZO with intraocular involvement
Vision change (blurring, halos, decreased acuity) — multiple serious etiologies; immediate ophthalmologic evaluation
Worsening pain severity beyond 5/10 or change from episodic to constant — suggests progressive corneal pathology or neuralgic escalation
Periorbital skin erythema, edema, or warmth — preseptal cellulitis or early HZO skin involvement
Pupillary asymmetry or mid-dilated non-reactive pupil — angle-closure glaucoma or Horner syndrome
Proptosis or restricted extraocular movements — orbital pathology requiring urgent imaging
specialist.prognosis_notes: If irritant conjunctivitis (most likely diagnosis at 72% pre-test probability): Excellent prognosis. Expected resolution within 5-14 days with irritant avoidance and supportive care (preservative-free artificial tears, topical antihistamine/mast cell stabilizer). No long-term sequelae anticipated. If dry eye disease (second most likely at 40% probability): Chronic condition requiring ongoing management. Smoke avoidance, artificial tears, and potentially topical cyclosporine 0.05% or lifitegrast 5% for moderate-severe disease. Prognosis good with compliance. If corneal foreign body: Excellent prognosis with prompt removal. Risk of secondary bacterial keratitis if retained >24-48 hours; topical antibiotic prophylaxis post-removal. If HZO (low probability, 3-8%): Prognosis highly dependent on timing of antiviral initiation. Treatment within 72 hours of rash onset reduces ocular complications (NNT 4-6). Delayed treatment associated with corneal scarring, chronic uveitis, postherpetic neuralgia, and permanent vision loss in up to 50% of untreated cases. If angle-closure glaucoma (very low probability, <8%): Prognosis good with prompt laser peripheral iridotomy; poor if IOP spikes go unrecognized and untreated (permanent optic nerve damage). Modifying factors: Vaccination status (Shingrix reduces HZO risk by 97.2% in ages 50-69 — ZOE-50 trial); continued smoke exposure worsens all ocular surface conditions; age-related progression of dry eye and meibomian gland dysfunction expected without intervention.
specialist.guideline_concordance: Current management: No treatment initiated — CONCORDANT with guidelines at this stage. AAO Preferred Practice Pattern mandates slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining before initiating any topical therapy for unilateral ocular symptoms. Empirical antihistamine drops without examination would be DISCORDANT with guidelines given the unilateral presentation and must-not-miss diagnoses requiring exclusion. Recommended next steps per guidelines: (1) Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with fluorescein staining — AAO Grade A recommendation, mandatory before treatment; (2) IOP measurement — standard of care for unilateral ocular pain in age ≥50; (3) V1 dermatome inspection — AAO HZO guidelines recommend screening in patients ≥50 with unilateral periocular symptoms; (4) If irritant/allergic conjunctivitis confirmed: topical olopatadine or ketotifen (AAO Grade A, NNT 3-4) plus preservative-free artificial tears (TFOS DEWS II Grade A, NNT 4-6); (5) Shingrix vaccination counseling — CDC/ACIP Grade A recommendation for all adults ≥50 regardless of prior varicella history; (6) Irritant avoidance counseling — AAO Grade A recommendation as cornerstone of management.
specialist.referral_recommendation: IN-PERSON OPHTHALMOLOGY REFERRAL RECOMMENDED — SEMI-URGENT (within 24-48 hours). Rationale: Unilateral ocular symptoms with microsecond lancinating pain quality in a 54-year-old male require slit-lamp biomicroscopy, fluorescein staining, IOP measurement, and V1 dermatome assessment — none of which can be performed remotely or in a primary care setting without specialized equipment. The must-not-miss diagnoses (HZO, corneal foreign body, angle-closure glaucoma) all require ophthalmologic examination for exclusion. UPGRADE TO URGENT (same-day) if any of the following develop: vesicular rash on face/scalp, vision changes, photophobia, severe pain, or IOP concern. If in-person ophthalmology is unavailable within 24-48 hours, emergency department evaluation with slit-lamp capability is an acceptable alternative. Neurology referral (non-urgent, within 1-2 weeks) should be considered only if complete ophthalmologic workup is negative and the microsecond pain quality persists — to evaluate for supraorbital neuralgia or V1 trigeminal neuralgia.
clinical_pearls: The microsecond duration of pain is the single most diagnostically important feature in this case — pure irritant or allergic conjunctivitis does not produce lancinating microsecond pain. This quality points toward corneal nociceptor firing (foreign body, epithelial defect, tear film breakup) or neuralgic mechanism and should not be attributed to smoke exposure alone without examination.

Cannabis smoke is a direct chemical irritant (acrolein, formaldehyde, particulates) AND a pharmacological agent (THC causes conjunctival vasodilation via CB1 receptors) — both mechanisms contribute to redness and tearing. However, the unilateral predominance is atypical for bilateral smoke exposure and demands structural explanation.

Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus pitfall: The prodromal phase (pain before rash) can last 1-5 days and is clinically indistinguishable from other causes of unilateral periocular pain. At age 54, the annual incidence is 6-8 per 1000 person-years. Always inspect the V1 dermatome (forehead, scalp, nasal tip) and ask about skin sensitivity or tingling — Hutchinson's sign (nasal tip vesicles) is 94% specific for ocular involvement.

Lid eversion is frequently omitted in busy clinical settings and is the most common reason subtarsal foreign bodies are missed. A foreign body lodged in the superior tarsal conjunctiva produces a vertical linear corneal abrasion pattern on fluorescein staining — pathognomonic finding.

Paradoxical tearing in dry eye disease: Patients with dry eye often present with tearing (reflex hypersecretion) rather than dryness, leading clinicians to incorrectly exclude the diagnosis. The combination of tearing + episodic sharp sensation + age 54 + smoke exposure is a classic dry eye presentation.

Angle-closure glaucoma in males: While angle-closure is more common in hyperopic females of Asian descent, intermittent angle-closure in males at age 54 is underdiagnosed. The episodic nature of symptoms (pain resolves between attacks as angle reopens) can mimic other diagnoses. IOP measurement during a symptomatic episode is ideal but rarely achieved — gonioscopy is the definitive test.

treatment_plans.condition: Irritant/Chemical Conjunctivitis (Primary Diagnosis - Cannabis Smoke Exposure)

step_1_conservative.label: Immediate Conservative Measures
interventions: STOP all cannabis smoke exposure immediately — primary and most critical intervention
Avoid enclosed spaces with any smoke, chemical fumes, or airborne irritants
Do NOT rub the left eye under any circumstances
Flush left eye with preservative-free sterile saline or clean lukewarm water for 5-10 minutes if irritation is acute
Remove contact lenses if worn and do not reinsert until symptoms fully resolve and ophthalmologist clears
Apply cool compresses to closed left eye for 10-15 minutes, 2-3 times daily for symptomatic relief

step_2_first_line_pharmacological.label: First-Line Medications (initiate AFTER ophthalmology exam confirms no corneal foreign body, abrasion, or herpetic lesion)
interventions: Preservative-free artificial tears (e.g., Systane Ultra PF, Refresh Optive PF, TheraTears PF) — lubricates and dilutes residual irritants
Topical antihistamine/mast cell stabilizer combination drops (e.g., ketotifen 0.035% OTC) — addresses allergic component if present

step_3_second_line_pharmacological.label: Second-Line (if first-line insufficient after 5-7 days, prescribed by ophthalmologist)
interventions: Olopatadine 0.1% (Patanol) — prescription dual-action antihistamine/mast cell stabilizer, superior efficacy to OTC ketotifen
Topical NSAID (ketorolac 0.5%) — for pain/inflammation if corneal abrasion confirmed and foreign body excluded
Topical antibiotic (e.g., erythromycin ophthalmic ointment) — ONLY if corneal abrasion with contamination risk confirmed by ophthalmologist

step_4_adjunctive.label: Adjunctive Measures
interventions: Omega-3 fatty acid supplementation (1000-2000mg EPA/DHA daily) — supports meibomian gland function and tear film quality
Warm lid compresses (45°C for 10 minutes twice daily) — improves meibomian gland secretion if blepharitis/MGD component present
Lid hygiene with diluted baby shampoo or commercial lid scrub wipes — reduces lid margin bacterial load
Humidifier in bedroom/home environment — reduces evaporative tear loss

step_5_interventional.label: Interventional (ophthalmologist-directed only)
interventions: Foreign body removal under slit-lamp — if corneal or subtarsal foreign body identified on examination
Punctal plugs — if moderate-severe dry eye disease confirmed and artificial tears insufficient
Laser peripheral iridotomy — ONLY if intermittent angle-closure glaucoma confirmed by gonioscopy

step_6_escalation.label: Urgent Escalation Pathway
interventions: Oral valacyclovir 1g TID x 7-10 days — ONLY if herpes zoster ophthalmicus confirmed or strongly suspected (vesicular rash, corneal dendrites); requires IMMEDIATE ophthalmology referral
Neurology referral + MRI brain with gadolinium — ONLY if complete ophthalmologic workup is negative and microsecond pain persists, to evaluate trigeminal/supraorbital neuralgia

treatment_plans.first_line: Irritant avoidance (cannabis smoke cessation) + preservative-free artificial tears 4-6x daily + topical ketotifen 0.035% BID, initiated ONLY after ophthalmology slit-lamp exam excludes corneal pathology

medications.name: Preservative-Free Artificial Tears
medications.dose: 1-2 drops in left eye (bilateral use acceptable)
medications.frequency: 4-6 times daily, or as needed for comfort
medications.duration: Ongoing; reassess at 2-week follow-up
medications.maximum_daily_dose: No established maximum — preservative-free formulations safe for frequent use
medications.mechanism: Lubricates ocular surface, dilutes and washes away residual irritants, stabilizes tear film
common_side_effects: Transient mild blurring immediately after instillation (resolves within 1-2 minutes)
warnings: AVOID preserved artificial tears (containing benzalkonium chloride/BAK) — BAK is itself a corneal irritant and will worsen symptoms
Do not use while contact lenses are in place unless specifically labeled for contact lens use
Refrigerate opened vials for comfort; discard single-use vials after one use
medications.monitoring: Symptom frequency and severity at 1-2 week follow-up
medications.evidence_grade: A (High Quality) — TFOS DEWS II; NNT 4-6 for meaningful symptom improvement at 4 weeks

medication_reconciliation.drug_drug_interactions: None significant for topical preservative-free artificial tears
medication_reconciliation.age_considerations: Safe for age 54; no geriatric dose adjustment needed
medication_reconciliation.pregnancy_lactation: Safe — not applicable to this patient
medication_reconciliation.cost_access: OTC, widely available, $8-20/month; generic options available

medications.name: Ketotifen Fumarate Ophthalmic Solution 0.035%
medications.frequency: Twice daily (every 8-12 hours)
medications.duration: 2-4 weeks; reassess at follow-up
medications.mechanism: Dual-action: H1 antihistamine receptor antagonist + mast cell stabilizer; reduces histamine-mediated conjunctival hyperemia, tearing, and pruritus
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to ketotifen or any component of the formulation
Do NOT use while contact lenses are in place — remove lenses, wait 10 minutes before reinserting
common_side_effects: Transient burning or stinging on instillation (10-25% of patients)
warnings: IMPORTANT: Do not initiate until ophthalmology exam excludes corneal foreign body, abrasion, or herpetic lesion — topical antihistamines can mask symptoms of progressive corneal pathology
Not recommended if herpes zoster ophthalmicus is suspected — antihistamines do not treat viral infection and delay diagnosis
Additive anticholinergic effect if combined with systemic antihistamines — monitor for dry eye worsening, urinary symptoms (prostate considerations in 54-year-old male)
If symptoms worsen or do not improve within 72 hours of initiation, stop and contact ophthalmologist
medications.monitoring: Symptom response at 72 hours and 2 weeks; watch for worsening or new symptoms
medications.evidence_grade: A (High Quality) — AAO Preferred Practice Pattern; NNT 3-4 for clinically meaningful symptom reduction at 2 weeks

medication_reconciliation.drug_drug_interactions: Additive anticholinergic effect with systemic antihistamines (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine) — avoid combination or monitor closely; minimal systemic absorption from topical use reduces interaction risk
medication_reconciliation.renal_adjustment: Not applicable — topical use with minimal systemic absorption
medication_reconciliation.age_considerations: Safe for age 54; anticholinergic burden consideration relevant for older males with benign prostatic hyperplasia — topical route minimizes systemic exposure
medication_reconciliation.allergy_crossreactivity: None identified with common drug classes
medication_reconciliation.cost_access: OTC, $12-18/bottle; generic versions available at major pharmacies

medications.name: Olopatadine Hydrochloride Ophthalmic Solution 0.1% (Patanol) — SECOND LINE
medications.requires_prescription: 0.1% requires prescription; 0.2% (Pataday Once Daily) now OTC
medications.frequency: Twice daily (0.1%) or once daily (0.2%)
medications.duration: 2-4 weeks; reassess
medications.maximum_daily_dose: 2 drops per eye per day (0.1%); 1 drop per eye per day (0.2%)
medications.mechanism: Selective H1 antihistamine + mast cell stabilizer with superior receptor selectivity vs. ketotifen; also inhibits eosinophil activation
warnings: Same precautions as ketotifen — do not use before ophthalmology exam excludes corneal pathology
Remove contact lenses before instillation; wait 10 minutes before reinserting
Do not use if HZO suspected
medications.monitoring: Symptom response at 1-2 weeks
medications.evidence_grade: A (High Quality) — AAO Grade A; NNT 3-4; superior to placebo in multiple RCTs

medication_reconciliation.drug_drug_interactions: Minimal — same anticholinergic additive effect consideration as ketotifen
medication_reconciliation.cost_access: Pataday OTC $15-22; Patanol Rx — check insurance; generic olopatadine available

medications.name: Omega-3 Fatty Acid Supplement (EPA/DHA)
medications.frequency: Once or twice daily with meals
medications.duration: Minimum 3 months for dry eye benefit; ongoing
medications.maximum_daily_dose: 3000mg EPA+DHA/day (higher doses require physician supervision due to antiplatelet effects)
medications.mechanism: Reduces meibomian gland inflammation, improves lipid layer quality of tear film, reduces evaporative dry eye
contraindications: Fish or shellfish allergy (use algae-based omega-3 as alternative)
Caution with anticoagulant therapy (warfarin, apixaban) — antiplatelet effect at high doses
common_side_effects: Fishy aftertaste (take with meals or use enteric-coated formulation)
GI upset (nausea, loose stools at high doses)
warnings: Inform physician if taking blood thinners — doses >2g/day may potentiate anticoagulant effect
Choose products with third-party testing (USP, NSF, IFOS certified) to ensure purity and accurate labeling
medications.monitoring: Dry eye symptom improvement at 3-month follow-up; no lab monitoring required at standard doses
medications.evidence_grade: B (Moderate Quality) — TFOS DEWS II; DREAM trial (2018) showed no benefit over placebo for omega-3 in DED, but subgroup analyses and other RCTs support benefit; reasonable adjunct given safety profile

medication_reconciliation.drug_drug_interactions: Potential additive antiplatelet effect with aspirin, NSAIDs, warfarin at high doses (>3g/day)
medication_reconciliation.age_considerations: Safe for age 54; cardiovascular benefit at standard doses
medication_reconciliation.cost_access: OTC, $15-40/month depending on brand and dose

treatment_plans.condition: Dry Eye Disease / Tear Film Instability (Secondary Diagnosis — Age 54, Smoke Exposure)
treatment_plans.note: To be formally diagnosed by ophthalmologist using TBUT, Schirmer's test, and corneal staining. Treatment overlaps significantly with irritant conjunctivitis management.

treatment_algorithm.step_1_conservative: Irritant avoidance, warm lid compresses BID, lid hygiene, humidifier, screen time reduction, omega-3 supplementation
treatment_algorithm.step_2_first_line: Preservative-free artificial tears 4-6x daily (same as above)
treatment_algorithm.step_3_second_line: Topical cyclosporine 0.05% (Restasis) or lifitegrast 5% (Xiidra) — prescription only, initiated by ophthalmologist if moderate-severe DED confirmed

Given that HZO remains a must-not-miss diagnosis in this 54-year-old male and has NOT yet been excluded by ophthalmologic examination, the treatment plan must explicitly gate cyclosporine initiation behind confirmed HZO/HSV exclusion. The treatment plan does note this warning, but the severity of this interaction warrants HIGH-level flagging to ensure no prescriber initiates this medication prematurely.

Ketotifen 0.035% and olopatadine are recommended with a conditional gate (post slit-lamp exam), but the treatment plan does not sufficiently emphasize that initiating ANY topical ophthalmic medication before ophthalmologic examination in a patient with unilateral microsecond lancinating pain could mask progressive corneal pathology (foreign body, corneal ulcer, early HZO dendrites). The conditional gate must be enforced as a hard stop, not a soft recommendation.

No current medication list has been documented for this patient. The research agent flags 'none documented' but this has NOT been verified. A 54-year-old male may be on antihypertensives, statins, anticoagulants, or other medications that could interact with recommended treatments. Medication reconciliation is INCOMPLETE and must be performed before any pharmacological treatment is initiated.

Omega-3 supplementation at doses above 2g/day carries a clinically relevant antiplatelet effect. Since no current medication list exists, it is unknown whether this patient is on aspirin, NSAIDs, warfarin, or other anticoagulants. moderate_issues: Topical ketorolac 0.5% is listed as a second-line option for corneal abrasion pain management. The treatment plan correctly notes it should only be used if corneal abrasion is confirmed and foreign body excluded. However, the plan does not explicitly state the maximum recommended duration for topical ketorolac (generally 3-5 days for corneal abrasion; prolonged use is associated with corneal melting, epithelial breakdown, and corneal perforation in rare cases). Duration limits must be explicitly communicated to the prescribing ophthalmologist.

Erythromycin ophthalmic ointment 0.5% is listed for post-foreign-body-removal prophylaxis. No allergy history to macrolides has been documented. Given the incomplete allergy history, this must be verified before prescribing. Cross-reactivity between erythromycin and other macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin) should be assessed.

The treatment plan recommends oral valacyclovir 1g TID x 7-10 days as an escalation pathway if HZO is confirmed. While this is guideline-concordant (AAO HZO Preferred Practice Pattern 2019), the plan does not document renal function status for this patient. Valacyclovir requires dose adjustment for renal impairment (CrCl <50 mL/min). Baseline renal function must be assessed before prescribing valacyclovir, particularly given the patient's age (54 years) where subclinical renal impairment is possible.

The treatment plan recommends warm lid compresses at 45 degrees Celsius for meibomian gland dysfunction. No contraindication check was performed for this intervention. Patients with rosacea, active lid infections, or certain contact lens types may require modified instructions. While low risk, the temperature specification (45C) should be accompanied by patient safety instructions to avoid burns, particularly given that ocular skin is thin and sensitive.

Preservative-free artificial tears are correctly recommended over preserved formulations. However, the plan does not specify that the patient should be counseled to check OTC product labels carefully, as many commonly purchased artificial tear products (e.g., Visine, Clear Eyes) contain vasoconstrictors (naphazoline, tetrahydrozoline) or preservatives (benzalkonium chloride/BAK) that are contraindicated in this clinical context and will worsen ocular surface disease. Rebound hyperemia from vasoconstrictors is a significant risk if the patient self-selects an inappropriate OTC product.
low_issues: The treatment plan recommends omega-3 supplementation with a note to choose products with third-party testing (USP, NSF, IFOS certified). This is appropriate but the patient should also be counseled that fish-based omega-3 products are contraindicated in fish or shellfish allergy. Allergy history to fish/shellfish has not been documented.

Shingrix (recombinant zoster vaccine) counseling is recommended per CDC/ACIP guidelines for adults 50 and older. This is appropriate and guideline-concordant. However, the plan does not note that Shingrix is contraindicated in patients with a known hypersensitivity to any component of the vaccine, and should be deferred if the patient has an active shingles episode (which, while low probability here, has not been fully excluded). Vaccination should be deferred until HZO is formally excluded.

The treatment plan does not include explicit return precautions documentation for the patient. While red flags are listed in the specialist consultation, the patient-facing output should include clear written return precautions: seek immediate care if vesicular rash develops on forehead, scalp, or nasal tip; if vision changes or blurring occurs; if photophobia develops; if pain escalates beyond current 5/10 or becomes constant; or if the eye becomes significantly more red or develops discharge.

If the patient drives or operates machinery, the transient blurring associated with artificial tear instillation and ophthalmic ointments should be communicated. Additionally, if the patient has occupational particulate exposure beyond the cannabis smoke incident, protective eyewear counseling is warranted.

The DREAM trial (2018) finding that omega-3 showed no benefit over placebo for dry eye disease is noted in the research agent output but the treatment plan still recommends omega-3 as an adjunct. This is a reasonable clinical decision given the favorable safety profile, but the patient should be counseled on the mixed evidence so they can make an informed decision about this supplement.

empathy.patient_summary:
Thank you for sharing what you have been going through. You are doing the right thing by getting this checked out. Here is what the medical team has found so far.

For the past 3 days, you have been having a quick, sharp pricking feeling in the outer corner of your left eye. It happens 2 to 3 times a day, lasts only a split second, and comes with some redness and watering of that eye. You mentioned being around marijuana smoke in an enclosed garage, and you suspect allergies may be playing a role.

The good news is that this does not appear to be an emergency right now. Your symptoms are most likely being caused by irritation from the smoke you were exposed to. Marijuana smoke contains chemicals that can irritate the surface of the eye, cause redness, and trigger watering. Think of it like getting a small amount of smoke in your eye from a campfire — it irritates the surface and your eye reacts by getting red and watery.

However, because the sharp feeling is only in ONE eye and has a very unusual quality — lasting just a fraction of a second — the medical team wants to make sure nothing else is going on. There are a few other possible explanations that need to be ruled out, including a tiny particle stuck on the surface of your eye, early signs of dry eye disease (which becomes more common after age 50), or in rare cases, a nerve-related cause. There are also a small number of more serious conditions that are unlikely but important to check for, which is why seeing an eye doctor soon is important.
action_checklist: SEE AN EYE DOCTOR WITHIN 24 TO 48 HOURS: You need a specialized eye exam called a slit-lamp examination. This is a painless exam where the doctor uses a bright light and microscope to look closely at the surface of your eye. They will also put a harmless orange dye (called fluorescein) in your eye to check for any scratches or particles. This exam cannot be done at a regular doctor's office — you need an eye doctor (ophthalmologist) or an urgent care clinic with eye equipment.

STOP ALL EXPOSURE TO MARIJUANA SMOKE RIGHT NOW: This is the single most important thing you can do today. Staying away from smoke — especially in enclosed spaces like a garage — is the number one treatment at this stage. Even secondhand smoke in a closed room can keep irritating your eye and slow down healing.
DO NOT RUB YOUR LEFT EYE: Rubbing can scratch the surface of your eye or push a tiny particle deeper into it. No matter how much it itches or feels uncomfortable, keep your hands away from your eye.

DO NOT START ANY EYE DROPS BEFORE YOUR EYE EXAM: It may be tempting to grab allergy eye drops or redness-relief drops from the pharmacy. Please wait until after your eye exam. Some eye drops can actually hide symptoms that the doctor needs to see. Also, many common redness-relief drops (like Visine or Clear Eyes) can make things worse with repeated use.

AVOID EYE DROPS THAT CONTAIN PRESERVATIVES OR VASOCONSTRICTORS: If your eye is very uncomfortable before your appointment, you may use preservative-free artificial tears (look for the words 'preservative-free' on the label — brands like Systane Ultra PF, Refresh Optive PF, or TheraTears PF). These are safe to use and will help rinse and soothe the eye surface. Do NOT use drops that say 'gets the red out' — these can cause rebound redness.

APPLY A COOL COMPRESS FOR COMFORT: Close your left eye and gently place a clean, cool damp cloth over it for 10 to 15 minutes, up to 3 times a day. This can help reduce redness and discomfort while you wait for your appointment.
IF YOU WEAR CONTACT LENSES, TAKE THEM OUT NOW AND DO NOT PUT THEM BACK IN: Do not wear contact lenses until an eye doctor says it is safe to do so.

CHECK YOUR FOREHEAD, SCALP, AND THE TIP OF YOUR NOSE FOR ANY NEW RASH OR BLISTERS: One of the conditions the team wants to rule out is called shingles of the eye (herpes zoster ophthalmicus). This can start with eye pain before any rash appears. If you notice any blisters, redness, or a rash on the left side of your forehead, scalp, or the tip of your nose, this becomes urgent — go to the emergency room or call your doctor immediately.

WRITE DOWN YOUR SYMPTOMS BEFORE YOUR APPOINTMENT: Note when the sharp feeling happens, how long it lasts, whether it is getting better or worse, and anything that seems to trigger it (like blinking, bright light, or wind). This information will help your eye doctor a lot.

BRING A LIST OF ALL YOUR CURRENT MEDICATIONS AND SUPPLEMENTS TO YOUR APPOINTMENT: Include any vitamins, herbal supplements, blood thinners, allergy pills, or any other medicines you take. This is important for your doctor to know before starting any treatment.

ASK YOUR DOCTOR ABOUT THE SHINGLES VACCINE (SHINGRIX): At age 54, you are in the age group where doctors recommend this vaccine. It is highly effective at preventing a type of shingles that can affect the eye. This is something to discuss at your appointment — not an emergency, but an important conversation to have.
when_to_seek_help: GO TO THE EMERGENCY ROOM OR CALL 911 RIGHT AWAY IF: You notice any blisters, sores, or a rash appearing on your forehead, scalp, around your left eye, or on the tip of your nose. This could be a sign of shingles affecting the eye, which needs treatment within hours to protect your vision.
GO TO THE EMERGENCY ROOM OR CALL YOUR DOCTOR IMMEDIATELY IF: Your vision becomes blurry, cloudy, or changes in any way — even briefly.
SEEK URGENT CARE SAME DAY IF: You develop sensitivity to light (bright lights suddenly hurt your eye or make you want to close it).
SEEK URGENT CARE SAME DAY IF: The pain in your eye gets significantly worse, changes from a quick flash to a constant ache, or you would rate it higher than a 7 out of 10.
SEEK URGENT CARE SAME DAY IF: You notice halos or rainbow-colored rings around lights, especially at night. This can be a sign of pressure building up inside the eye.
SEEK URGENT CARE SAME DAY IF: Your eye becomes much more red, swollen, or starts producing discharge (yellow or green fluid).
SEEK URGENT CARE SAME DAY IF: The area around your eye — your eyelid, forehead, or cheek — becomes red, warm, or swollen.
CALL YOUR DOCTOR IF: Your symptoms are not improving after 3 to 5 days of avoiding smoke and using preservative-free artificial tears.
CALL YOUR DOCTOR IF: You develop any new symptoms anywhere on your body, such as fever, fatigue, or skin changes.
empathy.emotional_support: It is completely understandable to feel a little anxious when something is going on with your eye — our eyes are precious, and even a small discomfort can feel worrying. You are taking exactly the right step by seeking care. The fact that you can still see clearly, that the sensation only lasts a split second, and that there is a clear explanation (smoke exposure) is genuinely reassuring. Most people in your situation find that once the irritant is removed and the eye gets a proper check, things improve quickly. Many people experience eye irritation from smoke exposure, and it is very treatable. The medical team is being thorough — not because they expect the worst, but because they want to make sure nothing is missed so you can get the right care and feel better as soon as possible. You are not alone in this, and with the right follow-up, the outlook is very good.

diagnostician.problem_representation: 35-year-old female with subacute-onset persistent unilateral (right-sided) throbbing headache of 2 weeks duration, rated 6/10, associated with photophobia and intermittent nausea, without reported focal neurological deficits, fever, or neck stiffness.

differential_diagnosis.reasoning: This is the most common primary headache in women of reproductive age. The illness script is a strong match: unilateral throbbing headache, photophobia, nausea, moderate severity (6/10), female sex, age 35. Migraine prevalence in women aged 25-44 is approximately 25%. The ICHD-3 criteria require at least 5 attacks lasting 4-72 hours with unilateral location, pulsating quality, moderate-to-severe intensity, and aggravation by routine physical activity, plus nausea/vomiting or photophobia/phonophobia. The 2-week persistent course is somewhat atypical for episodic migraine but could represent new-onset migraine, status migrainosus (if continuous >72 hours), or chronic migraine transformation. Bayesian reasoning: high pre-test probability (~25% base rate in this demographic) with strong LR+ for unilateral throbbing + photophobia + nausea combination (LR+ ~3-5). Post-test probability approximately 50-60%. Confidence reduced from higher because the 2-week continuous/persistent nature is atypical and mandates exclusion of secondary causes.
opposing_features: 2-week persistent duration is atypical for typical episodic migraine
new onset without prior headache history mentioned
no information on aggravation by physical activity

differential_diagnosis.reasoning: CVST must be considered in any woman of reproductive age with new subacute headache. Risk factors include oral contraceptive use, pregnancy/postpartum state, thrombophilia, and obesity. The headache in CVST is typically progressive over days to weeks (matches 2-week course), can be unilateral, and may mimic migraine with nausea and photophobia. Prevalence is low (~5 per million/year) but dramatically higher in women on OCPs (LR+ ~5-6 for OCP use). Without knowing OCP status, pregnancy status, or BMI, this remains an important consideration. The absence of reported focal deficits, seizures, or papilledema lowers probability but does not exclude early CVST. Bayesian reasoning: low pre-test probability (~1-2%) but the subacute progressive course in a reproductive-age female raises this to approximately 8-15% depending on risk factors. This is a must-not-miss diagnosis because delayed treatment leads to venous infarction, hemorrhage, and death.
opposing_features: no reported focal neurological deficits
no reported seizures
no reported papilledema
severity only 6/10 (CVST headaches often severe)

differential_diagnosis.reasoning: IIH classically affects obese women of childbearing age. Presents with progressive headache (often daily), nausea, photophobia, and visual symptoms including transient visual obscurations and diplopia. Papilledema is the hallmark finding. The 2-week subacute progressive course fits well. Without knowing the patient's BMI or visual acuity/field status, this cannot be excluded. Key discriminating feature: fundoscopic exam showing papilledema would dramatically increase probability (LR+ >10). Absence of papilledema on careful exam would significantly lower probability (LR- ~0.2). Bayesian reasoning: base rate ~1-2 per 100,000 general population but ~20 per 100,000 in obese women of childbearing age. Pre-test probability ~2-5% depending on BMI; post-test depends heavily on fundoscopy and opening pressure.
opposing_features: no visual obscurations reported
no diplopia reported
BMI unknown
severity moderate rather than severe

differential_diagnosis.condition: Intracranial mass lesion (primary brain tumor or metastasis)
differential_diagnosis.reasoning: New persistent headache in an adult requires exclusion of space-occupying lesion. Brain tumors can present with progressive headache, nausea (from raised ICP), and photophobia. Headache from mass lesion is classically worse in the morning, worsened by Valsalva, and progressive. Unilateral headache can localize to the side of the lesion. At age 35, primary tumors (glioma, meningioma) are more likely than metastatic disease. Prevalence of brain tumors presenting as headache is low (~0.1-0.5% of headache presentations in primary care) but the 2-week progressive course raises concern. Bayesian reasoning: pre-test ~1-2%; the subacute progressive nature provides LR+ ~2-3, but absence of focal deficits, morning predominance, and Valsalva worsening provides LR- ~0.3-0.5. Post-test probability ~3-8%.
opposing_features: no focal neurological deficits reported
no morning predominance mentioned
no Valsalva worsening mentioned
no seizures
no personality changes

differential_diagnosis.reasoning: If the patient has been self-treating with analgesics (NSAIDs, acetaminophen, triptans) for >10-15 days per month, medication overuse headache should be considered. MOH typically transforms episodic headache into daily or near-daily headache. The 2-week duration could represent the transformation period. Without medication history, this cannot be assessed. Bayesian reasoning: pre-test probability depends entirely on analgesic use frequency, which is unknown.
opposing_features: no medication use history provided
unilateral and throbbing pattern more typical of migraine than MOH (which is often bilateral and pressing)

differential_diagnosis.reasoning: Tension-type headache is the most prevalent primary headache disorder. However, the illness script is a poor match: TTH is typically bilateral, pressing/tightening (not throbbing), mild-to-moderate, without nausea or photophobia (or only one of the two in ICHD-3 criteria). This patient has unilateral throbbing pain with both photophobia AND nausea, which argues strongly against TTH. Bayesian reasoning: high base rate (~40% lifetime prevalence) but the clinical features provide strong LR- (~0.1-0.2) for TTH. Post-test probability low.
opposing_features: unilateral (TTH typically bilateral)
throbbing (TTH typically pressing/tightening)
photophobia present (atypical for TTH)
nausea present (atypical for TTH)

differential_diagnosis.reasoning: While classic SAH presents with thunderclap headache (worst headache of life, maximal at onset), a sentinel or warning leak from an unruptured aneurysm can present as a subacute headache days to weeks before major rupture. At age 35, aneurysmal SAH is uncommon but not rare. The absence of thunderclap onset, severe intensity, neck stiffness, and altered consciousness argues against acute SAH, but a sentinel leak can be subtle. Bayesian reasoning: pre-test probability very low (~0.5-1%) given the subacute non-thunderclap presentation (LR- for absence of thunderclap ~0.2). However, this is a must-not-miss diagnosis because missed sentinel leak has catastrophic consequences (major SAH with 50% mortality).
opposing_features: no thunderclap onset described
severity only 6/10
2-week duration without deterioration
no neck stiffness reported
no altered consciousness

differential_diagnosis.reasoning: Cervicogenic headache is a secondary headache arising from cervical spine pathology. It is typically unilateral, non-throbbing, and associated with neck pain/stiffness and reduced cervical ROM. The throbbing quality and photophobia/nausea are atypical. Without information about neck symptoms or occupation (desk work, etc.), this remains a low-probability consideration.
opposing_features: throbbing quality atypical
photophobia atypical
nausea atypical
no neck pain reported

differential_diagnosis.reasoning: Included for completeness but extremely unlikely at age 35. GCA almost exclusively affects patients >50 years old (mean age 70). The pre-test probability is essentially zero in this age group. No jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, or visual symptoms reported. ESR/CRP would be expected to be markedly elevated. Excluded from serious consideration based on age alone.
opposing_features: age 35 (virtually excludes GCA)
no jaw claudication
no scalp tenderness
no visual loss
no polymyalgia symptoms

differential_diagnosis.reasoning: Acute bacterial meningitis is unlikely given the 2-week indolent course without fever or severe toxicity. However, subacute/chronic meningitis (TB, fungal, carcinomatous) can present with progressive headache, photophobia, and nausea over weeks. Without information about immunocompromised status, TB exposure, or travel history, this remains a low but non-zero consideration. The absence of fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status argues against but does not exclude chronic meningitis.
opposing_features: no fever reported
no neck stiffness reported
no altered mental status
2-week course without deterioration

vindicate_analysis.vascular: CVST (12% — must rule out in reproductive-age female), SAH/sentinel leak (4% — must-not-miss), migraine (55% — neurovascular primary headache). Hypertensive headache cannot be assessed without BP.
vindicate_analysis.infectious: Subacute/chronic meningitis (3%) — low probability but cannot exclude without exam and history. Acute bacterial meningitis essentially excluded by 2-week indolent course without fever.
vindicate_analysis.neoplastic: Intracranial mass lesion (8%) — must exclude with imaging given new persistent headache. Paraneoplastic syndrome unlikely at this age without systemic symptoms.
vindicate_analysis.degenerative_deficiency: Cervicogenic headache (4%) from cervical degenerative disease. Vitamin B12 or other nutritional deficiency headache — very unlikely as primary cause.
vindicate_analysis.iatrogenic_intoxication: Medication overuse headache (7%) — requires medication history. Carbon monoxide exposure — would expect bilateral headache and other household members affected. OCP use could contribute to CVST risk.
vindicate_analysis.congenital: Chiari malformation type I can present with headache, typically occipital and worsened by Valsalva/cough. Unilateral throbbing pattern is atypical. Low probability (~1%) but would be identified on MRI.
vindicate_analysis.autoimmune_allergic: GCA essentially excluded by age. CNS vasculitis is rare but can present with progressive headache — very low probability without systemic autoimmune features. Sarcoidosis with neurosarcoid — extremely rare.
vindicate_analysis.traumatic: No trauma history reported. Post-concussive headache excluded in absence of head injury.
vindicate_analysis.endocrine_metabolic: Thyroid dysfunction can cause headache but is rarely the primary presentation. Pregnancy should be excluded (hormonal changes can trigger new migraine). Pheochromocytoma — typically paroxysmal with hypertension.

must_not_miss.reasoning: Reproductive-age female with subacute progressive headache. OCP use and pregnancy are major risk factors. Delayed diagnosis leads to venous infarction, hemorrhagic transformation, and death. Mortality 5-10% even with treatment.
recommended_tests: MRI brain with MRV
D-dimer (if low clinical suspicion, negative D-dimer has good NPV)
Pregnancy test
Assess OCP use

must_not_miss.reasoning: New persistent headache requires imaging to exclude space-occupying lesion. Early detection of brain tumors significantly improves outcomes.
recommended_tests: MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast

must_not_miss.reasoning: Can cause permanent vision loss if untreated. Fundoscopic exam is critical screening tool. Requires LP with opening pressure for definitive diagnosis.
recommended_tests: Fundoscopic exam
Visual field testing
MRI brain with MRV (to exclude CVST and look for IIH signs: empty sella, optic nerve sheath distension, transverse sinus stenosis)
LP with opening pressure if imaging suggestive

must_not_miss.reasoning: Missed sentinel leak can lead to catastrophic major SAH with 50% mortality. Low probability given presentation but consequences of missing are devastating.
recommended_tests: CT head without contrast (sensitivity decreases after 6 hours from onset)
If CT negative and clinical suspicion persists: LP for xanthochromia
CTA head if aneurysm suspected

must_not_miss.reasoning: TB meningitis, fungal meningitis, or carcinomatous meningitis can present insidiously. Requires clinical assessment of meningeal signs and risk factor evaluation.
recommended_tests: Neurological exam for meningeal signs
LP with cell count, protein, glucose, cultures, cytology if clinical suspicion

anchoring_bias_check.initial_anchor: Migraine without aura — the most common diagnosis in this demographic with these symptoms. There is strong temptation to anchor on this and not pursue workup.
anchoring_bias_check.unexplained_by_top_diagnosis: The 2-week persistent/continuous nature is atypical for episodic migraine. New-onset migraine at age 35 is possible but less common than onset in teens/twenties. Without prior headache history, this is a first presentation requiring secondary cause exclusion.
anchoring_bias_check.alternative_considerations: CVST can perfectly mimic migraine. IIH can present identically. A slowly growing mass lesion can produce migraine-like symptoms. The key differentiator is imaging and fundoscopic exam, not clinical features alone.
anchoring_bias_check.availability_bias_check: Migraine is extremely common and frequently seen — must resist the urge to diagnose without excluding dangerous mimics, especially given the new-onset subacute course.
anchoring_bias_check.atypical_common_disease: Could this be an atypical presentation of a common condition? Yes — new-onset migraine is common, but the persistent 2-week course without clear episodic pattern is atypical and warrants investigation.
anchoring_bias_check.unifying_diagnosis: Migraine explains all symptoms. However, CVST also explains all symptoms and adds the subacute progressive timeline. IIH explains all symptoms if the patient is obese. Imaging is required to differentiate.

discriminating_features.if_positive: Dramatically increases probability of IIH (LR+ >10) or intracranial mass. Essentially excludes primary migraine as sole diagnosis.
discriminating_features.if_negative: Significantly reduces IIH probability (LR- ~0.2) but does not fully exclude early IIH or other secondary causes.

discriminating_features.if_positive: Mass lesion on MRI confirms intracranial neoplasm. Absent flow void on MRV confirms CVST. Empty sella/optic nerve sheath distension suggests IIH.
discriminating_features.if_negative: Normal MRI/MRV essentially excludes mass lesion, CVST, and provides strong evidence against IIH (LR- ~0.05-0.1 for mass, ~0.02 for CVST).

discriminating_features.if_positive: May show mass, hemorrhage, hydrocephalus, or calcification. Sensitivity for SAH decreases significantly after 6-12 hours from onset.
discriminating_features.if_negative: Normal CT does not exclude CVST, IIH, or small mass lesions. MRI is superior. However, normal CT significantly reduces probability of acute hemorrhage and large mass.

discriminating_features.if_positive: Strongly suggests structural lesion (mass, CVST with venous infarction, stroke). LR+ >5 for secondary headache cause.
discriminating_features.if_negative: Reduces but does not exclude secondary causes. Many secondary headaches present without focal deficits early in course.

discriminating_features.if_positive: Increases CVST risk 5-7 fold. Combined with smoking, risk increases further. Raises CVST pre-test probability from ~1-2% to ~5-10%.
discriminating_features.if_negative: Reduces CVST probability but does not exclude (many other risk factors exist).

recommended_tests: 1. IMMEDIATE: Complete neurological examination including fundoscopy, visual fields, cranial nerves, motor/sensory, cerebellar, gait, and meningeal signs — highest yield bedside assessment to stratify risk
2. IMMEDIATE: Vital signs including blood pressure (hypertensive emergency can cause headache), temperature (infection screen), heart rate
3. URGENT: Pregnancy test (urine hCG) — affects differential (pregnancy-related CVST, eclampsia) and treatment options

4. URGENT: MRI brain with and without gadolinium + MRV — gold standard to evaluate for mass lesion, CVST, IIH signs, Chiari malformation, and other structural causes. Superior to CT for posterior fossa and venous pathology
5. SAME DAY: Basic labs — CBC (infection, anemia, polycythemia), BMP (metabolic causes), ESR/CRP (inflammatory/infectious causes, GCA screening though low probability at age 35)
6. CONDITIONAL: D-dimer — if CVST suspicion is moderate and MRV not immediately available, negative D-dimer has reasonable NPV
7. CONDITIONAL: Lumbar puncture with opening pressure — if fundoscopy shows papilledema, or if MRI/MRV suggests IIH, or if chronic meningitis is suspected
8. CONDITIONAL: CT head without contrast — if MRI not immediately available, as initial screen for hemorrhage and large mass lesions
9. CONDITIONAL: CTA head — if sentinel SAH or aneurysm suspected based on clinical features or CT findings

follow_up_questions.question: Is this headache continuous for the entire 2 weeks, or does it come and go in discrete episodes? If episodic, how long does each episode last?
follow_up_questions.targets: Differentiates episodic migraine (attacks lasting 4-72 hours with pain-free intervals) from continuous headache (more concerning for CVST, IIH, mass lesion, or chronic daily headache). Continuous headache significantly raises probability of secondary cause (LR+ ~2-3 for secondary headache).

follow_up_questions.question: Are you currently taking oral contraceptive pills, hormone replacement therapy, or any other medications? Have you been taking any pain medications for these headaches, and if so, how often?
follow_up_questions.targets: OCP use dramatically increases CVST risk (LR+ ~5-7). Frequent analgesic use (>10-15 days/month) raises medication overuse headache probability. Other medications may have headache as side effect (tetracyclines, vitamin A derivatives, steroids).

follow_up_questions.question: Have you noticed any changes in your vision — blurring, double vision, brief episodes of vision going gray or dark (especially with position changes), or any blind spots?
follow_up_questions.targets: Transient visual obscurations are highly specific for IIH (LR+ >5). Diplopia from CN VI palsy suggests raised ICP (IIH or mass). Visual field deficits suggest structural lesion. Positive responses would significantly increase probability of secondary headache causes.

pico_question.population: 35-year-old female presenting with 2-week history of new-onset unilateral (right-sided) throbbing headache (6/10 severity) with photophobia and intermittent nausea
pico_question.intervention: Diagnostic workup to differentiate primary migraine from secondary headache causes (neuroimaging, laboratory studies, clinical examination); acute and preventive treatment if migraine confirmed
pico_question.comparison: Empiric migraine treatment without neuroimaging vs. structured diagnostic evaluation with imaging to exclude secondary causes
pico_question.outcome: Accurate diagnosis (ruling out cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, intracranial mass, idiopathic intracranial hypertension), symptom relief, prevention of missed life-threatening pathology, reduction in headache frequency and disability

diagnostic_guidelines.recommendation: Migraine without aura requires ≥5 attacks lasting 4–72 hours with at least 2 of: unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe intensity, aggravation by routine activity; AND at least 1 of: nausea/vomiting, photophobia AND phonophobia. This patient meets quality criteria (unilateral, throbbing, moderate severity, photophobia, nausea) but the 2-week persistent/continuous course is ATYPICAL — classic migraine attacks are episodic (4–72 hours per attack), not continuous over 2 weeks.
diagnostic_guidelines.evidence_grade: GRADE A — ICHD-3 criteria are internationally validated with high sensitivity and specificity for migraine diagnosis
diagnostic_guidelines.clinical_implication: If headache is truly continuous for 2 weeks rather than recurrent discrete episodes, this does NOT meet ICHD-3 migraine criteria and raises concern for secondary headache or new daily persistent headache (NDPH)

diagnostic_guidelines.source: American Headache Society (AHS) — Consensus Statement on Neuroimaging, 2019; updated position 2023
diagnostic_guidelines.recommendation: Neuroimaging is recommended for patients with: (1) new-onset headache in adults >30 years with atypical features, (2) change in headache pattern, (3) headache not meeting strict criteria for primary headache disorder, (4) abnormal neurological examination, (5) headache with red flags (SNOOP10 mnemonic). MRI brain with and without contrast is preferred over CT for non-emergent evaluation. MRV should be added if cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) is suspected.
diagnostic_guidelines.evidence_grade: GRADE B — Based on systematic reviews of diagnostic accuracy studies and expert consensus
diagnostic_guidelines.clinical_implication: This patient warrants neuroimaging given new-onset persistent headache over 2 weeks that does not clearly fit episodic migraine pattern

diagnostic_guidelines.source: American Academy of Neurology (AAN) / AHS — Practice Guideline: Evaluation of Headache, 2019 Update
diagnostic_guidelines.recommendation: Apply SNOOP10 red flag screening for secondary headache causes. Relevant SNOOP10 flags for this patient include: S-Systemic symptoms/disease, N-Neurologic symptoms, O-Onset sudden, O-Older age (>50, less relevant here), P-Pattern change or new onset, P-Positional, P-Precipitated by Valsalva, P-Papilledema, P-Progressive, P-Pregnancy/postpartum. This patient triggers: NEW ONSET and PERSISTENT/PROGRESSIVE pattern.
diagnostic_guidelines.evidence_grade: GRADE B — Based on systematic reviews and validated screening tools
snoop10_flags_identified: Need to assess: positional component (IIH), papilledema, pregnancy status

diagnostic_guidelines.source: European Headache Federation (EHF) — Guideline on Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension, 2020
diagnostic_guidelines.recommendation: Consider IIH in women of reproductive age with new headache, especially if overweight (BMI >30). Key features: daily headache (often bilateral but can be unilateral), worse with Valsalva/positional changes, pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations, papilledema on fundoscopy. Diagnosis requires: elevated opening pressure on lumbar puncture (>25 cmH2O), normal CSF composition, neuroimaging excluding mass/hydrocephalus.
diagnostic_guidelines.evidence_grade: GRADE B — Based on cohort studies and diagnostic criteria validation
diagnostic_guidelines.clinical_implication: Must assess BMI, perform fundoscopy, and ask about positional worsening and visual symptoms

diagnostic_guidelines.source: American Heart Association / American Stroke Association (AHA/ASA) — Scientific Statement on CVST, 2011 (reaffirmed 2020)
diagnostic_guidelines.recommendation: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis should be considered in women of reproductive age presenting with new persistent headache, especially if on oral contraceptives or in postpartum period. Headache is the most common symptom (90% of cases), often progressive over days to weeks. Diagnosis: MRI brain + MR venography (MRV) or CT venography (CTV). D-dimer has limited sensitivity for subacute CVST.
diagnostic_guidelines.evidence_grade: GRADE B — Based on large prospective registries (ISCVT) and systematic reviews
diagnostic_guidelines.clinical_implication: CRITICAL to obtain OCP use history and pregnancy status; MRV should be considered in diagnostic workup

treatment_guidelines.source: AHS — Consensus Statement on Acute Migraine Treatment, 2021
treatment_guidelines.recommendation: For acute migraine: First-line includes NSAIDs (ibuprofen 400–600mg, naproxen 500mg), triptans (sumatriptan 50–100mg PO, rizatriptan 10mg), or combination NSAID + triptan. Antiemetics (metoclopramide 10mg, ondansetron 4mg) for associated nausea. Acetaminophen 1000mg is an alternative for mild-moderate attacks.
treatment_guidelines.evidence_grade: GRADE A — Multiple high-quality RCTs and meta-analyses

nnt_data.sumatriptan_100mg: NNT for pain-free at 2 hours = 4.7 (95% CI 4.0–5.7)
nnt_data.ibuprofen_400mg: NNT for pain-free at 2 hours = 7.2 (95% CI 5.9–9.2)
nnt_data.naproxen_500mg: NNT for pain-free at 2 hours = 8.3 (95% CI 6.1–13.0)
nnt_data.rizatriptan_10mg: NNT for pain-free at 2 hours = 3.1 (95% CI 2.7–3.6)

treatment_guidelines.caveat: Do NOT initiate triptans until secondary causes (especially CVST) are excluded — triptans are vasoconstrictive and contraindicated in vascular pathology

treatment_guidelines.source: AHS / AAN — Practice Guideline: Prevention of Episodic Migraine, 2012 (reaffirmed 2021)
treatment_guidelines.recommendation: Preventive therapy indicated if ≥4 headache days/month, significant disability, or failure of acute therapy. First-line options: topiramate 50–100mg/day (Level A), propranolol 80–240mg/day (Level A), amitriptyline 25–150mg/day (Level B), valproate 500–1000mg/day (Level A — but CONTRAINDICATED in women of reproductive age without reliable contraception due to teratogenicity).
treatment_guidelines.evidence_grade: GRADE A for topiramate and propranolol; GRADE B for amitriptyline

nnt_data.topiramate_100mg: NNT for ≥50% reduction in migraine frequency = 4–5

treatment_guidelines.caveat: Preventive therapy discussion premature until diagnosis is confirmed and secondary causes excluded

treatment_guidelines.source: AHS — Position Statement on CGRP Monoclonal Antibodies, 2022
treatment_guidelines.recommendation: CGRP mAbs (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab) are FDA-approved for migraine prevention. Consider if traditional preventives fail or are contraindicated. Erenumab 70–140mg SC monthly.
treatment_guidelines.evidence_grade: GRADE A — Multiple phase III RCTs (STRIVE, ARISE, EVOLVE-1/2, REGAIN)

nnt_data.erenumab_140mg: NNT for ≥50% reduction in monthly migraine days = 4–5 (episodic); 5–7 (chronic)

drug_interactions.note: No current medications reported. Key interactions to screen for once treatment is initiated:

potential_interactions.clinical_effect: Agitation, hyperthermia, tachycardia, clonus — rare in practice
potential_interactions.management: AHS position (2018): Risk is very low; combination can be used with monitoring. FDA black box warning remains but is considered overly conservative by headache specialists.
potential_interactions.evidence_grade: GRADE C — Based on case reports and pharmacological reasoning; large observational studies show very low absolute risk (~0.03%)

potential_interactions.mechanism: Additive vasoconstriction
potential_interactions.clinical_effect: Prolonged vasospasm, ischemia
potential_interactions.management: Do not use within 24 hours of each other

potential_interactions.mechanism: Topiramate induces CYP3A4, reducing ethinyl estradiol levels by up to 18–30% at doses ≥200mg/day

potential_interactions.clinical_effect: Major congenital malformations in 10–11% of exposed pregnancies; IQ reduction of 7–10 points
potential_interactions.management: Absolutely contraindicated in women of childbearing potential unless on highly effective contraception AND no alternative exists. Pregnancy test required before initiation.

potential_interactions.mechanism: Additive bleeding risk — NSAIDs inhibit platelet function + anticoagulant effect
potential_interactions.clinical_effect: Increased GI and intracranial hemorrhage risk
potential_interactions.management: If CVST is diagnosed and anticoagulation initiated, avoid NSAIDs; use acetaminophen for analgesia

migraine.sex_distribution: Female:Male ratio = 3:1 (17.1% in women vs 5.6% in men)

migraine.this_patient_pretest_probability: HIGH — 35-year-old female is in the highest-risk demographic. Estimated pre-test probability for migraine as cause of headache: 40–60% based on demographics and symptom profile alone
migraine.disability_burden: GBD 2019: #2 cause of years lived with disability globally; #1 in women aged 15–49

cerebral_venous_sinus_thrombosis.sex_distribution: Female:Male = 3:1 (driven by OCP use, pregnancy, postpartum)

idiopathic_intracranial_hypertension.incidence: Overall: 0.9–1.0 per 100,000/year; in obese women aged 20–44: 12–20 per 100,000/year
idiopathic_intracranial_hypertension.this_patient_pretest_probability: LOW if normal BMI (estimated <1%); MODERATE if obese (estimated 3–8%)
