intracranial_mass_lesion.incidence_primary_brain_tumor: 7.1 per 100,000/year (all types); meningioma most common in women (F:M = 2:1)
intracranial_mass_lesion.this_patient_pretest_probability: LOW — estimated 1–2% for new headache presentation in this age group
intracranial_mass_lesion.red_flags_increasing_probability: Progressive worsening, worse in morning/with Valsalva, focal neurological deficits, seizures, personality change

new_daily_persistent_headache.characteristics: Distinctive onset: patient can pinpoint exact day headache began. Continuous from onset. No prior headache history. Often refractory to treatment.
new_daily_persistent_headache.this_patient_relevance: If patient can identify exact onset date and headache has been truly continuous (not episodic), NDPH should be considered. Diagnosis of exclusion after secondary causes ruled out.

primary_diagnostic_consideration.pre_test_probability: 40–60% based on demographics and symptom profile

specialist.reason_for_consultation: Evaluation of new-onset persistent unilateral throbbing headache of 2 weeks duration in a 35-year-old female with photophobia and nausea, to differentiate primary migraine from secondary headache causes including cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST), idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), intracranial mass lesion, and sentinel subarachnoid hemorrhage.
specialist.specialist_assessment: This 35-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of new-onset right-sided throbbing headache (6/10 severity) with photophobia and intermittent nausea. From a neurology standpoint, the symptom profile is phenotypically consistent with migraine without aura — unilateral, pulsating quality, moderate intensity, with associated photophobia and nausea — which satisfies the qualitative ICHD-3 criteria. However, several features mandate a thorough secondary headache workup before accepting a primary headache diagnosis: (1) The 2-week persistent/subacute course is atypical for episodic migraine, which classically presents as discrete attacks lasting 4–72 hours with pain-free intervals. If this headache has been continuous for 14 days, it does NOT meet ICHD-3 criteria for migraine without aura and instead raises concern for new daily persistent headache (NDPH) or a secondary etiology. (2) This appears to be a new-onset headache without established prior headache history, which in an adult over 30 triggers SNOOP10 red flags for 'New onset' and 'Progressive/persistent pattern.' (3) The patient is a woman of reproductive age, placing her at elevated risk for CVST (especially if on combined oral contraceptives, RR 5.5–7.9x) and IIH (especially if obese, RR 11–20x). The ICHD-3 criterion 'not better accounted for by another ICHD-3 diagnosis' cannot be satisfied until secondary causes are excluded by appropriate investigation. My leading differential remains migraine without aura (~55% probability), but CVST (~12%), IIH (~10%), intracranial mass (~8%), medication overuse headache (~7%), sentinel SAH (~4%), and chronic meningitis (~3%) must be systematically excluded. The key discriminating investigations are fundoscopic examination (papilledema dramatically shifts probability toward IIH or mass effect) and MRI brain with MRV (which can simultaneously evaluate for mass lesion, CVST, IIH radiographic signs, Chiari malformation, and parenchymal abnormalities). A normal comprehensive neurological examination and normal MRI/MRV would raise post-test probability for primary migraine to >90% and allow confident initiation of migraine-specific therapy. Until secondary causes are excluded, triptans should be withheld given their vasoconstrictive properties and the possibility of underlying vascular pathology (CVST).
diagnostic_criteria_applied: ICHD-3 Criteria for Migraine Without Aura (1.1): Requires ≥5 attacks lasting 4–72 hours with ≥2 of (unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, aggravation by activity) AND ≥1 of (nausea/vomiting, photophobia AND phonophobia). Patient meets qualitative features (unilateral, pulsating, moderate, photophobia, nausea) but the 2-week persistent course is ATYPICAL — need clarification whether episodic or continuous. If first presentation, cannot meet the ≥5 attacks criterion. PARTIAL CRITERIA MET — diagnosis of 'probable migraine' (ICHD-3 1.5.1) may apply.

ICHD-3 Criteria for New Daily Persistent Headache (4.10): Persistent headache, daily from onset, clearly remembered onset date, present for >3 months. Patient has 2-week duration — too early for formal NDPH diagnosis but trajectory is concerning if headache remains continuous.

SNOOP10 Red Flag Screening (AAN/AHS 2019): S-Systemic symptoms: not reported (need to assess). N-Neurologic symptoms: photophobia present, need full neuro exam. O-Onset sudden: not thunderclap (reduces SAH concern). O-Older age >50: No (age 35). P-Pattern change/new onset: YES — NEW ONSET headache (RED FLAG TRIGGERED). P-Positional: not assessed (need to ask — relevant for IIH). P-Precipitated by Valsalva: not assessed. P-Papilledema: not assessed (CRITICAL to evaluate). P-Progressive: YES — persistent over 2 weeks (RED FLAG TRIGGERED). P-Pregnancy/postpartum: not assessed (MUST determine). Result: At least 2 of 10 SNOOP flags triggered, with 3 additional flags requiring assessment. Neuroimaging is indicated.

Modified Heros Rule for SAH Screening: Thunderclap onset absent, neck stiffness absent, severity 6/10 (not worst headache of life), no syncope, no focal deficits reported. Low clinical probability for acute SAH, but sentinel leak cannot be fully excluded without imaging.

CVST Clinical Probability Assessment: Female reproductive age (risk factor), subacute progressive headache (consistent), OCP status unknown (critical variable), no focal deficits reported (does not exclude early CVST — headache is isolated symptom in 25–30% of CVST cases per ISCVT registry), no seizures, no papilledema reported. Clinical probability: LOW-INTERMEDIATE pending risk factor assessment. MRV warranted.
specialist.risk_stratification: INTERMEDIATE RISK. Rationale: While the symptom phenotype is most consistent with migraine (high pre-test probability in this demographic), the patient triggers multiple SNOOP10 red flags (new onset, progressive/persistent pattern) and has unassessed critical risk factors (OCP use, BMI, pregnancy status, fundoscopic findings). The 2-week continuous/persistent course is atypical for episodic migraine and overlaps with the presentation of several must-not-miss diagnoses (CVST, IIH, intracranial mass). Risk cannot be downgraded to LOW until: (1) complete neurological examination including fundoscopy is normal, (2) MRI brain with MRV is normal, and (3) critical risk factors (OCP use, pregnancy, BMI) are assessed. Risk would be upgraded to HIGH if any of the following are found: papilledema, focal neurological deficits, OCP use with progressive headache, abnormal neuroimaging, or elevated blood pressure.
specialty_specific_tests: PRIORITY 1 — IMMEDIATE (Bedside): Complete neurological examination including: (a) Fundoscopic exam for papilledema — single highest-yield bedside test; papilledema LR+ >10 for raised ICP (IIH or mass). (b) Visual acuity and confrontation visual fields — visual field cuts suggest structural lesion or IIH with optic nerve involvement. (c) Cranial nerve examination — CN VI palsy (false localizing sign of raised ICP), CN III/IV/V assessment. (d) Pupillary examination including afferent pupillary defect. (e) Motor, sensory, cerebellar, and gait examination. (f) Meningeal signs: neck stiffness, Kernig sign, Brudzinski sign.

PRIORITY 2 — URGENT (Same day): MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast PLUS MR venography (MRV). This is the single most important imaging study — simultaneously evaluates for: intracranial mass lesion (sensitivity >95%), CVST (MRV sensitivity 95–97%), IIH radiographic signs (empty sella, optic nerve sheath distension, posterior globe flattening, transverse sinus stenosis), Chiari malformation, parenchymal abnormalities, meningeal enhancement (chronic meningitis). MRI is superior to CT for posterior fossa pathology, small lesions, and venous pathology.

PRIORITY 3 — URGENT (Same day): Laboratory studies: (a) Urine pregnancy test (hCG) — pregnancy affects differential (CVST risk 12–15x, eclampsia) and treatment options (teratogenicity of many headache medications). (b) CBC with differential — infection screen, polycythemia (CVST risk). (c) BMP — metabolic screen. (d) ESR and CRP — inflammatory markers (low yield at age 35 for GCA but screens for inflammatory/infectious etiologies). (e) Coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT) — baseline if anticoagulation may be needed for CVST.

PRIORITY 4 — CONDITIONAL: D-dimer — if CVST suspicion is moderate and MRV is not immediately available. Negative D-dimer has reasonable negative predictive value for acute CVST (sensitivity ~94% for acute, lower for subacute/chronic). However, MRV is definitive and preferred.

PRIORITY 5 — CONDITIONAL: CT head without contrast — only if MRI is unavailable or significantly delayed (>24–48 hours). CT is inferior to MRI for this clinical scenario but can screen for large mass lesions, acute hemorrhage, and hydrocephalus. Sensitivity for SAH decreases significantly after 6 hours from onset (not the primary concern here given 2-week course).

PRIORITY 6 — CONDITIONAL (Based on initial results): Lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement — indicated if: (a) Fundoscopy shows papilledema (to confirm IIH with opening pressure >25 cmH2O and normal CSF composition). (b) MRI shows IIH radiographic signs. (c) Clinical suspicion for chronic meningitis (send CSF for cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, bacterial/fungal/TB cultures, cytology, and consider viral PCR panel). (d) SAH cannot be excluded by imaging (xanthochromia analysis). IMPORTANT: LP should be performed AFTER neuroimaging to exclude mass lesion with risk of herniation.

PRIORITY 7 — CONDITIONAL: Formal neuro-ophthalmology assessment with automated perimetry (Humphrey visual field testing) and OCT of retinal nerve fiber layer — if fundoscopy is abnormal or equivocal, or if IIH is suspected. OCT can detect subclinical optic disc edema not visible on bedside fundoscopy.
PRIORITY 8 — CONDITIONAL: CT angiography (CTA) of head — if sentinel SAH or intracranial aneurysm is suspected based on clinical features or imaging findings.

PRIORITY 9 — SECOND-LINE (If initial workup negative): Thrombophilia screening (Factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A mutation, antithrombin III, protein C, protein S, antiphospholipid antibodies) — if CVST is diagnosed, to identify underlying prothrombotic state and guide duration of anticoagulation.

PRIORITY 10 — FOLLOW-UP: Headache diary — if primary migraine is confirmed after negative workup, patient should maintain a headache diary documenting frequency, duration, severity, triggers, menstrual correlation, and medication use for 4–8 weeks to guide preventive therapy decisions.
specialist_red_flags: NEW ONSET headache in an adult without established headache history — SNOOP10 red flag triggered; cannot assume primary headache without excluding secondary causes
PERSISTENT/PROGRESSIVE pattern over 2 weeks — atypical for episodic migraine; raises concern for CVST, IIH, mass lesion, or NDPH
Reproductive-age female — elevated risk for CVST (especially if on OCPs, RR 5.5–7.9x) and IIH (especially if obese, RR 11–20x)
OCP use status UNKNOWN — this is a critical missing variable; combined OCP use is the single most important modifiable risk factor for CVST in this demographic
Pregnancy status UNKNOWN — pregnancy/postpartum state increases CVST risk 12–15x and affects all treatment decisions
BMI UNKNOWN — obesity (BMI >30) increases IIH risk 11–20x; recent weight gain (>5% body weight) is an independent risk factor
Fundoscopic examination NOT YET PERFORMED — papilledema is the single most important bedside finding that would shift the differential dramatically toward raised ICP (IIH or mass)
Unilateral headache can be a lateralizing sign — right-sided headache could indicate ipsilateral pathology (mass, focal CVST) though migraine is also commonly unilateral
If headache worsens with Valsalva, coughing, bending, or positional changes — suggests raised intracranial pressure (IIH, mass, Chiari) and significantly increases probability of secondary cause
If patient reports pulsatile tinnitus — highly suggestive of IIH (present in ~60% of IIH cases, LR+ ~5)
Absence of focal neurological deficits does NOT exclude secondary causes — headache is the isolated presenting symptom in 25–30% of CVST cases and early IIH/mass lesions
specialist.prognosis_notes: PROGNOSIS IS DIAGNOSIS-DEPENDENT and varies dramatically based on etiology: (1) If MIGRAINE WITHOUT AURA is confirmed: Generally favorable prognosis. Episodic migraine is a chronic relapsing condition but is not life-threatening. ~50% of patients achieve ≥50% reduction in headache frequency with appropriate preventive therapy (NNT 4–5 for first-line agents). Migraine prevalence tends to decrease after menopause. However, migraine with aura in women on combined OCPs carries increased stroke risk (RR 2–4x), so contraceptive counseling is important. Disability burden is significant — migraine is the #1 cause of disability in women aged 15–49 globally (GBD 2019). (2) If CVST is diagnosed: With prompt anticoagulation, 79% achieve good functional outcome (mRS 0–1) per ISCVT registry. Mortality is 3–5% in acute phase, 8–10% at 1 year. Recurrence rate ~2–4% per year. Delayed diagnosis worsens outcomes significantly — median time to diagnosis is 7 days, and delays beyond 2 weeks are associated with higher rates of venous infarction and hemorrhagic transformation. (3) If IIH is diagnosed: With appropriate treatment (weight loss, acetazolamide, ± CSF diversion), headache improves in most patients. However, 10–25% develop permanent visual field deficits if untreated, and up to 10% have significant permanent visual loss. Weight loss of 5–10% body weight is the most effective long-term intervention. (4) If INTRACRANIAL MASS is identified: Prognosis depends entirely on tumor type, grade, location, and resectability. Meningiomas (most common in women) are typically benign and curable with surgery. Gliomas carry variable prognosis based on grade. (5) MODIFYING FACTORS: Early diagnosis and treatment improve outcomes across all secondary causes. Patient age (35) is favorable for recovery. Compliance with follow-up and medication adherence are critical modifiers.
specialist.guideline_concordance: CURRENT MANAGEMENT STATUS: The patient has not yet undergone formal diagnostic workup. Based on current guidelines, the following assessments of concordance apply: (1) AAN/AHS Headache Evaluation Guidelines (2019): Neuroimaging is INDICATED — patient triggers SNOOP10 red flags for new onset and progressive/persistent pattern. MRI with MRV is the preferred modality. NOT YET PERFORMED — guideline-discordant if imaging is not obtained. (2) AHS Consensus on Neuroimaging (2019/2023): New-onset headache in adult >30 with atypical features warrants MRI brain with and without contrast. CONCORDANT recommendation to image. (3) AHA/ASA CVST Scientific Statement (2011/2020): CVST should be considered in reproductive-age women with new persistent headache; MRV should be included. CONCORDANT with recommendation to obtain MRV. (4) EHF IIH Guideline (2020): Fundoscopic examination is mandatory in this clinical scenario. NOT YET PERFORMED — must be obtained urgently. (5) ICHD-3 Diagnostic Criteria: Formal migraine diagnosis CANNOT be made until secondary causes are excluded ('not better accounted for by another ICHD-3 diagnosis'). Premature to diagnose migraine without completing workup. (6) AHS Acute Migraine Treatment (2021): Symptomatic relief with NSAIDs (ibuprofen 400–600mg) and antiemetics (metoclopramide 10mg or ondansetron 4mg) is appropriate while workup proceeds. Triptans should be WITHHELD until vascular pathology (CVST) is excluded — this is guideline-concordant. (7) AHS/AAN Migraine Prevention Guidelines (2012/2021): Preventive therapy discussion is PREMATURE until diagnosis is confirmed. If migraine is confirmed and headache frequency is ≥4 days/month, preventive therapy should be offered. OVERALL: The recommended workup (neurological exam, fundoscopy, MRI/MRV, labs, pregnancy test) is fully concordant with current neurology guidelines. Failure to image this patient would be guideline-discordant and medico-legally indefensible given the red flags present.

referral_recommendation.urgency: URGENT (within 1–3 days if outpatient; same-day if emergency department presentation)
referral_recommendation.rationale: Patient requires specialist-level evaluation including: (1) Expert neurological examination with fundoscopy by a clinician experienced in detecting papilledema. (2) Interpretation of MRI/MRV findings in clinical context. (3) If CVST or IIH is diagnosed, specialist management is mandatory (anticoagulation for CVST, acetazolamide/LP for IIH). (4) If migraine is confirmed, neurology follow-up for preventive therapy optimization and headache diary review. (5) If lumbar puncture is needed, neurology should perform or supervise with opening pressure measurement.
referral_recommendation.escalation_criteria: EMERGENT referral (ED evaluation) if any of the following develop: sudden severe worsening of headache (thunderclap), new focal neurological deficits (weakness, numbness, speech difficulty, vision loss), seizure, altered consciousness, fever with neck stiffness, or papilledema found on examination.
referral_recommendation.additional_referrals: Neuro-ophthalmology referral if papilledema is found or IIH is suspected (for formal visual field testing and OCT monitoring). Hematology referral if CVST is diagnosed (for thrombophilia workup and anticoagulation management).

clinical_pearls: PEARL 1 — CVST mimics migraine: CVST is the great mimicker of migraine in young women. Headache is the presenting symptom in 89% of CVST cases, and in 25–30% it is the ONLY symptom. The headache can be unilateral, throbbing, and associated with photophobia and nausea — indistinguishable from migraine on clinical grounds alone. The only reliable way to differentiate is MRV. Never diagnose new-onset migraine in a reproductive-age woman without considering CVST.

PEARL 2 — The 2-week timeline is a diagnostic pivot point: Classic episodic migraine presents as discrete attacks lasting 4–72 hours with pain-free intervals. A truly continuous headache for 2 weeks does NOT meet ICHD-3 migraine criteria. Always ask: 'Is the headache there ALL the time, or does it come and go?' If continuous, the differential shifts significantly toward secondary causes or NDPH.

treatment_plans.condition: Acute Symptomatic Management (While Diagnostic Workup Is Pending — Secondary Causes NOT Yet Excluded)
treatment_plans.first_line: Safe symptomatic relief with NSAIDs and antiemetics ONLY. Triptans are WITHHELD until vascular pathology (cerebral venous sinus thrombosis) is excluded by MRI/MRV. This is a critical safety decision.

medications.name: Ibuprofen
medications.frequency: Every 6–8 hours as needed for headache
medications.duration: Use for no more than 10 days per month to avoid medication overuse headache
warnings: Take with food to reduce GI irritation
Avoid if pregnant (pregnancy test must be obtained first)
Avoid if history of peptic ulcer disease, GI bleeding, or renal impairment
If CVST is diagnosed and anticoagulation is started, ibuprofen must be DISCONTINUED immediately due to additive bleeding risk — switch to acetaminophen
Do not combine with aspirin or other NSAIDs
medications.monitoring: Monitor for GI symptoms (epigastric pain, dark stools), renal function if used beyond 5–7 days
medications.evidence_grade: Grade A — Cochrane Review: NNT for pain-free at 2 hours = 7.2

medications.name: Acetaminophen (alternative to ibuprofen)
medications.frequency: Every 6 hours as needed
medications.maximum_daily_dose: 3000 mg/day (conservative limit for safety; absolute max 4000 mg/day in healthy adults)
medications.duration: Use for no more than 10 days per month
warnings: Do NOT exceed maximum daily dose — hepatotoxicity risk
Avoid with alcohol use (>3 drinks/day)
Check all other medications for hidden acetaminophen content (cold medicines, combination products)
Safe in pregnancy if needed
Safe to use if anticoagulation is initiated for CVST
medications.monitoring: Liver function if prolonged use
medications.evidence_grade: Grade A — NNT for pain-free at 2 hours = 12 (less effective than ibuprofen but safer GI/bleeding profile)

medications.name: Metoclopramide
medications.frequency: Every 8 hours as needed for nausea
medications.duration: Short-term only (≤5 days to minimize extrapyramidal side effect risk)
warnings: Can cause drowsiness, restlessness, and rarely extrapyramidal symptoms (dystonia, akathisia)
Contraindicated in patients with seizure disorder, pheochromocytoma, or GI obstruction
Has prokinetic properties — also enhances absorption of oral analgesics, providing dual benefit in migraine
Avoid prolonged use (>12 weeks) due to tardive dyskinesia risk
medications.monitoring: Monitor for involuntary movements, restlessness
medications.evidence_grade: Grade B — effective antiemetic with adjunctive analgesic benefit in migraine

medications.name: Ondansetron (alternative antiemetic)
medications.frequency: Every 8 hours as needed for nausea
medications.duration: As needed during acute episodes
warnings: May cause constipation and headache (paradoxically)
QTc prolongation risk at higher doses — avoid in patients with known long QT syndrome or on QT-prolonging medications
No extrapyramidal side effects (advantage over metoclopramide)
medications.monitoring: ECG if using high doses or in patients with cardiac risk factors
medications.evidence_grade: Grade B

treatment_algorithm.step_1_conservative: Dark, quiet room during acute headache episodes. Cold compress to forehead/temples. Adequate hydration (minimum 2L water/day). Regular sleep schedule. Avoid known triggers (bright lights, strong odors, skipped meals).
treatment_algorithm.step_2_first_line_pharmacological: Ibuprofen 400–600 mg PO at headache onset + Metoclopramide 10 mg PO for nausea. Take medications EARLY in the headache — efficacy decreases if treatment is delayed.
treatment_algorithm.step_3_second_line_pharmacological: If ibuprofen is ineffective or contraindicated: Naproxen sodium 500 mg PO (longer duration of action, NNT 8.3). If NSAIDs contraindicated: Acetaminophen 1000 mg PO.
treatment_algorithm.step_4_triptan_therapy_CONDITIONAL: ONLY after MRI/MRV confirms NO vascular pathology: Sumatriptan 50–100 mg PO at headache onset (NNT 4.7 for pain-free at 2 hours). Rizatriptan 10 mg PO is an alternative with slightly better NNT (3.1). REQUIRES PRESCRIPTION. Contraindicated in uncontrolled hypertension, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, CVST, and pregnancy. Maximum 2 doses per 24 hours with ≥2-hour interval. Limit to ≤9 days per month to prevent medication overuse headache.
treatment_algorithm.step_5_preventive_therapy_CONDITIONAL: ONLY after diagnosis is confirmed as migraine and headache frequency is ≥4 days/month: First-line options (requires prescription, discuss with neurologist): (a) Propranolol 40 mg PO twice daily, titrate to 80–240 mg/day (NNT 4–5; avoid in asthma, bradycardia, depression). (b) Topiramate 25 mg PO at bedtime, titrate by 25 mg/week to 50–100 mg/day (NNT 4–5; side effects include paresthesias, cognitive dulling, weight loss; may reduce OCP efficacy at doses ≥200 mg/day). (c) Amitriptyline 10 mg PO at bedtime, titrate to 25–75 mg/day (NNT 3–4; side effects include sedation, dry mouth, weight gain). NOTE: Valproate is CONTRAINDICATED in this 35-year-old woman of reproductive age due to severe teratogenicity (10–11% major congenital malformation rate).
treatment_algorithm.step_6_advanced_preventive_CONDITIONAL: If first-line preventives fail or are not tolerated (after ≥8 weeks adequate trial): CGRP monoclonal antibodies — Erenumab 70–140 mg SC monthly (NNT 4–5 for ≥50% reduction). Requires prescription and specialist supervision. Generally well-tolerated; constipation is most common side effect.
treatment_algorithm.step_7_interventional_CONDITIONAL: For refractory cases: Greater occipital nerve block, Botox (onabotulinumtoxinA) for chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month for ≥3 months). Requires neurology referral.
treatment_algorithm.critical_safety_note: Steps 4–7 are CONDITIONAL on confirmed migraine diagnosis after secondary causes are excluded. Do NOT initiate triptans, ergotamines, or preventive therapy until MRI/MRV and neurological examination are completed and normal.

treatment_plans.condition: If Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis (CVST) Is Diagnosed
treatment_plans.first_line: Immediate anticoagulation with heparin followed by transition to oral anticoagulation. This is a medical emergency requiring inpatient management.

medications.name: Unfractionated Heparin (UFH) or Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (LMWH — Enoxaparin)
medications.dose: Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC every 12 hours OR UFH IV infusion per institutional protocol targeting aPTT 1.5–2.5x control
medications.frequency: Every 12 hours (enoxaparin) or continuous infusion (UFH)

immediate_actions: STEP 1 — RIGHT NOW: Obtain full vital signs including blood pressure (rule out hypertensive headache), temperature (rule out infectious etiology), heart rate, and oxygen saturation
STEP 2 — RIGHT NOW: Obtain urine pregnancy test (hCG) — this affects the entire differential diagnosis and all treatment decisions. Many headache medications are teratogenic.

STEP 3 — RIGHT NOW: Perform complete neurological examination including: (a) Fundoscopic exam for papilledema — SINGLE HIGHEST-YIELD BEDSIDE TEST; (b) Visual acuity and confrontation visual fields; (c) Cranial nerve examination (especially CN III, IV, VI); (d) Pupillary examination; (e) Motor, sensory, cerebellar, and gait examination; (f) Meningeal signs (neck stiffness, Kernig, Brudzinski)

STEP 4 — CRITICAL HISTORY: Ask about oral contraceptive pill use (increases CVST risk 5.5–7.9x), current medications including analgesic frequency (MOH screening), BMI/recent weight gain (IIH risk), visual symptoms (transient visual obscurations, diplopia), positional worsening (IIH), pulsatile tinnitus (IIH), and whether headache is continuous or episodic with pain-free intervals

STEP 5 — SAME DAY: Order MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast PLUS MR venography (MRV) — this is the single most important imaging study and simultaneously evaluates for mass lesion, CVST, IIH signs, and Chiari malformation
STEP 6 — SAME DAY: Order laboratory studies: CBC with differential, BMP, ESR, CRP, coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT as baseline)

STEP 7 — IMMEDIATE SYMPTOM RELIEF: Start ibuprofen 400–600 mg PO now (if not pregnant and no contraindications) + metoclopramide 10 mg PO for nausea. DO NOT give triptans until vascular pathology is excluded.

STEP 8 — PATIENT EDUCATION: Explain that while migraine is the most likely diagnosis, the 2-week persistent course requires testing to rule out less common but serious conditions. Reassure that the workup is precautionary and most results will likely be normal.

STEP 9 — HEADACHE DIARY: Begin immediately — record date, time of onset, duration, severity (0–10), location, quality, associated symptoms, triggers, and all medications taken with doses and times. This is essential for guiding future treatment decisions.
STEP 10 — ARRANGE URGENT NEUROLOGY REFERRAL: Within 1–3 days if outpatient; same-day if presenting to emergency department

warnings: CRITICAL — Pregnancy status UNKNOWN: Multiple recommended medications are teratogenic or contraindicated in pregnancy. Ibuprofen (contraindicated in 3rd trimester, caution throughout), metoclopramide (FDA category B but requires risk-benefit), triptans (limited safety data), topiramate (teratogenic — FDA category D, associated with cleft lip/palate), valproate (ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED — 10-11% major congenital malformation rate), warfarin (teratogenic if CVST diagnosed). A urine pregnancy test (hCG) MUST be obtained BEFORE administering any medications. This is a CRITICAL safety gate.

CRITICAL — Triptans must NOT be initiated until cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) and other vascular pathology are excluded by MRI/MRV. Triptans are vasoconstrictive (5-HT1B/1D agonists) and could worsen vascular pathology, potentially causing venous infarction or ischemic injury. The treatment team has correctly flagged this, but it must be reinforced as a hard stop — no triptan prescriptions until MRV is reviewed and reported as normal.

HIGH — Allergy history is COMPLETELY ABSENT from the patient record. No allergy information has been documented for any drug class including NSAIDs, sulfonamides, acetaminophen, or any other medication. This is a latent safety hazard (Swiss Cheese Model — missing defensive layer). Allergy history MUST be obtained before administering ibuprofen (NSAID allergy, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease), metoclopramide, ondansetron, or any other medication. If acetazolamide is later considered for IIH, sulfonamide allergy must be specifically screened as there is potential cross-reactivity.

HIGH — Oral contraceptive pill (OCP) status is UNKNOWN. This is both a diagnostic variable (CVST risk increased 5.5-7.9x with combined OCPs) and a treatment safety variable. If the patient is on combined OCPs: (1) CVST risk is significantly elevated and MRV becomes even more urgent, (2) Topiramate at doses ≥200 mg/day can reduce OCP efficacy via CYP3A4 induction, risking unintended pregnancy, (3) If migraine with aura is later identified, combined OCPs are contraindicated (increased stroke risk RR 2-4x per WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria). OCP status must be ascertained immediately.

HIGH — Ibuprofen must be IMMEDIATELY DISCONTINUED if CVST is diagnosed and anticoagulation is initiated. The treatment team has correctly noted this, but the transition plan must be explicit: switch to acetaminophen ≤3000 mg/day. NSAIDs inhibit platelet function via COX-1 inhibition and combined with heparin/warfarin create additive bleeding risk including increased intracranial hemorrhage risk — this is an ISMP high-alert medication interaction scenario (anticoagulants are ISMP high-alert medications).

HIGH — Valproate has been correctly identified as CONTRAINDICATED in this 35-year-old woman of reproductive age. However, it appears in the treatment plan discussion (Step 5 preventive therapy). To prevent prescribing errors, valproate should be explicitly listed on a 'DO NOT PRESCRIBE' list for this patient, not merely noted as contraindicated within a paragraph. This is a known prescribing error pattern — medications mentioned in treatment plans can be inadvertently ordered even when accompanied by contraindication warnings.

MODERATE — Ibuprofen maximum daily dose listed as 2400 mg/day. This is within the FDA-approved prescription range (max 3200 mg/day) but the OTC maximum is 1200 mg/day. For a patient self-managing at home without renal function assessment, the conservative recommendation should be 1200-1600 mg/day with explicit instruction not to exceed 2400 mg/day, and only under medical supervision. Renal function (BMP/creatinine) should be checked before endorsing higher doses, especially if used beyond 5-7 days.

MODERATE — Acetaminophen maximum daily dose listed as 3000 mg/day (conservative) with notation of absolute max 4000 mg/day. This is appropriate. However, the treatment plan must explicitly warn the patient to check ALL over-the-counter products for hidden acetaminophen (cold/flu medications, combination analgesics like Excedrin). Inadvertent acetaminophen stacking is a leading cause of acute liver failure in the US. Alcohol use history has not been obtained — if the patient consumes >3 alcoholic drinks/day, the maximum should be reduced to 2000 mg/day.

MODERATE — Metoclopramide duration limit of ≤5 days is appropriately conservative. However, the listed maximum daily dose of 30 mg/day should be verified against the patient's weight. The FDA recommends a maximum of 0.5 mg/kg/day (not to exceed 30 mg/day in most adults). Patient weight is UNKNOWN. Additionally, metoclopramide carries an FDA Black Box Warning for tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use — this warning should be communicated to the patient even for short-term use.

MODERATE — Ondansetron QTc prolongation risk: The treatment plan correctly notes QTc risk at higher doses. However, no baseline ECG has been recommended, and the patient's cardiac history and concurrent medication list (which could include QT-prolonging drugs) are unknown. If ondansetron is used at doses >4 mg, or if the patient is on any other QT-prolonging medication, an ECG should be obtained. The maximum single IV dose should not exceed 16 mg per FDA guidance (reduced from prior 32 mg recommendation due to QTc concerns).

MODERATE — Warfarin (if CVST diagnosed): Listed as ISMP high-alert medication. The treatment plan correctly notes teratogenicity and need for reliable contraception. However, the plan should also note: (1) Warfarin-acetaminophen interaction — high-dose acetaminophen (>2g/day for >3 days) can potentiate INR, which IS noted in one section but should be prominently flagged in the monitoring plan, (2) Extensive food-drug interactions (vitamin K-containing foods), (3) Need for patient education on bleeding signs, (4) Genetic testing (CYP2C9/VKORC1) may be considered to guide initial dosing. The starting dose of 5 mg may be too high for some patients — pharmacogenomic-guided dosing or a lower starting dose (2-3 mg) should be considered if genetic testing is not available.

MODERATE — Enoxaparin (if CVST diagnosed): Listed as ISMP high-alert medication. Dose of 1 mg/kg every 12 hours requires ACCURATE PATIENT WEIGHT. Patient weight is not documented. Incorrect weight-based dosing of LMWH is a known source of serious harm (under-dosing leads to treatment failure; over-dosing leads to hemorrhage). Weight must be obtained and documented before enoxaparin is administered. Additionally, renal function (CrCl) must be assessed — if CrCl <30 mL/min, enoxaparin dose must be reduced to 1 mg/kg once daily, or UFH should be used instead.

MODERATE — Dexamethasone (if mass lesion diagnosed): The treatment plan recommends adding a PPI (omeprazole 20 mg daily) for GI prophylaxis. While this is reasonable for short-term steroid use, the STOPP criteria note that PPIs should not be continued beyond 8 weeks without reassessment. This is a low-risk concern for short-term use but should be flagged for medication reconciliation at follow-up.

LOW — The treatment plan does not explicitly address caffeine intake. Caffeine withdrawal is a common cause of new-onset daily headache and should be screened for. Additionally, caffeine can be both a trigger and an acute treatment adjunct for migraine (caffeine-containing analgesic combinations have evidence). This is a minor completeness gap.

LOW — No explicit mention of driving safety counseling. Metoclopramide can cause drowsiness, and the headache itself with photophobia may impair driving ability. Patient should be counseled about operating vehicles/machinery while symptomatic or on sedating medications.

LOW — The treatment plan does not address potential need for work/activity restrictions during the diagnostic workup period. Given persistent headache with photophobia, the patient may benefit from a brief medical note for workplace accommodations (reduced screen time, lighting adjustments).

Triptans are CONTRAINDICATED in combination with ergotamines (must not be used within 24 hours of each other) — additive vasoconstriction risk

Triptans are CONTRAINDICATED in uncontrolled hypertension, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, and peripheral vascular disease — blood pressure must be measured before any triptan prescription
Valproate is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in this 35-year-old woman of reproductive age — 10-11% major congenital malformation rate, IQ reduction of 7-10 points in exposed offspring. DO NOT PRESCRIBE.

Ibuprofen (and all NSAIDs) are CONTRAINDICATED if: (a) patient is pregnant (especially 3rd trimester — premature ductus arteriosus closure), (b) history of NSAID allergy or aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, (c) active peptic ulcer disease or GI bleeding, (d) severe renal impairment (CrCl <30), (e) concurrent anticoagulation therapy (if CVST diagnosed)

recommendations: CRITICAL SAFETY GATE #1: Obtain urine pregnancy test (hCG) BEFORE administering ANY medications. Pregnancy status affects the entire treatment algorithm and multiple recommended medications are teratogenic. This is a non-negotiable prerequisite.

CRITICAL SAFETY GATE #2: Obtain comprehensive allergy history before administering any medications. Specifically screen for: NSAID/aspirin allergy, sulfonamide allergy, acetaminophen allergy, and any prior adverse drug reactions. Document allergy status prominently in the medical record.

CRITICAL SAFETY GATE #3: Do NOT prescribe or administer triptans until MRI brain with MRV is completed and reviewed as normal, excluding CVST and other vascular pathology. This must be a hard stop in the medication ordering system.
CRITICAL: Add valproate/divalproex to the patient's 'DO NOT PRESCRIBE' list to prevent inadvertent ordering. It should not appear as a treatment option in any order set for this patient.

HIGH: Obtain accurate patient weight (kg) and document prominently. Weight is required for: (a) weight-based dosing of enoxaparin if CVST is diagnosed, (b) BMI calculation for IIH risk stratification, (c) metoclopramide dose verification (max 0.5 mg/kg/day).
HIGH: Obtain baseline renal function (serum creatinine, estimated GFR) before endorsing ibuprofen use beyond 5-7 days and before any potential enoxaparin dosing.

HIGH: Obtain OCP/hormonal contraceptive status immediately — this is both a critical diagnostic variable (CVST risk) and a treatment safety variable (topiramate-OCP interaction, migraine with aura + OCP contraindication).

HIGH: Obtain blood pressure measurement before any medication administration. Hypertensive emergency can cause headache and is a contraindication to triptans. Severely elevated BP would also change the urgency of the workup.

HIGH: If anticoagulation is initiated for CVST, implement the following safety measures: (a) Immediately discontinue ibuprofen and all NSAIDs, (b) Switch to acetaminophen ≤3000 mg/day for analgesia, (c) Monitor INR closely if warfarin + acetaminophen >2g/day, (d) Verify patient weight for enoxaparin dosing, (e) Check renal function for LMWH dose adjustment, (f) Implement fall precautions.
MODERATE: Obtain alcohol use history to guide acetaminophen dosing (reduce max to 2000 mg/day if >3 drinks/day) and to assess for alcohol-related headache contribution.
MODERATE: Screen for caffeine intake and recent changes in caffeine consumption — caffeine withdrawal is a common and easily reversible cause of new-onset daily headache.

MODERATE: Provide explicit patient education on medication overuse headache prevention: limit ibuprofen/NSAID use to ≤10 days per month, limit triptans (if later prescribed) to ≤9 days per month. Document this counseling.
MODERATE: If ondansetron is used at doses >4 mg or if patient has any cardiac history or takes other QT-prolonging medications, obtain baseline ECG.

MODERATE: Ensure medication reconciliation is performed — obtain complete list of ALL current medications including over-the-counter products, supplements, and herbal remedies. Hidden acetaminophen in combination products is a specific hepatotoxicity risk. Herbal supplements (e.g., St. John's Wort, ginkgo) can interact with multiple recommended medications.
LOW: Counsel patient on driving safety while symptomatic and while taking metoclopramide (drowsiness risk).
LOW: Provide headache diary template with specific fields for medication tracking to support medication overuse headache prevention and future treatment optimization.

LOW: Document a clear follow-up plan: (a) Return to ED immediately if thunderclap headache, new neurological symptoms, seizure, fever with neck stiffness, or sudden vision loss, (b) Neurology follow-up within 1-3 days, (c) Review of imaging and lab results within 24-72 hours.

OVERALL SAFETY ASSESSMENT: The treatment team's recommendations are clinically sound, well-reasoned, and demonstrate appropriate caution regarding secondary headache exclusion before initiating migraine-specific therapy. The decision to withhold triptans pending MRV is the single most important safety decision in this case and is correct. The primary safety gaps are: (1) missing pregnancy status — a critical prerequisite for any pharmacotherapy, (2) missing allergy history — a fundamental safety requirement, (3) missing vital signs including blood pressure, (4) missing patient weight for potential weight-based dosing. These are latent conditions (Swiss Cheese Model) that must be addressed before medications are administered. No CRITICAL errors in the recommended medications or dosages were identified — all doses are within safe therapeutic ranges for a non-pregnant adult with normal renal/hepatic function. The conditional treatment algorithms (for CVST, IIH, mass lesion) are appropriate and guideline-concordant. The Beers Criteria and STOPP/START criteria are NOT applicable as the patient is 35 years old (these apply to patients ≥65 years).

empathy.patient_summary:
You are a 35-year-old woman who has been dealing with a persistent, throbbing headache on the right side of your head for the past two weeks, along with sensitivity to light and occasional nausea. We understand how frustrating and worrying it can be to have a headache that just won't go away — you are doing the right thing by seeking medical care.

The good news is that based on your symptoms, the most likely explanation is a type of headache called a migraine. Migraines are very common, especially in women your age, and they are highly treatable. Your symptoms — the one-sided throbbing pain, light sensitivity, and nausea — are classic signs of a migraine.

However, because this headache has lasted for two full weeks and appears to be new for you, your medical team wants to run some tests to make absolutely sure nothing else is going on. This is a precaution, not a reason to panic. Think of it like this: if you heard an unusual noise in your car, you'd still drive it to the mechanic, but you'd want them to check under the hood just to be safe. That's what we're doing here.

Specifically, your doctors want to rule out a few uncommon but important conditions:

• A blood clot in the veins of the brain (called cerebral venous sinus thrombosis or CVST) — this is rare but more common in women of childbearing age, especially those taking birth control pills. It is very treatable when caught early.

• A condition where pressure builds up inside the skull (called idiopathic intracranial hypertension or IIH) — this is also uncommon but important to check for, especially in women your age.

• A growth or mass in the brain — this is unlikely given your symptoms, but imaging will help rule it out completely.

The brain scan (MRI) and blood tests your team is recommending are standard and widely available. Most people in your situation receive completely normal results, and your doctors can then confidently treat you for migraines with very effective medications.
empathy.what_this_means:
Here is what is happening in simple terms:

A migraine is a type of headache caused by changes in brain activity and blood flow. It is NOT just a bad headache — it is a real medical condition that affects about 1 in 4 women your age. The throbbing pain, light sensitivity, and nausea you are experiencing are your brain's way of signaling that something has triggered this process.

The reason your doctors are being thorough with testing is that a headache lasting two straight weeks is a bit unusual for a typical migraine, which usually comes and goes in episodes lasting a few hours to a few days. When a headache sticks around this long, doctors want to look a little deeper — not because they think something is seriously wrong, but because it is the responsible thing to do.

Your doctor will want to look at the back of your eyes using a small light (called a fundoscopic exam). This quick, painless test can reveal whether there is any increased pressure inside your head. This single test gives your doctor a lot of important information.

The MRI scan is a painless imaging test that takes detailed pictures of your brain using magnets (no radiation). It will also look at the blood vessels in your brain to make sure blood is flowing normally. This test typically takes 30 to 60 minutes, and you simply lie still in the machine.

Blood tests will check your general health, look for signs of inflammation or infection, and include a pregnancy test (since pregnancy can affect both the diagnosis and which medications are safe for you).
action_checklist: RIGHT NOW — Tell your doctor about ALL medications you are currently taking, including birth control pills, over-the-counter pain relievers (like Advil, Tylenol, or Excedrin), vitamins, and supplements. This information is very important for your safety and diagnosis.
RIGHT NOW — Let your doctor know if there is any chance you could be pregnant. A quick urine pregnancy test will be done because it affects which medications are safe for you.
RIGHT NOW — Tell your doctor about any drug allergies you have, especially to pain relievers like ibuprofen or aspirin, or to sulfa drugs.

RIGHT NOW — For immediate pain relief, your doctor may recommend ibuprofen (Advil/Motrin) 400 to 600 mg with food. This helps reduce the inflammation that contributes to your pain. Take it as early as possible when the headache flares up — it works better the sooner you take it.

RIGHT NOW — If you feel nauseous, your doctor can prescribe an anti-nausea medication called metoclopramide (10 mg) or ondansetron (4 mg). These can help settle your stomach and may also help the pain medication work better.
RIGHT NOW — Rest in a dark, quiet room when the headache is at its worst. Apply a cold pack or cool cloth to your forehead or temples for 15 to 20 minutes at a time.

TODAY OR TOMORROW — Get the MRI brain scan with MRV (a special view of the blood vessels) that your doctor orders. This is the most important test to make sure everything looks normal inside your head.
TODAY OR TOMORROW — Get the blood tests your doctor orders, including a complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, and inflammation markers.

TODAY OR TOMORROW — Have your doctor do a thorough neurological exam, including looking at the back of your eyes with a special light, checking your vision, testing your strength and sensation, and checking your balance and coordination.

THIS WEEK — Start a headache diary. Every day, write down: (1) whether you had a headache, (2) how bad it was on a scale of 0 to 10, (3) where the pain was located, (4) what it felt like (throbbing, pressing, sharp), (5) any other symptoms like nausea or light sensitivity, (6) what you ate and drank, (7) how much sleep you got, (8) any medications you took and whether they helped. This diary will be incredibly helpful for your doctor.
THIS WEEK — See a neurologist (brain and nerve specialist) within 1 to 3 days. Your primary doctor can arrange this referral.

IMPORTANT — Do NOT take more than 10 days of pain medication per month (ibuprofen, Tylenol, or similar). Taking pain relievers too often can actually cause your headaches to get worse — a condition called medication overuse headache. Your doctor can explain more about this.

IMPORTANT — Do NOT take a medication called a triptan (such as sumatriptan or Imitrex) until your MRI results come back normal. These are excellent migraine medications, but your doctor needs to make sure your blood vessels are healthy first before prescribing them.
ONGOING — Stay well hydrated — aim for at least 8 glasses of water per day. Dehydration can make headaches worse.
ONGOING — Try to keep a regular sleep schedule — go to bed and wake up at the same time each day, even on weekends. Both too little and too much sleep can trigger migraines.

medications_explained.name: Ibuprofen (brand names: Advil, Motrin)
medications_explained.what_it_does: Reduces inflammation and pain. Think of it as calming down the swelling and irritation that is causing your headache.
medications_explained.how_to_take_it: Take 400 to 600 mg (2 to 3 over-the-counter tablets) by mouth with food every 6 to 8 hours as needed for headache pain. Do not take more than 1200 mg (6 tablets) in a day without your doctor's guidance.
medications_explained.important_tips: Always take with food or a glass of milk to protect your stomach. Take it as EARLY as possible when you feel a headache coming on — it works much better when taken early. Do not use for more than 10 days per month.
medications_explained.watch_out_for: Stomach pain, heartburn, or dark/tarry stools (signs of stomach irritation). Stop and call your doctor if these occur.
medications_explained.do_not_take_if: You are pregnant, have a history of stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or are allergic to aspirin or similar pain relievers.

medications_explained.name: Acetaminophen (brand name: Tylenol)
medications_explained.what_it_does: An alternative pain reliever that works differently from ibuprofen. It is gentler on the stomach and safe to use if ibuprofen is not an option.
medications_explained.how_to_take_it: Take 1000 mg (two 500 mg tablets) by mouth every 6 hours as needed. Do not take more than 3000 mg (six 500 mg tablets) in a day.
medications_explained.important_tips: CHECK all your other medications — many cold medicines, flu medicines, and combination pain relievers (like Excedrin) already contain acetaminophen. Taking too much total acetaminophen can seriously harm your liver.
medications_explained.watch_out_for: Do not drink more than 3 alcoholic drinks per day while taking this medication. If you drink alcohol regularly, tell your doctor — your maximum dose may need to be lower.
medications_explained.do_not_take_if: You have liver disease or drink alcohol heavily.

medications_explained.name: Metoclopramide (brand name: Reglan) — prescription needed
medications_explained.what_it_does: Controls nausea and vomiting. It also helps your stomach absorb pain medications faster, so they work better.
medications_explained.how_to_take_it: Take 10 mg by mouth up to 3 times a day as needed for nausea. Use for no more than 5 days at a time.
medications_explained.watch_out_for: May cause drowsiness or restlessness. Do not drive or operate heavy machinery if you feel drowsy. In rare cases, it can cause involuntary muscle movements — if you notice any unusual movements of your face, tongue, or body, stop taking it and contact your doctor right away.

medications_explained.name: Ondansetron (brand name: Zofran) — prescription needed
medications_explained.what_it_does: An alternative anti-nausea medication. It works differently from metoclopramide and does not cause the restlessness side effect.
medications_explained.how_to_take_it: Take 4 to 8 mg by mouth every 8 hours as needed for nausea. A dissolving tablet form is available that melts on your tongue — helpful if you feel too nauseous to swallow a pill.
medications_explained.watch_out_for: May cause constipation or (ironically) headache in some people.

lifestyle_tips: Hydration matters more than you might think. Many people find that simply drinking enough water throughout the day makes a noticeable difference in their headaches. Aim for at least 8 glasses a day. Keep a water bottle with you as a reminder.

Sleep is one of the most powerful tools you have. Try to go to bed and wake up at the same time every day — even on weekends. Both too little sleep and sleeping in too long can trigger migraines. Most adults do best with 7 to 8 hours.

Do not skip meals. When your blood sugar drops, it can trigger a headache. Eating regular, balanced meals throughout the day helps keep things stable. If you tend to get busy and forget to eat, try setting a reminder on your phone.

Manage stress in whatever way works for you. Stress is one of the most common migraine triggers. This could be deep breathing, a short walk, yoga, meditation, talking to a friend, or simply taking a few minutes for yourself each day. Even 10 minutes can help.

Pay attention to your screen time. If you work at a computer, take a break every 20 minutes — look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds (the 20-20-20 rule). Adjust your screen brightness and consider using blue-light filtering glasses.

Be mindful of strong smells, bright or flickering lights, and loud noises — these are common migraine triggers. If your workplace has harsh fluorescent lighting, you might ask about adjustments or wear lightly tinted glasses.

Keep track of what you eat and drink in your headache diary. Some people find that certain foods (aged cheese, red wine, processed meats, chocolate, or artificial sweeteners) can trigger their migraines. Everyone is different, so the diary will help you identify YOUR personal triggers.

Gentle, regular exercise can actually help prevent migraines over time. Start slowly — even a 20-minute walk most days of the week can make a difference. Avoid intense exercise during an active headache, as it can make the pain worse.

Limit caffeine to a consistent, moderate amount. Drinking a lot of coffee one day and none the next can trigger headaches. If you drink caffeine, try to have about the same amount at the same time each day. If you recently stopped or significantly reduced your caffeine intake, that could actually be contributing to your current headaches.
when_to_seek_help: Go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you experience a sudden, severe headache that feels like the worst headache of your life — especially if it comes on like a thunderclap (reaching maximum intensity within seconds to minutes). This is different from your current headache and needs immediate evaluation.

Go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you develop any new weakness, numbness, or tingling on one side of your body, or if you have trouble speaking or understanding speech. These could be signs of a stroke or blood clot.
Go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you have a seizure (convulsion or loss of consciousness with shaking).
Go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you develop a high fever (over 101°F / 38.3°C) along with a stiff neck and worsening headache. This combination could indicate an infection around the brain.
Go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you experience sudden vision loss in one or both eyes, or if you start seeing double.
Go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you become confused, excessively drowsy, or if someone notices that you are not acting like yourself.
Call your doctor the same day if your headache suddenly gets significantly worse (for example, jumping from a 6 out of 10 to a 9 or 10 out of 10).
Call your doctor the same day if you develop new symptoms that you have not had before, such as vomiting that will not stop, ringing in your ears, or pain that wakes you from sleep.
Call your doctor within 1 to 2 days if the pain medications are not helping at all, or if you find yourself needing to take them every day.
Call your doctor within 1 to 2 days if you notice any side effects from your medications, such as stomach pain, unusual restlessness, or involuntary movements.

anticipated_faqs.question: Could this be a brain tumor?
anticipated_faqs.answer: This is a very understandable worry, but brain tumors are an uncommon cause of headaches — they account for less than 1% of headache cases in primary care. Your symptoms are much more consistent with a migraine. That said, the MRI scan your doctor is ordering will give a very clear picture of your brain and can definitively rule this out. Most people who get this scan receive completely normal results.

anticipated_faqs.question: Why can't I just take a triptan (like Imitrex) right away? I've heard those work really well for migraines.
anticipated_faqs.answer: You're right — triptans are excellent migraine medications and may well be part of your treatment plan. However, triptans work by narrowing blood vessels in the brain. Before prescribing them, your doctor needs to make sure your blood vessels are healthy by reviewing your MRI results. This is a safety precaution. Once the scan comes back normal, your doctor can prescribe a triptan, and it may work significantly better than ibuprofen for your headaches.

anticipated_faqs.question: Why do I need an MRI if it's probably just a migraine?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Great question. For most people with a long history of typical migraines, an MRI is not always necessary. But in your case, this headache is new and has lasted for two weeks straight, which is a bit unusual for a typical migraine. Your doctor wants to take a careful look to make sure there is nothing else going on. It is the medical equivalent of 'better safe than sorry.' The MRI is painless and does not use radiation.

anticipated_faqs.question: Is this headache dangerous?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Based on your symptoms, the most likely cause is a migraine, which is not dangerous — it is painful and disruptive, but it does not cause lasting harm to your brain. The tests your doctor is ordering are to rule out the small chance of something more serious. The fact that your headache is moderate (6 out of 10), that you do not have any weakness or numbness, and that you are otherwise feeling well are all reassuring signs.

anticipated_faqs.question: Could my birth control pills be causing this?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Hormonal birth control can sometimes trigger or worsen migraines. It is also an important piece of information for your doctor because certain types of birth control pills can slightly increase the risk of blood clots, including in the brain. This is one reason your doctor will ask about your birth control method. Be sure to share this information — it helps your doctor make the best decisions about your care.

You are a 35-year-old woman who has been dealing with a persistent, throbbing headache on the right side of your head for the past two weeks, along with sensitivity to light and occasional nausea. We understand how frustrating and worrying it can be to have a headache that just won't go away — you are doing the right thing by seeking medical care.

The good news is that based on your symptoms, the most likely explanation is a type of headache called a migraine. Migraines are very common, especially in women your age, and they are highly treatable. Your symptoms — the one-sided throbbing pain, light sensitivity, and nausea — are classic signs of a migraine.

However, because this headache has lasted for two full weeks and appears to be new for you, your medical team wants to run some tests to make absolutely sure nothing else is going on. This is a precaution, not a reason to panic. Think of it like this: if you heard an unusual noise in your car, you'd still drive it to the mechanic, but you'd want them to check under the hood just to be safe. That's what we're doing here.

Specifically, your doctors want to rule out a few uncommon but important conditions:

• A blood clot in the veins of the brain (called cerebral venous sinus thrombosis or CVST) — this is rare but more common in women of childbearing age, especially those taking birth control pills. It is very treatable when caught early.

• A condition where pressure builds up inside the skull (called idiopathic intracranial hypertension or IIH) — this is also uncommon but important to check for, especially in women your age.

• A growth or mass in the brain — this is unlikely given your symptoms, but imaging will help rule it out completely.

The brain scan (MRI) and blood tests your team is recommending are standard and widely available. Most people in your situation receive completely normal results, and your doctors can then confidently treat you for migraines with very effective medications.

A migraine is a type of headache caused by changes in brain activity and blood flow. It is NOT just a bad headache — it is a real medical condition that affects about 1 in 4 women your age. The throbbing pain, light sensitivity, and nausea you are experiencing are your brain's way of signaling that something has triggered this process.

The reason your doctors are being thorough with testing is that a headache lasting two straight weeks is a bit unusual for a typical migraine, which usually comes and goes in episodes lasting a few hours to a few days. causes.explanation: This is the most common primary headache in women of reproductive age. The illness script is a strong match: unilateral throbbing headache, photophobia, nausea, moderate severity (6/10), female sex, age 35. Migraine prevalence in women aged 25-44 is approximately 25%. The ICHD-3 criteria require at least 5 attacks lasting 4-72 hours with unilateral location, pulsating quality, moderate-to-severe intensity, and aggravation by routine physical activity, plus nausea/vomiting or photophobia/phonophobia. The 2-week persistent course is somewhat atypical for episodic migraine but could represent new-onset migraine, status migrainosus (if continuous >72 hours), or chronic migraine transformation. Bayesian reasoning: high pre-test probability (~25% base rate in this demographic) with strong LR+ for unilateral throbbing + photophobia + nausea combination (LR+ ~3-5). Post-test probability approximately 50-60%. Confidence reduced from higher because the 2-week continuous/persistent nature is atypical and mandates exclusion of secondary causes.

new onset without prior headache history mentioned
no information on aggravation by physical activity

causes.explanation: CVST must be considered in any woman of reproductive age with new subacute headache. Risk factors include oral contraceptive use, pregnancy/postpartum state, thrombophilia, and obesity. The headache in CVST is typically progressive over days to weeks (matches 2-week course), can be unilateral, and may mimic migraine with nausea and photophobia. Prevalence is low (~5 per million/year) but dramatically higher in women on OCPs (LR+ ~5-6 for OCP use). Without knowing OCP status, pregnancy status, or BMI, this remains an important consideration. The absence of reported focal deficits, seizures, or papilledema lowers probability but does not exclude early CVST. Bayesian reasoning: low pre-test probability (~1-2%) but the subacute progressive course in a reproductive-age female raises this to approximately 8-15% depending on risk factors. This is a must-not-miss diagnosis because delayed treatment leads to venous infarction, hemorrhage, and death.

no reported papilledema

causes.explanation: IIH classically affects obese women of childbearing age. Presents with progressive headache (often daily), nausea, photophobia, and visual symptoms including transient visual obscurations and diplopia. Papilledema is the hallmark finding. The 2-week subacute progressive course fits well. Without knowing the patient's BMI or visual acuity/field status, this cannot be excluded. Key discriminating feature: fundoscopic exam showing papilledema would dramatically increase probability (LR+ >10). Absence of papilledema on careful exam would significantly lower probability (LR- ~0.2). Bayesian reasoning: base rate ~1-2 per 100,000 general population but ~20 per 100,000 in obese women of childbearing age. Pre-test probability ~2-5% depending on BMI; post-test depends heavily on fundoscopy and opening pressure.
opposing_features: no visual obscurations reported
no diplopia reported
BMI unknown

causes.explanation: New persistent headache in an adult requires exclusion of space-occupying lesion. Brain tumors can present with progressive headache, nausea (from raised ICP), and photophobia. Headache from mass lesion is classically worse in the morning, worsened by Valsalva, and progressive. Unilateral headache can localize to the side of the lesion. At age 35, primary tumors (glioma, meningioma) are more likely than metastatic disease. Prevalence of brain tumors presenting as headache is low (~0.1-0.5% of headache presentations in primary care) but the 2-week progressive course raises concern. recommended_tests: 1. IMMEDIATE: Complete neurological examination including fundoscopy, visual fields, cranial nerves, motor/sensory, cerebellar, gait, and meningeal signs — highest yield bedside assessment to stratify risk
2. IMMEDIATE: Vital signs including blood pressure (hypertensive emergency can cause headache), temperature (infection screen), heart rate
3. URGENT: Pregnancy test (urine hCG) — affects differential (pregnancy-related CVST, eclampsia) and treatment options

4. URGENT: MRI brain with and without gadolinium + MRV — gold standard to evaluate for mass lesion, CVST, IIH signs, Chiari malformation, and other structural causes. Superior to CT for posterior fossa and venous pathology
5. SAME DAY: Basic labs — CBC (infection, anemia, polycythemia), BMP (metabolic causes), ESR/CRP (inflammatory/infectious causes, GCA screening though low probability at age 35)
6. CONDITIONAL: D-dimer — if CVST suspicion is moderate and MRV not immediately available, negative D-dimer has reasonable NPV
7. CONDITIONAL: Lumbar puncture with opening pressure — if fundoscopy shows papilledema, or if MRI/MRV suggests IIH, or if chronic meningitis is suspected
8. CONDITIONAL: CT head without contrast — if MRI not immediately available, as initial screen for hemorrhage and large mass lesions
9. CONDITIONAL: CTA head — if sentinel SAH or aneurysm suspected based on clinical features or CT findings
