potential_interactions.management: Absolutely contraindicated in women of childbearing potential unless on highly effective contraception AND no alternative exists. Pregnancy test required before initiation.

potential_interactions.mechanism: Additive bleeding risk — NSAIDs inhibit platelet function + anticoagulant effect
potential_interactions.clinical_effect: Increased GI and intracranial hemorrhage risk
potential_interactions.management: If CVST is diagnosed and anticoagulation initiated, avoid NSAIDs; use acetaminophen for analgesia

migraine.global_prevalence: 14.7% overall (GBD 2019); leading cause of disability in women aged 15–49
migraine.sex_distribution: Female:Male ratio = 3:1 (17.1% in women vs 5.6% in men)
migraine.age_peak: Peak prevalence ages 25–55, with highest incidence in 30s–40s
migraine.this_patient_pretest_probability: HIGH — 35-year-old female is in the highest-risk demographic. Estimated pre-test probability for migraine as cause of headache: 40–60% based on demographics and symptom profile alone
migraine.disability_burden: GBD 2019: #2 cause of years lived with disability globally; #1 in women aged 15–49

cerebral_venous_sinus_thrombosis.incidence: 1.3–1.6 per 100,000 per year (higher in women of reproductive age: up to 2.8 per 100,000)
cerebral_venous_sinus_thrombosis.sex_distribution: Female:Male = 3:1 (driven by OCP use, pregnancy, postpartum)
cerebral_venous_sinus_thrombosis.this_patient_pretest_probability: LOW but non-negligible — estimated 1–3% in a young woman with new persistent headache, higher if on OCPs (5–7x increased risk with combined OCPs)
cerebral_venous_sinus_thrombosis.mortality: 3–5% in acute phase; 8–10% at 1 year (ISCVT data, n=624)
cerebral_venous_sinus_thrombosis.key_study: ISCVT (International Study on Cerebral Vein and Dural Sinus Thrombosis, Ferro et al., Stroke 2004): Largest prospective cohort (n=624). Headache present in 89% of cases. Median time to diagnosis: 7 days. 79% had good outcome (mRS 0–1) with anticoagulation.

idiopathic_intracranial_hypertension.incidence: Overall: 0.9–1.0 per 100,000/year; in obese women aged 20–44: 12–20 per 100,000/year
idiopathic_intracranial_hypertension.this_patient_pretest_probability: LOW if normal BMI (estimated <1%); MODERATE if obese (estimated 3–8%)
idiopathic_intracranial_hypertension.complications: Visual loss in 10–25% if untreated; permanent visual field defects in up to 10%

intracranial_mass_lesion.incidence_primary_brain_tumor: 7.1 per 100,000/year (all types); meningioma most common in women (F:M = 2:1)
intracranial_mass_lesion.this_patient_pretest_probability: LOW — estimated 1–2% for new headache presentation in this age group
intracranial_mass_lesion.red_flags_increasing_probability: Progressive worsening, worse in morning/with Valsalva, focal neurological deficits, seizures, personality change

new_daily_persistent_headache.characteristics: Distinctive onset: patient can pinpoint exact day headache began. Continuous from onset. No prior headache history. Often refractory to treatment.
new_daily_persistent_headache.this_patient_relevance: If patient can identify exact onset date and headache has been truly continuous (not episodic), NDPH should be considered. Diagnosis of exclusion after secondary causes ruled out.

primary_diagnostic_consideration.pre_test_probability: 40–60% based on demographics and symptom profile

warnings: CRITICAL — Pregnancy status UNKNOWN: Multiple recommended medications are teratogenic or contraindicated in pregnancy. Ibuprofen (contraindicated in 3rd trimester, caution throughout), metoclopramide (FDA category B but requires risk-benefit), triptans (limited safety data), topiramate (teratogenic — FDA category D, associated with cleft lip/palate), valproate (ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED — 10-11% major congenital malformation rate), warfarin (teratogenic if CVST diagnosed). A urine pregnancy test (hCG) MUST be obtained BEFORE administering any medications. This is a CRITICAL safety gate.

CRITICAL — Triptans must NOT be initiated until cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) and other vascular pathology are excluded by MRI/MRV. Triptans are vasoconstrictive (5-HT1B/1D agonists) and could worsen vascular pathology, potentially causing venous infarction or ischemic injury. The treatment team has correctly flagged this, but it must be reinforced as a hard stop — no triptan prescriptions until MRV is reviewed and reported as normal.

HIGH — Allergy history is COMPLETELY ABSENT from the patient record. No allergy information has been documented for any drug class including NSAIDs, sulfonamides, acetaminophen, or any other medication. This is a latent safety hazard (Swiss Cheese Model — missing defensive layer). Allergy history MUST be obtained before administering ibuprofen (NSAID allergy, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease), metoclopramide, ondansetron, or any other medication. If acetazolamide is later considered for IIH, sulfonamide allergy must be specifically screened as there is potential cross-reactivity.

HIGH — Oral contraceptive pill (OCP) status is UNKNOWN. This is both a diagnostic variable (CVST risk increased 5.5-7.9x with combined OCPs) and a treatment safety variable. If the patient is on combined OCPs: (1) CVST risk is significantly elevated and MRV becomes even more urgent, (2) Topiramate at doses ≥200 mg/day can reduce OCP efficacy via CYP3A4 induction, risking unintended pregnancy, (3) If migraine with aura is later identified, combined OCPs are contraindicated (increased stroke risk RR 2-4x per WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria). OCP status must be ascertained immediately.

HIGH — Ibuprofen must be IMMEDIATELY DISCONTINUED if CVST is diagnosed and anticoagulation is initiated. The treatment team has correctly noted this, but the transition plan must be explicit: switch to acetaminophen ≤3000 mg/day. NSAIDs inhibit platelet function via COX-1 inhibition and combined with heparin/warfarin create additive bleeding risk including increased intracranial hemorrhage risk — this is an ISMP high-alert medication interaction scenario (anticoagulants are ISMP high-alert medications).

HIGH — Valproate has been correctly identified as CONTRAINDICATED in this 35-year-old woman of reproductive age. However, it appears in the treatment plan discussion (Step 5 preventive therapy). To prevent prescribing errors, valproate should be explicitly listed on a 'DO NOT PRESCRIBE' list for this patient, not merely noted as contraindicated within a paragraph. This is a known prescribing error pattern — medications mentioned in treatment plans can be inadvertently ordered even when accompanied by contraindication warnings.

MODERATE — Ibuprofen maximum daily dose listed as 2400 mg/day. This is within the FDA-approved prescription range (max 3200 mg/day) but the OTC maximum is 1200 mg/day. For a patient self-managing at home without renal function assessment, the conservative recommendation should be 1200-1600 mg/day with explicit instruction not to exceed 2400 mg/day, and only under medical supervision. Renal function (BMP/creatinine) should be checked before endorsing higher doses, especially if used beyond 5-7 days.

MODERATE — Acetaminophen maximum daily dose listed as 3000 mg/day (conservative) with notation of absolute max 4000 mg/day. This is appropriate. However, the treatment plan must explicitly warn the patient to check ALL over-the-counter products for hidden acetaminophen (cold/flu medications, combination analgesics like Excedrin). Inadvertent acetaminophen stacking is a leading cause of acute liver failure in the US. Alcohol use history has not been obtained — if the patient consumes >3 alcoholic drinks/day, the maximum should be reduced to 2000 mg/day.

MODERATE — Metoclopramide duration limit of ≤5 days is appropriately conservative. However, the listed maximum daily dose of 30 mg/day should be verified against the patient's weight. The FDA recommends a maximum of 0.5 mg/kg/day (not to exceed 30 mg/day in most adults). Patient weight is UNKNOWN. Additionally, metoclopramide carries an FDA Black Box Warning for tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use — this warning should be communicated to the patient even for short-term use.

MODERATE — Ondansetron QTc prolongation risk: The treatment plan correctly notes QTc risk at higher doses. However, no baseline ECG has been recommended, and the patient's cardiac history and concurrent medication list (which could include QT-prolonging drugs) are unknown. If ondansetron is used at doses >4 mg, or if the patient is on any other QT-prolonging medication, an ECG should be obtained. The maximum single IV dose should not exceed 16 mg per FDA guidance (reduced from prior 32 mg recommendation due to QTc concerns).

MODERATE — Warfarin (if CVST diagnosed): Listed as ISMP high-alert medication. The treatment plan correctly notes teratogenicity and need for reliable contraception. However, the plan should also note: (1) Warfarin-acetaminophen interaction — high-dose acetaminophen (>2g/day for >3 days) can potentiate INR, which IS noted in one section but should be prominently flagged in the monitoring plan, (2) Extensive food-drug interactions (vitamin K-containing foods), (3) Need for patient education on bleeding signs, (4) Genetic testing (CYP2C9/VKORC1) may be considered to guide initial dosing. The starting dose of 5 mg may be too high for some patients — pharmacogenomic-guided dosing or a lower starting dose (2-3 mg) should be considered if genetic testing is not available.

MODERATE — Enoxaparin (if CVST diagnosed): Listed as ISMP high-alert medication. Dose of 1 mg/kg every 12 hours requires ACCURATE PATIENT WEIGHT. Patient weight is not documented. Incorrect weight-based dosing of LMWH is a known source of serious harm (under-dosing leads to treatment failure; over-dosing leads to hemorrhage). Weight must be obtained and documented before enoxaparin is administered. Additionally, renal function (CrCl) must be assessed — if CrCl <30 mL/min, enoxaparin dose must be reduced to 1 mg/kg once daily, or UFH should be used instead.

MODERATE — Dexamethasone (if mass lesion diagnosed): The treatment plan recommends adding a PPI (omeprazole 20 mg daily) for GI prophylaxis. While this is reasonable for short-term steroid use, the STOPP criteria note that PPIs should not be continued beyond 8 weeks without reassessment. This is a low-risk concern for short-term use but should be flagged for medication reconciliation at follow-up.

LOW — The treatment plan does not explicitly address caffeine intake. Caffeine withdrawal is a common cause of new-onset daily headache and should be screened for. Additionally, caffeine can be both a trigger and an acute treatment adjunct for migraine (caffeine-containing analgesic combinations have evidence). This is a minor completeness gap.

LOW — No explicit mention of driving safety counseling. Metoclopramide can cause drowsiness, and the headache itself with photophobia may impair driving ability. Patient should be counseled about operating vehicles/machinery while symptomatic or on sedating medications.

LOW — The treatment plan does not address potential need for work/activity restrictions during the diagnostic workup period. Given persistent headache with photophobia, the patient may benefit from a brief medical note for workplace accommodations (reduced screen time, lighting adjustments).
contraindications: Triptans (sumatriptan, rizatriptan) are CONTRAINDICATED until vascular pathology (CVST, aneurysm) is excluded by MRI/MRV — vasoconstrictive mechanism could worsen vascular pathology
Triptans are CONTRAINDICATED in combination with ergotamines (must not be used within 24 hours of each other) — additive vasoconstriction risk

Triptans are CONTRAINDICATED in uncontrolled hypertension, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, and peripheral vascular disease — blood pressure must be measured before any triptan prescription
Valproate is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in this 35-year-old woman of reproductive age — 10-11% major congenital malformation rate, IQ reduction of 7-10 points in exposed offspring. DO NOT PRESCRIBE.

Ibuprofen (and all NSAIDs) are CONTRAINDICATED if: (a) patient is pregnant (especially 3rd trimester — premature ductus arteriosus closure), (b) history of NSAID allergy or aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, (c) active peptic ulcer disease or GI bleeding, (d) severe renal impairment (CrCl <30), (e) concurrent anticoagulation therapy (if CVST diagnosed)
Warfarin is CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (teratogenic — warfarin embryopathy in 1st trimester, CNS abnormalities in 2nd/3rd trimester)
Acetazolamide (if IIH diagnosed) has potential cross-reactivity in patients with sulfonamide allergy — allergy history MUST be obtained before prescribing
Metoclopramide is CONTRAINDICATED in patients with seizure disorder, pheochromocytoma, GI obstruction, or concurrent use of other dopamine antagonists
NSAIDs are CONTRAINDICATED in combination with anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin, DOACs) due to additive bleeding risk — if CVST is diagnosed, immediately switch to acetaminophen
recommendations: CRITICAL SAFETY GATE #1: Obtain urine pregnancy test (hCG) BEFORE administering ANY medications. Pregnancy status affects the entire treatment algorithm and multiple recommended medications are teratogenic. This is a non-negotiable prerequisite.

CRITICAL SAFETY GATE #2: Obtain comprehensive allergy history before administering any medications. Specifically screen for: NSAID/aspirin allergy, sulfonamide allergy, acetaminophen allergy, and any prior adverse drug reactions. Document allergy status prominently in the medical record.

CRITICAL SAFETY GATE #3: Do NOT prescribe or administer triptans until MRI brain with MRV is completed and reviewed as normal, excluding CVST and other vascular pathology. This must be a hard stop in the medication ordering system.
CRITICAL: Add valproate/divalproex to the patient's 'DO NOT PRESCRIBE' list to prevent inadvertent ordering. It should not appear as a treatment option in any order set for this patient.

HIGH: Obtain accurate patient weight (kg) and document prominently. Weight is required for: (a) weight-based dosing of enoxaparin if CVST is diagnosed, (b) BMI calculation for IIH risk stratification, (c) metoclopramide dose verification (max 0.5 mg/kg/day).
HIGH: Obtain baseline renal function (serum creatinine, estimated GFR) before endorsing ibuprofen use beyond 5-7 days and before any potential enoxaparin dosing.

HIGH: Obtain OCP/hormonal contraceptive status immediately — this is both a critical diagnostic variable (CVST risk) and a treatment safety variable (topiramate-OCP interaction, migraine with aura + OCP contraindication).

HIGH: Obtain blood pressure measurement before any medication administration. Hypertensive emergency can cause headache and is a contraindication to triptans. Severely elevated BP would also change the urgency of the workup.

HIGH: If anticoagulation is initiated for CVST, implement the following safety measures: (a) Immediately discontinue ibuprofen and all NSAIDs, (b) Switch to acetaminophen ≤3000 mg/day for analgesia, (c) Monitor INR closely if warfarin + acetaminophen >2g/day, (d) Verify patient weight for enoxaparin dosing, (e) Check renal function for LMWH dose adjustment, (f) Implement fall precautions.
MODERATE: Obtain alcohol use history to guide acetaminophen dosing (reduce max to 2000 mg/day if >3 drinks/day) and to assess for alcohol-related headache contribution.
MODERATE: Screen for caffeine intake and recent changes in caffeine consumption — caffeine withdrawal is a common and easily reversible cause of new-onset daily headache.

MODERATE: Provide explicit patient education on medication overuse headache prevention: limit ibuprofen/NSAID use to ≤10 days per month, limit triptans (if later prescribed) to ≤9 days per month. Document this counseling.
MODERATE: If ondansetron is used at doses >4 mg or if patient has any cardiac history or takes other QT-prolonging medications, obtain baseline ECG.

MODERATE: Ensure medication reconciliation is performed — obtain complete list of ALL current medications including over-the-counter products, supplements, and herbal remedies. Hidden acetaminophen in combination products is a specific hepatotoxicity risk. Herbal supplements (e.g., St. John's Wort, ginkgo) can interact with multiple recommended medications.
LOW: Counsel patient on driving safety while symptomatic and while taking metoclopramide (drowsiness risk).
LOW: Provide headache diary template with specific fields for medication tracking to support medication overuse headache prevention and future treatment optimization.

LOW: Document a clear follow-up plan: (a) Return to ED immediately if thunderclap headache, new neurological symptoms, seizure, fever with neck stiffness, or sudden vision loss, (b) Neurology follow-up within 1-3 days, (c) Review of imaging and lab results within 24-72 hours.

OVERALL SAFETY ASSESSMENT: The treatment team's recommendations are clinically sound, well-reasoned, and demonstrate appropriate caution regarding secondary headache exclusion before initiating migraine-specific therapy. The decision to withhold triptans pending MRV is the single most important safety decision in this case and is correct. The primary safety gaps are: (1) missing pregnancy status — a critical prerequisite for any pharmacotherapy, (2) missing allergy history — a fundamental safety requirement, (3) missing vital signs including blood pressure, (4) missing patient weight for potential weight-based dosing. These are latent conditions (Swiss Cheese Model) that must be addressed before medications are administered. No CRITICAL errors in the recommended medications or dosages were identified — all doses are within safe therapeutic ranges for a non-pregnant adult with normal renal/hepatic function. The conditional treatment algorithms (for CVST, IIH, mass lesion) are appropriate and guideline-concordant. The Beers Criteria and STOPP/START criteria are NOT applicable as the patient is 35 years old (these apply to patients ≥65 years).

empathy.patient_summary:
You are a 35-year-old woman who has been dealing with a persistent, throbbing headache on the right side of your head for the past two weeks, along with sensitivity to light and occasional nausea. We understand how frustrating and worrying it can be to have a headache that just won't go away — you are doing the right thing by seeking medical care.

The good news is that based on your symptoms, the most likely explanation is a type of headache called a migraine. Migraines are very common, especially in women your age, and they are highly treatable. Your symptoms — the one-sided throbbing pain, light sensitivity, and nausea — are classic signs of a migraine.

However, because this headache has lasted for two full weeks and appears to be new for you, your medical team wants to run some tests to make absolutely sure nothing else is going on. This is a precaution, not a reason to panic. Think of it like this: if you heard an unusual noise in your car, you'd still drive it to the mechanic, but you'd want them to check under the hood just to be safe. That's what we're doing here.

Specifically, your doctors want to rule out a few uncommon but important conditions:

• A blood clot in the veins of the brain (called cerebral venous sinus thrombosis or CVST) — this is rare but more common in women of childbearing age, especially those taking birth control pills. It is very treatable when caught early.

• A condition where pressure builds up inside the skull (called idiopathic intracranial hypertension or IIH) — this is also uncommon but important to check for, especially in women your age.

• A growth or mass in the brain — this is unlikely given your symptoms, but imaging will help rule it out completely.

The brain scan (MRI) and blood tests your team is recommending are standard and widely available. Most people in your situation receive completely normal results, and your doctors can then confidently treat you for migraines with very effective medications.
empathy.what_this_means:
Here is what is happening in simple terms:

A migraine is a type of headache caused by changes in brain activity and blood flow. It is NOT just a bad headache — it is a real medical condition that affects about 1 in 4 women your age. The throbbing pain, light sensitivity, and nausea you are experiencing are your brain's way of signaling that something has triggered this process.

The reason your doctors are being thorough with testing is that a headache lasting two straight weeks is a bit unusual for a typical migraine, which usually comes and goes in episodes lasting a few hours to a few days. When a headache sticks around this long, doctors want to look a little deeper — not because they think something is seriously wrong, but because it is the responsible thing to do.

Your doctor will want to look at the back of your eyes using a small light (called a fundoscopic exam). This quick, painless test can reveal whether there is any increased pressure inside your head. This single test gives your doctor a lot of important information.

The MRI scan is a painless imaging test that takes detailed pictures of your brain using magnets (no radiation). It will also look at the blood vessels in your brain to make sure blood is flowing normally. This test typically takes 30 to 60 minutes, and you simply lie still in the machine.

Blood tests will check your general health, look for signs of inflammation or infection, and include a pregnancy test (since pregnancy can affect both the diagnosis and which medications are safe for you).
action_checklist: RIGHT NOW — Tell your doctor about ALL medications you are currently taking, including birth control pills, over-the-counter pain relievers (like Advil, Tylenol, or Excedrin), vitamins, and supplements. This information is very important for your safety and diagnosis.
RIGHT NOW — Let your doctor know if there is any chance you could be pregnant. A quick urine pregnancy test will be done because it affects which medications are safe for you.
RIGHT NOW — Tell your doctor about any drug allergies you have, especially to pain relievers like ibuprofen or aspirin, or to sulfa drugs.

RIGHT NOW — For immediate pain relief, your doctor may recommend ibuprofen (Advil/Motrin) 400 to 600 mg with food. This helps reduce the inflammation that contributes to your pain. Take it as early as possible when the headache flares up — it works better the sooner you take it.

RIGHT NOW — If you feel nauseous, your doctor can prescribe an anti-nausea medication called metoclopramide (10 mg) or ondansetron (4 mg). These can help settle your stomach and may also help the pain medication work better.
RIGHT NOW — Rest in a dark, quiet room when the headache is at its worst. Apply a cold pack or cool cloth to your forehead or temples for 15 to 20 minutes at a time.

TODAY OR TOMORROW — Get the MRI brain scan with MRV (a special view of the blood vessels) that your doctor orders. This is the most important test to make sure everything looks normal inside your head.
TODAY OR TOMORROW — Get the blood tests your doctor orders, including a complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, and inflammation markers.

TODAY OR TOMORROW — Have your doctor do a thorough neurological exam, including looking at the back of your eyes with a special light, checking your vision, testing your strength and sensation, and checking your balance and coordination.

THIS WEEK — Start a headache diary. Every day, write down: (1) whether you had a headache, (2) how bad it was on a scale of 0 to 10, (3) where the pain was located, (4) what it felt like (throbbing, pressing, sharp), (5) any other symptoms like nausea or light sensitivity, (6) what you ate and drank, (7) how much sleep you got, (8) any medications you took and whether they helped. This diary will be incredibly helpful for your doctor.
THIS WEEK — See a neurologist (brain and nerve specialist) within 1 to 3 days. Your primary doctor can arrange this referral.

IMPORTANT — Do NOT take more than 10 days of pain medication per month (ibuprofen, Tylenol, or similar). Taking pain relievers too often can actually cause your headaches to get worse — a condition called medication overuse headache. Your doctor can explain more about this.

IMPORTANT — Do NOT take a medication called a triptan (such as sumatriptan or Imitrex) until your MRI results come back normal. These are excellent migraine medications, but your doctor needs to make sure your blood vessels are healthy first before prescribing them.
ONGOING — Stay well hydrated — aim for at least 8 glasses of water per day. Dehydration can make headaches worse.
ONGOING — Try to keep a regular sleep schedule — go to bed and wake up at the same time each day, even on weekends. Both too little and too much sleep can trigger migraines.
ONGOING — Eat regular meals and do not skip meals. Low blood sugar can trigger headaches.

medications_explained.name: Ibuprofen (brand names: Advil, Motrin)
medications_explained.what_it_does: Reduces inflammation and pain. Think of it as calming down the swelling and irritation that is causing your headache.
medications_explained.how_to_take_it: Take 400 to 600 mg (2 to 3 over-the-counter tablets) by mouth with food every 6 to 8 hours as needed for headache pain. Do not take more than 1200 mg (6 tablets) in a day without your doctor's guidance.
medications_explained.important_tips: Always take with food or a glass of milk to protect your stomach. Take it as EARLY as possible when you feel a headache coming on — it works much better when taken early. Do not use for more than 10 days per month.
medications_explained.watch_out_for: Stomach pain, heartburn, or dark/tarry stools (signs of stomach irritation). Stop and call your doctor if these occur.
medications_explained.do_not_take_if: You are pregnant, have a history of stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or are allergic to aspirin or similar pain relievers.

medications_explained.name: Acetaminophen (brand name: Tylenol)
medications_explained.what_it_does: An alternative pain reliever that works differently from ibuprofen. It is gentler on the stomach and safe to use if ibuprofen is not an option.
medications_explained.how_to_take_it: Take 1000 mg (two 500 mg tablets) by mouth every 6 hours as needed. Do not take more than 3000 mg (six 500 mg tablets) in a day.
medications_explained.important_tips: CHECK all your other medications — many cold medicines, flu medicines, and combination pain relievers (like Excedrin) already contain acetaminophen. Taking too much total acetaminophen can seriously harm your liver.
medications_explained.watch_out_for: Do not drink more than 3 alcoholic drinks per day while taking this medication. If you drink alcohol regularly, tell your doctor — your maximum dose may need to be lower.
medications_explained.do_not_take_if: You have liver disease or drink alcohol heavily.

medications_explained.name: Metoclopramide (brand name: Reglan) — prescription needed
medications_explained.what_it_does: Controls nausea and vomiting. It also helps your stomach absorb pain medications faster, so they work better.
medications_explained.how_to_take_it: Take 10 mg by mouth up to 3 times a day as needed for nausea. Use for no more than 5 days at a time.
medications_explained.watch_out_for: May cause drowsiness or restlessness. Do not drive or operate heavy machinery if you feel drowsy. In rare cases, it can cause involuntary muscle movements — if you notice any unusual movements of your face, tongue, or body, stop taking it and contact your doctor right away.

medications_explained.name: Ondansetron (brand name: Zofran) — prescription needed
medications_explained.what_it_does: An alternative anti-nausea medication. It works differently from metoclopramide and does not cause the restlessness side effect.
medications_explained.how_to_take_it: Take 4 to 8 mg by mouth every 8 hours as needed for nausea. A dissolving tablet form is available that melts on your tongue — helpful if you feel too nauseous to swallow a pill.
medications_explained.watch_out_for: May cause constipation or (ironically) headache in some people.

lifestyle_tips: Hydration matters more than you might think. Many people find that simply drinking enough water throughout the day makes a noticeable difference in their headaches. Aim for at least 8 glasses a day. Keep a water bottle with you as a reminder.

Sleep is one of the most powerful tools you have. Try to go to bed and wake up at the same time every day — even on weekends. Both too little sleep and sleeping in too long can trigger migraines. Most adults do best with 7 to 8 hours.

Do not skip meals. When your blood sugar drops, it can trigger a headache. Eating regular, balanced meals throughout the day helps keep things stable. If you tend to get busy and forget to eat, try setting a reminder on your phone.

Manage stress in whatever way works for you. Stress is one of the most common migraine triggers. This could be deep breathing, a short walk, yoga, meditation, talking to a friend, or simply taking a few minutes for yourself each day. Even 10 minutes can help.

Pay attention to your screen time. If you work at a computer, take a break every 20 minutes — look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds (the 20-20-20 rule). Adjust your screen brightness and consider using blue-light filtering glasses.

Be mindful of strong smells, bright or flickering lights, and loud noises — these are common migraine triggers. If your workplace has harsh fluorescent lighting, you might ask about adjustments or wear lightly tinted glasses.

Keep track of what you eat and drink in your headache diary. Some people find that certain foods (aged cheese, red wine, processed meats, chocolate, or artificial sweeteners) can trigger their migraines. Everyone is different, so the diary will help you identify YOUR personal triggers.

Gentle, regular exercise can actually help prevent migraines over time. Start slowly — even a 20-minute walk most days of the week can make a difference. Avoid intense exercise during an active headache, as it can make the pain worse.

Limit caffeine to a consistent, moderate amount. Drinking a lot of coffee one day and none the next can trigger headaches. If you drink caffeine, try to have about the same amount at the same time each day. If you recently stopped or significantly reduced your caffeine intake, that could actually be contributing to your current headaches.
when_to_seek_help: Go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you experience a sudden, severe headache that feels like the worst headache of your life — especially if it comes on like a thunderclap (reaching maximum intensity within seconds to minutes). This is different from your current headache and needs immediate evaluation.

Go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you develop any new weakness, numbness, or tingling on one side of your body, or if you have trouble speaking or understanding speech. These could be signs of a stroke or blood clot.
Go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you have a seizure (convulsion or loss of consciousness with shaking).
Go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you develop a high fever (over 101°F / 38.3°C) along with a stiff neck and worsening headache. This combination could indicate an infection around the brain.
Go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you experience sudden vision loss in one or both eyes, or if you start seeing double.
Go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you become confused, excessively drowsy, or if someone notices that you are not acting like yourself.
Call your doctor the same day if your headache suddenly gets significantly worse (for example, jumping from a 6 out of 10 to a 9 or 10 out of 10).
Call your doctor the same day if you develop new symptoms that you have not had before, such as vomiting that will not stop, ringing in your ears, or pain that wakes you from sleep.
Call your doctor within 1 to 2 days if the pain medications are not helping at all, or if you find yourself needing to take them every day.
Call your doctor within 1 to 2 days if you notice any side effects from your medications, such as stomach pain, unusual restlessness, or involuntary movements.
empathy.reassurance:
We want you to know that you are taking exactly the right step by getting this checked out. The vast majority of headaches — even persistent ones like yours — turn out to be migraines or other treatable conditions, not something dangerous. Your symptoms are very common in women your age, and there are excellent treatments available that can help you feel much better.

The tests your doctor is recommending are not because anyone thinks something is seriously wrong — they are because good medicine means being thorough, especially when a headache lasts longer than usual. Think of it as your medical team being extra careful on your behalf.

Many people in your situation feel anxious while waiting for test results, and that is completely normal and understandable. It may help to know that the large majority of people who go through this workup receive reassuring, normal results. And even in the unlikely event that something else is found, the conditions your doctors are checking for are all treatable — especially when caught early, which is exactly what is happening here.

You are not alone in this. Migraine affects about 1 in 4 women, and it is the leading cause of disability in women aged 15 to 49 worldwide. There is no shame in having migraines, and there are many effective options — from medications to lifestyle changes — that can significantly reduce how often they happen and how much they affect your life.

Once your test results come back and your diagnosis is confirmed, your neurologist will work with you to create a personalized treatment plan. Most people with migraines see real improvement with the right combination of treatments. You have every reason to feel hopeful.

anticipated_faqs.question: Could this be a brain tumor?
anticipated_faqs.answer: This is a very understandable worry, but brain tumors are an uncommon cause of headaches — they account for less than 1% of headache cases in primary care. Your symptoms are much more consistent with a migraine. That said, the MRI scan your doctor is ordering will give a very clear picture of your brain and can definitively rule this out. Most people who get this scan receive completely normal results.

anticipated_faqs.question: Why can't I just take a triptan (like Imitrex) right away? I've heard those work really well for migraines.
anticipated_faqs.answer: You're right — triptans are excellent migraine medications and may well be part of your treatment plan. However, triptans work by narrowing blood vessels in the brain. Before prescribing them, your doctor needs to make sure your blood vessels are healthy by reviewing your MRI results. This is a safety precaution. Once the scan comes back normal, your doctor can prescribe a triptan, and it may work significantly better than ibuprofen for your headaches.

anticipated_faqs.question: Why do I need an MRI if it's probably just a migraine?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Great question. For most people with a long history of typical migraines, an MRI is not always necessary. But in your case, this headache is new and has lasted for two weeks straight, which is a bit unusual for a typical migraine. Your doctor wants to take a careful look to make sure there is nothing else going on. It is the medical equivalent of 'better safe than sorry.' The MRI is painless and does not use radiation.

anticipated_faqs.question: Is this headache dangerous?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Based on your symptoms, the most likely cause is a migraine, which is not dangerous — it is painful and disruptive, but it does not cause lasting harm to your brain. The tests your doctor is ordering are to rule out the small chance of something more serious. The fact that your headache is moderate (6 out of 10), that you do not have any weakness or numbness, and that you are otherwise feeling well are all reassuring signs.

anticipated_faqs.question: Could my birth control pills be causing this?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Hormonal birth control can sometimes trigger or worsen migraines. It is also an important piece of information for your doctor because certain types of birth control pills can slightly increase the risk of blood clots, including in the brain. This is one reason your doctor will ask about your birth control method. Be sure to share this information — it helps your doctor make the best decisions about your care.

primary_headache_diagnosis.recommendation: Migraine without aura requires ≥5 attacks lasting 4–72 hours with at least 2 of: unilateral location, pulsating quality, moderate-to-severe intensity, aggravation by routine activity; AND at least 1 of: nausea/vomiting, photophobia/phonophobia. This patient meets unilateral location, throbbing quality, photophobia, and nausea — however, 2-week continuous headache does NOT fit typical episodic migraine (4–72h per attack). Consider New Daily Persistent Headache (NDPH) or Status Migrainosus if migraine-like features persist >72h continuously.

primary_headache_diagnosis.clinical_note: ICHD-3 explicitly requires exclusion of secondary causes before diagnosing primary headache disorder. The 2-week unremitting course is atypical for episodic migraine and mandates secondary cause exclusion.

This patient triggers: NEW onset headache pattern in adult without prior diagnosis + 2-week persistence without resolution.

secondary_headache_exclusion.imaging_recommendation: Non-contrast CT head as initial screen in ED setting; MRI brain with and without contrast preferred if CT negative and clinical suspicion persists. MRA indicated if vascular lesion (AVM, aneurysm) suspected.

neuroimaging_guidelines.recommendation: CT head without contrast: Appropriate as initial imaging in new-onset headache in ED to exclude hemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus. MRI brain without/with contrast: More appropriate for subacute/chronic new headache, suspected IIH, meningeal disease, or posterior fossa pathology. MRA brain: Indicated when vascular malformation or aneurysm suspected.
neuroimaging_guidelines.evidence_grade: B (Moderate Quality — based on diagnostic accuracy studies and expert consensus)
neuroimaging_guidelines.sensitivity_note: CT sensitivity for subarachnoid hemorrhage: ~98% within 6 hours of onset, drops to ~85–90% at 24h, ~50% at 1 week. LP may be required if CT negative and SAH still suspected despite low thunderclap probability here.

iih_guidelines.treatment_if_confirmed: Acetazolamide 250–2000mg/day (first-line); weight loss (10% body weight reduction associated with IIH remission in 25% of cases); serial LP for acute symptom relief; surgical options (optic nerve sheath fenestration, CSF shunting) for vision-threatening cases

cerebral_venous_sinus_thrombosis.relevance: Reproductive-age female on potential OCP — CVT risk increased 5–7x with OCP use; headache is presenting symptom in >90% of CVT cases
cerebral_venous_sinus_thrombosis.recommendation: MRI brain with MR venography (MRV) is investigation of choice for CVT. D-dimer may be elevated but has limited sensitivity/specificity. Anticoagulation (LMWH then warfarin/DOAC) is treatment of choice even in presence of hemorrhagic infarction.

triptan_interactions.mechanism: Additive serotonergic effect — theoretical serotonin syndrome risk
triptan_interactions.clinical_effect: Serotonin syndrome (rare but serious): agitation, hyperthermia, clonus, autonomic instability
triptan_interactions.management: Monitor for serotonin syndrome symptoms; combination generally considered acceptable per AHS 2010 statement but use with caution; FDA warning issued 2006

triptan_interactions.mechanism: MAOIs inhibit triptan metabolism via MAO-A, leading to markedly elevated triptan levels
triptan_interactions.clinical_effect: Severe hypertension, serotonin syndrome, coronary vasospasm
triptan_interactions.management: Absolute contraindication — do not co-administer; 2-week washout required after MAOI discontinuation
Do not use within 24 hours of each other

triptan_interactions.mechanism: OCPs may reduce triptan clearance (CYP1A2 inhibition by estrogen component); also OCPs independently increase migraine frequency and stroke risk in migraineurs
triptan_interactions.clinical_effect: Potential increased triptan exposure; more clinically relevant: OCP + migraine with aura = significantly elevated ischemic stroke risk
triptan_interactions.management: Assess for aura; if migraine with aura confirmed, strongly consider OCP discontinuation per WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (Category 4 — unacceptable risk)

nsaid_interactions.drug_pair: NSAIDs + Anticoagulants (if CVT treated with anticoagulation)
nsaid_interactions.mechanism: Additive bleeding risk; NSAIDs inhibit platelet aggregation and damage GI mucosa
nsaid_interactions.clinical_effect: Increased GI and intracranial bleeding risk
nsaid_interactions.management: Avoid NSAIDs if anticoagulation initiated; use acetaminophen for analgesia

nsaid_interactions.drug_pair: NSAIDs (chronic use) — Medication Overuse Headache (MOH) Risk
nsaid_interactions.mechanism: Central sensitization from frequent analgesic use (>10–15 days/month)
nsaid_interactions.clinical_effect: Transformation to chronic daily headache; MOH affects ~1–2% of general population, up to 50% of chronic headache clinic patients
nsaid_interactions.management: Limit NSAID use to ≤10 days/month; educate patient on MOH risk; if MOH suspected, structured withdrawal program required

acetazolamide_interactions.drug_pair: Acetazolamide + Topiramate (if both used for IIH + migraine prevention)
acetazolamide_interactions.mechanism: Both are carbonic anhydrase inhibitors — additive effect
acetazolamide_interactions.clinical_effect: Increased risk of metabolic acidosis, nephrolithiasis, hypokalemia, paresthesias
acetazolamide_interactions.management: Monitor electrolytes, bicarbonate, renal function; avoid combination if possible or use lowest effective doses

drug_interactions.note: Full interaction profile requires complete medication reconciliation. OCP use status is clinically critical and not yet confirmed in this case.

specialist.reason_for_consultation: 35-year-old female with 2-week history of new-onset persistent right-sided throbbing headache (6/10), photophobia, and intermittent nausea. No prior headache diagnosis. Triage and diagnostician flagged need for secondary cause exclusion prior to primary headache diagnosis. Specific concerns include CVST, intracranial mass, IIH, SAH, and meningitis.
specialist.specialist_assessment:
This is a 35-year-old female presenting with a 2-week history of persistent right-sided throbbing headache rated 6/10, accompanied by photophobia and intermittent nausea. From a neurology standpoint, the phenotype is superficially consistent with migraine without aura (ICHD-3 criteria: unilateral location, pulsating quality, photophobia, nausea). However, several features deviate critically from a benign primary headache diagnosis and mandate urgent secondary cause exclusion before any primary headache label is applied.

KEY NEUROLOGICAL CONCERNS:

1. DURATION: The 2-week continuous course is fundamentally incompatible with episodic migraine (ICHD-3 requires 4-72 hours per attack). A 2-week unremitting headache in a previously undiagnosed adult is a neurological red flag. Differential considerations for this duration pattern include: Status Migrainosus (>72h continuous migraine — diagnosis of exclusion), New Daily Persistent Headache (NDPH — abrupt-onset daily headache from day 1, often with viral prodrome), Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis (CVST — progressive headache over days-weeks is the hallmark), Intracranial mass lesion (progressive course), IIH (chronic progressive headache in reproductive-age female), and Medication Overuse Headache (MOH — if analgesics used daily, though 2 weeks is early for MOH transformation).

2. FIXED UNILATERAL LOCALIZATION: While migraines are frequently unilateral, a headache that is consistently and exclusively right-sided over 2 weeks raises concern for an ipsilateral structural lesion. True migraine can alternate sides or remain unilateral, but fixed lateralization warrants structural exclusion.

3. NEW ONSET IN ADULT WITHOUT PRIOR DIAGNOSIS: Per SNOOP4 criteria (AHS/ACEP), new headache pattern in an adult without prior headache history is a red flag requiring neuroimaging. The absence of a prior migraine diagnosis means we cannot attribute this presentation to a known primary disorder.

4. REPRODUCTIVE-AGE FEMALE: This demographic carries specific neurological risk profiles — IIH (incidence 15-19/100,000/year in obese reproductive-age women vs. 0.9/100,000 general population) and CVST (OCP use increases risk 5-7x; headache is the presenting symptom in >90% of CVST cases). OCP use status is a CRITICAL unanswered question that materially changes the differential and urgency.

5. PHOTOPHOBIA: While classic for migraine, photophobia also occurs in meningitis, SAH, and IIH. In the context of a 2-week headache, it cannot be attributed to migraine without secondary cause exclusion.

NEUROLOGICAL EXAMINATION PRIORITIES:
The following examination findings would be immediately actionable:
- Fundoscopy: Papilledema (present → IIH, CVST with elevated ICP, mass lesion; absent → lowers but does not exclude IIH)
- Meningismus: Kernig/Brudzinski signs (present → LP mandatory after CT)
- Cranial nerve examination: CN VI palsy (IIH), CN III palsy with ptosis/mydriasis (posterior communicating artery aneurysm), visual field defects (mass lesion, IIH)
- Motor/sensory/cerebellar examination: Any focal deficit → emergent neuroimaging
- Blood pressure: Hypertensive urgency/emergency must be excluded immediately

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS (Neurology Perspective, Ranked by Clinical Priority):
1. Migraine Without Aura — New Onset (62% pre-imaging probability): Most likely phenotypically, but 2-week continuous course is atypical. Diagnosis of exclusion.
2. Hormonal/OCP-Related Migraine (18% if OCP confirmed): Estrogen-mediated migraine in reproductive-age female. Must confirm OCP use urgently — if confirmed, MRV mandatory before continuing OCP.
3. IIH / Pseudotumor Cerebri (14%): Female, reproductive age, photophobia, progressive headache. Fundoscopy is the critical bedside test. If papilledema present, diagnosis is strongly supported.
4. Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis (10-15% if OCP confirmed): Progressive 2-week headache in reproductive-age female. Can present with isolated headache before focal deficits develop. MRI/MRV is diagnostic. Time-sensitive — anticoagulation must be initiated promptly if confirmed.
5. Intracranial Mass Lesion (12%): New persistent unilateral headache in adult. MRI brain with gadolinium is gold standard. Absence of focal deficits and morning predominance argues against but does not exclude early lesion.
6. Status Migrainosus (diagnosis of exclusion): Continuous migraine >72 hours. Requires exclusion of all secondary causes before this label is applied.
7. New Daily Persistent Headache (NDPH): Headache present daily from onset, often following viral illness. Diagnosis of exclusion; requires neuroimaging.
8. SAH — Sentinel Bleed (5%): Low probability given absence of thunderclap onset, but must-not-miss. CT head without contrast is mandatory first step.
9. Meningitis — Viral/Subacute (5%): Low probability given absence of fever and meningismus, but photophobia warrants formal meningismus assessment.
10. Analgesic Overuse Headache (MOH): If patient has been taking analgesics daily for 2 weeks, early MOH transformation is possible — medication history is critical.

NEUROLOGY MANAGEMENT APPROACH:
Phase 1 (Immediate — ED): Vital signs including BP, focused neurological exam with fundoscopy and meningismus assessment, non-contrast CT head to exclude hemorrhage/mass/hydrocephalus, confirm OCP use status, obtain medication history (analgesic frequency).
Phase 2 (Urgent — within hours if CT negative): MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast + MR venography (MRV) — this is the single most important investigation in this patient. MRI/MRV will simultaneously evaluate for mass lesion, CVST, IIH features (empty sella, optic nerve sheath distension, transverse sinus stenosis), and posterior fossa pathology missed by CT.
Phase 3 (If MRI/MRV negative): LP with opening pressure measurement — critical to exclude IIH (opening pressure >25 cmH2O) and meningitis (CSF analysis). Also evaluates for xanthochromia if SAH still suspected.
Phase 4 (Outpatient Neurology): Headache diary, migraine trigger assessment, menstrual cycle correlation, preventive therapy consideration if migraine confirmed and frequency warrants it.

ACUTE SYMPTOMATIC TREATMENT (pending workup, assuming no contraindications identified):
- Antiemetic: Prochlorperazine 10mg IV (NNT ~2.9 for headache relief; superior to opioids in ED; independent anti-migraine effect) OR Metoclopramide 10mg IV
- Analgesic: Ketorolac 30mg IV (NNT ~3.9 in ED setting) — AVOID if anticoagulation anticipated (CVST concern)
- Triptan: Sumatriptan 6mg SC or 100mg PO if migraine diagnosis supported after initial workup and no contraindications (cardiovascular disease, uncontrolled HTN, hemiplegic/basilar migraine features)
- IV hydration: 1L NS if dehydration contributing
- Low-stimulation environment: Dim lighting, quiet room
- AVOID opioids: AHS Grade A recommendation against opioid use for migraine; inferior efficacy, MOH risk

OCP MANAGEMENT: If OCP use confirmed, do NOT continue combined oral contraceptive until CVST excluded by MRV. If migraine with aura is subsequently confirmed, combined OCP is WHO Category 4 (unacceptable risk) due to significantly elevated ischemic stroke risk (RR 2.08-8.72). Refer to OB-GYN for contraceptive counseling — progestin-only or non-hormonal methods preferred.

diagnostic_criteria_applied.result: PARTIAL FULFILLMENT — Patient meets: unilateral location (right-sided), pulsating/throbbing quality, photophobia, nausea. FAILS: 2-week continuous duration does not meet 4-72 hour attack duration criterion. Minimum 5 attacks required for diagnosis — single continuous 2-week episode does not qualify as episodic migraine. Diagnosis cannot be confirmed without secondary cause exclusion.
diagnostic_criteria_applied.interpretation: Cannot diagnose migraine without aura by ICHD-3 criteria given continuous 2-week course. Consider Status Migrainosus (>72h continuous) or NDPH as alternative primary headache diagnoses — both require secondary cause exclusion first.

diagnostic_criteria_applied.criteria: SNOOP4 Red Flag Criteria (AHS/ACEP Secondary Headache Screening)
diagnostic_criteria_applied.result: RED FLAGS PRESENT: (S) No systemic symptoms but new pattern; (N) Neurological symptoms — photophobia; (O) Onset not thunderclap but new in adult; (P) Prior headache history absent — NEW headache pattern without prior diagnosis; (P) Progressive 2-week course; (P) Papilledema — not yet assessed (CRITICAL gap); (P) Positional component — not yet assessed. Minimum 2-3 SNOOP4 criteria triggered.
diagnostic_criteria_applied.interpretation: SNOOP4 criteria triggered — neuroimaging is mandated before primary headache diagnosis. This patient should NOT be discharged with empirical migraine diagnosis without neuroimaging.

diagnostic_criteria_applied.result: NOT FULLY APPLICABLE — Ottawa SAH Rule applies to thunderclap or maximal-at-onset headache. This patient's headache is gradual onset over 2 weeks, not thunderclap. However, CT head without contrast is still indicated as first-line imaging to exclude hemorrhage. If any component of thunderclap onset is elicited on detailed history, Ottawa Rule becomes fully applicable (sensitivity 100%, specificity 13.6% for SAH).
diagnostic_criteria_applied.interpretation: Low probability for SAH given absence of thunderclap onset (LR- ~0.1). CT head still mandatory as initial screen. LP indicated if CT negative AND thunderclap onset confirmed on detailed history.

diagnostic_criteria_applied.result: CANNOT ASSESS WITHOUT EXAMINATION — Criteria require: (1) symptoms/signs of raised ICP, (2) papilledema on fundoscopy, (3) normal neurological exam except CN VI palsy, (4) LP opening pressure >25 cmH2O, (5) normal CSF composition, (6) no other cause on neuroimaging. Patient has symptoms consistent with raised ICP (headache, photophobia, nausea) but fundoscopy not yet performed — this is the critical missing data point.
diagnostic_criteria_applied.interpretation: IIH cannot be confirmed or excluded without fundoscopy and LP opening pressure. Fundoscopy is the most important immediate bedside test for this diagnosis.

diagnostic_criteria_applied.result: RISK FACTORS PRESENT BUT IMAGING NOT YET PERFORMED — Female sex, reproductive age, possible OCP use (unconfirmed). Headache as presenting symptom in >90% of CVST. Progressive 2-week course is classic. MRI/MRV required for definitive diagnosis (filling defect in dural venous sinus on MRV is diagnostic, LR+ >50).
diagnostic_criteria_applied.interpretation: CVST cannot be excluded without MRI/MRV. This is the most time-sensitive diagnosis in this case — if confirmed, anticoagulation must be initiated promptly. OCP use confirmation is urgently needed.

diagnostic_criteria_applied.result: INSUFFICIENT DATA — MIDAS requires information on headache days in past 3 months, missed work/school days, reduced productivity days, and missed household/social activity days. Cannot calculate without this information. Should be administered at neurology follow-up if primary migraine diagnosis confirmed.
diagnostic_criteria_applied.interpretation: MIDAS score will guide preventive therapy decision-making at outpatient neurology follow-up. Score ≥11 (Grade III-IV) indicates need for preventive therapy.

diagnostic_criteria_applied.result: INSUFFICIENT DATA — Cannot calculate without patient-reported impact questionnaire. Administer at follow-up.
diagnostic_criteria_applied.interpretation: HIT-6 score ≥60 indicates severe impact and supports preventive therapy initiation.

risk_stratification.rationale: While the most likely diagnosis remains new-onset migraine (62% probability), the 2-week continuous duration, fixed unilateral localization, new onset without prior diagnosis, and reproductive-age female demographics create an intermediate-to-high risk profile for serious secondary pathology. The unconfirmed OCP use status is the single most important unanswered question — if confirmed, CVST risk elevates this to HIGH risk requiring urgent MRI/MRV. The absence of thunderclap onset, focal neurological deficits, fever, meningismus, and papilledema (if confirmed absent on exam) would lower the risk profile toward intermediate. Current risk is intermediate-high pending examination findings and OCP status confirmation.

factors_increasing_risk: 2-week continuous headache duration (atypical for primary headache disorder)
New onset without prior headache diagnosis in adult
Fixed right-sided unilateral localization over 2 weeks
Reproductive-age female (IIH and CVST risk population)
OCP use status unconfirmed (if confirmed, CVST risk elevated 5-7x)
Papilledema status not yet assessed (critical gap)
factors_decreasing_risk: No morning predominance or positional worsening

specialty_specific_tests: IMMEDIATE (ED — within 1 hour): Blood pressure measurement bilateral arms — exclude hypertensive urgency/emergency (BP >180/120 mmHg)
IMMEDIATE (ED — within 1 hour): Focused neurological examination — cranial nerves (CN II, III, IV, VI), motor, sensory, cerebellar, gait, meningismus (Kernig/Brudzinski signs)
IMMEDIATE (ED — within 1 hour): Direct fundoscopy or slit-lamp examination — assess for papilledema (IIH, CVST with elevated ICP, mass lesion); this is the single most important bedside test
IMMEDIATE (ED — within 1 hour): Confirm OCP/hormonal contraceptive use status — critical for CVST risk stratification and management
IMMEDIATE (ED — within 1 hour): Confirm analgesic use frequency — assess for medication overuse headache (MOH) risk if analgesics used >10-15 days/month
URGENT IMAGING (within 2-4 hours): Non-contrast CT head — first-line to exclude hemorrhage (SAH, subdural/epidural hematoma), hydrocephalus, large mass lesion, midline shift

URGENT IMAGING (within 4-6 hours if CT negative or non-diagnostic): MRI brain without and with gadolinium contrast — gold standard for mass lesion (ring-enhancing lesion, LR+ >20), meningeal enhancement (meningitis, carcinomatosis), posterior fossa pathology, IIH features (empty sella, optic nerve sheath distension, flattening of posterior globe)

URGENT IMAGING (concurrent with MRI): MR Venography (MRV) of brain — mandatory in reproductive-age female with 2-week progressive headache to exclude CVST (filling defect in dural venous sinus, LR+ >50); especially critical if OCP use confirmed
URGENT LABS (within 2 hours): CBC with differential — leukocytosis (infection/inflammation), thrombocytopenia (thrombotic disorder)
URGENT LABS (within 2 hours): Comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) — electrolytes, renal function, glucose, liver function

URGENT LABS (within 2 hours): ESR and CRP — inflammatory/infectious etiology screening; ESR >50 mm/hr raises concern for GCA (low probability at age 35 but included for completeness) or other inflammatory process
URGENT LABS (within 2 hours): Coagulation studies (PT, PTT, INR) — baseline prior to potential anticoagulation if CVST confirmed; also screens for coagulopathy

URGENT LABS (if OCP use confirmed or CVST suspected): D-dimer — elevated in CVST but limited sensitivity/specificity; negative D-dimer has modest negative predictive value in low-pretest probability but does NOT exclude CVST

URGENT LABS (if OCP use confirmed or CVST suspected): Thrombophilia screen — Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin G20210A mutation, Protein C/S activity, Antithrombin III, Antiphospholipid antibodies (anticardiolipin IgG/IgM, anti-β2-glycoprotein I, lupus anticoagulant) — ideally before anticoagulation initiation

CONDITIONAL (if MRI/MRV negative and IIH or meningitis still suspected): Lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement — opening pressure >25 cmH2O diagnostic for IIH; CSF analysis (cell count, protein, glucose, culture, cytology, India ink if immunocompromised); xanthochromia assessment if SAH still suspected
CONDITIONAL (if LP performed): CSF opening pressure in lateral decubitus position — critical for IIH diagnosis; normal <20 cmH2O, borderline 20-25, elevated >25 cmH2O
CONDITIONAL (if focal deficits or mass lesion on MRI): CT angiography (CTA) head and neck — evaluate for vascular malformation (AVM), aneurysm, or arterial dissection
OUTPATIENT FOLLOW-UP (if primary migraine confirmed): Thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4) — hypothyroidism can cause or worsen headache; screen at outpatient visit
OUTPATIENT FOLLOW-UP (if primary migraine confirmed): Pregnancy test (urine or serum β-hCG) — reproductive-age female; pregnancy affects medication choices significantly
OUTPATIENT FOLLOW-UP (neurology clinic): MIDAS questionnaire administration — quantify headache-related disability to guide preventive therapy decision

STEP 3 — Immediate (within 1 hour): Direct fundoscopy — assess for papilledema (IIH, CVST with elevated ICP, mass lesion); single most important bedside test in this patient
STEP 4 — Immediate (within 1 hour): Confirm oral contraceptive pill (OCP) use status — CRITICAL for CVST risk stratification; if confirmed, MRI/MRV is mandatory before OCP continuation

medications.name: Prochlorperazine (Compazine)
medications.frequency: Once in ED; may repeat once after 30 minutes if inadequate response
medications.duration: Acute ED use only
medications.indication: Nausea relief AND independent anti-migraine analgesic effect (NNT ~2.9 for significant headache relief in ED); superior to opioids for migraine in ED setting
contraindications: QTc prolongation (obtain baseline ECG if concern)
medications.monitoring: Blood pressure before and after administration; observe for extrapyramidal symptoms for 30–60 minutes post-dose
drug_interactions: Additive CNS depression with benzodiazepines, opioids, alcohol
Additive QTc prolongation with other QTc-prolonging agents
May mask neurological deterioration — reassess neuro exam after administration
medications.pregnancy_safety: Category C — use with caution; benefit-risk assessment required
medications.evidence_grade: A — Level I evidence (AHS Consensus Statement 2021)

medications.name: Ketorolac (Toradol)
medications.frequency: Once in ED; may repeat 15–30 mg every 6 hours if needed
medications.max_daily_dose: 120 mg/day IV/IM; limit to 5 days total
medications.duration: Acute ED use only; do NOT prescribe for outpatient daily use
medications.indication: Acute migraine analgesia (NNT ~3.9 in ED setting); adjunct to antiemetic therapy
contraindications: Active peptic ulcer disease or GI bleeding
Known NSAID hypersensitivity or aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease
AVOID if anticoagulation anticipated (CVST concern — do not administer if CVST is strongly suspected before MRV results)
Pregnancy (especially third trimester — premature closure of ductus arteriosus)
medications.monitoring: Renal function if repeated dosing; blood pressure; GI symptoms
drug_interactions: CRITICAL: Do NOT combine with anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin, LMWH, DOACs) — significantly increased bleeding risk
Additive nephrotoxicity with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics
Reduces efficacy of antihypertensives
medications.clinical_note: HOLD ketorolac if CVST is strongly suspected on clinical grounds pending MRV results, as anticoagulation may be required imminently
medications.evidence_grade: A — Level I evidence

medications.name: Normal Saline (0.9% NaCl)
medications.frequency: Once over 1 hour in ED
medications.duration: Acute ED use
medications.indication: Dehydration is a common migraine trigger and perpetuating factor; IV hydration improves headache response to medications
common_side_effects: Fluid overload if excessive volumes given
medications.monitoring: Urine output, blood pressure, signs of fluid overload
medications.evidence_grade: B — Level II-III evidence

medications.name: Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) — PROPHYLACTIC
medications.frequency: Administer 15–30 minutes BEFORE prochlorperazine
medications.duration: Single prophylactic dose in ED
medications.indication: Prevention of akathisia and dystonic reactions from prochlorperazine; standard of care when administering dopamine antagonists for migraine in ED
medications.monitoring: Level of consciousness; fall risk
medications.evidence_grade: B — Level II evidence

treatment_plans.condition: Migraine Without Aura — New Onset (Most Likely Primary Diagnosis, 62% probability — DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION after workup)
treatment_plans.phase: Phase 2 — Acute Migraine Treatment (Initiate AFTER secondary causes excluded by imaging/exam)
treatment_plans.clinical_rationale: If CT head, MRI brain with contrast, and MRV are negative for secondary pathology, and neurological examination is normal with no papilledema and no meningismus, the diagnosis of new-onset migraine without aura is supported. Treatment follows AHS/NICE NG150 evidence-based stepped care algorithm. The 2-week continuous course may represent Status Migrainosus (continuous migraine >72 hours) or New Daily Persistent Headache (NDPH) — both are diagnoses of exclusion requiring outpatient neurology follow-up.
treatment_plans.first_line: Triptan therapy (5-HT1B/1D agonist) + NSAID combination for moderate-to-severe migraine

step_1_conservative: Rest in dark, quiet, low-stimulation environment
Cold or warm compress to head/neck per patient preference
Identify and avoid triggers (see lifestyle recommendations)
Headache diary initiation — track date, time, duration, severity (0–10), location, associated symptoms, potential triggers, medications taken
Sleep hygiene optimization — consistent sleep/wake schedule, 7–9 hours nightly
treatment_algorithm.step_2_first_line_pharmacological: Triptan + NSAID combination (superior to either agent alone; evidence grade A)
treatment_algorithm.step_3_second_line_pharmacological: CGRP receptor antagonist (gepant) if triptan contraindicated or not tolerated
treatment_algorithm.step_4_adjunctive: Antiemetic for nausea; behavioral therapy; biofeedback
treatment_algorithm.step_5_preventive: Initiate if ≥4 migraine days/month, significant disability (MIDAS ≥11), or acute medication overuse — assess at neurology follow-up
treatment_algorithm.step_6_interventional: Greater occipital nerve block; trigger point injections; Botox (onabotulinumtoxinA) for chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month)
treatment_algorithm.step_7_refractory: Inpatient DHE (dihydroergotamine) protocol for status migrainosus refractory to outpatient treatment

medications.name: Sumatriptan (Imitrex)

dose_options.subcutaneous: 6 mg SC (fastest onset, highest efficacy — NNT 3.3 for pain-free at 2 hours)
dose_options.nasal_spray: 20 mg intranasal (useful if nausea limits oral intake)

medications.frequency: At onset of migraine; may repeat once after 2 hours if partial response
medications.max_daily_dose: 200 mg/day PO; 12 mg/day SC; 40 mg/day nasal
medications.max_monthly_use: No more than 10 days per month to prevent medication overuse headache (MOH)
medications.duration: Acute use only — not for daily/preventive use

contraindications: Ischemic heart disease, coronary artery disease, or history of MI
Uncontrolled hypertension (BP must be controlled before prescribing)
Concurrent or recent (within 2 weeks) MAOI use — ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION
Concurrent ergotamine or ergot derivative use (within 24 hours)
IMPORTANT: If migraine WITH AURA is subsequently confirmed, reassess OCP use — combined OCP + migraine with aura = WHO Category 4 (unacceptable ischemic stroke risk, RR 2.08–8.72)

monitoring: Blood pressure before first dose
Cardiovascular risk assessment
Response at 2 hours — if no response, reassess diagnosis
Track monthly use days to prevent MOH

CONTRAINDICATED with ergotamine derivatives (within 24 hours — additive vasospasm)

medications.evidence_grade: A — Level I (AHS Consensus Statement 2021; NICE NG150 2021)

medications.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)

warnings: HIGH: Ketorolac IV 30mg must be HELD if CVST is clinically suspected pending MRV results — anticoagulation may be required imminently and concurrent NSAID use significantly increases intracranial and systemic bleeding risk. The treatment plan notes this caveat but it requires active clinical decision-making at bedside before administration.

HIGH: OCP (oral contraceptive pill) use status is unconfirmed and is the single most critical unanswered safety question in this case. If OCP use is confirmed: (1) combined OCP must be suspended immediately pending MRV to exclude CVST; (2) if migraine WITH aura is subsequently confirmed, combined OCP is WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria Category 4 — unacceptable ischemic stroke risk (RR 2.08–8.72) and must not be restarted; (3) sumatriptan prescribing safety profile changes in the context of OCP-related stroke risk.

HIGH: Sumatriptan is listed as a treatment option but must NOT be prescribed or administered until: (a) blood pressure is measured and confirmed controlled — uncontrolled hypertension is a contraindication; (b) CVST is excluded by MRV — triptans cause vasoconstriction and could worsen venous thrombosis; (c) hemiplegic or basilar migraine features are formally excluded on neurological examination; (d) cardiovascular risk is assessed. The treatment plan notes these contraindications but the sequential dependency must be enforced at the point of prescribing.

HIGH: Diphenhydramine 25mg IV is recommended prophylactically before prochlorperazine to prevent akathisia and dystonic reactions — this is appropriate and evidence-supported. However, diphenhydramine has anticholinergic properties and will cause sedation. Patient must be counseled not to drive or operate machinery after administration. Fall precautions must be in place post-administration.

MODERATE: Prochlorperazine lowers the seizure threshold. While seizure risk is low in this patient, this is relevant if CVST is subsequently confirmed (CVST carries seizure risk). Document baseline neurological status before administration and reassess neurological examination after dosing — prochlorperazine-induced sedation must not mask neurological deterioration.

MODERATE: Prochlorperazine and ondansetron are both listed as treatment options. If both are administered concurrently or in close succession, there is additive QTc prolongation risk. A baseline ECG should be obtained if there is any clinical concern for QTc prolongation, or if the patient is on any other QTc-prolonging medications (status unknown — medication reconciliation incomplete). Do NOT co-administer prochlorperazine and ondansetron without QTc assessment.

MODERATE: Ibuprofen 400–600mg PO is listed for outpatient acute migraine use with a maximum monthly use limit of 15 days/month to prevent medication overuse headache (MOH). The patient has already been experiencing headache for 2 weeks — analgesic use frequency over this period is UNKNOWN and not yet confirmed. If the patient has been self-medicating with NSAIDs, acetaminophen, or combination analgesics daily for the past 2 weeks, MOH may already be developing or present. This must be assessed before prescribing additional analgesics and before attributing the 2-week course solely to primary migraine.

MODERATE: Pregnancy status has not been confirmed. The patient is a 35-year-old female of reproductive age. Sumatriptan (Category C), prochlorperazine (Category C), and ketorolac (avoid in third trimester — premature ductus arteriosus closure) all carry pregnancy safety considerations. A urine or serum beta-hCG should be obtained before administering these medications. The specialist plan recommends this at outpatient follow-up — this safety officer recommends it be obtained in the ED prior to medication administration.

MODERATE: Thrombophilia screening (Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin G20210A, Protein C/S, Antithrombin III, antiphospholipid antibodies) is recommended if CVST is suspected. This screen should ideally be drawn BEFORE anticoagulation is initiated, as anticoagulation will alter Protein C, Protein S, and Antithrombin III levels. If CVST is confirmed and anticoagulation must be started urgently, document that thrombophilia screen was drawn prior to first anticoagulant dose.

MODERATE: No allergy history has been documented anywhere in the multi-agent output. This is a critical safety gap. Before administering prochlorperazine (phenothiazine class), ketorolac (NSAID class), diphenhydramine (antihistamine class), sumatriptan (triptan class), or ondansetron, allergy status must be confirmed. Phenothiazine hypersensitivity, NSAID/aspirin hypersensitivity (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease — Samter's triad), and sulfonamide cross-reactivity with triptans must be specifically queried.

LOW: Normal saline 1L IV is recommended for hydration. This is appropriate and low-risk in a hemodynamically stable patient. However, blood pressure has not yet been documented. If hypertensive urgency or emergency is identified on BP measurement, fluid administration strategy should be reassessed in context of overall hemodynamic management.

LOW: The treatment plan appropriately recommends AVOIDING opioids (AHS Grade A recommendation). This safety officer endorses and reinforces this recommendation. No opioid should be prescribed or administered for this presentation. If any other agent on the team or at the bedside suggests opioid use, this must be flagged as a safety concern.

LOW: Acetaminophen is listed as an alternative analgesic with a conservative maximum of 3000mg/day. Hepatic function status is unknown at this time. If CMP (ordered as part of the workup) reveals hepatic impairment, acetaminophen dose must be reduced further or avoided. This should be cross-referenced once lab results return.

LOW: The treatment plan does not explicitly address what to do if the patient has taken any medications in the past 14 days that could interact with the proposed regimen — specifically: (1) any MAOI use (absolute contraindication with sumatriptan and prochlorperazine — 2-week washout required); (2) any ergotamine-containing medications (contraindicated within 24 hours of triptan use); (3) any serotonergic agents (SSRIs, SNRIs, lithium — serotonin syndrome risk with triptans and prochlorperazine). Full medication reconciliation is required before prescribing.
contraindications: Sumatriptan is CONTRAINDICATED in: uncontrolled hypertension (BP not yet measured — must confirm before prescribing), ischemic heart disease or coronary artery disease, history of stroke or TIA, hemiplegic or basilar-type migraine (must be excluded on neurological exam), peripheral vascular disease, concurrent or recent MAOI use within 2 weeks (medication history not yet confirmed), concurrent ergotamine or ergot derivative use within 24 hours, severe hepatic impairment, and CVST (relative contraindication — vasoconstriction may worsen venous thrombosis).

Ketorolac IV is CONTRAINDICATED in: active peptic ulcer disease or GI bleeding (history not confirmed), renal impairment with CrCl <30 mL/min (renal function not yet confirmed — CMP pending), known NSAID hypersensitivity or aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (allergy history not documented), pregnancy especially third trimester (pregnancy status not confirmed), and should be HELD if anticoagulation is anticipated for CVST.

Ibuprofen PO is CONTRAINDICATED in: active GI bleeding or peptic ulcer disease, severe renal or hepatic impairment, NSAID hypersensitivity, pregnancy (third trimester), and must be AVOIDED if anticoagulation is initiated for CVST.

Prochlorperazine is CONTRAINDICATED in: known hypersensitivity to phenothiazines (allergy history not documented), CNS depression or comatose states, Parkinson's disease, and should be used with caution in patients with QTc prolongation or on other QTc-prolonging agents (baseline ECG recommended if concern exists).

Diphenhydramine is CONTRAINDICATED in: narrow-angle glaucoma (ophthalmologic history not confirmed), urinary retention, and concurrent MAOI use (medication history not confirmed). Note: diphenhydramine is listed on Beers Criteria as potentially inappropriate in elderly patients — NOT applicable here as patient is 35 years old, but documented for completeness.

Ondansetron is CONTRAINDICATED in: congenital long QT syndrome (cardiac history not confirmed), concurrent apomorphine use, and should be used with caution with other QTc-prolonging agents. Must NOT be co-administered with prochlorperazine without QTc assessment due to additive QTc prolongation risk.

Combined oral contraceptive pill (if currently prescribed): CONTRAINDICATED (WHO Category 4 — unacceptable risk) if migraine WITH AURA is confirmed. Must be suspended pending CVST exclusion by MRV regardless of aura status. This is a critical prescribing safety issue that must be communicated to the patient's prescribing physician.

Topiramate (listed as a preventive option): CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (Category D — teratogenic, associated with oral clefts and small for gestational age). Pregnancy must be excluded before initiating. Also: additive carbonic anhydrase inhibition if combined with acetazolamide (used for IIH) — increases risk of metabolic acidosis, nephrolithiasis, and hypokalemia.

Acetazolamide (listed for IIH if confirmed): CONTRAINDICATED in sulfonamide hypersensitivity (cross-reactivity risk — allergy history not documented), severe renal or hepatic impairment, hypokalemia, hyponatremia, and adrenocortical insufficiency. Electrolytes must be confirmed before initiation.
