empathy.patient_summary:
Thank you for reaching out about your headaches — two weeks of daily head pain is exhausting, and you are absolutely right to get it checked out. You are taking an important step by seeking care.

Here is what we know so far: You have been having a throbbing headache on the right side of your head for two weeks, along with sensitivity to light and some nausea. These symptoms look a lot like migraine — a type of headache that affects about 1 in 4 women your age. In fact, migraine is the most likely explanation for what you are experiencing.

However, because this is a brand-new headache pattern for you and it has lasted two weeks without stopping, your medical team wants to make sure nothing else is causing it before giving you a final diagnosis. This is not cause for alarm — it is simply good, careful medicine. Most of the time, tests like these come back normal and confirm that migraine is the answer. But ruling out other causes first means you get the right treatment faster and more safely.

Your care team is focused on two things right now: (1) making sure you are safe by doing some tests, and (2) helping you feel better as quickly as possible.
empathy.what_this_means:
Your symptoms — a one-sided throbbing headache, light sensitivity, and nausea — are the classic signs of migraine. Think of migraine as a storm in the brain's electrical and chemical system. It causes real, physical pain, not just stress or anxiety.

What makes your situation a little different from a typical migraine is that yours has lasted two full weeks without a break. Most migraines last between 4 and 72 hours and then ease up. A headache that keeps going for two weeks — especially one that is new for you — is something doctors want to investigate carefully.

Your team is checking for a few specific things:

• A blood clot in a vein in the brain (called CVST) — this is especially important if you take birth control pills, because the pill can slightly raise the risk of this type of clot. If you do take birth control pills, please tell your doctor right away.

• Increased pressure inside the skull (called IIH) — this is more common in women of childbearing age and can cause headaches that look just like yours.

• A growth or lesion in the brain — this is unlikely given your age and the fact that you have no other symptoms, but a scan will confirm it.

• Bleeding around the brain (SAH) — also unlikely because your headache came on gradually rather than suddenly, but the team wants to be thorough.

The good news: you have no warning signs like sudden severe pain, weakness, confusion, fever, or stiff neck — all of which would make this more urgent. Your medical team is being careful, not alarmed.

right_now: Go to the emergency department or urgent care today — do not wait. Your doctor needs to examine you and run some tests before starting treatment.
Tell the doctor or nurse right away if you take birth control pills or any hormonal contraception. This is one of the most important pieces of information for your care team.

Tell the doctor every medication you have taken for this headache over the past two weeks — including any over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen (Advil), acetaminophen (Tylenol), or aspirin, and how often you took them.
Tell the doctor about any other medications, vitamins, or supplements you take regularly.
Tell the doctor if you have any known allergies to medications.

Expect to have your blood pressure checked, a neurological exam (the doctor will check your eyes, reflexes, and coordination), and a CT scan of your head. You may also need an MRI scan and blood tests.
Rest in a quiet, dim room while you wait. Bright lights and noise can make the pain worse.
Drink water — staying hydrated can help with headache pain.
this_week: Follow up with a neurologist (a brain and nervous system specialist) as directed by your emergency team.

Start a headache diary. Each day, write down: what time the headache started, how bad it was on a scale of 0 to 10, where on your head it hurt, how long it lasted, any other symptoms (nausea, light sensitivity, blurry vision), what you ate or drank, how much sleep you got, where you were in your menstrual cycle, and any medications you took. This information is incredibly helpful for your doctor.

Ask your doctor about your birth control method — if you take combined birth control pills (estrogen and progestin), your doctor may want to discuss switching to a different method while your headaches are being investigated.
If you are prescribed a triptan medication (like sumatriptan) for migraine, take it at the very first sign of a headache — do not wait until the pain is severe. It works best early.
Avoid taking pain relievers more than 10 to 15 days per month. Using them too often can actually cause more headaches — this is called medication overuse headache or rebound headache.
ongoing: Keep your headache diary going — bring it to every doctor's appointment.
Try to keep a regular sleep schedule. Going to bed and waking up at the same time every day (even on weekends) is one of the most effective migraine prevention strategies.
Stay well hydrated — aim for 6 to 8 glasses of water per day.
Eat regular meals and avoid skipping meals, as low blood sugar is a common migraine trigger.

Identify your personal triggers. Common ones include: stress, bright or flickering lights, strong smells, caffeine changes, alcohol (especially red wine), hormonal changes around your period, and weather changes.
Manage stress with techniques that work for you — gentle exercise, deep breathing, meditation, or talking to someone you trust.

If your doctor recommends a daily preventive medication for migraine, take it every day as prescribed — even on days when you feel fine. These medications work by preventing headaches from starting, not by stopping them once they begin.
Attend all follow-up appointments, even if you are feeling better. Your doctor needs to track your progress and adjust your treatment plan if needed.

medications_explained.name: Prochlorperazine (Compazine)
medications_explained.what_it_does: This medication does two things at once — it stops nausea AND directly relieves migraine pain. It works by calming the chemical signals in your brain that cause both nausea and headache. Research shows it works better than opioid painkillers for migraine relief in the emergency setting.
medications_explained.how_to_take: Given by injection into a vein (IV) or muscle (IM) by a nurse in the emergency department. You will usually receive a small dose of Benadryl (diphenhydramine) first to prevent restlessness, which is a common side effect.
medications_explained.what_to_expect: You may feel drowsy and relaxed. Some people feel restless or have muscle stiffness — tell your nurse immediately if this happens, as it is easily treated.
medications_explained.important_note: Do not drive or operate machinery after receiving this medication. You will need someone to take you home.

medications_explained.name: Ketorolac (Toradol)
medications_explained.what_it_does: This is a powerful anti-inflammatory medication given through an IV. It reduces the inflammation that contributes to migraine pain. Think of it like a very strong version of ibuprofen delivered directly into your bloodstream for faster relief.
medications_explained.how_to_take: Given by injection into a vein (IV) by a nurse in the emergency department.
medications_explained.important_note: This medication will NOT be given if your doctor suspects a blood clot in the brain (CVST), because blood thinners may be needed in that case and this medication could increase bleeding risk. Your doctor will make this decision after reviewing your test results.

medications_explained.name: Sumatriptan (Imitrex)
medications_explained.what_it_does: Triptans are medications designed specifically for migraine. They work by narrowing blood vessels in the brain and blocking pain signals. They do not work for other types of headaches — only migraine. This is actually a good sign if they work for you, as it helps confirm the migraine diagnosis.
medications_explained.how_to_take: Available as a tablet you swallow (50–100mg), a self-injection under the skin (fastest option), or a nasal spray (useful if nausea makes swallowing difficult). Take it at the very first sign of a migraine — the sooner the better.
medications_explained.important_note: This medication will only be prescribed AFTER your tests come back and your doctor confirms it is safe for you. It cannot be used if you have certain heart conditions or uncontrolled high blood pressure. Your doctor will check these things first.
medications_explained.monthly_limit: Use no more than 10 days per month to avoid rebound headaches.

medications_explained.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)
medications_explained.what_it_does: Reduces inflammation and pain. For migraine, it works best for mild to moderate pain and is often used alongside a triptan for stronger attacks.
medications_explained.how_to_take: 400 to 600mg by mouth with food. Take with a full glass of water.
medications_explained.important_note: Do not use more than 15 days per month — using it more often than this can cause your headaches to get worse over time (called rebound or medication overuse headache). Always take with food to protect your stomach.

medications_explained.name: Ondansetron (Zofran)
medications_explained.what_it_does: Stops nausea so you can keep other medications down and feel more comfortable. It dissolves under your tongue, which is helpful when nausea makes swallowing difficult.
medications_explained.how_to_take: 4 to 8mg by mouth (dissolving tablet) or through an IV. Every 8 hours as needed for nausea.

empathy.lifestyle_tips:
Many people find that lifestyle changes make a real difference in how often migraines happen and how severe they are. You do not have to change everything at once — even small steps add up.

SLEEP: Try to go to bed and wake up at the same time every day. Your brain loves routine, and irregular sleep is one of the most common migraine triggers. Aim for 7 to 9 hours.

HYDRATION: Drink water throughout the day. Even mild dehydration can trigger a migraine. Keep a water bottle with you.

EATING REGULARLY: Do not skip meals. Low blood sugar is a well-known migraine trigger. Try to eat at regular times each day.

STRESS: Stress does not cause migraine, but it is a very common trigger. Find what helps you decompress — whether that is a walk, music, a warm bath, deep breathing, or talking to a friend. Even 10 minutes of quiet time can help.

CAFFEINE: If you drink coffee or tea, try to keep the amount consistent each day. Both too much caffeine and suddenly cutting back can trigger migraines.

LIGHT AND SCREENS: During a migraine, dim the lights and reduce screen time. Blue-light filtering glasses may help some people between attacks.

EXERCISE: Regular moderate exercise (like walking, swimming, or yoga) can reduce migraine frequency over time. However, very intense exercise can sometimes trigger a migraine — so build up gradually.

BIRTH CONTROL: If you take combined birth control pills (containing estrogen), this is worth discussing with your doctor. Estrogen changes can trigger migraines in some women, and there may be better options for you depending on your situation. This is not something to be embarrassed about — it is a very common and important conversation.

HEADACHE DIARY: This is probably the single most useful thing you can do. Tracking your headaches helps you and your doctor identify your personal triggers and find the best treatment.
when_to_get_help: Call 911 or go to the emergency room IMMEDIATELY if you experience a sudden, extremely severe headache — the worst headache of your life — especially if it comes on in seconds. This is sometimes called a 'thunderclap headache' and requires emergency evaluation right away.

Go to the emergency room immediately if your headache is accompanied by: fever AND stiff neck (you cannot touch your chin to your chest), confusion or difficulty thinking clearly, weakness or numbness on one side of your body, difficulty speaking or understanding speech, sudden vision changes or loss of vision, loss of consciousness or fainting, or seizures.

Go to the emergency room or call your doctor urgently if: your headache suddenly becomes much worse than it has been, you develop new symptoms you did not have before, you have a headache after a head injury or fall, your vision becomes blurry or you see double, or you feel pressure behind your eyes.

Call your doctor within 24 hours if: your prescribed medications are not helping at all, you are vomiting and cannot keep fluids down, your headache is significantly worse in the morning when you first wake up, or you notice your headache gets worse when you lie down or change positions.
Contact your doctor if you notice any new symptoms after starting a new medication, including chest tightness, racing heart, difficulty breathing, rash, or swelling.
empathy.reassurance:
Living with two weeks of daily head pain is genuinely hard, and it makes complete sense that you are worried and worn out. Please know that you are not alone — migraine affects about 1 in 4 women your age, making it one of the most common health conditions in the world. The fact that your symptoms look so much like migraine is actually reassuring.

The tests your doctors are recommending are not a sign that something is definitely wrong — they are a sign that your team is being thorough and careful. Most people who go through this workup find that everything comes back normal, and they leave with a clear migraine diagnosis and a treatment plan that actually works.

Migraine is a real, physical condition — not something you imagined, not something caused by stress alone, and not something you just have to live with. There are excellent treatments available, including medications that can stop a migraine in its tracks and daily preventive options that can dramatically reduce how often they happen.

You are taking exactly the right steps by seeking care. Many people with migraine go on to manage it very well and live full, active lives. You deserve to feel better, and your care team is here to help make that happen.

anticipated_faqs.answer: Your symptoms — a one-sided throbbing headache, light sensitivity, and nausea — match migraine very closely, and migraine is the most likely explanation (about a 62% probability based on your symptoms). However, because this is a new headache pattern for you and it has lasted two weeks without stopping, your doctors need to run some tests first to make sure nothing else is causing it. This is standard, careful practice — not a sign that something is definitely wrong. Once the tests come back, your doctor will be able to give you a clear answer.

anticipated_faqs.question: Why does it matter if I take birth control pills?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Combined birth control pills (the kind that contain estrogen) can slightly increase the risk of a rare type of blood clot in the brain called cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST). This type of clot can cause persistent headaches that look very similar to migraine. It is important for your doctor to know if you take the pill so they can decide whether to do a specific scan (called an MRI with MRV) to check for this. If you do take the pill, your doctor will likely ask you to pause it temporarily until the scan is done. This does not mean you definitely have a clot — it is simply a precaution.

anticipated_faqs.question: Could taking pain relievers every day have made my headaches worse?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Possibly, yes. This is called medication overuse headache, or rebound headache. When you take pain relievers (like ibuprofen or acetaminophen) more than 10 to 15 days per month, your brain can actually become more sensitive to pain over time, causing more frequent headaches. If this is happening, your doctor will help you safely reduce your pain reliever use as part of your treatment plan. It is not your fault — many people do not know about this risk.

anticipated_faqs.question: Do I need a brain scan?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Yes, most likely. Because your headache is new, has lasted two weeks, and you have never been diagnosed with migraine before, your doctors will want to do a CT scan of your head first to rule out bleeding or other urgent problems. They may also recommend an MRI scan, which gives a more detailed picture and can check for things a CT scan might miss. These scans are painless and will give your team important information to make sure you get the right treatment.

anticipated_faqs.question: Will I need to take medication every day?
anticipated_faqs.answer: That depends on how often your headaches occur. If your headaches happen four or more days per month, or if they significantly affect your daily life, your doctor may recommend a daily preventive medication. These are taken every day to reduce how often headaches happen — not to stop a headache once it starts. Common options include certain blood pressure medications, antidepressants (which also work for migraine prevention), or newer injectable medications called CGRP antibodies. Your doctor will discuss the best option for you at your follow-up appointment.

anticipated_faqs.question: Is migraine dangerous?
anticipated_faqs.answer: For most people, migraine is not dangerous — it is painful and disruptive, but it does not cause permanent damage to the brain. However, there are some important exceptions. Women who have migraines with aura (visual disturbances like flashing lights or blind spots before the headache) and who also take combined birth control pills have a higher risk of stroke. This is why your doctor will ask you specifically about aura symptoms and your contraception. If you do have migraine with aura, your doctor will likely recommend a different type of birth control.

anticipated_faqs.question: How long will it take to feel better?
anticipated_faqs.answer: With the right treatment, many people with migraine feel significantly better within a few days to a few weeks. Acute medications (like triptans) can stop a migraine within 2 hours for many people. If you start a daily preventive medication, it usually takes 4 to 8 weeks to see the full benefit. Lifestyle changes like regular sleep, hydration, and stress management can also make a noticeable difference over time. Recovery is very achievable — most people with migraine manage it well with proper care.

specialist.reason_for_consultation: 35-year-old female with 2-week history of new-onset persistent right-sided throbbing headache (6/10), photophobia, and intermittent nausea. No prior headache diagnosis. Triage and diagnostician flagged need for secondary cause exclusion prior to primary headache diagnosis. Specific concerns include CVST, intracranial mass, IIH, SAH, and meningitis.
specialist.specialist_assessment:
This is a 35-year-old female presenting with a 2-week history of persistent right-sided throbbing headache rated 6/10, accompanied by photophobia and intermittent nausea. From a neurology standpoint, the phenotype is superficially consistent with migraine without aura (ICHD-3 criteria: unilateral location, pulsating quality, photophobia, nausea). However, several features deviate critically from a benign primary headache diagnosis and mandate urgent secondary cause exclusion before any primary headache label is applied.

KEY NEUROLOGICAL CONCERNS:

1. DURATION: The 2-week continuous course is fundamentally incompatible with episodic migraine (ICHD-3 requires 4-72 hours per attack). A 2-week unremitting headache in a previously undiagnosed adult is a neurological red flag. Differential considerations for this duration pattern include: Status Migrainosus (>72h continuous migraine — diagnosis of exclusion), New Daily Persistent Headache (NDPH — abrupt-onset daily headache from day 1, often with viral prodrome), Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis (CVST — progressive headache over days-weeks is the hallmark), Intracranial mass lesion (progressive course), IIH (chronic progressive headache in reproductive-age female), and Medication Overuse Headache (MOH — if analgesics used daily, though 2 weeks is early for MOH transformation).

2. FIXED UNILATERAL LOCALIZATION: While migraines are frequently unilateral, a headache that is consistently and exclusively right-sided over 2 weeks raises concern for an ipsilateral structural lesion. True migraine can alternate sides or remain unilateral, but fixed lateralization warrants structural exclusion.

3. NEW ONSET IN ADULT WITHOUT PRIOR DIAGNOSIS: Per SNOOP4 criteria (AHS/ACEP), new headache pattern in an adult without prior headache history is a red flag requiring neuroimaging. The absence of a prior migraine diagnosis means we cannot attribute this presentation to a known primary disorder.

4. REPRODUCTIVE-AGE FEMALE: This demographic carries specific neurological risk profiles — IIH (incidence 15-19/100,000/year in obese reproductive-age women vs. 0.9/100,000 general population) and CVST (OCP use increases risk 5-7x; headache is the presenting symptom in >90% of CVST cases). OCP use status is a CRITICAL unanswered question that materially changes the differential and urgency.

5. PHOTOPHOBIA: While classic for migraine, photophobia also occurs in meningitis, SAH, and IIH. In the context of a 2-week headache, it cannot be attributed to migraine without secondary cause exclusion.

NEUROLOGICAL EXAMINATION PRIORITIES:
The following examination findings would be immediately actionable:
- Fundoscopy: Papilledema (present → IIH, CVST with elevated ICP, mass lesion; absent → lowers but does not exclude IIH)
- Meningismus: Kernig/Brudzinski signs (present → LP mandatory after CT)
- Cranial nerve examination: CN VI palsy (IIH), CN III palsy with ptosis/mydriasis (posterior communicating artery aneurysm), visual field defects (mass lesion, IIH)
- Motor/sensory/cerebellar examination: Any focal deficit → emergent neuroimaging
- Blood pressure: Hypertensive urgency/emergency must be excluded immediately

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS (Neurology Perspective, Ranked by Clinical Priority):
1. Migraine Without Aura — New Onset (62% pre-imaging probability): Most likely phenotypically, but 2-week continuous course is atypical. Diagnosis of exclusion.
2. Hormonal/OCP-Related Migraine (18% if OCP confirmed): Estrogen-mediated migraine in reproductive-age female. Must confirm OCP use urgently — if confirmed, MRV mandatory before continuing OCP.
3. IIH / Pseudotumor Cerebri (14%): Female, reproductive age, photophobia, progressive headache. Fundoscopy is the critical bedside test. If papilledema present, diagnosis is strongly supported.
4. Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis (10-15% if OCP confirmed): Progressive 2-week headache in reproductive-age female. Can present with isolated headache before focal deficits develop. MRI/MRV is diagnostic. Time-sensitive — anticoagulation must be initiated promptly if confirmed.
5. Intracranial Mass Lesion (12%): New persistent unilateral headache in adult. MRI brain with gadolinium is gold standard. Absence of focal deficits and morning predominance argues against but does not exclude early lesion.
6. Status Migrainosus (diagnosis of exclusion): Continuous migraine >72 hours. Requires exclusion of all secondary causes before this label is applied.
7. New Daily Persistent Headache (NDPH): Headache present daily from onset, often following viral illness. Diagnosis of exclusion; requires neuroimaging.
8. SAH — Sentinel Bleed (5%): Low probability given absence of thunderclap onset, but must-not-miss. CT head without contrast is mandatory first step.
9. Meningitis — Viral/Subacute (5%): Low probability given absence of fever and meningismus, but photophobia warrants formal meningismus assessment.
10. Analgesic Overuse Headache (MOH): If patient has been taking analgesics daily for 2 weeks, early MOH transformation is possible — medication history is critical.

NEUROLOGY MANAGEMENT APPROACH:
Phase 1 (Immediate — ED): Vital signs including BP, focused neurological exam with fundoscopy and meningismus assessment, non-contrast CT head to exclude hemorrhage/mass/hydrocephalus, confirm OCP use status, obtain medication history (analgesic frequency).
Phase 2 (Urgent — within hours if CT negative): MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast + MR venography (MRV) — this is the single most important investigation in this patient. MRI/MRV will simultaneously evaluate for mass lesion, CVST, IIH features (empty sella, optic nerve sheath distension, transverse sinus stenosis), and posterior fossa pathology missed by CT.
Phase 3 (If MRI/MRV negative): LP with opening pressure measurement — critical to exclude IIH (opening pressure >25 cmH2O) and meningitis (CSF analysis). Also evaluates for xanthochromia if SAH still suspected.
Phase 4 (Outpatient Neurology): Headache diary, migraine trigger assessment, menstrual cycle correlation, preventive therapy consideration if migraine confirmed and frequency warrants it.

ACUTE SYMPTOMATIC TREATMENT (pending workup, assuming no contraindications identified):
- Antiemetic: Prochlorperazine 10mg IV (NNT ~2.9 for headache relief; superior to opioids in ED; independent anti-migraine effect) OR Metoclopramide 10mg IV
- Analgesic: Ketorolac 30mg IV (NNT ~3.9 in ED setting) — AVOID if anticoagulation anticipated (CVST concern)
- Triptan: Sumatriptan 6mg SC or 100mg PO if migraine diagnosis supported after initial workup and no contraindications (cardiovascular disease, uncontrolled HTN, hemiplegic/basilar migraine features)
- IV hydration: 1L NS if dehydration contributing
- Low-stimulation environment: Dim lighting, quiet room
- AVOID opioids: AHS Grade A recommendation against opioid use for migraine; inferior efficacy, MOH risk

OCP MANAGEMENT: If OCP use confirmed, do NOT continue combined oral contraceptive until CVST excluded by MRV. If migraine with aura is subsequently confirmed, combined OCP is WHO Category 4 (unacceptable risk) due to significantly elevated ischemic stroke risk (RR 2.08-8.72). Refer to OB-GYN for contraceptive counseling — progestin-only or non-hormonal methods preferred.

risk_stratification.rationale: While the most likely diagnosis remains new-onset migraine (62% probability), the 2-week continuous duration, fixed unilateral localization, new onset without prior diagnosis, and reproductive-age female demographics create an intermediate-to-high risk profile for serious secondary pathology. The unconfirmed OCP use status is the single most important unanswered question — if confirmed, CVST risk elevates this to HIGH risk requiring urgent MRI/MRV. The absence of thunderclap onset, focal neurological deficits, fever, meningismus, and papilledema (if confirmed absent on exam) would lower the risk profile toward intermediate. Current risk is intermediate-high pending examination findings and OCP status confirmation.

specialty_specific_tests: IMMEDIATE (ED — within 1 hour): Blood pressure measurement bilateral arms — exclude hypertensive urgency/emergency (BP >180/120 mmHg)
IMMEDIATE (ED — within 1 hour): Focused neurological examination — cranial nerves (CN II, III, IV, VI), motor, sensory, cerebellar, gait, meningismus (Kernig/Brudzinski signs)
IMMEDIATE (ED — within 1 hour): Direct fundoscopy or slit-lamp examination — assess for papilledema (IIH, CVST with elevated ICP, mass lesion); this is the single most important bedside test
IMMEDIATE (ED — within 1 hour): Confirm OCP/hormonal contraceptive use status — critical for CVST risk stratification and management
IMMEDIATE (ED — within 1 hour): Confirm analgesic use frequency — assess for medication overuse headache (MOH) risk if analgesics used >10-15 days/month
URGENT IMAGING (within 2-4 hours): Non-contrast CT head — first-line to exclude hemorrhage (SAH, subdural/epidural hematoma), hydrocephalus, large mass lesion, midline shift

URGENT IMAGING (within 4-6 hours if CT negative or non-diagnostic): MRI brain without and with gadolinium contrast — gold standard for mass lesion (ring-enhancing lesion, LR+ >20), meningeal enhancement (meningitis, carcinomatosis), posterior fossa pathology, IIH features (empty sella, optic nerve sheath distension, flattening of posterior globe)

URGENT IMAGING (concurrent with MRI): MR Venography (MRV) of brain — mandatory in reproductive-age female with 2-week progressive headache to exclude CVST (filling defect in dural venous sinus, LR+ >50); especially critical if OCP use confirmed
URGENT LABS (within 2 hours): CBC with differential — leukocytosis (infection/inflammation), thrombocytopenia (thrombotic disorder)
URGENT LABS (within 2 hours): Comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) — electrolytes, renal function, glucose, liver function

URGENT LABS (within 2 hours): ESR and CRP — inflammatory/infectious etiology screening; ESR >50 mm/hr raises concern for GCA (low probability at age 35 but included for completeness) or other inflammatory process
URGENT LABS (within 2 hours): Coagulation studies (PT, PTT, INR) — baseline prior to potential anticoagulation if CVST confirmed; also screens for coagulopathy

URGENT LABS (if OCP use confirmed or CVST suspected): D-dimer — elevated in CVST but limited sensitivity/specificity; negative D-dimer has modest negative predictive value in low-pretest probability but does NOT exclude CVST

URGENT LABS (if OCP use confirmed or CVST suspected): Thrombophilia screen — Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin G20210A mutation, Protein C/S activity, Antithrombin III, Antiphospholipid antibodies (anticardiolipin IgG/IgM, anti-β2-glycoprotein I, lupus anticoagulant) — ideally before anticoagulation initiation

CONDITIONAL (if MRI/MRV negative and IIH or meningitis still suspected): Lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement — opening pressure >25 cmH2O diagnostic for IIH; CSF analysis (cell count, protein, glucose, culture, cytology, India ink if immunocompromised); xanthochromia assessment if SAH still suspected
CONDITIONAL (if LP performed): CSF opening pressure in lateral decubitus position — critical for IIH diagnosis; normal <20 cmH2O, borderline 20-25, elevated >25 cmH2O
CONDITIONAL (if focal deficits or mass lesion on MRI): CT angiography (CTA) head and neck — evaluate for vascular malformation (AVM), aneurysm, or arterial dissection
OUTPATIENT FOLLOW-UP (if primary migraine confirmed): Thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4) — hypothyroidism can cause or worsen headache; screen at outpatient visit
OUTPATIENT FOLLOW-UP (if primary migraine confirmed): Pregnancy test (urine or serum β-hCG) — reproductive-age female; pregnancy affects medication choices significantly
OUTPATIENT FOLLOW-UP (neurology clinic): MIDAS questionnaire administration — quantify headache-related disability to guide preventive therapy decision

treatment_plans.condition: New-Onset Persistent Unilateral Headache — Secondary Cause Exclusion (PRIORITY PHASE)
treatment_plans.phase: Phase 1 — Urgent Diagnostic Workup (ED / Urgent Care, Day 1)
treatment_plans.clinical_rationale: Before ANY primary headache treatment is initiated, secondary causes must be excluded. The 2-week continuous duration is fundamentally incompatible with episodic migraine (ICHD-3 requires 4–72 hours per attack). SNOOP4 red flags are triggered: new headache pattern in adult without prior diagnosis, persistent unilateral localization >2 weeks, reproductive-age female (IIH and CVST risk population). This patient CANNOT be discharged with empirical migraine diagnosis without neuroimaging.
treatment_plans.first_line: Urgent neuroimaging + neurological examination BEFORE pharmacological migraine treatment is finalized
diagnostic_steps: STEP 1 — Immediate (within 1 hour): Bilateral arm blood pressure measurement to exclude hypertensive urgency/emergency (BP >180/120 mmHg)
STEP 2 — Immediate (within 1 hour): Focused neurological examination — cranial nerves II/III/IV/VI, motor, sensory, cerebellar, meningismus (Kernig and Brudzinski signs)
STEP 3 — Immediate (within 1 hour): Direct fundoscopy — assess for papilledema (IIH, CVST with elevated ICP, mass lesion); single most important bedside test in this patient
STEP 4 — Immediate (within 1 hour): Confirm oral contraceptive pill (OCP) use status — CRITICAL for CVST risk stratification; if confirmed, MRI/MRV is mandatory before OCP continuation
STEP 5 — Immediate (within 1 hour): Confirm analgesic use frequency — assess for medication overuse headache (MOH) if analgesics used >10–15 days/month
STEP 6 — Urgent imaging (within 2–4 hours): Non-contrast CT head — first-line to exclude hemorrhage (SAH, subdural/epidural hematoma), hydrocephalus, large mass lesion, midline shift

STEP 7 — Urgent imaging (within 4–6 hours if CT negative): MRI brain without AND with gadolinium contrast — gold standard for mass lesion, meningeal enhancement, IIH features (empty sella, optic nerve sheath distension), posterior fossa pathology

STEP 8 — Urgent imaging (concurrent with MRI): MR Venography (MRV) of brain — mandatory in reproductive-age female with 2-week progressive headache to exclude CVST; especially critical if OCP use confirmed
STEP 9 — Urgent labs (within 2 hours): CBC with differential, CMP, ESR, CRP, coagulation studies (PT/PTT/INR)
STEP 10 — Conditional (if OCP confirmed or CVST suspected): D-dimer, thrombophilia screen (Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin G20210A, Protein C/S, Antithrombin III, antiphospholipid antibodies)

STEP 11 — Conditional (if MRI/MRV negative and IIH or meningitis still suspected): Lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement in lateral decubitus position — opening pressure >25 cmH2O diagnostic for IIH; CSF analysis for cell count, protein, glucose, culture, xanthochromia

medications.name: Prochlorperazine (Compazine)
medications.frequency: Once in ED; may repeat once after 30 minutes if inadequate response
medications.duration: Acute ED use only
medications.indication: Nausea relief AND independent anti-migraine analgesic effect (NNT ~2.9 for significant headache relief in ED); superior to opioids for migraine in ED setting
contraindications: QTc prolongation (obtain baseline ECG if concern)
medications.monitoring: Blood pressure before and after administration; observe for extrapyramidal symptoms for 30–60 minutes post-dose
drug_interactions: Additive CNS depression with benzodiazepines, opioids, alcohol
Additive QTc prolongation with other QTc-prolonging agents
May mask neurological deterioration — reassess neuro exam after administration
medications.pregnancy_safety: Category C — use with caution; benefit-risk assessment required
medications.evidence_grade: A — Level I evidence (AHS Consensus Statement 2021)

medications.name: Ketorolac (Toradol)
medications.frequency: Once in ED; may repeat 15–30 mg every 6 hours if needed
medications.max_daily_dose: 120 mg/day IV/IM; limit to 5 days total
medications.duration: Acute ED use only; do NOT prescribe for outpatient daily use
medications.indication: Acute migraine analgesia (NNT ~3.9 in ED setting); adjunct to antiemetic therapy
contraindications: Active peptic ulcer disease or GI bleeding
Known NSAID hypersensitivity or aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease
AVOID if anticoagulation anticipated (CVST concern — do not administer if CVST is strongly suspected before MRV results)
Pregnancy (especially third trimester — premature closure of ductus arteriosus)
medications.monitoring: Renal function if repeated dosing; blood pressure; GI symptoms
drug_interactions: CRITICAL: Do NOT combine with anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin, LMWH, DOACs) — significantly increased bleeding risk
Additive nephrotoxicity with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics
Reduces efficacy of antihypertensives
medications.clinical_note: HOLD ketorolac if CVST is strongly suspected on clinical grounds pending MRV results, as anticoagulation may be required imminently
medications.evidence_grade: A — Level I evidence

medications.name: Normal Saline (0.9% NaCl)
medications.frequency: Once over 1 hour in ED
medications.duration: Acute ED use
medications.indication: Dehydration is a common migraine trigger and perpetuating factor; IV hydration improves headache response to medications
common_side_effects: Fluid overload if excessive volumes given
medications.monitoring: Urine output, blood pressure, signs of fluid overload
medications.evidence_grade: B — Level II-III evidence

medications.name: Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) — PROPHYLACTIC
medications.frequency: Administer 15–30 minutes BEFORE prochlorperazine
medications.duration: Single prophylactic dose in ED
medications.indication: Prevention of akathisia and dystonic reactions from prochlorperazine; standard of care when administering dopamine antagonists for migraine in ED
medications.monitoring: Level of consciousness; fall risk
medications.evidence_grade: B — Level II evidence

treatment_plans.condition: Migraine Without Aura — New Onset (Most Likely Primary Diagnosis, 62% probability — DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION after workup)
treatment_plans.phase: Phase 2 — Acute Migraine Treatment (Initiate AFTER secondary causes excluded by imaging/exam)
treatment_plans.clinical_rationale: If CT head, MRI brain with contrast, and MRV are negative for secondary pathology, and neurological examination is normal with no papilledema and no meningismus, the diagnosis of new-onset migraine without aura is supported. Treatment follows AHS/NICE NG150 evidence-based stepped care algorithm. The 2-week continuous course may represent Status Migrainosus (continuous migraine >72 hours) or New Daily Persistent Headache (NDPH) — both are diagnoses of exclusion requiring outpatient neurology follow-up.
treatment_plans.first_line: Triptan therapy (5-HT1B/1D agonist) + NSAID combination for moderate-to-severe migraine

step_1_conservative: Rest in dark, quiet, low-stimulation environment
Cold or warm compress to head/neck per patient preference
Identify and avoid triggers (see lifestyle recommendations)
Headache diary initiation — track date, time, duration, severity (0–10), location, associated symptoms, potential triggers, medications taken
Sleep hygiene optimization — consistent sleep/wake schedule, 7–9 hours nightly
treatment_algorithm.step_2_first_line_pharmacological: Triptan + NSAID combination (superior to either agent alone; evidence grade A)
treatment_algorithm.step_3_second_line_pharmacological: CGRP receptor antagonist (gepant) if triptan contraindicated or not tolerated
treatment_algorithm.step_4_adjunctive: Antiemetic for nausea; behavioral therapy; biofeedback
treatment_algorithm.step_5_preventive: Initiate if ≥4 migraine days/month, significant disability (MIDAS ≥11), or acute medication overuse — assess at neurology follow-up
treatment_algorithm.step_6_interventional: Greater occipital nerve block; trigger point injections; Botox (onabotulinumtoxinA) for chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month)
treatment_algorithm.step_7_refractory: Inpatient DHE (dihydroergotamine) protocol for status migrainosus refractory to outpatient treatment

medications.name: Sumatriptan (Imitrex)

dose_options.subcutaneous: 6 mg SC (fastest onset, highest efficacy — NNT 3.3 for pain-free at 2 hours)
dose_options.nasal_spray: 20 mg intranasal (useful if nausea limits oral intake)

medications.frequency: At onset of migraine; may repeat once after 2 hours if partial response
medications.max_daily_dose: 200 mg/day PO; 12 mg/day SC; 40 mg/day nasal
medications.max_monthly_use: No more than 10 days per month to prevent medication overuse headache (MOH)
medications.duration: Acute use only — not for daily/preventive use
medications.indication: First-line acute treatment for moderate-to-severe migraine (NNT ~5 for pain-free at 2 hours PO; NNT ~3.3 SC)
contraindications: Ischemic heart disease, coronary artery disease, or history of MI
Uncontrolled hypertension (BP must be controlled before prescribing)
Concurrent or recent (within 2 weeks) MAOI use — ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION
Concurrent ergotamine or ergot derivative use (within 24 hours)
IMPORTANT: If migraine WITH AURA is subsequently confirmed, reassess OCP use — combined OCP + migraine with aura = WHO Category 4 (unacceptable ischemic stroke risk, RR 2.08–8.72)
common_side_effects: Chest tightness or pressure (usually musculoskeletal, not cardiac — but evaluate if persistent)
monitoring: Blood pressure before first dose
Cardiovascular risk assessment
Response at 2 hours — if no response, reassess diagnosis
Track monthly use days to prevent MOH
drug_interactions: CONTRAINDICATED with MAOIs (severe hypertension, serotonin syndrome)
CONTRAINDICATED with ergotamine derivatives (within 24 hours — additive vasospasm)
MODERATE interaction with SSRIs/SNRIs — theoretical serotonin syndrome risk (generally acceptable per AHS 2010 but monitor)
OCP interaction: estrogen component may reduce triptan clearance via CYP1A2 inhibition — monitor for increased triptan side effects
medications.pregnancy_safety: Category C — limited data; use only if benefit outweighs risk; consult OB-GYN
medications.evidence_grade: A — Level I (AHS Consensus Statement 2021; NICE NG150 2021)

medications.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)
medications.frequency: At onset of migraine; may repeat every 6–8 hours as needed
medications.max_monthly_use: No more than 15 days per month — CRITICAL to prevent MOH
medications.duration: Acute use only; take with food to reduce GI upset
medications.indication: First-line for mild-to-moderate migraine; adjunct to triptan for moderate-to-severe (NNT ~7.2 for pain-free at 2 hours as monotherapy)
contraindications: Active peptic ulcer disease or GI bleeding
NSAID hypersensitivity or aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease
AVOID if anticoagulation initiated for CVST
common_side_effects: GI upset, heartburn, nausea (take with food)
medications.monitoring: Renal function with regular use; blood pressure; GI symptoms
drug_interactions: AVOID with anticoagulants — increased bleeding risk
Reduces efficacy of antihypertensives (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics)
Additive nephrotoxicity with other nephrotoxic agents
medications.evidence_grade: A — Level I

medications.name: Ondansetron (Zofran)
medications.route: PO (oral dissolving tablet preferred if nausea limits swallowing) or IV
medications.frequency: Every 8 hours as needed for nausea
medications.duration: As needed for nausea during acute migraine attacks
medications.indication: Nausea management during migraine attacks; allows oral medication absorption; note: antiemetic effect only (no independent anti-migraine effect unlike prochlorperazine)
common_side_effects: QTc prolongation (dose-dependent, more relevant at higher doses)
medications.monitoring: QTc if on other QTc-prolonging medications
drug_interactions: Additive QTc prolongation with other QTc-prolonging agents
Serotonin syndrome risk with serotonergic agents (rare)
medications.pregnancy_safety: Category B — generally considered safe; consult OB-GYN
medications.evidence_grade: B — Level II (antiemetic effect; no independent anti-migraine effect)

medications.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol) — ALTERNATIVE ANALGESIC
medications.frequency: Every 6–8 hours as needed
medications.max_monthly_use: No more than 15 days per month to prevent MOH
medications.duration: Acute use; preferred analgesic if NSAIDs contraindicated or if anticoagulation initiated

pico_question.P: 35-year-old female with 2-week history of persistent unilateral right-sided throbbing headache (6/10), photophobia, and intermittent nausea; no prior headache diagnosis; no documented focal neurological deficits
pico_question.I: Clinical evaluation including neuroimaging (CT/MRI), neurological examination, and pharmacological treatment (triptans, NSAIDs, antiemetics) for suspected primary headache disorder
pico_question.C: Watchful waiting vs. empirical migraine treatment vs. urgent secondary cause workup (intracranial mass, vascular lesion, IIH, meningitis)
pico_question.O: Primary: accurate diagnosis and exclusion of secondary headache etiology; Secondary: headache frequency reduction ≥50%, pain-free at 2 hours, return to function, prevention of medication overuse headache (MOH)

primary_headache_diagnosis.recommendation: Migraine without aura requires ≥5 attacks lasting 4–72 hours with at least 2 of: unilateral location, pulsating quality, moderate-to-severe intensity, aggravation by routine activity; AND at least 1 of: nausea/vomiting, photophobia/phonophobia. This patient meets unilateral location, throbbing quality, photophobia, and nausea — however, 2-week continuous headache does NOT fit typical episodic migraine (4–72h per attack). Consider New Daily Persistent Headache (NDPH) or Status Migrainosus if migraine-like features persist >72h continuously.
primary_headache_diagnosis.evidence_grade: A (High Quality — consensus-based diagnostic criteria from systematic expert review)
primary_headache_diagnosis.clinical_note: ICHD-3 explicitly requires exclusion of secondary causes before diagnosing primary headache disorder. The 2-week unremitting course is atypical for episodic migraine and mandates secondary cause exclusion.

secondary_headache_exclusion.source: American Headache Society (AHS) / American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP) — 2019 Evidence-Based Guidelines
secondary_headache_exclusion.recommendation: Apply SNOOP4 red flag criteria for secondary headache screening: Systemic symptoms/disease, Neurological symptoms/signs, Onset sudden (thunderclap), Older age (>50), Prior headache history change, Positional component, Papilledema, Progressive worsening. This patient triggers: NEW onset headache pattern in adult without prior diagnosis + 2-week persistence without resolution.
red_flags_present: New headache pattern without prior diagnosis
secondary_headache_exclusion.imaging_recommendation: Non-contrast CT head as initial screen in ED setting; MRI brain with and without contrast preferred if CT negative and clinical suspicion persists. MRA indicated if vascular lesion (AVM, aneurysm) suspected.

neuroimaging_guidelines.source: American College of Radiology (ACR) Appropriateness Criteria — Headache, 2022; AAN Practice Parameter
neuroimaging_guidelines.recommendation: CT head without contrast: Appropriate as initial imaging in new-onset headache in ED to exclude hemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus. MRI brain without/with contrast: More appropriate for subacute/chronic new headache, suspected IIH, meningeal disease, or posterior fossa pathology. MRA brain: Indicated when vascular malformation or aneurysm suspected.
neuroimaging_guidelines.evidence_grade: B (Moderate Quality — based on diagnostic accuracy studies and expert consensus)
neuroimaging_guidelines.sensitivity_note: CT sensitivity for subarachnoid hemorrhage: ~98% within 6 hours of onset, drops to ~85–90% at 24h, ~50% at 1 week. LP may be required if CT negative and SAH still suspected despite low thunderclap probability here.

acute_migraine_treatment.source: American Headache Society (AHS) Consensus Statement 2021; NICE Guideline NG150 (2021); AAN/AHS Evidence-Based Guidelines

first_line_acute_treatments.examples: Sumatriptan 50–100mg PO, 6mg SC; Rizatriptan 10mg PO; Eletriptan 40mg PO
first_line_acute_treatments.recommendation: First-line for moderate-to-severe migraine or mild-to-moderate migraine not responding to NSAIDs
first_line_acute_treatments.nnt_pain_free_2h: NNT = 3.3–5.0 (sumatriptan 100mg PO: NNT ~5 for pain-free at 2h; SC sumatriptan: NNT ~3.3)
first_line_acute_treatments.contraindications: Cardiovascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, hemiplegic migraine, basilar migraine, concurrent MAOI use, pregnancy (relative)

first_line_acute_treatments.examples: Ibuprofen 400–600mg PO; Naproxen sodium 500–550mg PO; Ketorolac 30mg IV/IM
first_line_acute_treatments.recommendation: First-line for mild-to-moderate migraine; adjunct to triptans for moderate-to-severe
first_line_acute_treatments.nnt_pain_free_2h: Ibuprofen 400mg: NNT ~7.2 for pain-free at 2h; Ketorolac IV: NNT ~3.9 in ED setting

first_line_acute_treatments.examples: Metoclopramide 10mg IV/PO; Prochlorperazine 10mg IV/IM; Ondansetron 4–8mg IV/PO
first_line_acute_treatments.recommendation: Effective for nausea and as adjunct analgesic (prochlorperazine/metoclopramide have independent anti-migraine effect); prochlorperazine superior to opioids in ED
first_line_acute_treatments.evidence_grade: A (High Quality — prochlorperazine); B (Moderate — ondansetron for nausea only)
first_line_acute_treatments.nnt_headache_relief: Prochlorperazine 10mg IV: NNT ~2.9 for significant headache relief in ED

first_line_acute_treatments.recommendation: Alternative for patients with triptan contraindications or cardiovascular risk; also useful for MOH prevention

acute_migraine_treatment.opioid_recommendation: AVOID opioids for migraine management — associated with increased MOH risk, worse long-term outcomes, and inferior efficacy vs. dopamine antagonists in ED. (AHS Grade A recommendation against routine opioid use)

migraine_prevention_guidelines.source: AAN/AHS Evidence-Based Guideline for Migraine Prevention, 2012 (updated 2021 with CGRP mAbs); NICE NG150
migraine_prevention_guidelines.indication_for_prevention: ≥4 migraine days/month, significant disability, acute medication overuse, or patient preference

first_line_preventive_agents.nnt_50pct_reduction: NNT ~4.0 for ≥50% reduction in monthly migraine days

first_line_preventive_agents.evidence_grade: A (High Quality — multiple Phase III RCTs)
first_line_preventive_agents.note: Preferred in patients with contraindications to oral preventives or treatment-refractory migraine

migraine_prevention_guidelines.hormonal_consideration: If OCP use confirmed: combined oral contraceptives may increase migraine frequency and, in migraine with aura, significantly increase ischemic stroke risk (RR 2.08–8.72 depending on aura status). Progestin-only or non-hormonal contraception preferred in migraine with aura.

iih_guidelines.source: European Headache Federation / North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society (NANOS) IIH Guidelines 2021
iih_guidelines.relevance: 35-year-old female — IIH predominantly affects women of reproductive age; BMI not documented but key risk factor
iih_guidelines.diagnostic_criteria: Modified Dandy Criteria: symptoms/signs of raised ICP, papilledema on fundoscopy, normal neurological exam (except CN VI palsy), LP opening pressure >25 cmH2O, normal CSF composition, no other cause identified on neuroimaging
iih_guidelines.recommendation: Fundoscopic examination mandatory in all new headache presentations in reproductive-age females to exclude papilledema. MRI brain + MR venography preferred over CT to evaluate for venous sinus thrombosis and IIH features (empty sella, optic nerve sheath distension).
iih_guidelines.treatment_if_confirmed: Acetazolamide 250–2000mg/day (first-line); weight loss (10% body weight reduction associated with IIH remission in 25% of cases); serial LP for acute symptom relief; surgical options (optic nerve sheath fenestration, CSF shunting) for vision-threatening cases

cerebral_venous_sinus_thrombosis.source: European Stroke Organisation (ESO) Guidelines for CVT, 2017; AHA/ASA 2011
cerebral_venous_sinus_thrombosis.relevance: Reproductive-age female on potential OCP — CVT risk increased 5–7x with OCP use; headache is presenting symptom in >90% of CVT cases
cerebral_venous_sinus_thrombosis.recommendation: MRI brain with MR venography (MRV) is investigation of choice for CVT. D-dimer may be elevated but has limited sensitivity/specificity. Anticoagulation (LMWH then warfarin/DOAC) is treatment of choice even in presence of hemorrhagic infarction.

triptan_interactions.mechanism: Additive serotonergic effect — theoretical serotonin syndrome risk
triptan_interactions.clinical_effect: Serotonin syndrome (rare but serious): agitation, hyperthermia, clonus, autonomic instability
triptan_interactions.management: Monitor for serotonin syndrome symptoms; combination generally considered acceptable per AHS 2010 statement but use with caution; FDA warning issued 2006

triptan_interactions.mechanism: MAOIs inhibit triptan metabolism via MAO-A, leading to markedly elevated triptan levels
triptan_interactions.clinical_effect: Severe hypertension, serotonin syndrome, coronary vasospasm
triptan_interactions.management: Absolute contraindication — do not co-administer; 2-week washout required after MAOI discontinuation
Do not use within 24 hours of each other

triptan_interactions.mechanism: OCPs may reduce triptan clearance (CYP1A2 inhibition by estrogen component); also OCPs independently increase migraine frequency and stroke risk in migraineurs
triptan_interactions.clinical_effect: Potential increased triptan exposure; more clinically relevant: OCP + migraine with aura = significantly elevated ischemic stroke risk
triptan_interactions.management: Assess for aura; if migraine with aura confirmed, strongly consider OCP discontinuation per WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (Category 4 — unacceptable risk)

nsaid_interactions.drug_pair: NSAIDs + Anticoagulants (if CVT treated with anticoagulation)
nsaid_interactions.mechanism: Additive bleeding risk; NSAIDs inhibit platelet aggregation and damage GI mucosa
nsaid_interactions.clinical_effect: Increased GI and intracranial bleeding risk
nsaid_interactions.management: Avoid NSAIDs if anticoagulation initiated; use acetaminophen for analgesia

nsaid_interactions.drug_pair: NSAIDs (chronic use) — Medication Overuse Headache (MOH) Risk
nsaid_interactions.mechanism: Central sensitization from frequent analgesic use (>10–15 days/month)
nsaid_interactions.clinical_effect: Transformation to chronic daily headache; MOH affects ~1–2% of general population, up to 50% of chronic headache clinic patients
nsaid_interactions.management: Limit NSAID use to ≤10 days/month; educate patient on MOH risk; if MOH suspected, structured withdrawal program required

acetazolamide_interactions.drug_pair: Acetazolamide + Topiramate (if both used for IIH + migraine prevention)
acetazolamide_interactions.mechanism: Both are carbonic anhydrase inhibitors — additive effect
acetazolamide_interactions.clinical_effect: Increased risk of metabolic acidosis, nephrolithiasis, hypokalemia, paresthesias
acetazolamide_interactions.management: Monitor electrolytes, bicarbonate, renal function; avoid combination if possible or use lowest effective doses

drug_interactions.note: Full interaction profile requires complete medication reconciliation. OCP use status is clinically critical and not yet confirmed in this case.

migraine_epidemiology.global_prevalence: 14.7% of global population (1.04 billion people) — Lancet Neurology GBD 2016
migraine_epidemiology.sex_distribution: Female:Male ratio = 3:1 in adults; hormonal influence strongly implicated
migraine_epidemiology.peak_age: Peak prevalence ages 25–55; highest in women aged 30–39
migraine_epidemiology.this_patient_demographic: 35-year-old female — in highest prevalence demographic; estimated 1-year prevalence ~24–30% in this age-sex group
migraine_epidemiology.source: GBD 2016 Headache Collaborators, Lancet Neurology 2018; Lipton et al., Headache 2007

secondary_headache_prevalence_in_new_ons.overall_secondary_cause_rate: ~10–15% of patients presenting to ED with new/worst headache have a serious secondary cause
secondary_headache_prevalence_in_new_ons.intracranial_mass: Brain tumors account for ~0.1% of all headache presentations; headache as presenting symptom in ~60% of brain tumor patients
secondary_headache_prevalence_in_new_ons.subarachnoid_hemorrhage: ~1–3% of ED headache presentations; thunderclap onset in >80% — low probability here given gradual onset
secondary_headache_prevalence_in_new_ons.cerebral_venous_thrombosis: Incidence 1.32–1.57 per 100,000/year; women of reproductive age disproportionately affected (OCP use RR 5–7x); headache in >90% of cases

risk_factors: Female sex (RR ~8x vs. males)
Obesity BMI >30 (RR ~7.1 vs. normal BMI)
Recent weight gain
Reproductive age (15–44)
Certain medications: tetracyclines, vitamin A/retinoids, corticosteroid withdrawal, OCPs (controversial)

secondary_headache_prevalence_in_new_ons.meningitis: Bacterial meningitis incidence ~1.38/100,000/year in US; viral meningitis more common; fever + meningismus key distinguishing features — not reported here but absence does not fully exclude

warnings: HIGH: Ketorolac IV 30mg must be HELD if CVST is clinically suspected pending MRV results — anticoagulation may be required imminently and concurrent NSAID use significantly increases intracranial and systemic bleeding risk. The treatment plan notes this caveat but it requires active clinical decision-making at bedside before administration.

HIGH: OCP (oral contraceptive pill) use status is unconfirmed and is the single most critical unanswered safety question in this case. If OCP use is confirmed: (1) combined OCP must be suspended immediately pending MRV to exclude CVST; (2) if migraine WITH aura is subsequently confirmed, combined OCP is WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria Category 4 — unacceptable ischemic stroke risk (RR 2.08–8.72) and must not be restarted; (3) sumatriptan prescribing safety profile changes in the context of OCP-related stroke risk.

HIGH: Sumatriptan is listed as a treatment option but must NOT be prescribed or administered until: (a) blood pressure is measured and confirmed controlled — uncontrolled hypertension is a contraindication; (b) CVST is excluded by MRV — triptans cause vasoconstriction and could worsen venous thrombosis; (c) hemiplegic or basilar migraine features are formally excluded on neurological examination; (d) cardiovascular risk is assessed. The treatment plan notes these contraindications but the sequential dependency must be enforced at the point of prescribing.

HIGH: Diphenhydramine 25mg IV is recommended prophylactically before prochlorperazine to prevent akathisia and dystonic reactions — this is appropriate and evidence-supported. However, diphenhydramine has anticholinergic properties and will cause sedation. Patient must be counseled not to drive or operate machinery after administration. Fall precautions must be in place post-administration.

MODERATE: Prochlorperazine lowers the seizure threshold. While seizure risk is low in this patient, this is relevant if CVST is subsequently confirmed (CVST carries seizure risk). Document baseline neurological status before administration and reassess neurological examination after dosing — prochlorperazine-induced sedation must not mask neurological deterioration.

MODERATE: Prochlorperazine and ondansetron are both listed as treatment options. If both are administered concurrently or in close succession, there is additive QTc prolongation risk. A baseline ECG should be obtained if there is any clinical concern for QTc prolongation, or if the patient is on any other QTc-prolonging medications (status unknown — medication reconciliation incomplete). empathy.patient_summary:
Thank you for reaching out about your headaches — two weeks of daily head pain is exhausting, and you are absolutely right to get it checked out. You are taking an important step by seeking care.

Here is what we know so far: You have been having a throbbing headache on the right side of your head for two weeks, along with sensitivity to light and some nausea. These symptoms look a lot like migraine — a type of headache that affects about 1 in 4 women your age. In fact, migraine is the most likely explanation for what you are experiencing.

However, because this is a brand-new headache pattern for you and it has lasted two weeks without stopping, your medical team wants to make sure nothing else is causing it before giving you a final diagnosis. This is not cause for alarm — it is simply good, careful medicine. Most of the time, tests like these come back normal and confirm that migraine is the answer. But ruling out other causes first means you get the right treatment faster and more safely.

Your care team is focused on two things right now: (1) making sure you are safe by doing some tests, and (2) helping you feel better as quickly as possible.
empathy.what_this_means:
Your symptoms — a one-sided throbbing headache, light sensitivity, and nausea — are the classic signs of migraine. Think of migraine as a storm in the brain's electrical and chemical system. It causes real, physical pain, not just stress or anxiety.

What makes your situation a little different from a typical migraine is that yours has lasted two full weeks without a break. Most migraines last between 4 and 72 hours and then ease up. A headache that keeps going for two weeks — especially one that is new for you — is something doctors want to investigate carefully.

Your team is checking for a few specific things:

• A blood clot in a vein in the brain (called CVST) — this is especially important if you take birth control pills, because the pill can slightly raise the risk of this type of clot. If you do take birth control pills, please tell your doctor right away.

• Increased pressure inside the skull (called IIH) — this is more common in women of childbearing age and can cause headaches that look just like yours.

• A growth or lesion in the brain — this is unlikely given your age and the fact that you have no other symptoms, but a scan will confirm it.

• Bleeding around the brain (SAH) — also unlikely because your headache came on gradually rather than suddenly, but the team wants to be thorough.

The good news: you have no warning signs like sudden severe pain, weakness, confusion, fever, or stiff neck — all of which would make this more urgent. Your medical team is being careful, not alarmed.

right_now: Go to the emergency department or urgent care today — do not wait. Your doctor needs to examine you and run some tests before starting treatment.
Tell the doctor or nurse right away if you take birth control pills or any hormonal contraception. This is one of the most important pieces of information for your care team.

Tell the doctor every medication you have taken for this headache over the past two weeks — including any over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen (Advil), acetaminophen (Tylenol), or aspirin, and how often you took them.
Tell the doctor about any other medications, vitamins, or supplements you take regularly.
Tell the doctor if you have any known allergies to medications.

Expect to have your blood pressure checked, a neurological exam (the doctor will check your eyes, reflexes, and coordination), and a CT scan of your head. You may also need an MRI scan and blood tests.
Rest in a quiet, dim room while you wait. Bright lights and noise can make the pain worse.
Drink water — staying hydrated can help with headache pain.
this_week: Follow up with a neurologist (a brain and nervous system specialist) as directed by your emergency team.

Start a headache diary. Each day, write down: what time the headache started, how bad it was on a scale of 0 to 10, where on your head it hurt, how long it lasted, any other symptoms (nausea, light sensitivity, blurry vision), what you ate or drank, how much sleep you got, where you were in your menstrual cycle, and any medications you took. This information is incredibly helpful for your doctor.

Ask your doctor about your birth control method — if you take combined birth control pills (estrogen and progestin), your doctor may want to discuss switching to a different method while your headaches are being investigated.
If you are prescribed a triptan medication (like sumatriptan) for migraine, take it at the very first sign of a headache — do not wait until the pain is severe. It works best early.
Avoid taking pain relievers more than 10 to 15 days per month. Using them too often can actually cause more headaches — this is called medication overuse headache or rebound headache.
ongoing: Keep your headache diary going — bring it to every doctor's appointment.
Try to keep a regular sleep schedule. Going to bed and waking up at the same time every day (even on weekends) is one of the most effective migraine prevention strategies.
Stay well hydrated — aim for 6 to 8 glasses of water per day.
Eat regular meals and avoid skipping meals, as low blood sugar is a common migraine trigger.

Identify your personal triggers. Common ones include: stress, bright or flickering lights, strong smells, caffeine changes, alcohol (especially red wine), hormonal changes around your period, and weather changes.
Manage stress with techniques that work for you — gentle exercise, deep breathing, meditation, or talking to someone you trust.

If your doctor recommends a daily preventive medication for migraine, take it every day as prescribed — even on days when you feel fine. These medications work by preventing headaches from starting, not by stopping them once they begin.
Attend all follow-up appointments, even if you are feeling better. Your doctor needs to track your progress and adjust your treatment plan if needed.

medications_explained.name: Prochlorperazine (Compazine)
medications_explained.what_it_does: This medication does two things at once — it stops nausea AND directly relieves migraine pain. It works by calming the chemical signals in your brain that cause both nausea and headache. Research shows it works better than opioid painkillers for migraine relief in the emergency setting.
medications_explained.how_to_take: Given by injection into a vein (IV) or muscle (IM) by a nurse in the emergency department. You will usually receive a small dose of Benadryl (diphenhydramine) first to prevent restlessness, which is a common side effect.
medications_explained.what_to_expect: You may feel drowsy and relaxed. Some people feel restless or have muscle stiffness — tell your nurse immediately if this happens, as it is easily treated.
medications_explained.important_note: Do not drive or operate machinery after receiving this medication. You will need someone to take you home.

medications_explained.name: Ketorolac (Toradol)
medications_explained.what_it_does: This is a powerful anti-inflammatory medication given through an IV. It reduces the inflammation that contributes to migraine pain. Think of it like a very strong version of ibuprofen delivered directly into your bloodstream for faster relief.
medications_explained.how_to_take: Given by injection into a vein (IV) by a nurse in the emergency department.
medications_explained.important_note: This medication will NOT be given if your doctor suspects a blood clot in the brain (CVST), because blood thinners may be needed in that case and this medication could increase bleeding risk. Your doctor will make this decision after reviewing your test results.

medications_explained.name: Sumatriptan (Imitrex)
medications_explained.what_it_does: Triptans are medications designed specifically for migraine. They work by narrowing blood vessels in the brain and blocking pain signals. They do not work for other types of headaches — only migraine. This is actually a good sign if they work for you, as it helps confirm the migraine diagnosis.
medications_explained.how_to_take: Available as a tablet you swallow (50–100mg), a self-injection under the skin (fastest option), or a nasal spray (useful if nausea makes swallowing difficult). Take it at the very first sign of a migraine — the sooner the better.
medications_explained.important_note: This medication will only be prescribed AFTER your tests come back and your doctor confirms it is safe for you. It cannot be used if you have certain heart conditions or uncontrolled high blood pressure. Your doctor will check these things first.
medications_explained.monthly_limit: Use no more than 10 days per month to avoid rebound headaches.

medications_explained.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)
medications_explained.what_it_does: Reduces inflammation and pain. For migraine, it works best for mild to moderate pain and is often used alongside a triptan for stronger attacks.
medications_explained.how_to_take: 400 to 600mg by mouth with food. Take with a full glass of water.
medications_explained.important_note: Do not use more than 15 days per month — using it more often than this can cause your headaches to get worse over time (called rebound or medication overuse headache). Always take with food to protect your stomach.

medications_explained.name: Ondansetron (Zofran)
medications_explained.what_it_does: Stops nausea so you can keep other medications down and feel more comfortable. It dissolves under your tongue, which is helpful when nausea makes swallowing difficult.
medications_explained.how_to_take: 4 to 8mg by mouth (dissolving tablet) or through an IV. Every 8 hours as needed for nausea.

empathy.lifestyle_tips:
Many people find that lifestyle changes make a real difference in how often migraines happen and how severe they are. You do not have to change everything at once — even small steps add up.

SLEEP: Try to go to bed and wake up at the same time every day. Your brain loves routine, and irregular sleep is one of the most common migraine triggers. Aim for 7 to 9 hours.

HYDRATION: Drink water throughout the day. Even mild dehydration can trigger a migraine. Keep a water bottle with you.

EATING REGULARLY: Do not skip meals. Low blood sugar is a well-known migraine trigger. Try to eat at regular times each day.

STRESS: Stress does not cause migraine, but it is a very common trigger. Find what helps you decompress — whether that is a walk, music, a warm bath, deep breathing, or talking to a friend. Even 10 minutes of quiet time can help.

CAFFEINE: If you drink coffee or tea, try to keep the amount consistent each day. Both too much caffeine and suddenly cutting back can trigger migraines.

LIGHT AND SCREENS: During a migraine, dim the lights and reduce screen time. Blue-light filtering glasses may help some people between attacks.

EXERCISE: Regular moderate exercise (like walking, swimming, or yoga) can reduce migraine frequency over time. However, very intense exercise can sometimes trigger a migraine — so build up gradually.

BIRTH CONTROL: If you take combined birth control pills (containing estrogen), this is worth discussing with your doctor. Estrogen changes can trigger migraines in some women, and there may be better options for you depending on your situation. This is not something to be embarrassed about — it is a very common and important conversation.

HEADACHE DIARY: This is probably the single most useful thing you can do. Tracking your headaches helps you and your doctor identify your personal triggers and find the best treatment.
when_to_get_help: Call 911 or go to the emergency room IMMEDIATELY if you experience a sudden, extremely severe headache — the worst headache of your life — especially if it comes on in seconds. This is sometimes called a 'thunderclap headache' and requires emergency evaluation right away.

Go to the emergency room immediately if your headache is accompanied by: fever AND stiff neck (you cannot touch your chin to your chest), confusion or difficulty thinking clearly, weakness or numbness on one side of your body, difficulty speaking or understanding speech, sudden vision changes or loss of vision, loss of consciousness or fainting, or seizures.

Go to the emergency room or call your doctor urgently if: your headache suddenly becomes much worse than it has been, you develop new symptoms you did not have before, you have a headache after a head injury or fall, your vision becomes blurry or you see double, or you feel pressure behind your eyes.

Call your doctor within 24 hours if: your prescribed medications are not helping at all, you are vomiting and cannot keep fluids down, your headache is significantly worse in the morning when you first wake up, or you notice your headache gets worse when you lie down or change positions.
Contact your doctor if you notice any new symptoms after starting a new medication, including chest tightness, racing heart, difficulty breathing, rash, or swelling.
empathy.reassurance:
Living with two weeks of daily head pain is genuinely hard, and it makes complete sense that you are worried and worn out. Please know that you are not alone — migraine affects about 1 in 4 women your age, making it one of the most common health conditions in the world. The fact that your symptoms look so much like migraine is actually reassuring.

The tests your doctors are recommending are not a sign that something is definitely wrong — they are a sign that your team is being thorough and careful. Most people who go through this workup find that everything comes back normal, and they leave with a clear migraine diagnosis and a treatment plan that actually works.

Migraine is a real, physical condition — not something you imagined, not something caused by stress alone, and not something you just have to live with. There are excellent treatments available, including medications that can stop a migraine in its tracks and daily preventive options that can dramatically reduce how often they happen.

You are taking exactly the right steps by seeking care. Many people with migraine go on to manage it very well and live full, active lives. You deserve to feel better, and your care team is here to help make that happen.

anticipated_faqs.question: Is this definitely migraine?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Your symptoms — a one-sided throbbing headache, light sensitivity, and nausea — match migraine very closely, and migraine is the most likely explanation (about a 62% probability based on your symptoms). However, because this is a new headache pattern for you and it has lasted two weeks without stopping, your doctors need to run some tests first to make sure nothing else is causing it. This is standard, careful practice — not a sign that something is definitely wrong. Once the tests come back, your doctor will be able to give you a clear answer.

anticipated_faqs.question: Why does it matter if I take birth control pills?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Combined birth control pills (the kind that contain estrogen) can slightly increase the risk of a rare type of blood clot in the brain called cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST). This type of clot can cause persistent headaches that look very similar to migraine. It is important for your doctor to know if you take the pill so they can decide whether to do a specific scan (called an MRI with MRV) to check for this. If you do take the pill, your doctor will likely ask you to pause it temporarily until the scan is done. This does not mean you definitely have a clot — it is simply a precaution.

anticipated_faqs.question: Could taking pain relievers every day have made my headaches worse?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Possibly, yes. This is called medication overuse headache, or rebound headache. When you take pain relievers (like ibuprofen or acetaminophen) more than 10 to 15 days per month, your brain can actually become more sensitive to pain over time, causing more frequent headaches. If this is happening, your doctor will help you safely reduce your pain reliever use as part of your treatment plan. It is not your fault — many people do not know about this risk.

anticipated_faqs.question: Do I need a brain scan?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Yes, most likely. Because your headache is new, has lasted two weeks, and you have never been diagnosed with migraine before, your doctors will want to do a CT scan of your head first to rule out bleeding or other urgent problems. They may also recommend an MRI scan, which gives a more detailed picture and can check for things a CT scan might miss. These scans are painless and will give your team important information to make sure you get the right treatment.

anticipated_faqs.question: Will I need to take medication every day?
anticipated_faqs.answer: That depends on how often your headaches occur. If your headaches happen four or more days per month, or if they significantly affect your daily life, your doctor may recommend a daily preventive medication. These are taken every day to reduce how often headaches happen — not to stop a headache once it starts. Common options include certain blood pressure medications, antidepressants (which also work for migraine prevention), or newer injectable medications called CGRP antibodies. Your doctor will discuss the best option for you at your follow-up appointment.

anticipated_faqs.question: Is migraine dangerous?
anticipated_faqs.answer: For most people, migraine is not dangerous — it is painful and disruptive, but it does not cause permanent damage to the brain. However, there are some important exceptions. Women who have migraines with aura (visual disturbances like flashing lights or blind spots before the headache) and who also take combined birth control pills have a higher risk of stroke. This is why your doctor will ask you specifically about aura symptoms and your contraception. If you do have migraine with aura, your doctor will likely recommend a different type of birth control.

anticipated_faqs.question: How long will it take to feel better?
anticipated_faqs.answer: With the right treatment, many people with migraine feel significantly better within a few days to a few weeks. Acute medications (like triptans) can stop a migraine within 2 hours for many people. If you start a daily preventive medication, it usually takes 4 to 8 weeks to see the full benefit. Lifestyle changes like regular sleep, hydration, and stress management can also make a noticeable difference over time. Recovery is very achievable — most people with migraine manage it well with proper care.
