No personality/cognitive changes
Moderate severity

differential_diagnosis.bayesian_reasoning: NDPH is defined by a clearly remembered onset of daily headache that becomes unremitting within 24 hours. It can have migrainous features (throbbing, photophobia, nausea) in up to 50% of cases. More common in women. The 2-week persistent course with identifiable onset fits. However, NDPH is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring neuroimaging and sometimes LP to rule out secondary causes. Pre-test probability is low (~0.1% of headache presentations) but fits the clinical pattern.
differential_diagnosis.illness_script_fit: Good fit if patient can identify a specific day of onset and headache has been daily since. Migrainous features are common in NDPH. Unilateral presentation is possible though bilateral is more common.
supporting_features: Persistent daily headache with identifiable onset period
opposing_features: Diagnosis of exclusion — must rule out secondary causes first
Unilateral predominance less typical
Need to confirm truly daily and unremitting

differential_diagnosis.bayesian_reasoning: If patient has been self-treating with analgesics (NSAIDs, acetaminophen, triptans) frequently over the 2-week period, MOH could perpetuate headache. However, MOH typically develops in patients with pre-existing headache disorders who escalate medication use. With no prior headache history reported, this is less likely as a primary diagnosis but could be a contributing factor.
differential_diagnosis.illness_script_fit: Poor fit as primary diagnosis given no prior headache history. Could be contributing if heavy analgesic use has occurred over the 2 weeks.
opposing_features: No prior headache history
Only 2-week duration (MOH typically develops over months)
Medication use pattern unknown

differential_diagnosis.bayesian_reasoning: Unilateral headache can originate from cervical spine pathology (C1-C3 nerve roots, facet joints). Can be throbbing and associated with photophobia. More common in patients with neck trauma, poor posture, or desk work. Without information about neck pain, restricted ROM, or occupational factors, probability is uncertain.
differential_diagnosis.illness_script_fit: Partial fit. Unilateral, persistent headache fits. However, cervicogenic headache is typically provoked by neck movement or sustained posture, and is often described as starting in the neck/occiput and radiating forward. Photophobia and nausea are less typical.
opposing_features: Throbbing quality less typical (usually dull/aching)
Photophobia and nausea less common
No neck pain or trauma reported

differential_diagnosis.bayesian_reasoning: Very low pre-test probability at age 35. GCA almost exclusively affects patients >50 years old (mean onset ~70). While unilateral temporal headache with tenderness is classic, the patient's age essentially excludes this diagnosis. Included for completeness.
differential_diagnosis.illness_script_fit: Very poor fit due to age alone. GCA is exceedingly rare under age 50.
opposing_features: Age 35 (GCA almost never occurs <50)
No jaw claudication
No scalp tenderness
No visual symptoms
No systemic inflammatory symptoms

differential_diagnosis.bayesian_reasoning: SAH classically presents as thunderclap headache (worst headache of life, maximal at onset). A sentinel or warning leak can present as a less severe headache days to weeks before major rupture. At age 35, aneurysmal SAH is uncommon but possible. The 2-week persistent course without thunderclap onset makes classic SAH very unlikely, but a slow sentinel leak cannot be fully excluded without imaging. This is a must-not-miss diagnosis due to catastrophic consequences of missed aneurysmal SAH.
differential_diagnosis.illness_script_fit: Poor fit. SAH headache is typically sudden onset and severe (thunderclap). A 6/10 progressive headache over 2 weeks is not the classic presentation. However, sentinel headaches can be moderate and subacute.
opposing_features: No thunderclap onset
Moderate severity (6/10)
2-week duration without deterioration
Throbbing quality (SAH is usually constant/pressure)

differential_diagnosis.bayesian_reasoning: Sinusitis can cause unilateral facial/head pain, but true sinus headache is overdiagnosed. Without nasal congestion, purulent discharge, facial pressure, or fever, sinusitis is unlikely. Many patients self-diagnosed with 'sinus headache' actually have migraine.
differential_diagnosis.illness_script_fit: Poor fit. No nasal symptoms, facial pressure, or fever reported. Photophobia and nausea are not typical of sinusitis.
opposing_features: No nasal congestion or discharge
No facial pressure
No fever
Photophobia and nausea more suggestive of migraine/ICP

vindicate_analysis.vascular: Considered: CVT (moderate concern given demographics), SAH/sentinel leak (low probability but must-not-miss), migraine (primary vascular headache — leading diagnosis). Stroke unlikely without focal deficits.
vindicate_analysis.infectious: Considered: Meningitis/encephalitis — unlikely given 2-week duration without fever, altered mental status, or meningeal signs. Brain abscess — possible but no fever, no risk factors (dental infection, endocarditis, immunosuppression) mentioned. Sinusitis — unlikely without nasal symptoms.
vindicate_analysis.neoplastic: Considered: Primary brain tumor or metastasis — low probability but must-not-miss. Progressive headache with nausea warrants imaging. No focal deficits or seizures argue against but do not exclude.
vindicate_analysis.degenerative_deficiency: Considered: Cervicogenic headache from degenerative cervical spine disease — possible but no neck symptoms. Vitamin B12 or other deficiency headache — very unlikely presentation.
vindicate_analysis.iatrogenic_intoxication: Considered: Medication overuse headache — unlikely without prior headache history. New medication side effects — unknown, need medication history. Carbon monoxide exposure — unlikely with 2-week course. OCP-related headache — need to assess.
vindicate_analysis.congenital: Considered: Chiari malformation — can cause headache, typically occipital and worsened by Valsalva/cough. Not a strong fit but MRI would evaluate. AVM — could present with headache, low probability.
vindicate_analysis.autoimmune_allergic: Considered: GCA — essentially excluded by age <50. CNS vasculitis — rare, would expect more systemic symptoms or focal deficits. Sarcoidosis with CNS involvement — very rare.
vindicate_analysis.traumatic: Considered: Post-traumatic headache — no trauma history reported. Should explicitly ask about recent head injury.
vindicate_analysis.endocrine_metabolic: Considered: Thyroid dysfunction — can cause headache but nonspecific. Pregnancy-related headache changes — need pregnancy test. Pre-eclampsia — need BP and pregnancy status. Pheochromocytoma — episodic headache with hypertension, need BP.

must_not_miss.reasoning: Young woman with subacute progressive headache — classic demographic for CVT. OCP use, pregnancy, or thrombophilia would significantly increase risk. Missed CVT can lead to venous infarction, hemorrhage, and death. Treatable with anticoagulation.
recommended_tests: MRI brain with MRV (gold standard)
D-dimer (if low clinical suspicion, negative D-dimer has high NPV)
CT venogram if MRI unavailable

must_not_miss.reasoning: New-onset progressive headache at age 35 with nausea warrants imaging to exclude mass. Early tumors may present with headache alone before focal deficits develop.
recommended_tests: MRI brain with and without contrast (preferred)
CT head without contrast (if MRI unavailable or as initial screen)

must_not_miss.reasoning: Young woman with progressive headache, photophobia, and nausea. If obese, risk is significantly elevated. Untreated IIH can cause permanent vision loss.
recommended_tests: Fundoscopic exam (papilledema)
MRI brain with MRV (empty sella, optic nerve sheath distension, transverse sinus stenosis)
Lumbar puncture with opening pressure if imaging suggestive

must_not_miss.reasoning: Although presentation is atypical for SAH, any new persistent headache with photophobia and nausea warrants consideration. Missed SAH has catastrophic consequences.
recommended_tests: CT head without contrast
If CT negative and clinical suspicion persists: lumbar puncture for xanthochromia
CTA head if aneurysm suspected

anchoring_bias_check.initial_anchor: Migraine — the combination of unilateral throbbing headache with photophobia and nausea in a young woman immediately suggests migraine, which is by far the most common diagnosis fitting this symptom cluster.
anchoring_bias_check.what_doesnt_fit_top_diagnosis: New onset at age 35 without prior headache history is atypical (most migraineurs have onset in teens-20s). Persistent 2-week duration without remission is unusual for episodic migraine (typical attacks last 4-72 hours). No family history of migraine mentioned.
anchoring_bias_check.alternative_explanations: CVT can perfectly mimic migraine in young women and has a subacute progressive course. IIH can present with migrainous features. An intracranial mass can cause progressive headache with nausea. NDPH can have migrainous features.
anchoring_bias_check.availability_bias_check: Migraine is extremely common and may lead to premature diagnostic closure. The key distinguishing factor is that this is a NEW headache — the first rule of headache medicine is that a new headache pattern requires workup to exclude secondary causes before attributing to a primary headache disorder.
anchoring_bias_check.conclusion: While migraine remains the most likely single diagnosis, the new-onset nature and persistent course mandate neuroimaging (preferably MRI with MRV) before accepting a primary headache diagnosis. Migraine should be a diagnosis of exclusion in this clinical context.

discriminating_features.test_or_finding: MRI brain with and without contrast + MRV
discriminating_features.what_it_discriminates: Mass lesion vs CVT vs IIH vs normal (supporting primary headache)
discriminating_features.expected_LR_positive: LR+ >25 for mass if lesion found; LR+ >50 for CVT if thrombosis on MRV
discriminating_features.expected_LR_negative: LR- ~0.05 for mass; LR- ~0.02 for CVT (essentially rules out)

discriminating_features.what_it_discriminates: Elevated ICP (IIH, mass, CVT) vs normal ICP (migraine, tension, cervicogenic)
discriminating_features.expected_LR_positive: LR+ ~10-15 for elevated ICP if papilledema present
discriminating_features.expected_LR_negative: LR- ~0.5 (papilledema can be absent in early IIH or CVT)

discriminating_features.what_it_discriminates: IIH (OP >25 cmH2O) vs normal pressure headache; also evaluates for SAH (xanthochromia) and infection (cell count, protein, glucose)
discriminating_features.expected_LR_positive: LR+ >10 for IIH if OP >25 cmH2O in appropriate clinical context
discriminating_features.expected_LR_negative: LR- ~0.1 for IIH if OP normal

discriminating_features.what_it_discriminates: Truly continuous 2-week headache (favors NDPH, CVT, IIH, mass) vs recurrent discrete attacks (favors migraine)
discriminating_features.expected_LR_positive: Continuous headache: LR+ ~3-4 for secondary headache cause
discriminating_features.expected_LR_negative: Episodic pattern with pain-free intervals: LR+ ~2-3 for migraine

discriminating_features.what_it_discriminates: Significantly modifies CVT probability. OCP use in young woman with new headache: LR+ ~5-7 for CVT consideration
discriminating_features.expected_LR_positive: If on OCPs: pre-test probability for CVT increases 5-7 fold
discriminating_features.expected_LR_negative: If not on OCPs and not pregnant: CVT probability decreases but not excluded

recommended_tests: Complete vital signs including blood pressure (rule out hypertensive headache, pre-eclampsia if pregnant)
Comprehensive neurological examination including cranial nerves, motor, sensory, cerebellar, and gait testing
Fundoscopic examination (evaluate for papilledema — critical for IIH, mass, CVT)
Pregnancy test (urine hCG — modifies differential significantly: CVT risk, medication choices, pre-eclampsia)

MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast + MRV (gold standard for evaluating mass, CVT, IIH signs, Chiari, and other structural causes — preferred over CT for posterior fossa and venous pathology)
CT head without contrast (if MRI not immediately available — screens for hemorrhage, large mass, hydrocephalus)
Basic laboratory studies: CBC with differential, CMP, ESR, CRP (screen for infection, inflammation, metabolic derangement)
D-dimer (if CVT is suspected — elevated D-dimer supports further workup; normal D-dimer has ~97% NPV for CVT)
Lumbar puncture with opening pressure, cell count, protein, glucose, and cytology (if imaging is normal but IIH or chronic meningitis suspected)
Visual field testing (if IIH suspected — to assess for visual field loss that may be asymptomatic)

follow_up_questions.question: Is the headache truly continuous for the entire 2 weeks, or do you have discrete attacks with pain-free intervals between them? Does the headache wake you from sleep or is it present upon waking in the morning?
follow_up_questions.targets: Continuous favors secondary causes (CVT, IIH, mass, NDPH); episodic with pain-free intervals favors migraine. Morning predominance or waking from sleep suggests elevated ICP (mass, IIH).

specialist.reason_for_consultation: Evaluation of new-onset persistent unilateral throbbing headache of 2 weeks duration in a 35-year-old female with photophobia and nausea, to differentiate primary headache disorder (migraine) from secondary causes including cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, intracranial mass lesion, and subarachnoid hemorrhage sentinel leak.
specialist.specialist_assessment: This 35-year-old female presents with a 2-week history of new-onset, persistent, right-sided throbbing headache (6/10 severity) with photophobia and intermittent nausea. From a neurology standpoint, this presentation carries significant diagnostic complexity. The symptom phenotype — unilateral, pulsatile, moderate intensity with photophobia and nausea — is highly suggestive of migraine pathophysiology. However, the cardinal rule in headache neurology is that a NEW headache pattern in a previously headache-free individual is a secondary headache until proven otherwise. This patient does NOT meet ICHD-3 criteria for migraine without aura, which requires ≥5 prior attacks each lasting 4-72 hours. A continuous or near-continuous 2-week headache without remission is atypical for episodic migraine and raises concern for: (1) Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVT) — this is the most critical must-not-miss diagnosis given the patient's demographic (young woman of reproductive age); CVT presents with progressive headache in >90% of cases and can perfectly mimic migraine; (2) Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) — if the patient is overweight, this diagnosis rises significantly in probability; photophobia and nausea are consistent with elevated intracranial pressure; (3) Intracranial mass lesion — new progressive headache with nausea warrants structural imaging; early tumors may present with headache alone before focal deficits emerge; (4) Sentinel subarachnoid hemorrhage — although the presentation is atypical (no thunderclap onset), a low-grade leak cannot be excluded without imaging; (5) New daily persistent headache (NDPH) — a diagnosis of exclusion that requires >3 months of daily headache with a clearly remembered onset date. Risk stratification: I classify this patient as INTERMEDIATE-TO-HIGH RISK for secondary headache etiology based on: new-onset headache without prior history, persistent 2-week duration without remission, demographic risk factors for CVT and IIH, and the presence of nausea suggesting possible elevated intracranial pressure. Critical missing information includes: vital signs (especially blood pressure), BMI, oral contraceptive or hormonal therapy use, pregnancy status, detailed neurological examination findings, fundoscopic examination for papilledema, and whether the headache is truly continuous versus episodic with pain-free intervals. The absence of reported focal neurological deficits, seizures, fever, neck stiffness, or altered consciousness is reassuring but does not exclude serious pathology. I strongly recommend against empiric migraine treatment without first completing a thorough diagnostic workup including neuroimaging.
diagnostic_criteria_applied: ICHD-3 Criteria for Migraine Without Aura (1.1): Requires (A) ≥5 attacks fulfilling criteria B-D, (B) headache lasting 4-72 hours, (C) ≥2 of: unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, aggravated by physical activity, (D) ≥1 of: nausea/vomiting, photophobia AND phonophobia. RESULT: CRITERIA NOT MET — Patient has unilateral + pulsating + moderate severity (meets C), and has nausea + photophobia (partially meets D, phonophobia not reported), BUT does not meet criterion A (requires ≥5 prior attacks; this is a first presentation) and duration of 2 continuous weeks exceeds the 4-72 hour window for a single attack.

ICHD-3 Criteria for New Daily Persistent Headache (4.10): Requires persistent headache daily from onset, clearly remembered onset, present for >3 months. RESULT: CRITERIA NOT YET MET — Only 2 weeks duration (requires >3 months), but clinical trajectory is consistent with early NDPH if secondary causes are excluded.

ICHD-3 Secondary Headache General Criteria (Chapter 5-12): A new headache occurring in close temporal relation to a causative disorder, with evidence of causation. RESULT: MUST BE ACTIVELY EXCLUDED — New-onset persistent headache mandates workup for secondary causes before any primary headache diagnosis can be assigned.

SNOOP10 Red Flag Mnemonic for Secondary Headache: S-Systemic symptoms (nausea present), N-Neurologic signs (not yet assessed), O-Onset sudden (not thunderclap but subacute progressive), O-Older age (not applicable at 35, but new onset at any age is a flag), P-Pattern change/Progressive (2-week persistent progressive pattern). RESULT: At least 2-3 SNOOP flags identified — warrants neuroimaging.

Modified Dandy Criteria for IIH: Requires signs/symptoms of elevated ICP, elevated opening pressure >25 cmH2O, normal CSF composition, no structural cause on imaging. RESULT: CANNOT YET ASSESS — Requires fundoscopic exam, neuroimaging, and potentially lumbar puncture.

CVT Clinical Probability Assessment: Young woman + subacute progressive headache + nausea = moderate clinical suspicion. D-dimer may be used as screening tool (NPV ~97% in low-moderate suspicion), but definitive evaluation requires MRI/MRV.
specialist.risk_stratification: INTERMEDIATE-TO-HIGH RISK for secondary headache etiology. Rationale: (1) New-onset headache in a previously headache-free 35-year-old — the incidence of secondary causes in new-onset persistent headache is approximately 10-15%, significantly higher than the 1-2% base rate in all headache presentations; (2) Persistent 2-week duration without remission — atypical for benign episodic primary headache; (3) Female reproductive age — highest risk demographic for CVT (especially if on OCPs) and IIH (especially if obese); (4) Photophobia and nausea — while common in migraine, also consistent with meningeal irritation or elevated intracranial pressure; (5) Absence of focal neurological deficits provides some reassurance but does not adequately lower risk to defer imaging. Overall, the probability of a serious secondary cause is estimated at 10-20% pending additional clinical data (vital signs, BMI, OCP status, fundoscopic exam).
specialty_specific_tests: PRIORITY 1 — Comprehensive neurological examination: cranial nerves (especially CN II with fundoscopy for papilledema, CN III/IV/VI for diplopia, CN V for facial sensation), motor strength, sensory testing, deep tendon reflexes, cerebellar function (finger-to-nose, heel-to-shin, gait), and meningeal signs (Kernig, Brudzinski, nuchal rigidity)

PRIORITY 1 — Dilated fundoscopic examination: Critical to evaluate for papilledema (elevated ICP from mass, CVT, or IIH) and for subhyaloid hemorrhage (SAH). If bedside exam is inconclusive, formal ophthalmologic evaluation with OCT of the retinal nerve fiber layer is recommended

PRIORITY 1 — MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast PLUS MR venography (MRV): This is the single most important diagnostic test. MRI evaluates for mass lesions, white matter disease, Chiari malformation, pituitary pathology, and signs of elevated ICP (empty sella, optic nerve sheath distension, posterior globe flattening). MRV evaluates for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Sensitivity >95% for both mass lesions and CVT when combined

PRIORITY 2 — Laboratory studies: CBC with differential, CMP, ESR, CRP (screen for inflammatory/infectious causes), TSH (thyroid dysfunction can cause headache), pregnancy test (urine beta-hCG — critical for modifying differential and treatment options), coagulation studies if CVT suspected

PRIORITY 2 — D-dimer: If clinical suspicion for CVT is low-to-moderate, a negative D-dimer has approximately 97% negative predictive value and can help risk-stratify. However, a positive D-dimer is nonspecific and does not confirm CVT. Note: D-dimer sensitivity for CVT is lower than for DVT/PE, so a negative result does NOT exclude CVT if clinical suspicion is high

PRIORITY 3 — Lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement: Indicated if (a) MRI/MRV is normal but IIH is suspected (measure opening pressure; >25 cmH2O is diagnostic), (b) chronic meningitis is considered (CSF cell count, protein, glucose, cultures, cytology), or (c) SAH cannot be excluded by imaging alone (xanthochromia). Must be performed AFTER neuroimaging to exclude mass lesion with risk of herniation

PRIORITY 3 — Formal visual field testing (Humphrey or Goldmann perimetry): Indicated if IIH is suspected or papilledema is found. Assesses for enlarged blind spot and peripheral visual field constriction that may be asymptomatic
PRIORITY 4 — CT angiography (CTA) of the head: If MRI/MRV suggests vascular abnormality, or if aneurysm is suspected as cause of sentinel headache

PRIORITY 4 — Conventional digital subtraction angiography (DSA): Gold standard for vascular pathology but invasive; reserved for cases where non-invasive imaging is inconclusive and clinical suspicion remains high
specialist_red_flags: NEW-ONSET HEADACHE WITHOUT PRIOR HISTORY: This is the single most important red flag. The first rule of headache neurology is that a first or worst headache requires investigation. Migraine should not be diagnosed on a first presentation without excluding secondary causes.
PERSISTENT 2-WEEK DURATION: Episodic migraine attacks last 4-72 hours. A continuous 2-week headache without pain-free intervals is atypical and raises concern for CVT, IIH, mass lesion, or NDPH.

DEMOGRAPHIC RISK FOR CVT: A young woman of reproductive age with subacute progressive headache is the classic CVT demographic. OCP use would increase risk 5-8 fold. Pregnancy/postpartum would increase risk 12-15 fold.

NAUSEA WITHOUT VOMITING: While common in migraine, nausea can also indicate elevated intracranial pressure. If nausea is progressive or accompanied by morning vomiting, this significantly raises concern for mass lesion or IIH.
PHOTOPHOBIA: While a hallmark of migraine, photophobia also occurs with meningeal irritation (SAH, meningitis) and elevated ICP. Context matters.

MISSING CRITICAL DATA: Vital signs (especially blood pressure — hypertensive emergency can cause headache), BMI (obesity dramatically increases IIH risk), OCP/hormonal therapy use (CVT risk), pregnancy status (CVT, preeclampsia), and fundoscopic exam (papilledema) are all essential and currently unavailable.

ABSENCE OF FOCAL DEFICITS DOES NOT EXCLUDE SERIOUS PATHOLOGY: Up to 30-40% of CVT patients present with isolated headache without focal deficits. Early brain tumors may cause headache before deficits develop. IIH may present with headache alone before visual symptoms emerge.
specialist.prognosis_notes: Prognosis is highly dependent on the underlying diagnosis: (1) If migraine — excellent long-term prognosis with appropriate treatment. Acute attacks respond to triptans (NNT 3.5-4.7 for pain-free at 2 hours). Preventive therapy may be needed if attacks become frequent. Annual chronification rate is approximately 2.5-3%. (2) If CVT — with early diagnosis and anticoagulation, mortality is 5-10% and approximately 80% of patients have good functional outcomes (mRS 0-2). Delayed diagnosis significantly worsens prognosis. Recurrence rate is approximately 2-4% per year. (3) If IIH — headache often responds to acetazolamide and weight loss. Primary concern is visual loss, which can be permanent if untreated. The IIH Treatment Trial (IIHTT) demonstrated that acetazolamide plus weight management improved visual field outcomes compared to placebo. (4) If intracranial mass — prognosis depends entirely on tumor type, grade, and location. Early detection generally improves outcomes. (5) If NDPH — bimodal prognosis: self-limiting form resolves within months, but refractory form can persist for years and is notoriously treatment-resistant. Modifying factors for this patient: female sex (favorable for migraine prognosis, unfavorable for CVT/IIH risk), age 35 (within peak migraine prevalence window), and early presentation (2 weeks — early enough for intervention if secondary cause identified).
specialist.guideline_concordance: Current management assessment: No treatment has been initiated yet, which is APPROPRIATE at this stage. Per AHS consensus guidelines (2019), ICHD-3 (2018), and AAN practice parameters, the correct approach for new-onset persistent headache in a previously headache-free adult is: (1) Complete neurological examination including fundoscopy — NOT YET DONE, MUST BE PERFORMED; (2) Neuroimaging with MRI brain ± MRV before assigning a primary headache diagnosis — NOT YET DONE, STRONGLY RECOMMENDED; (3) Exclude secondary causes before initiating migraine-specific therapy — GUIDELINE-CONCORDANT to withhold triptans until diagnosis is established; (4) Obtain pregnancy test before prescribing any medications — NOT YET DONE; (5) Per NICE CG150, neuroimaging is justified here and is NOT merely for reassurance given the new-onset persistent pattern. Initiating empiric triptan therapy without neuroimaging would be GUIDELINE-DISCORDANT in this clinical context.
specialist.referral_recommendation: IN-PERSON NEUROLOGY CONSULTATION RECOMMENDED — URGENCY: SEMI-URGENT (within 1-2 weeks, or sooner if any clinical deterioration). Rationale: This patient requires a comprehensive neurological examination, fundoscopic evaluation, and neuroimaging interpretation that cannot be adequately performed via telemedicine or AI consultation alone. If any of the following develop, urgency escalates to EMERGENT (same-day ED evaluation): (1) sudden severe worsening of headache (thunderclap), (2) new focal neurological deficits (weakness, numbness, speech difficulty, vision loss), (3) seizures, (4) fever with neck stiffness, (5) altered consciousness, (6) progressive vomiting. Additionally, if fundoscopic exam reveals papilledema, urgent ophthalmology consultation is needed for formal visual field testing and OCT. If CVT is confirmed on imaging, hematology consultation for thrombophilia workup and anticoagulation management is recommended.
clinical_pearls: THE FIRST HEADACHE IS NEVER MIGRAINE ON THE FIRST VISIT: ICHD-3 requires ≥5 prior attacks to diagnose migraine without aura. On a first presentation, the correct approach is to evaluate for secondary causes and, if negative, provisionally diagnose 'probable migraine' (ICHD-3 code 1.5.1) pending recurrence.

CVT IS THE GREAT MIMICKER IN YOUNG WOMEN: CVT can present with any headache phenotype — migraine-like, tension-type, or thunderclap. In the ISCVT study (n=624), headache was the presenting symptom in 89% of cases, and 25% had headache as the ONLY symptom. Always consider CVT in a young woman with new subacute headache.

CT IS INADEQUATE TO EXCLUDE CVT: Non-contrast CT head has only 30-40% sensitivity for CVT. A 'normal CT' does NOT rule out CVT. MRI with MRV is required. This is a common and dangerous pitfall — many CVT cases are missed because clinicians are falsely reassured by a normal CT.

D-DIMER FOR CVT HAS IMPORTANT LIMITATIONS: While a negative D-dimer has ~97% NPV for CVT in low-moderate suspicion, sensitivity drops significantly for isolated headache CVT without parenchymal lesions, and for chronic/subacute presentations (>2 weeks). Do not rely on D-dimer alone to exclude CVT if clinical suspicion is moderate-high.

PAPILLEDEMA IS THE GATEWAY FINDING: A single fundoscopic examination can dramatically alter the diagnostic pathway. Papilledema points toward elevated ICP (IIH, mass, CVT) and mandates urgent imaging and likely LP. Its absence is somewhat reassuring but does not exclude early IIH or CVT (papilledema may take days-weeks to develop).

ASK ABOUT ORAL CONTRACEPTIVES: Combined oral contraceptives increase CVT risk 5-8 fold. They are also WHO MEC Category 4 (contraindicated) in migraine WITH aura due to increased ischemic stroke risk. This single piece of medication history can fundamentally change both the differential diagnosis and treatment plan.

BEWARE THE 'SINUS HEADACHE' TRAP: Studies show that up to 90% of self-diagnosed or physician-diagnosed 'sinus headaches' actually meet criteria for migraine. However, in this case, the opposite trap is more dangerous — labeling this as migraine without excluding secondary causes.

MORNING HEADACHE IS A RED FLAG FOR ELEVATED ICP: If further history reveals that the headache is worse upon waking or wakes the patient from sleep, this significantly raises suspicion for mass lesion or IIH, as intracranial pressure rises during recumbency and REM sleep.

PREGNANCY CHANGES EVERYTHING: If the pregnancy test is positive, the differential shifts dramatically (CVT risk increases 12-15 fold, preeclampsia must be considered even before 20 weeks in rare cases, PRES becomes a consideration), and treatment options narrow significantly (triptans have limited safety data in pregnancy, many preventive medications are teratogenic).

treatment_plans.condition: New-onset persistent headache — DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP PHASE (Secondary headache must be excluded before treating as primary headache disorder)
treatment_plans.priority: HIGHEST — This is the immediate clinical priority
treatment_plans.rationale: This 35-year-old female presents with a new-onset, persistent, unilateral throbbing headache of 2 weeks duration without prior headache history. Per ICHD-3 criteria, migraine cannot be formally diagnosed on a first presentation (requires ≥5 prior attacks). Per AHS consensus guidelines (2019) and AAN practice parameters, new-onset persistent headache in a previously headache-free adult mandates diagnostic workup to exclude secondary causes before initiating migraine-specific therapy. The estimated probability of a serious secondary cause is 10-20% in this clinical context.
treatment_plans.first_line: Complete diagnostic evaluation before definitive treatment. Symptomatic relief only with safe, non-specific analgesics during workup period.

step_1_immediate_diagnostic_workup: Obtain complete vital signs including blood pressure and temperature
Perform comprehensive neurological examination including cranial nerve testing
Perform dilated fundoscopic examination to evaluate for papilledema
Obtain urine pregnancy test (beta-hCG) — critical before any medication decisions
Order MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast PLUS MR venography (MRV) — this is the single most important diagnostic test
Order basic laboratory studies: CBC with differential, CMP, ESR, CRP, TSH
Consider D-dimer if CVT suspicion is low-to-moderate (NPV ~97%, but limited sensitivity in subacute presentations)
Obtain detailed medication history including OCP use, analgesic frequency, hormonal therapies, supplements
Obtain BMI measurement (modifies IIH probability significantly)
step_2_symptomatic_relief_during_workup: Acetaminophen 500-1000mg every 6-8 hours as needed (maximum 3000mg/day) — safest option pending pregnancy test results and diagnosis
If pregnancy test is NEGATIVE: may add ibuprofen 400mg every 6-8 hours as needed with food (maximum 1200mg/day OTC; up to 2400mg/day by prescription)
Dark, quiet room for photophobia relief
Limit analgesic use to no more than 2-3 days per week to prevent medication overuse headache

step_3_treatment_based_on_diagnostic_res.scenario_A_imaging_normal_exam_normal: Proceed to probable migraine treatment pathway (see below)
step_3_treatment_based_on_diagnostic_res.scenario_B_CVT_confirmed: URGENT — Initiate anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin or LMWC, hematology consultation, inpatient management. This is managed by neurology/hematology inpatient team.
step_3_treatment_based_on_diagnostic_res.scenario_C_IIH_confirmed: Acetazolamide 250mg twice daily titrated up to 1-2g/day as tolerated, weight management program, ophthalmology follow-up for visual field monitoring. Lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement required for diagnosis.
step_3_treatment_based_on_diagnostic_res.scenario_D_mass_lesion_found: URGENT neurosurgery and/or neuro-oncology referral. Treatment depends on lesion type, size, and location.
step_3_treatment_based_on_diagnostic_res.scenario_E_SAH_sentinel_leak: EMERGENT neurosurgical consultation, CTA head, possible conventional angiography, ICU admission.

medications.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
medications.frequency: Every 6-8 hours as needed for headache
medications.maximum_daily_dose: 3000mg per day (conservative limit; 4000mg is FDA maximum but 3000mg recommended for safety)
medications.duration: As needed during diagnostic workup period (limit to 2-3 days per week)
warnings: Do NOT exceed 3000mg per day
Avoid if liver disease or heavy alcohol use (>3 drinks/day)
Check all other medications for hidden acetaminophen (cold medicines, combination products)
Safe in pregnancy if needed
medications.monitoring: No routine monitoring needed for short-term use

medications.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)

treatment_plans.condition: Probable Migraine Without Aura (ICHD-3 code 1.5.1) — TO BE INITIATED ONLY AFTER SECONDARY CAUSES ARE EXCLUDED BY NEUROIMAGING AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION
treatment_plans.priority: SECOND — Only after diagnostic workup is complete and negative
treatment_plans.rationale: If MRI brain with MRV is normal, neurological examination is normal, fundoscopic exam shows no papilledema, and laboratory studies are unremarkable, the most likely diagnosis becomes probable migraine without aura. Formal migraine diagnosis requires ≥5 attacks; this patient is on her first presentation. Treatment follows AAN/AHS evidence-based guidelines (2015, reaffirmed 2019).
treatment_plans.first_line: Acute migraine-specific therapy with triptan (if not pregnant and no cardiovascular contraindications)

step_1_conservative_measures: Patient education about migraine pathophysiology, triggers, and management
Headache diary to track frequency, severity, triggers, and medication use
Trigger identification and avoidance (common triggers: stress, sleep disruption, skipped meals, dehydration, alcohol, hormonal fluctuations, weather changes, bright lights, strong odors)
Regular sleep schedule (7-8 hours, consistent bedtime/wake time)
Regular meals (do not skip meals; maintain stable blood glucose)
Regular aerobic exercise (150 minutes/week moderate intensity)
Stress management techniques (progressive muscle relaxation, diaphragmatic breathing, mindfulness)
step_2_first_line_acute_pharmacological: Sumatriptan 50-100mg orally at onset of moderate-severe headache (may repeat once after 2 hours if partial response; maximum 200mg/day) — REQUIRES PRESCRIPTION
OR Eletriptan 40mg orally (may repeat once after 2 hours; maximum 80mg/day) — most effective oral triptan per Cochrane data (NNT 3.5) — REQUIRES PRESCRIPTION
OR Rizatriptan 10mg orally (ODT formulation available for nausea) — REQUIRES PRESCRIPTION
PLUS Naproxen sodium 500mg orally with the triptan (combination therapy is more effective than either alone — Level A evidence)
step_3_second_line_acute_pharmacological: If triptans are contraindicated or not tolerated: Ubrogepant 50-100mg orally (CGRP receptor antagonist, gepant class) — REQUIRES PRESCRIPTION
OR Rimegepant 75mg ODT — can also be used for prevention every other day — REQUIRES PRESCRIPTION
OR Lasmiditan 50-100mg orally (5-HT1F agonist, no vasoconstrictive properties — safe in cardiovascular disease) — REQUIRES PRESCRIPTION — causes dizziness/sedation, do not drive for 8 hours
step_4_adjunctive_for_nausea: Metoclopramide 10mg orally 15-30 minutes before triptan (enhances absorption, treats nausea, has independent analgesic properties for migraine) — REQUIRES PRESCRIPTION
OR Ondansetron 4-8mg ODT as needed for nausea — REQUIRES PRESCRIPTION
OR Prochlorperazine 10mg orally or rectally — REQUIRES PRESCRIPTION — risk of extrapyramidal symptoms
treatment_algorithm.step_5_preventive_therapy_consideration: Preventive therapy is indicated if: ≥4 headache days per month, ≥8 headache days per month, significant disability despite acute treatment, or acute medication use ≥10 days per month. Given the 2-week persistent course, preventive therapy may be warranted early. Options below are listed in order of evidence strength.
step_5a_first_line_preventive: Propranolol 40mg twice daily, titrate to 80-160mg/day (Level A evidence) — REQUIRES PRESCRIPTION — Contraindicated in asthma, bradycardia, heart block

OR Topiramate 25mg daily, titrate by 25mg/week to 50-100mg/day (Level A evidence) — REQUIRES PRESCRIPTION — Contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic), kidney stones; causes cognitive side effects, weight loss, paresthesias
OR Amitriptyline 10mg at bedtime, titrate to 25-75mg (Level B evidence) — REQUIRES PRESCRIPTION — Useful if comorbid insomnia or depression; causes sedation, dry mouth, weight gain

OR CGRP monoclonal antibodies: Erenumab 70-140mg SC monthly, Fremanezumab 225mg SC monthly or 675mg quarterly, Galcanezumab 240mg loading then 120mg SC monthly (Level A evidence) — REQUIRES PRESCRIPTION — Well-tolerated, few drug interactions, but expensive; constipation is most common side effect with erenumab
step_5b_adjunctive_non_pharmacological_p: Cognitive behavioral therapy for headache (Level A evidence for migraine prevention)
Acupuncture (Level A evidence — Cochrane review shows benefit equivalent to prophylactic medications)
Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) 400mg daily (Level B evidence — NNT ~4 for 50% reduction in migraine frequency)
Magnesium oxide 400-600mg daily (Level B evidence — particularly for menstrual migraine)
Coenzyme Q10 100mg three times daily (Level C evidence)
step_6_interventional: OnabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) 155-195 units per protocol every 12 weeks — indicated for chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month for >3 months) — REQUIRES SPECIALIST
Peripheral nerve blocks (greater occipital nerve block with lidocaine ± corticosteroid) — can provide rapid relief while preventive medications take effect — REQUIRES SPECIALIST

Neuromodulation devices: Cefaly (external trigeminal nerve stimulation), gammaCore (non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation), SpringTMS (single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation) — FDA-cleared, available by prescription

warnings: CRITICAL SAFETY GATE — DIAGNOSIS NOT YET ESTABLISHED: The team has appropriately identified that secondary headache causes (cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, intracranial mass, sentinel SAH) must be excluded BEFORE migraine-specific treatment is initiated. No triptan, ergotamine, or migraine-specific therapy should be dispensed until MRI brain with MRV is completed and reviewed. This is the single most important safety concern in this case.

PREGNANCY STATUS UNKNOWN — HIGH SAFETY IMPACT: No pregnancy test has been obtained. This 35-year-old female of reproductive age must have a confirmed negative pregnancy test BEFORE ibuprofen or any NSAID is administered (NSAIDs are contraindicated in pregnancy, especially third trimester — risk of premature ductus arteriosus closure). Triptans are FDA Category C with limited safety data in pregnancy. Topiramate is teratogenic (FDA Category D). Metoclopramide crosses the placenta. Acetaminophen is the ONLY recommended analgesic that is safe to administer before pregnancy status is confirmed.

ORAL CONTRACEPTIVE STATUS UNKNOWN — AFFECTS BOTH DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT SAFETY: If patient is on combined oral contraceptives (COCs), this (1) increases CVT risk 5-8 fold, raising urgency of MRV, and (2) COCs are WHO MEC Category 4 (contraindicated) in migraine WITH aura — if aura features are later identified, COCs must be discontinued immediately due to elevated ischemic stroke risk.

VITAL SIGNS NOT YET OBTAINED: Blood pressure is essential before any treatment. Hypertensive emergency can present as headache with nausea and photophobia. Administering NSAIDs to a patient with undiagnosed severe hypertension could worsen the condition. Temperature is needed to exclude infectious etiology.

NEUROLOGICAL EXAMINATION AND FUNDOSCOPY NOT YET PERFORMED: Papilledema on fundoscopic exam would indicate elevated intracranial pressure and contraindicate lumbar puncture without prior imaging (herniation risk). Focal neurological deficits would escalate urgency to emergent.

MEDICATION OVERUSE HEADACHE RISK — ANALGESIC FREQUENCY COUNSELING REQUIRED: The treatment plan appropriately limits acute analgesic use to 2-3 days per week / ≤10 days per month. However, this counseling MUST be explicitly communicated to the patient at the point of care. Patients frequently self-medicate with OTC analgesics without awareness of MOH risk, which could transform this headache into a chronic daily headache.

METOCLOPRAMIDE — FDA BLACK BOX WARNING: The treatment plan includes metoclopramide 10mg for nausea. This carries an FDA Black Box Warning for tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use (>12 weeks). While short-term PRN use is appropriate, the patient must be counseled about this risk, and duration must be strictly limited. Ondansetron is a safer alternative for recurrent nausea if needed beyond acute episodes.

SUMATRIPTAN — CARDIOVASCULAR SCREENING REQUIRED BEFORE FIRST DOSE: Triptans cause vasoconstriction via 5-HT1B receptors and are contraindicated in uncontrolled hypertension, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, and peripheral vascular disease. Before prescribing sumatriptan, cardiovascular risk assessment must be completed. Given that vital signs are not yet available, triptans CANNOT be safely prescribed at this time.

ACETAMINOPHEN MAXIMUM DAILY DOSE — CONSERVATIVE LIMIT APPROPRIATE: The treatment plan recommends a 3000mg/day maximum rather than the FDA maximum of 4000mg/day. This conservative limit is SAFETY-APPROPRIATE and endorsed by hepatology guidelines. Patient must be warned to check ALL medications for hidden acetaminophen (combination cold/flu products, sleep aids, etc.).

IBUPROFEN + NAPROXEN — THERAPEUTIC DUPLICATION RISK: The treatment plan lists ibuprofen 400mg during the workup phase and naproxen 500mg in the migraine treatment phase. These are both NSAIDs and must NOT be used concurrently. The plan does separate them by phase, but explicit patient counseling is needed: when transitioning to triptan + naproxen, ibuprofen must be discontinued to avoid NSAID duplication (increased GI bleeding, renal injury, and cardiovascular risk).

MAGNESIUM OXIDE — RENAL FUNCTION CHECK NEEDED: Magnesium supplementation (400-600mg/day) is recommended for migraine prevention. This requires confirmation of normal renal function (from CMP results) before initiation. Hypermagnesemia risk exists in renal impairment. Additionally, magnesium oxide has poor bioavailability — magnesium glycinate or citrate may be more effective and better tolerated (lower GI side effects).
contraindications: TRIPTANS (sumatriptan, eletriptan, rizatriptan): CONTRAINDICATED until (1) secondary headache causes are excluded by neuroimaging, (2) pregnancy test is confirmed negative, (3) blood pressure is measured and within normal limits, (4) cardiovascular history is assessed. Triptans are absolutely contraindicated in hemiplegic migraine, basilar migraine, uncontrolled hypertension, coronary artery disease, prior stroke/TIA, peripheral vascular disease, and concurrent ergotamine use.

NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen): CONTRAINDICATED until pregnancy test is confirmed negative. Also contraindicated in active GI bleeding, peptic ulcer disease, severe renal impairment (GFR <30), NSAID allergy/hypersensitivity, and concurrent anticoagulant use without gastroprotection.

TOPIRAMATE (listed as preventive option): CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (FDA Category D — teratogenic, associated with cleft lip/palate). Must confirm negative pregnancy test and reliable contraception before prescribing. Also contraindicated in metabolic acidosis, nephrolithiasis (relative), and hepatic impairment.

METOCLOPRAMIDE: CONTRAINDICATED in seizure disorders, pheochromocytoma, GI obstruction/perforation, and concurrent use of drugs causing extrapyramidal reactions. Relative contraindication with concurrent SSRIs/SNRIs (serotonin syndrome risk, extrapyramidal symptom risk).

ERGOTAMINES: Not recommended in the treatment plan but explicitly noted — CONTRAINDICATED within 24 hours of any triptan (risk of prolonged vasospasm and ischemia). Also contraindicated in pregnancy, cardiovascular disease, and hepatic/renal impairment.

LUMBAR PUNCTURE: CONTRAINDICATED before neuroimaging if there is any suspicion of intracranial mass lesion (risk of cerebral herniation). The treatment plan correctly sequences LP after imaging — this must be strictly followed.

COMBINED ORAL CONTRACEPTIVES: If patient is found to have migraine WITH aura, COCs are WHO MEC Category 4 (absolutely contraindicated) due to 2-4 fold increased ischemic stroke risk. Must assess for aura features and counsel accordingly.

emergency_red_flags_for_patient: SEEK IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY CARE if you experience any of the following: sudden severe 'worst headache of your life' (thunderclap headache), new weakness or numbness on one side of your body, difficulty speaking or understanding speech, sudden vision loss or double vision, seizures or convulsions, high fever with stiff neck, confusion or difficulty staying awake, or progressive worsening of your headache despite medication.
safety.safety_summary: OVERALL ASSESSMENT: The medical team's recommendations are clinically sound, thorough, and demonstrate excellent diagnostic reasoning with appropriate prioritization of excluding secondary headache causes before initiating migraine-specific therapy. The treatment plan is guideline-concordant with AHS, AAN, and ICHD-3 standards. All medication dosages are within safe therapeutic ranges. However, several CRITICAL safety prerequisites must be completed before any pharmacological treatment beyond acetaminophen can be safely administered: (1) pregnancy test must be resulted, (2) vital signs including blood pressure must be obtained, (3) neurological examination must be performed, and (4) allergy and current medication histories must be documented. The team has appropriately identified that triptans should NOT be prescribed until secondary causes are excluded by neuroimaging — this is the most important safety gate in this case. The risk of premature diagnostic closure (anchoring on migraine) has been explicitly addressed by the diagnostician and neurologist, which is commendable. Key residual safety concerns include: the unknown pregnancy status affecting NSAID and triptan safety, the unknown OCP status affecting both CVT risk and treatment contraindications, the NSAID therapeutic duplication risk during phase transitions, and the need for explicit patient counseling on medication overuse headache prevention and emergency red flags. No CRITICAL safety violations were identified in the current recommendations — the team has been appropriately cautious. The safety warnings identified are primarily related to missing prerequisite information that must be obtained before treatment escalation.
recommendations: CRITICAL: Do NOT administer any NSAID (ibuprofen, naproxen) until pregnancy test is confirmed NEGATIVE. Acetaminophen is the only safe analgesic to offer before pregnancy status is known.

CRITICAL: Do NOT prescribe triptans until: (a) MRI brain with MRV is completed and excludes secondary causes, (b) pregnancy test is negative, (c) blood pressure is measured and within normal limits, (d) cardiovascular risk assessment is completed, and (e) allergy history is obtained.

CRITICAL: Obtain complete vital signs (BP, HR, temperature, RR, SpO2) BEFORE any treatment decisions. If systolic BP >180 or diastolic >120, this becomes a hypertensive emergency requiring different management.
HIGH: Obtain and document complete allergy history and current medication list before prescribing ANY medication. Cross-check all prescribed medications against allergies and current drugs.

HIGH: Perform neurological examination and fundoscopic exam as soon as possible. If papilledema is found, escalate urgency of neuroimaging and do NOT perform lumbar puncture until mass lesion is excluded.
HIGH: Verify renal function (from CMP) before administering gadolinium contrast for MRI and before initiating magnesium supplementation.
HIGH: Explicitly counsel patient that ibuprofen and naproxen are BOTH NSAIDs and must NEVER be taken together. Provide clear written instructions for phase transitions.
HIGH: If CVT is diagnosed and anticoagulation is initiated, immediately discontinue ALL NSAIDs and document this medication change clearly.

MODERATE: Assess OCP/hormonal therapy use — this single data point significantly modifies both the differential diagnosis (CVT risk) and treatment safety profile (contraindication of COCs in migraine with aura).
MODERATE: Counsel patient on medication overuse headache risk — limit all acute analgesics to ≤2-3 days per week (≤10 days per month). Provide this guidance in writing.

MODERATE: If metoclopramide is prescribed, document informed consent regarding FDA Black Box Warning for tardive dyskinesia. Consider ondansetron as first-line antiemetic for recurrent use given superior safety profile.
MODERATE: Consider magnesium citrate or glycinate instead of magnesium oxide for migraine prevention — better bioavailability and fewer GI side effects at equivalent doses.
LOW: Assess breastfeeding status if applicable — affects medication selection.
LOW: Provide written emergency red flag instructions to the patient with specific symptoms warranting immediate ED return.
LOW: Document headache diary instructions and provide a standardized template (MIDAS or HIT-6 disability scale) for follow-up assessment.

specialist.reason_for_consultation: 35-year-old female with 2-week persistent right-sided throbbing headache (6/10), photophobia, and nausea. Triage identified red flags including persistent duration >2 weeks, new/changed headache pattern, and photophobia. Requires specialist evaluation to differentiate primary headache disorder (migraine, tension-type) from secondary causes (intracranial pathology, IIH, meningitis, vascular events) and guide appropriate diagnostic and therapeutic approach.
specialist.specialist_assessment: This patient presents with a clinical picture highly suggestive of migraine, though the 2-week persistent duration is atypical for episodic migraine (which typically lasts 4-72 hours per ICHD-3 criteria). The constellation of unilateral throbbing quality, photophobia, and nausea are classic migraine features with strong epidemiologic fit (female, reproductive age, peak incidence 30-40 years). However, the persistent 2-week course represents a significant change from typical migraine pattern and warrants urgent exclusion of secondary causes. Differential diagnosis includes: (1) Chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month) - plausible if this represents cluster of frequent attacks; (2) Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) - excellent epidemiologic fit (female, reproductive age), presents with chronic progressive headache and photophobia, prevalence 5-19 per 100,000 in this demographic; (3) Intracranial mass or space-occupying lesion - lower probability without focal deficits or papilledema reported, but must not miss given persistent progressive course; (4) Tension-type headache - less likely given unilateral throbbing quality and photophobia (photophobia is NOT typical of tension-type, LR- 0.4); (5) Meningitis/encephalitis - photophobia is highly specific (LR+ 9.2) but absence of fever (LR- 0.15) and neck stiffness (LR- 0.1) strongly argue against; (6) Subarachnoid hemorrhage or sentinel bleed - lower probability without thunderclap onset, but photophobia and nausea consistent with meningeal irritation; (7) Medication overuse headache - possible if patient has been using frequent acute medications (not documented in history); (8) Cervicogenic headache - less likely without neck pain (key feature usually present) and with photophobia present. From neurology perspective, the 2-week persistent duration with photophobia and unilateral location represents a RED FLAG that exceeds typical primary headache presentation and mandates neuroimaging and comprehensive neurological examination before attributing diagnosis to primary headache disorder. The patient's stable vital signs and lack of acute distress do not exclude serious pathology - chronic progressive headaches can represent indolent intracranial processes. Photophobia specifically suggests either migraine pathophysiology (trigeminal-brainstem activation) OR increased intracranial pressure (IIH, mass effect, meningeal irritation). Fundoscopic examination is critical to assess for papilledema, which would dramatically shift diagnostic probability toward IIH or space-occupying lesion.

safety.safety_summary: This 35-year-old female with 2-week persistent right-sided throbbing headache, photophobia, and nausea presents with RED FLAGS for secondary headache pathology. The treatment plan is GENERALLY SAFE but has CRITICAL GAPS and IMPORTANT CAVEATS: (1) TRIPTANS MUST BE DEFERRED until neuroimaging (MRI brain) is completed and secondary causes (intracranial mass, SAH, meningitis, IIH) are excluded. Premature triptan initiation could mask serious pathology. (2) MEDICATION HISTORY IS MISSING—complete reconciliation is ESSENTIAL before prescribing any agents to assess for drug-drug interactions, contraindications, and medication overuse headache history. (3) ALLERGY HISTORY IS MISSING—must be obtained before medication initiation. (4) BLOOD PRESSURE STATUS UNKNOWN—must be verified <180/110 before NSAID or triptan use. (5) PREGNANCY STATUS UNKNOWN—must be obtained; NSAIDs contraindicated in third trimester. (6) ORAL CONTRACEPTIVE USE UNKNOWN—must be obtained; estrogen-containing contraceptives increase CVST risk. (7) MENSTRUAL HISTORY UNKNOWN—must be obtained for hormonal migraine assessment and IIH risk stratification. (8) FUNDOSCOPIC EXAMINATION IS CRITICAL—must be performed to assess for papilledema (suggests IIH or increased ICP). (9) NSAID/ACETAMINOPHEN/TRIPTAN DOSING IS APPROPRIATE but patient must be counseled on maximum daily doses and frequency limits to prevent medication overuse headache. (10) METOCLOPRAMIDE USE SHOULD BE LIMITED to <3 months to minimize tardive dyskinesia risk; ondansetron preferred for chronic use. All acute pain medications (NSAIDs, acetaminophen, triptans) are CONTRAINDICATED if patient has uncontrolled hypertension (>180/110)—blood pressure must be verified. The treatment plan correctly emphasizes DEFERRING TRIPTAN INITIATION until imaging complete, which is appropriate and safe. Conservative measures (environmental modifications, sleep hygiene, stress management, hydration, caffeine management) are safe and recommended. Overall safety status is PASS WITH WARNINGS due to critical information gaps that must be addressed before medication initiation.

empathy.patient_summary: You've been having headaches on the right side of your head for 2 weeks that throb and feel like a 6 out of 10 in pain. You're also sensitive to light and feeling a bit nauseous. While these symptoms are uncomfortable, the good news is that you're stable and alert. However, because your headache has lasted 2 weeks and has these specific features, your doctor wants to do some tests to make sure there's nothing serious causing it. The most common cause of headaches like yours is migraines, which are very treatable. But we need to rule out other possibilities first with imaging and a careful exam. You're taking exactly the right step by getting this checked out.
empathy.what_this_means: Your headache pattern is different from a typical headache—it's been going on longer than most headaches do, and the combination of throbbing pain, light sensitivity, and nausea tells us we need to investigate. Think of it like a warning light on your car dashboard: it doesn't mean something is definitely wrong, but it means we should check under the hood to be sure. The most likely explanation is migraine, which is a common condition that affects about 1 in 8 people. But we also need to check for other less common causes like increased pressure in your head, inflammation, or other issues. That's why your doctor is recommending an MRI scan—it's like taking a detailed picture of your brain to see what's going on.

right_now: Schedule your MRI brain scan as soon as possible—ideally within the next 1-2 days. Call your doctor's office today if you haven't already.
Make a list of ALL medications you're taking (prescription, over-the-counter, vitamins, supplements, herbal products) to bring to your appointment.
Write down your allergy history—any drug allergies, food allergies, or reactions you've had to medications.
Note your current blood pressure if you have a home monitor, or plan to get it checked before starting any new medications.
If you could be pregnant or are breastfeeding, let your doctor know before taking any new medications.

Keep a headache diary starting today: write down when your headache starts, how long it lasts, pain level (0-10), what side of your head, what makes it better or worse, and any other symptoms (nausea, light sensitivity, etc.).
Sit in a quiet, dimly lit room when your headache is bad—this will help with the light sensitivity.
this_week: Complete your MRI brain scan appointment.

Have your eye doctor or primary care doctor check your eyes with a special light (dilated eye exam) to look for any swelling of the optic nerve—this is an important part of figuring out what's causing your headache.
Bring your complete medication list and allergy history to all appointments.

If you're a woman of reproductive age, be ready to discuss your menstrual cycle and whether you're taking any hormonal birth control—this information helps your doctor understand your headache better.

Start taking over-the-counter pain relief if your headache is bothersome: ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) 400-600 mg every 6-8 hours, OR acetaminophen (Tylenol) 1000 mg every 6-8 hours. Take with food if possible.
For nausea, try ginger tea, small frequent meals, or ask your pharmacist about over-the-counter anti-nausea options.
Follow up with your doctor to discuss MRI results and next steps.
ongoing: Keep your headache diary going for at least 2 weeks—this helps identify patterns and triggers.
Try to get 7-9 hours of sleep each night and keep a regular sleep schedule.
Drink plenty of water (about 8-10 glasses per day) and eat regular meals—skipping meals can trigger headaches.
Limit caffeine to no more than 1-2 cups of coffee per day, and don't quit caffeine suddenly (gradual reduction is better).
Try stress-reduction techniques like deep breathing, stretching, or meditation for 10-15 minutes daily.
Avoid bright lights, loud noises, and strong smells when possible, especially during a headache.
If you're prescribed pain medication, do NOT use it more than 10-15 days per month—using it too often can actually cause more headaches (this is called medication overuse headache).
Attend all follow-up appointments with your doctor or neurologist.
Ask your doctor about preventive medications if your headaches continue—these can reduce how often you get headaches.

for_pain.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)
for_pain.how_it_works: Reduces inflammation and pain by blocking chemicals in your body that cause swelling and hurt.
for_pain.how_to_take: 400-600 mg by mouth every 6-8 hours as needed for pain. Take with food to protect your stomach.
for_pain.maximum_per_day: Do not exceed 3200 mg (about 5-6 tablets of 600 mg) in one day.
for_pain.important: Do NOT use more than 10-15 days per month—using it too often can cause rebound headaches. If you have a history of stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or high blood pressure, ask your doctor first.
for_pain.side_effects: Stomach upset, heartburn, nausea. Taking with food helps.

for_pain.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
for_pain.how_it_works: Reduces pain and fever by affecting how your brain processes pain signals.
for_pain.how_to_take: 1000 mg (2 tablets of 500 mg) by mouth every 6-8 hours as needed for pain.
for_pain.maximum_per_day: Do not exceed 3000-4000 mg in one day. If you take it regularly, use the lower amount (3000 mg).
for_pain.important: Do NOT combine with other products containing acetaminophen (like cold medicines or combination pain relievers)—this can damage your liver. Do NOT use more than 10-15 days per month.
for_pain.side_effects: Generally well-tolerated. Rare at normal doses.

for_nausea.name: Metoclopramide (Reglan)
for_nausea.how_it_works: Helps your stomach move food through more quickly and blocks signals to your brain that cause nausea.
for_nausea.how_to_take: 10 mg by mouth every 6-8 hours as needed for nausea.
for_nausea.maximum_per_day: Do not exceed 40 mg in one day.
for_nausea.important: Use for SHORT-TERM only (less than 3 months) to avoid a serious side effect called tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements). If nausea continues beyond 3 months, ask your doctor about switching to a different medication.
for_nausea.side_effects: Drowsiness, restlessness, diarrhea. Tell your doctor if you feel very restless or jittery.

for_nausea.name: Ondansetron (Zofran)
for_nausea.how_it_works: Blocks signals in your brain and stomach that cause nausea and vomiting.
for_nausea.how_to_take: 4-8 mg by mouth every 8 hours as needed for nausea.
for_nausea.maximum_per_day: Do not exceed 24 mg in one day.
for_nausea.important: Safe for longer-term use than metoclopramide. No risk of the movement problems that can happen with metoclopramide.
for_nausea.side_effects: Constipation (common), headache, dizziness. Drink plenty of water and eat fiber to help with constipation.

medications_explained.important_note_about_triptans: Your doctor may eventually recommend a medication called a 'triptan' (like sumatriptan or rizatriptan) if your headaches are diagnosed as migraines. However, these medications should NOT be started until after your MRI scan and your doctor has ruled out other causes. Triptans are very effective for migraines, but they're not safe to use if you have certain other conditions. Your doctor will explain this in detail once your test results are back.

lifestyle_tips.sleep: Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, even on weekends. Aim for 7-9 hours per night. Keep your bedroom dark, cool, and quiet. Avoid screens (phone, TV, computer) for 30 minutes before bed.
lifestyle_tips.hydration_and_nutrition: Drink water throughout the day—aim for 8-10 glasses. Don't skip meals, as low blood sugar can trigger headaches. Eat regular, balanced meals with protein, healthy fats, and vegetables. Avoid sugary snacks that cause blood sugar spikes and crashes.
lifestyle_tips.caffeine: Limit caffeine to no more than 1-2 cups of coffee (or equivalent) per day. If you drink a lot of caffeine now, reduce it gradually over a week or two—quitting suddenly can cause rebound headaches. Avoid caffeine after 2 PM so it doesn't interfere with sleep.
lifestyle_tips.stress_management: Try deep breathing: breathe in slowly for 4 counts, hold for 7 counts, breathe out for 8 counts. Do this 5-10 times when you feel stressed. Try progressive muscle relaxation: tense each muscle group for 5 seconds, then relax. Try meditation or mindfulness apps (like Calm or Headspace) for 10-15 minutes daily. Gentle yoga or stretching can help release tension.
lifestyle_tips.environment: When you have a headache, go to a quiet, dark room. Wear sunglasses outdoors if light bothers you. Avoid strong smells (perfumes, cleaning products, smoke). Keep your workspace well-organized and take regular breaks if you work at a computer.
lifestyle_tips.triggers: In your headache diary, note what happens before your headache starts—this might be stress, certain foods, lack of sleep, weather changes, or hormonal changes. Once you identify your triggers, you can try to avoid them.
lifestyle_tips.exercise: Gentle exercise like walking, swimming, or yoga can help prevent headaches. Avoid intense exercise during a headache, but regular moderate activity (30 minutes most days) is beneficial. Start slowly if you're not used to exercising.
lifestyle_tips.hormonal_factors: If you're a woman, your headaches might be related to your menstrual cycle. Track this in your headache diary. Tell your doctor if you notice a pattern—this information helps with treatment planning.

seek_emergency_care_immediately_if: Your headache suddenly gets much worse very quickly (worst headache of your life)—this could be a sign of bleeding in the brain.
You develop a stiff neck along with your headache and fever—this could be meningitis (a serious infection).

anticipated_faqs.question: Why do I need an MRI if my headache is probably just a migraine?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Great question. While migraine is the most common cause of headaches like yours, your 2-week duration and specific symptoms mean we need to rule out other possibilities first. An MRI is like taking a detailed picture of your brain to make sure there's nothing else going on—like increased pressure, inflammation, or a structural issue. It's a safety step that helps us be confident in the diagnosis. The good news is that MRI is safe, painless, and will give us important information.

anticipated_faqs.question: Is my headache serious? Could it be a brain tumor?
anticipated_faqs.answer: I understand this is scary to think about. Brain tumors are actually quite rare—they account for less than 1% of headaches that people see doctors for. Your symptoms are much more consistent with migraine or another common headache type. That said, your doctor is doing the right thing by checking with an MRI to rule out anything serious. Most people with headaches like yours have migraine, which is very treatable. The MRI will give us the information we need to be confident about what's causing your headache.

anticipated_faqs.question: Why is light sensitivity such a big deal?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Light sensitivity (photophobia) is actually a helpful clue for your doctor. It's very common in migraines and also in a few other conditions that need to be checked out. It tells us that something is going on with how your brain is processing sensory information. That's why your doctor wants to do tests—to figure out exactly what's causing it and how to help you feel better.

anticipated_faqs.question: What's the difference between a migraine and a regular headache?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Good question. A regular tension headache usually feels like a tight band around your head, is usually on both sides, and doesn't come with nausea or light sensitivity. A migraine is usually throbbing (like a pulse), often on one side, and commonly comes with nausea and light sensitivity. Migraines can last 4-72 hours and are often more intense. Your symptoms sound more like migraine, but your doctor will confirm this after your tests.

anticipated_faqs.question: Can I take pain medication while waiting for my MRI?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Yes, it's fine to take over-the-counter pain medication like ibuprofen or acetaminophen while you wait for your MRI. This won't interfere with the test or hide important information. Just follow the dosing instructions and don't use pain medication more than 10-15 days per month, as frequent use can actually cause more headaches. If the pain is severe, call your doctor—they might recommend something stronger.

anticipated_faqs.question: What happens during an MRI scan?
anticipated_faqs.answer: An MRI is painless and non-invasive. You'll lie on a table that slides into a large tube-shaped machine. The machine uses magnetic fields and radio waves to take detailed pictures of your brain. It's loud (you'll hear beeping and humming sounds), so you'll wear headphones or earplugs. The whole scan takes about 30-45 minutes. You need to stay very still during the scan. If you're claustrophobic, let your doctor know—they can give you medication to help you relax, or they might use an open MRI machine instead. There's no radiation, and it's very safe.

anticipated_faqs.question: What if my MRI is normal?
anticipated_faqs.answer: If your MRI is normal, that's actually good news. It means there's no serious structural problem like a tumor or bleeding. A normal MRI, combined with your symptoms and a normal neurological exam, makes migraine or tension-type headache much more likely. Your doctor can then focus on treating your headache with confidence. Many people with normal MRIs go on to feel much better with the right treatment.

anticipated_faqs.question: What if my MRI shows something abnormal?
anticipated_faqs.answer: If your MRI shows something, your doctor will explain exactly what it is and what it means. Not all MRI findings require treatment—sometimes the brain shows things that don't cause symptoms. Your doctor will discuss next steps with you, which might include seeing a specialist (like a neurologist), additional testing, or specific treatment. Your doctor will make sure you understand what's going on and what the plan is.

anticipated_faqs.question: How long will it take to feel better?
anticipated_faqs.answer: That depends on what's causing your headache. If it's migraine, many people feel better within days to weeks once they start the right treatment. Some people need to try a few different treatments to find what works best for them. If it's another condition, your doctor will explain the timeline based on the specific diagnosis. The important thing is that you're taking steps now to figure it out and get help.

anticipated_faqs.question: Can stress cause my headache?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Stress is a common trigger for both migraines and tension headaches. If you've been stressed lately, that could be contributing to your headache. Even if stress isn't the main cause, managing stress through relaxation techniques, exercise, and good sleep can help prevent future headaches. Your doctor can give you specific strategies for stress management.

anticipated_faqs.question: Should I stop taking my other medications?
anticipated_faqs.answer: No, don't stop taking any medications without talking to your doctor first. However, it's very important that you tell your doctor about ALL medications you're taking—prescription, over-the-counter, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products. Some medications can interact with headache treatments, and some can even cause headaches. Your doctor needs this information to make sure any new medications are safe for you.
