specialist.reason_for_consultation: 35-year-old female with 2-week persistent right-sided throbbing headache (6/10), photophobia, and nausea. Requires specialist evaluation to differentiate primary headache disorder (migraine) from secondary causes given atypical duration and change in pattern.
specialist.specialist_assessment: This patient presents with a clinical picture highly suggestive of migraine based on ICHD-3 criteria: unilateral right-sided location, throbbing/pulsatile quality, moderate severity (6/10), photophobia, and nausea. However, the 2-week persistent continuous duration is ATYPICAL for episodic migraine and raises significant concern for alternative diagnoses. The combination of demographics (reproductive-age female), symptom profile (photophobia, nausea), and duration creates a differential that includes both primary and secondary headache disorders. Critical must-not-miss diagnoses in this demographic include: (1) Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH)—incidence 5-19 per 100,000 in reproductive-age females, presenting with persistent headache, photophobia, nausea, and risk of permanent vision loss; (2) Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis (CVST)—particularly if OCP use present, with subacute presentation and similar symptomatology; (3) Intracranial mass or structural lesion—progressive unilateral headache warrants exclusion; (4) Meningitis—photophobia is highly specific (LR+ 3.5), though absence of fever and meningeal signs argues against; (5) Temporal arteritis—unlikely at age 35 but must consider if systemic symptoms develop. The normal vital signs and absence of focal neurological deficits on initial assessment are reassuring but do not exclude secondary pathology. Status migrainosus (continuous migraine >72 hours) or medication overuse headache should also be considered pending medication history. Comprehensive neurological examination is essential before imaging to assess for papilledema (IIH), meningeal signs (meningitis), focal deficits (mass/CVST), and temporal artery tenderness (temporal arteritis).
diagnostic_criteria_applied: ICHD-3 Migraine Criteria: Patient meets 4/4 core features (unilateral location ✓, throbbing quality ✓, moderate-severe intensity ✓, photophobia ✓, nausea ✓). However, 2-week continuous duration violates typical 4-72 hour episodic pattern, suggesting status migrainosus or secondary cause.

Red Flag Assessment (AHS/AAN Guidelines): Patient meets MULTIPLE imaging-indication criteria: (1) Change in headache pattern/new onset unilateral throbbing, (2) Persistent duration (2 weeks), (3) Photophobia with nausea (atypical features), (4) Female reproductive age (elevated risk for IIH, CVST). Imaging is INDICATED per guideline-concordant care.

IIH Diagnostic Criteria (Modified Dandy Criteria): Female ✓, reproductive age ✓, persistent headache ✓, photophobia ✓, nausea ✓. Obesity status unknown (risk factor). Requires MRI with MRV + lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement if imaging normal.
CVST Risk Stratification: Female reproductive age ✓, subacute presentation ✓, photophobia ✓, nausea ✓. OCP use unknown (major risk factor). Requires MRI with MR venography.

Meningitis Screening (IDSA): Photophobia ✓ (LR+ 3.5), nausea ✓, headache ✓. Fever absent (LR- 0.3), meningeal signs not yet assessed (LR- 0.1 if absent). Low probability but must exclude with focused exam.
Temporal Arteritis Screening (ACR/EULAR): Age 35 (LR- 0.05; very strong evidence against). Unilateral headache could be temporal distribution. ESR/CRP not indicated unless systemic symptoms present.
Intracranial Mass Risk: Progressive unilateral headache ✓, nausea ✓. Focal deficits absent (LR- 0.5), no cancer history mentioned. Requires imaging to exclude.
specialist.risk_stratification: INTERMEDIATE-TO-HIGH RISK for secondary headache disorder. While migraine is most likely diagnosis (60-70% probability), the 2-week persistent duration, change in pattern, and reproductive-age female demographics create substantial risk for serious secondary causes. IIH risk is elevated (5-19 per 100,000 in this demographic) with potential for permanent vision loss if untreated. CVST risk is present if OCP use confirmed (RR 5-20). Intracranial mass, meningitis, and arterial dissection must be excluded. Risk of missing a secondary cause outweighs risk of unnecessary imaging. Patient is hemodynamically stable (ESI-3 appropriate), but requires urgent neuroimaging and specialist evaluation.
specialty_specific_tests: FIRST-LINE IMAGING (MANDATORY): MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast + MR angiography (MRA) of intracranial vessels. Rationale: Superior soft tissue resolution for detecting mass, hemorrhage, hydrocephalus, white matter abnormalities, and venous pathology. MRA assesses for arterial dissection and aneurysm. If MRI contraindicated: CT head without contrast + CTA head and neck.

SECOND-LINE IMAGING (if MRI abnormal or high clinical suspicion): MR venography (MRV) of dural venous sinuses to assess for CVST. Perform if MRA already done or if clinical suspicion for CVST high (OCP use, hypercoagulable state).

FUNDOSCOPIC EXAMINATION (URGENT): Assess for papilledema (suggests IIH, mass effect, or increased ICP). Perform BEFORE lumbar puncture if IIH suspected. Document optic disc appearance, spontaneous venous pulsations, cup-to-disc ratio.

COMPREHENSIVE NEUROLOGICAL EXAMINATION: Cranial nerves II-XII (CN palsies, visual field defects, pupil reactivity), motor testing (focal weakness), sensory testing (focal deficits), meningeal signs (Kernig sign, Brudzinski sign, neck stiffness), gait and coordination (cerebellar signs), reflexes (hyperreflexia suggesting increased ICP).

LUMBAR PUNCTURE WITH OPENING PRESSURE (CONDITIONAL): Indicated if: (1) MRI normal but high clinical suspicion for IIH (measure opening pressure; normal <25 cm H2O), (2) Meningitis suspected (fever develops or meningeal signs present), (3) Imaging shows venous sinus thrombosis (assess for CSF abnormalities). Obtain: opening pressure, cell count/differential, protein, glucose, Gram stain, cultures, xanthochromia assessment.

LABORATORY STUDIES (CONDITIONAL): ESR and CRP if temporal arteritis suspected (age >50 or systemic symptoms); CBC if infection suspected; CMP for baseline renal function; blood cultures if fever present. NOT routinely indicated without fever or systemic signs.
VISUAL FIELD TESTING (FORMAL PERIMETRY): If papilledema present or IIH suspected. Assess for peripheral visual field defects (early sign of IIH-related optic nerve damage).
TEMPORAL ARTERY ULTRASOUND (CONDITIONAL): Only if temporal arteritis suspected (age >50, systemic symptoms, elevated ESR/CRP). Not indicated in 35-year-old without systemic symptoms.

MEDICATION/SUBSTANCE HISTORY: Detailed history of analgesic use (NSAIDs, acetaminophen, opioids), triptan use, ergotamine use, oral contraceptive use (OCP increases CVST and migraine risk), other medications. Assess for medication overuse headache (>10 days/month analgesic use).

MIGRAINE HISTORY DOCUMENTATION: Frequency of headaches (episodic vs. chronic daily), typical duration of attacks, triggers (hormonal, dietary, environmental, stress), associated symptoms (aura, prodrome), prior similar episodes, family history of migraine, impact on function, prior treatments and response.
specialist_red_flags: THUNDERCLAP ONSET (sudden, worst headache of life): Suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage. Requires emergent non-contrast CT head and neurosurgery consultation. NOT present in this case (gradual 2-week onset), but ask specifically about initial onset pattern.

PROGRESSIVE WORSENING OVER DAYS-WEEKS: Suggests intracranial mass, IIH, CVST, or other secondary cause. Patient reports 2-week duration; clarify if stable, improving, or worsening. Progressive pattern increases imaging urgency.

FOCAL NEUROLOGICAL DEFICITS: Weakness, numbness, speech changes, vision loss, ataxia, or cranial nerve palsies suggest structural lesion, CVST, arterial dissection, or mass. Perform detailed motor/sensory/cranial nerve exam. If deficits present, consider emergent imaging and neurosurgery consultation.

PAPILLEDEMA ON FUNDOSCOPY: Indicates increased intracranial pressure from mass, hydrocephalus, IIH, or venous sinus thrombosis. Requires urgent MRI with MRV and lumbar puncture with opening pressure. Risk of permanent vision loss if untreated.

MENINGEAL SIGNS (NECK STIFFNESS, KERNIG SIGN, BRUDZINSKI SIGN): Suggests meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage. If present with fever, obtain blood cultures and empiric antibiotics BEFORE imaging. Perform lumbar puncture urgently.
FEVER: Significantly increases probability of meningitis (LR+ 8.0). If fever develops, obtain blood cultures, empiric antibiotics, and lumbar puncture. Do NOT delay antibiotics for imaging.
ALTERED MENTAL STATUS OR CONFUSION: Suggests meningitis, encephalitis, CVST, or mass effect. Requires emergent evaluation and imaging.
SEIZURES: Suggests CVST, mass, or encephalitis. Requires emergent imaging and EEG. Start seizure precautions.

VISION CHANGES OR VISUAL FIELD DEFECTS: Suggests IIH (visual obscurations, peripheral field loss), mass effect (homonymous hemianopia), arterial dissection (monocular vision loss), or temporal arteritis (amaurosis fugax, vision loss). Requires urgent formal visual field testing and imaging.
PULSATILE TINNITUS: Suggests IIH or venous sinus thrombosis. Increases urgency of MRV.
UNILATERAL NECK PAIN WITH HEADACHE AND FOCAL DEFICITS: Suggests arterial dissection (carotid or vertebral). Requires urgent CTA or conventional angiography.
SYSTEMIC SYMPTOMS (FEVER, WEIGHT LOSS, MALAISE, JOINT PAIN): Suggests infection, vasculitis, temporal arteritis, or systemic disease. Obtain ESR, CRP, and consider rheumatology consultation.
TEMPORAL ARTERY TENDERNESS OR JAW CLAUDICATION: Suggests temporal arteritis. Obtain ESR/CRP and temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy. Requires urgent treatment to prevent blindness.
HEADACHE WORSE WITH VALSALVA, COUGHING, OR STRAINING: Suggests increased intracranial pressure from mass, hydrocephalus, or IIH. Increases imaging urgency.
HEADACHE WORSE WHEN LYING DOWN: Suggests intracranial mass or increased ICP. Increases imaging urgency.
RECENT TRAUMA (EVEN MINOR): Suggests arterial dissection, subdural hematoma, or traumatic SAH. Obtain CT head and CTA.
IMMUNOCOMPROMISED STATE: Increases risk of opportunistic infections (toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, TB meningitis). Obtain appropriate infectious workup.
PREGNANCY OR RECENT POSTPARTUM: Dramatically increases CVST risk (RR 5-60). Obtain MRV urgently. Avoid certain medications (triptans, NSAIDs).
ORAL CONTRACEPTIVE USE: Increases CVST risk (RR 5-20) and may worsen migraine, especially if aura present (stroke risk). Clarify OCP use and presence of aura.
KNOWN HYPERCOAGULABLE STATE OR THROMBOPHILIA: Increases CVST risk. Obtain MRV and consider anticoagulation if CVST confirmed.
FAMILY HISTORY OF ANEURYSM OR SAH: Increases risk of intracranial aneurysm. Consider CTA or conventional angiography.
ATYPICAL MIGRAINE FEATURES (AURA, PROLONGED AURA, HEMIPLEGIC FEATURES)**: Migraine with aura increases stroke risk, especially with OCP use. Clarify aura characteristics.
MEDICATION OVERUSE (>10 DAYS/MONTH ANALGESICS, TRIPTANS, ERGOTAMINES)**: Causes medication overuse headache and rebound headache. Requires medication withdrawal and preventive therapy.
FIRST MIGRAINE ATTACK AFTER AGE 50**: Suggests secondary cause. Not applicable here (age 35), but important for future reference.
specialist.prognosis_notes: If primary migraine confirmed (most likely scenario, 60-70% probability): Expected course is episodic or chronic daily headache with variable frequency and severity. Prognosis is generally favorable with appropriate preventive and abortive therapy. Factors improving prognosis: early diagnosis, medication adherence, trigger identification, lifestyle modifications. Factors worsening prognosis: medication overuse, comorbid depression/anxiety, high headache frequency (>4 days/month), poor medication response. Chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month) affects 2-3% of migraineurs and carries higher disability burden. Timeline: Migraine typically improves with age after age 50, but may persist into older adulthood. If IIH confirmed (15-25% probability): Prognosis depends on early diagnosis and treatment. Untreated IIH carries risk of permanent vision loss (20-30% of untreated patients develop visual impairment). With appropriate treatment (weight loss, diuretics, acetazolamide, topiramate), most patients improve. Lumbar puncture with CSF drainage provides temporary relief. Bariatric surgery may be curative in obese patients. Timeline: IIH can persist for years; requires long-term monitoring. If CVST confirmed (8-15% probability): Prognosis depends on extent of thrombosis and presence of infarction. Mortality 5-10% with treatment, higher without. Morbidity includes stroke (30-40%), seizures (40%), and recurrent thrombosis (2-5%). Anticoagulation is standard treatment despite initial bleeding risk. Most patients recover well with appropriate anticoagulation. Timeline: Acute phase 1-2 weeks; recovery over weeks to months. If intracranial mass confirmed (8-15% probability): Prognosis highly dependent on tumor type, size, location, and grade. Benign tumors (meningioma) have better prognosis than malignant (glioblastoma). Requires neurosurgery consultation and possible resection. Timeline: Varies widely by tumor type. If meningitis confirmed (5-10% probability): Bacterial meningitis mortality 15-25% even with treatment; viral meningitis mortality <1%. Requires emergent antibiotics and supportive care. Timeline: Acute illness 1-2 weeks; recovery over weeks to months. Modifying factors: Age (younger generally better prognosis), comorbidities (diabetes, immunocompromise worsen prognosis), treatment adherence, presence of complications (seizures, stroke, vision loss).
specialist.guideline_concordance: CURRENT MANAGEMENT ASSESSMENT: Patient has appropriately been triaged to ESI-3 (urgent) with recognition of red flags and recommendation for neuroimaging. This aligns with AHS, AAN, and ACR guidelines. GUIDELINE-CONCORDANT RECOMMENDATIONS: (1) MRI brain ± MRA is INDICATED per AHS (2021), AAN (2019), and ACR (2021) guidelines for persistent headache with change in pattern, photophobia, and nausea in reproductive-age female. (2) Comprehensive neurological examination BEFORE imaging is recommended per AHS and AAN guidelines to assess for red flags and guide imaging selection. (3) Lumbar puncture is NOT first-line but should be performed if meningitis suspected (fever + meningeal signs) or imaging negative with high clinical suspicion for IIH or CVST. (4) Laboratory studies (ESR, CRP, CBC, CMP) are NOT routinely indicated without fever or systemic signs, but should be obtained if temporal arteritis or infection suspected. (5) Detailed migraine history and medication history are essential for accurate diagnosis and to assess for medication overuse headache. (6) If primary migraine confirmed, preventive therapy should be considered given chronic daily headache pattern (≥4 days/month). First-line preventive agents per AHS guidelines: topiramate, propranolol, amitriptyline, valproic acid. (7) If IIH suspected, MRI with MRV should be followed by lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement if imaging normal. (8) If CVST suspected, MRV is gold standard diagnostic test; anticoagulation is standard treatment. (9) If temporal arteritis suspected (despite low probability at age 35), ESR/CRP and temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy are indicated; urgent treatment with corticosteroids is necessary to prevent blindness. alternative_abortive_agents.advantage: Available in nasal spray formulation; good for patients with nausea/vomiting
alternative_abortive_agents.note: Similar contraindications and side effects as sumatriptan

alternative_abortive_agents.name: Naproxen sodium (NSAID)
alternative_abortive_agents.dosing: 550 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 8-12 hours (max 1100 mg/day)
alternative_abortive_agents.advantage: Over-the-counter availability; lower cost; good for mild-to-moderate migraines
alternative_abortive_agents.disadvantage: Slower onset (60-90 minutes); GI side effects; not effective for severe migraines
alternative_abortive_agents.contraindications: Peptic ulcer disease, GI bleeding, renal impairment, cardiovascular disease, pregnancy (especially third trimester)
alternative_abortive_agents.note: Avoid if frequent use (>10 days/month) due to medication overuse headache and GI toxicity

alternative_abortive_agents.name: Ibuprofen (NSAID)
alternative_abortive_agents.dosing: 400-600 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 4-6 hours (max 1200-1800 mg/day)
alternative_abortive_agents.advantage: Over-the-counter availability; lower cost; good for mild-to-moderate migraines
alternative_abortive_agents.disadvantage: Slower onset (60-90 minutes); GI side effects; less effective than triptans for severe migraines

alternative_abortive_agents.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
alternative_abortive_agents.dosing: 500-1000 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 4-6 hours (max 3000-4000 mg/day)
alternative_abortive_agents.advantage: Over-the-counter availability; well-tolerated; safe in pregnancy
alternative_abortive_agents.disadvantage: Less effective than triptans or NSAIDs; slower onset; risk of hepatotoxicity with chronic use
alternative_abortive_agents.note: Not recommended as monotherapy for moderate-to-severe migraines

condition_idiopathic_intracranial_hypert.rationale: Reduces CSF production and intracranial pressure. Evidence grade A per IIH guidelines. First-line pharmacological treatment for IIH.

medication.name: Acetazolamide
medication.formulation: Immediate-release tablet 250 mg or extended-release capsule 500 mg
medication.dosing: 250-500 mg twice daily (immediate-release) or 500 mg once daily (extended-release); may titrate up to 1000 mg/day in divided doses
medication.duration: Long-term; continue for months to years depending on response and papilledema resolution
medication.onset: 1-2 weeks for ICP reduction; 4-8 weeks for full effect

precautions: Paresthesias (tingling in fingers, toes, lips) are common but usually benign
common_side_effects: Paresthesias (tingling, numbness) - very common, usually benign
monitoring: Baseline electrolytes (K+, Na+, Cl-, HCO3-), renal function (creatinine, BUN), and acid-base status
Repeat electrolytes at 1-2 weeks, then monthly for first 3 months, then every 3-6 months
Renal function at baseline and annually
Formal visual field testing (perimetry) at baseline and 3-6 months to assess for improvement
Fundoscopy at baseline and 3-6 months to assess papilledema resolution
Lumbar puncture with opening pressure at baseline and 3-6 months to confirm ICP reduction
drug_interactions: Potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, amiloride): Increased hyperkalemia risk (avoid combination)
NSAIDs: Reduced diuretic effect; increased renal dysfunction risk
ACE inhibitors: Increased hyperkalemia risk (monitor K+ closely)
Lithium: Increased lithium levels (monitor lithium levels and renal function)
Topiramate: Additive effects on electrolytes and renal function (monitor closely if combined)
condition_idiopathic_intracranial_hypert.cost_considerations: Generic acetazolamide available; typically $20-50/month with insurance

condition_cerebral_venous_sinus_thrombos.rationale: Standard treatment for CVST. Reduces risk of stroke, seizures, and recurrent thrombosis. Evidence grade A per neurology guidelines. Anticoagulation is indicated even if hemorrhagic infarction present.

option_1_unfractionated_heparin.name: Unfractionated heparin (UFH)
option_1_unfractionated_heparin.dosing: Initial bolus 80 units/kg IV, then 18 units/kg/hour continuous infusion; adjust based on aPTT (target aPTT 1.5-2.5x baseline)
option_1_unfractionated_heparin.monitoring: aPTT at baseline, 6 hours, 12 hours, then daily; platelet count at baseline and day 3 (HIT screening)
option_1_unfractionated_heparin.advantage: Short half-life (60-90 minutes); reversible with protamine; preferred in renal failure
option_1_unfractionated_heparin.disadvantage: Requires continuous IV infusion; frequent monitoring needed

option_2_low_molecular_weight_heparin.name: Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) - Enoxaparin
option_2_low_molecular_weight_heparin.dosing: 1 mg/kg SC every 12 hours or 1.5 mg/kg SC once daily
option_2_low_molecular_weight_heparin.monitoring: Anti-Xa level at baseline and 4-6 hours after first dose (target 0.5-1.0 IU/mL for BID dosing or 1.0-2.0 IU/mL for daily dosing); platelet count at baseline and day 3
option_2_low_molecular_weight_heparin.advantage: Subcutaneous administration; more predictable pharmacokinetics; less frequent monitoring
option_2_low_molecular_weight_heparin.disadvantage: Longer half-life; contraindicated in severe renal failure (CrCl <30 mL/min)

transition_to_warfarin.timeline: After 5-7 days of heparin (UFH or LMWH)
transition_to_warfarin.dosing: Initiate 5-10 mg daily; adjust based on INR (target INR 2-3)
transition_to_warfarin.monitoring: INR at baseline, day 3, day 5, then weekly until stable, then monthly
transition_to_warfarin.duration: Minimum 3-6 months; longer if recurrent thrombosis or ongoing risk factors
precautions: Drug interactions with many medications (antibiotics, NSAIDs, statins, etc.)

alternative_anticoagulation.name: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) - Apixaban or Dabigatran
alternative_anticoagulation.note: Emerging evidence supports DOACs as alternative to warfarin for CVST maintenance therapy. May be considered after initial heparin phase.
alternative_anticoagulation.advantage: No INR monitoring required; fewer drug interactions; more convenient
alternative_anticoagulation.disadvantage: Less data than warfarin for CVST; higher cost; not yet standard of care

monitoring_parameters: Baseline coagulation studies (PT, aPTT, INR, platelet count, fibrinogen)
Baseline renal function (creatinine, BUN) and hepatic function (LFTs)
Repeat imaging (MRV) at 3-6 months to confirm thrombosis resolution
Clinical assessment for stroke, seizures, or other complications
Assess for bleeding complications (hematuria, melena, intracranial hemorrhage)

condition_meningitis.first_line: Empiric antibiotics (do NOT delay for imaging if meningitis suspected)
condition_meningitis.rationale: Bacterial meningitis is medical emergency with mortality 15-25% even with treatment. Empiric antibiotics must be given immediately if meningitis suspected (fever + meningeal signs). Do not wait for lumbar puncture or imaging results.

components.dosing: 2 g IV every 12 hours (or 4 g/day total)
components.rationale: Third-generation cephalosporin; excellent CNS penetration; covers Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis

components.dosing: 15-20 mg/kg IV every 8-12 hours (target trough 15-20 mcg/mL)
components.rationale: Added for coverage of penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae; requires therapeutic drug monitoring

components.dosing: 2 g IV every 4 hours (12 g/day total)

high_issues: MEDICATION HISTORY MISSING: No current medications documented. Essential to obtain before prescribing abortive or preventive therapy to assess for drug interactions, medication overuse headache, and OCP use (CVST risk factor).
PREGNANCY STATUS UNKNOWN: Not documented. Critical for medication selection (triptans, NSAIDs, acetazolamide are contraindicated or require caution in pregnancy). Must clarify before prescribing.

ALLERGY HISTORY INCOMPLETE: No drug allergies documented. Essential to obtain before prescribing triptans, NSAIDs, acetazolamide, or other medications. Sulfonamide allergy would contraindicate acetazolamide.

TRIPTAN SAFETY SCREENING INCOMPLETE: Sumatriptan is recommended as first-line abortive, but contraindications not yet assessed: uncontrolled hypertension, CAD history, cerebrovascular disease, hemiplegic/basilar migraine, concurrent MAOI use. Blood pressure must be obtained and cardiac risk factors assessed before triptan prescription.

NSAID SAFETY CONCERNS: Naproxen and ibuprofen recommended as alternatives, but renal function, GI history, and cardiovascular status not documented. NSAIDs contraindicated in renal impairment, peptic ulcer disease, and cardiovascular disease. Baseline renal function (creatinine, BUN) should be obtained.

ACETAZOLAMIDE CONDITIONAL RECOMMENDATION: If IIH diagnosed, acetazolamide requires baseline electrolytes (K+, Na+, Cl-, HCO3-), renal function (creatinine, BUN), and acid-base status. Sulfonamide allergy must be ruled out (cross-reactivity risk). Hypokalemia monitoring essential during therapy.

WARFARIN INTERACTION RISK: If CVST diagnosed and warfarin initiated, multiple drug interactions possible. Current medication list essential to identify conflicts with antibiotics, NSAIDs, statins, and other common medications.

SEROTONIN SYNDROME RISK: If patient on SSRI/SNRI for depression/anxiety (not documented), triptan use carries rare but serious serotonin syndrome risk. Medication history must clarify psychiatric medications.

MEDICATION OVERUSE HEADACHE RISK: Treatment plan recommends triptans/NSAIDs for acute migraine, but no baseline frequency of analgesic use documented. If patient already using >10 days/month, medication overuse headache likely; requires medication withdrawal strategy, not escalation.

LUMBAR PUNCTURE SAFETY: If meningitis suspected and LP performed, opening pressure measurement critical for IIH assessment. However, LP contraindicated if papilledema present (risk of herniation). Fundoscopy MUST be performed before LP.

IMAGING CONTRAST ALLERGY: MRI with gadolinium contrast recommended, but contrast allergy history not documented. Iodinated contrast for CT also carries allergy risk. Allergy history essential before imaging.
RENAL FUNCTION BASELINE MISSING: Multiple medications (acetazolamide, NSAIDs, triptans, warfarin) require renal function assessment. Baseline creatinine and BUN should be obtained.
HEPATIC FUNCTION BASELINE MISSING: Acetaminophen, warfarin, and other medications require hepatic function assessment. Baseline LFTs should be obtained.
moderate_issues: BLOOD PRESSURE NOT DOCUMENTED: Vital signs mentioned as 'presumed normal' but not explicitly obtained. BP critical for triptan safety assessment (contraindicated if SBP >180 or DBP >110). Must obtain before abortive therapy.
TEMPERATURE NOT DOCUMENTED: Fever is key red flag for meningitis (LR+ 8.0). Temperature must be obtained to assess meningitis probability.
FUNDOSCOPIC EXAMINATION NOT YET PERFORMED: Essential to assess for papilledema (IIH, mass effect, increased ICP). Must be performed before LP and before diagnosing primary migraine.
MENINGEAL SIGNS NOT YET ASSESSED: Kernig sign and Brudzinski sign not documented. Critical for meningitis screening. Must be assessed during neurological exam.

MEDICATION OVERUSE HEADACHE NOT ASSESSED: Treatment plan recommends triptans/NSAIDs, but no baseline analgesic use frequency documented. If patient already using analgesics >10 days/month, medication overuse headache is likely diagnosis; requires different management approach (medication withdrawal, not escalation).
MIGRAINE AURA STATUS UNKNOWN: If patient has migraine with aura and uses OCPs, stroke risk significantly increased. Aura status must be clarified before OCP continuation or triptan use.

TEMPORAL ARTERY EXAMINATION NOT DOCUMENTED: While temporal arteritis unlikely at age 35, temporal artery tenderness should be assessed given unilateral right-sided headache. Examination not yet performed.
OBESITY STATUS NOT DOCUMENTED: IIH risk factor. BMI should be assessed to stratify IIH probability.
HYPERCOAGULABLE STATE NOT ASSESSED: CVST risk factor. History of thrombosis, family history of thrombophilia, or known hypercoagulable state should be obtained.
RECENT TRAUMA HISTORY NOT DOCUMENTED: Arterial dissection risk factor. Must clarify if any recent head/neck trauma.
IMMUNOCOMPROMISED STATUS NOT DOCUMENTED: Affects meningitis risk and treatment approach. Must clarify if immunocompromised.
TRIPTAN DOSING FREQUENCY LIMIT: Treatment plan recommends sumatriptan but does not emphasize medication overuse headache risk (>10 days/month). Patient education essential on frequency limits.
NSAID DOSING FREQUENCY LIMIT: Naproxen and ibuprofen recommended but frequency limits not emphasized. Risk of medication overuse headache and GI toxicity with chronic use.
ACETAZOLAMIDE ELECTROLYTE MONITORING: If IIH diagnosed and acetazolamide initiated, hypokalemia is common side effect. Potassium supplementation may be needed. Baseline K+ essential.
WARFARIN DIETARY COUNSELING: If CVST diagnosed and warfarin initiated, patient must maintain consistent vitamin K intake and avoid NSAIDs. Counseling not yet documented.

ANTICOAGULATION BLEEDING RISK: If CVST diagnosed and anticoagulation initiated, patient must be counseled on bleeding precautions and signs of bleeding (hematuria, melena, severe headache, vision changes).
SEIZURE PRECAUTIONS NOT MENTIONED: If CVST or meningitis suspected, seizure risk present (40% in CVST, variable in meningitis). Seizure precautions should be implemented.
IMAGING TIMING: MRI recommended as urgent (within 24 hours), but no specific timeline documented. If meningitis suspected with fever, imaging should not delay antibiotics.
LUMBAR PUNCTURE TIMING: If meningitis suspected, LP should be performed urgently (after blood cultures, concurrent with antibiotics). Timing not specified in treatment plan.
FOLLOW-UP IMAGING: If IIH diagnosed, repeat MRI with MRV at 3-6 months recommended to assess for venous sinus thrombosis resolution. Not mentioned in treatment plan.
PREVENTIVE THERAPY TIMING: If primary migraine confirmed, preventive therapy should be considered given chronic daily headache pattern (≥4 days/month). Timing and agent selection not specified.
low_issues: SUMATRIPTAN FORMULATION SELECTION: Multiple formulations available (oral, subcutaneous, intranasal). Intranasal preferred if nausea prominent, but patient preference and access should guide selection.

ALTERNATIVE TRIPTAN OPTIONS: Rizatriptan and zolmitriptan mentioned as alternatives with potential advantages (faster onset, nasal spray availability). Patient-specific factors should guide selection.

NSAID SELECTION: Both naproxen and ibuprofen recommended. Naproxen has longer half-life (better for migraine duration), but ibuprofen more commonly available OTC. Patient preference and access should guide selection.
ACETAZOLAMIDE FORMULATION: Both immediate-release (250 mg BID) and extended-release (500 mg daily) available. Extended-release may improve adherence but immediate-release allows dose titration.

WARFARIN MONITORING FREQUENCY: INR monitoring schedule specified (baseline, day 3, day 5, then weekly until stable, then monthly). Frequency appropriate but patient must understand importance of adherence.
HEPARIN MONITORING: aPTT monitoring specified for UFH, anti-Xa for LMWH. Frequency appropriate but patient must understand importance of adherence.
PATIENT EDUCATION: No mention of patient education on migraine triggers, medication side effects, warning signs requiring emergency evaluation, or lifestyle modifications.

PREVENTIVE THERAPY OPTIONS: If primary migraine confirmed, first-line preventive agents listed (topiramate, propranolol, amitriptyline, valproic acid) but no guidance on selection based on comorbidities or patient factors.

TOPIRAMATE INTERACTION WITH OCPs: If topiramate used for migraine prevention and patient on OCPs, reduced OCP efficacy possible. Counseling on breakthrough bleeding and alternative contraception needed.
PROPRANOLOL CONTRAINDICATIONS: If propranolol used for migraine prevention, contraindicated in asthma/COPD and caution in diabetes (masks hypoglycemia symptoms). Not yet assessed.
AMITRIPTYLINE SIDE EFFECTS: If amitriptyline used for migraine prevention, anticholinergic side effects common (dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation). Patient counseling needed.
VALPROIC ACID TERATOGENICITY: If valproic acid used for migraine prevention, highly teratogenic (Category X). Pregnancy status and contraception counseling essential.
FOLLOW-UP APPOINTMENT: No follow-up timeline specified for reassessment of imaging results, medication efficacy, or side effect tolerance.
SPECIALIST FOLLOW-UP: Neurology consultation recommended but no timeline specified. Should be scheduled within 1-2 weeks of imaging results.

sumatriptan_subcutaneous.notes: Dosing within standard range. Faster onset than oral formulation.

sumatriptan_intranasal.recommended_dose: 20 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 2 hours if needed (max 40 mg/day)
sumatriptan_intranasal.notes: Dosing within standard range. Preferred if nausea prominent.

naproxen_sodium.recommended_dose: 550 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 8-12 hours (max 1100 mg/day)
naproxen_sodium.notes: Dosing within standard range. Frequency limit appropriate to prevent medication overuse headache and GI toxicity.

ibuprofen.notes: Dosing within standard range. Frequency limit appropriate.

empathy.patient_summary: You've been having a throbbing headache on the right side of your head for 2 weeks now, with pain around 6 out of 10. You're also sensitive to light and feeling a bit nauseous. This combination of symptoms needs to be checked out carefully because while it could be a migraine (a common type of headache), we need to rule out some other conditions that can cause similar symptoms. The good news is that your vital signs are stable, which is reassuring. We're going to do some imaging (a special scan of your brain) and a thorough exam to figure out exactly what's going on so we can get you the right treatment.
empathy.what_this_means: Your headache pattern—throbbing, one-sided, with light sensitivity and nausea—matches what doctors see with migraines, which are very common and very treatable. However, because your headache has lasted 2 weeks (longer than a typical migraine), we need to make sure it's not something else. There are several other conditions that can cause similar symptoms, like increased pressure in your brain, blood clots, or inflammation. None of these are emergencies right now based on what we know, but they do need to be identified so you get the right care. Think of it like this: your symptoms are like a puzzle, and we need to see the whole picture before we can solve it.

right_now: **Get a brain scan (MRI or CT)** — This is the most important next step. It will show us what's causing your headache. This should happen within the next 24 hours.

**Have a complete neurological exam** — Your doctor will check your eyes, reflexes, strength, and sensation to look for any other signs. They'll also check for neck stiffness and look at the back of your eyes.
**Tell your doctor about all your medications** — This is critical. Include birth control pills, pain relievers, vitamins, supplements, and anything else you take regularly.

**Share your full medical history** — Let your doctor know if you've ever had blood clots, if you're pregnant or could be pregnant, if you have any allergies (especially to sulfa drugs), and if you have any family history of stroke or aneurysm.
this_week: **Follow up on your imaging results** — Once your scan is done, your doctor will review it with you. This usually happens within 24-48 hours.
**See a neurologist (brain specialist)** — Your primary doctor will refer you. This should be scheduled within 1-2 weeks.
**Get baseline blood work** — Your doctor may want to check your kidney function, electrolytes, and blood counts to make sure it's safe to start any new medications.
**Keep a headache diary** — Write down when your headaches happen, how long they last, what makes them better or worse, and any other symptoms. This helps your doctor understand your pattern.
ongoing: **Avoid your headache triggers** — Common triggers include skipped meals, caffeine, alcohol, stress, poor sleep, and bright lights. Once you identify yours, try to avoid them.
**Stay hydrated** — Drink plenty of water throughout the day. Dehydration is a common migraine trigger.
**Maintain a regular sleep schedule** — Aim for 7-9 hours of sleep each night. Irregular sleep can trigger migraines.
**Manage stress** — Try relaxation techniques like deep breathing, meditation, yoga, or whatever works for you.

**Take medications exactly as prescribed** — If your doctor prescribes something for acute headaches or prevention, follow the instructions carefully. Don't use pain relievers more than 10 days per month (this can actually make headaches worse).
**Attend all follow-up appointments** — Regular check-ins help your doctor track how you're doing and adjust treatment if needed.

sumatriptan_triptan.what_it_does: This medication narrows blood vessels and reduces brain inflammation to stop a migraine in progress. It works best if you take it as soon as the headache starts.
sumatriptan_triptan.how_to_take_it: Take 50-100 mg by mouth when your headache begins. You can take another dose 2 hours later if needed, but don't take more than 200 mg in one day.
sumatriptan_triptan.when_it_works: You should feel better within 30-60 minutes.
sumatriptan_triptan.side_effects: You might feel tingling in your fingers or toes, dizziness, flushing (warmth in your face), or chest tightness. Most of these are mild and go away quickly.
sumatriptan_triptan.important: Don't use this more than 10 days per month, or it can backfire and cause more headaches. Tell your doctor if you have high blood pressure, heart disease, or if you're pregnant.

naproxen_or_ibuprofen_nsaid.what_it_does: These are over-the-counter pain relievers that reduce inflammation and pain.
naproxen_or_ibuprofen_nsaid.how_to_take_it: Naproxen: 550 mg at the start of your headache, then 550 mg every 8-12 hours if needed (max 1100 mg/day). Ibuprofen: 400-600 mg every 4-6 hours (max 1200-1800 mg/day).
naproxen_or_ibuprofen_nsaid.side_effects: Stomach upset, heartburn, or nausea are most common.
naproxen_or_ibuprofen_nsaid.important: Don't use more than 10 days per month. Avoid if you have stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or heart disease. Don't take with blood thinners.

for_prevention.note: If you're having headaches 4 or more days per month, your doctor may recommend a daily preventive medication to reduce how often and how severe your headaches are.
for_prevention.common_options: Your doctor might suggest topiramate, propranolol, amitriptyline, or valproic acid. Each works differently and has different side effects, so your doctor will choose based on your specific situation.

acetazolamide.what_it_does: This medication reduces the fluid pressure inside your brain by decreasing the amount of fluid your brain makes.
acetazolamide.how_to_take_it: Usually 250-500 mg twice a day by mouth. Your doctor may adjust the dose.
acetazolamide.when_it_works: 1-2 weeks to start working; full effect in 4-8 weeks.
acetazolamide.side_effects: Tingling in your fingers, toes, or lips is very common but usually harmless. You might also feel thirsty, need to urinate more, or have a funny taste in your mouth.
acetazolamide.important: You'll need regular blood tests to check your potassium and kidney function. Tell your doctor if you're allergic to sulfa drugs. Don't use if you're pregnant.
acetazolamide.monitoring: Blood work at baseline, 1-2 weeks, then monthly for the first 3 months, then every 3-6 months.

anticoagulation_blood_thinners.what_it_does: These medications prevent blood clots from growing and reduce the risk of stroke.
anticoagulation_blood_thinners.initial_phase: You'll start with injectable heparin (given in the hospital) for 5-7 days.
anticoagulation_blood_thinners.maintenance_phase: Then you'll switch to warfarin (a pill) to take at home for at least 3-6 months.
anticoagulation_blood_thinners.how_to_take_warfarin: Take exactly as prescribed. Dose varies by person based on blood tests (INR).
anticoagulation_blood_thinners.side_effects: Bleeding is the main risk. You might have nosebleeds, bruising, or blood in urine.
anticoagulation_blood_thinners.important: You'll need regular blood tests (INR checks) to make sure the dose is right. Tell your doctor about all medications and supplements. Avoid NSAIDs and excess alcohol. Maintain consistent vitamin K intake (don't suddenly eat lots of leafy greens or avoid them).
anticoagulation_blood_thinners.monitoring: Blood tests at baseline, day 3, day 5, then weekly until stable, then monthly.

antibiotics.what_it_does: These kill bacteria that cause meningitis (brain inflammation from infection).
antibiotics.how_given: Through an IV in the hospital.
antibiotics.timeline: Started immediately if infection suspected—don't wait for test results.

lifestyle_tips.manage_light_sensitivity: Wear sunglasses outdoors. Use blue-light blocking glasses if you spend time on screens. Dim the lights at home. Avoid fluorescent lighting if possible.
lifestyle_tips.reduce_nausea: Eat small, frequent meals. Stay hydrated. Avoid strong smells. Rest in a quiet, cool room during headaches.
lifestyle_tips.sleep_well: Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, even on weekends. Aim for 7-9 hours. Avoid screens 1 hour before bed.
lifestyle_tips.manage_stress: Try deep breathing: breathe in slowly for 4 counts, hold for 4, breathe out for 4. Do this 5-10 times when you feel stressed. Yoga, meditation, or gentle exercise can help. Spend time doing things you enjoy.
lifestyle_tips.stay_hydrated: Drink water throughout the day. A good rule: drink enough so your urine is pale yellow. Avoid excessive caffeine and alcohol, which can trigger headaches.
lifestyle_tips.identify_triggers: Keep a headache diary. Write down what you ate, what you did, how much you slept, and your stress level before each headache. Look for patterns.
lifestyle_tips.be_active: Regular gentle exercise like walking, swimming, or yoga can help prevent migraines. Avoid intense exercise during a headache.
lifestyle_tips.eat_regularly: Don't skip meals. Eat balanced meals with protein, healthy fats, and carbohydrates. Low blood sugar can trigger headaches.
lifestyle_tips.limit_medication_use: Don't use pain relievers more than 10 days per month. Overuse actually causes more headaches. Talk to your doctor about prevention if you need pain relief frequently.
lifestyle_tips.create_a_comfortable_environment: During a headache, rest in a cool, dark, quiet room. Use a cold compress on your forehead or neck. Avoid strong smells and loud noises.

seek_emergency_care_immediately: **Sudden, severe 'thunderclap' headache** — The worst headache of your life that comes on suddenly. This could indicate bleeding in the brain.
**Fever over 101°F (38.3°C) with headache and stiff neck** — This combination suggests meningitis (brain infection), which is a medical emergency.
**Confusion, difficulty speaking, or difficulty understanding** — These suggest a serious problem that needs immediate evaluation.
**Weakness or numbness on one side of your body** — This could indicate a stroke.
**Vision loss or double vision** — Especially if sudden or severe.
**Severe dizziness or loss of balance** — Especially if new or worsening.
**Seizures (convulsions)** — Uncontrolled shaking or loss of consciousness.
**Severe vomiting** — Especially if you can't keep anything down.
**Headache after a head injury** — Even if the injury seemed minor.
**Headache with high fever and rash** — Especially a rash that doesn't blanch (turn white) when you press on it.
call_your_doctor_same_day: **Headache is getting worse despite treatment** — Especially if it's progressively worsening over hours.
**New symptoms develop** — Such as vision changes, weakness, numbness, or difficulty speaking.
**You develop a fever** — Even without neck stiffness.
**Medication side effects are severe** — Such as severe tingling, chest pain, or severe dizziness.
**You're having headaches more than 4 days per week** — This suggests you may need preventive medication.
**Your headache pattern changes significantly** — If it's different from your usual headaches in location, severity, or associated symptoms.
schedule_appointment_this_week: **To discuss imaging results** — Once your brain scan is done.

anticipated_faqs.why_do_i_need_a_brain_scan_if_it_might_j: Great question. While migraines are common and usually not serious, your symptoms have lasted 2 weeks, which is longer than typical migraines. We need to make sure there's nothing else going on—like increased pressure in your brain, a blood clot, or inflammation—that needs different treatment. Think of the scan as a safety check. It's much better to rule out serious causes than to miss something important.
anticipated_faqs.what_is_the_difference_between_a_migrain: A migraine is a specific type of headache caused by changes in blood vessels and brain chemistry. It's usually throbbing, one-sided, and often comes with sensitivity to light, sound, or nausea. A regular tension headache is usually a steady pressure feeling, often on both sides, and doesn't usually have those extra symptoms. Migraines tend to be more intense and disabling.
anticipated_faqs.how_long_will_it_take_to_feel_better: That depends on what's causing your headache. If it's a migraine, some people feel better within hours of taking medication. If it's something else, treatment time varies. Your doctor will give you a better timeline once they know what's going on. Be patient—healing takes time.
anticipated_faqs.will_i_need_to_take_medication_forever: Not necessarily. If it's a migraine, some people need medication only when they have a headache. Others benefit from taking a daily preventive medication. If it's something else, the duration of treatment depends on the cause. Your doctor will discuss the best long-term plan for you.
anticipated_faqs.can_i_still_work_and_do_my_normal_activi: During a headache, you may need to rest. But once you're treated and your headaches improve, most people return to normal activities. If you're having frequent headaches, talk to your doctor about options to reduce how often they happen. Many people with migraines work full-time and live normal lives.
anticipated_faqs.is_this_headache_serious: Based on what we know so far, you're not in immediate danger—your vital signs are stable and you don't have the most alarming symptoms. However, we do need to figure out what's causing it so we can treat it properly. That's why the brain scan is important. Most causes of persistent headaches are manageable.
anticipated_faqs.could_this_be_a_brain_tumor: It's unlikely, but it's one of the things we're checking for with the brain scan. Brain tumors are relatively rare, and your symptoms don't perfectly match what we typically see with tumors. But the scan will give us a definitive answer.
anticipated_faqs.could_this_be_meningitis: Meningitis usually comes with fever and a stiff neck, which you don't have right now. However, we'll check for this during your exam. If you develop a fever, especially with a stiff neck, that would be a reason to go to the emergency room immediately.
anticipated_faqs.what_if_the_brain_scan_is_normal: That's actually good news. It means there's no tumor, bleeding, or other structural problem. If the scan is normal, your doctor will likely diagnose you with a primary headache disorder like migraine and focus on treating and preventing your headaches.
anticipated_faqs.why_do_i_need_blood_work: Blood work helps your doctor make sure it's safe to start certain medications and gives a baseline to compare against if needed. It also helps rule out other causes of headache like thyroid problems or infections.
anticipated_faqs.can_i_take_over_the_counter_pain_relieve: Yes, you can take ibuprofen or naproxen as directed on the package. However, don't use pain relievers more than 10 days per month, as overuse can actually cause more headaches. If you need pain relief more often than that, tell your doctor.
anticipated_faqs.what_should_i_avoid_while_i_have_this_he: Avoid bright lights, loud noises, strong smells, and strenuous exercise. Try to rest in a cool, dark, quiet room. Avoid skipping meals and stay hydrated. Limit caffeine and alcohol.
anticipated_faqs.is_this_related_to_stress: Stress is a common migraine trigger, but it's usually not the only cause. Your doctor will help you understand what's triggering your headaches.
anticipated_faqs.could_this_be_related_to_my_birth_contro: Birth control pills can sometimes trigger or worsen migraines, especially if you have aura (visual symptoms before the headache). Tell your doctor if you're on birth control so they can assess this.
anticipated_faqs.will_my_headache_go_away_on_its_own: Some headaches do improve on their own, but a 2-week headache needs evaluation. Once we know what's causing it, we can treat it properly rather than just waiting and hoping it goes away.
anticipated_faqs.what_does_photophobia_mean: Photophobia is sensitivity to light. It means bright light bothers your eyes and makes your headache worse. It's common with migraines. During a headache, dim the lights or wear sunglasses.

specialist.reason_for_consultation: 35-year-old female with 2-week persistent right-sided throbbing headache (6/10), photophobia, and nausea. Requires specialist evaluation to differentiate primary headache disorder (migraine) from secondary causes given atypical duration and change in pattern.
specialist.specialist_assessment: This patient presents with a clinical picture highly suggestive of migraine based on ICHD-3 criteria: unilateral right-sided location, throbbing/pulsatile quality, moderate severity (6/10), photophobia, and nausea. However, the 2-week persistent continuous duration is ATYPICAL for episodic migraine and raises significant concern for alternative diagnoses. The combination of demographics (reproductive-age female), symptom profile (photophobia, nausea), and duration creates a differential that includes both primary and secondary headache disorders. Critical must-not-miss diagnoses in this demographic include: (1) Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH)—incidence 5-19 per 100,000 in reproductive-age females, presenting with persistent headache, photophobia, nausea, and risk of permanent vision loss; (2) Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis (CVST)—particularly if OCP use present, with subacute presentation and similar symptomatology; (3) Intracranial mass or structural lesion—progressive unilateral headache warrants exclusion; (4) Meningitis—photophobia is highly specific (LR+ 3.5), though absence of fever and meningeal signs argues against; (5) Temporal arteritis—unlikely at age 35 but must consider if systemic symptoms develop. The normal vital signs and absence of focal neurological deficits on initial assessment are reassuring but do not exclude secondary pathology. Status migrainosus (continuous migraine >72 hours) or medication overuse headache should also be considered pending medication history. Comprehensive neurological examination is essential before imaging to assess for papilledema (IIH), meningeal signs (meningitis), focal deficits (mass/CVST), and temporal artery tenderness (temporal arteritis).

specialist.risk_stratification: INTERMEDIATE-TO-HIGH RISK for secondary headache disorder. While migraine is most likely diagnosis (60-70% probability), the 2-week persistent duration, change in pattern, and reproductive-age female demographics create substantial risk for serious secondary causes. IIH risk is elevated (5-19 per 100,000 in this demographic) with potential for permanent vision loss if untreated. CVST risk is present if OCP use confirmed (RR 5-20). Intracranial mass, meningitis, and arterial dissection must be excluded. Risk of missing a secondary cause outweighs risk of unnecessary imaging. specialty_specific_tests: FIRST-LINE IMAGING (MANDATORY): MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast + MR angiography (MRA) of intracranial vessels. Rationale: Superior soft tissue resolution for detecting mass, hemorrhage, hydrocephalus, white matter abnormalities, and venous pathology. MRA assesses for arterial dissection and aneurysm. If MRI contraindicated: CT head without contrast + CTA head and neck.

SECOND-LINE IMAGING (if MRI abnormal or high clinical suspicion): MR venography (MRV) of dural venous sinuses to assess for CVST. Perform if MRA already done or if clinical suspicion for CVST high (OCP use, hypercoagulable state).

FUNDOSCOPIC EXAMINATION (URGENT): Assess for papilledema (suggests IIH, mass effect, or increased ICP). Perform BEFORE lumbar puncture if IIH suspected. Document optic disc appearance, spontaneous venous pulsations, cup-to-disc ratio.

COMPREHENSIVE NEUROLOGICAL EXAMINATION: Cranial nerves II-XII (CN palsies, visual field defects, pupil reactivity), motor testing (focal weakness), sensory testing (focal deficits), meningeal signs (Kernig sign, Brudzinski sign, neck stiffness), gait and coordination (cerebellar signs), reflexes (hyperreflexia suggesting increased ICP).

LUMBAR PUNCTURE WITH OPENING PRESSURE (CONDITIONAL): Indicated if: (1) MRI normal but high clinical suspicion for IIH (measure opening pressure; normal <25 cm H2O), (2) Meningitis suspected (fever develops or meningeal signs present), (3) Imaging shows venous sinus thrombosis (assess for CSF abnormalities). Obtain: opening pressure, cell count/differential, protein, glucose, Gram stain, cultures, xanthochromia assessment.

LABORATORY STUDIES (CONDITIONAL): ESR and CRP if temporal arteritis suspected (age >50 or systemic symptoms); CBC if infection suspected; CMP for baseline renal function; blood cultures if fever present. NOT routinely indicated without fever or systemic signs.
VISUAL FIELD TESTING (FORMAL PERIMETRY): If papilledema present or IIH suspected. Assess for peripheral visual field defects (early sign of IIH-related optic nerve damage).
TEMPORAL ARTERY ULTRASOUND (CONDITIONAL): Only if temporal arteritis suspected (age >50, systemic symptoms, elevated ESR/CRP). Not indicated in 35-year-old without systemic symptoms.

MEDICATION/SUBSTANCE HISTORY: Detailed history of analgesic use (NSAIDs, acetaminophen, opioids), triptan use, ergotamine use, oral contraceptive use (OCP increases CVST and migraine risk), other medications. Assess for medication overuse headache (>10 days/month analgesic use).

MIGRAINE HISTORY DOCUMENTATION: Frequency of headaches (episodic vs. chronic daily), typical duration of attacks, triggers (hormonal, dietary, environmental, stress), associated symptoms (aura, prodrome), prior similar episodes, family history of migraine, impact on function, prior treatments and response.
specialist_red_flags: THUNDERCLAP ONSET (sudden, worst headache of life): Suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage. Requires emergent non-contrast CT head and neurosurgery consultation. NOT present in this case (gradual 2-week onset), but ask specifically about initial onset pattern.

PROGRESSIVE WORSENING OVER DAYS-WEEKS: Suggests intracranial mass, IIH, CVST, or other secondary cause. Patient reports 2-week duration; clarify if stable, improving, or worsening. Progressive pattern increases imaging urgency.

FOCAL NEUROLOGICAL DEFICITS: Weakness, numbness, speech changes, vision loss, ataxia, or cranial nerve palsies suggest structural lesion, CVST, arterial dissection, or mass. Perform detailed motor/sensory/cranial nerve exam. If deficits present, consider emergent imaging and neurosurgery consultation.

PAPILLEDEMA ON FUNDOSCOPY: Indicates increased intracranial pressure from mass, hydrocephalus, IIH, or venous sinus thrombosis. Requires urgent MRI with MRV and lumbar puncture with opening pressure. Risk of permanent vision loss if untreated.

MENINGEAL SIGNS (NECK STIFFNESS, KERNIG SIGN, BRUDZINSKI SIGN): Suggests meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage. If present with fever, obtain blood cultures and empiric antibiotics BEFORE imaging. Perform lumbar puncture urgently.
FEVER: Significantly increases probability of meningitis (LR+ 8.0). If fever develops, obtain blood cultures, empiric antibiotics, and lumbar puncture. Do NOT delay antibiotics for imaging.
ALTERED MENTAL STATUS OR CONFUSION: Suggests meningitis, encephalitis, CVST, or mass effect. Requires emergent evaluation and imaging.
SEIZURES: Suggests CVST, mass, or encephalitis. Requires emergent imaging and EEG. Start seizure precautions.

VISION CHANGES OR VISUAL FIELD DEFECTS: Suggests IIH (visual obscurations, peripheral field loss), mass effect (homonymous hemianopia), arterial dissection (monocular vision loss), or temporal arteritis (amaurosis fugax, vision loss). Requires urgent formal visual field testing and imaging.
PULSATILE TINNITUS: Suggests IIH or venous sinus thrombosis. Increases urgency of MRV.
UNILATERAL NECK PAIN WITH HEADACHE AND FOCAL DEFICITS: Suggests arterial dissection (carotid or vertebral). Requires urgent CTA or conventional angiography.
SYSTEMIC SYMPTOMS (FEVER, WEIGHT LOSS, MALAISE, JOINT PAIN): Suggests infection, vasculitis, temporal arteritis, or systemic disease. Obtain ESR, CRP, and consider rheumatology consultation.
TEMPORAL ARTERY TENDERNESS OR JAW CLAUDICATION: Suggests temporal arteritis. Obtain ESR/CRP and temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy. Requires urgent treatment to prevent blindness.
HEADACHE WORSE WITH VALSALVA, COUGHING, OR STRAINING: Suggests increased intracranial pressure from mass, hydrocephalus, or IIH. Increases imaging urgency.
HEADACHE WORSE WHEN LYING DOWN: Suggests intracranial mass or increased ICP. Increases imaging urgency.
RECENT TRAUMA (EVEN MINOR): Suggests arterial dissection, subdural hematoma, or traumatic SAH. Obtain CT head and CTA.
IMMUNOCOMPROMISED STATE: Increases risk of opportunistic infections (toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, TB meningitis). Obtain appropriate infectious workup.
PREGNANCY OR RECENT POSTPARTUM: Dramatically increases CVST risk (RR 5-60). Obtain MRV urgently. Avoid certain medications (triptans, NSAIDs).
ORAL CONTRACEPTIVE USE: Increases CVST risk (RR 5-20) and may worsen migraine, especially if aura present (stroke risk). Clarify OCP use and presence of aura.
KNOWN HYPERCOAGULABLE STATE OR THROMBOPHILIA: Increases CVST risk. Obtain MRV and consider anticoagulation if CVST confirmed.
FAMILY HISTORY OF ANEURYSM OR SAH: Increases risk of intracranial aneurysm. Consider CTA or conventional angiography.
ATYPICAL MIGRAINE FEATURES (AURA, PROLONGED AURA, HEMIPLEGIC FEATURES)**: Migraine with aura increases stroke risk, especially with OCP use. Clarify aura characteristics.
MEDICATION OVERUSE (>10 DAYS/MONTH ANALGESICS, TRIPTANS, ERGOTAMINES)**: Causes medication overuse headache and rebound headache. Requires medication withdrawal and preventive therapy.
FIRST MIGRAINE ATTACK AFTER AGE 50**: Suggests secondary cause. Not applicable here (age 35), but important for future reference.
specialist.prognosis_notes: If primary migraine confirmed (most likely scenario, 60-70% probability): Expected course is episodic or chronic daily headache with variable frequency and severity. Prognosis is generally favorable with appropriate preventive and abortive therapy. Factors improving prognosis: early diagnosis, medication adherence, trigger identification, lifestyle modifications. Factors worsening prognosis: medication overuse, comorbid depression/anxiety, high headache frequency (>4 days/month), poor medication response. Chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month) affects 2-3% of migraineurs and carries higher disability burden. Timeline: Migraine typically improves with age after age 50, but may persist into older adulthood. If IIH confirmed (15-25% probability): Prognosis depends on early diagnosis and treatment. Untreated IIH carries risk of permanent vision loss (20-30% of untreated patients develop visual impairment). With appropriate treatment (weight loss, diuretics, acetazolamide, topiramate), most patients improve. Lumbar puncture with CSF drainage provides temporary relief. Bariatric surgery may be curative in obese patients. Timeline: IIH can persist for years; requires long-term monitoring. If CVST confirmed (8-15% probability): Prognosis depends on extent of thrombosis and presence of infarction. Mortality 5-10% with treatment, higher without. Morbidity includes stroke (30-40%), seizures (40%), and recurrent thrombosis (2-5%). Anticoagulation is standard treatment despite initial bleeding risk. Most patients recover well with appropriate anticoagulation. Timeline: Acute phase 1-2 weeks; recovery over weeks to months. If intracranial mass confirmed (8-15% probability): Prognosis highly dependent on tumor type, size, location, and grade. Benign tumors (meningioma) have better prognosis than malignant (glioblastoma). Requires neurosurgery consultation and possible resection. Timeline: Varies widely by tumor type. If meningitis confirmed (5-10% probability): Bacterial meningitis mortality 15-25% even with treatment; viral meningitis mortality <1%. Requires emergent antibiotics and supportive care. Timeline: Acute illness 1-2 weeks; recovery over weeks to months. Modifying factors: Age (younger generally better prognosis), comorbidities (diabetes, immunocompromise worsen prognosis), treatment adherence, presence of complications (seizures, stroke, vision loss).
specialist.guideline_concordance: CURRENT MANAGEMENT ASSESSMENT: Patient has appropriately been triaged to ESI-3 (urgent) with recognition of red flags and recommendation for neuroimaging. This aligns with AHS, AAN, and ACR guidelines. GUIDELINE-CONCORDANT RECOMMENDATIONS: (1) MRI brain ± MRA is INDICATED per AHS (2021), AAN (2019), and ACR (2021) guidelines for persistent headache with change in pattern, photophobia, and nausea in reproductive-age female. (2) Comprehensive neurological examination BEFORE imaging is recommended per AHS and AAN guidelines to assess for red flags and guide imaging selection. (3) Lumbar puncture is NOT first-line but should be performed if meningitis suspected (fever + meningeal signs) or imaging negative with high clinical suspicion for IIH or CVST. (4) Laboratory studies (ESR, CRP, CBC, CMP) are NOT routinely indicated without fever or systemic signs, but should be obtained if temporal arteritis or infection suspected. (5) Detailed migraine history and medication history are essential for accurate diagnosis and to assess for medication overuse headache. (6) If primary migraine confirmed, preventive therapy should be considered given chronic daily headache pattern (≥4 days/month). First-line preventive agents per AHS guidelines: topiramate, propranolol, amitriptyline, valproic acid. (7) If IIH suspected, MRI with MRV should be followed by lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement if imaging normal. (8) If CVST suspected, MRV is gold standard diagnostic test; anticoagulation is standard treatment. (9) If temporal arteritis suspected (despite low probability at age 35), ESR/CRP and temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy are indicated; urgent treatment with corticosteroids is necessary to prevent blindness. CURRENT CARE ALIGNMENT: Triage assessment appropriately recognizes need for neuroimaging and specialist consultation. Recommended immediate actions (vital signs, focused neuro exam, IV access, neuroimaging, labs if indicated) align with guideline-concordant care. Recommendation for neurologist consultation is appropriate. GAPS IN CURRENT ASSESSMENT: (1) Medication history not yet obtained (assess for medication overuse headache, OCP use, other medications). (2) Detailed migraine history not documented (frequency, triggers, prior episodes, family history, aura). (3) Fundoscopic examination not yet performed (assess for papilledema). (4) Meningeal signs not yet assessed (Kernig, Brudzinski). (5) Obesity status not documented (relevant for IIH risk). (6) Pregnancy status not documented (relevant for CVST risk). (7) Temporal artery examination not documented (relevant for temporal arteritis, though low probability).

medication.name: Sumatriptan

dosing.oral: 50-100 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 2 hours if needed (max 200 mg/day)
dosing.subcutaneous: 6 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 1 hour if needed (max 12 mg/day)
dosing.intranasal: 20 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 2 hours if needed (max 40 mg/day)

medication.frequency: As needed for acute migraine; not to exceed 10 days/month (risk of medication overuse headache)
medication.duration: Single dose per migraine attack; use for acute episodes only
medication.efficacy: Pain relief in 60-70% of patients at 2 hours; complete pain freedom in 40-50%

contraindications: Coronary artery disease or history of MI
Cerebrovascular disease or history of stroke
Hemiplegic or basilar migraine (risk of stroke)
Concurrent ergot derivatives or other triptans
Pregnancy (Category C - use only if benefits outweigh risks; generally avoid first trimester)
precautions: Use with caution in patients with uncontrolled hypertension
Risk of serotonin syndrome with concurrent SSRIs/SNRIs (rare but serious)
May cause coronary vasospasm in susceptible patients
Medication overuse headache if used >10 days/month
common_side_effects: Chest tightness or pressure (usually benign but concerning)
monitoring: Blood pressure before first dose (if hypertension history)
Cardiac assessment if risk factors present (age >40, hypertension, smoking, family history of CAD)
Frequency of use (monitor for medication overuse headache)
Efficacy and side effect tolerance at follow-up
drug_interactions: SSRIs/SNRIs: Risk of serotonin syndrome (monitor closely; rare but serious)
MAOIs: Absolute contraindication (severe hypertensive crisis risk)
Ergot derivatives: Contraindicated (additive vasoconstrictive effects)
Other triptans: Contraindicated (additive effects)
Lithium: May increase lithium levels (monitor lithium levels)
abortive_therapy.cost_considerations: Generic sumatriptan available; typically $10-30 per dose with insurance; may be expensive without coverage

alternative_abortive_agents.name: Rizatriptan (alternative triptan)
alternative_abortive_agents.dosing: 5-10 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 2 hours (max 30 mg/day)
alternative_abortive_agents.advantage: Faster onset than sumatriptan (30 minutes); may be more effective in some patients
alternative_abortive_agents.note: Similar contraindications and side effects as sumatriptan

alternative_abortive_agents.name: Zolmitriptan (alternative triptan)
alternative_abortive_agents.dosing: 2.5 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 2 hours (max 10 mg/day)
alternative_abortive_agents.advantage: Available in nasal spray formulation; good for patients with nausea/vomiting
alternative_abortive_agents.note: Similar contraindications and side effects as sumatriptan

alternative_abortive_agents.name: Naproxen sodium (NSAID)
alternative_abortive_agents.dosing: 550 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 8-12 hours (max 1100 mg/day)
alternative_abortive_agents.advantage: Over-the-counter availability; lower cost; good for mild-to-moderate migraines
alternative_abortive_agents.disadvantage: Slower onset (60-90 minutes); GI side effects; not effective for severe migraines
alternative_abortive_agents.contraindications: Peptic ulcer disease, GI bleeding, renal impairment, cardiovascular disease, pregnancy (especially third trimester)
alternative_abortive_agents.note: Avoid if frequent use (>10 days/month) due to medication overuse headache and GI toxicity

alternative_abortive_agents.name: Ibuprofen (NSAID)
alternative_abortive_agents.dosing: 400-600 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 4-6 hours (max 1200-1800 mg/day)
alternative_abortive_agents.advantage: Over-the-counter availability; lower cost; good for mild-to-moderate migraines
alternative_abortive_agents.disadvantage: Slower onset (60-90 minutes); GI side effects; less effective than triptans for severe migraines

alternative_abortive_agents.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
alternative_abortive_agents.dosing: 500-1000 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 4-6 hours (max 3000-4000 mg/day)
alternative_abortive_agents.advantage: Over-the-counter availability; well-tolerated; safe in pregnancy
alternative_abortive_agents.disadvantage: Less effective than triptans or NSAIDs; slower onset; risk of hepatotoxicity with chronic use
alternative_abortive_agents.note: Not recommended as monotherapy for moderate-to-severe migraines

condition_idiopathic_intracranial_hypert.rationale: Reduces CSF production and intracranial pressure. Evidence grade A per IIH guidelines. First-line pharmacological treatment for IIH.

medication.name: Acetazolamide
medication.formulation: Immediate-release tablet 250 mg or extended-release capsule 500 mg
medication.dosing: 250-500 mg twice daily (immediate-release) or 500 mg once daily (extended-release); may titrate up to 1000 mg/day in divided doses
medication.duration: Long-term; continue for months to years depending on response and papilledema resolution
medication.onset: 1-2 weeks for ICP reduction; 4-8 weeks for full effect

precautions: Paresthesias (tingling in fingers, toes, lips) are common but usually benign
common_side_effects: Paresthesias (tingling, numbness) - very common, usually benign
monitoring: Baseline electrolytes (K+, Na+, Cl-, HCO3-), renal function (creatinine, BUN), and acid-base status
Repeat electrolytes at 1-2 weeks, then monthly for first 3 months, then every 3-6 months
Renal function at baseline and annually
Formal visual field testing (perimetry) at baseline and 3-6 months to assess for improvement
Fundoscopy at baseline and 3-6 months to assess papilledema resolution
Lumbar puncture with opening pressure at baseline and 3-6 months to confirm ICP reduction
drug_interactions: Potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, amiloride): Increased hyperkalemia risk (avoid combination)
NSAIDs: Reduced diuretic effect; increased renal dysfunction risk
ACE inhibitors: Increased hyperkalemia risk (monitor K+ closely)
Lithium: Increased lithium levels (monitor lithium levels and renal function)
Topiramate: Additive effects on electrolytes and renal function (monitor closely if combined)
condition_idiopathic_intracranial_hypert.cost_considerations: Generic acetazolamide available; typically $20-50/month with insurance

condition_cerebral_venous_sinus_thrombos.rationale: Standard treatment for CVST. Reduces risk of stroke, seizures, and recurrent thrombosis. Evidence grade A per neurology guidelines. Anticoagulation is indicated even if hemorrhagic infarction present.

option_1_unfractionated_heparin.name: Unfractionated heparin (UFH)
option_1_unfractionated_heparin.dosing: Initial bolus 80 units/kg IV, then 18 units/kg/hour continuous infusion; adjust based on aPTT (target aPTT 1.5-2.5x baseline)
option_1_unfractionated_heparin.monitoring: aPTT at baseline, 6 hours, 12 hours, then daily; platelet count at baseline and day 3 (HIT screening)
option_1_unfractionated_heparin.advantage: Short half-life (60-90 minutes); reversible with protamine; preferred in renal failure
option_1_unfractionated_heparin.disadvantage: Requires continuous IV infusion; frequent monitoring needed

option_2_low_molecular_weight_heparin.name: Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) - Enoxaparin
option_2_low_molecular_weight_heparin.dosing: 1 mg/kg SC every 12 hours or 1.5 mg/kg SC once daily
option_2_low_molecular_weight_heparin.monitoring: Anti-Xa level at baseline and 4-6 hours after first dose (target 0.5-1.0 IU/mL for BID dosing or 1.0-2.0 IU/mL for daily dosing); platelet count at baseline and day 3
option_2_low_molecular_weight_heparin.advantage: Subcutaneous administration; more predictable pharmacokinetics; less frequent monitoring
option_2_low_molecular_weight_heparin.disadvantage: Longer half-life; contraindicated in severe renal failure (CrCl <30 mL/min)

transition_to_warfarin.timeline: After 5-7 days of heparin (UFH or LMWH)
transition_to_warfarin.dosing: Initiate 5-10 mg daily; adjust based on INR (target INR 2-3)
transition_to_warfarin.monitoring: INR at baseline, day 3, day 5, then weekly until stable, then monthly
transition_to_warfarin.duration: Minimum 3-6 months; longer if recurrent thrombosis or ongoing risk factors
precautions: Drug interactions with many medications (antibiotics, NSAIDs, statins, etc.)

alternative_anticoagulation.name: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) - Apixaban or Dabigatran
alternative_anticoagulation.note: Emerging evidence supports DOACs as alternative to warfarin for CVST maintenance therapy. May be considered after initial heparin phase.
alternative_anticoagulation.advantage: No INR monitoring required; fewer drug interactions; more convenient
alternative_anticoagulation.disadvantage: Less data than warfarin for CVST; higher cost; not yet standard of care

high_issues: MEDICATION HISTORY MISSING: No current medications documented. Essential to obtain before prescribing abortive or preventive therapy to assess for drug interactions, medication overuse headache, and OCP use (CVST risk factor).
PREGNANCY STATUS UNKNOWN: Not documented. Critical for medication selection (triptans, NSAIDs, acetazolamide are contraindicated or require caution in pregnancy). Must clarify before prescribing.

ALLERGY HISTORY INCOMPLETE: No drug allergies documented. Essential to obtain before prescribing triptans, NSAIDs, acetazolamide, or other medications. Sulfonamide allergy would contraindicate acetazolamide.

TRIPTAN SAFETY SCREENING INCOMPLETE: Sumatriptan is recommended as first-line abortive, but contraindications not yet assessed: uncontrolled hypertension, CAD history, cerebrovascular disease, hemiplegic/basilar migraine, concurrent MAOI use. Blood pressure must be obtained and cardiac risk factors assessed before triptan prescription.

NSAID SAFETY CONCERNS: Naproxen and ibuprofen recommended as alternatives, but renal function, GI history, and cardiovascular status not documented. NSAIDs contraindicated in renal impairment, peptic ulcer disease, and cardiovascular disease. Baseline renal function (creatinine, BUN) should be obtained.

ACETAZOLAMIDE CONDITIONAL RECOMMENDATION: If IIH diagnosed, acetazolamide requires baseline electrolytes (K+, Na+, Cl-, HCO3-), renal function (creatinine, BUN), and acid-base status. Sulfonamide allergy must be ruled out (cross-reactivity risk). Hypokalemia monitoring essential during therapy.

WARFARIN INTERACTION RISK: If CVST diagnosed and warfarin initiated, multiple drug interactions possible. Current medication list essential to identify conflicts with antibiotics, NSAIDs, statins, and other common medications.

SEROTONIN SYNDROME RISK: If patient on SSRI/SNRI for depression/anxiety (not documented), triptan use carries rare but serious serotonin syndrome risk. Medication history must clarify psychiatric medications.

LUMBAR PUNCTURE SAFETY: If meningitis suspected and LP performed, opening pressure measurement critical for IIH assessment. However, LP contraindicated if papilledema present (risk of herniation). Fundoscopy MUST be performed before LP.

IMAGING CONTRAST ALLERGY: MRI with gadolinium contrast recommended, but contrast allergy history not documented. Iodinated contrast for CT also carries allergy risk. Allergy history essential before imaging.

low_issues: SUMATRIPTAN FORMULATION SELECTION: Multiple formulations available (oral, subcutaneous, intranasal). Intranasal preferred if nausea prominent, but patient preference and access should guide selection.

ALTERNATIVE TRIPTAN OPTIONS: Rizatriptan and zolmitriptan mentioned as alternatives with potential advantages (faster onset, nasal spray availability). Patient-specific factors should guide selection.

NSAID SELECTION: Both naproxen and ibuprofen recommended. Naproxen has longer half-life (better for migraine duration), but ibuprofen more commonly available OTC. Patient preference and access should guide selection.
ACETAZOLAMIDE FORMULATION: Both immediate-release (250 mg BID) and extended-release (500 mg daily) available. Extended-release may improve adherence but immediate-release allows dose titration.

sumatriptan_subcutaneous.recommended_dose: 6 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 1 hour if needed (max 12 mg/day)
sumatriptan_subcutaneous.notes: Dosing within standard range. Faster onset than oral formulation.

sumatriptan_intranasal.recommended_dose: 20 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 2 hours if needed (max 40 mg/day)
sumatriptan_intranasal.notes: Dosing within standard range. Preferred if nausea prominent.

naproxen_sodium.recommended_dose: 550 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 8-12 hours (max 1100 mg/day)
naproxen_sodium.notes: Dosing within standard range. Frequency limit appropriate to prevent medication overuse headache and GI toxicity.

ibuprofen.recommended_dose: 400-600 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 4-6 hours (max 1200-1800 mg/day)
ibuprofen.notes: Dosing within standard range. Frequency limit appropriate.

acetaminophen.recommended_dose: 500-1000 mg at headache onset; may repeat after 4-6 hours (max 3000-4000 mg/day)
acetaminophen.notes: Dosing within standard range. Daily maximum 3000-4000 mg appropriate to prevent hepatotoxicity.

acetazolamide_immediate_release.recommended_dose: 250-500 mg twice daily; may titrate up to 1000 mg/day in divided doses

acetazolamide_extended_release.notes: Dosing within standard range. Extended-release formulation may improve adherence.

unfractionated_heparin.recommended_dose: Initial bolus 80 units/kg IV, then 18 units/kg/hour continuous infusion; adjust based on aPTT (target aPTT 1.5-2.5x baseline)
unfractionated_heparin.notes: Dosing within standard range for CVST anticoagulation. Requires aPTT monitoring and dose adjustment.

enoxaparin.recommended_dose: 1 mg/kg SC every 12 hours or 1.5 mg/kg SC once daily
enoxaparin.notes: Dosing within standard range for CVST anticoagulation. Requires anti-Xa monitoring. Contraindicated in severe renal failure (CrCl <30 mL/min).

warfarin.recommended_dose: Initiate 5-10 mg daily; adjust based on INR (target INR 2-3)
warfarin.notes: Dosing within standard range for CVST maintenance anticoagulation. Requires INR monitoring and dose adjustment. Minimum 3-6 months duration recommended.

ceftriaxone.recommended_dose: 2 g IV every 12 hours (or 4 g/day total)
ceftriaxone.notes: Dosing within standard range for meningitis empiric therapy. Excellent CNS penetration.

vancomycin.recommended_dose: 15-20 mg/kg IV every 8-12 hours (target trough 15-20 mcg/mL)
vancomycin.notes: Dosing within standard range for meningitis empiric therapy. Requires therapeutic drug monitoring (trough levels). Added for penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae coverage.

ampicillin.recommended_dose: 2 g IV every 4 hours (12 g/day total)
ampicillin.notes: Dosing within standard range for meningitis empiric therapy. Covers Listeria monocytogenes in certain populations.
