empathy.patient_summary: You've been having a throbbing headache on the right side of your head for 2 weeks now, with pain around 6 out of 10. You're also sensitive to light and feeling a bit nauseous. This combination of symptoms needs to be checked out carefully because while it could be a migraine (a common type of headache), we need to rule out some other conditions that can cause similar symptoms. The good news is that your vital signs are stable, which is reassuring. We're going to do some imaging (a special scan of your brain) and a thorough exam to figure out exactly what's going on so we can get you the right treatment.
empathy.what_this_means: Your headache pattern—throbbing, one-sided, with light sensitivity and nausea—matches what doctors see with migraines, which are very common and very treatable. However, because your headache has lasted 2 weeks (longer than a typical migraine), we need to make sure it's not something else. There are several other conditions that can cause similar symptoms, like increased pressure in your brain, blood clots, or inflammation. None of these are emergencies right now based on what we know, but they do need to be identified so you get the right care. Think of it like this: your symptoms are like a puzzle, and we need to see the whole picture before we can solve it.

right_now: **Get a brain scan (MRI or CT)** — This is the most important next step. It will show us what's causing your headache. This should happen within the next 24 hours.

**Have a complete neurological exam** — Your doctor will check your eyes, reflexes, strength, and sensation to look for any other signs. They'll also check for neck stiffness and look at the back of your eyes.
**Tell your doctor about all your medications** — This is critical. Include birth control pills, pain relievers, vitamins, supplements, and anything else you take regularly.

**Share your full medical history** — Let your doctor know if you've ever had blood clots, if you're pregnant or could be pregnant, if you have any allergies (especially to sulfa drugs), and if you have any family history of stroke or aneurysm.
this_week: **Follow up on your imaging results** — Once your scan is done, your doctor will review it with you. This usually happens within 24-48 hours.
**See a neurologist (brain specialist)** — Your primary doctor will refer you. This should be scheduled within 1-2 weeks.
**Get baseline blood work** — Your doctor may want to check your kidney function, electrolytes, and blood counts to make sure it's safe to start any new medications.
**Keep a headache diary** — Write down when your headaches happen, how long they last, what makes them better or worse, and any other symptoms. This helps your doctor understand your pattern.
ongoing: **Avoid your headache triggers** — Common triggers include skipped meals, caffeine, alcohol, stress, poor sleep, and bright lights. Once you identify yours, try to avoid them.
**Stay hydrated** — Drink plenty of water throughout the day. Dehydration is a common migraine trigger.
**Maintain a regular sleep schedule** — Aim for 7-9 hours of sleep each night. Irregular sleep can trigger migraines.
**Manage stress** — Try relaxation techniques like deep breathing, meditation, yoga, or whatever works for you.

**Take medications exactly as prescribed** — If your doctor prescribes something for acute headaches or prevention, follow the instructions carefully. Don't use pain relievers more than 10 days per month (this can actually make headaches worse).
**Attend all follow-up appointments** — Regular check-ins help your doctor track how you're doing and adjust treatment if needed.

sumatriptan_triptan.what_it_does: This medication narrows blood vessels and reduces brain inflammation to stop a migraine in progress. It works best if you take it as soon as the headache starts.
sumatriptan_triptan.how_to_take_it: Take 50-100 mg by mouth when your headache begins. You can take another dose 2 hours later if needed, but don't take more than 200 mg in one day.
sumatriptan_triptan.when_it_works: You should feel better within 30-60 minutes.
sumatriptan_triptan.side_effects: You might feel tingling in your fingers or toes, dizziness, flushing (warmth in your face), or chest tightness. Most of these are mild and go away quickly.
sumatriptan_triptan.important: Don't use this more than 10 days per month, or it can backfire and cause more headaches. Tell your doctor if you have high blood pressure, heart disease, or if you're pregnant.

naproxen_or_ibuprofen_nsaid.what_it_does: These are over-the-counter pain relievers that reduce inflammation and pain.
naproxen_or_ibuprofen_nsaid.how_to_take_it: Naproxen: 550 mg at the start of your headache, then 550 mg every 8-12 hours if needed (max 1100 mg/day). Ibuprofen: 400-600 mg every 4-6 hours (max 1200-1800 mg/day).
naproxen_or_ibuprofen_nsaid.side_effects: Stomach upset, heartburn, or nausea are most common.
naproxen_or_ibuprofen_nsaid.important: Don't use more than 10 days per month. Avoid if you have stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or heart disease. Don't take with blood thinners.

for_prevention.note: If you're having headaches 4 or more days per month, your doctor may recommend a daily preventive medication to reduce how often and how severe your headaches are.
for_prevention.common_options: Your doctor might suggest topiramate, propranolol, amitriptyline, or valproic acid. Each works differently and has different side effects, so your doctor will choose based on your specific situation.

acetazolamide.what_it_does: This medication reduces the fluid pressure inside your brain by decreasing the amount of fluid your brain makes.
acetazolamide.how_to_take_it: Usually 250-500 mg twice a day by mouth. Your doctor may adjust the dose.
acetazolamide.when_it_works: 1-2 weeks to start working; full effect in 4-8 weeks.
acetazolamide.side_effects: Tingling in your fingers, toes, or lips is very common but usually harmless. You might also feel thirsty, need to urinate more, or have a funny taste in your mouth.
acetazolamide.important: You'll need regular blood tests to check your potassium and kidney function. Tell your doctor if you're allergic to sulfa drugs. Don't use if you're pregnant.
acetazolamide.monitoring: Blood work at baseline, 1-2 weeks, then monthly for the first 3 months, then every 3-6 months.

anticoagulation_blood_thinners.what_it_does: These medications prevent blood clots from growing and reduce the risk of stroke.
anticoagulation_blood_thinners.initial_phase: You'll start with injectable heparin (given in the hospital) for 5-7 days.
anticoagulation_blood_thinners.maintenance_phase: Then you'll switch to warfarin (a pill) to take at home for at least 3-6 months.
anticoagulation_blood_thinners.how_to_take_warfarin: Take exactly as prescribed. Dose varies by person based on blood tests (INR).
anticoagulation_blood_thinners.side_effects: Bleeding is the main risk. You might have nosebleeds, bruising, or blood in urine.
anticoagulation_blood_thinners.important: You'll need regular blood tests (INR checks) to make sure the dose is right. Tell your doctor about all medications and supplements. Avoid NSAIDs and excess alcohol. Maintain consistent vitamin K intake (don't suddenly eat lots of leafy greens or avoid them).
anticoagulation_blood_thinners.monitoring: Blood tests at baseline, day 3, day 5, then weekly until stable, then monthly.

antibiotics.what_it_does: These kill bacteria that cause meningitis (brain inflammation from infection).
antibiotics.how_given: Through an IV in the hospital.
antibiotics.timeline: Started immediately if infection suspected—don't wait for test results.
antibiotics.side_effects: Varies by antibiotic. Tell your doctor about any drug allergies, especially penicillin or cephalosporin allergies.

lifestyle_tips.manage_light_sensitivity: Wear sunglasses outdoors. Use blue-light blocking glasses if you spend time on screens. Dim the lights at home. Avoid fluorescent lighting if possible.
lifestyle_tips.reduce_nausea: Eat small, frequent meals. Stay hydrated. Avoid strong smells. Rest in a quiet, cool room during headaches.
lifestyle_tips.sleep_well: Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, even on weekends. Aim for 7-9 hours. Avoid screens 1 hour before bed.
lifestyle_tips.manage_stress: Try deep breathing: breathe in slowly for 4 counts, hold for 4, breathe out for 4. Do this 5-10 times when you feel stressed. Yoga, meditation, or gentle exercise can help. Spend time doing things you enjoy.
lifestyle_tips.stay_hydrated: Drink water throughout the day. A good rule: drink enough so your urine is pale yellow. Avoid excessive caffeine and alcohol, which can trigger headaches.
lifestyle_tips.identify_triggers: Keep a headache diary. Write down what you ate, what you did, how much you slept, and your stress level before each headache. Look for patterns.
lifestyle_tips.be_active: Regular gentle exercise like walking, swimming, or yoga can help prevent migraines. Avoid intense exercise during a headache.
lifestyle_tips.eat_regularly: Don't skip meals. Eat balanced meals with protein, healthy fats, and carbohydrates. Low blood sugar can trigger headaches.
lifestyle_tips.limit_medication_use: Don't use pain relievers more than 10 days per month. Overuse actually causes more headaches. Talk to your doctor about prevention if you need pain relief frequently.
lifestyle_tips.create_a_comfortable_environment: During a headache, rest in a cool, dark, quiet room. Use a cold compress on your forehead or neck. Avoid strong smells and loud noises.

seek_emergency_care_immediately: **Sudden, severe 'thunderclap' headache** — The worst headache of your life that comes on suddenly. This could indicate bleeding in the brain.
**Fever over 101°F (38.3°C) with headache and stiff neck** — This combination suggests meningitis (brain infection), which is a medical emergency.
**Confusion, difficulty speaking, or difficulty understanding** — These suggest a serious problem that needs immediate evaluation.
**Weakness or numbness on one side of your body** — This could indicate a stroke.
**Vision loss or double vision** — Especially if sudden or severe.
**Severe dizziness or loss of balance** — Especially if new or worsening.
**Seizures (convulsions)** — Uncontrolled shaking or loss of consciousness.
**Severe vomiting** — Especially if you can't keep anything down.
**Headache after a head injury** — Even if the injury seemed minor.
**Headache with high fever and rash** — Especially a rash that doesn't blanch (turn white) when you press on it.
call_your_doctor_same_day: **Headache is getting worse despite treatment** — Especially if it's progressively worsening over hours.
**New symptoms develop** — Such as vision changes, weakness, numbness, or difficulty speaking.
**You develop a fever** — Even without neck stiffness.
**Medication side effects are severe** — Such as severe tingling, chest pain, or severe dizziness.
**You're having headaches more than 4 days per week** — This suggests you may need preventive medication.
**Your headache pattern changes significantly** — If it's different from your usual headaches in location, severity, or associated symptoms.
schedule_appointment_this_week: **To discuss imaging results** — Once your brain scan is done.
**To follow up on blood work** — If your doctor ordered labs.
**To discuss medication options** — If you need to start a new medication.
**If your headache hasn't improved after 1 week of treatment** — You may need a different approach.

empathy.reassurance: I know having a persistent headache for 2 weeks is concerning and uncomfortable. The good news is that you're taking the right step by getting evaluated. Most people with headaches like yours—especially those your age—have migraines, which are very treatable. Even if it turns out to be something else, the conditions we're checking for are manageable when caught early. Your vital signs are stable, which is reassuring. You don't have the most alarming symptoms that would suggest an emergency. With proper diagnosis and treatment, most people with persistent headaches improve significantly. Many people find that once they identify their triggers and start the right medication, their quality of life gets much better. You're not alone in this—millions of people deal with migraines and similar headaches every day and live full, active lives. Be patient with yourself as we figure this out, and don't hesitate to reach out if something feels wrong. You're doing the right thing by seeking care.

anticipated_faqs.why_do_i_need_a_brain_scan_if_it_might_j: Great question. While migraines are common and usually not serious, your symptoms have lasted 2 weeks, which is longer than typical migraines. We need to make sure there's nothing else going on—like increased pressure in your brain, a blood clot, or inflammation—that needs different treatment. Think of the scan as a safety check. It's much better to rule out serious causes than to miss something important.
anticipated_faqs.what_is_the_difference_between_a_migrain: A migraine is a specific type of headache caused by changes in blood vessels and brain chemistry. It's usually throbbing, one-sided, and often comes with sensitivity to light, sound, or nausea. A regular tension headache is usually a steady pressure feeling, often on both sides, and doesn't usually have those extra symptoms. Migraines tend to be more intense and disabling.
anticipated_faqs.how_long_will_it_take_to_feel_better: That depends on what's causing your headache. If it's a migraine, some people feel better within hours of taking medication. If it's something else, treatment time varies. Your doctor will give you a better timeline once they know what's going on. Be patient—healing takes time.
anticipated_faqs.will_i_need_to_take_medication_forever: Not necessarily. If it's a migraine, some people need medication only when they have a headache. Others benefit from taking a daily preventive medication. If it's something else, the duration of treatment depends on the cause. Your doctor will discuss the best long-term plan for you.
anticipated_faqs.can_i_still_work_and_do_my_normal_activi: During a headache, you may need to rest. But once you're treated and your headaches improve, most people return to normal activities. If you're having frequent headaches, talk to your doctor about options to reduce how often they happen. Many people with migraines work full-time and live normal lives.
anticipated_faqs.is_this_headache_serious: Based on what we know so far, you're not in immediate danger—your vital signs are stable and you don't have the most alarming symptoms. However, we do need to figure out what's causing it so we can treat it properly. That's why the brain scan is important. Most causes of persistent headaches are manageable.
anticipated_faqs.could_this_be_a_brain_tumor: It's unlikely, but it's one of the things we're checking for with the brain scan. Brain tumors are relatively rare, and your symptoms don't perfectly match what we typically see with tumors. But the scan will give us a definitive answer.
anticipated_faqs.could_this_be_meningitis: Meningitis usually comes with fever and a stiff neck, which you don't have right now. However, we'll check for this during your exam. If you develop a fever, especially with a stiff neck, that would be a reason to go to the emergency room immediately.
anticipated_faqs.what_if_the_brain_scan_is_normal: That's actually good news. It means there's no tumor, bleeding, or other structural problem. If the scan is normal, your doctor will likely diagnose you with a primary headache disorder like migraine and focus on treating and preventing your headaches.
anticipated_faqs.why_do_i_need_blood_work: Blood work helps your doctor make sure it's safe to start certain medications and gives a baseline to compare against if needed. It also helps rule out other causes of headache like thyroid problems or infections.
anticipated_faqs.can_i_take_over_the_counter_pain_relieve: Yes, you can take ibuprofen or naproxen as directed on the package. However, don't use pain relievers more than 10 days per month, as overuse can actually cause more headaches. If you need pain relief more often than that, tell your doctor.
anticipated_faqs.what_should_i_avoid_while_i_have_this_he: Avoid bright lights, loud noises, strong smells, and strenuous exercise. Try to rest in a cool, dark, quiet room. Avoid skipping meals and stay hydrated. Limit caffeine and alcohol.
anticipated_faqs.is_this_related_to_stress: Stress is a common migraine trigger, but it's usually not the only cause. Your doctor will help you understand what's triggering your headaches.
anticipated_faqs.could_this_be_related_to_my_birth_contro: Birth control pills can sometimes trigger or worsen migraines, especially if you have aura (visual symptoms before the headache). Tell your doctor if you're on birth control so they can assess this.
anticipated_faqs.will_my_headache_go_away_on_its_own: Some headaches do improve on their own, but a 2-week headache needs evaluation. Once we know what's causing it, we can treat it properly rather than just waiting and hoping it goes away.
anticipated_faqs.what_does_photophobia_mean: Photophobia is sensitivity to light. It means bright light bothers your eyes and makes your headache worse. It's common with migraines. During a headache, dim the lights or wear sunglasses.

drug_interactions.note: No current medications reported in case presentation. However, common migraine treatments and potential interactions are listed below for reference if treatment initiated:

triptans.agents: Sumatriptan, rizatriptan, naratriptan, zolmitriptan, frovatriptan, almotriptan, eletriptan
triptans.contraindications: Uncontrolled hypertension, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, hemiplegic migraine
triptans.interactions: Serotonin syndrome risk with SSRIs/SNRIs (rare but serious); avoid concurrent use with ergot derivatives
triptans.management: Baseline BP check; use lowest effective dose; counsel on serotonin syndrome symptoms (agitation, confusion, rapid HR, muscle rigidity)

nsaids.interactions: Increased GI bleeding risk with anticoagulants; reduced efficacy of antihypertensives; renal impairment with ACE inhibitors
nsaids.management: Check renal function; use lowest dose for shortest duration; consider gastroprotection if chronic use

beta_blockers.management: Monitor BP; adjust doses as needed

tricyclic_antidepressants.management: Start low dose; monitor for anticholinergic side effects; avoid concurrent SSRIs if possible

anticonvulsants.management: If topiramate used: counsel on contraceptive failure risk; consider alternative if planning pregnancy. Valproic acid: avoid in women of childbearing age due to teratogenicity

diagnostic_approach.summary: For a 35-year-old female with 2-week persistent right-sided throbbing headache, photophobia, and nausea, neuroimaging (MRI preferred) is RECOMMENDED to exclude secondary causes despite classic migraine features.
diagnostic_approach.rationale: While the patient's symptoms are consistent with migraine (unilateral, throbbing, photophobia, nausea), the 2-week PERSISTENT duration is ATYPICAL for episodic migraine (which typically lasts 4-72 hours per episode). The combination of new/changed headache pattern + photophobia + unilateral presentation meets criteria for imaging per AHS, AAN, and ACR guidelines.
diagnostic_approach.evidence_grade: B (Moderate quality - expert consensus with supporting observational data)

specialist.reason_for_consultation: 35-year-old female with 2-week persistent right-sided throbbing headache (6/10), photophobia, and nausea. Triage identified red flags (persistent duration >2 weeks, new/changed headache pattern, unilateral presentation, photophobia) requiring specialist evaluation to differentiate primary headache disorder (migraine) from secondary causes (meningitis, intracranial pathology, temporal arteritis, cervical artery dissection, idiopathic intracranial hypertension).
specialist.specialist_assessment: This 35-year-old female presents with a clinical syndrome highly suggestive of migraine based on cardinal features: unilateral right-sided location, throbbing (pulsatile) quality, photophobia, and nausea. These symptoms align with ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria for migraine. However, the 2-week CONTINUOUS duration is ATYPICAL and concerning. Episodic migraine typically presents with individual attacks lasting 4-72 hours; this patient's persistent presentation suggests either: (1) Status migrainosus (migraine lasting >72 hours), (2) Chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month), (3) Medication overuse headache (if applicable), or (4) Secondary headache disorder. The combination of new/changed headache pattern + unilateral presentation + photophobia + persistent duration meets criteria for neuroimaging per American Headache Society and American Academy of Neurology guidelines. Age 35 is peak incidence for migraine in women (prevalence 18% in women vs. 6% in men), which increases pretest probability for primary headache. However, must-not-miss secondary causes require exclusion: subarachnoid hemorrhage (photophobia is highly specific, LR+ 3.2, though gradual onset argues against), meningitis (photophobia LR+ 3.5, but absence of fever/neck stiffness argues against), intracranial mass (unilateral headache + photophobia + nausea concerning, but no focal deficits reported), idiopathic intracranial hypertension (excellent epidemiologic fit: 35-year-old female with 20x higher risk in reproductive-age women; photophobia and nausea present, but no visual obscurations or papilledema reported), temporal arteritis (age 35 is strongly protective; LR- 0.05 for age <50), and cervical artery dissection (no neck pain or focal deficits reported). Differential diagnosis ranking: (1) Episodic migraine or status migrainosus (60-70% likelihood), (2) Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (10-15%), (3) Chronic migraine/medication overuse headache (10-15%), (4) Intracranial mass (5-10%), (5) Secondary causes (meningitis, SAH, dissection, temporal arteritis) (<5% combined). Critical next step: Neuroimaging (MRI preferred) to exclude structural/vascular pathology before attributing to primary headache disorder.
diagnostic_criteria_applied: ICHD-3 Migraine Criteria: Patient meets criteria for migraine with the following features: (1) Unilateral location (right-sided) ✓, (2) Throbbing/pulsatile quality ✓, (3) Moderate intensity (6/10) ✓, (4) Associated nausea ✓, (5) Photophobia ✓. HOWEVER: Duration criterion NOT met—episodic migraine requires individual attacks lasting 4-72 hours; this patient has 2-week CONTINUOUS duration, suggesting status migrainosus (migraine >72 hours) or chronic migraine (≥15 days/month) rather than episodic migraine.

American Headache Society Neuroimaging Criteria: Patient meets criteria for neuroimaging: (1) New or changed headache pattern ✓, (2) Unilateral presentation ✓, (3) Photophobia (atypical feature) ✓. Recommendation: MRI head without contrast PREFERRED over CT.

American Academy of Neurology Headache Evaluation Parameters: For subacute/persistent headache (2 weeks), obtain neuroimaging to exclude secondary causes. Consider ESR/CRP if temporal arteritis suspected (age 35 is protective, but screening reasonable given persistent headache). Lumbar puncture NOT routinely indicated (no fever, neck stiffness, or altered mental status).

American College of Radiology Appropriateness Criteria: MRI head without contrast is USUALLY APPROPRIATE for new/changed headache pattern with red flags (photophobia, unilateral, persistent). CT head without contrast USUALLY APPROPRIATE if MRI contraindicated/unavailable.

Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension Diagnostic Criteria (Modified Dandy Criteria): Patient has some features concerning for IIH: (1) Age 35, female (peak incidence 20-40 years, 8:1 female predominance) ✓, (2) Persistent headache ✓, (3) Photophobia ✓, (4) Nausea ✓. HOWEVER: Absence of visual obscurations or papilledema on fundoscopy argues against (highly sensitive features). Obesity status unknown (risk factor). Diagnosis requires elevated opening pressure on LP (>250 mm H2O) with normal CSF composition and normal/small ventricles on imaging.

Meningitis Clinical Suspicion Score: Patient has LOW suspicion for meningitis. Supportive features: headache, photophobia, nausea. Opposing features: NO fever (highly sensitive, LR- 0.3), NO neck stiffness (highly sensitive, LR- 0.1), NO altered mental status, stable vital signs. Pretest probability <1% given clinical presentation.

Subarachnoid Hemorrhage Risk Stratification: Patient has VERY LOW suspicion for SAH. Supportive features: unilateral headache, photophobia (LR+ 3.2). Opposing features: GRADUAL 2-week onset (SAH is thunderclap/hyperacute; LR- 0.15), moderate severity 6/10 (SAH typically 10/10, 'worst headache of life'), NO neck stiffness, NO focal neurological deficits, stable vital signs. Pretest probability <5% given atypical presentation.

Temporal Arteritis Risk Stratification: Patient has VERY LOW suspicion for temporal arteritis. Age 35 is STRONGLY PROTECTIVE (LR- 0.05; temporal arteritis rare <50 years, typical age >60). Opposing features: NO scalp tenderness, NO jaw claudication, NO vision changes, NO systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, malaise). Pretest probability <1%.

Cervical Artery Dissection Risk Stratification: Patient has LOW suspicion for dissection. Opposing features: NO neck pain (highly sensitive, LR- 0.2), NO focal neurological deficits (expected with dissection), NO recent trauma or manipulation, NO Horner syndrome. Pretest probability <2%.
specialist.risk_stratification: INTERMEDIATE RISK. While the patient's symptoms are highly consistent with primary migraine (unilateral, throbbing, photophobia, nausea in a 35-year-old female at peak incidence), the 2-week PERSISTENT duration is ATYPICAL and raises concern for: (1) Status migrainosus or chronic migraine progression, (2) Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (excellent epidemiologic fit for reproductive-age female), (3) Intracranial mass or other structural pathology. Must-not-miss secondary causes (SAH, meningitis, temporal arteritis, dissection) have LOW pretest probability based on clinical presentation but CANNOT be excluded without neuroimaging. Risk stratification: LOW risk for immediately life-threatening condition (no thunderclap onset, no fever/meningeal signs, no focal deficits, stable vitals), but INTERMEDIATE risk for significant secondary pathology requiring imaging and specialist evaluation. Neuroimaging is MANDATORY before attributing to primary headache disorder.
specialty_specific_tests: MRI head without contrast (FIRST-LINE, PREFERRED): Superior soft tissue resolution for detecting mass, demyelination, vascular lesions, edema, and other structural abnormalities. Sensitivity for intracranial pathology >95% for most lesions. Preferred over CT per AHS, AAN, and ACR guidelines. If MRI contraindicated (pacemaker, metallic implants, claustrophobia), proceed to CT.

CT head without contrast (FIRST-LINE ALTERNATIVE if MRI unavailable/contraindicated): Rapid imaging to exclude acute hemorrhage, mass effect, or hydrocephalus. Sensitivity for SAH 95% if <6 hours, decreases over time. Less sensitive than MRI for subtle pathology but acceptable alternative.

Fundoscopic examination (BEDSIDE SPECIALIST TEST): Assess for papilledema (sign of elevated intracranial pressure, concerning for IIH or mass). Examine optic disc margins, venous pulsations, retinal hemorrhages. Critical if IIH suspected.

Formal visual field testing (SECOND-LINE if IIH suspected): Perimetry to assess for visual field defects (enlarged blind spot, peripheral constriction) consistent with IIH. Indicated if papilledema present or high clinical suspicion.

Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis (SECOND-LINE if meningitis suspected or imaging inconclusive): Opening pressure measurement (elevated in IIH >250 mm H2O), cell count/differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, bacterial culture, viral PCR. Xanthochromia on visual inspection or spectrophotometry is pathognomonic for SAH. NOT routinely indicated in this case (low meningitis suspicion, no fever/neck stiffness), but consider if imaging normal and clinical suspicion remains high.

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) (OPTIONAL SECOND-LINE): Screen for vasculitis or inflammatory conditions. Low pretest probability for temporal arteritis at age 35 (LR- 0.05), but reasonable to obtain given persistent headache. If ESR >50 mm/hr or CRP significantly elevated, consider temporal artery biopsy or imaging.
Complete blood count (CBC) (FIRST-LINE LABORATORY): Screen for infection (elevated WBC), anemia (can worsen headache), or other hematologic abnormalities.
Comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) (FIRST-LINE LABORATORY): Assess renal function, electrolytes, glucose, liver function. Abnormalities may contribute to headache or affect medication choices.

Temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy (THIRD-LINE if temporal arteritis suspected): Ultrasound shows halo sign (hypoechoic thickening of arterial wall) with high specificity. Temporal artery biopsy is gold standard but invasive. NOT indicated in this case (age 35, no systemic symptoms, low pretest probability).

Carotid/vertebral artery imaging (CTA or MRA neck) (SECOND-LINE if dissection suspected): CTA or MRA with neck protocol to visualize arterial walls and detect dissection flap, intimal tear, or pseudoaneurysm. NOT routinely indicated (no neck pain, no focal deficits), but consider if clinical suspicion increases.

Cerebral angiography (THIRD-LINE if vascular pathology suspected): Gold standard for detecting vascular lesions (aneurysm, AVM, vasculitis). Invasive with small risk of stroke. Reserved for cases with high suspicion and inconclusive non-invasive imaging.

Ophthalmology referral with formal visual field testing and optical coherence tomography (OCT) (SECOND-LINE if IIH suspected): OCT of optic nerve head to assess for papilledema and measure optic nerve head elevation. Formal perimetry for visual field defects. Indicated if papilledema present or high clinical suspicion for IIH.

Pregnancy test (hCG) (FIRST-LINE if reproductive-age female): CRITICAL before neuroimaging with contrast or certain medications. MRI is safe in pregnancy; CT with contrast requires risk-benefit analysis. Hormonal status relevant to migraine pathophysiology (estrogen fluctuations trigger migraines in 60% of women).

Medication/substance use history (BEDSIDE ASSESSMENT): Detailed history of analgesic, triptan, ergotamine, or other medication use to assess for medication overuse headache (MOH). Frequency and duration of use critical. Also assess for caffeine, stimulant, or illicit drug use.

Migraine trigger assessment (BEDSIDE ASSESSMENT): Detailed history of potential triggers (stress, menses, sleep disruption, foods, environmental factors, hormonal changes). Helps confirm migraine diagnosis and guide preventive strategies.
specialist_red_flags: THUNDERCLAP ONSET (sudden, maximal at onset): Highly specific for SAH (LR+ 10-15). This patient has GRADUAL 2-week onset, which argues against SAH, but any report of sudden worsening should prompt urgent imaging and neurosurgery consultation.

FEVER + HEADACHE + NECK STIFFNESS (classic meningitis triad): Highly specific for meningitis. This patient lacks fever and neck stiffness, but if fever develops, obtain blood cultures and consider empiric antibiotics pending LP/imaging.

FOCAL NEUROLOGICAL DEFICITS (weakness, numbness, vision loss, ataxia, aphasia): Concerning for stroke, mass, or other structural pathology. This patient reports no focal deficits, but any new focal finding warrants urgent imaging and neurology consultation.
PAPILLEDEMA ON FUNDOSCOPY: Sign of elevated intracranial pressure. Concerning for IIH, mass, or other space-occupying lesion. Requires urgent imaging and possible LP.

PROGRESSIVE WORSENING OVER DAYS-WEEKS: Concerning for mass, infection, or other progressive pathology. This patient has 2-week persistent headache; if worsening trajectory documented, increases concern for secondary cause.

ALTERED MENTAL STATUS OR CONFUSION: Concerning for meningitis, encephalitis, intoxication, or metabolic derangement. This patient reports no altered mental status, but any change warrants urgent evaluation.
SEIZURES: Concerning for structural lesion, infection, or metabolic abnormality. This patient reports no seizures, but any seizure activity warrants urgent imaging and EEG.

VISION CHANGES (visual obscurations, diplopia, amaurosis fugax, visual field defects): Concerning for IIH (visual obscurations, enlarged blind spot), dissection (amaurosis fugax), or mass (visual field defects). This patient reports no vision changes, but any visual symptoms warrant ophthalmology referral and imaging.

NECK PAIN OR STIFFNESS: Concerning for meningitis, dissection, or other cervical pathology. This patient reports no neck pain, but any neck pain warrants imaging of neck vessels and consideration of dissection.

UNCONTROLLED HYPERTENSION (BP >180/120): Concerning for hypertensive emergency or secondary hypertension from pheochromocytoma, renal artery stenosis, or other cause. This patient's vital signs are stable, but severe hypertension warrants urgent evaluation.

IMMUNOCOMPROMISED STATE (HIV, malignancy, immunosuppressive therapy): Increases risk of opportunistic infections (toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, PML) and malignancy. This patient's immune status unknown; obtain history of immunosuppression.
RECENT TRAUMA OR MANIPULATION: Risk factor for dissection or subdural hematoma. This patient reports no trauma, but any recent head/neck trauma warrants imaging.
CONNECTIVE TISSUE DISORDER (Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, fibromuscular dysplasia): Risk factor for dissection. This patient's connective tissue status unknown; obtain history.

UNILATERAL TEMPORAL HEADACHE + SCALP TENDERNESS + JAW CLAUDICATION + VISION CHANGES: Classic for temporal arteritis. This patient is age 35 (protective), but any combination of these features warrants ESR/CRP and possible temporal artery imaging/biopsy.
HEADACHE + FEVER + RASH: Concerning for meningococcal meningitis. This patient reports no rash, but any petechial/purpuric rash warrants blood cultures and empiric antibiotics.

PHOTOPHOBIA + NECK STIFFNESS + FEVER (meningitis triad): This patient has photophobia but lacks fever and neck stiffness, lowering meningitis suspicion. However, if fever or neck stiffness develops, treat as meningitis until proven otherwise.

UNILATERAL HEADACHE + IPSILATERAL NECK PAIN + FOCAL NEUROLOGICAL DEFICITS (dissection triad): This patient has unilateral headache but no neck pain or focal deficits, lowering dissection suspicion. However, if neck pain or focal deficits develop, obtain CTA/MRA neck.

PERSISTENT HEADACHE IN PATIENT ON CHRONIC ANALGESICS/TRIPTANS: Concerning for medication overuse headache (MOH). Medication history critical; if MOH suspected, gradual medication withdrawal indicated.

HEADACHE + VISUAL OBSCURATIONS + PAPILLEDEMA IN REPRODUCTIVE-AGE FEMALE: Classic for IIH. This patient has headache and is reproductive-age female, but lacks visual obscurations and papilledema. However, if visual symptoms or papilledema develop, obtain LP with opening pressure measurement.

HEADACHE REFRACTORY TO STANDARD ABORTIVE/PREVENTIVE THERAPY: Concerning for secondary cause or inadequate treatment. If migraine diagnosis confirmed on imaging, ensure adequate triptan dosing, preventive therapy optimization, and specialist follow-up.

treatment_plans.condition: Migraine (Episodic vs. Status Migrainosus vs. Chronic Migraine)

interventions.details: Patient to track daily: headache onset/duration, severity (0-10), location, associated symptoms (photophobia, nausea, vomiting), potential triggers (stress, menses, sleep, foods, weather, hormonal changes), medication use, and response to treatment. Duration: ongoing, minimum 2 weeks.
interventions.rationale: Identifies patterns, triggers, and medication overuse; guides preventive therapy selection

interventions.details: Maintain consistent sleep schedule (7-9 hours/night), avoid sleep deprivation and oversleeping, establish bedtime routine, optimize sleep environment (dark, cool, quiet). Avoid caffeine after 2 PM.
interventions.rationale: Sleep disruption is major migraine trigger; optimization reduces attack frequency by 20-30%

interventions.details: Progressive muscle relaxation, deep breathing exercises (4-7-8 technique), mindfulness meditation (10-15 min daily), yoga, or tai chi. Consider biofeedback therapy.
interventions.rationale: Stress is major migraine trigger; relaxation techniques reduce attack frequency and severity

interventions.details: Identify and avoid common migraine triggers: aged cheeses, cured meats, MSG, artificial sweeteners, excessive caffeine, alcohol (especially red wine, beer). Maintain regular meal schedule; avoid skipping meals. Stay well-hydrated (2-3 L water daily).
interventions.rationale: Dietary triggers account for 30-40% of migraine attacks; elimination reduces frequency

interventions.details: Reduce light exposure (use sunglasses, dim screens, avoid bright lights), minimize loud noises, maintain comfortable temperature, use air purifier if environmental sensitivities present.
interventions.rationale: Photophobia present; environmental control reduces symptom severity

interventions.details: Detailed menstrual history: cycle regularity, relationship of headaches to menses, oral contraceptive use, hormone replacement therapy. Consider hormonal triggers in 60% of women with migraine.
interventions.rationale: Estrogen fluctuations trigger migraines in 60% of women; hormonal management may reduce frequency

interventions.details: Limit caffeine to <200 mg/day (equivalent to 1-2 cups coffee). Gradual reduction if currently high intake to avoid withdrawal headaches. Avoid caffeine-containing analgesics.
interventions.rationale: Caffeine overuse paradoxically triggers headaches; withdrawal can cause rebound headaches

interventions.details: Aerobic exercise 150 min/week (brisk walking, swimming, cycling) at moderate intensity. Avoid intense exercise during acute migraine. Gradual warm-up to prevent exercise-induced migraine.
interventions.rationale: Regular aerobic exercise reduces migraine frequency by 20-30%; improves overall health

TRIPTAN USE REQUIRES BASELINE ASSESSMENT: Before initiating triptan therapy (sumatriptan, rizatriptan, naratriptan), obtain baseline blood pressure and confirm absence of uncontrolled hypertension (BP >180/120), coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, or hemiplegic migraine. These are absolute contraindications.

SEROTONIN SYNDROME RISK: If patient is on SSRIs or SNRIs (not documented but must verify), concurrent triptan use carries rare but serious serotonin syndrome risk. Symptoms include agitation, confusion, rapid heart rate, and muscle rigidity. Patient education essential.

MEDICATION OVERUSE HEADACHE RISK: If abortive medications (triptans, NSAIDs) are used, frequency must be monitored. Use >10 days/month for triptans or >15 days/month for NSAIDs increases risk of medication overuse headache (MOH), which paradoxically worsens headaches. Clear frequency limits must be communicated to patient.
moderate_issues: NSAID SAFETY IN REPRODUCTIVE-AGE FEMALE: If ibuprofen or naproxen prescribed for acute migraine, counsel on: (1) avoid in 3rd trimester if pregnant, (2) use lowest dose for shortest duration, (3) take with food to reduce GI upset, (4) do not exceed frequency limits (ibuprofen max 1200 mg/day OTC, naproxen max 660 mg/day OTC). Renal function should be normal before chronic NSAID use.

If MRI with gadolinium contrast used, confirm: (1) no severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min; gadolinium contraindicated due to nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk), (2) pregnancy status (gadolinium Category C; use only if benefits outweigh risks). rizatriptan.details: 5-10 mg at migraine onset; may repeat after 2 hours (max 30 mg/day) — within safe range. Appropriate for this patient. NOTE: If patient on propranolol, reduce dose to 5 mg (propranolol increases rizatriptan levels).

naratriptan.details: 1-2.5 mg at migraine onset; may repeat after 4 hours (max 5 mg/day) — within safe range. Appropriate for this patient.

ibuprofen.details: 400-600 mg at migraine onset; may repeat every 4-6 hours (max 1200 mg/day OTC, 2400 mg/day prescription) — within safe range. Appropriate for this patient assuming normal renal/hepatic function and no contraindications.

naproxen.details: 220-550 mg at migraine onset; may repeat after 8-12 hours (max 660 mg/day OTC, 1000 mg/day prescription) — within safe range. Appropriate for this patient.

amitriptyline_preventive.details: Typical starting dose 10-25 mg at bedtime; titrate to 50-100 mg/day for migraine prevention — within safe range. Appropriate for reproductive-age female (safer than valproic acid or topiramate). Monitor for anticholinergic side effects.

propranolol_preventive.details: Typical starting dose 40-80 mg/day divided; titrate to 120-240 mg/day for migraine prevention — within safe range. Appropriate for reproductive-age female. Monitor blood pressure and heart rate.

topiramate_preventive.details: Typical starting dose 25 mg at bedtime; titrate to 50-100 mg/day for migraine prevention — dosages within safe range. HOWEVER: CAUTION in reproductive-age female due to reduced oral contraceptive efficacy and teratogenicity concerns. Consider alternative (amitriptyline or propranolol) if patient of childbearing age planning pregnancy.

valproic_acid_preventive.details: CONTRAINDICATED in reproductive-age female due to high teratogenicity risk (neural tube defects, developmental delays). DO NOT USE in this 35-year-old female. Alternative preventive agents (amitriptyline, propranolol, topiramate with caution) strongly preferred.

safety.safety_summary: OVERALL SAFETY STATUS: PASS WITH WARNINGS. The diagnostic and treatment recommendations from the medical team are generally appropriate and evidence-based for a 35-year-old female with 2-week persistent right-sided throbbing headache, photophobia, and nausea. Neuroimaging (MRI preferred) is appropriately recommended to exclude secondary causes despite classic migraine features. Proposed abortive medications (triptans, NSAIDs) and preventive agents (amitriptyline, propranolol) are within safe dosage ranges and appropriate for this patient population. HOWEVER, CRITICAL SAFETY GAPS exist: (1) NO CURRENT MEDICATION HISTORY DOCUMENTED — must obtain complete list of current medications, supplements, and herbal products before prescribing abortive/preventive therapy to assess for drug-drug interactions (especially SSRIs/SNRIs with triptans, anticoagulants with NSAIDs, oral contraceptives with topiramate). (2) NO DRUG ALLERGY HISTORY DOCUMENTED — must obtain complete allergy history before prescribing any medications. (3) PREGNANCY STATUS NOT CONFIRMED — patient is 35 years old (reproductive age); pregnancy status must be confirmed before neuroimaging with contrast or certain medications (valproic acid, topiramate, NSAIDs in 3rd trimester). (4) REPRODUCTIVE-AGE FEMALE MEDICATION CONSIDERATIONS — if preventive migraine therapy initiated, AVOID valproic acid (teratogenic) and use caution with topiramate (reduces oral contraceptive efficacy); amitriptyline or beta-blockers are safer alternatives. (5) TRIPTAN SAFETY REQUIRES BASELINE ASSESSMENT — before initiating triptan therapy, obtain baseline blood pressure and confirm absence of contraindications (uncontrolled hypertension, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, hemiplegic migraine). (6) MEDICATION OVERUSE HEADACHE RISK — if abortive medications used, frequency must be monitored and clearly communicated to patient (max 10 days/month for triptans, max 15 days/month for NSAIDs). (7) SEROTONIN SYNDROME RISK — if patient on SSRIs/SNRIs, concurrent triptan use carries rare but serious serotonin syndrome risk; patient education essential. Once these safety gaps are addressed, the treatment plan is appropriate and safe for this patient.
recommendations: CRITICAL: Obtain complete current medication history BEFORE prescribing any abortive or preventive migraine therapy. Document: (1) all analgesics/NSAIDs/triptans currently used (assess for medication overuse headache), (2) SSRIs/SNRIs (serotonin syndrome risk with triptans), (3) anticoagulants (NSAID interaction risk), (4) oral contraceptives (topiramate reduces efficacy), (5) herbal supplements (St. John's Wort interacts with triptans), (6) other medications.

empathy.patient_summary: You've been experiencing a right-sided throbbing headache for 2 weeks that gets worse with light and causes nausea. While these symptoms are consistent with migraines—which are very common and treatable—the fact that your headache has lasted this long is unusual. We need to do some imaging tests to make sure there's nothing else going on. The good news is that your vital signs are stable, and most people with this type of headache do very well with proper care and treatment.
empathy.what_this_means: Your symptoms fit a pattern called migraine, which happens when blood vessels in your brain become inflamed and sensitive. This causes the throbbing pain, makes you sensitive to light, and can trigger nausea. Migraines are very common—about 1 in 5 women experience them. However, most migraines come and go in a few hours to a couple of days. Since yours has been going on for 2 weeks straight, we want to rule out other possibilities first. That's why we're doing imaging (a special picture of your brain) to make sure everything is okay. Once we confirm what's causing this, we can start treatment to help you feel better.

right_now: Schedule your MRI or CT scan of your head as soon as possible—ideally within the next few days. This is the most important step to figure out what's causing your headache.
Get blood work done (basic blood tests) to check for infection or other issues. Your doctor will order this.
Write down when your headaches started, how long they last, what makes them better or worse, and any patterns you notice. This information helps your doctor understand your headaches better.
Confirm with your doctor that you're not pregnant before you have the imaging test, especially if contrast dye will be used.
this_week: Start keeping a headache diary: Write down the date, time of day, pain level (0-10), location, what you were doing when it started, and what you ate that day. Note if light bothers you, if you feel nauseous, and what helps (if anything).
Try to improve your sleep: Go to bed and wake up at the same time each day, aim for 7-9 hours of sleep, and keep your bedroom dark and cool.
Reduce stress: Try deep breathing exercises (breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 7, breathe out for 8), take a 15-minute walk, or try a relaxation app. Stress is a major migraine trigger.

Avoid common migraine triggers: Limit caffeine to 1-2 cups of coffee per day, eat regular meals (don't skip breakfast), drink plenty of water, and avoid aged cheeses, cured meats, and artificial sweeteners if these bother you.
Make an appointment with a neurologist (brain specialist) if you don't already have one. Your primary care doctor can refer you.
Tell your doctor about ALL medications and supplements you're currently taking—this is very important for safety.
ongoing: Once imaging is done and we know what's causing your headache, your doctor will talk with you about treatment options. This might include medications to stop a headache when it starts, or medications to prevent headaches from happening.
Continue your headache diary for at least 2-4 weeks. This helps your doctor see patterns and adjust your treatment if needed.
Practice the lifestyle changes that help: good sleep, stress management, regular meals, staying hydrated, and avoiding your personal triggers.

If your doctor prescribes migraine medication, use it exactly as directed. Don't use pain relievers more than 10-15 days per month, as this can actually make headaches worse (called medication overuse headache).
Follow up with your neurologist or doctor in 2-4 weeks to discuss your imaging results and start a treatment plan.
Keep track of which treatments work best for you so you and your doctor can fine-tune your plan over time.

if_prescribed_for_acute_headache.name: Sumatriptan (Imitrex) or other triptans (Maxalt, Amerge)
if_prescribed_for_acute_headache.what_it_does: These medications work by narrowing blood vessels in your brain and blocking pain signals. They're designed to stop a migraine attack once it starts.
if_prescribed_for_acute_headache.how_to_use: Take it at the very first sign of a headache—don't wait for the pain to get worse. You can take it as a pill, nasal spray, or injection depending on which form your doctor prescribes. If the headache comes back after 2 hours, you can take another dose.
if_prescribed_for_acute_headache.important_limits: Do NOT use these more than 10 days per month. Using them too often can actually cause more headaches (medication overuse headache).
if_prescribed_for_acute_headache.side_effects: Some people feel dizzy, sleepy, or have tingling sensations. A few people feel chest tightness—if this happens, tell your doctor right away.
if_prescribed_for_acute_headache.safety_notes: Tell your doctor if you have high blood pressure, heart disease, or have had a stroke. These medications are not safe for everyone. If you're taking antidepressants (SSRIs or SNRIs), let your doctor know before using triptans.

if_prescribed_for_acute_headache.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) or Naproxen (Aleve)
if_prescribed_for_acute_headache.what_it_does: These are over-the-counter pain relievers that reduce inflammation and pain.
if_prescribed_for_acute_headache.how_to_use: Take 400-600 mg of ibuprofen (or 220-550 mg of naproxen) at the first sign of a headache. You can repeat the dose after 4-6 hours if needed, but don't exceed 1,200 mg of ibuprofen per day (or 660 mg of naproxen per day) without a prescription.
if_prescribed_for_acute_headache.important_limits: Do NOT use these more than 15 days per month. Like triptans, overuse can cause medication overuse headache.
if_prescribed_for_acute_headache.side_effects: These can upset your stomach, so take them with food. Some people feel nauseous or dizzy.
if_prescribed_for_acute_headache.safety_notes: Avoid these if you have a history of stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or are taking blood thinners. If you're pregnant (especially in the last 3 months), talk to your doctor before using these.
if_prescribed_for_acute_headache.cost: Very inexpensive—usually $3-5 for a bottle of 30 tablets.

if_prescribed_for_prevention.name: Amitriptyline (Elavil)
if_prescribed_for_prevention.what_it_does: This is an older antidepressant that also helps prevent migraines. It works by calming overactive nerve signals in your brain.
if_prescribed_for_prevention.how_to_use: Take it once a day, usually at bedtime. Your doctor will start with a low dose (10-25 mg) and slowly increase it over weeks. It takes 4-6 weeks to see the full benefit.
if_prescribed_for_prevention.expected_benefit: About 50% of people who take this medication have at least half as many migraines.
if_prescribed_for_prevention.side_effects: Drowsiness (which is why you take it at night), dry mouth, constipation, and weight gain are possible. These often improve over time.
if_prescribed_for_prevention.safety_notes: This is safe for women of childbearing age, including if you're planning to get pregnant. Tell your doctor if you're on other antidepressants.

if_prescribed_for_prevention.name: Propranolol (Inderal)
if_prescribed_for_prevention.what_it_does: This is a beta-blocker (a blood pressure medication) that also prevents migraines by calming blood vessel activity.
if_prescribed_for_prevention.how_to_use: Take it once or twice a day as directed by your doctor. Your doctor will start with a low dose and increase it gradually. It takes 2-4 weeks to see benefit.
if_prescribed_for_prevention.expected_benefit: About 50% of people have at least half as many migraines.
if_prescribed_for_prevention.side_effects: Fatigue, dizziness, and slower heart rate are possible. Some people notice their hands feel cold.
if_prescribed_for_prevention.safety_notes: This is safe for women of childbearing age. Your doctor will monitor your blood pressure and heart rate. Tell your doctor if you have asthma or heart problems.

medications_explained.important_safety_information: Tell your doctor about ALL medications and supplements you're taking before starting any migraine medication. Some combinations can be dangerous. If you're on birth control pills and your doctor suggests topiramate (Topamax), know that topiramate can make birth control less effective—talk to your doctor about this. Do NOT take valproic acid (Depakote) if you're a woman of childbearing age, as it can harm a developing baby.

lifestyle_tips.sleep: Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, even on weekends. Aim for 7-9 hours. Keep your bedroom dark, cool, and quiet. Avoid screens 30 minutes before bed. Sleep deprivation is a major migraine trigger.
lifestyle_tips.stress_management: Try deep breathing (breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 7, breathe out for 8), progressive muscle relaxation, meditation, yoga, or tai chi. Even 10-15 minutes a day helps. Many people find that regular exercise reduces migraines by 20-30%.
lifestyle_tips.exercise: Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity per week (like brisk walking, swimming, or cycling). Warm up slowly to avoid exercise-triggered migraines. Regular exercise improves overall health and reduces headache frequency.
lifestyle_tips.diet: Eat regular meals—skipping meals is a trigger. Stay hydrated (drink 2-3 liters of water daily). Avoid or limit common triggers: aged cheeses, cured meats, MSG, artificial sweeteners, excessive caffeine, and alcohol (especially red wine). Keep a food diary to identify your personal triggers.
lifestyle_tips.caffeine: Limit caffeine to less than 200 mg per day (about 1-2 cups of coffee). If you drink a lot of caffeine now, gradually reduce it—sudden withdrawal can cause headaches. Avoid caffeine-containing pain relievers.
lifestyle_tips.hormonal_factors: If your headaches seem to happen around your period, write this down and tell your doctor. Hormonal changes trigger migraines in about 60% of women. Your doctor can help manage this.
lifestyle_tips.light_sensitivity: Since light bothers you, wear sunglasses outdoors, dim your computer screen, use blue light glasses if you work on screens, and reduce bright lighting at home. These simple changes can help.
lifestyle_tips.environment: Avoid loud noises, strong smells, and extreme temperatures when possible. These can trigger migraines. Keep your environment comfortable.
lifestyle_tips.tracking: Keep a headache diary for at least 2-4 weeks. Write down: date, time, pain level (0-10), location, what you were doing, what you ate, sleep quality, stress level, and whether it's around your period. This helps you and your doctor spot patterns and identify your personal triggers.

seek_immediate_emergency_care_if: Your headache suddenly gets much worse very quickly (like a thunderbolt or the worst headache of your life)—this could be a sign of bleeding in the brain
You develop a stiff neck along with your headache and fever—this could be meningitis (a serious infection)
You have weakness, numbness, or difficulty speaking—these could be signs of a stroke
You have vision changes, double vision, or loss of vision
You feel confused, have trouble thinking clearly, or lose consciousness
You have a seizure (convulsion or loss of consciousness with shaking)
You have severe vomiting and can't keep anything down
Your headache is accompanied by a rash (especially a purple or red rash that doesn't blanch when you press on it)
call_your_doctor_soon_if: Your headache pattern changes significantly (gets worse, happens more often, or feels different than usual)
Your headache lasts longer than 3 weeks despite treatment
You're having headaches more than 4 days per week
You develop new symptoms like fever, weight loss, or night sweats
You're using pain medication more than 10-15 days per month (this can cause medication overuse headache)
You have side effects from your migraine medication that bother you
You think you might be pregnant (important before imaging or certain medications)
routine_follow_up: Schedule your imaging (MRI or CT scan) within the next few days
Follow up with your doctor within 1-2 weeks to discuss imaging results
See a neurologist (brain specialist) within 2-4 weeks if recommended by your doctor
Return for a follow-up visit 2-4 weeks after starting any new migraine medication to see how it's working

empathy.reassurance: I know having a headache that won't go away is frustrating and scary. But here's the good news: you're taking exactly the right step by getting evaluated. Most people with persistent headaches like yours do very well once we figure out what's causing them. Even if this turns out to be migraines—which are very common and very treatable—there are many effective options to help you feel better. Many people find that a combination of lifestyle changes (better sleep, stress management, avoiding triggers) plus the right medication makes a huge difference. You're not alone in this. Millions of people experience migraines, and most of them live normal, active lives with proper treatment. The fact that you're 35 and otherwise healthy is a positive sign. We're going to work together to get you answers and relief. You've got this.

anticipated_faqs.question: Why do I need imaging if my symptoms sound like a migraine?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Great question. While your symptoms do sound like a migraine, the fact that your headache has lasted 2 weeks straight is unusual. Most migraines come and go in a few hours to a couple of days. We need imaging to make sure there's nothing else going on—like an infection, inflammation, or a structural problem. Once we rule those out, we can confidently treat this as a migraine and help you feel better. Think of it like getting an X-ray for a twisted ankle—we want to make sure it's just a sprain and not a fracture.

anticipated_faqs.question: Is a migraine dangerous?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Migraines are not dangerous in the sense that they won't cause permanent damage to your brain. However, they can be very uncomfortable and affect your quality of life. That's why we treat them. The good news is that migraines are very treatable, and most people do well with the right combination of medication and lifestyle changes.

anticipated_faqs.question: Will I need to take medication forever?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Some people take migraine medication for a while and then can stop. Others find that lifestyle changes (better sleep, stress management, avoiding triggers) reduce their migraines enough that they don't need medication. Some people need medication long-term. It really depends on your individual situation. Your doctor will work with you to find what works best and adjust your treatment over time.

anticipated_faqs.question: What's the difference between a migraine and a regular headache?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Regular tension headaches usually feel like a tight band around your head and are caused by muscle tension. Migraines are different—they're caused by changes in blood vessels and nerve activity in your brain. Migraines typically throb, happen on one side of the head, and come with other symptoms like light sensitivity, nausea, or vomiting. Migraines also tend to be more severe and last longer than regular headaches.

anticipated_faqs.question: Can stress cause my migraines?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Yes, stress is one of the most common migraine triggers. Interestingly, it's not just stress itself—sometimes it's the relief from stress that triggers a migraine (like on a weekend after a stressful week). That's why stress management techniques like deep breathing, meditation, yoga, and regular exercise are so important. Even 10-15 minutes of relaxation a day can help.

anticipated_faqs.question: Why does light bother me when I have a migraine?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Light sensitivity (called photophobia) happens because the same nerves that process pain in your brain also process light. During a migraine, these nerves become extra sensitive, so normal light feels painful. This is why wearing sunglasses, dimming lights, and reducing screen time can help during a migraine.

anticipated_faqs.question: Can I prevent migraines from happening?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Absolutely. Prevention is a big part of migraine management. This includes: (1) Lifestyle changes like good sleep, stress management, regular meals, staying hydrated, and avoiding your personal triggers. (2) Preventive medications that reduce how often migraines happen. Your doctor can help you figure out which approach works best for you.

anticipated_faqs.question: Is it safe to take pain relievers every time I have a headache?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Not really. If you use pain relievers (including triptans) more than 10-15 days per month, you can develop medication overuse headache, which actually makes headaches worse. That's why it's important to track how often you're using these medications and talk to your doctor if you're using them frequently. This is another reason why preventive medications and lifestyle changes are so important.

anticipated_faqs.question: Why does my doctor ask about my menstrual cycle?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Because hormonal changes trigger migraines in about 60% of women. If your migraines happen around your period, your doctor might suggest timing your medication differently or adjusting your birth control. This is really important information that helps your doctor help you.

anticipated_faqs.question: Will my imaging show if I have a brain tumor?
anticipated_faqs.answer: Yes, the imaging (MRI or CT scan) will show if there's a tumor or any other structural problem in your brain. However, brain tumors are very rare, and based on your symptoms and the fact that your vital signs are normal, your doctor doesn't think this is likely. The imaging is really to rule out other treatable causes of persistent headache and give you peace of mind.

anticipated_faqs.question: How long does it take for migraine medication to work?
anticipated_faqs.answer: It depends on the type of medication. Abortive medications (like triptans) that stop a migraine once it starts usually work within 30-60 minutes. Preventive medications that reduce how often migraines happen take longer—usually 4-6 weeks to see the full benefit. Your doctor will discuss what to expect with whatever medication they recommend.

The combination of new/changed headache pattern + unilateral presentation + photophobia + persistent duration meets criteria for neuroimaging per American Headache Society and American Academy of Neurology guidelines. Age 35 is peak incidence for migraine in women (prevalence 18% in women vs. 6% in men), which increases pretest probability for primary headache. However, must-not-miss secondary causes require exclusion: subarachnoid hemorrhage (photophobia is highly specific, LR+ 3.2, though gradual onset argues against), meningitis (photophobia LR+ 3.5, but absence of fever/neck stiffness argues against), intracranial mass (unilateral headache + photophobia + nausea concerning, but no focal deficits reported), idiopathic intracranial hypertension (excellent epidemiologic fit: 35-year-old female with 20x higher risk in reproductive-age women; photophobia and nausea present, but no visual obscurations or papilledema reported), temporal arteritis (age 35 is strongly protective; LR- 0.05 for age <50), and cervical artery dissection (no neck pain or focal deficits reported). specialty_specific_tests: MRI head without contrast (FIRST-LINE, PREFERRED): Superior soft tissue resolution for detecting mass, demyelination, vascular lesions, edema, and other structural abnormalities. Sensitivity for intracranial pathology >95% for most lesions. Preferred over CT per AHS, AAN, and ACR guidelines. If MRI contraindicated (pacemaker, metallic implants, claustrophobia), proceed to CT.

CT head without contrast (FIRST-LINE ALTERNATIVE if MRI unavailable/contraindicated): Rapid imaging to exclude acute hemorrhage, mass effect, or hydrocephalus. Sensitivity for SAH 95% if <6 hours, decreases over time. Less sensitive than MRI for subtle pathology but acceptable alternative.

Fundoscopic examination (BEDSIDE SPECIALIST TEST): Assess for papilledema (sign of elevated intracranial pressure, concerning for IIH or mass). Examine optic disc margins, venous pulsations, retinal hemorrhages. Critical if IIH suspected.

Formal visual field testing (SECOND-LINE if IIH suspected): Perimetry to assess for visual field defects (enlarged blind spot, peripheral constriction) consistent with IIH. Indicated if papilledema present or high clinical suspicion.

Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis (SECOND-LINE if meningitis suspected or imaging inconclusive): Opening pressure measurement (elevated in IIH >250 mm H2O), cell count/differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, bacterial culture, viral PCR. Xanthochromia on visual inspection or spectrophotometry is pathognomonic for SAH. NOT routinely indicated in this case (low meningitis suspicion, no fever/neck stiffness), but consider if imaging normal and clinical suspicion remains high.

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) (OPTIONAL SECOND-LINE): Screen for vasculitis or inflammatory conditions. Low pretest probability for temporal arteritis at age 35 (LR- 0.05), but reasonable to obtain given persistent headache. If ESR >50 mm/hr or CRP significantly elevated, consider temporal artery biopsy or imaging.
Complete blood count (CBC) (FIRST-LINE LABORATORY): Screen for infection (elevated WBC), anemia (can worsen headache), or other hematologic abnormalities.
Comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) (FIRST-LINE LABORATORY): Assess renal function, electrolytes, glucose, liver function. Abnormalities may contribute to headache or affect medication choices.

Temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy (THIRD-LINE if temporal arteritis suspected): Ultrasound shows halo sign (hypoechoic thickening of arterial wall) with high specificity. Temporal artery biopsy is gold standard but invasive. NOT indicated in this case (age 35, no systemic symptoms, low pretest probability).

Carotid/vertebral artery imaging (CTA or MRA neck) (SECOND-LINE if dissection suspected): CTA or MRA with neck protocol to visualize arterial walls and detect dissection flap, intimal tear, or pseudoaneurysm. NOT routinely indicated (no neck pain, no focal deficits), but consider if clinical suspicion increases.

Cerebral angiography (THIRD-LINE if vascular pathology suspected): Gold standard for detecting vascular lesions (aneurysm, AVM, vasculitis). Invasive with small risk of stroke. Reserved for cases with high suspicion and inconclusive non-invasive imaging.

Ophthalmology referral with formal visual field testing and optical coherence tomography (OCT) (SECOND-LINE if IIH suspected): OCT of optic nerve head to assess for papilledema and measure optic nerve head elevation. Formal perimetry for visual field defects. Indicated if papilledema present or high clinical suspicion for IIH.

Pregnancy test (hCG) (FIRST-LINE if reproductive-age female): CRITICAL before neuroimaging with contrast or certain medications. MRI is safe in pregnancy; CT with contrast requires risk-benefit analysis. Hormonal status relevant to migraine pathophysiology (estrogen fluctuations trigger migraines in 60% of women).

Medication/substance use history (BEDSIDE ASSESSMENT): Detailed history of analgesic, triptan, ergotamine, or other medication use to assess for medication overuse headache (MOH). Frequency and duration of use critical. Also assess for caffeine, stimulant, or illicit drug use.

Migraine trigger assessment (BEDSIDE ASSESSMENT): Detailed history of potential triggers (stress, menses, sleep disruption, foods, environmental factors, hormonal changes). Helps confirm migraine diagnosis and guide preventive strategies.

Consider lumbar puncture if meningitis suspected (fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status). ESR/CRP if temporal arteritis suspected (age >50, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, vision changes).

key_points: This patient meets ICHD-3 criteria for migraine (unilateral, throbbing, photophobia, nausea)
HOWEVER: 2-week continuous duration is ATYPICAL for episodic migraine (which is typically 4-72 hours per episode)
Differential: Status migrainosus (migraine lasting >72 hours), chronic migraine (≥15 days/month), or secondary cause

high_issues: REPRODUCTIVE-AGE FEMALE MEDICATION CONSIDERATION: Patient is 35 years old (reproductive age). If preventive migraine therapy initiated, AVOID valproic acid (teratogenic) and use caution with topiramate (reduces oral contraceptive efficacy). Amitriptyline or beta-blockers are safer alternatives. Pregnancy status should be confirmed before neuroimaging with contrast agents.

TRIPTAN USE REQUIRES BASELINE ASSESSMENT: Before initiating triptan therapy (sumatriptan, rizatriptan, naratriptan), obtain baseline blood pressure and confirm absence of uncontrolled hypertension (BP >180/120), coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, or hemiplegic migraine. These are absolute contraindications.

SEROTONIN SYNDROME RISK: If patient is on SSRIs or SNRIs (not documented but must verify), concurrent triptan use carries rare but serious serotonin syndrome risk. Symptoms include agitation, confusion, rapid heart rate, and muscle rigidity. Patient education essential.

MEDICATION OVERUSE HEADACHE RISK: If abortive medications (triptans, NSAIDs) are used, frequency must be monitored. Use >10 days/month for triptans or >15 days/month for NSAIDs increases risk of medication overuse headache (MOH), which paradoxically worsens headaches. Clear frequency limits must be communicated to patient.
moderate_issues: NSAID SAFETY IN REPRODUCTIVE-AGE FEMALE: If ibuprofen or naproxen prescribed for acute migraine, counsel on: (1) avoid in 3rd trimester if pregnant, (2) use lowest dose for shortest duration, (3) take with food to reduce GI upset, (4) do not exceed frequency limits (ibuprofen max 1200 mg/day OTC, naproxen max 660 mg/day OTC). Renal function should be normal before chronic NSAID use.

IMAGING CONTRAST CONSIDERATIONS: Patient requires neuroimaging (MRI preferred per guidelines). If MRI with gadolinium contrast used, confirm: (1) no severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min; gadolinium contraindicated due to nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk), (2) pregnancy status (gadolinium Category C; use only if benefits outweigh risks). MRI without contrast is preferred if possible.

MISSING MEDICATION HISTORY: No current medications documented in case presentation. CRITICAL SAFETY GAP: Must obtain complete medication history including: (1) current analgesics/NSAIDs/triptans (assess for medication overuse headache), (2) SSRIs/SNRIs (serotonin syndrome risk with triptans), (3) anticoagulants (NSAID interaction risk), (4) oral contraceptives (topiramate reduces efficacy), (5) herbal supplements (St. John's Wort interacts with triptans). This information is ESSENTIAL before prescribing abortive or preventive therapy.

MISSING ALLERGY HISTORY: No drug allergies documented. CRITICAL SAFETY GAP: Must obtain complete allergy history including: (1) triptan allergies (cross-reactivity possible within triptan class), (2) NSAID allergies (aspirin sensitivity increases NSAID risk), (3) contrast allergies (if imaging with contrast planned), (4) other drug allergies. Sulfonamide allergy should be noted if topiramate considered (theoretical cross-reactivity).

MISSING PREGNANCY STATUS: Patient is 35-year-old female of reproductive age. Pregnancy status NOT documented. CRITICAL SAFETY GAP: Must confirm: (1) current pregnancy status (affects imaging and medication choices), (2) contraceptive use (relevant to topiramate if preventive therapy considered), (3) plans for pregnancy (affects medication selection). Pregnancy test (hCG) recommended before neuroimaging with contrast or certain medications.
low_issues: BEERS CRITERIA NOT APPLICABLE: Patient is 35 years old; Beers Criteria apply only to patients ≥65 years. No age-related medication safety concerns identified.
STOPP/START CRITERIA NOT APPLICABLE: Patient is 35 years old; STOPP/START apply only to patients ≥65 years.

CAFFEINE MANAGEMENT: Patient should limit caffeine to <200 mg/day (equivalent to 1-2 cups coffee). Caffeine overuse paradoxically triggers headaches; gradual reduction recommended if currently high intake to avoid withdrawal headaches. Avoid caffeine-containing analgesics.
