Preferred imaging modality for this subacute presentation.

PRIORITY 1 — MR Venography (MRV) of the brain: Gold standard for CVST diagnosis. Demonstrates filling defects in dural venous sinuses (superior sagittal sinus, transverse sinuses, sigmoid sinuses most commonly affected). Should be ordered simultaneously with MRI brain — combined MRI/MRV is the single most important diagnostic test in this case.

PRIORITY 2 — D-dimer: Highly sensitive (>97%) but non-specific for CVST. A normal D-dimer in a low-pretest-probability patient may help exclude CVST, but elevated D-dimer requires MRV confirmation. Not a standalone diagnostic test.

PRIORITY 2 — Lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement: Indicated if: (a) CT negative and SAH still suspected — send CSF for xanthochromia (spectrophotometry preferred over visual inspection), RBC count, cell count, protein, glucose, culture; (b) MRI/MRV normal and IIH suspected — opening pressure >25 cmH2O (>20 cmH2O with symptoms in non-obese patients) is diagnostic for IIH; (c) Meningismus present — send CSF for full infectious workup. LP must be preceded by CT to exclude mass lesion with herniation risk.
PRIORITY 2 — Complete blood count (CBC): Evaluate for thrombocytosis (CVST risk), anemia (headache trigger), leukocytosis (infectious etiology), polycythemia.
PRIORITY 2 — Comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP): Electrolytes, renal function, liver function, glucose. Metabolic derangements can cause or exacerbate headache.

PRIORITY 2 — ESR and CRP: Inflammatory markers. ESR >50 mm/hr in a patient >50 would raise temporal arteritis concern (not applicable at age 35 but baseline inflammatory markers useful). Elevated CRP may suggest infectious or inflammatory etiology.
PRIORITY 2 — Coagulation studies (PT, PTT, INR): Baseline prior to potential anticoagulation if CVST confirmed. Also screens for coagulopathy.

PRIORITY 3 — Hypercoagulability panel (if CVST confirmed or strongly suspected): Factor V Leiden mutation, Prothrombin G20210A mutation, Protein C and S levels, Antithrombin III, Antiphospholipid antibodies (anticardiolipin IgG/IgM, anti-beta2-glycoprotein I, lupus anticoagulant), homocysteine. Note: Protein C, S, and antithrombin levels should ideally be measured before anticoagulation initiation or 4-6 weeks after completion.

PRIORITY 3 — Formal visual field testing (Humphrey perimetry): If IIH is suspected — visual field defects (enlarged blind spot, inferior nasal step, arcuate scotoma) are the primary vision-threatening complication of IIH. Ophthalmology referral for formal perimetry.

PRIORITY 3 — CT Angiography (CTA) head and neck: If SAH confirmed on CT or LP — identifies aneurysm location and morphology for neurosurgical planning. Also useful if arteriovenous malformation (AVM) suspected.
PRIORITY 3 — TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone): Hypothyroidism is a recognized secondary cause of headache and can precipitate IIH. Obtain as part of IIH workup.

PRIORITY 3 — Pregnancy test (urine or serum beta-hCG): Mandatory in reproductive-age female before CT radiation exposure and before prescribing triptans, topiramate, or valproate. Pregnancy is also a risk factor for CVST.

PRIORITY 3 — Medication history and analgesic use quantification: Specifically query daily analgesic use over the past 2 weeks. Medication overuse headache (MOH) requires >10 days/month of triptan/ergotamine use or >15 days/month of simple analgesic use for >3 months — patient may be in early MOH development if self-treating daily.

triage.triage_summary: 35-year-old female presenting with a 2-week history of persistent right-sided throbbing headache (6/10), photophobia, and nausea. Symptom constellation is consistent with migraine with aura; however, the subacute persistent course, fixed unilateral location, and associated meningeal irritation signs (photophobia, nausea) mandate exclusion of secondary causes including: subarachnoid hemorrhage (sentinel headache), cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, intracranial mass, hypertensive emergency, and meningitis. No vital signs provided — BP and full neurological exam are immediately required. ESI-3 assigned based on stable presentation requiring multiple resources (neuroimaging + labs ± LP); would upgrade to ESI-2 if any danger-zone vitals, focal neuro deficits, meningismus, or papilledema identified.

Perform focused neurological exam: GCS, cranial nerves, motor/sensory, cerebellar, fundoscopy for papilledema

Inquire about: thunderclap onset, fever/chills, oral contraceptive use, recent trauma, visual changes, weakness/numbness, prior similar headaches

differential_diagnosis.condition: Migraine without aura (or with unrecognized aura)
differential_diagnosis.bayesian_reasoning: Pre-test probability ~55% given peak demographic (35F), unilateral throbbing pain, photophobia, nausea — classic ICHD-3 criteria. LR+ for unilateral throbbing + photophobia + nausea constellation ~8-10. Post-test probability ~62%. Slightly discounted due to 2-week continuous duration (typical migraine attacks last 4-72 hours, not 2 weeks continuously), raising concern for new persistent daily headache or secondary cause.
differential_diagnosis.illness_script_fit: Strong epidemiological fit (35F, peak migraine prevalence). Pathophysiology: trigeminovascular activation, cortical spreading depression. Time course partially fits (recurrent attacks possible) but continuous 2-week course is atypical. Key features present: unilateral, throbbing, photophobia, nausea. Missing: prior migraine history not documented, aura not reported, typical attack duration not clarified.

Pain severity 6/10 — moderate, consistent with migraine
opposing_features: 2-week continuous duration exceeds typical migraine attack duration (4-72 hours)
No prior migraine history documented
Fixed unilateral location over 2 weeks raises concern for structural lesion
New headache pattern in adult warrants secondary cause exclusion

differential_diagnosis.bayesian_reasoning: Pre-test probability ~5-8% in 35F with subacute headache, elevated significantly if on oral contraceptives (OCP use not yet documented — critical gap). LR+ for subacute progressive unilateral headache in reproductive-age female on OCP ~6-8. Post-test probability 18-25% pending OCP status. CVST classically presents with progressive headache over days-weeks, can mimic migraine, and is catastrophically missed. Must be excluded.
differential_diagnosis.illness_script_fit: Epidemiology: reproductive-age females, especially OCP users, hypercoagulable states, postpartum. Pathophysiology: venous outflow obstruction → increased ICP → headache. Time course: subacute over days to weeks — FITS this presentation perfectly. Key features: progressive headache, may have papilledema, focal deficits, seizures (absent here but not required early). The 2-week progressive course is a hallmark.
supporting_features: Subacute 2-week progressive course — classic CVST timeline
OCP use status unknown — critical risk factor
opposing_features: No focal neurological deficits reported
No seizures reported

Pain only 6/10 — CVST often more severe

differential_diagnosis.bayesian_reasoning: Pre-test probability ~2-3% for brain tumor in 35F with new headache. LR+ for progressive unilateral headache without positional component or morning predominance is modest (~2-3). Post-test probability ~10%. Included as must-not-miss given catastrophic consequences of delay. Primary tumors (glioma, meningioma) and metastases (breast, lung) must be considered.
differential_diagnosis.illness_script_fit: Epidemiology: meningioma peaks in middle-aged females; glioma less common at 35. Pathophysiology: mass effect, peritumoral edema → elevated ICP → headache. Time course: typically progressive over weeks-months — partially fits. Key features: morning headache, positional worsening, papilledema, focal deficits — most absent here but early lesions may lack these.

No positional worsening
No focal neurological deficits
No papilledema documented

differential_diagnosis.bayesian_reasoning: Pre-test probability for SAH in 35F with subacute headache ~1-3%. Significantly reduced by absence of thunderclap onset (LR- ~0.1 for SAH without thunderclap). However, sentinel headaches from small aneurysmal leaks can present as recurrent moderate headaches over days-weeks before catastrophic rupture. Post-test probability ~8% — low but catastrophic if missed.
differential_diagnosis.illness_script_fit: Epidemiology: SAH peaks 40-60 years, but aneurysms can rupture at 35. Pathophysiology: blood in subarachnoid space → meningeal irritation → headache, photophobia, nausea. Time course: classic thunderclap (absent here) but sentinel headaches are subacute. Key features: thunderclap onset (absent), meningismus (not yet assessed), photophobia (present), nausea (present). Absence of thunderclap significantly reduces probability.

opposing_features: No thunderclap onset reported (strongest argument against)
Pain only 6/10 — SAH typically 10/10 'worst headache of life'

differential_diagnosis.illness_script_fit: Epidemiology: bacterial meningitis peaks in young adults; viral more common overall. Pathophysiology: meningeal inflammation → headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, fever. Time course: bacterial = hours to days (2 weeks without fever/deterioration argues strongly against); viral = days to 1-2 weeks (possible). Key features: fever (absent), nuchal rigidity (not assessed), Kernig's/Brudzinski's (not assessed).

recommended_tests.rationale: First-line to exclude acute hemorrhage (SAH, ICH), large mass with herniation risk
recommended_tests.confirms_excludes: Confirms acute hemorrhage, large mass; negative CT does not exclude CVST, small mass, or SAH >6 hours old

specialist.reason_for_consultation: 35-year-old female with 2-week persistent right-sided throbbing headache (6/10), photophobia, and nausea. Triage and diagnostician have flagged concern for secondary headache etiologies including CVST, SAH sentinel headache, intracranial mass, IIH, and meningitis. Neurology consultation requested to apply specialty-level diagnostic criteria, risk stratification, and management guidance.
specialist.specialist_assessment:
This is a 35-year-old female presenting with a 2-week history of persistent, unilateral right-sided throbbing headache rated 6/10, accompanied by photophobia and nausea. From a neurology standpoint, this presentation sits at a critical diagnostic crossroads between primary headache disorder (migraine, NDPH) and several serious secondary etiologies that must be systematically excluded before any primary headache diagnosis is assigned.

The symptom triad of unilateral throbbing headache, photophobia, and nausea is phenotypically consistent with migraine without aura per ICHD-3 criteria. However, the 2-week continuous duration is the pivotal atypical feature that fundamentally challenges a pure migraine diagnosis. Migraine attacks by definition last 4-72 hours; a 2-week unremitting course suggests either: (1) new daily persistent headache (NDPH) with migrainous features, (2) status migrainosus (>72 hours continuous migraine), (3) chronic migraine superimposed on a new pattern, or most critically, (4) a secondary structural or vascular etiology masquerading as migraine.

CEREBRAL VENOUS SINUS THROMBOSIS (CVST) is my highest-priority must-not-miss diagnosis. The subacute 2-week progressive headache course in a reproductive-age female is the textbook CVST presentation. CVST accounts for up to 0.5-1% of all strokes but is dramatically overrepresented in women aged 20-35, particularly those using oral contraceptives (OCP use not yet documented — this is a critical clinical gap). The ISCVT registry demonstrated that headache was the presenting symptom in 90% of CVST cases, and the headache is frequently described as progressive, unilateral, and migrainous in character. Crucially, early CVST may present WITHOUT focal neurological deficits, seizures, or papilledema — the absence of these features does not exclude the diagnosis. MRI brain with MR Venography (MRV) is the diagnostic gold standard and must be obtained urgently.

IDIOPATHIC INTRACRANIAL HYPERTENSION (IIH) is the second priority in this demographic. IIH incidence is 15-19 per 100,000 in obese reproductive-age women. The subacute progressive headache with nausea and photophobia fits the IIH phenotype. OCP use is a recognized precipitant. Fundoscopic examination for papilledema is mandatory — its presence would dramatically elevate IIH probability. Visual field testing and formal ophthalmology evaluation would follow. Lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement (>25 cmH2O diagnostic) is required for confirmation after neuroimaging excludes a mass lesion.

INTRACRANIAL MASS LESION must be excluded by neuroimaging. While the pre-test probability is low (~2-3% in this age group without systemic symptoms), the consequences of a missed diagnosis are catastrophic. Meningioma is the most common intracranial tumor in women and peaks in middle-aged females; early meningiomas may present with isolated progressive unilateral headache without focal deficits or papilledema. MRI with gadolinium is far superior to CT for detecting small extra-axial lesions, posterior fossa pathology, and leptomeningeal disease.

SUBARACHNOID HEMORRHAGE (sentinel headache) remains on the differential despite the absence of thunderclap onset. Approximately 20-50% of SAH patients report a preceding sentinel headache — a moderate-severity headache occurring days to weeks before catastrophic aneurysmal rupture. The absence of 'worst headache of life' quality and thunderclap onset significantly reduces SAH probability (LR- ~0.1), but the 2-week duration with photophobia and nausea warrants CT head without contrast as the immediate first step. If CT is negative and clinical suspicion persists, LP for xanthochromia is mandatory.

MIGRAINE (primary diagnosis) remains the leading statistical probability at approximately 60-65% given the demographic and phenotypic features. However, this is a diagnosis of exclusion in this clinical context. The ICHD-3 criteria are met for individual attack features, but the 2-week continuous course requires explanation. If secondary causes are excluded, the diagnosis would be refined to either: new daily persistent headache with migrainous features (if continuous from onset), status migrainosus (if a single prolonged attack), or chronic migraine with medication overuse headache (if analgesics have been used daily for 2 weeks — this must be specifically queried).

NEUROLOGICAL EXAMINATION PRIORITIES: The bedside neurological exam is the most immediately actionable diagnostic tool. Fundoscopy for papilledema, assessment for meningismus (nuchal rigidity, Kernig's sign, Brudzinski's sign), cranial nerve examination (particularly CN VI palsy as a false localizing sign of elevated ICP, and CN III palsy suggesting posterior communicating artery aneurysm), visual field confrontation testing, and a complete motor/sensory/cerebellar examination must be performed immediately. Any abnormality on this exam upgrades urgency to emergent.
diagnostic_criteria_applied: ICHD-3 Migraine Without Aura Criteria (IHS 2018): Patient meets — unilateral location (right-sided), pulsating/throbbing quality, moderate-severe intensity (6/10), photophobia, nausea. PARTIALLY MET — duration criterion (4-72 hours per attack) NOT met given 2-week continuous course. Conclusion: Phenotypically migrainous but duration criterion failure mandates secondary cause exclusion before primary migraine diagnosis is assigned.

ICHD-3 New Daily Persistent Headache (NDPH) Criteria: Requires daily headache from onset persisting >3 months. Patient at 2 weeks — does NOT yet meet duration threshold. Diagnosis cannot be formally applied but clinical pattern is consistent with early NDPH; reassessment at 3-month mark required if secondary causes excluded.

ICHD-3 Status Migrainosus Criteria: Migraine attack lasting >72 hours. Possible if this represents a single prolonged attack — requires clarification of whether headache has been truly continuous or episodic with incomplete resolution.

SNOOP4 Red Flag Criteria (AHS/ACEP): Evaluating for secondary headache red flags — S (Systemic symptoms): No fever documented, no weight loss — NOT MET. N (Neurological signs): Focal deficits not reported but exam not yet completed — PENDING. O (Onset sudden/thunderclap): Not reported — NOT MET. O (Older age >50): Patient is 35 — NOT MET. P (Progressive pattern): 2-week persistent course — SOFT FLAG PRESENT. P (Positional component): Not assessed — PENDING. P (Precipitated by Valsalva): Not assessed — PENDING. P (Papilledema): Not assessed — PENDING. Assessment: At least 1 soft SNOOP4 flag present (progressive/persistent new pattern) — neuroimaging is indicated per AHS guidelines.

Ottawa SAH Rule (Perry et al., JAMA 2011): Applies to patients >15 years with non-traumatic headache reaching maximum intensity within 1 hour. Criteria include: age >40, neck pain/stiffness, witnessed loss of consciousness, onset with exertion, thunderclap onset, limited neck flexion on exam. Patient does not clearly trigger Ottawa Rule given absence of thunderclap onset — however, sentinel headache pattern (gradual onset, 2-week course) is a recognized SAH variant not fully captured by Ottawa Rule. CT head still indicated.

Modified Dandy Criteria for IIH: (1) Symptoms/signs of elevated ICP — headache, nausea, photophobia PRESENT. (2) No localizing neurological signs other than CN VI palsy — not yet assessed. (3) CSF opening pressure >25 cmH2O — not yet measured. (4) Normal CSF composition — not yet obtained. (5) No mass lesion on neuroimaging — not yet performed. Patient meets symptomatic criteria; formal IIH diagnosis requires LP opening pressure after neuroimaging exclusion of mass.

CVST Risk Stratification (ISCVT Registry Criteria): High-risk features present — female sex, reproductive age (20-35 years), subacute progressive headache over 2 weeks. Critical risk factor UNKNOWN — oral contraceptive use not documented. Thrombophilia status unknown. Risk score cannot be fully calculated without OCP history — this is the single most important missing data point for CVST risk stratification.

Migraine Disability Assessment (MIDAS Score): Cannot be formally calculated without knowing number of headache days in past 3 months, days of missed work/school, and days of reduced productivity. Estimated MIDAS Grade II-III (moderate-severe disability) based on 2-week continuous headache at 6/10 severity — formal calculation required at follow-up.
specialist.risk_stratification: INTERMEDIATE-HIGH RISK — Rationale: This patient cannot be classified as low-risk until secondary causes are excluded by neuroimaging and clinical examination. Risk is elevated to intermediate-high based on the following: (1) Subacute 2-week continuous headache course — atypical for primary migraine, classic for CVST and IIH. (2) Reproductive-age female — highest-risk demographic for CVST (especially with unknown OCP status). (3) Photophobia and nausea — present in both primary migraine AND elevated ICP syndromes (CVST, IIH, mass lesion). (4) Absence of vital signs and neurological exam findings — critical data gaps that prevent downgrading to low risk. (5) No prior migraine history documented — new headache pattern in adult requires secondary cause exclusion per AHS Grade A recommendation. Risk would be DOWNGRADED to LOW-INTERMEDIATE if: BP normal, neurological exam completely normal, no papilledema, no meningismus, MRI/MRV normal, OCP not in use. Risk would be UPGRADED to HIGH/EMERGENT if: papilledema found on fundoscopy, focal neurological deficit identified, meningismus present, BP >180 systolic, or MRI/MRV shows venous sinus filling defect.
specialty_specific_tests: IMMEDIATE — Blood pressure measurement (both arms): Critical data gap; must exclude hypertensive emergency (SBP >180) before any other workup proceeds. OCP-induced hypertension is a specific concern in this demographic.

IMMEDIATE — Complete neurological examination: GCS, cranial nerves (especially CN III, CN VI), motor strength, sensory testing, cerebellar function, gait. Focal deficits would mandate emergent CT/MRI.

IMMEDIATE — Fundoscopic examination (direct ophthalmoscopy or slit-lamp): Assess for papilledema (elevated ICP), hypertensive retinopathy, venous pulsations. Papilledema presence would mandate emergent neuroimaging and IIH/CVST workup.

IMMEDIATE — Meningismus assessment: Nuchal rigidity, Kernig's sign (resistance to knee extension with hip flexed), Brudzinski's sign (involuntary hip/knee flexion with passive neck flexion). Positive findings mandate LP after CT.

PRIORITY 1 — Non-contrast CT head: First-line imaging to exclude acute hemorrhage (SAH, ICH), large mass with herniation risk, hydrocephalus. Sensitivity 98% for SAH within 6 hours of onset; sensitivity decreases to 85-90% at 24 hours and further declines over 2 weeks.

PRIORITY 1 — MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast: Superior to CT for detecting small mass lesions, posterior fossa pathology, leptomeningeal enhancement, cortical vein thrombosis, white matter changes, and early ischemic changes. Preferred imaging modality for this subacute presentation.

PRIORITY 1 — MR Venography (MRV) of the brain: Gold standard for CVST diagnosis. Demonstrates filling defects in dural venous sinuses (superior sagittal sinus, transverse sinuses, sigmoid sinuses most commonly affected). Should be ordered simultaneously with MRI brain — combined MRI/MRV is the single most important diagnostic test in this case.

PRIORITY 2 — D-dimer: Highly sensitive (>97%) but non-specific for CVST. A normal D-dimer in a low-pretest-probability patient may help exclude CVST, but elevated D-dimer requires MRV confirmation. Not a standalone diagnostic test.

PRIORITY 2 — Lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement: Indicated if: (a) CT negative and SAH still suspected — send CSF for xanthochromia (spectrophotometry preferred over visual inspection), RBC count, cell count, protein, glucose, culture; (b) MRI/MRV normal and IIH suspected — opening pressure >25 cmH2O (>20 cmH2O with symptoms in non-obese patients) is diagnostic for IIH; (c) Meningismus present — send CSF for full infectious workup. LP must be preceded by CT to exclude mass lesion with herniation risk.
PRIORITY 2 — Complete blood count (CBC): Evaluate for thrombocytosis (CVST risk), anemia (headache trigger), leukocytosis (infectious etiology), polycythemia.
PRIORITY 2 — Comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP): Electrolytes, renal function, liver function, glucose. Metabolic derangements can cause or exacerbate headache.

PRIORITY 2 — ESR and CRP: Inflammatory markers. ESR >50 mm/hr in a patient >50 would raise temporal arteritis concern (not applicable at age 35 but baseline inflammatory markers useful). Elevated CRP may suggest infectious or inflammatory etiology.
PRIORITY 2 — Coagulation studies (PT, PTT, INR): Baseline prior to potential anticoagulation if CVST confirmed. Also screens for coagulopathy.

PRIORITY 3 — Hypercoagulability panel (if CVST confirmed or strongly suspected): Factor V Leiden mutation, Prothrombin G20210A mutation, Protein C and S levels, Antithrombin III, Antiphospholipid antibodies (anticardiolipin IgG/IgM, anti-beta2-glycoprotein I, lupus anticoagulant), homocysteine. Note: Protein C, S, and antithrombin levels should ideally be measured before anticoagulation initiation or 4-6 weeks after completion.

PRIORITY 3 — Formal visual field testing (Humphrey perimetry): If IIH is suspected — visual field defects (enlarged blind spot, inferior nasal step, arcuate scotoma) are the primary vision-threatening complication of IIH. Ophthalmology referral for formal perimetry.

PRIORITY 3 — CT Angiography (CTA) head and neck: If SAH confirmed on CT or LP — identifies aneurysm location and morphology for neurosurgical planning. Also useful if arteriovenous malformation (AVM) suspected.
PRIORITY 3 — TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone): Hypothyroidism is a recognized secondary cause of headache and can precipitate IIH. Obtain as part of IIH workup.

PRIORITY 3 — Pregnancy test (urine or serum beta-hCG): Mandatory in reproductive-age female before CT radiation exposure and before prescribing triptans, topiramate, or valproate. Pregnancy is also a risk factor for CVST.

PRIORITY 3 — Medication history and analgesic use quantification: Specifically query daily analgesic use over the past 2 weeks. Medication overuse headache (MOH) requires >10 days/month of triptan/ergotamine use or >15 days/month of simple analgesic use for >3 months — patient may be in early MOH development if self-treating daily.
specialist_red_flags: EMERGENT — New focal neurological deficit (unilateral weakness, facial droop, speech difficulty, visual field cut): Suggests venous infarction from CVST, mass effect, or ischemic stroke — immediate CT/MRI and neurology/neurosurgery activation.
EMERGENT — Papilledema on fundoscopy: Confirms elevated intracranial pressure — immediately narrows differential to CVST, IIH, intracranial mass, or hypertensive emergency. Emergent MRI/MRV required.
EMERGENT — Meningismus (nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig's or Brudzinski's): Raises concern for SAH or meningitis — emergent CT followed by LP if CT negative.

EMERGENT — Sudden severe headache escalation ('thunderclap' component): Even if baseline headache has been moderate, any sudden escalation to 'worst headache of life' quality mandates immediate SAH workup.
EMERGENT — Altered level of consciousness or confusion: Suggests elevated ICP with impending herniation, venous infarction, or encephalitis — immediate CT and neurosurgery/neurology activation.
EMERGENT — Seizure: New seizure in context of 2-week headache strongly suggests CVST with cortical irritation, mass lesion, or encephalitis — emergent MRI/MRV.
URGENT — CN VI palsy (lateral gaze palsy, diplopia): False localizing sign of elevated ICP — suggests CVST, IIH, or mass lesion causing diffuse ICP elevation.
URGENT — CN III palsy (ptosis, mydriasis, 'down and out' eye): Suggests posterior communicating artery aneurysm compression — emergent CTA/MRA.
URGENT — Pulsatile tinnitus: Highly specific for IIH (venous hum from elevated CSF pressure transmitted to sigmoid sinus) — if present, IIH becomes leading diagnosis.
URGENT — Transient visual obscurations (brief graying/blackening of vision lasting seconds): Pathognomonic for papilledema and elevated ICP — urgent ophthalmology and neurology evaluation.
URGENT — Oral contraceptive use confirmed: Immediately elevates CVST probability 13-22x — MRV becomes mandatory rather than optional.
URGENT — Headache worsening with recumbency or Valsalva maneuver: Suggests elevated ICP from any cause (mass, CVST, IIH, hydrocephalus).
URGENT — Headache worse in morning upon awakening: Classic pattern for elevated ICP — CO2 accumulation during sleep causes cerebral vasodilation and ICP elevation.
WATCH — Progressive headache severity over the 2-week course: Distinguishes secondary (progressive) from primary (episodic with resolution) headache — must be specifically characterized.
WATCH — Postpartum state (within 6 weeks of delivery): Dramatically elevates CVST risk — must be queried.

treatment_plans.condition: Suspected Primary Migraine (Diagnosis of Exclusion — Secondary Causes Must Be Ruled Out First)
treatment_plans.diagnosis_status: PROVISIONAL — Treatment initiation contingent on negative secondary cause workup

step_1_conservative.label: Conservative & Supportive Measures (Initiate Immediately)
interventions: Place patient in quiet, dimly lit room — reduce photic and auditory stimulation immediately
Oral or IV hydration — dehydration is a common migraine trigger and exacerbant
Cold compress to right temporal/occipital region — vasoconstriction, symptomatic relief
Eliminate dietary triggers: caffeine (or cautious caffeine use if habitual consumer), alcohol, MSG, aged cheeses, processed meats
Sleep hygiene optimization — consistent sleep-wake cycle, 7-9 hours nightly
Stress reduction: identify and document triggers in a headache diary starting today
Screen for medication overuse: quantify analgesic use over past 2 weeks — if daily use, MOH must be addressed

step_2_first_line_pharmacological_acute.label: First-Line Acute Pharmacological Treatment (After Secondary Causes Excluded)
interventions: Sumatriptan 50-100mg oral (first-line triptan — Level A evidence, NNT 3.1 for 2-hour pain freedom)
Ibuprofen 400-600mg oral with food (Level A evidence, NNT 7.2 — use only if no anticoagulation initiated)
Metoclopramide 10mg IV/oral for nausea AND headache adjunct (Level B, NNT 3.2 in ED setting)
Combination Sumatriptan 85mg + Naproxen 500mg (Treximet) — superior to monotherapy if available (Level A, NNT 4.9)

step_2_first_line_pharmacological_preven.label: First-Line Preventive Therapy (Initiate if ≥4 migraine days/month confirmed at follow-up)
interventions: Propranolol 40-240mg/day — Level A evidence, NNT 4.0 for ≥50% frequency reduction (preferred if no asthma/bradycardia)
Topiramate 25-100mg/day — Level A evidence, NNT 3.5 (CAUTION: reduces OCP efficacy at ≥200mg/day; teratogenic — requires pregnancy counseling)
Amitriptyline 10-75mg nightly — Level B evidence (useful if comorbid insomnia or depression)

step_3_second_line_pharmacological.label: Second-Line Options (If First-Line Fails or Contraindicated)
interventions: Gepants — Ubrogepant (Ubrelvy) 50-100mg oral OR Rimegepant (Nurtec ODT) 75mg — Level A; preferred if triptans contraindicated (cardiovascular risk, vasospasm history); NNT ~8.9
Lasmiditan (Reyvow) 100-200mg — Level A; serotonin 1F agonist, no vasoconstrictive properties; NNT ~8.7; NOTE: impairs driving for 8 hours
Prochlorperazine 10mg IV — Level A in ED setting, NNT 2.9; superior to opioids for migraine
Valproate 500-1000mg/day (preventive) — Level A; CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — mandatory pregnancy test before initiation
CGRP monoclonal antibodies (Erenumab/Aimovig, Fremanezumab/Ajovy, Galcanezumab/Emgality) — Level A preventive; NNT 4.3; consider if 2+ preventive agents fail

step_4_adjunctive_therapy.label: Adjunctive Non-Pharmacological Therapy
interventions: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) for headache — Level A evidence for migraine prevention; addresses pain catastrophizing and stress triggers
Biofeedback therapy — Level A evidence; thermal and EMG biofeedback reduce migraine frequency by 40-50%
Acupuncture — Level B evidence; comparable to prophylactic drug therapy in some trials (Cochrane 2016)
Magnesium glycinate 400-600mg/day — Level B preventive; safe, well-tolerated; addresses magnesium deficiency common in migraineurs
Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) 400mg/day — Level B preventive; mitochondrial energy metabolism support
Coenzyme Q10 300mg/day — Level C preventive; antioxidant mechanism

step_5_interventional.label: Interventional Options (If Steps 1-4 Fail)
interventions: OnabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) 155-195 units IM — FDA-approved for chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month); Level A evidence; administered every 12 weeks by neurologist
Greater occipital nerve (GON) block — 1% lidocaine ± methylprednisolone injection; Level B evidence for acute migraine rescue and short-term prevention
Sphenopalatine ganglion (SPG) block — Level B evidence; minimally invasive, performed by pain specialist or neurologist
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) — FDA-cleared device (SpringTMS/eNeura); Level B evidence for acute and preventive migraine treatment
Non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation (nVNS — gammaCore) — FDA-cleared; Level B evidence for acute migraine

step_6_surgical.label: Surgical (Reserved for Refractory Cases or Confirmed Secondary Etiology)
interventions: Neurosurgical intervention — ONLY if intracranial mass, aneurysm, or AVM confirmed on imaging
Anticoagulation (LMWH/UFH then warfarin/DOAC) — if CVST confirmed; this is medical not surgical but life-saving
CSF diversion (lumboperitoneal or ventriculoperitoneal shunt) OR optic nerve sheath fenestration — if IIH confirmed with progressive visual loss refractory to acetazolamide
Surgical decompression — if Chiari malformation identified as cause (low probability in this case)

treatment_plans.first_line: PHASE 1 (Emergency Department — Before Diagnosis Confirmed): IV hydration, dimly lit room, metoclopramide 10mg IV for nausea/headache, ketorolac 15-30mg IV for pain (avoid if anticoagulation anticipated). PHASE 2 (After Secondary Causes Excluded by Imaging): Sumatriptan 50-100mg oral for acute attacks + ibuprofen 400mg. PHASE 3 (Outpatient Preventive — if ≥4 migraine days/month): Propranolol 40mg BID titrated to effect OR topiramate 25mg nightly titrated to 50-100mg/day.

medications.name: Metoclopramide (Reglan)
medications.class: Dopamine D2 antagonist — antiemetic and analgesic adjunct
medications.frequency: Every 6-8 hours as needed
medications.duration: Acute use only — 24-48 hours maximum; do NOT use >5 days continuously
medications.indication: Nausea relief AND headache adjunct in acute migraine
medications.evidence_grade: Level B — NNT 3.2 for headache relief in ED
warnings: Extrapyramidal symptoms (akathisia, acute dystonia) — especially in young women
Co-administer diphenhydramine 25mg IV prophylactically to prevent akathisia
Tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use — limit to short-term only
QT prolongation — avoid with other QT-prolonging agents
Contraindicated with MAO inhibitors
Additive effect with antipsychotics — increased EPS risk
medications.monitoring: Monitor for restlessness, involuntary movements, sedation during administration
medications.pregnancy_safety: Category B — generally considered safe in pregnancy; consult OB if pregnant
medications.renal_adjustment: Reduce dose by 50% if CrCl <40 mL/min

medications.name: Ketorolac (Toradol)
medications.frequency: Every 6 hours as needed
medications.duration: Acute ED use — maximum 5 days total (all routes combined)
medications.indication: Acute migraine pain relief in ED when oral medications not tolerated
medications.evidence_grade: Level B — effective for acute migraine in ED setting
warnings: CONTRAINDICATED if CVST confirmed and anticoagulation initiated — bleeding risk
CONTRAINDICATED in renal impairment, active GI bleeding, peptic ulcer disease
Avoid in pregnancy (especially third trimester — premature closure of ductus arteriosus)
Increases bleeding risk — do NOT use if LP anticipated or anticoagulation planned
NSAIDs + anticoagulants = MAJOR interaction — avoid combination
Maximum 5-day course — renal toxicity with prolonged use
medications.monitoring: Renal function if prolonged use; GI symptoms
medications.pregnancy_safety: Category C (first/second trimester); Category D (third trimester) — AVOID

medications.name: Sumatriptan (Imitrex)
medications.dose: 50mg or 100mg oral; 6mg subcutaneous (faster onset, higher efficacy)
medications.frequency: Once at headache onset; may repeat after 2 hours if partial response
medications.duration: Acute use — maximum 2 doses per attack; maximum 9 days/month to avoid MOH
medications.indication: Acute moderate-severe migraine attack — first-line triptan
medications.evidence_grade: Level A — NNT 3.1 (oral 100mg, 2-hour pain freedom); NNT 2.3 (SC 6mg)
warnings: CONTRAINDICATED in: ischemic heart disease, coronary vasospasm, uncontrolled hypertension, hemiplegic migraine, basilar migraine, stroke/TIA history, peripheral vascular disease
CONTRAINDICATED with MAO inhibitors (within 2 weeks) — severe hypertension and serotonin syndrome risk
CONTRAINDICATED within 24 hours of ergotamine derivatives — additive vasospasm
MODERATE interaction with SSRIs/SNRIs — theoretical serotonin syndrome risk; monitor for agitation, hyperthermia, clonus
DO NOT USE until BP is measured and hypertensive emergency excluded — vasoconstrictive properties dangerous in uncontrolled hypertension
DO NOT USE until CVST excluded — vasoconstrictive properties may worsen venous thrombosis
Medication overuse headache (MOH) risk if used >9 days/month
Chest tightness/pressure sensation common — usually benign but cardiac cause must be excluded
Pregnancy: Category C — limited data; discuss risk/benefit with OB
medications.monitoring: BP before each use; headache diary to track frequency and response; watch for MOH pattern
medications.pregnancy_safety: Category C — use only if benefits outweigh risks; sumatriptan pregnancy registry data generally reassuring but consult OB
medications.renal_adjustment: No dose adjustment required for mild-moderate renal impairment
medications.hepatic_adjustment: Use with caution in severe hepatic impairment; maximum 50mg oral dose
medications.cost: Moderate — generic available; SC auto-injector more expensive

medications.name: Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)
medications.frequency: Every 6-8 hours as needed
medications.duration: Acute use — as needed; avoid daily use >10 days/month to prevent MOH
medications.indication: Mild-moderate migraine; adjunct to triptans
medications.evidence_grade: Level A — NNT 7.2 for 2-hour pain freedom (400mg dose)
warnings: CONTRAINDICATED if CVST confirmed and anticoagulation initiated — major bleeding risk
CONTRAINDICATED in active GI bleeding, peptic ulcer disease, severe renal/hepatic impairment
Avoid in third trimester pregnancy
GI irritation — always take with food
Cardiovascular risk with prolonged use
NSAIDs + anticoagulants = MAJOR interaction
Medication overuse headache if used >15 days/month
medications.monitoring: GI symptoms; renal function with prolonged use
medications.pregnancy_safety: Category C (first/second trimester); Category D (third trimester) — AVOID

medications.name: Ondansetron (Zofran)
medications.frequency: Every 8 hours as needed for nausea
medications.duration: As needed for nausea — acute use
medications.indication: Nausea associated with migraine — alternative to metoclopramide if EPS risk concern
medications.evidence_grade: Level B — effective antiemetic; less evidence for headache relief than metoclopramide
warnings: QT prolongation — avoid with other QT-prolonging agents (antipsychotics, fluoroquinolones, macrolides)
Serotonin syndrome risk when combined with serotonergic agents (triptans, SSRIs) — monitor
Headache (paradoxical) reported as side effect
Less effective than metoclopramide for migraine-specific headache relief
medications.monitoring: ECG if QT prolongation risk; nausea response
medications.pregnancy_safety: Category B — generally considered safe; widely used in pregnancy for hyperemesis

medications.name: Propranolol (Inderal)
medications.dose: Start 40mg BID; titrate to 80-240mg/day in divided doses or extended-release formulation
medications.frequency: BID (immediate-release) or once daily (extended-release)
medications.duration: Minimum 3-month trial to assess efficacy; continue 6-12 months if effective
medications.indication: Migraine prevention — initiate at outpatient follow-up if ≥4 migraine days/month confirmed
medications.evidence_grade: Level A — NNT 4.0 for ≥50% reduction in migraine frequency
warnings: CONTRAINDICATED in: asthma, COPD, decompensated heart failure, heart block (2nd/3rd degree), bradycardia (<60 bpm), cardiogenic shock
CONTRAINDICATED with cocaine use — paradoxical hypertension
Masks hypoglycemia symptoms in diabetics
Do NOT abruptly discontinue — rebound hypertension and angina risk; taper over 2 weeks
May worsen depression — monitor mood
Fatigue, cold extremities, sexual dysfunction common
Interacts with calcium channel blockers — additive bradycardia/hypotension
Pregnancy: Category C — neonatal bradycardia, hypoglycemia reported; use with caution
medications.monitoring: Heart rate and BP at each visit; depression screening; glucose in diabetics
medications.pregnancy_safety: Category C — neonatal effects possible; discuss with OB if pregnancy planned
medications.hepatic_adjustment: Reduce dose in severe hepatic impairment

medications.name: Topiramate (Topamax)
medications.dose: Start 25mg nightly; titrate by 25mg/week to target 50-100mg/day
medications.frequency: Once or twice daily
medications.duration: Minimum 3-month trial; continue 6-12 months if effective
medications.indication: Migraine prevention — second-line or first-line alternative to propranolol
medications.evidence_grade: Level A — NNT 3.5 for ≥50% reduction in migraine frequency

pico_question.P: 35-year-old female presenting with 2-week history of persistent unilateral right-sided throbbing headache (6/10), photophobia, and nausea — no documented fever, focal neurological deficits, or thunderclap onset
pico_question.I: Clinical evaluation including neuroimaging (CT/MRI), laboratory workup, lumbar puncture if indicated, and pharmacological treatment (triptans, NSAIDs, antiemetics)
pico_question.C: Empirical migraine treatment without secondary cause workup vs. full diagnostic evaluation prior to treatment
pico_question.O: Primary outcomes: accurate diagnosis, exclusion of life-threatening secondary headache causes (SAH, CVST, meningitis, intracranial mass), symptom resolution, prevention of recurrence, functional restoration. Secondary outcomes: time-to-diagnosis, medication overuse, quality of life

primary_headache_diagnosis.source: International Headache Society (IHS) — ICHD-3 Diagnostic Criteria, 2018

migraine_without_aura_criteria.criteria: ≥5 attacks lasting 4–72 hours with ≥2 of: unilateral location, pulsating quality, moderate-severe intensity, aggravation by routine activity; AND ≥1 of: nausea/vomiting, photophobia/phonophobia
migraine_without_aura_criteria.applicability_to_case: Patient meets: unilateral location (right-sided), pulsating/throbbing quality, 6/10 intensity, photophobia, nausea. Duration of 2 weeks is atypical for single attack — suggests either chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month) or new persistent daily headache (NDPH) pattern requiring further characterization
migraine_without_aura_criteria.evidence_grade: A — Consensus-based diagnostic criteria with high inter-rater reliability (Level VII expert consensus, but universally adopted)

safety.safety_summary: This 35-year-old female presenting with a 2-week persistent right-sided throbbing headache (6/10), photophobia, and nausea has received a comprehensive multi-agent workup that is clinically thorough and largely appropriate. However, the safety review has identified four CRITICAL safety gaps and multiple HIGH and MODERATE concerns that must be resolved before the treatment plan is finalized or communicated to the patient. The most urgent critical issues are: (1) Topiramate's warnings array is completely empty in the treatment plan — a documentation failure that could result in this teratogenic medication being prescribed to a pregnant patient or a patient on oral contraceptives without appropriate counseling; (2) Blood pressure has not been obtained, making sumatriptan and NSAIDs potentially unsafe to administer; (3) Pregnancy status is unknown, creating contraindication risk for topiramate, valproate, ketorolac, and CT radiation; and (4) Oral contraceptive use is undocumented, which is the single most important risk factor for CVST in this demographic and affects multiple treatment decisions. The treatment plan's sequencing — withholding sumatriptan until secondary causes are excluded — is clinically correct and represents sound safety practice. The diagnostic workup recommended (CT head, MRI/MRV, LP if indicated) is appropriate and evidence-based. The drug interaction warnings documented by the research agent are accurate and well-characterized. The primary safety failures are in documentation completeness (topiramate warnings), missing prerequisite clinical data (BP, pregnancy test, OCP history, full medication reconciliation), and two undocumented drug interactions (ondansetron + sumatriptan serotonin syndrome risk; ondansetron + metoclopramide QT prolongation risk). These issues must be corrected before output reaches the patient. Overall safety status is PASS_WITH_WARNINGS — the plan is clinically sound in structure but requires the identified corrections before safe implementation.

empathy.patient_summary:
You came in today because you have been dealing with a throbbing headache on the right side of your head for the past 2 weeks, along with sensitivity to light and some nausea. You are doing the right thing by getting this checked out — and we want you to know that you are in good hands.

Your symptoms look a lot like migraine, which is one of the most common health conditions in women your age. In fact, about 1 in 4 women between the ages of 25 and 55 experience migraines. The throbbing pain on one side, light sensitivity, and nausea are classic signs.

However, because your headache has lasted 2 full weeks without going away — which is longer than a typical migraine — your medical team wants to do some important tests first. This is not meant to alarm you. It is simply good, careful medicine. The goal is to make sure nothing else is causing your headache before starting treatment. Most people in your situation turn out to have a primary headache disorder like migraine, and the outlook for that is very good with the right care.

Here is what your care team is focused on right now: getting your blood pressure checked, doing a careful neurological exam (checking your eyes, reflexes, and coordination), and likely ordering a brain scan. These steps will help your doctors give you the most accurate diagnosis and the safest, most effective treatment plan.
empathy.what_this_means:
Your symptoms — a one-sided throbbing headache, light sensitivity, and nausea — fit the pattern of migraine very well. Migraine is not just a bad headache. It is a neurological condition where certain nerves and blood vessels in the brain become overactivated, causing intense, often one-sided pain along with other symptoms like nausea and sensitivity to light or sound.

Think of it like a temporary electrical storm in part of your brain. The storm causes real, physical symptoms — and it can be treated.

The reason your doctors are being thorough is that a headache lasting 2 weeks straight is slightly unusual for a typical migraine attack, which usually lasts between 4 hours and 3 days. So before labeling this as migraine, they want to rule out a few other possible causes. Some of these causes are rare but important to check for, especially in women your age. The most important ones your team is watching for include:

• A condition called CVST (Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis) — this is a rare type of blood clot in the veins of the brain. It is more common in women of reproductive age, especially those who use birth control pills. It causes a gradually worsening headache over days to weeks — which matches your timeline. It is treatable with blood thinners if caught.

• Increased pressure inside the skull (called Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension or IIH) — this can cause headaches, nausea, and light sensitivity. It is more common in women your age and is diagnosed with a special spinal fluid test.

• A brain scan is also being done to make sure there is no other structural cause for your headache, such as a growth or swelling. This is very unlikely given your age and symptoms, but it is a standard and important step.

The good news: most people with your symptoms are diagnosed with migraine, which is very manageable. Even if another cause is found, most of these conditions are treatable when caught early.

right_now: Let the nurse or doctor take your blood pressure in both arms right away — this is the first and most important step before any medication is given
Tell your doctor or nurse if you are currently taking any birth control pills, patches, or hormonal devices — this is very important information for your diagnosis

Tell your doctor about ALL medications you are currently taking, including over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen (Advil), acetaminophen (Tylenol), or naproxen (Aleve), and any vitamins or supplements
Tell your doctor if there is any chance you could be pregnant — a simple urine test will be done before any scans or certain medications are given

Tell your doctor if you have been taking pain relievers every day for the past 2 weeks to manage this headache — this is important because daily pain reliever use can actually make headaches worse over time
Rest in a quiet, dimly lit room while you wait — reducing light and noise can help ease your symptoms right now
Drink water if you are able to — staying hydrated can help with headache pain
Apply a cool, damp cloth to your right temple or the back of your neck for comfort
this_week: Complete any brain imaging your doctor orders — likely a CT scan first, then possibly an MRI with a special test to look at the veins in your brain (called an MRV). These are painless tests that take pictures of your brain
Have your blood drawn for lab tests — these check for infection, inflammation, blood counts, and other possible causes of your headache
Follow up with your doctor or a neurologist (a brain and nervous system specialist) within the next few days to review your test results

Start a headache diary — write down each day: how bad the headache is (0-10), how long it lasts, what you were doing when it started, what you ate or drank, how much sleep you got, and any medications you took. This information is very helpful for your doctor
Avoid taking over-the-counter pain relievers more than 2-3 times per week — using them too often can cause 'rebound headaches' that are harder to treat
Avoid known headache triggers this week: alcohol, caffeine changes, skipped meals, poor sleep, and bright lights or loud environments
ongoing: Attend all follow-up appointments with your neurologist or primary care doctor — migraine is a condition that benefits greatly from ongoing, personalized care

If migraine is confirmed, discuss a prevention plan with your doctor — there are very effective daily medications (like propranolol or topiramate) that can significantly reduce how often migraines happen
Ask your doctor about a rescue medication to use at the start of a migraine attack — triptans (like sumatriptan) are very effective when taken early and are safe for most people
Continue your headache diary every day — tracking patterns helps identify your personal triggers and helps your doctor adjust your treatment

Stay well hydrated — aim for 6-8 glasses of water daily

medications_explained.name: Metoclopramide (brand name: Reglan)
medications_explained.what_it_is: A medication that helps with nausea AND headache pain at the same time
medications_explained.how_it_works: It calms the part of your brain that triggers nausea and also helps reduce headache pain by blocking certain chemical signals
medications_explained.how_it_is_given: Usually through an IV (a small needle in your vein) in the emergency or urgent care setting, or as a pill
medications_explained.important_to_know: Some people — especially younger women — can experience restlessness or muscle stiffness after this medication. To prevent this, your doctor will likely give you a second medication called diphenhydramine (Benadryl) at the same time. This is a routine precaution, not a sign that anything is wrong. Do not use this medication for more than a few days in a row.
medications_explained.safety_note: Tell your doctor if you take any antipsychotic medications, as this can interact with metoclopramide

medications_explained.name: Ketorolac (brand name: Toradol)
medications_explained.what_it_is: A strong anti-inflammatory pain reliever given through an IV or injection — similar to ibuprofen but much stronger and faster-acting
medications_explained.how_it_works: It reduces inflammation and blocks pain signals
medications_explained.how_it_is_given: Through an IV or injection in the medical setting
medications_explained.important_to_know: This medication can only be used for a maximum of 5 days. It cannot be used if you are on blood thinners. Always take it with food if switching to an oral form.
medications_explained.safety_note: This medication will NOT be given until your blood pressure is checked and your pregnancy test result is known

medications_explained.name: Sumatriptan (brand name: Imitrex)
medications_explained.what_it_is: A migraine-specific medication called a 'triptan' — one of the most effective treatments for migraine attacks
medications_explained.how_it_works: It works directly on the pain pathways involved in migraine by calming overactivated nerves and narrowing blood vessels that have widened during a migraine. Think of it as a targeted 'off switch' for the migraine process.
medications_explained.how_it_is_given: As a pill (50mg or 100mg) or as a self-injection under the skin for faster relief
medications_explained.how_to_use_it: Take it as early as possible when a migraine starts — the sooner you take it, the better it works. You can take a second dose after 2 hours if the headache comes back or only partially improves.
medications_explained.important_to_know: Do not use more than 9 days per month — using it too often can cause 'medication overuse headaches.' Do not drive after taking the injection form until you know how it affects you.
medications_explained.safety_note: IMPORTANT: This medication will NOT be prescribed until your blood pressure is checked and your brain scan results are reviewed. It is not safe to use if you have very high blood pressure or certain vascular conditions. Tell your doctor if you have heart disease, have had a stroke, or take antidepressants.

medications_explained.name: Ibuprofen (brand names: Advil, Motrin)
medications_explained.what_it_is: An over-the-counter anti-inflammatory pain reliever
medications_explained.how_it_works: Reduces inflammation and blocks pain signals throughout the body
medications_explained.how_to_use_it: 400-600mg with food, every 6-8 hours as needed. Always take with food or milk to protect your stomach.
medications_explained.important_to_know: Do not use more than 15 days per month — daily use can cause 'rebound headaches' that are harder to treat. Cannot be used if you are on blood thinners.
medications_explained.safety_note: Do not use if your doctor starts you on blood thinners for any reason

medications_explained.name: Ondansetron (brand name: Zofran)
medications_explained.what_it_is: An anti-nausea medication
medications_explained.how_it_works: Blocks the chemical signals in your brain and gut that cause nausea and vomiting
medications_explained.how_it_is_given: As a dissolving tablet that melts under your tongue, or through an IV
medications_explained.important_to_know: Very effective for nausea. Tell your doctor if you take any heart medications, antibiotics, or antipsychotic medications, as some combinations require extra monitoring.
medications_explained.safety_note: Generally safe and well-tolerated. Widely used during pregnancy for severe nausea.

medications_explained.name: Propranolol (brand name: Inderal) — for PREVENTION only
medications_explained.what_it_is: A blood pressure medication that is also one of the most proven migraine prevention medications
medications_explained.how_it_works: It calms overactive nerve signals that trigger migraines. Think of it as turning down the 'volume' on your brain's sensitivity.
medications_explained.how_to_use_it: Taken as a daily pill — usually starting at a low dose and gradually increasing. It takes 4-8 weeks to see the full benefit.
medications_explained.important_to_know: Do NOT stop this medication suddenly — always taper off slowly under your doctor's guidance. Tell your doctor if you have asthma, a slow heart rate, or diabetes.
medications_explained.safety_note: This is a preventive medication — it will not help during an active migraine attack. It is meant to reduce how often migraines happen.

medications_explained.name: Topiramate (brand name: Topamax) — for PREVENTION only
medications_explained.what_it_is: An anti-seizure medication that is also FDA-approved for migraine prevention
medications_explained.how_it_works: Stabilizes overactive nerve activity in the brain that contributes to migraines
medications_explained.how_to_use_it: Taken as a daily pill, starting at a very low dose and slowly increasing over several weeks
medications_explained.important_to_know: This medication has several important safety considerations your doctor will discuss with you in detail: (1) It can cause birth defects — a pregnancy test is required before starting, and reliable contraception is essential while taking it. (2) It can reduce the effectiveness of birth control pills — your doctor will discuss alternative contraception options. (3) Some people experience memory or word-finding difficulties — this is usually mild and dose-related. (4) It can cause kidney stones — drink plenty of water. (5) It can cause tingling in the hands and feet — usually temporary.
medications_explained.safety_note: CRITICAL: This medication CANNOT be started if you are pregnant or trying to become pregnant. Please discuss your family planning goals with your doctor before starting this medication. Do not start this medication without a full discussion with your doctor about these safety points.

empathy.lifestyle_tips:
Living with migraines can feel exhausting and frustrating — especially when they interrupt your work, your relationships, and the things you love to do. You are not alone in this. Migraine is the leading cause of disability in women under 50, which means millions of people understand exactly what you are going through.

The good news is that lifestyle changes can make a real, meaningful difference — sometimes as much as medication. Here are some of the most effective things you can do:

**Sleep is your most powerful tool.** Going to bed and waking up at the same time every day — even on weekends — is one of the single most effective ways to reduce migraine frequency. Your brain thrives on routine.

**Stay hydrated.** Even mild dehydration is a well-known migraine trigger. Aim for 6-8 glasses of water daily. If you drink coffee regularly, do not skip it suddenly — caffeine withdrawal is also a trigger. Either maintain a consistent amount or reduce very gradually.

**Eat regular meals.** Skipping meals causes blood sugar drops that can trigger migraines. Try to eat at consistent times each day, and keep a small snack available.

**Manage stress — even a little bit helps.** You do not need to eliminate stress (that is not realistic). But even 10 minutes of deep breathing, gentle stretching, or quiet time daily can reduce your nervous system's overall reactivity. Many people find that apps like Headspace or Calm are helpful starting points.

**Keep a headache diary.** This is one of the most valuable things you can do. Write down each day: your headache level (0-10), sleep hours, meals, stress level, weather changes, menstrual cycle phase, and any medications taken. Over time, patterns will emerge that help you and your doctor identify your personal triggers.

**Common triggers to watch for:** Bright or flickering lights, strong smells, alcohol (especially red wine), aged cheeses, processed meats, MSG, hormonal changes around your menstrual cycle, weather changes, and stress.

**Consider magnesium.** Many people with migraines have low magnesium levels. A daily supplement of magnesium glycinate (400mg) is safe, inexpensive, and has good scientific evidence for reducing migraine frequency. Ask your doctor before starting.

**Many people find it helpful to** work with a therapist trained in biofeedback or cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for headache. These are non-medication approaches with strong scientific support — they teach your brain and body to respond differently to pain signals.
when_to_get_help: Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room IMMEDIATELY if your headache suddenly becomes the worst headache of your life — especially if it feels like it came on in seconds like a 'thunderclap' or 'explosion' in your head. This can be a sign of bleeding in the brain.
Go to the emergency room IMMEDIATELY if you develop any weakness, numbness, or tingling on one side of your body or face
Go to the emergency room IMMEDIATELY if you have trouble speaking, understanding speech, or finding words
Go to the emergency room IMMEDIATELY if you have sudden vision changes, double vision, or loss of vision in one or both eyes
Go to the emergency room IMMEDIATELY if you have a seizure (shaking you cannot control, loss of consciousness)
Go to the emergency room IMMEDIATELY if you become confused, unusually drowsy, or difficult to wake up
Go to the emergency room IMMEDIATELY if you develop a stiff neck along with your headache — especially if combined with fever or sensitivity to light
Go to the emergency room IMMEDIATELY if your headache is accompanied by a fever above 38.5°C (101.3°F)
Call your doctor or go to urgent care TODAY if your headache suddenly becomes significantly worse than it has been over the past 2 weeks

Call your doctor TODAY if you develop new symptoms you did not have before, such as ringing in your ears, brief episodes where your vision goes gray or black for a few seconds, or a whooshing sound in your ears
Call your doctor TODAY if you vomit and cannot keep fluids down
Call your doctor if your headache does not improve after taking prescribed medications as directed
Call your doctor if you notice your headache is consistently worse when you first wake up in the morning, or worse when you lie down
Trust your instincts — if something feels different or more serious than usual, seek help. You know your body best.
