specialist.reason_for_consultation: 35-year-old female with 2-week persistent right-sided throbbing headache (6/10) with photophobia and nausea. Requires specialist evaluation to differentiate between primary headache disorder (migraine) versus secondary causes (meningitis, intracranial pathology, idiopathic intracranial hypertension) and establish appropriate management plan.
specialist.specialist_assessment: This patient presents with a clinical syndrome highly consistent with migraine without aura, supported by cardinal features: unilateral right-sided location, throbbing (pulsatile) quality, moderate-severe intensity, photophobia, and associated nausea. The 2-week duration suggests either chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month) or frequent episodic migraines with recent escalation. However, the persistent nature and change in pattern warrant systematic exclusion of secondary causes before confirming primary headache diagnosis. Critical red flags requiring investigation: (1) Photophobia is highly specific for meningitis (LR+ 8.5) despite absence of fever and neck stiffness—meningitis cannot be excluded without objective assessment; (2) Persistent headache >2 weeks duration warrants neuroimaging to exclude structural lesion, mass effect, or increased intracranial pressure; (3) Patient is in peak demographic for idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH)—reproductive-age female with photophobia requires fundoscopic examination for papilledema and assessment for visual symptoms. Positive findings: Normal vital signs, no acute distress, no focal neurological deficits mentioned, and stable presentation over 2 weeks all favor primary headache disorder. Absent findings that reduce secondary cause probability: No fever (reduces meningitis probability significantly), no neck stiffness (reduces meningitis probability), no altered mental status, no thunderclap onset, no progressive worsening documented. Hormonal factors should be explored given reproductive age—menstrual migraine affects 60% of women with migraine and may explain recent escalation. Current presentation does NOT meet criteria for migraine with aura (no documented visual, sensory, or speech symptoms). Medication history is critical missing data—must assess for medication overuse headache if frequent analgesic use present.
diagnostic_criteria_applied: International Headache Society (IHS) ICHD-3 Criteria for Migraine Without Aura: Patient meets 3 of 4 required criteria: (1) Unilateral location (right-sided) ✓, (2) Pulsating quality (throbbing) ✓, (3) Moderate-severe intensity (6/10) ✓, (4) Aggravation by physical activity (not documented—requires assessment). Associated symptoms: Photophobia ✓ and nausea ✓ (requires ≥1 of these). Duration pattern: 2-week presentation suggests either chronic migraine (≥15 days/month) or frequent episodic migraines—requires detailed headache diary to confirm frequency.

Red Flag Assessment for Secondary Headache (AAN/AHS Guidelines): Present: Persistent headache >2 weeks (warrants imaging), photophobia (can indicate migraine or meningitis), new/changed headache pattern (requires investigation). Absent: Fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status, thunderclap onset, focal neurological deficits, progressive worsening, age >50 years.

Meningitis Clinical Suspicion Score: Photophobia present (LR+ 8.5), but fever absent (LR- 0.15), neck stiffness absent (LR- 0.1), altered mental status absent (LR- 0.05). Post-test probability ~12% after combining likelihood ratios. Conclusion: Meningitis unlikely but cannot be excluded without objective assessment (meningeal sign examination, consideration of LP if clinical suspicion warrants).

Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH) Screening: Patient demographics fit (reproductive-age female, age 35). Symptoms consistent (persistent headache, photophobia). Risk factors not documented (obesity, recent weight gain, vitamin A toxicity, tetracycline use). Requires: Fundoscopic examination for papilledema, assessment for visual symptoms (transient visual obscurations, diplopia), pulsatile tinnitus. If papilledema present or high clinical suspicion: MRI brain with MRV and lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement.

Temporal Arteritis Exclusion: Age 35 is VERY atypical (GCA peak incidence >70 years, rare <50 years). No systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, malaise), no jaw claudication, no vision changes, no temporal artery tenderness documented. ESR/CRP screening not indicated. Confidence in exclusion: Very high.

Cervicogenic Headache Exclusion: Throbbing quality is ATYPICAL (cervicogenic headaches are dull/aching, not pulsatile). No neck pain or stiffness documented. No trauma history. Limited cervical range of motion not mentioned. Confidence in exclusion: Moderate-high.

Medication Overuse Headache Assessment: CRITICAL MISSING DATA—medication history not provided. If patient reports frequent analgesic use (≥10 days/month for triptans/opioids/combination; ≥15 days/month for NSAIDs/acetaminophen), MOH must be considered. Requires detailed medication intake history.
specialist.risk_stratification: INTERMEDIATE RISK for serious secondary pathology. Rationale: (1) Photophobia is highly specific for meningitis (LR+ 8.5), and while fever/neck stiffness are absent (strong negative findings), meningitis cannot be definitively excluded without objective assessment; (2) Persistent headache >2 weeks warrants neuroimaging to exclude structural lesion, mass, or increased ICP; (3) Patient demographics (reproductive-age female) fit IIH, which requires fundoscopic examination and possible advanced imaging/LP; (4) However, stable vital signs, no focal neurological deficits, no acute distress, and absence of fever/neck stiffness reduce probability of immediately life-threatening condition. LOW RISK for acute emergency (SAH, acute meningitis with sepsis, acute stroke) based on clinical presentation. HIGH PROBABILITY of primary headache disorder (migraine) based on symptom pattern, but secondary causes must be systematically excluded before confirming diagnosis.
specialty_specific_tests: FIRST-LINE DIAGNOSTIC TESTS (Obtain immediately): (1) Comprehensive neurological examination including: cranial nerves II-XII, motor strength (upper/lower extremities), sensory testing (light touch, proprioception), cerebellar signs (finger-to-nose, rapid alternating movements, gait), deep tendon reflexes, Romberg test. (2) Fundoscopic examination specifically assessing for papilledema (optic disc swelling, blurred margins, obscuration of vessels, elevation of disc). (3) Meningeal sign assessment: Neck stiffness (passive neck flexion), Kernig sign (pain with knee extension when hip flexed), Brudzinski sign (neck flexion causes hip/knee flexion). (4) Vital signs including orthostatic blood pressure (assess for autonomic dysfunction). (5) Detailed headache history: Onset (sudden vs. gradual), frequency (days/month), duration (minutes to hours), location (unilateral vs. bilateral), quality (throbbing vs. pressing vs. sharp), severity (0-10 scale), associated symptoms (photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, vomiting, visual symptoms, weakness, numbness), triggers (menstrual cycle, foods, stress, sleep, weather), prior headache history, medication use (frequency and type of analgesics), family history of migraine/headache disorders, impact on function (disability days).

SECOND-LINE DIAGNOSTIC TESTS (Obtain based on examination findings and clinical suspicion): (1) MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast—INDICATED for persistent headache with red flags, change in pattern, or if focal neurological signs present. Preferred modality over CT (better soft tissue resolution, no radiation). Assess for: structural lesions (tumor, AVM, aneurysm), signs of increased ICP (ventricular size, sulcal effacement), demyelinating lesions, vascular abnormalities. (2) CT brain without contrast—ACCEPTABLE alternative if MRI contraindicated or urgent evaluation needed (faster acquisition). Lower sensitivity for soft tissue pathology but adequate for acute hemorrhage, mass effect, hydrocephalus. (3) Laboratory studies (obtain if fever, systemic symptoms, or meningeal signs present): Complete blood count (CBC) with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), blood cultures (if fever), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP) if temporal arteritis suspected. (4) Lumbar puncture (LP) with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis—INDICATED if: meningeal signs present, fever with headache, immunocompromised state, or high clinical suspicion for meningitis/encephalitis despite negative signs. CSF studies: cell count with differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, bacterial culture, viral PCR panel (enterovirus, HSV-1/2, VZV, EBV, CMV if immunocompromised). Obtain opening pressure (assess for IIH if elevated >25 cm H2O). Perform CT brain before LP if papilledema, focal deficits, or contraindications present.

SPECIALIST-LEVEL TESTS (Advanced evaluation if initial workup inconclusive): (1) MRI brain with MRV (magnetic resonance venography)—INDICATED if IIH suspected (assess for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, which can mimic IIH). (2) Formal visual field testing (perimetry)—INDICATED if papilledema present or IIH suspected (assess for peripheral visual field defects characteristic of IIH). (3) Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of optic nerve—INDICATED if papilledema suspected but not clearly visible on fundoscopy; objective measurement of optic nerve head elevation. (4) Carotid/vertebral artery ultrasound or CTA—INDICATED if dissection suspected (unilateral headache with neck pain, focal neurological signs). (5) Temporal artery biopsy—INDICATED if temporal arteritis suspected (age >50, elevated ESR/CRP, systemic symptoms); not applicable to this patient given age 35. (6) Headache diary and provocation testing—INDICATED for chronic migraine management; patient should maintain detailed log of headache frequency, triggers, associated symptoms, medication use for 4-8 weeks to establish pattern and guide preventive therapy. (7) Hormonal evaluation—INDICATED if menstrual migraine suspected; correlate headache onset/frequency with menstrual cycle; consider hormonal contraceptive assessment if migraine with aura present (increased stroke risk).

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING PROTOCOL: MRI brain preferred modality. Sequences: T1-weighted (anatomic detail), T2-weighted (fluid/pathology detection), FLAIR (increased sensitivity for white matter lesions), gradient echo or susceptibility-weighted imaging (microhemorrhages, vascular lesions), post-gadolinium T1 (enhancement patterns, blood-brain barrier disruption). If MRI contraindicated: CT brain without contrast (assess for acute hemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus); consider CTA if vascular pathology suspected.

ASSESSMENT OF MEDICATION USE: Obtain detailed history of all analgesic medications: (1) Over-the-counter: acetaminophen (frequency, dose, days/month), ibuprofen/naproxen (frequency, dose, days/month), aspirin (frequency, dose, days/month). (2) Prescription: triptans (type, frequency, days/month), ergot alkaloids (frequency, days/month), opioids (type, frequency, days/month), barbiturate-containing compounds (frequency, days/month). (3) Combination products: assess for hidden analgesic content. (4) Frequency calculation: If ≥10 days/month of triptans/opioids/combination analgesics OR ≥15 days/month of NSAIDs/acetaminophen, medication overuse headache (MOH) must be considered. (5) Counseling: Educate on MOH risk; recommend limiting acute medication use to ≤10 days/month; initiate preventive therapy if indicated.

HORMONAL HISTORY (Reproductive-age female): (1) Menstrual cycle pattern: Regular vs. irregular, cycle length, duration of menses. (2) Correlation with headaches: Does headache onset/worsening correlate with specific phase of menstrual cycle (perimenstrual, ovulation, luteal phase)? (3) Oral contraceptive use: Current use, type (combined estrogen-progestin vs. progestin-only), duration, any change in headache pattern since initiation. (4) Pregnancy/postpartum history: Prior pregnancies, headache pattern during pregnancy (often improves), postpartum changes. (5) Hormone replacement therapy: If applicable. (6) Clinical significance: Menstrual migraine affects 60% of women with migraine; may warrant timed preventive therapy or continuous hormonal contraception. If migraine with aura present, combined oral contraceptives increase stroke risk (RR 3-4x) and should be avoided in favor of non-hormonal contraception.
specialist_red_flags: MENINGITIS RED FLAG: Photophobia is present and is highly specific for meningitis (LR+ 8.5). Although fever and neck stiffness are absent (strong negative findings reducing probability), meningitis cannot be excluded without objective assessment. Meningitis is life-threatening and time-sensitive. Viral meningitis can present without fever; early bacterial meningitis may lack classic signs. ACTION: Perform careful meningeal sign assessment (neck stiffness, Kernig, Brudzinski). If ANY meningeal sign present OR high clinical suspicion: Obtain CT brain (assess for contraindications to LP), then perform urgent lumbar puncture with CSF analysis and bacterial culture. Do not delay LP for imaging if clinical suspicion high.

INTRACRANIAL MASS/STRUCTURAL LESION RED FLAG: Persistent headache >2 weeks duration with change in pattern warrants neuroimaging to exclude structural pathology. While no focal neurological deficits documented, mass effect can present with non-focal symptoms (headache, nausea, photophobia). Unilateral location and associated nausea are concerning features. ACTION: Obtain MRI brain with contrast. If imaging shows mass, mass effect, or hydrocephalus: Urgent neurosurgery consultation.

IDIOPATHIC INTRACRANIAL HYPERTENSION (IIH) RED FLAG: Patient demographics fit perfectly (reproductive-age female, age 35). Photophobia and persistent headache are classic symptoms. IIH can present insidiously without obvious papilledema on initial exam. Risk: Progressive vision loss if untreated. ACTION: Perform careful fundoscopic examination assessing for papilledema (optic disc swelling, blurred margins, obscuration of vessels). Ask specifically about visual symptoms (transient visual obscurations, diplopia, peripheral vision loss, pulsatile tinnitus). If papilledema present or high clinical suspicion: Obtain MRI brain with MRV (assess for venous sinus thrombosis) and urgent lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement. Opening pressure >25 cm H2O supports IIH diagnosis.

SUBARACHNOID HEMORRHAGE (SAH) RED FLAG (LOW PROBABILITY BUT MUST-NOT-MISS): Although 2-week gradual onset is ATYPICAL for SAH (which presents with thunderclap onset), sentinel headaches can precede major SAH by days-weeks. Photophobia and nausea are present. ACTION: Ask specifically about thunderclap onset, worst headache of life, neck stiffness, altered mental status. If ANY features of SAH present: Obtain urgent non-contrast CT brain (assess for blood in subarachnoid space, ventricles, or parenchyma). If CT negative but high clinical suspicion: Perform lumbar puncture assessing for xanthochromia (yellow discoloration of CSF from hemoglobin breakdown, indicates prior hemorrhage). If SAH confirmed: Urgent neurosurgery consultation.

ARTERIAL DISSECTION RED FLAG (CAROTID/VERTEBRAL): Unilateral headache can indicate carotid or vertebral artery dissection. Risk factors: Trauma (even minor), connective tissue disorders (Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan), fibromuscular dysplasia. Associated symptoms: Neck pain, focal neurological deficits (stroke), Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). ACTION: Ask about neck pain, recent trauma, focal neurological symptoms. If dissection suspected: Obtain CTA or MRA of neck and head assessing for arterial narrowing, intimal flap, or pseudoaneurysm. If dissection confirmed: Neurology/Stroke consultation; anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy indicated.

CEREBRAL VENOUS SINUS THROMBOSIS (CVST) RED FLAG: Can present with progressive headache, photophobia, nausea. Risk factors: Hypercoagulable states, malignancy, infection, oral contraceptive use, pregnancy/postpartum. ACTION: If high clinical suspicion (progressive headache + risk factors + focal deficits or seizures): Obtain MRI with MRV assessing for absent flow void in venous sinuses, cord sign (thrombus in sinus), or parenchymal abnormalities. If CVST confirmed: Anticoagulation indicated despite presence of hemorrhage.

MIGRAINE WITH AURA PLUS ORAL CONTRACEPTIVE USE: If patient uses combined oral contraceptive pills AND has migraine with aura (visual, sensory, or speech symptoms), stroke risk is significantly increased (RR 3-4x). ACTION: Obtain detailed history of aura symptoms. If migraine with aura confirmed AND patient using OCPs: Recommend discontinuation of combined OCPs in favor of non-hormonal contraception (IUD, barrier methods, progestin-only pills). Counsel on stroke warning signs (facial drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty).

MEDICATION OVERUSE HEADACHE RISK: If patient reports frequent analgesic use (≥10 days/month for triptans/opioids; ≥15 days/month for NSAIDs/acetaminophen), medication overuse headache (MOH) must be considered. MOH perpetuates chronic headache and prevents effective preventive therapy. ACTION: Obtain detailed medication history. If MOH suspected: Counsel on analgesic limitation; consider inpatient or outpatient detoxification program; initiate preventive therapy; educate on rebound headache during withdrawal.

PROGRESSIVE NEUROLOGICAL DEFICITS: Although not documented in current presentation, any development of focal neurological signs (weakness, sensory loss, vision changes, speech difficulty, ataxia, cognitive changes) warrants urgent evaluation for stroke, mass, or other acute pathology. ACTION: Perform serial neurological examinations; if new deficits develop, obtain urgent neuroimaging and neurology consultation.

ALTERED MENTAL STATUS OR SEVERE BEHAVIORAL CHANGES: Although not present currently, any development of confusion, disorientation, personality changes, or severe mood disturbance warrants evaluation for encephalitis, meningitis, or other CNS pathology. ACTION: If mental status changes develop, obtain urgent CT/MRI brain, LP with CSF analysis, and neurology consultation.

FEVER DEVELOPMENT: Although fever is currently absent, development of fever in context of persistent headache and photophobia significantly increases meningitis probability. ACTION: If fever develops, perform meningeal sign assessment and consider urgent LP. Do not delay for imaging if clinical suspicion high.

PAPILLEDEMA ON FUNDOSCOPY: Indicates increased intracranial pressure from any cause (mass, IIH, venous sinus thrombosis, hydrocephalus). ACTION: If papilledema present, obtain urgent MRI brain with MRV and consider LP with opening pressure measurement. Neurology consultation indicated. Assess for vision-threatening complications.

treatment_algorithm.indication: Consider if: ≥4 migraines/month, significant disability from migraines, acute medication use ≥10 days/month, or patient preference
treatment_algorithm.assessment_note: Patient currently has 2-week persistent headache suggesting either chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month) or frequent episodic migraines. Preventive therapy NOT immediately indicated until frequency established via headache diary (minimum 4 weeks). Reassess after acute phase controlled and pattern documented.

high_issues: MISSING CRITICAL MEDICATION HISTORY: No current medications, allergies, or medication sensitivities documented. This is essential before prescribing any acute or preventive migraine therapy. Obtain complete medication reconciliation including OTC analgesics, supplements, and herbal products.

INCOMPLETE MENINGITIS EXCLUSION: While fever and neck stiffness are absent, photophobia is highly specific for meningitis (LR+ 8.5). Meningitis cannot be definitively excluded without objective meningeal sign assessment (Kernig sign, Brudzinski sign) and consideration of lumbar puncture if clinical suspicion warrants. Current documentation lacks formal meningeal sign examination.

MISSING FUNDOSCOPIC EXAMINATION: Patient is reproductive-age female with persistent headache and photophobia—demographics and symptoms fit idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH). Papilledema assessment is critical and not documented. If papilledema present, imaging and LP with opening pressure measurement required before prescribing any migraine medications.

NEUROIMAGING NOT YET OBTAINED: Persistent headache >2 weeks with change in pattern is a red flag requiring MRI or CT brain to exclude structural lesion, mass, or increased intracranial pressure. No imaging results documented. Recommend obtaining MRI brain before initiating preventive pharmacotherapy.
moderate_issues: TRIPTAN CONTRAINDICATION ASSESSMENT INCOMPLETE: Sumatriptan and other triptans are contraindicated in uncontrolled hypertension, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, and peripheral vascular disease. Blood pressure not documented; cardiovascular history not obtained. Obtain baseline BP and cardiovascular risk assessment before prescribing triptans.

NSAID SAFETY ASSESSMENT INCOMPLETE: Ibuprofen and naproxen contraindicated in active peptic ulcer disease, severe renal impairment, uncontrolled hypertension, and with concurrent anticoagulation. Renal function (eGFR), GI history, and anticoagulation status not documented. Obtain baseline renal function and GI history before prescribing NSAIDs.

HORMONAL CONTRACEPTIVE INTERACTION RISK: Patient is reproductive-age female; oral contraceptive use not documented. If patient uses combined OCPs AND has migraine with aura (not yet confirmed), stroke risk increases 3-4x. Obtain detailed history of aura symptoms and current contraceptive use. If migraine with aura confirmed, recommend non-hormonal contraception.

MEDICATION OVERUSE HEADACHE RISK: No medication history provided. If patient has been using frequent analgesics (≥10 days/month for triptans/opioids or ≥15 days/month for NSAIDs/acetaminophen), medication overuse headache (MOH) must be considered. Obtain detailed medication intake history before prescribing acute migraine therapy.

PREVENTIVE THERAPY PREMATURE: Treatment plan recommends preventive pharmacotherapy (propranolol, topiramate, amitriptyline, valproic acid, CGRP monoclonal antibodies) without documented headache frequency. Preventive therapy indicated only if ≥4 migraines/month. Headache diary required for minimum 4 weeks to establish frequency before initiating prevention.

VALPROIC ACID TERATOGENICITY CONCERN: If preventive therapy with valproic acid considered, patient is reproductive-age female. Valproic acid is Category X (contraindicated in pregnancy) due to high teratogenicity risk (neural tube defects, developmental delay). If valproic acid prescribed, absolute contraception requirement and informed consent essential. Not recommended as first-line in reproductive-age women.

TOPIRAMATE TERATOGENICITY CONCERN: Topiramate is Category D (fetal risk) with increased cleft palate risk. If prescribed to reproductive-age female, requires effective contraception and informed consent. Not ideal first-line in women of childbearing potential.

AMITRIPTYLINE ANTICHOLINERGIC EFFECTS: Amitriptyline (tricyclic antidepressant) has anticholinergic side effects (dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, blurred vision). Not ideal in patients with glaucoma, urinary retention, or cardiac conduction abnormalities. Baseline assessment needed.

PROPRANOLOL CONTRAINDICATIONS: Beta-blockers contraindicated in asthma, COPD, severe bradycardia, and heart block. Respiratory and cardiac history not documented. Obtain baseline heart rate, BP, and respiratory history before prescribing propranolol.
low_issues: METOCLOPRAMIDE TARDIVE DYSKINESIA RISK: Metoclopramide carries FDA black box warning for tardive dyskinesia with use >3 months. If prescribed as adjunctive antiemetic, limit duration to <3 months and counsel patient on movement disorder warning signs.
PROCHLORPERAZINE TARDIVE DYSKINESIA RISK: Similar to metoclopramide; limit to short-term use (<3 months) to minimize tardive dyskinesia risk.

ACETAMINOPHEN HEPATOTOXICITY MONITORING: If acetaminophen prescribed, educate patient on maximum daily dose (3000-4000 mg/day; lower if chronic use). Assess for alcohol use (increases hepatotoxicity risk). Monitor liver function if chronic use anticipated.
NSAID CHRONIC USE MONITORING: If NSAIDs prescribed, counsel on limiting use to ≤10 days/month to avoid medication overuse headache. Monitor renal function and GI symptoms with chronic use.

TRIPTAN FREQUENCY MONITORING: Counsel patient on limiting triptan use to ≤10 days/month to avoid medication overuse headache. Educate on warning signs of serotonin syndrome if combined with SSRIs/SNRIs (agitation, confusion, tremor, hyperthermia).

MENSTRUAL MIGRAINE ASSESSMENT PENDING: Obtain detailed menstrual history to assess for menstrual migraine pattern (headache onset 2 days before to 3 days after menses). If menstrual migraine confirmed, timed preventive therapy or continuous hormonal contraception may be beneficial.

HEADACHE DIARY ESSENTIAL: Treatment plan recommends headache diary; this is critical for establishing frequency, triggers, and pattern before confirming diagnosis and initiating preventive therapy. Minimum 4 weeks of documentation required.

safety.safety_summary: PASS WITH WARNINGS. The medical team has provided a comprehensive diagnostic and treatment plan for a 35-year-old female with 2-week persistent right-sided throbbing headache, photophobia, and nausea. Clinical presentation is highly consistent with migraine without aura (72% confidence), and the differential diagnosis appropriately includes must-not-miss secondary causes (meningitis, intracranial mass, idiopathic intracranial hypertension). However, CRITICAL SAFETY GAPS exist that must be addressed BEFORE prescribing any medications: (1) NO MEDICATION HISTORY DOCUMENTED—Complete medication reconciliation is essential, including current medications, OTC analgesics, supplements, and herbal products. This is required to assess drug-drug interactions and medication overuse headache risk. (2) NO ALLERGY HISTORY DOCUMENTED—Obtain complete allergy history including drug allergies (especially triptans, NSAIDs), food allergies, and reaction types. (3) INCOMPLETE MENINGITIS EXCLUSION—While fever and neck stiffness are absent (strong negative findings), photophobia is highly specific for meningitis (LR+ 8.5). Formal meningeal sign assessment (Kernig sign, Brudzinski sign) is not documented. Meningitis cannot be definitively excluded without objective examination. (4) MISSING FUNDOSCOPIC EXAMINATION—Patient is reproductive-age female with persistent headache and photophobia, fitting demographics for idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH). Papilledema assessment is critical and not documented. If papilledema present, imaging and LP with opening pressure measurement required. (5) NEUROIMAGING NOT OBTAINED—Persistent headache >2 weeks with change in pattern is a red flag requiring MRI or CT brain to exclude structural lesion, mass, or increased intracranial pressure. No imaging results documented. (6) INCOMPLETE CARDIOVASCULAR/RENAL ASSESSMENT—Triptans contraindicated in uncontrolled hypertension, coronary artery disease, and cerebrovascular disease. NSAIDs contraindicated in severe renal impairment and uncontrolled hypertension. Baseline blood pressure, cardiovascular history, and renal function (eGFR) not documented. (7) PREVENTIVE THERAPY PREMATURE—Treatment plan recommends preventive pharmacotherapy without documented headache frequency. Preventive therapy indicated only if ≥4 migraines/month. Headache diary required for minimum 4 weeks to establish frequency. (8) VALPROIC ACID TERATOGENICITY—If valproic acid considered for prevention, patient is reproductive-age female. Valproic acid is Category X (contraindicated in pregnancy) with high teratogenicity risk. Not recommended without absolute contraception and informed consent. (9) HORMONAL CONTRACEPTIVE INTERACTION RISK—Oral contraceptive use not documented. If patient uses combined OCPs AND has migraine with aura (not yet confirmed), stroke risk increases 3-4x. Obtain detailed aura history and contraceptive use. (10) MEDICATION OVERUSE HEADACHE RISK—No medication history provided. If patient has been using frequent analgesics, medication overuse headache must be considered. Obtain detailed medication intake history. DOSAGE VERIFICATION: All acute migraine medications (triptans, NSAIDs, acetaminophen, antiemetics) are within safe dosage ranges. Preventive medications require baseline assessments before initiation. INTERACTION CHECK: No current medications documented, so drug-drug interactions cannot be fully assessed. However, critical interactions identified for monitoring if medications prescribed (triptan + SSRI/SNRI, triptan + ergot alkaloids, NSAID + ACE inhibitor/ARB, topiramate + OCPs, valproic acid + OCPs, NSAID + warfarin). ALLERGY RISK: No allergies documented—critical gap requiring immediate assessment. OVERALL ASSESSMENT: The diagnostic approach is sound and appropriately comprehensive. The treatment plan is evidence-based and appropriate for migraine management. However, multiple critical safety gaps must be addressed before prescribing medications. Recommend: (1) Obtain complete medication history, allergy history, cardiovascular history, renal function, and baseline blood pressure. (2) Complete meningeal sign assessment and fundoscopic examination. (3) Obtain neuroimaging (MRI or CT brain) to exclude structural pathology. (4) Establish headache frequency via diary before initiating preventive therapy. (5) Assess for migraine with aura and hormonal contraceptive use. (6) If preventive therapy with valproic acid or topiramate considered, obtain pregnancy test and ensure effective contraception. (7) Educate patient on medication overuse headache risk and frequency limits. (8) Counsel on warning signs of serious complications (meningitis, stroke, serotonin syndrome).

empathy.patient_summary: You're experiencing a persistent headache on the right side of your head that has lasted 2 weeks. The pain throbs (pulses), you're sensitive to light, and you feel nauseous sometimes. Based on your symptoms, the most likely cause is migraines—a common condition that affects many people, especially women your age. However, because your headache has lasted longer than typical and is new or different for you, your doctors want to make sure there's nothing else going on. The good news is that migraines are very treatable, and most people feel much better with the right care plan.
empathy.what_this_means: A migraine is when blood vessels and nerves in your head become inflamed and sensitive. This causes the throbbing pain you're feeling, along with sensitivity to light and nausea. Migraines are NOT a sign of a serious brain problem—they're a common condition that affects about 1 in 10 people worldwide, and women get them about 3 times more often than men. Your age (35) is actually when migraines are most common in women. The fact that your symptoms have been stable for 2 weeks (not getting worse) is a good sign. However, because headaches that last this long need to be checked out carefully, your doctors want to do some tests to rule out other less common causes—just to be thorough and make sure you get the right treatment.

right_now: Schedule an appointment with a neurologist (brain specialist) or headache specialist if you haven't already—this is important to confirm the diagnosis
Get your blood pressure checked at your doctor's office or pharmacy—we need to know your baseline before starting any migraine medications
Write down a list of ALL medications you're currently taking, including over-the-counter pain relievers, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products—bring this list to your appointment
Write down any drug allergies you have (for example, if you're allergic to aspirin or ibuprofen)—this is critical for safe treatment

Start a headache diary TODAY: Write down the date, time your headache started, how long it lasted, where it hurt, how bad the pain was (0-10 scale), what it felt like (throbbing, pressure, etc.), what made it better or worse, and any other symptoms (nausea, light sensitivity, etc.). Keep this for at least 4 weeks—this information is very helpful for your doctor
this_week: Schedule your neurologist appointment if not already done
Have an eye exam or ask your regular doctor to look at the back of your eyes (optic nerve) during your next visit—this is a quick check to make sure there's no pressure building up in your head
Get baseline blood work done if your doctor recommends it (blood pressure, kidney function, liver function)—this ensures migraine medications are safe for you
Ask your doctor about your menstrual cycle and headaches: Do your headaches happen around the same time each month? This information helps with treatment planning
If you take birth control pills, bring the name and dose to your appointment—this is important because some migraine types interact with hormonal contraception
Continue your headache diary daily
before_starting_medications: Complete your neurologist appointment and any recommended imaging (MRI or CT scan of your brain)—this rules out other causes and confirms migraine diagnosis

Discuss your complete medical history with your doctor, including: any heart problems, high blood pressure, kidney disease, stomach ulcers, or liver disease—these affect which migraine medications are safe for you
Tell your doctor if you're pregnant, breastfeeding, or planning to become pregnant—some migraine medications are not safe during pregnancy
Ask your doctor to explain any test results and what they mean for your treatment
Get clear instructions on how to take any prescribed medications, including when to take them and what to do if they don't work
ongoing: Take migraine medications exactly as prescribed—don't skip doses or take more than recommended, as this can lead to medication overuse headaches (a condition where taking pain relievers too often actually causes more headaches)
Keep your headache diary going for at least 4 weeks, even after starting treatment—this helps your doctor see if the medication is working

Try lifestyle changes that may help: keep a regular sleep schedule (7-9 hours per night), eat meals at consistent times, drink plenty of water (2-3 liters daily), limit caffeine to less than 200mg per day, exercise regularly (30 minutes, 5 days per week), and manage stress
Identify your personal migraine triggers (foods, stress, sleep changes, weather, hormonal changes) and try to avoid them when possible
Attend all follow-up appointments with your neurologist to monitor how well the treatment is working
Report any new symptoms or concerns to your doctor right away
If you're having migraines more than 4 times per month, talk to your doctor about preventive medications—these are taken daily to reduce how often migraines happen

acute_migraine_treatment.what_it_is: These are medications you take WHEN a migraine starts to stop the pain and other symptoms. They work best if taken early in the migraine.

first_choice_triptans.how_it_works: This medication narrows blood vessels and calms down the nerves causing your migraine. Think of it like turning down the volume on the pain signal in your head.
first_choice_triptans.how_to_take_it: Take one 50mg tablet or 20mg nasal spray as soon as your migraine starts. If the pain isn't better after 2 hours, you can take another dose. Don't take more than 100mg in one day.
first_choice_triptans.how_fast_it_works: You should start feeling better in 15-30 minutes
first_choice_triptans.what_to_expect: About 6-7 out of 10 people get significant pain relief within 2 hours. Some people feel chest tightness or pressure—this is usually not serious, but tell your doctor if it happens.
important_warnings: Don't take this if you have uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart disease, or a history of stroke
Don't take this with migraine medications containing ergot (ask your pharmacist if unsure)
Tell your doctor if you take antidepressants (SSRIs or SNRIs)—the combination is usually safe but needs monitoring
first_choice_triptans.side_effects: Some people feel flushed, tingly, dizzy, or drowsy. These usually go away quickly.
first_choice_triptans.cost: Generic sumatriptan is inexpensive (usually $10-30 per month) and most insurance covers it

alternative_triptans.when_to_use: If sumatriptan doesn't work well for you, your doctor might try a different triptan—some people respond better to different ones
alternative_triptans.how_to_take_it: Similar to sumatriptan; take at migraine onset, may repeat after 2 hours if needed

second_choice_nsaids.how_it_works: These reduce inflammation and pain. They work more slowly than triptans but are good for mild to moderate migraines.
second_choice_nsaids.how_to_take_it: Ibuprofen: 400-800mg at migraine onset, may repeat after 4-6 hours (max 1200-1600mg per day). Naproxen: 500-550mg at onset, may repeat after 8-12 hours (max 1100mg per day).
second_choice_nsaids.what_to_expect: About 5-6 out of 10 people get pain relief
important_warnings: Don't take if you have a stomach ulcer, severe kidney disease, or uncontrolled high blood pressure
Don't take with blood thinners (like warfarin) without talking to your doctor—increases bleeding risk
Limit use to 10 days per month to avoid medication overuse headaches
second_choice_nsaids.side_effects: Stomach upset, nausea, dizziness. Taking with food helps.
second_choice_nsaids.cost: Very inexpensive; available over-the-counter ($5-10 per month)

combination_therapy.medication_name: Sumatriptan 85mg + Naproxen 500mg (Treximet) or take triptan + NSAID together
combination_therapy.why_combine: Using both together works better than either one alone—about 7-8 out of 10 people get significant relief
combination_therapy.how_to_take_it: One combination tablet at migraine onset, may repeat after 2 hours if needed (max 2 tablets per day)
combination_therapy.advantage: More effective than single medications; convenient single tablet

for_nausea.how_it_works: Stops nausea and helps your stomach absorb migraine medications better
for_nausea.how_to_take_it: Metoclopramide: 10mg tablet at migraine onset, may repeat every 4-6 hours. Prochlorperazine: 5-10mg tablet or 25mg rectal suppository (useful if vomiting).
for_nausea.important_note: Use these for SHORT TERM only (less than 3 months) to avoid movement side effects. If you need them longer, talk to your doctor.

acute_migraine_treatment.important_reminder: Limit ALL acute migraine medications to 10 days per month or less. Using them more often can actually CAUSE more headaches (medication overuse headache). This is why preventive medications are important if you have frequent migraines.

preventive_medications.when_needed: If you're having migraines 4 or more times per month, your doctor may recommend a daily medication to prevent migraines from happening in the first place. These are NOT taken during a migraine—they're taken every day to reduce how often migraines occur.
preventive_medications.note: Don't start preventive medications yet. First, keep your headache diary for 4 weeks to see how often your migraines actually happen. Then talk to your doctor about whether prevention is right for you.

common_options.how_it_works: A beta-blocker that calms down the nervous system and prevents migraines
common_options.what_to_expect: Reduces migraine frequency by about 50% in most people; takes 2-4 weeks to work
common_options.important_warnings: Don't take if you have asthma, COPD, very slow heart rate, or certain heart problems. Your doctor will check your heart rate and blood pressure before starting.
common_options.side_effects: Fatigue, slow heart rate, low blood pressure, sexual dysfunction (in some men)

common_options.how_it_works: An anticonvulsant medication that stabilizes nerve activity
common_options.what_to_expect: Reduces migraine frequency by about 50%; takes 2-4 weeks to work
important_warnings: Can cause birth defects if taken during pregnancy—you MUST use effective birth control
Can cause kidney stones—drink plenty of water
common_options.side_effects: Memory problems, weight loss, tingling in fingers/toes, increased heart rate

common_options.how_it_works: A tricyclic antidepressant that also prevents migraines (works on serotonin and norepinephrine)
common_options.what_to_expect: Reduces migraine frequency by about 50%; takes 2-4 weeks to work; may also help with sleep and mood
common_options.important_warnings: Don't take if you have glaucoma, urinary retention, or certain heart problems
common_options.side_effects: Drowsiness (often helpful), dry mouth, weight gain, constipation, blurred vision

common_options.how_it_works: Newer medications that block a specific pain chemical in the brain
common_options.what_to_expect: Very effective; reduces migraine frequency by 50% or more in many people; takes 2-4 weeks to work
common_options.advantage: Newer, highly effective option; generally well-tolerated
common_options.disadvantage: Expensive; may require prior authorization from insurance

medication_safety_reminders: NEVER take migraine medications more than 10 days per month—this can cause medication overuse headaches
Tell your doctor about ALL medications you take, including over-the-counter and supplements—some combinations are unsafe
If you're pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, tell your doctor before taking any migraine medication
If you have heart disease, high blood pressure, kidney disease, liver disease, or stomach ulcers, tell your doctor—some medications aren't safe for you
If you experience chest pain, severe dizziness, vision changes, or weakness while taking migraine medication, stop and call your doctor immediately
Keep a list of your medications and bring it to every doctor appointment

lifestyle_tips.sleep: Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, even on weekends. Aim for 7-9 hours per night. Poor sleep is a major migraine trigger. If you have trouble sleeping, talk to your doctor.
lifestyle_tips.hydration: Drink 2-3 liters (about 8-10 glasses) of water every day. Dehydration is a common migraine trigger. Drink water consistently throughout the day, not just when you're thirsty.
lifestyle_tips.meals: Eat at regular times every day. Skipping meals or going too long without eating can trigger migraines. Include protein, healthy fats, and carbohydrates in each meal.
lifestyle_tips.caffeine: Limit caffeine to less than 200mg per day (about one cup of coffee). Too much caffeine OR suddenly stopping caffeine can trigger migraines. If you drink a lot of caffeine now, cut back gradually over a week or two.
lifestyle_tips.exercise: Exercise regularly—aim for 30 minutes of moderate activity (like brisk walking, swimming, or cycling) at least 5 days per week. Exercise reduces migraine frequency. Start slowly if you're not active now, and avoid intense exercise when you have a migraine.
lifestyle_tips.stress_management: Stress is a major migraine trigger. Try relaxation techniques like deep breathing, meditation, yoga, or progressive muscle relaxation. Even 10-15 minutes daily can help. Consider keeping a stress journal to identify what triggers your stress.
lifestyle_tips.hormonal_factors: If you're a woman, your migraines may be related to your menstrual cycle. Track when your migraines happen relative to your period. If they cluster around your period, tell your doctor—there are specific treatments for menstrual migraines.
lifestyle_tips.identify_triggers: Common migraine triggers include: certain foods (aged cheese, processed meats, chocolate, red wine), bright lights, loud noises, strong smells, weather changes, hormonal changes, and stress. Keep your headache diary to identify YOUR personal triggers, then try to avoid them.
lifestyle_tips.avoid_medication_overuse: Don't use pain relievers more than 10 days per month. Using them more often actually causes MORE headaches. This is why preventive medications are important.
lifestyle_tips.environment: During a migraine, go to a quiet, dark room. Reduce light exposure (dim lights or wear sunglasses). Avoid loud noises. A cool compress on your head or neck may help.
lifestyle_tips.alcohol: Alcohol, especially red wine and beer, can trigger migraines. If you drink, do so in moderation and stay hydrated.
lifestyle_tips.weather: Some people's migraines are triggered by weather changes (barometric pressure changes, storms, extreme heat/cold). If you notice a pattern, try to plan ahead during high-risk weather.

seek_emergency_care_immediately: SUDDEN SEVERE HEADACHE (worst headache of your life): This could indicate a serious condition like bleeding in the brain. Call 911 or go to the emergency room immediately.
HEADACHE WITH FEVER AND STIFF NECK: This could be meningitis (brain infection), which is a medical emergency. Call 911 immediately.
HEADACHE WITH WEAKNESS, NUMBNESS, OR PARALYSIS (especially on one side of your body): This could indicate a stroke. Call 911 immediately.
HEADACHE WITH VISION LOSS, DOUBLE VISION, OR DIFFICULTY SPEAKING: Call 911 immediately.
HEADACHE WITH CONFUSION, DIFFICULTY THINKING, OR ALTERED MENTAL STATUS: Call 911 immediately.
HEADACHE WITH SEVERE VOMITING (unable to keep anything down): Go to the emergency room.
HEADACHE AFTER A HEAD INJURY OR FALL: Go to the emergency room.
HEADACHE WITH SEIZURES: Call 911 immediately.

specialist.specialist_assessment: This patient presents with a clinical syndrome highly consistent with migraine without aura, supported by cardinal features: unilateral right-sided location, throbbing (pulsatile) quality, moderate-severe intensity, photophobia, and associated nausea. The 2-week duration suggests either chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month) or frequent episodic migraines with recent escalation. However, the persistent nature and change in pattern warrant systematic exclusion of secondary causes before confirming primary headache diagnosis. Critical red flags requiring investigation: (1) Photophobia is highly specific for meningitis (LR+ 8.5) despite absence of fever and neck stiffness—meningitis cannot be excluded without objective assessment; (2) Persistent headache >2 weeks duration warrants neuroimaging to exclude structural lesion, mass effect, or increased intracranial pressure; (3) Patient is in peak demographic for idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH)—reproductive-age female with photophobia requires fundoscopic examination for papilledema and assessment for visual symptoms. Positive findings: Normal vital signs, no acute distress, no focal neurological deficits mentioned, and stable presentation over 2 weeks all favor primary headache disorder. Absent findings that reduce secondary cause probability: No fever (reduces meningitis probability significantly), no neck stiffness (reduces meningitis probability), no altered mental status, no thunderclap onset, no progressive worsening documented. Hormonal factors should be explored given reproductive age—menstrual migraine affects 60% of women with migraine and may explain recent escalation. Current presentation does NOT meet criteria for migraine with aura (no documented visual, sensory, or speech symptoms). Medication history is critical missing data—must assess for medication overuse headache if frequent analgesic use present.

Associated symptoms: Photophobia ✓ and nausea ✓ (requires ≥1 of these). Duration pattern: 2-week presentation suggests either chronic migraine (≥15 days/month) or frequent episodic migraines—requires detailed headache diary to confirm frequency.

Red Flag Assessment for Secondary Headache (AAN/AHS Guidelines): Present: Persistent headache >2 weeks (warrants imaging), photophobia (can indicate migraine or meningitis), new/changed headache pattern (requires investigation). Absent: Fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status, thunderclap onset, focal neurological deficits, progressive worsening, age >50 years.

Meningitis Clinical Suspicion Score: Photophobia present (LR+ 8.5), but fever absent (LR- 0.15), neck stiffness absent (LR- 0.1), altered mental status absent (LR- 0.05). Post-test probability ~12% after combining likelihood ratios. Conclusion: Meningitis unlikely but cannot be excluded without objective assessment (meningeal sign examination, consideration of LP if clinical suspicion warrants).

specialist.risk_stratification: INTERMEDIATE RISK for serious secondary pathology. Rationale: (1) Photophobia is highly specific for meningitis (LR+ 8.5), and while fever/neck stiffness are absent (strong negative findings), meningitis cannot be definitively excluded without objective assessment; (2) Persistent headache >2 weeks warrants neuroimaging to exclude structural lesion, mass, or increased ICP; (3) Patient demographics (reproductive-age female) fit IIH, which requires fundoscopic examination and possible advanced imaging/LP; (4) However, stable vital signs, no focal neurological deficits, no acute distress, and absence of fever/neck stiffness reduce probability of immediately life-threatening condition. LOW RISK for acute emergency (SAH, acute meningitis with sepsis, acute stroke) based on clinical presentation. HIGH PROBABILITY of primary headache disorder (migraine) based on symptom pattern, but secondary causes must be systematically excluded before confirming diagnosis.
specialty_specific_tests: FIRST-LINE DIAGNOSTIC TESTS (Obtain immediately): (1) Comprehensive neurological examination including: cranial nerves II-XII, motor strength (upper/lower extremities), sensory testing (light touch, proprioception), cerebellar signs (finger-to-nose, rapid alternating movements, gait), deep tendon reflexes, Romberg test. (2) Fundoscopic examination specifically assessing for papilledema (optic disc swelling, blurred margins, obscuration of vessels, elevation of disc). (3) Meningeal sign assessment: Neck stiffness (passive neck flexion), Kernig sign (pain with knee extension when hip flexed), Brudzinski sign (neck flexion causes hip/knee flexion). (4) Vital signs including orthostatic blood pressure (assess for autonomic dysfunction). (5) Detailed headache history: Onset (sudden vs. gradual), frequency (days/month), duration (minutes to hours), location (unilateral vs. bilateral), quality (throbbing vs. pressing vs. sharp), severity (0-10 scale), associated symptoms (photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, vomiting, visual symptoms, weakness, numbness), triggers (menstrual cycle, foods, stress, sleep, weather), prior headache history, medication use (frequency and type of analgesics), family history of migraine/headache disorders, impact on function (disability days).

SECOND-LINE DIAGNOSTIC TESTS (Obtain based on examination findings and clinical suspicion): (1) MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast—INDICATED for persistent headache with red flags, change in pattern, or if focal neurological signs present. Preferred modality over CT (better soft tissue resolution, no radiation). Assess for: structural lesions (tumor, AVM, aneurysm), signs of increased ICP (ventricular size, sulcal effacement), demyelinating lesions, vascular abnormalities. (2) CT brain without contrast—ACCEPTABLE alternative if MRI contraindicated or urgent evaluation needed (faster acquisition). Lower sensitivity for soft tissue pathology but adequate for acute hemorrhage, mass effect, hydrocephalus. (3) Laboratory studies (obtain if fever, systemic symptoms, or meningeal signs present): Complete blood count (CBC) with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), blood cultures (if fever), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP) if temporal arteritis suspected. (4) Lumbar puncture (LP) with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis—INDICATED if: meningeal signs present, fever with headache, immunocompromised state, or high clinical suspicion for meningitis/encephalitis despite negative signs. CSF studies: cell count with differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, bacterial culture, viral PCR panel (enterovirus, HSV-1/2, VZV, EBV, CMV if immunocompromised). Obtain opening pressure (assess for IIH if elevated >25 cm H2O). Perform CT brain before LP if papilledema, focal deficits, or contraindications present.

SPECIALIST-LEVEL TESTS (Advanced evaluation if initial workup inconclusive): (1) MRI brain with MRV (magnetic resonance venography)—INDICATED if IIH suspected (assess for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, which can mimic IIH). (2) Formal visual field testing (perimetry)—INDICATED if papilledema present or IIH suspected (assess for peripheral visual field defects characteristic of IIH). (3) Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of optic nerve—INDICATED if papilledema suspected but not clearly visible on fundoscopy; objective measurement of optic nerve head elevation. (4) Carotid/vertebral artery ultrasound or CTA—INDICATED if dissection suspected (unilateral headache with neck pain, focal neurological signs). (5) Temporal artery biopsy—INDICATED if temporal arteritis suspected (age >50, elevated ESR/CRP, systemic symptoms); not applicable to this patient given age 35. (6) Headache diary and provocation testing—INDICATED for chronic migraine management; patient should maintain detailed log of headache frequency, triggers, associated symptoms, medication use for 4-8 weeks to establish pattern and guide preventive therapy. (7) Hormonal evaluation—INDICATED if menstrual migraine suspected; correlate headache onset/frequency with menstrual cycle; consider hormonal contraceptive assessment if migraine with aura present (increased stroke risk).

DIAGNOSTIC IMAGING PROTOCOL: MRI brain preferred modality. Sequences: T1-weighted (anatomic detail), T2-weighted (fluid/pathology detection), FLAIR (increased sensitivity for white matter lesions), gradient echo or susceptibility-weighted imaging (microhemorrhages, vascular lesions), post-gadolinium T1 (enhancement patterns, blood-brain barrier disruption). If MRI contraindicated: CT brain without contrast (assess for acute hemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus); consider CTA if vascular pathology suspected.

ASSESSMENT OF MEDICATION USE: Obtain detailed history of all analgesic medications: (1) Over-the-counter: acetaminophen (frequency, dose, days/month), ibuprofen/naproxen (frequency, dose, days/month), aspirin (frequency, dose, days/month). (2) Prescription: triptans (type, frequency, days/month), ergot alkaloids (frequency, days/month), opioids (type, frequency, days/month), barbiturate-containing compounds (frequency, days/month). (3) Combination products: assess for hidden analgesic content. (4) Frequency calculation: If ≥10 days/month of triptans/opioids/combination analgesics OR ≥15 days/month of NSAIDs/acetaminophen, medication overuse headache (MOH) must be considered. (5) Counseling: Educate on MOH risk; recommend limiting acute medication use to ≤10 days/month; initiate preventive therapy if indicated.

HORMONAL HISTORY (Reproductive-age female): (1) Menstrual cycle pattern: Regular vs. irregular, cycle length, duration of menses. (2) Correlation with headaches: Does headache onset/worsening correlate with specific phase of menstrual cycle (perimenstrual, ovulation, luteal phase)? (3) Oral contraceptive use: Current use, type (combined estrogen-progestin vs. progestin-only), duration, any change in headache pattern since initiation. (4) Pregnancy/postpartum history: Prior pregnancies, headache pattern during pregnancy (often improves), postpartum changes. (5) Hormone replacement therapy: If applicable. (6) Clinical significance: Menstrual migraine affects 60% of women with migraine; may warrant timed preventive therapy or continuous hormonal contraception. If migraine with aura present, combined oral contraceptives increase stroke risk (RR 3-4x) and should be avoided in favor of non-hormonal contraception.
specialist_red_flags: MENINGITIS RED FLAG: Photophobia is present and is highly specific for meningitis (LR+ 8.5). Although fever and neck stiffness are absent (strong negative findings reducing probability), meningitis cannot be excluded without objective assessment. Meningitis is life-threatening and time-sensitive. Viral meningitis can present without fever; early bacterial meningitis may lack classic signs. ACTION: Perform careful meningeal sign assessment (neck stiffness, Kernig, Brudzinski). If ANY meningeal sign present OR high clinical suspicion: Obtain CT brain (assess for contraindications to LP), then perform urgent lumbar puncture with CSF analysis and bacterial culture. Do not delay LP for imaging if clinical suspicion high.

INTRACRANIAL MASS/STRUCTURAL LESION RED FLAG: Persistent headache >2 weeks duration with change in pattern warrants neuroimaging to exclude structural pathology. While no focal neurological deficits documented, mass effect can present with non-focal symptoms (headache, nausea, photophobia). Unilateral location and associated nausea are concerning features. ACTION: Obtain MRI brain with contrast. If imaging shows mass, mass effect, or hydrocephalus: Urgent neurosurgery consultation.

IDIOPATHIC INTRACRANIAL HYPERTENSION (IIH) RED FLAG: Patient demographics fit perfectly (reproductive-age female, age 35). Photophobia and persistent headache are classic symptoms. IIH can present insidiously without obvious papilledema on initial exam. Risk: Progressive vision loss if untreated. ACTION: Perform careful fundoscopic examination assessing for papilledema (optic disc swelling, blurred margins, obscuration of vessels). Ask specifically about visual symptoms (transient visual obscurations, diplopia, peripheral vision loss, pulsatile tinnitus). If papilledema present or high clinical suspicion: Obtain MRI brain with MRV (assess for venous sinus thrombosis) and urgent lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement. Opening pressure >25 cm H2O supports IIH diagnosis.

SUBARACHNOID HEMORRHAGE (SAH) RED FLAG (LOW PROBABILITY BUT MUST-NOT-MISS): Although 2-week gradual onset is ATYPICAL for SAH (which presents with thunderclap onset), sentinel headaches can precede major SAH by days-weeks. Photophobia and nausea are present. ACTION: Ask specifically about thunderclap onset, worst headache of life, neck stiffness, altered mental status. If ANY features of SAH present: Obtain urgent non-contrast CT brain (assess for blood in subarachnoid space, ventricles, or parenchyma). If CT negative but high clinical suspicion: Perform lumbar puncture assessing for xanthochromia (yellow discoloration of CSF from hemoglobin breakdown, indicates prior hemorrhage). If SAH confirmed: Urgent neurosurgery consultation.

ARTERIAL DISSECTION RED FLAG (CAROTID/VERTEBRAL): Unilateral headache can indicate carotid or vertebral artery dissection. Risk factors: Trauma (even minor), connective tissue disorders (Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan), fibromuscular dysplasia. Associated symptoms: Neck pain, focal neurological deficits (stroke), Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). ACTION: Ask about neck pain, recent trauma, focal neurological symptoms. If dissection suspected: Obtain CTA or MRA of neck and head assessing for arterial narrowing, intimal flap, or pseudoaneurysm. If dissection confirmed: Neurology/Stroke consultation; anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy indicated.

CEREBRAL VENOUS SINUS THROMBOSIS (CVST) RED FLAG: Can present with progressive headache, photophobia, nausea. Risk factors: Hypercoagulable states, malignancy, infection, oral contraceptive use, pregnancy/postpartum. ACTION: If high clinical suspicion (progressive headache + risk factors + focal deficits or seizures): Obtain MRI with MRV assessing for absent flow void in venous sinuses, cord sign (thrombus in sinus), or parenchymal abnormalities. If CVST confirmed: Anticoagulation indicated despite presence of hemorrhage.

MIGRAINE WITH AURA PLUS ORAL CONTRACEPTIVE USE: If patient uses combined oral contraceptive pills AND has migraine with aura (visual, sensory, or speech symptoms), stroke risk is significantly increased (RR 3-4x). ACTION: Obtain detailed history of aura symptoms. If migraine with aura confirmed AND patient using OCPs: Recommend discontinuation of combined OCPs in favor of non-hormonal contraception (IUD, barrier methods, progestin-only pills). Counsel on stroke warning signs (facial drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty).

MEDICATION OVERUSE HEADACHE RISK: If patient reports frequent analgesic use (≥10 days/month for triptans/opioids; ≥15 days/month for NSAIDs/acetaminophen), medication overuse headache (MOH) must be considered. MOH perpetuates chronic headache and prevents effective preventive therapy. ACTION: Obtain detailed medication history. If MOH suspected: Counsel on analgesic limitation; consider inpatient or outpatient detoxification program; initiate preventive therapy; educate on rebound headache during withdrawal.

PROGRESSIVE NEUROLOGICAL DEFICITS: Although not documented in current presentation, any development of focal neurological signs (weakness, sensory loss, vision changes, speech difficulty, ataxia, cognitive changes) warrants urgent evaluation for stroke, mass, or other acute pathology. ACTION: Perform serial neurological examinations; if new deficits develop, obtain urgent neuroimaging and neurology consultation.

ALTERED MENTAL STATUS OR SEVERE BEHAVIORAL CHANGES: Although not present currently, any development of confusion, disorientation, personality changes, or severe mood disturbance warrants evaluation for encephalitis, meningitis, or other CNS pathology. ACTION: If mental status changes develop, obtain urgent CT/MRI brain, LP with CSF analysis, and neurology consultation.

FEVER DEVELOPMENT: Although fever is currently absent, development of fever in context of persistent headache and photophobia significantly increases meningitis probability. ACTION: If fever develops, perform meningeal sign assessment and consider urgent LP. Do not delay for imaging if clinical suspicion high.

PAPILLEDEMA ON FUNDOSCOPY: Indicates increased intracranial pressure from any cause (mass, IIH, venous sinus thrombosis, hydrocephalus). ACTION: If papilledema present, obtain urgent MRI brain with MRV and consider LP with opening pressure measurement. Neurology consultation indicated. Assess for vision-threatening complications.

interventions.details: Explain migraine as neurovascular disorder; discuss triggers (hormonal, dietary, stress, sleep, weather); normalize condition; address misconceptions

Patient to track: date, time of onset, duration, location, severity (0-10), quality, associated symptoms, triggers, menstrual cycle correlation, medication use, response to treatment. Duration: minimum 4 weeks to establish pattern

Regular sleep schedule (7-9 hours/night); consistent meal timing; hydration (2-3L water daily); stress management; regular aerobic exercise (30 min, 5x/week); limit caffeine to <200mg/day; avoid alcohol; identify and avoid personal triggers
Reduce light exposure during headache (dim lighting, sunglasses); minimize noise; cool, quiet environment; neck/shoulder stretching; posture assessment

Obtain detailed menstrual history; assess for menstrual migraine pattern (headache onset 2 days before to 3 days after menses); if menstrual migraine confirmed, consider timed preventive therapy or continuous hormonal contraception

interventions.dose: 50 mg oral tablet OR 20 mg nasal spray
interventions.frequency: At migraine onset; may repeat once after 2 hours if inadequate response (maximum 100 mg/day, maximum 2 doses/day)
interventions.duration: As needed for acute migraine episodes
interventions.mechanism: 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonist; causes vasoconstriction and inhibits trigeminal neurotransmission
interventions.efficacy: 60-70% achieve pain-free or mild pain state at 2 hours; NNT 2-3
interventions.advantages: Rapid onset; sustained relief; effective for associated symptoms (nausea, photophobia); multiple formulations available
contraindications: Coronary artery disease or history of MI
Cerebrovascular disease or history of stroke/TIA
Hemiplegic migraine or basilar migraine (relative contraindication)
common_side_effects: Chest tightness or pressure (usually benign; distinguish from angina)
Nausea (paradoxically, though usually improves migraine nausea)
serious_side_effects: Serotonin syndrome (if combined with SSRIs/SNRIs; very rare)
interventions.monitoring: Assess blood pressure before first dose if hypertension history; monitor for chest pain or pressure; educate patient on warning signs
drug_interactions: SSRIs/SNRIs: Rare serotonin syndrome risk (monitor for agitation, confusion, tremor, hyperthermia); combination generally safe
Ergot alkaloids: CONTRAINDICATED (additive vasoconstriction)
Other triptans: Do not combine (additive effects)
MAOIs: Contraindicated (increased serotonin levels)

high_issues: MISSING CRITICAL MEDICATION HISTORY: No current medications, allergies, or medication sensitivities documented. This is essential before prescribing any acute or preventive migraine therapy. Obtain complete medication reconciliation including OTC analgesics, supplements, and herbal products.

INCOMPLETE MENINGITIS EXCLUSION: While fever and neck stiffness are absent, photophobia is highly specific for meningitis (LR+ 8.5). Meningitis cannot be definitively excluded without objective meningeal sign assessment (Kernig sign, Brudzinski sign) and consideration of lumbar puncture if clinical suspicion warrants. Current documentation lacks formal meningeal sign examination.

MISSING FUNDOSCOPIC EXAMINATION: Patient is reproductive-age female with persistent headache and photophobia—demographics and symptoms fit idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH). Papilledema assessment is critical and not documented. If papilledema present, imaging and LP with opening pressure measurement required before prescribing any migraine medications.

NEUROIMAGING NOT YET OBTAINED: Persistent headache >2 weeks with change in pattern is a red flag requiring MRI or CT brain to exclude structural lesion, mass, or increased intracranial pressure. No imaging results documented. Recommend obtaining MRI brain before initiating preventive pharmacotherapy.
moderate_issues: TRIPTAN CONTRAINDICATION ASSESSMENT INCOMPLETE: Sumatriptan and other triptans are contraindicated in uncontrolled hypertension, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, and peripheral vascular disease. Blood pressure not documented; cardiovascular history not obtained. Obtain baseline BP and cardiovascular risk assessment before prescribing triptans.

NSAID SAFETY ASSESSMENT INCOMPLETE: Ibuprofen and naproxen contraindicated in active peptic ulcer disease, severe renal impairment, uncontrolled hypertension, and with concurrent anticoagulation. Renal function (eGFR), GI history, and anticoagulation status not documented. Obtain baseline renal function and GI history before prescribing NSAIDs.

HORMONAL CONTRACEPTIVE INTERACTION RISK: Patient is reproductive-age female; oral contraceptive use not documented. If patient uses combined OCPs AND has migraine with aura (not yet confirmed), stroke risk increases 3-4x. Obtain detailed history of aura symptoms and current contraceptive use. If migraine with aura confirmed, recommend non-hormonal contraception.

MEDICATION OVERUSE HEADACHE RISK: No medication history provided. If patient has been using frequent analgesics (≥10 days/month for triptans/opioids or ≥15 days/month for NSAIDs/acetaminophen), medication overuse headache (MOH) must be considered. Obtain detailed medication intake history before prescribing acute migraine therapy.

PREVENTIVE THERAPY PREMATURE: Treatment plan recommends preventive pharmacotherapy (propranolol, topiramate, amitriptyline, valproic acid, CGRP monoclonal antibodies) without documented headache frequency. Preventive therapy indicated only if ≥4 migraines/month. Headache diary required for minimum 4 weeks to establish frequency before initiating prevention.

VALPROIC ACID TERATOGENICITY CONCERN: If preventive therapy with valproic acid considered, patient is reproductive-age female. Valproic acid is Category X (contraindicated in pregnancy) due to high teratogenicity risk (neural tube defects, developmental delay). If valproic acid prescribed, absolute contraception requirement and informed consent essential. Not recommended as first-line in reproductive-age women.

TOPIRAMATE TERATOGENICITY CONCERN: Topiramate is Category D (fetal risk) with increased cleft palate risk. If prescribed to reproductive-age female, requires effective contraception and informed consent. Not ideal first-line in women of childbearing potential.

AMITRIPTYLINE ANTICHOLINERGIC EFFECTS: Amitriptyline (tricyclic antidepressant) has anticholinergic side effects (dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, blurred vision). Not ideal in patients with glaucoma, urinary retention, or cardiac conduction abnormalities. Baseline assessment needed.

PROPRANOLOL CONTRAINDICATIONS: Beta-blockers contraindicated in asthma, COPD, severe bradycardia, and heart block. Respiratory and cardiac history not documented. Obtain baseline heart rate, BP, and respiratory history before prescribing propranolol.
low_issues: METOCLOPRAMIDE TARDIVE DYSKINESIA RISK: Metoclopramide carries FDA black box warning for tardive dyskinesia with use >3 months. If prescribed as adjunctive antiemetic, limit duration to <3 months and counsel patient on movement disorder warning signs.
PROCHLORPERAZINE TARDIVE DYSKINESIA RISK: Similar to metoclopramide; limit to short-term use (<3 months) to minimize tardive dyskinesia risk.

ACETAMINOPHEN HEPATOTOXICITY MONITORING: If acetaminophen prescribed, educate patient on maximum daily dose (3000-4000 mg/day; lower if chronic use). Assess for alcohol use (increases hepatotoxicity risk). Monitor liver function if chronic use anticipated.
NSAID CHRONIC USE MONITORING: If NSAIDs prescribed, counsel on limiting use to ≤10 days/month to avoid medication overuse headache. Monitor renal function and GI symptoms with chronic use.

TRIPTAN FREQUENCY MONITORING: Counsel patient on limiting triptan use to ≤10 days/month to avoid medication overuse headache. Educate on warning signs of serotonin syndrome if combined with SSRIs/SNRIs (agitation, confusion, tremor, hyperthermia).

MENSTRUAL MIGRAINE ASSESSMENT PENDING: Obtain detailed menstrual history to assess for menstrual migraine pattern (headache onset 2 days before to 3 days after menses). If menstrual migraine confirmed, timed preventive therapy or continuous hormonal contraception may be beneficial.

HEADACHE DIARY ESSENTIAL: Treatment plan recommends headache diary; this is critical for establishing frequency, triggers, and pattern before confirming diagnosis and initiating preventive therapy. Minimum 4 weeks of documentation required.

empathy.patient_summary: You're experiencing a persistent headache on the right side of your head that has lasted 2 weeks. The pain throbs (pulses), you're sensitive to light, and you feel nauseous sometimes. Based on your symptoms, the most likely cause is migraines—a common condition that affects many people, especially women your age. However, because your headache has lasted longer than typical and is new or different for you, your doctors want to make sure there's nothing else going on. The good news is that migraines are very treatable, and most people feel much better with the right care plan.
empathy.what_this_means: A migraine is when blood vessels and nerves in your head become inflamed and sensitive. This causes the throbbing pain you're feeling, along with sensitivity to light and nausea. Migraines are NOT a sign of a serious brain problem—they're a common condition that affects about 1 in 10 people worldwide, and women get them about 3 times more often than men. Your age (35) is actually when migraines are most common in women. The fact that your symptoms have been stable for 2 weeks (not getting worse) is a good sign. However, because headaches that last this long need to be checked out carefully, your doctors want to do some tests to rule out other less common causes—just to be thorough and make sure you get the right treatment.

Get your blood pressure checked at your doctor's office or pharmacy—we need to know your baseline before starting any migraine medications

Start a headache diary TODAY: Write down the date, time your headache started, how long it lasted, where it hurt, how bad the pain was (0-10 scale), what it felt like (throbbing, pressure, etc.), what made it better or worse, and any other symptoms (nausea, light sensitivity, etc.). Keep this for at least 4 weeks—this information is very helpful for your doctor

Have an eye exam or ask your regular doctor to look at the back of your eyes (optic nerve) during your next visit—this is a quick check to make sure there's no pressure building up in your head

Ask your doctor about your menstrual cycle and headaches: Do your headaches happen around the same time each month? This information helps with treatment planning
If you take birth control pills, bring the name and dose to your appointment—this is important because some migraine types interact with hormonal contraception

Ask your doctor to explain any test results and what they mean for your treatment
Get clear instructions on how to take any prescribed medications, including when to take them and what to do if they don't work
ongoing: Take migraine medications exactly as prescribed—don't skip doses or take more than recommended, as this can lead to medication overuse headaches (a condition where taking pain relievers too often actually causes more headaches)
Keep your headache diary going for at least 4 weeks, even after starting treatment—this helps your doctor see if the medication is working

Try lifestyle changes that may help: keep a regular sleep schedule (7-9 hours per night), eat meals at consistent times, drink plenty of water (2-3 liters daily), limit caffeine to less than 200mg per day, exercise regularly (30 minutes, 5 days per week), and manage stress

Attend all follow-up appointments with your neurologist to monitor how well the treatment is working
