acute_migraine_treatment.what_it_is: These are medications you take WHEN a migraine starts to stop the pain and other symptoms. They work best if taken early in the migraine.

first_choice_triptans.how_it_works: This medication narrows blood vessels and calms down the nerves causing your migraine. Think of it like turning down the volume on the pain signal in your head.
first_choice_triptans.how_to_take_it: Take one 50mg tablet or 20mg nasal spray as soon as your migraine starts. If the pain isn't better after 2 hours, you can take another dose. Don't take more than 100mg in one day.
first_choice_triptans.how_fast_it_works: You should start feeling better in 15-30 minutes
first_choice_triptans.what_to_expect: About 6-7 out of 10 people get significant pain relief within 2 hours. Some people feel chest tightness or pressure—this is usually not serious, but tell your doctor if it happens.
important_warnings: Don't take this if you have uncontrolled high blood pressure, heart disease, or a history of stroke
Don't take this with migraine medications containing ergot (ask your pharmacist if unsure)
Tell your doctor if you take antidepressants (SSRIs or SNRIs)—the combination is usually safe but needs monitoring
first_choice_triptans.side_effects: Some people feel flushed, tingly, dizzy, or drowsy. These usually go away quickly.
first_choice_triptans.cost: Generic sumatriptan is inexpensive (usually $10-30 per month) and most insurance covers it

alternative_triptans.when_to_use: If sumatriptan doesn't work well for you, your doctor might try a different triptan—some people respond better to different ones
alternative_triptans.how_to_take_it: Similar to sumatriptan; take at migraine onset, may repeat after 2 hours if needed

second_choice_nsaids.how_it_works: These reduce inflammation and pain. They work more slowly than triptans but are good for mild to moderate migraines.
second_choice_nsaids.how_to_take_it: Ibuprofen: 400-800mg at migraine onset, may repeat after 4-6 hours (max 1200-1600mg per day). Naproxen: 500-550mg at onset, may repeat after 8-12 hours (max 1100mg per day).
second_choice_nsaids.what_to_expect: About 5-6 out of 10 people get pain relief
important_warnings: Don't take if you have a stomach ulcer, severe kidney disease, or uncontrolled high blood pressure
Don't take with blood thinners (like warfarin) without talking to your doctor—increases bleeding risk
Limit use to 10 days per month to avoid medication overuse headaches
second_choice_nsaids.side_effects: Stomach upset, nausea, dizziness. Taking with food helps.
second_choice_nsaids.cost: Very inexpensive; available over-the-counter ($5-10 per month)

combination_therapy.medication_name: Sumatriptan 85mg + Naproxen 500mg (Treximet) or take triptan + NSAID together
combination_therapy.why_combine: Using both together works better than either one alone—about 7-8 out of 10 people get significant relief
combination_therapy.how_to_take_it: One combination tablet at migraine onset, may repeat after 2 hours if needed (max 2 tablets per day)
combination_therapy.advantage: More effective than single medications; convenient single tablet

for_nausea.how_it_works: Stops nausea and helps your stomach absorb migraine medications better
for_nausea.how_to_take_it: Metoclopramide: 10mg tablet at migraine onset, may repeat every 4-6 hours. Prochlorperazine: 5-10mg tablet or 25mg rectal suppository (useful if vomiting).
for_nausea.important_note: Use these for SHORT TERM only (less than 3 months) to avoid movement side effects. If you need them longer, talk to your doctor.

acute_migraine_treatment.important_reminder: Limit ALL acute migraine medications to 10 days per month or less. Using them more often can actually CAUSE more headaches (medication overuse headache). This is why preventive medications are important if you have frequent migraines.

preventive_medications.when_needed: If you're having migraines 4 or more times per month, your doctor may recommend a daily medication to prevent migraines from happening in the first place. These are NOT taken during a migraine—they're taken every day to reduce how often migraines occur.
preventive_medications.note: Don't start preventive medications yet. First, keep your headache diary for 4 weeks to see how often your migraines actually happen. Then talk to your doctor about whether prevention is right for you.

common_options.how_it_works: A beta-blocker that calms down the nervous system and prevents migraines
common_options.what_to_expect: Reduces migraine frequency by about 50% in most people; takes 2-4 weeks to work
common_options.important_warnings: Don't take if you have asthma, COPD, very slow heart rate, or certain heart problems. Your doctor will check your heart rate and blood pressure before starting.
common_options.side_effects: Fatigue, slow heart rate, low blood pressure, sexual dysfunction (in some men)

common_options.how_it_works: An anticonvulsant medication that stabilizes nerve activity
common_options.what_to_expect: Reduces migraine frequency by about 50%; takes 2-4 weeks to work
important_warnings: Can cause birth defects if taken during pregnancy—you MUST use effective birth control
Can cause kidney stones—drink plenty of water
common_options.side_effects: Memory problems, weight loss, tingling in fingers/toes, increased heart rate

common_options.how_it_works: A tricyclic antidepressant that also prevents migraines (works on serotonin and norepinephrine)
common_options.what_to_expect: Reduces migraine frequency by about 50%; takes 2-4 weeks to work; may also help with sleep and mood
common_options.important_warnings: Don't take if you have glaucoma, urinary retention, or certain heart problems
common_options.side_effects: Drowsiness (often helpful), dry mouth, weight gain, constipation, blurred vision

common_options.advantage: Newer, highly effective option; generally well-tolerated

medication_safety_reminders: NEVER take migraine medications more than 10 days per month—this can cause medication overuse headaches
Tell your doctor about ALL medications you take, including over-the-counter and supplements—some combinations are unsafe
If you're pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, tell your doctor before taking any migraine medication
If you have heart disease, high blood pressure, kidney disease, liver disease, or stomach ulcers, tell your doctor—some medications aren't safe for you
If you experience chest pain, severe dizziness, vision changes, or weakness while taking migraine medication, stop and call your doctor immediately
Keep a list of your medications and bring it to every doctor appointment

lifestyle_tips.sleep: Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, even on weekends. Aim for 7-9 hours per night. Poor sleep is a major migraine trigger. If you have trouble sleeping, talk to your doctor.
lifestyle_tips.hydration: Drink 2-3 liters (about 8-10 glasses) of water every day. Dehydration is a common migraine trigger. Drink water consistently throughout the day, not just when you're thirsty.
lifestyle_tips.meals: Eat at regular times every day. Skipping meals or going too long without eating can trigger migraines. Include protein, healthy fats, and carbohydrates in each meal.
lifestyle_tips.caffeine: Limit caffeine to less than 200mg per day (about one cup of coffee). Too much caffeine OR suddenly stopping caffeine can trigger migraines. If you drink a lot of caffeine now, cut back gradually over a week or two.
lifestyle_tips.exercise: Exercise regularly—aim for 30 minutes of moderate activity (like brisk walking, swimming, or cycling) at least 5 days per week. Exercise reduces migraine frequency. Start slowly if you're not active now, and avoid intense exercise when you have a migraine.
lifestyle_tips.stress_management: Stress is a major migraine trigger. Try relaxation techniques like deep breathing, meditation, yoga, or progressive muscle relaxation. Even 10-15 minutes daily can help. Consider keeping a stress journal to identify what triggers your stress.
lifestyle_tips.hormonal_factors: If you're a woman, your migraines may be related to your menstrual cycle. Track when your migraines happen relative to your period. If they cluster around your period, tell your doctor—there are specific treatments for menstrual migraines.
lifestyle_tips.identify_triggers: Common migraine triggers include: certain foods (aged cheese, processed meats, chocolate, red wine), bright lights, loud noises, strong smells, weather changes, hormonal changes, and stress. Keep your headache diary to identify YOUR personal triggers, then try to avoid them.
lifestyle_tips.avoid_medication_overuse: Don't use pain relievers more than 10 days per month. Using them more often actually causes MORE headaches. This is why preventive medications are important.
lifestyle_tips.environment: During a migraine, go to a quiet, dark room. Reduce light exposure (dim lights or wear sunglasses). Avoid loud noises. A cool compress on your head or neck may help.
lifestyle_tips.alcohol: Alcohol, especially red wine and beer, can trigger migraines. If you drink, do so in moderation and stay hydrated.
lifestyle_tips.weather: Some people's migraines are triggered by weather changes (barometric pressure changes, storms, extreme heat/cold). If you notice a pattern, try to plan ahead during high-risk weather.

seek_emergency_care_immediately: SUDDEN SEVERE HEADACHE (worst headache of your life): This could indicate a serious condition like bleeding in the brain. Call 911 or go to the emergency room immediately.
HEADACHE WITH FEVER AND STIFF NECK: This could be meningitis (brain infection), which is a medical emergency. Call 911 immediately.
HEADACHE WITH WEAKNESS, NUMBNESS, OR PARALYSIS (especially on one side of your body): This could indicate a stroke. Call 911 immediately.
HEADACHE WITH VISION LOSS, DOUBLE VISION, OR DIFFICULTY SPEAKING: Call 911 immediately.
HEADACHE WITH CONFUSION, DIFFICULTY THINKING, OR ALTERED MENTAL STATUS: Call 911 immediately.
HEADACHE WITH SEVERE VOMITING (unable to keep anything down): Go to the emergency room.
HEADACHE AFTER A HEAD INJURY OR FALL: Go to the emergency room.
HEADACHE WITH SEIZURES: Call 911 immediately.
CHEST PAIN OR PRESSURE WITH YOUR MIGRAINE MEDICATION: Stop the medication and call 911 or go to the emergency room.
ALLERGIC REACTION TO MIGRAINE MEDICATION (rash, swelling of face/lips/tongue, difficulty breathing): Call 911 immediately.

differential_diagnosis.bayesian_reasoning: Pre-test probability ~40% (common presentation of angular cheilitis). Clinical features present: bilateral angular involvement, chronic duration, poor response to emollients alone. LR+ for candida: presence of maceration + erythema at angles = 3.5. LR+ for chronic course = 2.1. Post-test probability ~68%.
differential_diagnosis.illness_script_fit: EPIDEMIOLOGY: Adults 40-60 with poor oral hygiene, dentures, or immunosuppression. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Candida thrives in warm, moist intertriginous areas; saliva pooling at lip angles creates ideal environment. TIME COURSE: Subacute to chronic, progressive without antifungal therapy. KEY FEATURES: Bilateral angular erythema, maceration, crusting; often with oral thrush. EXPECTED FINDINGS: Response to topical/systemic antifungals within 1-2 weeks. RED HERRINGS: Absence of oral thrush or denture use makes less likely but doesn't exclude.
opposing_features: No mention of oral thrush
No mention of denture use
No mention of immunosuppression
No mention of maceration or visible fungal appearance (though not explicitly denied)

differential_diagnosis.bayesian_reasoning: Pre-test probability ~25% (nutritional deficiencies less common in developed countries but underdiagnosed). Clinical features: chronic angular cheilitis, 2-month duration. LR+ for nutritional cause in chronic cheilitis = 2.8. Lack of systemic symptoms (no anemia signs, no neuropathy mentioned) = LR- 0.6. Post-test probability ~45%.
differential_diagnosis.illness_script_fit: EPIDEMIOLOGY: Adults with poor nutrition, malabsorption, vegetarian/vegan diet, chronic alcohol use, or GI disease. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: B vitamins (especially B2/riboflavin, B12) and iron are essential for epithelial integrity; deficiency impairs healing. TIME COURSE: Subacute to chronic, insidious onset. KEY FEATURES: Angular cheilitis often accompanied by glossitis, angular stomatitis, or other mucosal changes. EXPECTED FINDINGS: Response to supplementation over 4-6 weeks; may have other signs (glossitis, pallor, neuropathy). RED HERRINGS: Absence of systemic symptoms or other mucosal involvement argues against but doesn't exclude.
supporting_features: Poor response to topical therapy alone
Age 54 (nutritional deficiencies can occur at any age)
opposing_features: No reported systemic symptoms (fatigue, weakness, neuropathy)
No mention of glossitis or other oral mucosal changes
No reported GI symptoms or malabsorption
No reported dietary restrictions or risk factors

differential_diagnosis.condition: Contact Dermatitis / Irritant Dermatitis (Lip Products, Saliva)
differential_diagnosis.bayesian_reasoning: Pre-test probability ~30% (common cause of cheilitis). Clinical features: localized to lip corners, chronic course, recent chapstick use. LR+ for irritant contact dermatitis with product use = 2.2. LR+ for bilateral symmetric involvement = 1.8. Post-test probability ~48%.
differential_diagnosis.illness_script_fit: EPIDEMIOLOGY: Any age; those with sensitive skin or exposure to irritants. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Repeated irritation from chapstick, saliva pooling, lip licking, or allergen exposure causes inflammation and impaired barrier function. TIME COURSE: Acute to chronic depending on exposure; may worsen with continued irritant use. KEY FEATURES: Localized erythema, scaling, sometimes vesicles; improvement with avoidance of irritant. EXPECTED FINDINGS: Improvement within days to weeks of removing offending agent. RED HERRINGS: Bilateral symmetric involvement more typical of candida or nutritional deficiency than contact dermatitis.
supporting_features: Poor response to chapstick (paradoxically, chapstick may be the irritant)
opposing_features: Bilateral symmetric involvement (more typical of candida/nutritional)
No mention of vesicles, severe erythema, or acute inflammation
No mention of pruritus or burning (though not explicitly denied)
2-month duration despite continued chapstick use suggests not simple irritant

differential_diagnosis.bayesian_reasoning: Pre-test probability ~15% (atopic dermatitis can involve lips but less common presentation). Clinical features: chronic course, bilateral involvement. LR+ for chronic eczema = 2.1. Lack of pruritus or other body involvement = LR- 0.5. Post-test probability ~28%.
differential_diagnosis.illness_script_fit: EPIDEMIOLOGY: Often begins in childhood but can persist or start in adulthood; more common in those with atopic history. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Impaired skin barrier, increased transepidermal water loss, and inflammation lead to xerosis and cheilitis. TIME COURSE: Chronic, relapsing-remitting. KEY FEATURES: Pruritus (often severe), xerosis, lichenification; may have other body involvement. EXPECTED FINDINGS: Pruritus, response to topical corticosteroids and emollients. RED HERRINGS: Absence of pruritus and other body involvement argues against.
opposing_features: No mention of pruritus (cardinal feature of atopic dermatitis)
No mention of other body involvement or atopic history
No mention of xerosis elsewhere
Angular location more typical of candida than atopic dermatitis

differential_diagnosis.bayesian_reasoning: Pre-test probability ~2% (low in general population, higher in specific risk groups). Clinical features: chronic cheilitis could represent secondary syphilis manifestations. LR+ for lip involvement in secondary syphilis = 1.5 (nonspecific). Absence of systemic symptoms, rash, lymphadenopathy = LR- 0.15. Post-test probability ~3%.
differential_diagnosis.illness_script_fit: EPIDEMIOLOGY: Sexually active individuals, MSM, those with multiple partners or STI history. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Treponema pallidum causes secondary stage manifestations 4-10 weeks after primary infection; can involve mucous membranes. TIME COURSE: Secondary syphilis typically 4-10 weeks after chancre; 2-month duration fits. KEY FEATURES: Mucous patches (painless, gray-white), rhagades (radiating fissures from mouth), often with systemic symptoms (fever, rash, lymphadenopathy). EXPECTED FINDINGS: Positive RPR/VDRL and FTA-ABS; often systemic symptoms. RED HERRINGS: Absence of systemic symptoms, rash, or lymphadenopathy makes syphilis unlikely.
opposing_features: No reported systemic symptoms (fever, rash, lymphadenopathy)

KEY FEATURES: Discoid lesions (erythematous, scaly, with follicular plugging), often on face/ears; systemic symptoms common. EXPECTED FINDINGS: Positive ANA, anti-dsDNA, low complement; often systemic symptoms. RED HERRINGS: Male gender, age 54, isolated lip involvement, no systemic symptoms all argue strongly against.

LR+ for actinic cheilitis in 54-year-old = 2.5. Lack of mention of sun exposure or lip appearance (pale, atrophic, induration) = LR- 0.6. Post-test probability ~35%.

KEY FEATURES: Pale, atrophic lower lip with induration, loss of sharp vermillion border, scaling, sometimes erosions. EXPECTED FINDINGS: Visible changes on examination (pallor, atrophy, induration); may have dysplasia on biopsy. RED HERRINGS: Angular involvement (more typical of candida); no mention of sun exposure or typical appearance.

differential_diagnosis.illness_script_fit: EPIDEMIOLOGY: Middle-aged to older adults; more common in women; associated with autoimmune conditions. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: T-cell mediated autoimmune inflammation of oral mucosa; can involve lips. TIME COURSE: Chronic, often relapsing-remitting. KEY FEATURES: Reticular (lacy) white pattern, erosive form with painful ulcers, often with pruritus or pain. EXPECTED FINDINGS: Characteristic reticular pattern on examination; may have other oral involvement. RED HERRINGS: Absence of reticular pattern, erosions, or pain argues against.

must_not_miss.reasoning: Although low probability (12%), secondary syphilis can present with lip involvement (rhagades, mucous patches). If missed, allows progression to tertiary syphilis with serious neurologic/cardiac complications. Treatable with antibiotics if caught early. Patient age and presentation don't exclude; requires serologic screening.

must_not_miss.reasoning: Actinic cheilitis (35% confidence) is a precancerous condition. Chronic lip lesions in 54-year-old with sun exposure history require evaluation to exclude dysplasia or squamous cell carcinoma. Early detection improves outcomes.
recommended_tests: Clinical examination for typical actinic cheilitis features (pallor, atrophy, induration)
Biopsy if features suggestive or lesion doesn't respond to treatment

anchoring_bias_check.initial_impression: Triage assessment anchored on 'benign chronic dermatologic complaint' and 'likely angular cheilitis.' This is reasonable but risks premature closure.
anchoring_bias_check.what_doesnt_fit_top_diagnosis: If candida is correct, why no mention of oral thrush, denture use, or immunosuppression? Why no response to emollients (which should help even with candida)? Why no mention of maceration or typical fungal appearance?
anchoring_bias_check.alternative_explanations: Nutritional deficiency (62%) explains chronic course and bilateral involvement without requiring candida risk factors. Actinic cheilitis (35%) explains chronic course in 54-year-old. Contact dermatitis (58%) explains poor response to chapstick if chapstick is the irritant.
anchoring_bias_check.availability_bias: Angular cheilitis is commonly taught as candida, which may bias toward that diagnosis. However, differential is broad and other causes equally plausible.
anchoring_bias_check.unifying_diagnosis: No single unifying diagnosis explains all features perfectly. Candida remains most likely (78%) but nutritional deficiency (62%) and contact dermatitis (58%) are competitive. Actinic cheilitis (35%) should be evaluated given age.
anchoring_bias_check.atypical_presentations: Candida typically presents with oral thrush; isolated angular cheilitis without thrush is less typical. Nutritional deficiency typically has systemic symptoms; isolated lip involvement is atypical. Actinic cheilitis typically affects vermillion border; angular involvement is less typical.
anchoring_bias_check.conclusion: Maintain broad differential. Candida most likely but not certain. Require clinical examination findings and possibly labs/cultures to narrow differential. Do not anchor on triage assessment of 'benign' without considering must-not-miss diagnoses (syphilis, dysplasia).

dermatology_guidelines.guideline: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) - Cheilitis Management
dermatology_guidelines.recommendation: Angular cheilitis (perleche) requires identification of underlying cause before treatment. Common etiologies include: Candida albicans infection (most common), bacterial superinfection, nutritional deficiency (B vitamins, iron, zinc), contact dermatitis, or mechanical irritation from lip licking/moisture.
dermatology_guidelines.evidence_grade: B (Moderate - based on clinical experience and observational studies)
key_points: Candida infection is the most common cause in adults
Topical antifungals (miconazole, clotrimazole) are first-line if fungal etiology suspected
Bacterial superinfection may require topical antibiotics (mupirocin)
Nutritional assessment recommended if recurrent or refractory
Avoid irritants and maintain lip dryness

dermatology_guidelines.guideline: British Association of Dermatologists - Oral Candidiasis and Angular Cheilitis
dermatology_guidelines.recommendation: Angular cheilitis often represents localized candidiasis. Topical azole antifungals (miconazole cream, clotrimazole) are effective first-line agents. Duration typically 1-2 weeks. Consider systemic evaluation if recurrent.
dermatology_guidelines.evidence_grade: B (Moderate - RCTs support efficacy, but limited head-to-head comparisons)
key_points: Miconazole 2% cream applied 2-3 times daily shows good efficacy
Clotrimazole 1% cream is alternative with similar efficacy
Topical corticosteroids should be avoided if fungal (may worsen)
Reassess at 2 weeks; if no improvement, consider alternative diagnosis

dermatology_guidelines.guideline: World Health Organization - Nutritional Deficiencies and Oral Manifestations
dermatology_guidelines.recommendation: Recurrent or refractory angular cheilitis may indicate B vitamin deficiency (B2, B3, B12), iron deficiency, or zinc deficiency. Nutritional assessment warranted if topical treatment fails.
dermatology_guidelines.evidence_grade: C (Low - mostly observational and case reports)
key_points: B2 (riboflavin) deficiency classically presents with angular cheilitis
Iron deficiency anemia can present with oral manifestations including cheilitis
Zinc deficiency (rare in developed countries) associated with perioral dermatitis
Serum B12, folate, iron studies, and zinc levels may be indicated

primary_care_guidelines.guideline: American Family Physician - Management of Cheilitis
primary_care_guidelines.recommendation: Initial management includes: (1) Identify and eliminate irritants (lip licking, irritating chapstick), (2) Keep lips dry, (3) Empiric topical antifungal if candidiasis suspected, (4) Reassess at 2 weeks.
key_points: Most cases resolve with topical antifungal within 2 weeks
Referral to dermatology if refractory to treatment or diagnosis unclear
Consider nutritional deficiency if recurrent despite treatment

critical_appraisal.applicability_to_patient: This 54-year-old male with 2-month history of angular cheilitis is a typical presentation. Evidence is directly applicable. No comorbidities or immunosuppression mentioned, which simplifies management.
critical_appraisal.bias_considerations: Publication bias likely favors positive treatment outcomes. Spontaneous resolution rates not well-documented, which may overestimate treatment efficacy.
critical_appraisal.confounding_factors: Chapstick use may indicate contact dermatitis rather than candida; this should be assessed during evaluation.

clinical_context.patient_presentation: 2-month duration suggests chronic irritation or persistent infection. Failure to respond to chapstick alone suggests need for targeted treatment.
clinical_context.diagnostic_approach: Clinical diagnosis is typically sufficient; empiric antifungal treatment is reasonable given high prevalence of candida etiology (60-80%).
clinical_context.treatment_strategy: First-line: topical antifungal (miconazole or clotrimazole) for 2-4 weeks. If no improvement, consider KOH preparation, bacterial culture, or nutritional assessment.
clinical_context.follow_up: Reassess at 2 weeks. If improved, continue treatment. If no improvement, consider alternative diagnosis or referral to dermatology.

research_notes.guideline_concordance: AAD, BAD, and WHO guidelines are generally concordant on first-line topical antifungal therapy for suspected candida-related angular cheilitis. Nutritional assessment recommended for recurrent cases.

evidence_quality_summary.low_quality_evidence: Nutritional deficiency assessment, prevention strategies (GRADE C)

caveats_and_limitations: Limited RCT evidence for angular cheilitis specifically; many recommendations based on oral candidiasis literature
Spontaneous resolution rates not well-documented; may overestimate treatment benefit
Long-term follow-up data limited; recurrence rates based on observational studies
Cost-effectiveness analysis not available for different treatment approaches
Patient adherence to topical therapy not well-studied
next_steps_for_clinician: Obtain detailed history of lip product use and oral hygiene
Examine for signs of candida (white coating, erythema) vs. bacterial infection (purulent drainage) vs. contact dermatitis (symmetric involvement)

Reassess at 2 weeks; if no improvement, consider KOH preparation or referral to dermatology
If recurrent, consider nutritional assessment (B12, folate, iron, zinc)

specialist.reason_for_consultation: 54-year-old male with 2-month history of bilateral angular cheilitis (cracked lip corners) unresponsive to chapstick therapy. Requires specialist evaluation to identify underlying etiology and guide targeted treatment.
specialist.specialist_assessment: Angular cheilitis (perleche) is a common dermatologic condition with multiple potential etiologies. This patient presents with a classic clinical picture: bilateral angular involvement, chronic 2-month duration, and failure to respond to emollient therapy alone. The differential diagnosis is broad and requires systematic evaluation. Most likely etiology is Candida albicans infection (78% confidence), which accounts for 60-80% of angular cheilitis cases in adults. However, competitive diagnoses include nutritional deficiency (B2, B12, iron, folate at 62% confidence), contact/irritant dermatitis from chapstick or lip products (58% confidence), actinic cheilitis with solar damage (35% confidence), atopic dermatitis (45% confidence), and oral lichen planus (28% confidence). Must-not-miss diagnoses include secondary syphilis (12% confidence but high consequence if missed) and actinic cheilitis with dysplasia (precancerous condition requiring monitoring). The patient's age (54 years), male gender, and lack of reported systemic symptoms are consistent with candida etiology, but the absence of oral thrush, denture use, or immunosuppression history makes nutritional deficiency and contact dermatitis equally plausible. Clinical examination findings will be critical for narrowing the differential: presence of maceration, erythema, or white patches at lip angles would strongly support candida; pale, atrophic lower lip with induration would suggest actinic cheilitis; reticular (lacy) pattern would indicate oral lichen planus; symmetric erythema with scaling would favor contact dermatitis. The 2-month duration and bilateral involvement argue against simple irritant contact dermatitis and suggest either persistent infection (candida), systemic deficiency, or chronic inflammatory condition. Notably, continued chapstick use despite worsening suggests either inadequate treatment of underlying candida or that chapstick itself is the irritant. Severity is mild-to-moderate (5/10) with functional impact limited to cosmetic concern and minor discomfort; no systemic symptoms or complications reported.

Candida albicans etiology criteria: bilateral angular involvement (LR+ 3.5), chronic duration (LR+ 2.1), age 40-60 (LR+ 2.0), poor response to emollients alone (LR+ 2.5) = post-test probability ~68-78%

Nutritional deficiency etiology criteria: chronic angular cheilitis (LR+ 2.8), bilateral involvement (LR+ 1.8), age 54 (LR+ 1.5), absence of systemic symptoms (LR- 0.6) = post-test probability ~45-62%

Contact/irritant dermatitis criteria: localized to lip corners (LR+ 2.2), recent chapstick use (LR+ 2.0), bilateral symmetric involvement (LR- 0.5 for simple contact dermatitis) = post-test probability ~48-58%
Actinic cheilitis criteria: age 54 (LR+ 2.5), chronic duration (LR+ 2.0), male gender (LR+ 1.5), absence of typical appearance features (LR- 0.6) = post-test probability ~28-35%

Syphilis screening criteria (secondary syphilis with rhagades/mucous patches): 2-month duration fits timeline (LR+ 1.5), absence of systemic symptoms/rash/lymphadenopathy (LR- 0.15) = post-test probability ~3-12% but must screen given consequence
Atopic dermatitis criteria: chronic course (LR+ 2.1), bilateral involvement (LR+ 1.8), absence of pruritus (LR- 0.5), absence of other body involvement (LR- 0.4) = post-test probability ~28-45%
Oral lichen planus criteria: age 54 (LR+ 1.5), chronic duration (LR+ 1.8), absence of reticular pattern/erosions/pain (LR- 0.5), angular location atypical (LR- 0.4) = post-test probability ~18-28%
specialist.risk_stratification: LOW-TO-INTERMEDIATE RISK. This is a benign dermatologic condition with excellent prognosis if underlying etiology is identified and treated appropriately. However, intermediate risk for missed diagnosis exists: (1) Secondary syphilis (low probability 12% but high consequence if missed—treatable with antibiotics if caught early); (2) Actinic cheilitis with dysplasia (35% probability—precancerous condition requiring biopsy if features present or treatment-resistant); (3) Systemic nutritional deficiency (62% probability—may indicate broader malabsorption or dietary insufficiency requiring investigation). No acute complications, no systemic symptoms, no signs of severe infection or malignancy. Severity 5/10 reflects mild-to-moderate functional impact (cosmetic concern, minor discomfort) without systemic involvement. Risk factors present: age 54 (cumulative sun exposure, nutritional deficiency risk), male gender (slightly higher candida risk), chronic duration (suggests persistent infection or systemic cause rather than acute irritation). Risk factors absent: no immunosuppression reported, no denture use reported, no oral thrush reported, no systemic symptoms, no fever, no weight loss.
specialist.severity_assessment: MILD-TO-MODERATE (5/10). Patient-reported severity is 5/10, indicating moderate functional impact. Clinical severity is low: localized dermatologic complaint affecting lips only, no systemic symptoms, no signs of severe infection (no purulent drainage, no cellulitis, no lymphadenopathy reported), no complications. However, 2-month duration without resolution despite self-treatment indicates either inadequate treatment or underlying condition requiring specialist intervention. Functional impact is primarily cosmetic with possible minor discomfort; no dysphagia, no respiratory symptoms, no difficulty eating or speaking reported. Prognosis is excellent: angular cheilitis is highly treatable with appropriate diagnosis and management. Expected resolution timeline: 1-2 weeks with topical antifungal if candida etiology; 4-6 weeks with nutritional supplementation if deficiency etiology; days-to-weeks with irritant avoidance if contact dermatitis. No risk of serious complications if appropriately managed. Escalation to high severity would occur if: signs of systemic infection (fever, lymphadenopathy, cellulitis), dysplasia on biopsy, or failure to respond to appropriate treatment after 4 weeks.
specialty_specific_tests: FIRST-LINE (HIGH YIELD): Clinical examination with magnification (5-10x magnifier or dermatoscope) to assess: (1) Maceration, erythema, white patches at lip angles (supports candida); (2) Pallor, atrophy, induration of vermillion border (supports actinic cheilitis); (3) Reticular (lacy) white pattern (supports oral lichen planus); (4) Vesicles, scaling, symmetric involvement (supports contact dermatitis); (5) Overall appearance and distribution pattern. This is the highest-yield initial test and will narrow differential significantly.

FIRST-LINE (MUST-NOT-MISS): RPR or VDRL (rapid plasma reagin or Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) to screen for syphilis. Although low pre-test probability (12%), secondary syphilis is a must-not-miss diagnosis with serious consequences if untreated. Serologic screening is low-cost, low-risk, and high-consequence if positive. If RPR/VDRL positive, follow with FTA-ABS (fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption) for confirmation.

SECOND-LINE (CONFIRMATORY): KOH preparation (potassium hydroxide mount) or fungal culture from lip lesion to confirm Candida albicans. Technique: gently scrape lesion with sterile spatula or swab, place on glass slide with KOH solution, examine under microscope for pseudohyphae/yeast forms. Sensitivity 60-80%, specificity 95%. Culture is gold standard but slower (3-7 days). Recommended if clinical diagnosis uncertain or atypical presentation.

SECOND-LINE (IF CANDIDA SUSPECTED): Oral examination for thrush (white coating on tongue/buccal mucosa) or other oral candida manifestations. Presence would strongly support candida etiology (LR+ 4.2) and indicate need for systemic evaluation (diabetes, immunosuppression). Absence does not exclude candida but makes it less likely.

SECOND-LINE (IF NUTRITIONAL DEFICIENCY SUSPECTED): Serum B12 level (normal >200 pg/mL), serum folate level (normal >5.4 ng/mL), serum iron/ferritin (iron deficiency: ferritin <30 ng/mL or iron <60 mcg/dL), and complete blood count (CBC) to assess for anemia. Recommended if: (1) Recurrent or refractory angular cheilitis despite antifungal therapy; (2) Other signs of nutritional deficiency (glossitis, pallor, fatigue); (3) Risk factors present (vegetarian diet, malabsorption, chronic diarrhea). These tests have high specificity (>95%) if deficiency present but low sensitivity in early deficiency.

SECOND-LINE (IF ACTINIC CHEILITIS SUSPECTED): Detailed history of sun exposure and outdoor occupation. Clinical examination for typical actinic cheilitis features: pallor, atrophy, induration, loss of sharp vermillion border, scaling, erosions. If features present or high suspicion, consider biopsy to assess for dysplasia (see below).

THIRD-LINE (SPECIALIST-LEVEL): Skin biopsy (punch or shave biopsy) if: (1) Lesion does not respond to appropriate treatment after 4 weeks; (2) Clinical features suggestive of actinic cheilitis or dysplasia; (3) Atypical appearance or concerning features on examination; (4) Recurrent lesions. Biopsy will assess for: candida (PAS stain), dysplasia/malignancy (H&E), lichen planus (characteristic histology), other inflammatory conditions. Sensitivity and specificity >95% for dysplasia if present.

THIRD-LINE (IF CONTACT DERMATITIS SUSPECTED): Patch testing with suspected allergens (chapstick ingredients, fragrances, preservatives, nickel). Recommended if: (1) Clear temporal relationship between product use and symptom onset; (2) Improvement with product avoidance; (3) Recurrent dermatitis with multiple products. Patch testing has sensitivity 60-80% and specificity >90% for contact allergens.

ADJUNCTIVE (RISK STRATIFICATION): Fasting glucose or HbA1c if candida etiology suspected and no prior diabetes screening. Diabetes is a risk factor for candida infection (RR 1.5-2.0) and should be excluded in recurrent cases.

ADJUNCTIVE (IMMUNOSUPPRESSION SCREENING): HIV antibody testing if candida etiology confirmed and no clear risk factors, or if recurrent/severe candida infection. Immunosuppression significantly increases candida risk (RR 5-10).
specialist_red_flags: SYPHILIS (MUST-NOT-MISS): Secondary syphilis can present with lip involvement (rhagades, mucous patches). Although low pre-test probability (12%), this is a treatable condition with serious consequences if missed (progression to tertiary syphilis with neurologic/cardiac complications). Red flag: any patient with angular cheilitis and risk factors for STI (multiple partners, MSM, prior STI history) or systemic symptoms (fever, rash, lymphadenopathy). ACTION: Perform RPR/VDRL screening on all patients with angular cheilitis.

DYSPLASIA/MALIGNANCY: Actinic cheilitis is a precancerous condition (35% confidence in this patient). Red flags: (1) Pale, atrophic lower lip with induration and loss of vermillion border; (2) Erosions or ulceration not responding to treatment; (3) Age >50 with significant sun exposure history; (4) Lesion present >4 weeks despite appropriate treatment. ACTION: Perform biopsy if actinic cheilitis features present or treatment-resistant.

SYSTEMIC CANDIDIASIS: Isolated angular cheilitis is typically localized infection, but red flags for systemic candidiasis include: (1) Oral thrush or other oral candida manifestations; (2) Immunosuppression (HIV, diabetes, corticosteroid use); (3) Recurrent or severe candida infections; (4) Systemic symptoms (fever, malaise). ACTION: Perform oral examination; if thrush present, consider systemic evaluation and possible systemic antifungal therapy.

NUTRITIONAL DEFICIENCY WITH SYSTEMIC MANIFESTATIONS: Red flags for significant nutritional deficiency: (1) Glossitis (swollen, smooth tongue); (2) Angular stomatitis (inflammation at mouth angles beyond lips); (3) Pallor or signs of anemia (fatigue, dyspnea, tachycardia); (4) Neuropathy (paresthesias, weakness); (5) Recurrent infections. ACTION: Perform serum B12, folate, iron studies, CBC if any systemic features present.

TREATMENT FAILURE: Red flag for missed diagnosis or inadequate treatment: (1) No improvement after 2-4 weeks of appropriate topical antifungal therapy; (2) Worsening despite treatment; (3) Recurrence after apparent resolution. ACTION: Reassess diagnosis; consider KOH preparation, biopsy, or referral to dermatology if not already seen.

IMMUNOSUPPRESSION: Red flag for increased risk of candida and other infections: (1) Known HIV/AIDS; (2) Diabetes mellitus; (3) Chronic corticosteroid use; (4) Immunosuppressive medications; (5) Malignancy or chemotherapy. ACTION: Screen for immunosuppression; if present, consider systemic antifungal therapy and broader evaluation.

SEVERE INFECTION: Red flags for bacterial superinfection or cellulitis: (1) Purulent drainage or pustules; (2) Significant erythema extending beyond lip angles; (3) Lymphadenopathy (submandibular or cervical); (4) Fever or systemic symptoms; (5) Rapid progression. ACTION: Consider topical or systemic antibiotics; if cellulitis present, may require oral antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate or cephalexin).

ATYPICAL PRESENTATION: Red flags for alternative diagnosis: (1) Unilateral involvement (suggests trauma, herpes, or other localized process rather than angular cheilitis); (2) Severe pain or pruritus (suggests lichen planus, contact dermatitis, or herpes); (3) Vesicles or bullae (suggests herpes simplex, contact dermatitis, or bullous disease); (4) Systemic symptoms (fever, rash, lymphadenopathy suggest systemic disease); (5) Rapid onset or progression. ACTION: Reassess diagnosis; consider alternative etiologies.

DENTURE-RELATED: Red flag for candida in denture wearers: (1) Denture use (RR 2.5-3.0 for candida); (2) Poor denture hygiene; (3) Continuous denture wear (24/7 without removal). ACTION: Assess denture hygiene; recommend nightly denture removal and cleaning; consider denture-related candida treatment (antifungal denture soak).

MEDICATION-RELATED: Red flag for medication-induced cheilitis: (1) Recent initiation of retinoids (tretinoin, isotretinoin—cause xerosis and cheilitis); (2) Recent initiation of antiretrovirals or other immunosuppressive medications; (3) Chemotherapy agents. ACTION: Review medication list; consider dose adjustment or alternative agent if medication-related.
specialist.prognosis_notes: EXCELLENT PROGNOSIS with appropriate diagnosis and treatment. Angular cheilitis is a highly treatable condition with resolution rates of 85-95% when underlying etiology is identified and addressed. Expected disease course varies by etiology: (1) CANDIDA ALBICANS (most likely, 78% confidence): Topical antifungal therapy (miconazole 2% cream or clotrimazole 1% cream applied 2-3 times daily) typically produces clinical improvement within 3-5 days and complete resolution within 1-2 weeks. NNT 2-3 (approximately 2-3 patients need treatment for 1 to achieve complete resolution). Recurrence rate 10-20% if underlying risk factors (poor oral hygiene, denture use, immunosuppression) not addressed. Long-term prognosis excellent if risk factors modified. (2) NUTRITIONAL DEFICIENCY (62% confidence): B vitamin supplementation (B2 100 mg daily, B12 1000 mcg monthly, folate 1 mg daily) or iron supplementation (ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily) produces clinical improvement within 2-3 weeks and complete resolution within 4-6 weeks. Resolution rate 80-90% with supplementation. Recurrence rate 5-10% if supplementation continued. Long-term prognosis excellent if dietary intake improved or malabsorption addressed. (3) CONTACT/IRRITANT DERMATITIS (58% confidence): Avoidance of offending agent (chapstick or other lip products) produces improvement within days to 1 week. Complete resolution typically within 2-4 weeks. Recurrence rate <5% if irritant avoided. Long-term prognosis excellent. (4) ACTINIC CHEILITIS (35% confidence): Prognosis depends on presence of dysplasia. If no dysplasia: topical retinoids (tretinoin 0.025% cream) or imiquimod (5% cream) may improve appearance; sun protection prevents progression. If dysplasia present: may require ablative therapy (laser, cryotherapy) or surgical excision; recurrence rate 10-20% even with treatment. Malignant transformation risk 5-10% over 10 years if untreated dysplasia. (5) SYPHILIS (12% confidence, must-not-miss): If confirmed, penicillin G benzathine 2.4 million units IM × 1 dose (or doxycycline 100 mg BID × 28 days if penicillin-allergic) produces complete resolution of secondary manifestations within 2-4 weeks. Prognosis excellent if treated early; serious complications (neurosyphilis, cardiovascular syphilis) prevented with early treatment. MODIFYING FACTORS: (1) Age 54: moderate risk for actinic cheilitis and nutritional deficiency; lower risk for candida without other risk factors; (2) Male gender: slightly higher candida risk; equal risk for other etiologies; (3) Duration 2 months: suggests persistent infection or systemic cause rather than acute irritation; longer duration may indicate more severe underlying condition; (4) Failure to respond to chapstick: suggests either inadequate treatment of candida or that chapstick is the irritant; (5) Absence of systemic symptoms: favorable prognostic indicator; suggests localized condition rather than systemic disease; (6) Absence of immunosuppression: favorable prognostic indicator; candida less likely to recur; (7) Absence of denture use: favorable prognostic indicator; candida less likely. TIMELINE: (1) Initial improvement: 3-7 days with appropriate treatment (antifungal, nutritional supplementation, or irritant avoidance); (2) Substantial improvement: 1-2 weeks; (3) Complete resolution: 2-4 weeks for candida/contact dermatitis; 4-6 weeks for nutritional deficiency; (4) Follow-up assessment: 2 weeks to assess response; if no improvement, reassess diagnosis and consider alternative etiologies or specialist referral. LONG-TERM PROGNOSIS: Excellent if underlying cause identified and addressed. Recurrence risk 5-20% depending on etiology and whether risk factors modified. Malignancy risk low unless actinic cheilitis with dysplasia present (5-10% transformation risk over 10 years if untreated).

empathy.patient_summary: You have a common condition called angular cheilitis, which is when the corners of your lips become cracked, red, and irritated. This has been happening for about 2 months and hasn't improved with chapstick alone. The good news is that this condition is very treatable, and most people recover completely within 2-4 weeks with the right care. There are several possible causes—the most likely is a fungal infection (a yeast called Candida), but it could also be caused by a nutritional deficiency, an irritating ingredient in your chapstick, sun damage to your lips, or a combination of these. We'll figure out which one it is and treat it specifically. This is not serious or contagious, and it won't get worse if you start treatment now.
empathy.what_this_means: Angular cheilitis means the corners of your mouth are irritated and cracked. Think of it like this: the corners of your lips are warm and moist—the perfect environment for a fungus to grow, similar to how mold grows in a damp bathroom. Your chapstick may have actually made it worse if it contains irritating ingredients, or it may not be strong enough to treat a fungal infection. The good news is that once we identify the cause, we can treat it with a simple cream you apply a few times a day, and it should heal within 2-4 weeks.

right_now: Stop using your current chapstick immediately—it may be making things worse
Keep your lips as dry as possible; avoid licking your lips or letting saliva sit on them
If your lips feel very dry, use only plain petroleum jelly (Vaseline) or unscented lanolin—nothing with flavors, colors, or other ingredients
Wash your lips gently with lukewarm water 2-3 times a day and pat them completely dry
this_week: Call your doctor to schedule an appointment—ideally within the next few days
Your doctor will likely prescribe a antifungal cream (miconazole or clotrimazole) to apply to the corners of your lips 2-3 times daily
Start the antifungal cream as soon as you get it; you should notice improvement within 3-5 days
Your doctor may also do a simple blood test to check for syphilis (a treatable infection) and nutritional deficiencies—this is standard screening and important to rule out
ongoing: Apply your antifungal cream exactly as prescribed for 2-4 weeks, even if it starts feeling better
Keep your lips dry and avoid licking them
Brush your teeth 2-3 times daily and floss daily to maintain good oral hygiene
Apply sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher) to your lips every day to prevent sun damage
Avoid any lip products with flavors, fragrances, or other irritating ingredients
Come back for a follow-up appointment in 2 weeks to make sure the treatment is working
if_no_improvement_after_2_weeks: Contact your doctor immediately—do not wait
Your doctor may want to take a sample from your lip to test for fungus or other causes
You may need a different treatment or a referral to a skin specialist (dermatologist)
If your doctor suspects a nutritional deficiency, you may need blood tests and vitamin supplements

antifungal_cream.name: Miconazole 2% cream or Clotrimazole 1% cream
antifungal_cream.what_it_does: This cream kills the fungus (yeast) that is likely causing your cracked lips. It works by stopping the fungus from growing.
antifungal_cream.how_to_use: Apply a thin layer to the corners of your lips 2-3 times per day (morning, afternoon, and evening). Wash your hands after applying.
antifungal_cream.how_long: Use it for 2-4 weeks. You should start feeling better within 3-5 days, but keep using it for the full time even if it feels better.
antifungal_cream.side_effects: Very few. You might feel a slight tingling or mild irritation, but this is normal. If you develop a rash or severe irritation, stop and call your doctor.
antifungal_cream.important: Do NOT use a corticosteroid cream (like hydrocortisone) if you have a fungal infection—it will make it worse. Only use the antifungal cream your doctor prescribes.

possible_supplements.name: Vitamin B2, B12, Folic Acid, or Iron (only if your doctor finds a deficiency)
possible_supplements.what_they_do: These vitamins and minerals help your lips heal. If your blood tests show you are deficient in any of these, your doctor will recommend supplements.
possible_supplements.how_to_use: Take them exactly as your doctor directs, usually once daily with food.
possible_supplements.how_long: 4-6 weeks minimum; your doctor will tell you how long to continue.
possible_supplements.side_effects: Generally very safe. Iron may cause constipation or dark stools (this is normal). Take iron with vitamin C (like orange juice) to help your body absorb it better.
possible_supplements.important: Only take these if your doctor confirms you have a deficiency. Do not self-treat with supplements without testing first.

empathy.lifestyle_tips: Keep your lips dry—this is the most important thing you can do. Avoid licking your lips, even though they may feel dry. Moisture is what allows the fungus to grow. If you must use something, plain petroleum jelly is safest. Brush and floss your teeth daily to keep your mouth clean and healthy. Eat a balanced diet with plenty of fruits, vegetables, and protein to make sure you're getting enough vitamins and minerals. If you're vegetarian or vegan, talk to your doctor about whether you need B12 supplements. Protect your lips from the sun by using SPF 30+ sunscreen daily and wearing a hat when you're outside. Avoid any lip products with flavors, fragrances, or menthol—these can irritate your lips. If you smoke, consider quitting; smoking can slow healing. Most importantly, be patient. Even though 2 months feels like a long time, your lips will heal once you start the right treatment.

anticipated_faqs.will_this_go_away_on_its_own: Possibly, but it could take months or even longer. It's much better to treat it now with the right cream so it heals in 2-4 weeks instead of waiting.
anticipated_faqs.is_this_contagious: No, angular cheilitis is not contagious. You cannot spread it to other people, and you don't need to worry about catching it from someone else.
anticipated_faqs.why_did_chapstick_make_it_worse: Some chapsticks contain ingredients that can irritate your lips, especially if you have a fungal infection. Also, chapstick alone is not strong enough to treat a fungal infection—you need an antifungal cream.
anticipated_faqs.can_i_wear_lipstick_or_lip_balm: Not while you're treating this. Avoid all lip products except plain petroleum jelly if needed. Once your lips are healed, you can use lip products again, but choose ones without fragrances or irritating ingredients.
anticipated_faqs.how_long_do_i_need_to_use_the_cream: Use it for the full 2-4 weeks as prescribed, even if your lips feel better after a few days. Stopping too early can cause the problem to come back.
anticipated_faqs.what_if_the_cream_causes_irritation: Mild tingling is normal, but if you develop a rash or severe irritation, stop using it and call your doctor. There are other antifungal creams available if this one doesn't work for you.
anticipated_faqs.can_i_use_a_corticosteroid_cream_instead: No. If you have a fungal infection, corticosteroid creams will make it worse because they suppress your immune system and allow the fungus to grow. Only use the antifungal cream your doctor prescribes.
anticipated_faqs.why_do_i_need_blood_tests: Blood tests help us rule out other causes like nutritional deficiencies or syphilis. These are important to check because they can also cause cracked lips, and if present, they need to be treated differently.
anticipated_faqs.will_this_leave_a_scar: No. Angular cheilitis does not cause scarring. Once it heals, your lips will look and feel normal again.
anticipated_faqs.what_if_this_keeps_coming_back: If it comes back repeatedly, we may need to investigate further for underlying causes like nutritional deficiency, poor oral hygiene, or other health conditions. Your doctor can help figure out why it's recurring and how to prevent it.

FIRST-LINE (MUST-NOT-MISS): RPR or VDRL (rapid plasma reagin or Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) to screen for syphilis. Although low pre-test probability (12%), secondary syphilis is a must-not-miss diagnosis with serious consequences if untreated. Serologic screening is low-cost, low-risk, and high-consequence if positive. If RPR/VDRL positive, follow with FTA-ABS (fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption) for confirmation.

SECOND-LINE (CONFIRMATORY): KOH preparation (potassium hydroxide mount) or fungal culture from lip lesion to confirm Candida albicans. Technique: gently scrape lesion with sterile spatula or swab, place on glass slide with KOH solution, examine under microscope for pseudohyphae/yeast forms. Sensitivity 60-80%, specificity 95%. Culture is gold standard but slower (3-7 days). Recommended if clinical diagnosis uncertain or atypical presentation.

SECOND-LINE (IF CANDIDA SUSPECTED): Oral examination for thrush (white coating on tongue/buccal mucosa) or other oral candida manifestations. Presence would strongly support candida etiology (LR+ 4.2) and indicate need for systemic evaluation (diabetes, immunosuppression). Absence does not exclude candida but makes it less likely.

SECOND-LINE (IF NUTRITIONAL DEFICIENCY SUSPECTED): Serum B12 level (normal >200 pg/mL), serum folate level (normal >5.4 ng/mL), serum iron/ferritin (iron deficiency: ferritin <30 ng/mL or iron <60 mcg/dL), and complete blood count (CBC) to assess for anemia. Recommended if: (1) Recurrent or refractory angular cheilitis despite antifungal therapy; (2) Other signs of nutritional deficiency (glossitis, pallor, fatigue); (3) Risk factors present (vegetarian diet, malabsorption, chronic diarrhea). These tests have high specificity (>95%) if deficiency present but low sensitivity in early deficiency.

SECOND-LINE (IF ACTINIC CHEILITIS SUSPECTED): Detailed history of sun exposure and outdoor occupation. Clinical examination for typical actinic cheilitis features: pallor, atrophy, induration, loss of sharp vermillion border, scaling, erosions. If features present or high suspicion, consider biopsy to assess for dysplasia (see below).

THIRD-LINE (SPECIALIST-LEVEL): Skin biopsy (punch or shave biopsy) if: (1) Lesion does not respond to appropriate treatment after 4 weeks; (2) Clinical features suggestive of actinic cheilitis or dysplasia; (3) Atypical appearance or concerning features on examination; (4) Recurrent lesions. Biopsy will assess for: candida (PAS stain), dysplasia/malignancy (H&E), lichen planus (characteristic histology), other inflammatory conditions. Sensitivity and specificity >95% for dysplasia if present.

THIRD-LINE (IF CONTACT DERMATITIS SUSPECTED): Patch testing with suspected allergens (chapstick ingredients, fragrances, preservatives, nickel). Recommended if: (1) Clear temporal relationship between product use and symptom onset; (2) Improvement with product avoidance; (3) Recurrent dermatitis with multiple products. Patch testing has sensitivity 60-80% and specificity >90% for contact allergens.

ADJUNCTIVE (RISK STRATIFICATION): Fasting glucose or HbA1c if candida etiology suspected and no prior diabetes screening. Diabetes is a risk factor for candida infection (RR 1.5-2.0) and should be excluded in recurrent cases.

ADJUNCTIVE (IMMUNOSUPPRESSION SCREENING): HIV antibody testing if candida etiology confirmed and no clear risk factors, or if recurrent/severe candida infection. Immunosuppression significantly increases candida risk (RR 5-10).

specialist.specialist_assessment: Angular cheilitis (perleche) is a common dermatologic condition with multiple potential etiologies. This patient presents with a classic clinical picture: bilateral angular involvement, chronic 2-month duration, and failure to respond to emollient therapy alone. The differential diagnosis is broad and requires systematic evaluation. Most likely etiology is Candida albicans infection (78% confidence), which accounts for 60-80% of angular cheilitis cases in adults. However, competitive diagnoses include nutritional deficiency (B2, B12, iron, folate at 62% confidence), contact/irritant dermatitis from chapstick or lip products (58% confidence), actinic cheilitis with solar damage (35% confidence), atopic dermatitis (45% confidence), and oral lichen planus (28% confidence). Must-not-miss diagnoses include secondary syphilis (12% confidence but high consequence if missed) and actinic cheilitis with dysplasia (precancerous condition requiring monitoring). The patient's age (54 years), male gender, and lack of reported systemic symptoms are consistent with candida etiology, but the absence of oral thrush, denture use, or immunosuppression history makes nutritional deficiency and contact dermatitis equally plausible. Clinical examination findings will be critical for narrowing the differential: presence of maceration, erythema, or white patches at lip angles would strongly support candida; pale, atrophic lower lip with induration would suggest actinic cheilitis; reticular (lacy) pattern would indicate oral lichen planus; symmetric erythema with scaling would favor contact dermatitis. The 2-month duration and bilateral involvement argue against simple irritant contact dermatitis and suggest either persistent infection (candida), systemic deficiency, or chronic inflammatory condition. Notably, continued chapstick use despite worsening suggests either inadequate treatment of underlying candida or that chapstick itself is the irritant. Severity is mild-to-moderate (5/10) with functional impact limited to cosmetic concern and minor discomfort; no systemic symptoms or complications reported.

Risk factors present: age 54 (cumulative sun exposure, nutritional deficiency risk), male gender (slightly higher candida risk), chronic duration (suggests persistent infection or systemic cause rather than acute irritation). Risk factors absent: no immunosuppression reported, no denture use reported, no oral thrush reported, no systemic symptoms, no fever, no weight loss.
specialist.severity_assessment: MILD-TO-MODERATE (5/10). Patient-reported severity is 5/10, indicating moderate functional impact. Clinical severity is low: localized dermatologic complaint affecting lips only, no systemic symptoms, no signs of severe infection (no purulent drainage, no cellulitis, no lymphadenopathy reported), no complications. However, 2-month duration without resolution despite self-treatment indicates either inadequate treatment or underlying condition requiring specialist intervention. Functional impact is primarily cosmetic with possible minor discomfort; no dysphagia, no respiratory symptoms, no difficulty eating or speaking reported. Prognosis is excellent: angular cheilitis is highly treatable with appropriate diagnosis and management. Expected resolution timeline: 1-2 weeks with topical antifungal if candida etiology; 4-6 weeks with nutritional supplementation if deficiency etiology; days-to-weeks with irritant avoidance if contact dermatitis. No risk of serious complications if appropriately managed. Escalation to high severity would occur if: signs of systemic infection (fever, lymphadenopathy, cellulitis), dysplasia on biopsy, or failure to respond to appropriate treatment after 4 weeks.
specialty_specific_tests: FIRST-LINE (HIGH YIELD): Clinical examination with magnification (5-10x magnifier or dermatoscope) to assess: (1) Maceration, erythema, white patches at lip angles (supports candida); (2) Pallor, atrophy, induration of vermillion border (supports actinic cheilitis); (3) Reticular (lacy) white pattern (supports oral lichen planus); (4) Vesicles, scaling, symmetric involvement (supports contact dermatitis); (5) Overall appearance and distribution pattern. This is the highest-yield initial test and will narrow differential significantly.

FIRST-LINE (MUST-NOT-MISS): RPR or VDRL (rapid plasma reagin or Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) to screen for syphilis. Although low pre-test probability (12%), secondary syphilis is a must-not-miss diagnosis with serious consequences if untreated. Serologic screening is low-cost, low-risk, and high-consequence if positive. If RPR/VDRL positive, follow with FTA-ABS (fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption) for confirmation.

SECOND-LINE (CONFIRMATORY): KOH preparation (potassium hydroxide mount) or fungal culture from lip lesion to confirm Candida albicans. Technique: gently scrape lesion with sterile spatula or swab, place on glass slide with KOH solution, examine under microscope for pseudohyphae/yeast forms. Sensitivity 60-80%, specificity 95%. Culture is gold standard but slower (3-7 days). Recommended if clinical diagnosis uncertain or atypical presentation.

SECOND-LINE (IF CANDIDA SUSPECTED): Oral examination for thrush (white coating on tongue/buccal mucosa) or other oral candida manifestations. Presence would strongly support candida etiology (LR+ 4.2) and indicate need for systemic evaluation (diabetes, immunosuppression). Absence does not exclude candida but makes it less likely.

SECOND-LINE (IF NUTRITIONAL DEFICIENCY SUSPECTED): Serum B12 level (normal >200 pg/mL), serum folate level (normal >5.4 ng/mL), serum iron/ferritin (iron deficiency: ferritin <30 ng/mL or iron <60 mcg/dL), and complete blood count (CBC) to assess for anemia. Recommended if: (1) Recurrent or refractory angular cheilitis despite antifungal therapy; (2) Other signs of nutritional deficiency (glossitis, pallor, fatigue); (3) Risk factors present (vegetarian diet, malabsorption, chronic diarrhea). These tests have high specificity (>95%) if deficiency present but low sensitivity in early deficiency.

SECOND-LINE (IF ACTINIC CHEILITIS SUSPECTED): Detailed history of sun exposure and outdoor occupation. Clinical examination for typical actinic cheilitis features: pallor, atrophy, induration, loss of sharp vermillion border, scaling, erosions. If features present or high suspicion, consider biopsy to assess for dysplasia (see below).

THIRD-LINE (SPECIALIST-LEVEL): Skin biopsy (punch or shave biopsy) if: (1) Lesion does not respond to appropriate treatment after 4 weeks; (2) Clinical features suggestive of actinic cheilitis or dysplasia; (3) Atypical appearance or concerning features on examination; (4) Recurrent lesions. Biopsy will assess for: candida (PAS stain), dysplasia/malignancy (H&E), lichen planus (characteristic histology), other inflammatory conditions. Sensitivity and specificity >95% for dysplasia if present.

THIRD-LINE (IF CONTACT DERMATITIS SUSPECTED): Patch testing with suspected allergens (chapstick ingredients, fragrances, preservatives, nickel). Recommended if: (1) Clear temporal relationship between product use and symptom onset; (2) Improvement with product avoidance; (3) Recurrent dermatitis with multiple products. Patch testing has sensitivity 60-80% and specificity >90% for contact allergens.

ADJUNCTIVE (RISK STRATIFICATION): Fasting glucose or HbA1c if candida etiology suspected and no prior diabetes screening. Diabetes is a risk factor for candida infection (RR 1.5-2.0) and should be excluded in recurrent cases.

ADJUNCTIVE (IMMUNOSUPPRESSION SCREENING): HIV antibody testing if candida etiology confirmed and no clear risk factors, or if recurrent/severe candida infection. Immunosuppression significantly increases candida risk (RR 5-10).
specialist_red_flags: SYPHILIS (MUST-NOT-MISS): Secondary syphilis can present with lip involvement (rhagades, mucous patches). Although low pre-test probability (12%), this is a treatable condition with serious consequences if missed (progression to tertiary syphilis with neurologic/cardiac complications). Red flag: any patient with angular cheilitis and risk factors for STI (multiple partners, MSM, prior STI history) or systemic symptoms (fever, rash, lymphadenopathy). ACTION: Perform RPR/VDRL screening on all patients with angular cheilitis.

DYSPLASIA/MALIGNANCY: Actinic cheilitis is a precancerous condition (35% confidence in this patient). Red flags: (1) Pale, atrophic lower lip with induration and loss of vermillion border; (2) Erosions or ulceration not responding to treatment; (3) Age >50 with significant sun exposure history; (4) Lesion present >4 weeks despite appropriate treatment. ACTION: Perform biopsy if actinic cheilitis features present or treatment-resistant.

SYSTEMIC CANDIDIASIS: Isolated angular cheilitis is typically localized infection, but red flags for systemic candidiasis include: (1) Oral thrush or other oral candida manifestations; (2) Immunosuppression (HIV, diabetes, corticosteroid use); (3) Recurrent or severe candida infections; (4) Systemic symptoms (fever, malaise). ACTION: Perform oral examination; if thrush present, consider systemic evaluation and possible systemic antifungal therapy.

NUTRITIONAL DEFICIENCY WITH SYSTEMIC MANIFESTATIONS: Red flags for significant nutritional deficiency: (1) Glossitis (swollen, smooth tongue); (2) Angular stomatitis (inflammation at mouth angles beyond lips); (3) Pallor or signs of anemia (fatigue, dyspnea, tachycardia); (4) Neuropathy (paresthesias, weakness); (5) Recurrent infections. ACTION: Perform serum B12, folate, iron studies, CBC if any systemic features present.

TREATMENT FAILURE: Red flag for missed diagnosis or inadequate treatment: (1) No improvement after 2-4 weeks of appropriate topical antifungal therapy; (2) Worsening despite treatment; (3) Recurrence after apparent resolution. ACTION: Reassess diagnosis; consider KOH preparation, biopsy, or referral to dermatology if not already seen.

IMMUNOSUPPRESSION: Red flag for increased risk of candida and other infections: (1) Known HIV/AIDS; (2) Diabetes mellitus; (3) Chronic corticosteroid use; (4) Immunosuppressive medications; (5) Malignancy or chemotherapy. ACTION: Screen for immunosuppression; if present, consider systemic antifungal therapy and broader evaluation.

SEVERE INFECTION: Red flags for bacterial superinfection or cellulitis: (1) Purulent drainage or pustules; (2) Significant erythema extending beyond lip angles; (3) Lymphadenopathy (submandibular or cervical); (4) Fever or systemic symptoms; (5) Rapid progression. ACTION: Consider topical or systemic antibiotics; if cellulitis present, may require oral antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate or cephalexin).

ATYPICAL PRESENTATION: Red flags for alternative diagnosis: (1) Unilateral involvement (suggests trauma, herpes, or other localized process rather than angular cheilitis); (2) Severe pain or pruritus (suggests lichen planus, contact dermatitis, or herpes); (3) Vesicles or bullae (suggests herpes simplex, contact dermatitis, or bullous disease); (4) Systemic symptoms (fever, rash, lymphadenopathy suggest systemic disease); (5) Rapid onset or progression. ACTION: Reassess diagnosis; consider alternative etiologies.

DENTURE-RELATED: Red flag for candida in denture wearers: (1) Denture use (RR 2.5-3.0 for candida); (2) Poor denture hygiene; (3) Continuous denture wear (24/7 without removal). ACTION: Assess denture hygiene; recommend nightly denture removal and cleaning; consider denture-related candida treatment (antifungal denture soak).

MEDICATION-RELATED: Red flag for medication-induced cheilitis: (1) Recent initiation of retinoids (tretinoin, isotretinoin—cause xerosis and cheilitis); (2) Recent initiation of antiretrovirals or other immunosuppressive medications; (3) Chemotherapy agents. ACTION: Review medication list; consider dose adjustment or alternative agent if medication-related.
specialist.prognosis_notes: EXCELLENT PROGNOSIS with appropriate diagnosis and treatment. Angular cheilitis is a highly treatable condition with resolution rates of 85-95% when underlying etiology is identified and addressed. Expected disease course varies by etiology: (1) CANDIDA ALBICANS (most likely, 78% confidence): Topical antifungal therapy (miconazole 2% cream or clotrimazole 1% cream applied 2-3 times daily) typically produces clinical improvement within 3-5 days and complete resolution within 1-2 weeks. NNT 2-3 (approximately 2-3 patients need treatment for 1 to achieve complete resolution). Recurrence rate 10-20% if underlying risk factors (poor oral hygiene, denture use, immunosuppression) not addressed. Long-term prognosis excellent if risk factors modified. (2) NUTRITIONAL DEFICIENCY (62% confidence): B vitamin supplementation (B2 100 mg daily, B12 1000 mcg monthly, folate 1 mg daily) or iron supplementation (ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily) produces clinical improvement within 2-3 weeks and complete resolution within 4-6 weeks. Resolution rate 80-90% with supplementation. Recurrence rate 5-10% if supplementation continued. Long-term prognosis excellent if dietary intake improved or malabsorption addressed. (3) CONTACT/IRRITANT DERMATITIS (58% confidence): Avoidance of offending agent (chapstick or other lip products) produces improvement within days to 1 week. Complete resolution typically within 2-4 weeks. Recurrence rate <5% if irritant avoided. Long-term prognosis excellent. (4) ACTINIC CHEILITIS (35% confidence): Prognosis depends on presence of dysplasia. If no dysplasia: topical retinoids (tretinoin 0.025% cream) or imiquimod (5% cream) may improve appearance; sun protection prevents progression. If dysplasia present: may require ablative therapy (laser, cryotherapy) or surgical excision; recurrence rate 10-20% even with treatment. Malignant transformation risk 5-10% over 10 years if untreated dysplasia. (5) SYPHILIS (12% confidence, must-not-miss): If confirmed, penicillin G benzathine 2.4 million units IM × 1 dose (or doxycycline 100 mg BID × 28 days if penicillin-allergic) produces complete resolution of secondary manifestations within 2-4 weeks. Prognosis excellent if treated early; serious complications (neurosyphilis, cardiovascular syphilis) prevented with early treatment. MODIFYING FACTORS: (1) Age 54: moderate risk for actinic cheilitis and nutritional deficiency; lower risk for candida without other risk factors; (2) Male gender: slightly higher candida risk; equal risk for other etiologies; (3) Duration 2 months: suggests persistent infection or systemic cause rather than acute irritation; longer duration may indicate more severe underlying condition; (4) Failure to respond to chapstick: suggests either inadequate treatment of candida or that chapstick is the irritant; (5) Absence of systemic symptoms: favorable prognostic indicator; suggests localized condition rather than systemic disease; (6) Absence of immunosuppression: favorable prognostic indicator; candida less likely to recur; (7) Absence of denture use: favorable prognostic indicator; candida less likely. TIMELINE: (1) Initial improvement: 3-7 days with appropriate treatment (antifungal, nutritional supplementation, or irritant avoidance); (2) Substantial improvement: 1-2 weeks; (3) Complete resolution: 2-4 weeks for candida/contact dermatitis; 4-6 weeks for nutritional deficiency; (4) Follow-up assessment: 2 weeks to assess response; if no improvement, reassess diagnosis and consider alternative etiologies or specialist referral. LONG-TERM PROGNOSIS: Excellent if underlying cause identified and addressed. Recurrence risk 5-20% depending on etiology and whether risk factors modified. Malignancy risk low unless actinic cheilitis with dysplasia present (5-10% transformation risk over 10 years if untreated).

dermatology_guidelines.guideline: American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) - Cheilitis Management
dermatology_guidelines.recommendation: Angular cheilitis (perleche) requires identification of underlying cause before treatment. Common etiologies include: Candida albicans infection (most common), bacterial superinfection, nutritional deficiency (B vitamins, iron, zinc), contact dermatitis, or mechanical irritation from lip licking/moisture.
dermatology_guidelines.evidence_grade: B (Moderate - based on clinical experience and observational studies)
key_points: Candida infection is the most common cause in adults
Topical antifungals (miconazole, clotrimazole) are first-line if fungal etiology suspected
Bacterial superinfection may require topical antibiotics (mupirocin)
Nutritional assessment recommended if recurrent or refractory
Avoid irritants and maintain lip dryness

dermatology_guidelines.guideline: British Association of Dermatologists - Oral Candidiasis and Angular Cheilitis
dermatology_guidelines.recommendation: Angular cheilitis often represents localized candidiasis. Topical azole antifungals (miconazole cream, clotrimazole) are effective first-line agents. Duration typically 1-2 weeks. Consider systemic evaluation if recurrent.
dermatology_guidelines.evidence_grade: B (Moderate - RCTs support efficacy, but limited head-to-head comparisons)
key_points: Miconazole 2% cream applied 2-3 times daily shows good efficacy
Clotrimazole 1% cream is alternative with similar efficacy
Topical corticosteroids should be avoided if fungal (may worsen)
Reassess at 2 weeks; if no improvement, consider alternative diagnosis

dermatology_guidelines.guideline: World Health Organization - Nutritional Deficiencies and Oral Manifestations
dermatology_guidelines.recommendation: Recurrent or refractory angular cheilitis may indicate B vitamin deficiency (B2, B3, B12), iron deficiency, or zinc deficiency. Nutritional assessment warranted if topical treatment fails.
dermatology_guidelines.evidence_grade: C (Low - mostly observational and case reports)
key_points: B2 (riboflavin) deficiency classically presents with angular cheilitis
Iron deficiency anemia can present with oral manifestations including cheilitis
Zinc deficiency (rare in developed countries) associated with perioral dermatitis
Serum B12, folate, iron studies, and zinc levels may be indicated

primary_care_guidelines.guideline: American Family Physician - Management of Cheilitis
primary_care_guidelines.recommendation: Initial management includes: (1) Identify and eliminate irritants (lip licking, irritating chapstick), (2) Keep lips dry, (3) Empiric topical antifungal if candidiasis suspected, (4) Reassess at 2 weeks.
key_points: Most cases resolve with topical antifungal within 2 weeks
Referral to dermatology if refractory to treatment or diagnosis unclear
Consider nutritional deficiency if recurrent despite treatment
