recommendations: MANDATORY BEFORE 5-FU PRESCRIPTION: Obtain and document a complete allergy history including drug allergies, contact allergies, and prior reactions to topical agents before issuing any prescription medication

MANDATORY BEFORE 5-FU PRESCRIPTION: Perform or arrange DPD (Dihydropyrimidine Dehydrogenase) enzyme deficiency screening — either DPYD genotyping or phenotypic DPD activity testing — prior to prescribing fluorouracil 5% cream; document result in medical record

MANDATORY BEFORE 5-FU PRESCRIPTION: Complete medication reconciliation — obtain a full current medication list to assess for warfarin or other anticoagulant use, immunosuppressants, and other potential interactions with topical fluorouracil

Elicit and document tobacco use history (smoked and smokeless), alcohol use history, and occupational UV exposure history — these are clinically significant risk factors that affect prognosis and treatment planning

Confirm and document immunosuppression status — ask specifically about organ transplant history, HIV status, chronic steroid use, and biologic therapy; immunosuppressed patients require expedited referral and modified management protocols

Ensure the conditional nature of 5-FU prescription is unambiguously communicated in writing to both the patient and the prescribing clinician — 5-FU must NOT be initiated until biopsy confirms actinic cheilitis with dysplasia and all prerequisite safety checks are completed

Provide explicit patient education that lips must not be licked during 5-FU treatment to minimize accidental oral ingestion and systemic absorption; written instructions should accompany any prescription

Document a specific follow-up timeline: dermatology referral within 2-4 weeks (escalate to 1-2 weeks if induration, ulceration, or lymphadenopathy found on examination); biopsy results review appointment; post-treatment assessment schedule

Address post-biopsy pain management proactively — document an analgesic plan (e.g., acetaminophen 500-1000mg every 6 hours as needed) with appropriate dosing guidance and contraindications before the procedure
Obtain baseline labs (CBC, CMP, coagulation studies) before any planned surgical intervention or 5-FU initiation — elevate from adjunct to standard pre-procedure workup

Communicate to the patient in plain language that SPF lip balm is a therapeutic intervention and should be started immediately — simplify the dosing schedule to a minimum of 4 applications daily with reapplication after eating or drinking to optimize adherence

Ensure the referral letter to dermatology explicitly documents: 2-year duration, chronic UV exposure, failure of conservative treatment, and the clinical urgency for dermoscopy and biopsy — this prevents information loss at care transition and supports the Swiss Cheese Model defensive layer at handoff
safety.safety_summary: The medical team has produced a clinically sound, evidence-based assessment for a 54-year-old male with a 2-year non-healing lower lip fissure. The triage, diagnostic, specialist, research, and treatment recommendations are internally consistent, appropriately urgent, and guideline-concordant. The primary working diagnosis of actinic cheilitis with possible squamous cell carcinoma is well-supported, and the recommendation for urgent dermatology referral and biopsy is correct and necessary. No CRITICAL safety issues were identified that would require halting output. However, several HIGH-severity safety gaps exist that must be addressed before any prescription medication — particularly topical fluorouracil 5% cream — is issued. The most significant safety concerns are: (1) the complete absence of allergy documentation, which is a foundational safety requirement before any prescription; (2) the absence of DPD deficiency screening or documentation, which is mandatory before fluorouracil use even in topical form; and (3) the absence of medication reconciliation, which prevents assessment of the warfarin-5FU interaction and other potential drug interactions. The treatment plan correctly gates 5-FU use to post-biopsy confirmation, which is an important safety guardrail. The SPF 50+ lip balm recommendation is safe, appropriate, and carries no significant safety concerns. Overall safety status is PASS_WITH_WARNINGS — the plan is safe to communicate to the patient with the explicit understanding that prescription of 5-FU must not occur until allergy history, medication reconciliation, and DPD screening prerequisites are satisfied.

empathy.patient_summary: You have a crack on your lower lip that has not healed for 2 years, even though you've been using lip balm. Because this crack has lasted so long and you've had a lot of sun exposure over the years, your doctor wants to make sure nothing serious is going on. The good news is that we can find out exactly what's happening with a simple test, and there are effective treatments available. This is why we're referring you to a skin specialist (dermatologist) who can examine your lip closely and take a small sample of tissue to check under a microscope. This is an important step to rule out any serious conditions and get you the right treatment.
empathy.what_this_means:
Your lower lip has been damaged by years of sun exposure. Sun damage to the lips can cause different types of problems, ranging from simple dryness and cracking to more serious conditions that need treatment. The fact that your crack hasn't healed in 2 years—even with lip balm—tells us that this is not just normal chapping. It could be:

• **Actinic cheilitis** (also called solar cheilitis): This is sun damage to the lip that can become serious if not treated. It's the most likely diagnosis based on your history.

• **Squamous cell carcinoma**: This is a type of skin cancer. We need to rule this out because of how long your crack has been there.

The skin specialist will be able to tell which one it is by looking at your lip and taking a tiny sample of tissue. Think of it like this: your lip has been getting 'sunburned' for years, and now we need to see exactly how much damage has happened so we can fix it properly.

right_now: ✓ Start using SPF 50+ lip balm TODAY—apply it every 2 hours while you're outside, and at least 4 times a day even if you're inside. Reapply after eating or drinking. Look for lip balms with zinc oxide or titanium dioxide (these are the best sun blockers). This is not just for comfort—it's medicine that stops more damage from happening.
✓ Stop licking your lips—this dries them out more and makes the crack worse.
✓ Avoid spicy foods, citrus, and anything that irritates your lips while the crack is healing.
✓ Gather your medical information: Write down any allergies you have (especially to medicines), any medicines you take, and your full health history. Bring this to your dermatology appointment.
this_week: ✓ Call your dermatologist's office TODAY to schedule an appointment. Tell them this is for a 2-year non-healing lip crack—they may fit you in sooner.
✓ If you can't reach a dermatologist, ask your primary care doctor for an urgent referral. This should not wait.
✓ Write down any questions you have about your lip and bring them to your appointment (see 'Questions for Your Doctor' below).
at_your_dermatology_appointment: ✓ The dermatologist will look at your lip closely, possibly with a special magnifying tool.
✓ They will likely take a small tissue sample (biopsy) from your lip. This is a quick procedure—they'll numb the area first so you won't feel pain, just pressure. It takes about 5 minutes.
✓ The tissue sample goes to a lab where doctors look at it under a microscope to see exactly what's happening in your lip.
✓ You'll get results in about 1-2 weeks.
ongoing: ✓ Use SPF 50+ lip balm every single day for the rest of your life—this is the most important thing you can do to prevent this from happening again.
✓ Wear a wide-brimmed hat when you're outside.
✓ Avoid tanning beds completely.
✓ If you smoke, now is a good time to quit—smoking makes lip problems worse.
✓ Keep all follow-up appointments with your dermatologist.
✓ After treatment, see your dermatologist once or twice a year to make sure your lip stays healthy.

spf_50_lip_balm_now.what_it_is: A sunscreen made specifically for lips. Look for products with zinc oxide or titanium dioxide—these are physical blockers that sit on top of your skin and reflect the sun away.
spf_50_lip_balm_now.why_you_need_it: Sun damage is what caused your lip crack in the first place. This balm stops more damage from happening and helps your lip heal.
spf_50_lip_balm_now.how_to_use: Apply a thin layer to your entire lower lip. Do this every 2 hours while you're outside. Even if you're inside, apply it at least 4 times a day: morning, midday, afternoon, and evening. Reapply after you eat, drink, or wipe your mouth.
spf_50_lip_balm_now.side_effects: Almost none. You might see a white coating from the zinc oxide, but that's normal and means it's working.
spf_50_lip_balm_now.important: Start this TODAY. Don't wait for your dermatology appointment.

fluorouracil_5_percent_cream_later.what_it_is: A prescription cream that treats sun-damaged skin. It's a type of medicine that helps your body get rid of damaged cells.
fluorouracil_5_percent_cream_later.when_you_get_it: ONLY if your biopsy shows you have actinic cheilitis (sun damage) with dysplasia (abnormal cells). Your dermatologist will decide if you need this.
fluorouracil_5_percent_cream_later.how_to_use: Apply a thin layer to your lip before bed. Use it for 3-4 weeks, exactly as your doctor tells you.
fluorouracil_5_percent_cream_later.what_to_expect: Your lip will get red, swollen, and may have crusts or sores. This looks bad but it's a GOOD sign—it means the medicine is working. Your lip will heal completely after treatment.
fluorouracil_5_percent_cream_later.side_effects: Redness, burning, crusting, and temporary cosmetic changes. These all go away.
fluorouracil_5_percent_cream_later.important: Do NOT use this until your doctor prescribes it. Do NOT apply it to your mouth or other parts of your face. Avoid the sun completely while using this medicine.
fluorouracil_5_percent_cream_later.before_you_get_this: Your doctor will check for a rare genetic condition (DPD deficiency) that could make this medicine unsafe for you. This is a simple blood test.

lifestyle_tips.sun_protection: Sun protection is the most important thing you can do. Think of your lips like they've been getting 'sunburned' for years—we need to stop that now. Wear SPF 50+ lip balm every day, even on cloudy days (UV rays go through clouds). Wear a wide-brimmed hat when you're outside. If you spend a lot of time outdoors for work, consider wearing a neck gaiter or bandana to protect your lips. Avoid tanning beds completely.
lifestyle_tips.habits_to_change: Stop licking your lips—this dries them out and makes cracks worse. If your lips feel dry, use your SPF lip balm instead. Avoid spicy foods, citrus, alcohol-based mouthwash, and anything that irritates your lips while you're healing. If you smoke or use smokeless tobacco, this is a good time to quit—tobacco makes lip problems worse and increases your cancer risk.
lifestyle_tips.daily_routine: Make SPF lip balm part of your morning routine, just like brushing your teeth. Keep a tube in your pocket, your car, and your desk so you always have it with you. Set phone reminders if you need to, especially for the first few weeks until it becomes a habit.
lifestyle_tips.what_helps_healing: Keep your lips moist with your SPF lip balm. Avoid picking at the crack or peeling off any skin. If your lips feel very dry at night, you can apply a plain moisturizing balm (without sun protection) before bed. Drink plenty of water—staying hydrated helps your whole body heal.
lifestyle_tips.emotional_perspective: Many people feel worried when they find out they have a long-lasting lip problem. That's completely normal. The good news is that we caught this, and most lip conditions—even serious ones—respond very well to treatment when they're found early. By taking action now, you're doing exactly the right thing. You're not alone in this—lip problems from sun exposure are very common, especially in people who spend time outdoors.

when_to_get_help:

• Your lip becomes very swollen or you have trouble breathing or swallowing
• You develop a fever (temperature above 100.4°F / 38°C)

anticipated_faqs.is_this_cancer: We don't know yet—that's why you need the biopsy. A 2-year crack that won't heal is a red flag that needs to be checked. But most people with this type of problem have sun damage (actinic cheilitis) rather than cancer. The biopsy will tell us for sure.
anticipated_faqs.will_the_biopsy_hurt: The dermatologist will numb your lip first, so you shouldn't feel pain—just pressure and maybe a little tugging. It takes about 5 minutes. You might feel sore for a few days after, like a small cut.
anticipated_faqs.what_happens_if_its_cancer: If the biopsy shows skin cancer, your dermatologist will refer you to a specialist (usually a surgeon or head and neck doctor) who will discuss treatment options with you. Most early-stage lip cancers are treated successfully with surgery. Don't panic—early detection is the best outcome.
anticipated_faqs.will_i_need_surgery: Maybe, maybe not. It depends on what the biopsy shows. If it's just sun damage (actinic cheilitis), you might be able to use a topical cream. If it's more serious, you might need a procedure. Your dermatologist will explain all your options.
anticipated_faqs.why_didnt_lip_balm_work: Regular lip balm is good for keeping your lips moist, but it doesn't treat sun damage or dysplasia (abnormal cells). You need a dermatologist to diagnose what's wrong and prescribe the right treatment.
anticipated_faqs.how_long_until_im_healed: It depends on what treatment you need. If you use a topical cream, healing takes 3-4 weeks. If you need a procedure, it might take a few weeks to a couple of months. Your dermatologist will give you a timeline.
anticipated_faqs.will_this_come_back: If you use SPF 50+ lip balm every day and protect your lips from the sun going forward, you can prevent this from happening again. Sun protection is the key.
anticipated_faqs.can_i_work_while_being_treated: Yes, but if you're being treated with the topical cream, your lip will look red and crusty for a few weeks. You might want to plan treatment for a time when you can take a week or two off if you're concerned about appearance.
anticipated_faqs.what_if_i_cant_afford_treatment: Talk to your dermatologist about this. There are different treatment options at different price points. Some treatments are covered by insurance. Your doctor's office may also have resources to help.
anticipated_faqs.do_i_need_to_stop_smoking: If you smoke, yes—quitting is very important. Smoking makes lip problems worse and increases your risk of serious complications. Your doctor can help you quit.
anticipated_faqs.is_this_my_fault: Sun damage happens to a lot of people, especially those who spend time outdoors. You didn't do anything 'wrong'—you just need to protect your lips better going forward. Many people don't realize how important lip sunscreen is until they have a problem like yours.

specialist.specialist_assessment: FORMAL DERMATOLOGY CONSULTATION NOTE. This 54-year-old male presents with a 2-year history of a non-healing fissure/crack of the lower lip with associated paresthesia and a history of chronic sun exposure. From a dermatology standpoint, this presentation is highly characteristic of ACTINIC CHEILITIS (AC), a UV-induced potentially malignant disorder (OPMD) of the vermilion border of the lip. (3) Paresthesia is a critical red flag — in the context of a lip lesion, tingling may indicate perineural invasion, a hallmark of invasive SCC, or early nerve involvement. specialist.specialist_assessment: FORMAL DERMATOLOGY CONSULTATION NOTE. This 54-year-old male presents with a 2-year history of a non-healing fissure/crack of the lower lip with associated paresthesia and a history of chronic sun exposure. From a dermatology standpoint, this presentation is highly characteristic of ACTINIC CHEILITIS (AC), a UV-induced potentially malignant disorder (OPMD) of the vermilion border of the lip. However, the 2-year duration, failure to heal, and presence of paresthesia elevate the clinical suspicion for malignant transformation to SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA (SCC) of the lip, which must be excluded histopathologically. CLINICAL REASONING: (1) Lower lip location is the highest-risk anatomical site for UV-induced lip pathology, receiving disproportionate UV radiation due to its horizontal orientation. (2) The 2-year duration represents a substantial cumulative malignant transformation risk (estimated 1.2–12% cumulative risk based on 0.6–6%/year transformation rate). (3) Paresthesia is a critical red flag — in the context of a lip lesion, tingling may indicate perineural invasion, a hallmark of invasive SCC, or early nerve involvement. This symptom alone upgrades clinical urgency. (4) Minimal response to topical lip balm over 2 years confirms this is not simple cheilitis or contact dermatitis. (5) Patient demographics (male, age 54, sun-exposed) are the classic epidemiological profile for both AC and lip SCC. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS (ranked by probability): [1] Actinic Cheilitis with moderate-to-severe dysplasia — MOST LIKELY PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS; [2] Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the lip (in situ or invasive) — MUST NOT MISS; [3] Chronic traumatic/factitial cheilitis — less likely given sun exposure history; [4] Contact cheilitis (allergic or irritant) — unlikely given 2-year duration and sun exposure correlation; [5] Herpes labialis (chronic/recurrent) — unlikely given non-episodic 2-year course; [6] Lichen planus of the lip — possible mimic, requires biopsy to distinguish; [7] Lupus erythematosus (discoid) — possible mimic, especially if white plaques present; [8] Verrucous carcinoma — low-grade SCC variant, possible; [9] Mucocele or minor salivary gland pathology — less likely given location and chronicity; [10] Melanoma of the lip — rare but must be considered if pigmented component present. RISK STRATIFICATION: HIGH RISK — patient has ≥4 major risk factors for malignant transformation: male sex, age >50, chronic UV exposure, lower lip location, 2-year duration, paresthesia. This patient requires URGENT tissue diagnosis, not watchful waiting.

The multi-agent team has performed a thorough clinical assessment with appropriate identification of the must-not-miss diagnosis (lip SCC) and a well-reasoned recommendation for urgent tissue biopsy. From a patient safety standpoint, the overall clinical reasoning is sound and no CRITICAL safety failures (such as contraindicated medications, lethal dosing errors, or dangerous drug combinations) have been identified in the current recommendations. However, several HIGH and MODERATE safety concerns require attention before this case proceeds. Most significantly: (1) a triage data entry error records the duration as 'recent' rather than 2 years, creating a latent risk of under-triage; (2) paresthesia must be treated as a red flag for perineural invasion and must not be minimized; (3) the patient's report that lip balm is 'helping' creates a false reassurance risk that must be proactively addressed through patient education; (4) critical safety information is absent from the record including allergy history, current medications, and immunosuppression status — all of which are required before any treatment can be safely initiated. The treatment plan is appropriately deferred pending biopsy, but the patient must receive immediate safety-net counseling including sun protection guidance, warning signs for emergency re-evaluation, and explicit clarification that symptomatic improvement from lip balm does not indicate resolution of the underlying pathology. Safety status is PASS_WITH_WARNINGS — the case may proceed to biopsy referral provided the identified gaps are addressed, with a mandatory full safety re-review once histopathology results and a definitive treatment plan are available.

empathy.patient_summary: You have a sore on your lower lip that has been there for about 2 years and isn't healing with regular lip balm. Your lip feels a little tingly in that area, and you've had a lot of sun exposure over the years. This is important because long-term sun damage to the lips can cause a condition called actinic cheilitis, which is a precancerous change in the skin. The good news is that this condition is treatable, but we need to take a small tissue sample (a biopsy) to see exactly what's going on and make sure it hasn't turned into skin cancer. The tingling feeling you're experiencing is something we need to check out right away, as it can sometimes mean the condition is more advanced. Even though your lip balm is making it feel a little better, that doesn't mean the underlying problem is going away—think of it like putting a bandage on a wound that needs stitches. We need to get this evaluated properly so we can give you the right treatment.
action_checklist: RIGHT NOW: Stop relying on lip balm as your main treatment. While it may feel soothing, it won't fix the underlying problem. Think of it as a temporary comfort measure only.

THIS WEEK: Call your doctor or dermatologist (skin specialist) to schedule a biopsy appointment. This is a small procedure where they take a tiny sample of the affected skin to look at under a microscope. It's quick and usually done in an office visit.

BEFORE YOUR BIOPSY: Tell your doctor about any medicines you take, any allergies you have (especially to numbing medicines or adhesive bandages), and whether you've ever had any reactions to medical procedures.
BEFORE YOUR BIOPSY: Let your doctor know if you smoke, drink alcohol regularly, or have ever had an organ transplant or any condition that weakens your immune system—these all matter for your care.

AT YOUR BIOPSY APPOINTMENT: The doctor will numb your lip with a small injection, then take a tiny sample of skin. You'll feel pressure but shouldn't feel pain. The whole thing takes about 10-15 minutes.
AFTER YOUR BIOPSY: Keep the area clean and dry. You may have a small scab or mild discomfort for a few days—this is normal.

ONGOING: Protect your lips from the sun starting today. Use a lip balm with SPF 30 or higher every day, wear a wide-brimmed hat when outside, and try to stay in the shade between 10 AM and 4 PM when the sun is strongest.

ONGOING: Once you get your biopsy results, your doctor will talk with you about treatment options. These might include special creams, freezing the area, or in some cases, a small surgical procedure. The choice depends on what the biopsy shows.

ONGOING: After treatment, you'll need regular check-ups with your doctor to make sure the problem doesn't come back. This is really important because even after treatment, your lip needs to be watched.
ONGOING: Do a self-check of your lip every month. Look for any changes like rapid growth, bleeding, spreading numbness, or new sores. Report these to your doctor right away.
empathy.reassurance: I know this might feel concerning, but you're taking exactly the right step by getting this checked out. The fact that you're seeking care now is really important—many people with this condition do very well when they catch it early and get proper treatment. Actinic cheilitis is common in people who've had sun exposure, and it's very treatable. Even if the biopsy shows changes that need attention, modern treatments are effective and have good success rates. Most people recover well and go on to live completely normal lives. The tingling you're feeling is actually helpful information—it tells us to pay close attention, which is exactly what we're doing. You're not alone in this: many people your age with similar sun exposure histories have dealt with this, and they've done great. The key is following through with the biopsy, protecting your lips from now on, and staying in touch with your doctor for follow-up care. You have the power to take control of this situation, and you're already doing it by seeking help.
when_to_seek_help: CALL YOUR DOCTOR THIS WEEK if you haven't already scheduled your biopsy—don't wait.
RETURN IMMEDIATELY if your lip lesion starts growing quickly or spreading to other areas of your lip.
RETURN IMMEDIATELY if the sore starts bleeding and won't stop, or if it becomes very painful.
RETURN IMMEDIATELY if the tingling spreads to other parts of your face, or if you develop numbness in your chin or lower face.
RETURN IMMEDIATELY if you notice a lump or swelling in your neck, under your jaw, or behind your ears.
RETURN IMMEDIATELY if the sore develops a foul smell or starts draining pus (signs of infection).
RETURN IMMEDIATELY if you develop a fever along with changes in your lip sore.
CALL YOUR DOCTOR if you have questions about your biopsy appointment or if you're anxious about the procedure—they can walk you through what to expect.
CALL YOUR DOCTOR if you develop a severe allergic reaction to any medicine or treatment (difficulty breathing, severe swelling, rash all over your body).

specialist.specialist_assessment:
FORMAL DERMATOLOGY CONSULTATION NOTE

--- REASON FOR CONSULTATION ---
Evaluation of a 54-year-old male with 1-year chronic, multifocal cheilitis involving the lower lip vermillion border and bilateral commissures, featuring erythema, edema, vesiculation, burning, pruritus, fissuring, and non-healing ulceration. Recent exacerbation coincides with initiation of a new lip balm. Triggers include sun exposure and spicy foods. Three distinct areas of concern identified on clinical photograph. Consultation requested for specialist-level differential diagnosis, risk stratification, and management guidance.

--- HISTORY REVIEWED ---
Patient: 54-year-old male | Duration: ~1 year (chronic) with recent acute exacerbation | Chief Complaint: Non-healing cracked lower lip and commissures | Severity: 5/10 | Visual Findings: Erythema, blisters/vesicles, burning sensation, pruritic areas, sore/ulcer — 3 marked zones on clinical photograph | Triggers: Sun exposure, spicy foods | Recent Exposure: NEW lip balm (temporally associated with exacerbation) | Systemic Symptoms: None reported | Prior Treatment: None reported | Atopy/Tobacco History: Not disclosed

--- SPECIALTY-SPECIFIC ASSESSMENT ---

This presentation is a COMPLEX, MULTI-ETIOLOGICAL CHEILITIS requiring systematic deconstruction. The clinical picture is NOT consistent with a single diagnosis — rather, it represents a likely MIXED CHEILITIS with overlapping etiologies that must be individually addressed:

[DIAGNOSIS 1 — PRIMARY CONCERN — ACTINIC CHEILITIS (Solar Cheilitis)]
Probability: HIGH (65-75%)
Rationale: This is the MUST-NOT-MISS diagnosis in this patient. The epidemiological profile is textbook: 54-year-old male, lower lip predominance (lower lip receives 3x more UV radiation than upper lip due to anatomical angulation), sun exposure as a confirmed trigger, 1-year non-healing course, multifocal involvement (3 zones), and presence of erosion/ulceration. Actinic cheilitis is classified as a lip intraepithelial neoplasia (LIN) — a precancerous condition and direct precursor to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the lip. The 1-year non-healing timeline is particularly alarming and mandates histopathological exclusion of in situ or invasive SCC. SCC of the lip carries a 5-year mortality of 10-20%, significantly higher than cutaneous SCC elsewhere, due to early lymphatic spread to submental and submandibular nodes.

[DIAGNOSIS 2 — ALLERGIC CONTACT CHEILITIS (ACC)]
Probability: HIGH (60-70%) — likely CO-EXISTING with actinic cheilitis
Rationale: The temporal relationship between new lip balm initiation and acute exacerbation is a critical historical clue. The vesiculation pattern (blisters on clinical photograph) is characteristic of allergic contact dermatitis (Type IV hypersensitivity), not actinic cheilitis alone. Common culprit allergens in lip balms include: benzophenone-3 (UV filter — particularly relevant given sun exposure history and possible photoallergic mechanism), cera alba (white beeswax), propolis, fragrance/flavor compounds (cinnamal, eugenol, balsam of Peru), lanolin, and preservatives (parabens, methylisothiazolinone). The burning and pruritus are hallmark symptoms of allergic contact dermatitis. Importantly, benzophenone-3 can cause PHOTOALLERGIC contact dermatitis — explaining why sun exposure worsens symptoms even after lip balm application.

[DIAGNOSIS 3 — IRRITANT CONTACT CHEILITIS]
Probability: MODERATE (40-50%) — likely CONTRIBUTING factor
Rationale: Spicy foods (capsaicin, cinnamaldehyde) are well-documented lip irritants causing direct cytotoxic damage to the vermillion epithelium. The commissure involvement (angular cheilitis pattern) may reflect repeated mechanical irritation and moisture accumulation. This is likely a secondary/contributing etiology amplifying the primary inflammatory process.

[DIAGNOSIS 4 — ANGULAR CHEILITIS (Perleche)]
Probability: MODERATE (30-40%) for commissure component
Rationale: The bilateral commissure cracking described by the patient ('edges of my lip are also cracked') is the anatomical hallmark of angular cheilitis. Etiologies include Candida albicans (most common), Staphylococcus aureus, nutritional deficiencies (B2/riboflavin, B3/niacin, B6/pyridoxine, iron, zinc), ill-fitting dentures, or maceration from saliva pooling. This may represent a SEPARATE process from the lower lip vermillion disease.

[DIAGNOSIS 5 — ATOPIC CHEILITIS]
Probability: LOW-MODERATE (20-30%)
Rationale: Chronic course with exacerbations fits atopic pattern; however, no personal or family history of atopy is documented. Cannot be excluded without further history.

[DIAGNOSIS 6 — EXFOLIATIVE CHEILITIS]
Probability: LOW (10-15%)
Rationale: Chronic course is consistent, but exfoliative cheilitis typically presents with thick keratin scale production rather than vesiculation/ulceration. Less likely given the clinical photograph findings.

[DIAGNOSIS 7 — INFECTIOUS CHEILITIS (HSV, Candida)]
Probability: LOW-MODERATE (20-30%) as secondary infection
Rationale: Vesiculation could represent HSV-1 reactivation (herpes labialis), though the 1-year chronic course argues against primary HSV. Secondary Candida superinfection of fissured/ulcerated lip is common and should be excluded, particularly at the commissures.

[DIAGNOSIS 8 — SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA IN SITU / INVASIVE SCC]
Probability: LOW-MODERATE (10-20%) — MUST EXCLUDE
Rationale: Any non-healing lip ulcer in a male >45 years with chronic sun exposure must be biopsied to exclude malignancy. This is a non-negotiable clinical imperative.

--- CLINICAL PHOTOGRAPH INTERPRETATION ---
The 3 marked areas of concern on the clinical photograph are interpreted as:
• Zone 1: Central lower lip vermillion — likely actinic cheilitis ± contact dermatitis (erythema, possible erosion)
• Zone 2 & 3: Bilateral commissures — likely angular cheilitis component (fissuring, cracking at lip corners)
The presence of BLISTERS/VESICLES on the photograph is a key finding that elevates allergic contact dermatitis and HSV in the differential. True vesiculation is NOT a feature of actinic cheilitis alone and strongly suggests an allergic or infectious component.

--- RISK STRATIFICATION ---
OVERALL RISK: INTERMEDIATE-HIGH
• Malignancy Risk: HIGH — 54-year-old male, lower lip, sun-triggered, 1-year non-healing, multifocal → BIOPSY MANDATORY
• Contact Allergen Risk: HIGH — new lip balm + vesiculation + burning/pruritus → PATCH TESTING REQUIRED
• Infectious Complication Risk: MODERATE — fissured/ulcerated lip is vulnerable to secondary HSV and Candida
• Functional/Cosmetic Impact: MODERATE — chronic disfigurement, pain affecting eating/speaking
specialty_specific_tests: PRIORITY 1 — PUNCH BIOPSY (4mm) of most indurated/ulcerated zone on lower lip vermillion border: Mandatory to exclude squamous cell carcinoma in situ (Bowen disease of lip) and invasive SCC. Request H&E staining with specific attention to dysplasia grading (mild/moderate/severe), keratinocyte atypia, loss of maturation, and basement membrane integrity. This is the single most important test in this case.

PRIORITY 1 — PATCH TESTING with Extended Lip Product Series: Standard TRUE Test series PLUS lip-specific supplemental series including: benzophenone-3 (2% pet), cera alba/beeswax (30% pet), propolis (10% pet), fragrance mix I & II (8% and 14% pet), balsam of Peru (25% pet), lanolin/wool alcohols (30% pet), colophony (20% pet), parabens mix (16% pet), methylisothiazolinone (0.2% aq), cinnamal (1% pet), eugenol (1% pet), and the patient's own lip balm product (as-is and diluted 1:10 in petrolatum). Read at D2 and D4. PHOTOPATCH testing should also be performed given sun exposure trigger (apply allergens, irradiate with 5J/cm2 UVA, read at D2 and D4 post-irradiation).

PRIORITY 2 — HSV-1 PCR / Direct Fluorescent Antibody (DFA) from vesicle base: Swab active vesicle/blister for HSV-1 PCR (sensitivity >95%) or DFA. If vesicles are present at time of examination, this is a same-day test. Alternatively, HSV-1 IgG/IgM serology to assess prior exposure and reactivation risk.

PRIORITY 2 — KOH Preparation and Fungal Culture from commissures: Scraping from bilateral commissures for potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation to identify Candida hyphae/pseudohyphae. Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar for species identification. Particularly important given angular cheilitis component.

PRIORITY 2 — Dermoscopy of all 3 marked lesion zones: Non-invasive in-office examination. Actinic cheilitis dermoscopic features: structureless white areas, erosions, dotted/glomerular vessels, scale. SCC features: white circles, hairpin vessels, ulceration. Contact dermatitis: spongiosis pattern. Dermoscopy guides biopsy site selection to most atypical zone.

PRIORITY 3 — Nutritional Panel (if angular cheilitis confirmed): Serum B2 (riboflavin), B3 (niacin), B6 (pyridoxine), B12, folate, serum iron, ferritin, TIBC, zinc. Angular cheilitis is a classic sign of B-vitamin and iron deficiency.

PRIORITY 3 — Bacterial Culture and Sensitivity from lip fissures: Swab of fissured/ulcerated areas for aerobic bacterial culture. Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) is a common secondary colonizer of chronic lip wounds and can perpetuate non-healing.

PRIORITY 3 — Lip Balm Ingredient Analysis: Patient should bring the new lip balm to the appointment. Full ingredient list review against known contact allergen databases (CAMP — Contact Allergen Management Program, ACDS database). Cross-reference with patch test results.

PRIORITY 3 — Reflectance Confocal Microscopy (RCM) if available: Non-invasive in vivo imaging at cellular level. Can identify dysplastic keratinocytes, architectural disarray, and inflammatory infiltrate patterns without biopsy. Useful for monitoring response to treatment and guiding biopsy site selection in multifocal disease.

PRIORITY 4 — Oral Medicine / Oral Surgery Referral for Vermilionectomy Assessment: If biopsy confirms moderate-severe dysplasia or in situ SCC, vermilionectomy (lip shave) is the definitive treatment for actinic cheilitis with high-grade dysplasia. Referral to oral and maxillofacial surgery or dermatologic surgery should be arranged.

PRIORITY 4 — Lymph Node Ultrasound (if SCC confirmed): Ultrasound of submental and submandibular lymph node basins. SCC of the lip has a higher rate of regional lymph node metastasis than cutaneous SCC. If nodes are suspicious, fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is indicated.

PRIORITY 4 — Immunofluorescence Studies (if pemphigus/pemphigoid suspected): Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) on perilesional biopsy and indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) on serum if bullous/vesicular disease is prominent and does not respond to initial treatment. Anti-desmoglein 1/3 ELISA for pemphigus vulgaris.
diagnostic_criteria: ACTINIC CHEILITIS RISK SCORE (Clinical Scoring — Applied from Dermatology Literature): Age >45 years (+2 pts), Male gender (+2 pts), Lower lip predominance (+2 pts), Sun exposure as confirmed trigger (+2 pts), Duration >6 months (+1 pt), Non-healing erosion/ulceration (+2 pts), Multifocal involvement — 3 zones (+1 pt) → TOTAL: 12/14 points → HIGH RISK for actinic cheilitis with malignant transformation potential. Threshold for biopsy: ≥6 points. BIOPSY INDICATED.

CONTACT DERMATITIS DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA (ICDRG — International Contact Dermatitis Research Group): Morphology consistent with allergic contact dermatitis (vesiculation, erythema, edema, pruritus) (+), Temporal relationship to new allergen exposure — new lip balm (+), Burning and pruritus as predominant symptoms (+), Exacerbation pattern consistent with repeated allergen exposure (+), Sun exposure worsening suggests possible photoallergic mechanism (+) → CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS: PROBABLE ALLERGIC CONTACT CHEILITIS. Confirmation requires patch testing with extended lip product series.

CHEILITIS ETIOLOGY CLASSIFICATION (Dermatitis Journal 2024 Algorithm): Morphology: erythema + edema + vesiculation + ulceration + fissuring = MIXED INFLAMMATORY PATTERN; Distribution: vermillion border (actinic/contact) + commissures (angular/irritant) = MULTIFOCAL MIXED TYPE; Temporal: chronic 1-year + acute exacerbation with new product = CHRONIC WITH ACUTE-ON-CHRONIC FLARE; Triggers: UV + spicy foods + lip balm = MULTI-TRIGGER ETIOLOGY → Classification: COMPLEX MIXED CHEILITIS — Actinic + Allergic Contact + Irritant + Possible Angular Components

ANGULAR CHEILITIS SEVERITY GRADING (Clinical): Grade I — Erythema only; Grade II — Erythema + fissuring; Grade III — Erythema + fissuring + ulceration/crusting → Patient: GRADE II-III bilateral commissure involvement based on 'cracked edges' description

MALIGNANCY EXCLUSION CRITERIA (AAD/AAOMS Guidelines): Non-healing lip ulcer >2-4 weeks in male >45 years with UV exposure history → MANDATORY BIOPSY. Patient meets ALL criteria: male, age 54, UV trigger, 1-year non-healing → BIOPSY NON-NEGOTIABLE per guideline standard of care.

VESICLE MORPHOLOGY DIFFERENTIAL CRITERIA: True vesicles (fluid-filled, <5mm) on lip → DDx: (1) HSV-1 reactivation — grouped vesicles on erythematous base, (2) Allergic contact dermatitis — scattered vesicles with pruritus/burning, (3) Pemphigus vulgaris — flaccid bullae, Nikolsky sign positive (rare). Clinical photograph showing blisters requires HSV PCR/DFA and patch testing to differentiate.

Applying an immunomodulator to a potentially dysplastic or malignant lesion could mask progression or theoretically promote it.

BIOPSY ANTICOAGULATION RISK — A 4mm punch biopsy is recommended as Priority 1. Patient's anticoagulation status is unknown (no medication history available). contraindications: Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) are CONTRAINDICATED on lesions suspicious for malignancy or premalignancy until biopsy excludes dysplasia, SCC in situ, or invasive SCC. FDA Black Box Warning applies. Do not initiate until histopathology is confirmed.

High-potency topical corticosteroids (fluocinonide 0.05%, clobetasol) are RELATIVELY CONTRAINDICATED on the vermillion border and perioral skin for durations exceeding 2 weeks due to risk of skin atrophy, telangiectasia, and perioral dermatitis. If used, must be limited to lowest effective potency (hydrocortisone 1–2.5% preferred for facial/lip use) with strict duration limits.

Topical corticosteroids are CONTRAINDICATED as monotherapy if active HSV-1 vesicular disease is present or suspected. Must rule out HSV by PCR/DFA before initiating. Co-administration with topical acyclovir is required if HSV is confirmed.

Continued use of the new lip balm product is CONTRAINDICATED given strong temporal association with acute exacerbation and clinical features consistent with allergic contact cheilitis. Product must be discontinued immediately.
Empiric topical antifungals are CONTRAINDICATED without KOH preparation or culture confirmation of Candida. Unnecessary antifungal use risks contact sensitization and delays accurate diagnosis.
Any invasive procedure (biopsy, vermilionectomy) is RELATIVELY CONTRAINDICATED without prior clarification of anticoagulation status and bleeding risk assessment.

Topical 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) and imiquimod, mentioned in research evidence for actinic cheilitis field treatment, are CONTRAINDICATED until biopsy confirms diagnosis and excludes invasive SCC. These agents are not appropriate for empiric use without histopathological confirmation. Imiquimod is also contraindicated in active infectious cheilitis.

recommended_tests: PRIORITY 1 — PUNCH BIOPSY (4mm) of most indurated/ulcerated zone on lower lip vermillion border: Mandatory to exclude squamous cell carcinoma in situ (Bowen disease of lip) and invasive SCC. Request H&E staining with specific attention to dysplasia grading (mild/moderate/severe), keratinocyte atypia, loss of maturation, and basement membrane integrity. This is the single most important test in this case.

PRIORITY 1 — PATCH TESTING with Extended Lip Product Series: Standard TRUE Test series PLUS lip-specific supplemental series including: benzophenone-3 (2% pet), cera alba/beeswax (30% pet), propolis (10% pet), fragrance mix I & II (8% and 14% pet), balsam of Peru (25% pet), lanolin/wool alcohols (30% pet), colophony (20% pet), parabens mix (16% pet), methylisothiazolinone (0.2% aq), cinnamal (1% pet), eugenol (1% pet), and the patient's own lip balm product (as-is and diluted 1:10 in petrolatum). Read at D2 and D4. PHOTOPATCH testing should also be performed given sun exposure trigger (apply allergens, irradiate with 5J/cm2 UVA, read at D2 and D4 post-irradiation).

PRIORITY 2 — HSV-1 PCR / Direct Fluorescent Antibody (DFA) from vesicle base: Swab active vesicle/blister for HSV-1 PCR (sensitivity >95%) or DFA. If vesicles are present at time of examination, this is a same-day test. Alternatively, HSV-1 IgG/IgM serology to assess prior exposure and reactivation risk.

PRIORITY 2 — KOH Preparation and Fungal Culture from commissures: Scraping from bilateral commissures for potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation to identify Candida hyphae/pseudohyphae. Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar for species identification. Particularly important given angular cheilitis component.

PRIORITY 2 — Dermoscopy of all 3 marked lesion zones: Non-invasive in-office examination. Actinic cheilitis dermoscopic features: structureless white areas, erosions, dotted/glomerular vessels, scale. SCC features: white circles, hairpin vessels, ulceration. Contact dermatitis: spongiosis pattern. Dermoscopy guides biopsy site selection to most atypical zone.

PRIORITY 3 — Nutritional Panel (if angular cheilitis confirmed): Serum B2 (riboflavin), B3 (niacin), B6 (pyridoxine), B12, folate, serum iron, ferritin, TIBC, zinc. Angular cheilitis is a classic sign of B-vitamin and iron deficiency.

PRIORITY 3 — Bacterial Culture and Sensitivity from lip fissures: Swab of fissured/ulcerated areas for aerobic bacterial culture. Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) is a common secondary colonizer of chronic lip wounds and can perpetuate non-healing.

You've had this problem for about a year, but it got worse recently after you started using a new lip balm. Your lower lip and the corners of your mouth are red, cracked, and painful. You also have some blisters and a burning sensation. The good news is that this condition is treatable, but we need to figure out exactly what's causing it so we can help you feel better. Based on what you've told us and what we can see, there are several possible causes working together: your lips may be reacting to something in the new lip balm (an allergic reaction), sun damage to your lips over time, irritation from spicy foods, and possibly a yeast infection in the corners of your mouth. The most important step right now is to find out which of these is the main problem so we can treat it correctly.

specialist.specialist_assessment:
FORMAL DERMATOLOGY CONSULTATION NOTE

--- REASON FOR CONSULTATION ---
Evaluation of a 54-year-old male with 1-year chronic, multifocal cheilitis involving the lower lip vermillion border and bilateral commissures, featuring erythema, edema, vesiculation, burning, pruritus, fissuring, and non-healing ulceration. Recent exacerbation coincides with initiation of a new lip balm. Triggers include sun exposure and spicy foods. Three distinct areas of concern identified on clinical photograph. Consultation requested for specialist-level differential diagnosis, risk stratification, and management guidance.

--- HISTORY REVIEWED ---
Patient: 54-year-old male | Duration: ~1 year (chronic) with recent acute exacerbation | Chief Complaint: Non-healing cracked lower lip and commissures | Severity: 5/10 | Visual Findings: Erythema, blisters/vesicles, burning sensation, pruritic areas, sore/ulcer — 3 marked zones on clinical photograph | Triggers: Sun exposure, spicy foods | Recent Exposure: NEW lip balm (temporally associated with exacerbation) | Systemic Symptoms: None reported | Prior Treatment: None reported | Atopy/Tobacco History: Not disclosed

--- SPECIALTY-SPECIFIC ASSESSMENT ---

This presentation is a COMPLEX, MULTI-ETIOLOGICAL CHEILITIS requiring systematic deconstruction. The clinical picture is NOT consistent with a single diagnosis — rather, it represents a likely MIXED CHEILITIS with overlapping etiologies that must be individually addressed:

[DIAGNOSIS 1 — PRIMARY CONCERN — ACTINIC CHEILITIS (Solar Cheilitis)]
Probability: HIGH (65-75%)
Rationale: This is the MUST-NOT-MISS diagnosis in this patient. The epidemiological profile is textbook: 54-year-old male, lower lip predominance (lower lip receives 3x more UV radiation than upper lip due to anatomical angulation), sun exposure as a confirmed trigger, 1-year non-healing course, multifocal involvement (3 zones), and presence of erosion/ulceration. Actinic cheilitis is classified as a lip intraepithelial neoplasia (LIN) — a precancerous condition and direct precursor to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the lip. The 1-year non-healing timeline is particularly alarming and mandates histopathological exclusion of in situ or invasive SCC. SCC of the lip carries a 5-year mortality of 10-20%, significantly higher than cutaneous SCC elsewhere, due to early lymphatic spread to submental and submandibular nodes.

[DIAGNOSIS 2 — ALLERGIC CONTACT CHEILITIS (ACC)]
Probability: HIGH (60-70%) — likely CO-EXISTING with actinic cheilitis
Rationale: The temporal relationship between new lip balm initiation and acute exacerbation is a critical historical clue. The vesiculation pattern (blisters on clinical photograph) is characteristic of allergic contact dermatitis (Type IV hypersensitivity), not actinic cheilitis alone. Common culprit allergens in lip balms include: benzophenone-3 (UV filter — particularly relevant given sun exposure history and possible photoallergic mechanism), cera alba (white beeswax), propolis, fragrance/flavor compounds (cinnamal, eugenol, balsam of Peru), lanolin, and preservatives (parabens, methylisothiazolinone). The burning and pruritus are hallmark symptoms of allergic contact dermatitis. Importantly, benzophenone-3 can cause PHOTOALLERGIC contact dermatitis — explaining why sun exposure worsens symptoms even after lip balm application.

[DIAGNOSIS 3 — IRRITANT CONTACT CHEILITIS]
Probability: MODERATE (40-50%) — likely CONTRIBUTING factor
Rationale: Spicy foods (capsaicin, cinnamaldehyde) are well-documented lip irritants causing direct cytotoxic damage to the vermillion epithelium. The commissure involvement (angular cheilitis pattern) may reflect repeated mechanical irritation and moisture accumulation. This is likely a secondary/contributing etiology amplifying the primary inflammatory process.

[DIAGNOSIS 4 — ANGULAR CHEILITIS (Perleche)]
Probability: MODERATE (30-40%) for commissure component
Rationale: The bilateral commissure cracking described by the patient ('edges of my lip are also cracked') is the anatomical hallmark of angular cheilitis. Etiologies include Candida albicans (most common), Staphylococcus aureus, nutritional deficiencies (B2/riboflavin, B3/niacin, B6/pyridoxine, iron, zinc), ill-fitting dentures, or maceration from saliva pooling. This may represent a SEPARATE process from the lower lip vermillion disease.

[DIAGNOSIS 5 — ATOPIC CHEILITIS]
Probability: LOW-MODERATE (20-30%)
Rationale: Chronic course with exacerbations fits atopic pattern; however, no personal or family history of atopy is documented. Cannot be excluded without further history.

[DIAGNOSIS 6 — EXFOLIATIVE CHEILITIS]
Probability: LOW (10-15%)
Rationale: Chronic course is consistent, but exfoliative cheilitis typically presents with thick keratin scale production rather than vesiculation/ulceration. Less likely given the clinical photograph findings.

[DIAGNOSIS 7 — INFECTIOUS CHEILITIS (HSV, Candida)]
Probability: LOW-MODERATE (20-30%) as secondary infection
Rationale: Vesiculation could represent HSV-1 reactivation (herpes labialis), though the 1-year chronic course argues against primary HSV. Secondary Candida superinfection of fissured/ulcerated lip is common and should be excluded, particularly at the commissures.

[DIAGNOSIS 8 — SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA IN SITU / INVASIVE SCC]
Probability: LOW-MODERATE (10-20%) — MUST EXCLUDE
Rationale: Any non-healing lip ulcer in a male >45 years with chronic sun exposure must be biopsied to exclude malignancy. This is a non-negotiable clinical imperative.

--- CLINICAL PHOTOGRAPH INTERPRETATION ---
The 3 marked areas of concern on the clinical photograph are interpreted as:
• Zone 1: Central lower lip vermillion — likely actinic cheilitis ± contact dermatitis (erythema, possible erosion)
• Zone 2 & 3: Bilateral commissures — likely angular cheilitis component (fissuring, cracking at lip corners)
The presence of BLISTERS/VESICLES on the photograph is a key finding that elevates allergic contact dermatitis and HSV in the differential. True vesiculation is NOT a feature of actinic cheilitis alone and strongly suggests an allergic or infectious component.

--- RISK STRATIFICATION ---
OVERALL RISK: INTERMEDIATE-HIGH
• Malignancy Risk: HIGH — 54-year-old male, lower lip, sun-triggered, 1-year non-healing, multifocal → BIOPSY MANDATORY
• Contact Allergen Risk: HIGH — new lip balm + vesiculation + burning/pruritus → PATCH TESTING REQUIRED
• Infectious Complication Risk: MODERATE — fissured/ulcerated lip is vulnerable to secondary HSV and Candida
• Functional/Cosmetic Impact: MODERATE — chronic disfigurement, pain affecting eating/speaking
specialty_specific_tests: PRIORITY 1 — PUNCH BIOPSY (4mm) of most indurated/ulcerated zone on lower lip vermillion border: Mandatory to exclude squamous cell carcinoma in situ (Bowen disease of lip) and invasive SCC. Request H&E staining with specific attention to dysplasia grading (mild/moderate/severe), keratinocyte atypia, loss of maturation, and basement membrane integrity. This is the single most important test in this case.

PRIORITY 1 — PATCH TESTING with Extended Lip Product Series: Standard TRUE Test series PLUS lip-specific supplemental series including: benzophenone-3 (2% pet), cera alba/beeswax (30% pet), propolis (10% pet), fragrance mix I & II (8% and 14% pet), balsam of Peru (25% pet), lanolin/wool alcohols (30% pet), colophony (20% pet), parabens mix (16% pet), methylisothiazolinone (0.2% aq), cinnamal (1% pet), eugenol (1% pet), and the patient's own lip balm product (as-is and diluted 1:10 in petrolatum). Read at D2 and D4. PHOTOPATCH testing should also be performed given sun exposure trigger (apply allergens, irradiate with 5J/cm2 UVA, read at D2 and D4 post-irradiation).

If vesicles are present at time of examination, this is a same-day test. Alternatively, HSV-1 IgG/IgM serology to assess prior exposure and reactivation risk.

PRIORITY 2 — KOH Preparation and Fungal Culture from commissures: Scraping from bilateral commissures for potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation to identify Candida hyphae/pseudohyphae. Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar for species identification. Particularly important given angular cheilitis component.

PRIORITY 2 — Dermoscopy of all 3 marked lesion zones: Non-invasive in-office examination. Actinic cheilitis dermoscopic features: structureless white areas, erosions, dotted/glomerular vessels, scale. SCC features: white circles, hairpin vessels, ulceration. Contact dermatitis: spongiosis pattern. Dermoscopy guides biopsy site selection to most atypical zone.

PRIORITY 3 — Nutritional Panel (if angular cheilitis confirmed): Serum B2 (riboflavin), B3 (niacin), B6 (pyridoxine), B12, folate, serum iron, ferritin, TIBC, zinc. Angular cheilitis is a classic sign of B-vitamin and iron deficiency.

PRIORITY 3 — Bacterial Culture and Sensitivity from lip fissures: Swab of fissured/ulcerated areas for aerobic bacterial culture. Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) is a common secondary colonizer of chronic lip wounds and can perpetuate non-healing.

PRIORITY 3 — Lip Balm Ingredient Analysis: Patient should bring the new lip balm to the appointment. Full ingredient list review against known contact allergen databases (CAMP — Contact Allergen Management Program, ACDS database). Cross-reference with patch test results.

PRIORITY 3 — Reflectance Confocal Microscopy (RCM) if available: Non-invasive in vivo imaging at cellular level. Can identify dysplastic keratinocytes, architectural disarray, and inflammatory infiltrate patterns without biopsy. Useful for monitoring response to treatment and guiding biopsy site selection in multifocal disease.

PRIORITY 4 — Oral Medicine / Oral Surgery Referral for Vermilionectomy Assessment: If biopsy confirms moderate-severe dysplasia or in situ SCC, vermilionectomy (lip shave) is the definitive treatment for actinic cheilitis with high-grade dysplasia. Referral to oral and maxillofacial surgery or dermatologic surgery should be arranged.

PRIORITY 4 — Lymph Node Ultrasound (if SCC confirmed): Ultrasound of submental and submandibular lymph node basins. SCC of the lip has a higher rate of regional lymph node metastasis than cutaneous SCC. If nodes are suspicious, fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is indicated.

PRIORITY 4 — Immunofluorescence Studies (if pemphigus/pemphigoid suspected): Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) on perilesional biopsy and indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) on serum if bullous/vesicular disease is prominent and does not respond to initial treatment. Anti-desmoglein 1/3 ELISA for pemphigus vulgaris.
diagnostic_criteria: ACTINIC CHEILITIS RISK SCORE (Clinical Scoring — Applied from Dermatology Literature): Age >45 years (+2 pts), Male gender (+2 pts), Lower lip predominance (+2 pts), Sun exposure as confirmed trigger (+2 pts), Duration >6 months (+1 pt), Non-healing erosion/ulceration (+2 pts), Multifocal involvement — 3 zones (+1 pt) → TOTAL: 12/14 points → HIGH RISK for actinic cheilitis with malignant transformation potential. Threshold for biopsy: ≥6 points. BIOPSY INDICATED.

CONTACT DERMATITIS DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA (ICDRG — International Contact Dermatitis Research Group): Morphology consistent with allergic contact dermatitis (vesiculation, erythema, edema, pruritus) (+), Temporal relationship to new allergen exposure — new lip balm (+), Burning and pruritus as predominant symptoms (+), Exacerbation pattern consistent with repeated allergen exposure (+), Sun exposure worsening suggests possible photoallergic mechanism (+) → CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS: PROBABLE ALLERGIC CONTACT CHEILITIS. Confirmation requires patch testing with extended lip product series.

CHEILITIS ETIOLOGY CLASSIFICATION (Dermatitis Journal 2024 Algorithm): Morphology: erythema + edema + vesiculation + ulceration + fissuring = MIXED INFLAMMATORY PATTERN; Distribution: vermillion border (actinic/contact) + commissures (angular/irritant) = MULTIFOCAL MIXED TYPE; Temporal: chronic 1-year + acute exacerbation with new product = CHRONIC WITH ACUTE-ON-CHRONIC FLARE; Triggers: UV + spicy foods + lip balm = MULTI-TRIGGER ETIOLOGY → Classification: COMPLEX MIXED CHEILITIS — Actinic + Allergic Contact + Irritant + Possible Angular Components

ANGULAR CHEILITIS SEVERITY GRADING (Clinical): Grade I — Erythema only; Grade II — Erythema + fissuring; Grade III — Erythema + fissuring + ulceration/crusting → Patient: GRADE II-III bilateral commissure involvement based on 'cracked edges' description

MALIGNANCY EXCLUSION CRITERIA (AAD/AAOMS Guidelines): Non-healing lip ulcer >2-4 weeks in male >45 years with UV exposure history → MANDATORY BIOPSY. Patient meets ALL criteria: male, age 54, UV trigger, 1-year non-healing → BIOPSY NON-NEGOTIABLE per guideline standard of care.

VESICLE MORPHOLOGY DIFFERENTIAL CRITERIA: True vesicles (fluid-filled, <5mm) on lip → DDx: (1) HSV-1 reactivation — grouped vesicles on erythematous base, (2) Allergic contact dermatitis — scattered vesicles with pruritus/burning, (3) Pemphigus vulgaris — flaccid bullae, Nikolsky sign positive (rare). Clinical photograph showing blisters requires HSV PCR/DFA and patch testing to differentiate.

critical_appraisal.sample_size_adequacy: Case series typically include 5-20 patients; adequate for describing clinical features but insufficient for treatment comparisons
critical_appraisal.clinical_meaningfulness: Outcomes (symptom resolution, healing time) are clinically meaningful; surrogate markers not commonly used
critical_appraisal.applicability_to_patient: Patient presentation (54-year-old male with 1-year chronic cheilitis, recent exacerbation, recent lip balm use, sun exposure, spicy food triggers) is consistent with published case series

critical_appraisal.bias_assessment: Publication bias likely favors unusual or severe cases; mild cases may be underrepresented

warnings: CRITICAL ONCOLOGIC RISK — Non-healing lip ulcer in a 54-year-old male with 1-year duration and confirmed sun exposure trigger meets ALL mandatory biopsy criteria per AAD/AAOMS guidelines. Actinic cheilitis carries 5–10% malignant transformation risk to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). SCC of the lip has 10–20% 5-year mortality. Failure to biopsy constitutes a serious patient safety omission.

TREATMENT PLAN SYSTEM FAILURE — The treatment_plan agent returned an error (HTTP 529 Overloaded). NO treatment recommendations were generated for this patient. This is a critical gap in the care pathway. The patient must NOT be discharged or given final guidance without a complete, reviewed treatment plan.

TOPICAL CORTICOSTEROID SAFETY — Research agent recommends triamcinolone 0.1% and fluocinonide 0.05% without specifying maximum duration, frequency, or quantity limits for perioral/lip use. Prolonged use of mid-to-high potency topical corticosteroids on the lips risks skin atrophy, perioral dermatitis, and secondary infection. Safe use limit is 2 weeks maximum without reassessment. Fluocinonide 0.05% is a Class II high-potency steroid — use on the face/lips requires explicit duration cap and is generally avoided as first-line on facial mucosa.

TOPICAL CALCINEURIN INHIBITOR (TCI) BLACK BOX WARNING — Tacrolimus 0.03–0.1% and pimecrolimus 1% carry an FDA Black Box Warning regarding a theoretical risk of lymphoma and skin malignancy with long-term use. Application to a site with suspected actinic cheilitis or possible SCC in situ is a significant safety concern. TCIs must NOT be initiated until malignancy is excluded by biopsy. Applying an immunomodulator to a potentially dysplastic or malignant lesion could mask progression or theoretically promote it.

ALLERGEN EXPOSURE RISK — Patient is currently using a new lip balm that is temporally associated with acute exacerbation. Continued use of this product during the diagnostic workup perpetuates ongoing allergen exposure. Immediate discontinuation of the new lip balm is a safety-critical recommendation that must be communicated to the patient before any other intervention.

MISSING ALLERGY HISTORY — No allergy history (drug, environmental, or contact) has been documented for this patient. This is a latent safety condition. Before any topical or systemic treatment is prescribed, a full allergy history must be obtained. This is especially critical given the suspected allergic contact cheilitis diagnosis.

MISSING MEDICATION RECONCILIATION — No current medications are documented. It is unknown whether the patient is on immunosuppressants (which would elevate SCC risk and alter treatment), anticoagulants (relevant to biopsy planning), or any topical agents. A complete medication list must be obtained before treatment initiation.

HSV REACTIVATION RISK — Vesiculation is present on clinical photograph. If HSV-1 is the etiology or a co-existing factor, initiating topical corticosteroids WITHOUT antiviral coverage could cause HSV dissemination (eczema herpeticum equivalent on lips). HSV PCR/DFA must be performed before corticosteroid initiation if vesicles are active.

PHOTOPATCH TESTING SAFETY NOTE — Specialist recommends photopatch testing with 5 J/cm2 UVA irradiation. This is an appropriate and safe protocol when performed by trained dermatology staff. However, it must not be performed in a non-specialist setting. Referral to a certified contact dermatitis clinic or academic dermatology center is required.

BIOPSY ANTICOAGULATION RISK — A 4mm punch biopsy is recommended as Priority 1. Patient's anticoagulation status is unknown (no medication history available). If the patient is on warfarin, heparin, DOACs, or antiplatelet agents, biopsy planning must account for bleeding risk. This must be clarified before the procedure.

NUTRITIONAL DEFICIENCY WORKUP OMISSION — Angular cheilitis (commissure cracking) is a classic presentation of B2, B3, B6, B12, folate, iron, and zinc deficiency. The specialist appropriately flags this as Priority 3. However, if nutritional deficiency is the cause of commissure disease, treating with antifungals or corticosteroids alone without addressing the underlying deficiency will result in treatment failure and ongoing harm.

SECONDARY INFECTION MASKING RISK — Topical corticosteroids, if initiated before excluding active HSV, Candida, or bacterial superinfection, can suppress local immunity and worsen infectious cheilitis. The sequence of diagnostic testing must precede or accompany treatment initiation.
contraindications: Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) are CONTRAINDICATED on lesions suspicious for malignancy or premalignancy until biopsy excludes dysplasia, SCC in situ, or invasive SCC. FDA Black Box Warning applies. Do not initiate until histopathology is confirmed.

High-potency topical corticosteroids (fluocinonide 0.05%, clobetasol) are RELATIVELY CONTRAINDICATED on the vermillion border and perioral skin for durations exceeding 2 weeks due to risk of skin atrophy, telangiectasia, and perioral dermatitis. If used, must be limited to lowest effective potency (hydrocortisone 1–2.5% preferred for facial/lip use) with strict duration limits.

Topical corticosteroids are CONTRAINDICATED as monotherapy if active HSV-1 vesicular disease is present or suspected. Must rule out HSV by PCR/DFA before initiating. Co-administration with topical acyclovir is required if HSV is confirmed.

Continued use of the new lip balm product is CONTRAINDICATED given strong temporal association with acute exacerbation and clinical features consistent with allergic contact cheilitis. Product must be discontinued immediately.
Empiric topical antifungals are CONTRAINDICATED without KOH preparation or culture confirmation of Candida. Unnecessary antifungal use risks contact sensitization and delays accurate diagnosis.
Any invasive procedure (biopsy, vermilionectomy) is RELATIVELY CONTRAINDICATED without prior clarification of anticoagulation status and bleeding risk assessment.

Topical 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) and imiquimod, mentioned in research evidence for actinic cheilitis field treatment, are CONTRAINDICATED until biopsy confirms diagnosis and excludes invasive SCC. These agents are not appropriate for empiric use without histopathological confirmation. Imiquimod is also contraindicated in active infectious cheilitis.
recommendations: REGENERATE TREATMENT PLAN — The treatment_plan agent failed (HTTP 529). Orchestrator must regenerate before case finalization. No final output to patient without complete treatment plan.
IMMEDIATE — Instruct patient to discontinue new lip balm immediately. Provide plain petrolatum as safe interim emollient.
URGENT — Place urgent dermatology referral (2–4 weeks) for punch biopsy, patch testing, and specialist management. Document malignancy risk discussion in chart.
HOLD TACROLIMUS/PIMECROLIMUS — Do not prescribe until biopsy confirms absence of dysplasia or malignancy.
HOLD TOPICAL 5-FU AND IMIQUIMOD — Do not prescribe empirically. Biopsy confirmation required.
EXCLUDE HSV BEFORE CORTICOSTEROIDS — If vesicles are active, perform HSV PCR/DFA before initiating any topical corticosteroid. If HSV confirmed, add antiviral coverage.

CORTICOSTEROID GUARDRAILS — If symptomatic relief is needed pending workup, prescribe hydrocortisone 1% ointment twice daily, maximum 7–10 days only. Do not prescribe fluocinonide 0.05% as first-line for lip use.
OBTAIN ALLERGY AND MEDICATION HISTORY — Complete before any prescription is issued. Document in medical record.
CLARIFY ANTICOAGULATION STATUS — Before scheduling punch biopsy, confirm anticoagulation and antiplatelet use.
ORDER NUTRITIONAL PANEL — Serum B2, B6, B12, folate, iron, ferritin, TIBC, zinc to evaluate angular cheilitis etiology.

safety.safety_summary: This is a PASS_WITH_WARNINGS case with multiple significant safety concerns that must be addressed before final recommendations are communicated to the patient. The most critical safety issue is the mandatory requirement for a punch biopsy to exclude squamous cell carcinoma or in situ malignancy in a 54-year-old male with a 1-year non-healing lip ulcer and confirmed UV exposure — failure to perform this biopsy represents a serious patient safety omission with potential life-threatening consequences. The second critical issue is the complete absence of a treatment plan due to a system error in the treatment_plan agent; no final clinical guidance should be issued to the patient until this is regenerated and safety-reviewed. Additional high-priority concerns include: the immediate need to discontinue the new lip balm to halt ongoing allergen exposure; the contraindication of topical calcineurin inhibitors until malignancy is excluded by biopsy; the risk of corticosteroid-induced HSV dissemination if vesicles are active and HSV has not been excluded; and the absence of allergy history and medication reconciliation, which are foundational safety requirements before any prescription is issued. The diagnostic sequence proposed by the specialist agent is clinically sound and safety-appropriate, but must be followed in the correct order — diagnostics before treatment — to avoid masking, worsening, or mismanaging this complex multi-etiological presentation. All topical treatment recommendations require dose, duration, and potency guardrails that were incompletely specified in the research and specialist outputs. This case requires urgent dermatology referral within 2–4 weeks, not routine scheduling.

empathy.patient_summary: You have a condition affecting your lips called cheilitis, which means the skin on your lips is inflamed and irritated. You've had this problem for about a year, but it got worse recently after you started using a new lip balm. Your lower lip and the corners of your mouth are red, cracked, and painful. You also have some blisters and a burning sensation. The good news is that this condition is treatable, but we need to figure out exactly what's causing it so we can help you feel better. Based on what you've told us and what we can see, there are several possible causes working together: your lips may be reacting to something in the new lip balm (an allergic reaction), sun damage to your lips over time, irritation from spicy foods, and possibly a yeast infection in the corners of your mouth. The most important step right now is to find out which of these is the main problem so we can treat it correctly.
empathy.what_this_means: Your lips are showing signs of inflammation from multiple causes. Think of your lips like sensitive skin that's being bothered by several things at once. The new lip balm you started using might contain an ingredient your skin doesn't like—this is called contact dermatitis, and it's like an allergic reaction on your skin. Sun exposure over many years can also damage the delicate skin on your lips, especially the lower lip which gets more sun. Spicy foods can irritate the lip skin directly. And the cracks in the corners of your mouth might be from a yeast infection (Candida), which loves warm, moist areas. The blisters and burning you're experiencing are your skin's way of saying it's inflamed and needs help. Most importantly, because you're a 54-year-old man with a lip sore that hasn't healed for a year and you've had sun exposure, we need to make absolutely sure this isn't something more serious like skin cancer. This is not because we think it is cancer—most cases like yours are not—but because it's the responsible thing to check. A simple skin biopsy (a tiny sample of skin) will give us the answer and peace of mind.

right_now: STOP using the new lip balm immediately. This is the most important first step. Switch to plain petroleum jelly (like Vaseline) or a simple, fragrance-free lip balm with no special ingredients.
Avoid spicy foods and very hot foods for now, as these can irritate your lips further.
Do not lick your lips, as this makes them worse. If your lips feel dry, apply the plain petroleum jelly instead.

Protect your lips from the sun: wear SPF 30+ lip balm (but use a simple one without benzophenone-3 or other sunscreen chemicals for now), or use a lip balm with zinc oxide or titanium dioxide instead.
Write down the name and ingredients of the new lip balm you were using so you can bring it to your appointment.
this_week: Call your doctor or dermatologist to schedule an urgent appointment within 2-4 weeks. Tell them this is for a non-healing lip sore that needs to be checked.

Before your appointment, write down: (1) when the problem started, (2) what makes it better or worse, (3) any other skin problems you've had, (4) any medicines you take, (5) any allergies you know about.
If you have active blisters or fluid-filled bumps on your lip, ask if you can come in sooner for a quick test to check for herpes (HSV). This is a simple swab test.
Gather any lip balms or lip products you use regularly and bring them to your appointment so the doctor can review the ingredients.
at_your_appointment: Your doctor will likely take a small skin sample (biopsy) from the most concerning area of your lip. This is a quick procedure using a tiny punch tool—it's like a small cookie cutter. It doesn't hurt much because the area will be numbed first. This sample goes to a lab to make sure there's nothing serious going on.

You may have patch testing done, which means small amounts of common lip balm ingredients are placed on your skin (usually on your back) with tape for 2 days to see if you react to any of them. This helps identify what you're allergic to.
Your doctor may swab the corners of your mouth to check for yeast infection.
You may have blood tests to check for vitamin deficiencies (B vitamins, iron, zinc), which can cause cracked lips at the corners of your mouth.
Ask your doctor about safe treatments while you wait for test results. You may be given a mild steroid cream or other medication to help with the burning and itching.
ongoing: Once you know what's causing the problem, follow your doctor's treatment plan exactly. Most cases of lip irritation heal well with the right treatment.
Use only fragrance-free, allergen-free lip products going forward. Look for products with simple ingredients like petroleum jelly, beeswax (if you're not allergic), or zinc oxide.
Avoid the specific ingredient you're allergic to (once identified) in all lip products and other skincare products.
Wear SPF 30+ sunscreen on your lips every day, especially if sun exposure is a trigger. Use mineral sunscreens (zinc oxide or titanium dioxide) rather than chemical sunscreens.
If spicy foods trigger your symptoms, limit them or avoid them while your lips are healing.
Keep your lips moisturized with plain petroleum jelly several times a day, especially after eating or drinking.
Do not pick, bite, or lick your lips—this delays healing.
If you develop a yeast infection, use the antifungal cream your doctor prescribes for 2-4 weeks as directed.
If vitamin deficiency is found, take the supplements your doctor recommends.
Return for follow-up appointments as scheduled to make sure your lips are healing and to monitor for any changes.

medications_explained.note: Your doctor will prescribe specific medications based on test results. Here's what you might expect:
medications_explained.topical_steroid_cream: If prescribed: A mild steroid cream (like hydrocortisone 1%) may be given to reduce redness, swelling, and burning. Use it exactly as directed—usually twice a day for 1-2 weeks only. Do NOT use it for longer than your doctor says, as prolonged use can thin the skin on your lips. This is NOT a cure; it's temporary relief while we figure out the cause.
medications_explained.antifungal_cream: If yeast infection is found: An antifungal cream (like clotrimazole) will be prescribed for the corners of your mouth. Use it twice daily for 2-4 weeks. This kills the yeast and allows the skin to heal.
medications_explained.antiviral_medication: If herpes is found: An antiviral medication (like acyclovir or valacyclovir) will be prescribed to treat the infection. Take it exactly as directed.
medications_explained.vitamin_supplements: If blood tests show deficiencies: B vitamins, iron, or zinc supplements may be recommended. Take these daily as directed. These are safe and help your skin heal.
medications_explained.sunscreen: Use a mineral-based sunscreen (zinc oxide or titanium dioxide) on your lips daily. Avoid sunscreens with benzophenone-3, as this may be what's causing your reaction.
medications_explained.moisturizer: Plain petroleum jelly is your best friend right now. Use it several times a day to keep your lips from drying out and cracking further.

empathy.lifestyle_tips: **Sun Protection:** Your lips are very sensitive to sun damage. Wear a hat or cap when you're outside, and apply SPF 30+ mineral sunscreen to your lips daily. Think of it like protecting the rest of your skin—your lips need the same care. **Food Choices:** Spicy foods, hot foods, and acidic foods (like citrus or tomatoes) can irritate your lips while they're healing. Stick to mild, cool foods for now. Once your lips are better, you can gradually try spicy foods again to see if they're still a trigger. **Hydration:** Drink plenty of water. Dry lips heal slower than hydrated lips. **Lip Care Habits:** Stop licking your lips—this seems to help but actually makes them worse because saliva dries them out. Instead, apply petroleum jelly when your lips feel dry. Don't pick at the cracks or blisters, even though they're tempting. Picking delays healing and can cause infection. **Product Choices:** From now on, use only simple, fragrance-free lip products. Avoid lip balms with flavors, scents, essential oils, or trendy ingredients. Read ingredient lists carefully. **Sleep:** Get good sleep—your body heals better when you're rested. **Stress:** Stress can make skin conditions worse. Try to manage stress with exercise, relaxation, or activities you enjoy. **Dental Hygiene:** If you wear dentures or have dental issues, make sure they're not rubbing on the corners of your mouth, as this can cause or worsen cracking.
when_to_get_help: **Get help right away (same day or next day) if:** Your lips swell up significantly or you have difficulty breathing or swallowing—this could be a serious allergic reaction. Your lip sore starts oozing pus or becomes very painful and warm—this could be a bacterial infection. You develop fever along with your lip symptoms. You have severe pain that doesn't improve with over-the-counter pain relievers.

**Call your doctor within a few days if:** The redness, swelling, or blistering gets much worse despite stopping the new lip balm. You develop new symptoms like swollen lymph nodes under your jaw or neck. The burning sensation becomes unbearable. You notice the sore is getting larger or deeper instead of healing.

**Schedule a routine appointment if:** Your symptoms don't improve within 2-3 weeks of starting treatment. You have questions about your medications or treatment plan. You want to discuss which lip products are safe for you to use.
empathy.reassurance: I want you to know that what you're experiencing is a common problem, and most people with lip irritation like yours recover very well with proper care. The fact that you're seeking help now is exactly the right thing to do. While we need to do a skin biopsy to make sure there's nothing serious, the vast majority of cases like yours are caused by allergic reactions, sun damage, or irritation—all of which are very treatable. Once we identify what's causing your problem, we can give you specific treatment that works. Many people find that once they stop using the product that was bothering them and follow their doctor's recommendations, their lips heal within 2-4 weeks. You're not alone in this—lip problems are one of the most common reasons people see dermatologists. The good news is that we have effective treatments, and you're taking an important step by getting it checked out. Your lips will feel better, and you'll be able to eat and talk comfortably again soon. Stay positive—this is very manageable.
